SERENISSIMO CELSISSIMOQUE PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, D. FRIDERICO LUDOVICO, Comiti Palatino ad Rhenum, Duci Bavariae, Juliae, Clivie ac Montium, Comiti Veldentiae & Sponhemii, Marchiae & Ravenspurgi, Domino Ravenstenii, &c.
units.tr: TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST EXALTED PRINCE AND LORD, LORD FRIEDRICH LUDWIG, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, of Jülich, Cleves and Berg, Count of Veldenz and Sponheim, of Mark and Ravensberg, Lord of Ravenstein, etc.

units.la: Tibi, PRINCEPS SERENISSIME, librum offero, quem, ut ingenue fatear, mortalium nulli aperte, sed Soli Illi cui omnes omnia debent, ta-cite constitueram dicare, cum ego per totum tempus quod ei compo-nendo impendi, & ultra, verissime in animo ha-buerim nomen meum reticere, ut vel ex ipso stylo patet, qui cum per primam personam tanquam de se ipsa loquentem (meditantium more) sit expressus, non videtur pati ut Lectori cum modestia exhi-beat ideam personae sese nomine suo designantis. Sed cum ii ex amicis, quos perfectiores novi, ratio-nibus postmodum urgerent ut nomen profiterer, quanquam non amplius vacaret discursus stylum immutare, consensi, quia ingenue processum est, sine studio cuivis placendi aut displicendi. Quem-admodum autem me eo rationes alienae impule-runt; runt; sic propria ratio me volentem eo adduxit ut Nominis Tui, Princeps, patrocinio opus com-mitterem, quippe qui favore tuo me meaque com-plecti sis dignatus, & sub cujus ditione atque tutela hæc ortum habuerint. Et quamquam scio Te so-lidæ Veritati atque Pietati, quæ ex Sacris oraculis hauriuntur, potissimum inhiare, nec videri posse apprime opportunum Speculationes Philosophicas proponere, ubi, post casum Illustrissimæ familiæ charissimorum Capitum, Ducatum Tuum Bipon-tinum vastavit militaris furor; attamen, & ipsa Di-vina revelatio nos vel in mediis calamitatibus ad naturales considerationes, imo ad ciconiæ, boum, aliorumque animalium, elementorum, regimina provocat, quibus ad Deum revocati, illum pro-pitium experiamur.
units.tr: To you, most serene Prince, I offer this book, which, to confess candidly, I had quietly resolved to dedicate to no mortal openly, but to Him alone to whom all owe everything. For throughout the whole time I spent composing it, and beyond, I truly intended to keep my name hidden, as the style itself makes clear: it is written in the first person, as if the author were speaking of himself in the manner of meditators, and so it does not seem to allow the reader, with decency, to form an idea of a person who names himself. But when certain friends whom I know to be more learned pressed me with arguments to declare my name, I consented, although I no longer had the leisure to change the style, since the inquiry was carried out openly and without any desire to please or displease anyone. Just as other people's reasons drove me to this, so my own reason led me, willingly, to commit this work to the protection of your name, Prince, since you have deigned to embrace me and my writings with your favour, and under whose rule and guardianship these things have come into being. And although I know that you chiefly long for solid Truth and for the Piety that is drawn from the sacred oracles, and that it may not seem especially fitting to set out philosophical speculations, when, after the fall of the most illustrious family of your most beloved chiefs, military fury has laid waste your Duchy of Zweibrücken; nevertheless, even the Divine revelation itself calls us, even in the midst of calamities, to natural considerations, indeed to the governances of the stork, the ox and other animals, and of the elements, by which, being called back to God, we may experience him as gracious.

units.la: Quanto minus igitur impor-tunus censeri debebit serius (quem & sacræ pagi-næ inculcant) ad Mentem nostram recursus, in qua se Divina Mens non reliquit ἀμάρτητον[?]; ubi so-lidiora & æternum permansura bona ostenduntur, præ quibus cætera ita evanescunt, ut cum horum privatio accidit, minus ea tangamus; ubi etiam ve-rorum malorum origo latet, atque sic detegi potest, ut clarum fiat, externas calamitates inter præcipuas non debere annumerari; at bene eas quibus mentes, objectorum & affectuum tumultu, confunduntur & dissipantur: cui malo sine mora medendum est si soluto cadavere cum Æterna Mente ad solatia dura-tura aspiremus. Hæc in ipsa Mentis nostræ natura Deus aperta fecit: ad quæ utinam attendissent Christiani, qui Naturæ atque Scripturæ dictaminibus jam pariter valedixere, (quod animadvertere & dolere soles) quo crassæ molis collapsuræ cura una occuparentur. Forte ex iis solidiora ad sui instructionem deprompsissent, quam sint ea quæ ex Divino Scripturæ Codice male lacerant, pejus interpretantur, & pessime accommodant atque obtrudunt populis plerique Animarum Ductores, quorum intellectus & conscientia ne lumine quidem & rectitudine naturali illustrantur: nam quamvis hi, cum cæteris qui pro more solito studiis incumbunt, dicantur acquisisse inScholis rerum Divinarum & humanarum cognitionem in quantum per lumen naturæ haberi potest (quo pacto suam indigitant Philosophiam) nil tamen revera præter steriles Sophisticationum nugas plerumque ibi coacervant, unde ad omnia cætera corrumpenda, aut jam corrupta in posterum fovenda, aptiores redduntur, quam secus fuissent; paucique dantur qui cum sana ratione inde evadant, etsi maxime eam illuc apportassent: qui vero evadunt, & certiora Naturæ rationisque principia nancisçuntur[?], in scopulos alios solent ut plurimum impingere, nempe ad minuta objecta, quæ satius esset prætermittere, descendunt; totumque vitæ temtempus, vel praecipuum, in eorum speculatione impendunt, dum quod maximum, maximeque necessarium est, neglectui & oblivioni perniciose traditur. A quo mille scopulorum mari cum me utcunque Divina gratia coeperit liberare, hanc è naufragio, vel è naufragii periculo, Tabellam Liberatori meo appendo, in qua quae recta, quae avia vel devia, quid boni malive in ejusmodi viis sit reperire, conatus sum quantum mihi licuit designare, ad cautelam eorum qui sunt liberioris indolis, & ad veriora aspirant, nullarum ullius cogitationum mancipia. Quodsi nonnullis profuero, erit quo Au-ctori omnis boni gratiae habeantur: Sin minus, suf-fecerit mihi candide boni quippiam intendisse, atque ea occasione publice testatum esse, me solidae & fructuosae Veritatis amantem Principem colere dum vere profiteor me esse,
units.tr: How much less, therefore, ought it to be judged an unreasonable turn to our Mind (which the sacred pages also urge upon us as well), in which the Divine Mind has not left itself without witness; where more solid goods that will remain forever are shown, in comparison with which other things so fade away that, when their loss occurs, we are less moved by them; where also the origin of true evils lies hidden, and so can be uncovered, so that it becomes clear that external calamities should not be counted among the chief ones, but rather those by which minds are confounded and scattered by the tumult of objects and passions. This evil must be remedied without delay, if, with the corpse cast off, we aspire to consolations that will endure with the Eternal Mind. God has made these things plain in the very nature of our mind. Would that Christians had attended to them, who have now equally bid farewell to the dictates of Nature and of Scripture (as you are wont to observe and lament), so that they might occupy themselves with the care of one thing that is to collapse like a gross mass. Perhaps they would have drawn from these more solid materials for their own instruction than those that most of the guides of souls tear badly from the Divine Codex of Scripture, interpret worse, and most wretchedly adapt and thrust upon the peoples, whose understanding and conscience are not illuminated even by the light and natural rectitude. For although these, along with the others who devote themselves to study in the customary way, are said to have acquired in the Schools "knowledge of divine and human things so far as it can be had through the light of nature" (by which they designate their Philosophy), yet in truth they mostly heap up there nothing but the sterile trifles of sophistry, from which they become more apt to corrupt everything else, or to foster what is already corrupt for the future, than they would otherwise have been; and few are given who come out of it with sound reason, even if they had brought that very thing there in the greatest measure. Those who do come out, and who obtain more certain principles of Nature and reason, usually run aground on other rocks: they descend to minute objects, which it would be better to pass over, and spend most or all of their life's time on their study, while what is greatest and most necessary is handed over to neglect and oblivion, to ruinous effect. Since divine grace has in some measure begun to free me from this sea of a thousand rocks, I hang this little tablet, from the shipwreck or from the danger of shipwreck, as an offering to my Deliverer, in which I have tried, as far as I was permitted, to mark out what is straight, what is off the road or astray, and what good or evil is to be found on such paths, for the caution of those of a freer disposition who aspire to truer things, and who are not slaves to any thoughts whatever. If I shall have profited some, the thanks for all good will be owed to the Author. But if not, it will suffice me to have candidly intended something good and, on that occasion, to have publicly testified, as I truly profess, that I am a lover of solid and fruitful Truth, and that I honour a Prince who is the same.

units.la: MI Lector, ne terrearis libri mole. Magnum ea malum ubi res alibi sæpe eadem expositæ, continuo solo verborum augmento incrustantur, & diversitate ordinis inversæ atque interpolatæ, reponuntur. forte hic, ubi de materia non ita vulgari agitur, simile quid non reperies. Interim, qui præjudiciis liber est, possit brevitatis causa totum librum primum, & aliquot capita secundi, prætermittere: nam magis in destruendo quam in construendo impenduntur. non est res adeo jucunda lutum removere, quod ibi non sine tædio, sed nec sine necessitate imo & coactione factum esse scio. Philosophorum quorundam opiniones non alia de causa interdum, quanquam raro, retuli, nisi quod ob Nominis celebritatem præjudicia valde noxia faciant apud multos. In tricas Scholasticas aliquoties descendendum fuit, ut qui ab illis impediti, solverentur. Nam istis præcipue hæc scripta sunt. In cæteris personas non sequor, sed indicia veritatis à Deo in Mentium intimis insculpta & ad Deum ducentia non ut in illum qui est incomprehensibilis rationi subjicerem, sed rationem illi, ut testimonia sui quæ in illa reliquit, patefiant ad ejus gloriam. quare eos qui putant non esse genuinæ Philosophiæ ex notionibus rebusque naturalibus ad Deum noscendum & amandum erigi, nil moror. Diabolicum stratagema! ut omnis ad scientiam aspirans longè à Deo evanescat. Illud cassum reddere hic sum conatus. De materia assumpta scripsi quæ cum ea adhuc ignorarem & præjudiciis oppositis atque difficultatibus angerer, optassem mihi ab aliis ostendi. Cæterum tenuitatem, vel, si vis, barbariem styli, nil curo. Auribus non scripsi, nec verborum præstigiis inhiantibus, iisque sese pascentibus, neque etiam contentiosis, qui ex eo quod quædam voces diverso sensu variis in locis sint adhibitæ, non habent quod vel contradictionem, vel æquivocationem obtendant: cum data sit opera ut ex ipso loci discurdiscursu pateat sensus vocis non ambiguus. Si quæ prætereà dif-ficultates occurrunt, certus sum eas, saltem plerasque, ex itera-ta meditatione evaniturâs. Si quis errores in hisce demonstrationibus sibi detegere videatur, idque vere demonstret, non refragabor, nam opto amare veritatem ob Divinum suum fontem, sine respectu ad me, adeoque & mihi adversantem: sed certus sum ejus potiores partes hic esse. Quod si Tu, Amice, iis ad Deum ferri possis, iis ad hunc scopum utere: sin alia viæ sint tibi commo-diores, hæc vero tibi non conveniens, alias elige: Sed nolis hæc media, quæ ignorare posses, quaque forte præter opinionem tuam vera & bona esse possint, traducere; ne ita adversèris plurimis iisque genuinis testimoniis quæ hic sunt de Deo ejusque mirabilibus, quod ob veritatem ipsam dictum sit. Bene vale.
units.tr: My reader, do not be frightened by the bulk of the book. That is a great evil, when matters already set out elsewhere are often encrusted with a mass of extra words and, reordered and interpolated in a different arrangement, are presented again. Perhaps here, where the subject is not so commonplace, you will find nothing like this. Meanwhile, whoever is free of prejudices may, for the sake of brevity, skip the whole first book and some chapters of the second, for these are spent more on demolition than on construction. It is not a pleasant task to remove mud, which I know was done here not without weariness, but not without necessity and even compulsion. I have sometimes, though rarely, recounted the opinions of certain philosophers for no other reason than that, because of the celebrity of their names, they do great harm by creating prejudices among many people. It was sometimes necessary to descend into the Scholastic subtleties, so that those hindered by them might be freed. For these writings are chiefly directed at them. Elsewhere I do not follow persons, but the signs of truth, engraved by God in the innermost parts of minds and leading to God, not so as to subject God, who is incomprehensible, to reason, but so that reason may be laid open to him, as the witnesses of himself which he has left in it, to his glory. Therefore I care nothing for those who think that no genuine philosophy rises from notions and natural things to the knowledge and love of God. This is a diabolical stratagem, that everyone who aspires to knowledge should vanish far from God. I have tried here to render that device void. I have written on a borrowed subject, which, while I was still ignorant of it and troubled by opposing prejudices and difficulties, I would have wished to have been shown to me by others. Otherwise, I care nothing for the thinness, or, if you like, the barbarity, of my style. I have not written for the ears, nor for those who gape after tricks of words and feed on them, nor for the contentious, who, because certain terms have been used in different senses in various places, have no ground for objecting either contradiction or equivocation, since care has been taken that the meaning of a term is unambiguous from the course of the argument itself. If any further difficulties occur, I am certain that most of them, at least, will vanish upon repeated meditation. If anyone seems to himself to detect errors in these demonstrations, and really demonstrates them, I will not object, for I desire to love truth for its divine source, without regard to myself, even when it is against me; but I am certain that the stronger part is here. And if you, friend, can be carried to God by these things, use them to this end; but if other ways are more convenient for you, and these do not suit you, choose others. Yet do not distort these means, which you may not know, and which perhaps, beyond your opinion, may be true and good; lest you oppose so many and such genuine testimonies, which are here, concerning God and his wonders, for the sake of truth itself. Farewell.

units.la: 1. Rei praecipuae tractandae dignitas & difficultas. 2. Media diversa. 3. Quorum posteriora huius sunt loci. 4. Res admitttendae. 5. Excludendae. 6. Partitio operis in Libros quatuor.
units.tr: 1. The dignity and difficulty of the principal subject to be treated. 2. Various means. 3. Of which the latter are the concern of this place. 4. Matters to be admitted. 5. Matters to be excluded. 6. Division of the work into four Books.

units.la: I. Si bene sapienterque à Sapiente Rege monitum, ne, cum coram Deo loqui animus est, festinantes in verba dissolvamur, non dubium est quin ubi, non tantum coram illo, sed & de illo est loquendum, cogitata verbaque nostra sint maxime serio pensitanda, & caute proferenda. In his quippe errare, non leve est. Quid enim tribuere Enti Summo, Perfectissimoque imperfectiones, (quod ab errore in his non differt) aliud esse possit, quam ejus Naturam negare, aut in idolum transformare, & dedecore afficere? Sibi aliisve Deum sistere deformatum, gravius est & absurdius homini, quam si se ipsum coram Deo male formatum sistat: quod ultimum tamen temeritatis, ut minimum, culpa tenetur.
units.tr: I. If the Wise King has rightly and wisely warned us that, when we intend to speak before God, we should not be hasty in our words, there is no doubt that, when we must speak not only before him but also about him, our thoughts and words ought to be weighed most seriously and uttered with caution. For to err in these matters is no slight thing. For what could it be to ascribe imperfections to the Supreme Being, most perfect (which differs in no way from error in these matters), other than to deny his nature, or to transform him into an idol and dishonour him? To set forth God to oneself or to others in a distorted form is more grievous and more absurd for a man than to present himself before God in a badly formed condition; yet even the latter is held to be, at the very least, a fault of rashness.

units.la: II. Non dubium est quin illi quiDeum debito honore sunt prosecuti, eum etiam debite agnoverint, & cum sibi, tum aliis magis ac magis agnoscendum proponere sint annixi. Sed inter media quibus hoc promoverent, illa quae opere & affectu interno constant, ab illis quae ratiocinio & discursu absolvuntur studiose distinxere, hisque illa praeposuere. Deum isti mente sua amplexi, simili opere aliis admittendum praesentabant, quaquatenus, discursu etiam semoto, vitæ agendæ modus (signum effectusque agniti affectu & opere intimo Numinis) talis erat, ut Dei (ejus efficientis & exemplaris) pulcritudinem, decentiam, modumque eum amplectendi, cognoscendi, & in ea cognitione provehendi certissimum propalaret. Cætera, si cum his quibus continuo nec interrupte vacabant comparentur, raro & ex intervallo, utpote minus præ-cipua & requisita, adhibebant. Imo notabile est, eorum discursus, quos reliquerunt paucos, ita nobiscum comparatos esse, ut non possint recte capi ab illis, quorum mentes affectus & operatio Numinis Summi non prius tetigere, quique ad illos percipiendos facilem animum ad se-quendum Deum illum clarius postmodum agnoscendum, non serio of-ferunt. Quapropter ubi in priori illa via securitatem omnimodam, in posteriori contra, sæpe multum incerti & periculosi offendere est, tum proponenti, tum audienti ratiocinationum discursus: Nisi enim uter-que ut mox dictum est disponatur, vel disponi peroptet, in utroque ratum illud est, In ratiociniis & differtationibus suis evanuerunt.
units.tr: II. There is no doubt that those who have paid God due honour have also acknowledged him duly, and have striven to set him forth more and more for acknowledgement, both to themselves and to others. But among the means by which they would advance this, they carefully distinguished those which consist in work and inner affection from those which are accomplished by reasoning and discourse, and they placed the former before the latter. Having embraced God in their minds, they presented him to others to be admitted by a similar work; for even when discourse was set aside, the manner of living (the sign and effect of knowing God through inner affection and work of the Divinity) was such that it most certainly revealed the beauty and fitness of God (his efficient and exemplary cause), and the manner of embracing him, knowing him, and advancing in that knowledge. Other things, if they are compared with those to which they devoted themselves continually and without interruption, they employed rarely and at intervals, as being less principal and less required. Indeed it is noteworthy that the discourses they left behind, few as they are, are so constituted in relation to us that they cannot rightly be grasped by those whose minds have not first been touched by the affection and working of the Supreme Divinity, and who do not seriously offer themselves, with a mind ready to follow God, to perceive them, so as to recognise him more clearly afterwards. Wherefore, whereas on the former way one meets with complete security, on the latter one often meets with much uncertainty and danger, both for the one who proposes and for the one who hears the course of reasonings. For unless each is disposed (as has just been said), or desires to be disposed, that saying holds true in both cases: They vanished in their reasonings and disputations.

units.la: III. Inde tamen non sequitur nos ita à Deo abduci, ut ratione & loquela circa eum ex principiis innatis versari non liceat. Quin potius sic ad componendam mentem excitemur, ut harum facultatum, quas ipse nequaquam concessit in cassum, usum habeamus quamoptimum & utilissimum. Et cum quidem talem concedere velit ipse, omnis boni fons, Deus: ut nebulis & nubibus phantasmatum corporeorum, & his deteriorum, depulsis à quorundam mentibus, quæ per illa in conci-piendis rebus spiritualibus impediuntur, obruuntur, & nonnunquam importune admodum vexantur, ea ex mentis absconditis eruantur, quæ tabernaculo menti increatæ in mente creata exstruendo, vel condeco-rando, aliquatenus possint inservire.
units.tr: III. Yet it does not follow from this that we are so drawn away from God that it is not permitted to be occupied with him by reason and speech, from innate principles. Rather, we are so roused to compose the mind that we may have the most excellent and most useful use of these faculties, which he himself by no means granted in vain. And since the fountain of every good, God, is indeed willing to grant such a use, the clouds and mists of corporeal phantasms, and of things worse than these, are to be driven away from the minds of some who, being hindered and sometimes very troublesomely vexed by them in conceiving spiritual things, are overwhelmed; and those things are to be drawn out from the hidden recesses of the mind which, in building or adorning the tabernacle of the uncreated mind within the created mind, may in some measure serve.

units.la: IV. Animus est ea in sequentibus verbis breviter satis complecti, quæ Dei, Entis Summi, ejusque tum excellentissimi operis, animi nostri, tum adversarii & hostis perpetui, mali scilicet, sive peccati, ideas, seu conceptus, quantum quidem fieri poterit, claros excitent. Ad hoc autem non erit necesse, ut singula quæ in istis sunt, recenseantur, quod maximi effet operis. Ideoque ut limitibus brevioribus circumcingamur, à sequentibus excludentur; (1) Ubi de Deo, ejus existentiæ demonstratio ex professo, de qua Cartesianæ meditationes consulantur, Mysterium Trinitatis, Dei attributa & actiones quæ relationem ad creaturarum statum particularem, salutem vel perditionem, involvunt, qualia sunt decreta, creatio, conservatio, providentia, amor, misericordia, & si quæ similia, particularius spectata in respectu ad res quales jam se habent: (2) Ubi de mente creata, quia illa non est tractatus hujus objectum principale, non agetur de explicandis specialius ejus facultatibus, maxime iis quae in relatione ad corpus cui unitur, considerari debent. (3) Similiter nec in specialibus peccatis enumerandis, nec in modis quibus Deus circa illa agit exponendis, nec in eorum duratione, poenis, contrariisve recensendis, versabitur opera. Nolim tamen hoc ita rigide accipi, ac si nullo modo de istis mentio esset facienda: nam si lucem materiae praecipuae affundant, & explicandae rei inserviant, forte interdum ea cum illis quae circa ea notabiliora occurrunt, oculis subjicientur, quanquam non sit de illis ex professo agendi locus.
units.tr: IV. It is my intention to comprehend briefly enough, in the following words, those things which will, as far as it can be done, stir up clear ideas or conceptions of God, the Supreme Being, and of his excellent work, our soul, and also of the adversary and perpetual enemy, namely evil or sin. To do this, however, it will not be necessary to enumerate each of the things that are in these matters, which would be the work of very great length. And so that we may be bounded by shorter limits, the following are excluded: (1) Where it concerns God, the demonstration of his existence as such, for which the Cartesian Meditations may be consulted; the Mystery of the Trinity; the attributes of God and the actions which involve a relation to the particular state of creatures, their salvation or perdition, such as decrees, creation, conservation, providence, love, mercy, and any similar things, considered more particularly in respect to things as they now stand. (2) Where it concerns the created mind: since that is not the principal object of this treatise, we shall not treat more specially of the explanation of its faculties, especially those which must be considered in relation to the body to which it is united. (3) Likewise the work will not be engaged in enumerating particular sins, nor in setting forth the ways in which God acts with respect to them, nor in recounting their duration, punishments, or contraries. I would not, however, wish this to be taken so rigidly as if no mention whatever were to be made of these things: for if they shed light on the principal matter and serve to explain the thing, perhaps at times they will be placed before the eyes together with those more notable matters that occur concerning them, although there is no place for treating them expressly.

units.la: V. His igitur ita exclusis, assumimus Deum, eaque illius attributa, quae, si potentiam quodam sensu excipias, ita concipiuntur, ut in iis concipiendis non sit necessario attendendum ad positionem actualem creaturarum, praesentemque earum statum, quamvis ex istiusmodi creaturarum consideratione occasio oriatur de illis cogitandi. Et hoc modo quaecunque de mente creata dicentur ut plurimum sunt spectanda, quatenus scilicet ex ejus inspectione sumetur occasio noscendi Deum distin-ctius. Ut jam non sit opus ut diu vagemur extra mentem nostram,&,quae in illa sunt, diversarum rerum ideas: nam seu existant, sive non existant extra nos, jam perinde est; cum ad nostrum scopum solae earum notiones, quarum mens intime conscia est, sufficiant. De malo sive peccato seorsim ea dicentur quae cum ante dictis nectantur sequela & generaliori tractandi modo.
units.tr: V. With these things thus excluded, we assume God, and those attributes of his which, if you except power in a certain sense, are so conceived that in conceiving them one need not necessarily attend to the actual position of creatures and their present state, although from the consideration of such creatures an occasion arises of thinking about them. And in this way whatever will be said about the created mind is for the most part to be regarded as far as, namely, from its inspection an occasion will be taken of knowing God more distinctly. So there is no need that we wander for long outside our mind, and the ideas of diverse things which are in it; for whether they exist outside us or do not, it is now all the same, since for our purpose their notions alone, of which the mind is inwardly conscious, suffice. Concerning evil or sin, these things will be said separately, which are connected with what has been said before by a consequence and by a more general mode of treatment.

units.la: VI. Ea autem ut nonnullus servetur ordo sic disponentur, ut primo, nebulae quae impediunt quominus mens rerum spiritualium ideam veram possit formare, discutiantur; quibus superatis, generalis notio utriusque mentis, increatae videlicet, & creatae, harumque agnoscendarum cum suis perfectionibus imperfectionibusque, si quae essent, via in genere proponetur: Quam tertio, sequetur specialior Dei & Mentis creatae deductio; rejectis ad ultimum locum quae de peccato sunt dicenda. Atque haec quatuor totidem Libris comprehensa, ut Deo placitum fuerit, subjicientur.
units.tr: VI. So that a certain order may be kept, these matters will be arranged so that, first, the mists which hinder the mind from forming a true idea of spiritual things are dispelled; these being overcome, a general notion of both minds, the uncreated namely and the created, and of these as they are to be recognised with their perfections and imperfections, if any there were, will be proposed by way of general method. Thirdly, there will follow a more particular deduction of God and of the created mind; the things that are to be said about sin being set aside to the last place. And these four things, comprehended in as many Books, will be subjoined, as it shall please God.

units.la: LIBER PRIMUS
units.tr: BOOK ONE

units.la: IN QUO Obstacula removentur quæ impediunt conceptus Rerum Spiritualium.
units.tr: IN WHICH the obstacles are removed that hinder the concepts of spiritual things.

units.la: 1. De notitia rerum spiritualium sententiæ quinque. 2. Refel-litur prima. 3.4. 5. repulsis hujus assertionis causis tribus.
units.tr: 1. Five opinions concerning the knowledge of spiritual things. 2. The first is refuted. 3., 4., 5. Three causes of this assertion are set aside.

units.la: I. QUæ rerum spiritualium cognitioni offuciæ oppo-nuntur, non unius sunt generis. Sunt qui nullam plane, sunt qui meris verbis, sunt qui sensibili-bus externis, sunt qui imaginatione Mentium notitiam acquiri volunt, sunt qui & puriori cogi-tatione seu intellectu; neque hisce,qui stant à vero, deest, quod in sequentibus interdum videbitur, suus nævus, in illis quæ sæpe ut vera proponunt. Cæteris jam ibitur obviam.
units.tr: I. The things that are set against the knowledge of spiritual things by way of obstruction are not all of one kind. Some want no knowledge of them at all; some want it from mere words; some from external sensible things; some want the knowledge of minds to be acquired by imagination; and some by a purer thought or understanding. Nor do those who stand with the truth lack their own blemish, as will sometimes appear in what follows, in those things which they often put forward as true. The others will now be met in turn.

units.la: II. Etsi illi qui verba mera, aut ea quæ sensibus vel imaginatione si-stuntur, pro idea seu notitia rerum spiritualium obtrudunt, iidem sint consequenter cum aliis qui nullam plane earum notitiam asseverant, in hoc tamen differunt,quod illi cognitionem earum verbo profitentes,sua phantasmata pro ea venditent : hi vero expresse eam inficientur. quæ sen-tentia cum absurditate impietatem conjungit: ut ne jam dicam id esse amplecti principium Atheismi, & doctrinæ de Animarum exstinctione, (quis enim rei plane ignotæ vitam tribuat ? alioqui si vivere agnoscitur, jam utique agnoscitur) imo & omnem veri bonique cognitionem ne-gare. Sufficiat talibus emendandis in mentem revocare se conscios esse cogitationis, cogitantes de se, vel de chimæra, aut de rebus corporeis, si velint; se volitionis (sic liceat actum exprimere) se affirmationis, assen-sus, dissensus, & similium conscientiam habere. Conscium esse alicujus non-nihili cogitantis, affirmantis, dissentientis, figuram, chymæram sibi repræsentare potentis, id vero jam est rem spiritualem aliquatenus cognoscere. Sed quia in omnibus quæ sequentur, hi in actu exercito (ut cum scholis loquar) repellentur, alios compellabimus, si modo prius notaverimus, quidnam huic ignorantiæ professioni potuerit obstetricari.
units.tr: II. Although those who thrust upon us mere words, or those things which are presented to the senses or to the imagination, as the idea or knowledge of spiritual things, are consistently the same as others who assert that there is no knowledge of them at all, they differ in this: the former profess knowledge of them in name and peddle their own fancies as that knowledge, while the latter openly deny it. This opinion joins impiety to absurdity, not to mention that it is the principle of atheism and of the doctrine of the extinction of souls. For who would ascribe life to a thing wholly unknown? If life is acknowledged in it, then surely it is already known. Indeed it even denies all knowledge of truth and good. It will suffice, for correcting such people, to call to mind that they are conscious of thinking, of thinking about themselves, or about a chimera, or about corporeal things if they wish; and that they have consciousness of willing (let me so express the act), of affirming, of assenting, of dissenting, and of similar things. To be conscious of some thinking, affirming, dissenting thing, which is able to represent to itself a figure or a chimera, is indeed already to know a spiritual thing in some measure. But since in everything that follows these people will be refuted in actual exercise (as the schools say), we will address others, provided we first note what could have given birth to this profession of ignorance.

units.la: III. Nempe multorum præjudicium est, res spirituales esse incogitabiles, hoc est, tales quarum natura non possit cogitatione repræsen-tari, sed sit ultra omnem cogitationem. Hinc, quicquid cogitari potest, quia cogitatur, & quidem clarè, negatur ideo ab illis esse de natura rerum spiritualium, ut tandem nihil aliud sit ipsis natura spiritualis quam id quod neque concipitur, neque concipi potest: cujus, fateor, non datur notitia; Eodem prorsus modo quo formæ corporum, quas substantiales vocant, à suis defensoribus finguntur ita incogitabiles, ut quicquid in corporibus clare concipitur, forma esse negetur, & nil superfit quam quod nosci nequit, inani formarum nomine, quas etiam ignotas esse fatentur, insignitum. Notare licet (quem modum dedu-cendi hinc inde quædam minus abstracta interdum sequemur, ne cæte-ra nimis jejuna, & nullius usus videantur), licet inquam notare morbi hujus in multis contagium. etenim, vel in Theologicis, si quid nova, eaque facili claritate concipiendum exponatur, à quibusdam ob istam claritatis evidentiam sæpe timebitur ne non sit ibi veritas, quam tamen adesse sibi persuadebunt, ubi obscuritas & terminorum nebulæ rem eandem ita involvent ut non possit intellectum iri, superfitque indebito stupori locus. Sic in praxi, vita simplicissima, & quæ ut claræ ideæ à confusis, sic à turbæ & calliditatis confusione remota est, nulla vita vulgo habetur. & in universum, quælibet clara, plana, facilia & sim-plicia, quæ ob naturalem cum intelligendi facultate convenientiam non multum nec diu faciunt impetum, turbant, vel commovent, pro nihi-lo reputantur. alia ignota supponenda sunt pro rebus, quæ majora & magis mira possint præsumi. Quamvis autem talis ignorantiæ jactatio ideo forte quibusdam placere possit, quod sinceritatis, humilitatis, & modestiæ speciem videatur habere, dum defectus suos ita aperte fate-tur; tamen, si dicendum quod res est, verendum est ne ea sit indicium animi tum prophani, non curantis (ut sacris verbis utar) Deum habere in notitia; tum superbi & simul rudis, qui cum ea quæ in se sunt non animadvertat, non tantum non vult cæteris, qui ea noscunt, inferior videri, vel etiam æqualis, sed & superior, omnem omnium scientiam gaudens conculcare, & cuique dicere, Tu non modo nil scis, ut Ego: sed & ego hoc præ te habeo quod sciam te & alios mecum nil scire, tu vero id nescias.
units.tr: III. Indeed it is the prejudice of many that spiritual things are unthinkable, that is, that their nature cannot be represented by thought but lies beyond all thought. Hence, whatever can be thought, because it is thought, and indeed clearly, they deny on that account to belong to the nature of spiritual things; so that in the end the spiritual nature is for them nothing other than that which is neither conceived nor can be conceived, of which, I confess, there is no knowledge. In exactly the same way, the forms of bodies, which they call substantial, are feigned by their defenders to be so unthinkable that whatever is clearly conceived in bodies is denied to be form, and nothing remains but what cannot be known, marked with the empty name of forms, which they also confess to be unknown. It is permitted to note the contagion of this disease in many people. (Here and there I will follow a manner of deducing certain things less abstractly, lest the rest seem too dry and of no use.) I say it is permitted to note the contagion of this disease in many people. For even in theological matters, if something new, and easy to conceive with clarity, is set forth, some will often fear, on account of this very evidence of clarity, that there is no truth there; yet they will persuade themselves that truth is present where obscurity and the clouds of terms so wrap up the same thing that it cannot be understood, and room is left for undue amazement. So in practice, the most simple life, which is as remote from the confusion of crowds and cunning as clear ideas are from confused ones, is held by the common people to be no life at all. And in general, whatever is clear, plain, easy and simple, which because of its natural agreement with the faculty of understanding does not make much or lasting impression, or disturbs or moves us, is counted as nothing. Other unknown things must be supposed in place of things that can be presumed to be greater and more wonderful. Although the boasting of such ignorance may perhaps please some, because it seems to have the appearance of sincerity, humility and modesty, since it so openly confesses its defects; yet, if we must say what the matter is, it is to be feared that it is a sign of a mind both profane, not caring (to use the sacred words) to have God in knowledge, and proud and at the same time crude, which, since it does not notice what is in itself, not only does not wish to seem inferior to, or even equal to, those who know these things, but superior, rejoicing to trample underfoot all the knowledge of all, and to say to each: "You not only know nothing, as I do; but I have this over you, that I know you and the others with me know nothing, while you do not know this."

units.la: IV. Sunt alii qui ideo negant rerum spiritualium dari notitiam, quod eas instar corporum nosse non possint. Hi cum in mentium notitiam volunt assurgere, ex consuetudine prava sibi illico aliquod subtile corporeum imaginantur, quod pro natura mentis sive spiritus (nam his vocibus indifferenter utimur) assumant. Sed cum absurda sine numero vident ex illa suppositione consequi, nec plane possint in istis imaginibus, quibus solis veram notitiam adipisci posse putabant, quiescere; maluerunt profiteri nil de rebus illis posse sciri, quam, ut absurda alii, istas imaginationes pro notitia mentium venditare, quod est candoris ingenui; verum enim est nullam dari mentium notitiam, eo scilicet modo quem sibi imaginantur, nullamque omnino si is solus esset, sed aliam, eamque veram superesse ad eas cognoscendas viam, pluribus in posterum dicetur.
units.tr: IV. There are others who deny that knowledge of spiritual things is given, because they cannot know them after the manner of bodies. When these want to rise to the knowledge of minds, from a bad habit they straightway imagine for themselves some subtle corporeal thing, which they take as the nature of mind or spirit (for we use these words interchangeably). But when they see that countless absurdities follow from that supposition, and cannot at all rest in those images, in which alone they thought true knowledge could be obtained, they have preferred to profess that nothing about those things can be known, rather than, like others who are absurd, to peddle those imaginations as the knowledge of minds. This is an ingenuous candour: for it is true that there is no knowledge of minds in the way they imagine it, and none at all if that were the only way; but that there remains another, true way of knowing them, will be said in what follows.

units.la: V. Denique quidam cum viderent se non posse intellectu comprehendere omnia quæ in mentibus sunt, vel esse possunt, puta omnes perfectiones in Deo, omnesque facultates ac variationes in mente creata, negarunt idcirco illarum dari notitiam. Quo sensu fatendum est non tantum mentium, sed & cujusvis corpusculi, non dari notitiam, cognitionem nempe ita adæquatam, ut omnium quæ in aliqua re sunt & esse possunt conscii simus: nam vel minimi pulviculi particulas omnes, motus, ejusque gradus & vias, figuras, possibiles quoque, & similia quæ ipsius sunt determinare ne forte angelus possit. Deus quidem ejus notitiam habet adæquatam, cum singula, quæ in illo, perfecte noscat, singulosque modos quibus affici potest: sed cum nulla sit ratio qua probetur notitias, quascunque mens creata de ulla re possit habere, æque perfectas esse censendas atque illa est quam Deus de quavis re habet; cumque cognitio Dei sit adæquata, non est igitur cur notitia ulla quam mens creata habet præsumenda sit adæquata. (Sed de hac re in lib. iii. ubi de cognitione Dei). Prout autem, quamvis inadæquate corpora concipiantur, non sequitur inde, vel ipsis fatentibus, non dari corporum notitiam; sic neque obstat ea ratio, quominus afferendum sit, dari de rebus spiritualibus notitiam, mediocrem quidem illam, & a principiis primis ad ultimos recessus non diffusam, sed quæ tamen sit vere notitia, non mera ignorantia. Superbiæ est nolle in mediocribus manere, & nisi summa tenere tibi concedatur, cuncta fastidiose repulsare.
units.tr: V. Finally, some, seeing that they cannot comprehend with the understanding all that is or can be in minds, for example all the perfections in God, and all the faculties and modifications in a created mind, have on that account denied that knowledge of them is given. In this sense it must be granted that there is no knowledge of not only minds but of any tiny body whatever, namely knowledge so adequate that we are aware of all that is and can be in a thing. For perhaps not even an angel could determine all the particles of the smallest speck of dust, its motions and their degrees and paths, its figures, including the possible ones, and similar things that belong to it. God indeed has adequate knowledge of it, since he perfectly knows each thing that is in him and each mode by which he can be affected. But since there is no reason by which it can be proved that any knowledge a created mind may have of any thing is to be judged as perfect as that which God has of any thing; and since the knowledge of God is adequate, there is therefore no reason why any knowledge a created mind has should be presumed adequate. (But of this matter, in Book III, where we treat of the knowledge of God.) Just as, although bodies are conceived inadequately, it does not follow from this, even by their own admission, that there is no knowledge of bodies; so this reason does not hinder us from asserting that there is knowledge of spiritual things, a moderate knowledge indeed, not spread out from first principles to the furthest recesses, but which is nonetheless truly knowledge and not mere ignorance. It is the mark of pride to refuse to remain in moderate things, and, unless you are granted to hold the highest, to reject everything with disdain.

units.la: VI. His accenseri possent illi qui spiritualia non nisi modo negativo cognosci ferunt: sed commodius cum illis agemus alibi.
units.tr: VI. Among these could be counted those who hold that spiritual things can be known only in a negative way; but we shall deal with them more conveniently elsewhere.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Secunda sententia, quæ est partim Hobbii. 2. Refellitur ex suis hypothesibus. 3. & ex rei veritate. 4. ejus causæ effectisque plurimis, ut occurrendum sit.
units.tr: 1. The second opinion, which is partly that of Hobbes. 2. It is refuted from his own hypotheses. 3. And from the truth of the matter. 4. Its many causes and effects, which must be met.

units.la: I. Inter illos qui opinionem modo rejectam fovent, non parum eminet Hobbes, Philosophus Anglus, qui non tantum notitiam, sed & existentiam rerum spiritualium negavit, statuens omnia, etiam ipsum Deum, esse corpora, seu res extensas & quantas, ut diserte ait in appendice ad suum Leviathan. Hic vir ita pertinaciter errori suo, (unde omnis Dei vera notitia atque pietas evertitur) adhæsit, ut omnia scripta sua inde coinquinaverit. Sed cum natura non possit ita abjurari, quin vel furcâ expulsa recurrat, hinc est quod multis passim de istis discurrat. Verum non una dicit, sed quasi palpans in tenebris miscet diversa, ut si una refutentur[?] alia obtrudat, quæ, ut ex uno hydræ capite amputato, septena renascantur. Dicit notitiam discursivam fieri per nominum combinationes, nomina autem esse signa cogitationum, cogitationes omnes esse, vel sensionem, vel imaginationem, & neutra Deum nosci (cujus contrarium asserit ubi Deum affirmat esse corpus, omnem substantiam esse corpus, nos in Deo moveri ut extensum in extenso, quæ imaginabilia sunt) & nihilominus tribuit Deo nomina. Vult ergo illa esse voces insignificantes quibus cogitatio nulla respondeat, cujus classis esse ait voces substantia incorporea, immaterialis, quæ, & similia,{a} non semel apud eum reperire est. Quæ cum impedimento constanter fuerint viro qui subtilissimus habetur, operæ pretium fuerit, ne aliis etiam remoram injiciant, removere.
units.tr: I. Among those who cherish the opinion just rejected, Hobbes, the English philosopher, stands out no little, for he denied not only the knowledge but also the existence of spiritual things, holding that all things, even God himself, are bodies, or extended and quantified things, as he states plainly in the appendix to his Leviathan. This man clung so stubbornly to his error (from which all true knowledge and piety of God is overthrown) that he has defiled all his writings with it. But since nature cannot be so abjured that it does not return even when driven out with a pitchfork, it comes about that he runs on about these matters here and there in many places. Yet he does not say one thing; rather, groping as in the dark, he mixes diverse things together, so that if one is refuted he thrusts another forward, which, like the seven heads of the Hydra with one cut off, grow back. He says that discursive knowledge comes about through combinations of names, that names are signs of thoughts, and that all thoughts are either sensation or imagination, and that God is known by neither (the contrary of which he asserts where he affirms that God is a body, that every substance is a body, and that we are moved in God as the extended in the extended, things which are imaginable); and nevertheless he ascribes names to God. He therefore wants those to be insignificant words to which no thought corresponds, and he says the words "incorporeal substance" and "immaterial" belong to this class, along with others like them, which are found in him more than once. Since these notions have been a constant hindrance to a man held to be most subtle, it will be worth the effort to remove them, lest they also throw an obstacle in the way of others.

units.la: II. Si qui cum ipso ejusdem sint sententiæ, eos facile est ex propriis hypothesibus convincere. Dari res spirituales non negaverit ipse, si mo-neatur, nil aliud per illas intelligi quam res cogitantes. An vero illæ à corpore differant, necne? alterius est loci, sufficiat hic ex ipso probare, non esse mera verba quæ de illis per ratiocinationem, aliumve modum, noscuntur: quod sic conficitur. Primo, dicit verba seu nomina esse signa cogitationum animi. Talia autem signa seu nomina Deo attribuit plurima. Igitur ejus (Dei, rei spiritualis) notitia, non in verbis, sed in cogitatis consistit. Nec jam refert an cogitata illa Deo sint similia, necne: quicquid id sit, ultra verba aliquid est. Imo, quod pluseft, cum fateatur Deum non nosci sensu, nec imaginatione, sequitur illud quod in animo est, & nomine signatur, esse cogitatum sensu & imaginatione pu-rius & superius. Secundo, asserit, Deum existere, esse natura notum: sed nulla nomina, etiam Dei, sunt natura nota, seu demonstrabilia, hoc est, non patet ex naturæ inspectione quo sono designandus sit Deus; & omnia nomina sunt ex pacto, ut ait. quod igitur de Deo natura nosci potest, aliquid est præter nomen. Tertio, cum dicat Deum existere esse certum natura; alibi vero, nempe in objectionibus in Meditatio-nes Cartesii tertiis, (ubi iis collatis cum cæteris ipsius scriptis, patet eum ex animo loqui) concedat incertum esse ulla corpora, ulla sensibilia, ul-la imaginatione effecta, existere; cum de illis omnibus, quæ à Scepti-cis in dubium revocantur, dicat, veritatem hujus meditationis agnoscimus; sequitur, illam Dei notitiam quæ certa ipsi est, non esse in verbis cor-poreis incertis, siquidem eorum subjectum, corpus omne, incertum sit. Ex concessis licet, quarto, concludere, dari notitiam non tantum de Deo, sed & de pluribus rebus quas patet non esse corpora, eamque notitiam non esse verbalem. Certo noscit se cogitare, velle, nolle (quod & plurimis commune est), & interim non noscit an dentur corpora, sen-sibilia & imaginabilia, adeoque per consequens, voces & nomina: datur ergo notitia rei absque corpore & nomine. Imo convincitur dari ratio-cinationem absque sensu, imaginatione & nomine, ex suis verbis: Si sensus nostros sine alia ratiocinatione sequamur, merito dubitabimus, an aliquid existat, nec ne. Si ratiocinatio sit se-quela nominum, nomina imagina-tionis, imaginatio sensuum, quomodo demonstrabis quædam existere non sequendo solos sensus? Ratiocinatio igitur non est verborum, quæ sensus sunt, & corporum motorum: alioqui volens hæc probare, tu eadem in antecessum per tuam ratiocinationem, quæ sensuum esset se-quela, præsupponeres; neque etiam est imaginationis, quam vocat sensum dilutum. Sed de his ad hominem satis: imo vereor ne hæc, non-nullis forte tædiosa, eos à sequentibus, acsi in similium nugarum dis-cussione consisterent, absterreant. Hæc tamen, quia plurimi cum illo decipiuntur, ideo dicta sunto. Quæ de cæteris hujus Philosophi opi-nionibus circa sensualem & imaginariam notitiam possent dici, hisce quoque satis superque refutata sunt, ut non sit opus ea in sequentibus de novo recensere.
units.tr: II. If there are any who share his opinion, they can easily be convinced from his own hypotheses. He himself would not deny that spiritual things exist, if he were reminded that by them nothing else is understood than thinking things. Whether those differ from body or not belongs to another place; it is enough here to prove from his own words that the things known about them through reasoning, or in some other way, are not mere words. This is shown as follows. First, he says that words or names are signs of the thoughts of the mind. He ascribes many such signs or names to God. Therefore the knowledge of him (of God, a spiritual thing) does not consist in words but in thoughts. Nor does it now matter whether those thoughts are like God or not; whatever they are, they are something beyond words. Indeed, what is more, since he confesses that God is not known by sense or by imagination, it follows that what is in the mind and signified by a name is a thought purer and higher than sense and imagination. Second, he asserts that the existence of God is known by nature; but no names, not even God's, are known by nature or demonstrable, that is, it is not evident from inspecting nature by what sound God is to be named; and all names are by agreement, as he says. Therefore what can be known of God by nature is something beyond the name. Third, since he says that the existence of God is certain by nature, but elsewhere, namely in the objections to Descartes' Third Meditations (where, comparing these with his other writings, it is clear that he speaks from his heart), he concedes that it is uncertain whether any bodies, any sensible things, any things produced by imagination, exist, while of all those things which the Sceptics call into doubt he says, "we acknowledge the truth of this meditation"; it follows that that knowledge of God which is certain to him is not in uncertain bodily words, since the subject of those words, every body, is uncertain. From what has been conceded, one may, fourth, conclude that there is knowledge not only of God but also of many things which evidently are not bodies, and that this knowledge is not verbal. He certainly knows that he thinks, wills and does not will (which is common to very many), and meanwhile he does not know whether there are bodies, sensible and imaginable, and consequently words and names: therefore there is knowledge of a thing without body and without name. Indeed, it is proved from his own words that there is reasoning without sense, imagination and name: "If we follow our senses without any other reasoning, we shall rightly doubt whether anything exists or not." If reasoning is a consequence of names, names of imagination, and imagination of the senses, how will you demonstrate that certain things exist without following the senses alone? Reasoning, therefore, is not of words, which are of the senses, and of moving bodies; otherwise, wishing to prove these things, you would presuppose beforehand the same things through your reasoning, which would be a consequence of the senses. Nor is it of imagination, which he calls diluted sense. But enough of these matters as addressed to the man himself: indeed I fear that these things, perhaps tedious to some, may frighten them away from what follows, as if it consisted in the discussion of similar trifles. Yet these things have been said because very many are deceived along with him. What could be said about his other opinions of this philosopher concerning sensual and imaginary knowledge has also been refuted sufficiently and more than sufficiently by these things, so that there is no need to review them again in what follows.

units.la: III. Nec minus à sana ratione discedunt quicunque in rebus spiri-tualibus nominalem illam notitiam obtrudunt. Cur potius in nomine, in verbis, consistat cognitio ratiocinio, aliove modo, parata, quam in motu linguæ, aut aëris? quam in characteribus, aut atramento, ejusve ad chartam applicatione? Brutum est, & Psittacorum dare sine mente sonos, quorum usus, ni ex eorum occasione alicujus rei sis conscius, nullus est. Sed & quoties inter somnum, aut etiam vigiliam, absque verbis reperitur in nobis multorum conscientia? quæ ipsa, cum à nobis agnoscatur, utrumque, & rem spiritualem, & notitiam non verbalem, exhibet. Et quamvis per verba mentium notitia promoveri aut retardari possit, non tamen demonstratur hanc illis absolvi, sed potius aliquid quod in animo est, illis notari, quod illis præsentibus sæpe excitatur, sæpe quiescit absentibus.
units.tr: III. Those who foist that nominal knowledge upon spiritual things depart no less from sound reason. Why should knowledge, ready for reasoning, consist rather in a name, in words, or in some other way, than in the motion of the tongue or of the air? Than in letters or ink, or in its application to paper? It is brutish, and fit for parrots, to give sounds without mind, whose use, unless you are aware of some thing on the occasion of them, is nothing. But also, how often in sleep, or even in waking, is there found in us an awareness of many things without words? This awareness itself, since it is acknowledged by us, exhibits both a spiritual thing and a non-verbal knowledge. And although the knowledge of minds can be advanced or retarded by words, it is not thereby shown that it is completed by them; rather, something which is in the mind is merely noted by them, which is often stirred up when they are present and often lies quiet when they are absent.

units.la: IV. Inter sententiæ hujus causas præcipua est, quod mens sibi, suisque actibus, satis non attendat; sed levitate quadam extra se quasi evolans, in externis vagetur: inter quæ degens, cum nil magis audiat commendari scientia, præsertim de spiritualibus, eam, cum ob defectum attentionis non possit capere, in solis, quæ audit, verbis subsistere putat. Ex hoc fonte est quod multi pietatem & sacra sua quam spiritualissima collocent in preculis, seu verbis, certo tempore, numero, certoque modo alligandis, pronunciandis, decantandis, vel audiendis; quod infantium mentem conemur ab incunabulis obruere verbis. Sed & doctorum altercationes innumeræ, studium linguarum immodicum, ut quis decem modis nominare possit rem ne semel quidem cognitam, non aliunde manant. Inde est & illud nunquam satis deplorandum, quod nulli fere in seipsis scientiam, in primis mentium, quærant; sed omnem in libris, & in authoritate verborum humanorum, rixarum fundamentis, latitare putent: non aliud agentes ubi aliquid scire cupiunt, quam quod mentem suam quærant onerare alienis dictis & vocibus, sibi nunquam restituti per puram, liberam, atque solutam meditationem, quæ omnium scopus: ad quam etsi extranea ista interdum conferant, ei tamen ubi istis adhæretur [?], nocent potentissime, haud secus ac perpetua statio in via impedit quominus perveniatur ad metam. Quæ omnia incommoda si quis evitare volet, abstrahat à verbis omnino necesse est, idque non modo cum ad propria mentis suæ cogitata vult attendere, verum etiam cum ex aliorum scriptis aliquem fructum tranquille colligere tentat. Nam cum duas diversas cogitationes interdum una voce signent, aut unam diversis vocibus, sæpe videntur eadem in re opponi ubi de verbis solis certant: adeoque non tam attendendum est verbis, quam cogitatis quæ probabile est eos habere, utut non appositè exprimantur. Et in universum fere certum est, eos qui de primis cognitis, ideis, differentiisque dissentiunt, solis verbis dissentire, ut facillime id appareret, fi verborum, quibus utun-tur, peterentur definitiones ideam claram in mente excitare aptæ. exem-pli causa: dicit Hobbes non dari substantiam incorpoream; nos vero, contra: donemus ipsi sua verba, sed attendamus ad id quod quisque in mente habet. Is per substantiam intelligit corpus, rem extensam: sic, do tibi non dari corpus incorporeum. Sed ego per eas voces significo esse aliquid, seu non-nihil, quod est conscium eorum quæ sunt in ipso, quod non negas dari. Dicis hoc ipsum (quod mentem voco) à corpore non differre realiter, alius affirmat: An vis ideam, seu conceptum, seu attentionem non posse haberi de cogitatione, quin eo ipso habeatur de extensione, & vice versa? ut non possit unum concipi sine altero? ut conscium esse alterutrius fit eo ipso conscium esse utriusque? Non dicit. bene: hoc ipsum est quod vocamus re & substantia differre, quam locutionem, nisi fis indocilis, recusare non debes, de ejus sensu prius edoctus. Quod fi tu per vocem mens designare vis corpus, seu extensum, bene concepta male five non usitate exprimis. Atque ita de cæteris, quæ in dictionariis sic deberent proponi, ut cogitationibus distinguendis inservirent, non vero præter vocum pronunciationem sub-stitutionemque vix quicquam docerent.
units.tr: IV. Among the causes of this opinion the chief is that the mind does not attend sufficiently to itself and its own acts, but, flitting outward as if by a certain lightness, wanders among external things; dwelling among these, since it hears nothing more commended than knowledge, especially of spiritual things, and since on account of lack of attention it cannot grasp it, it thinks that knowledge subsists in the words alone which it hears. From this source it comes that many place their piety and their most spiritual sacred things in prayers, that is, in words to be bound to a fixed time, number and manner, to be pronounced, chanted or heard; and that we try to overwhelm the minds of infants with words from the cradle. But also the countless wranglings of the learned, and an immoderate zeal for languages, so that someone can name in ten ways a thing not even once known, flow from no other source. Hence also that never sufficiently deplored fact, that almost no one seeks knowledge in himself, above all of minds, but thinks it lies hidden in books and in the authority of human words, the foundations of quarrels; not acting otherwise when they desire to know something, than seeking to burden their mind with other people's sayings and voices, never restored to themselves through pure, free and unloosed meditation, which is the aim of all. Although these external things sometimes contribute to that, yet where one clings to them they harm most powerfully, just as a permanent stop on the road prevents one from reaching the goal. If anyone wishes to avoid all these inconveniences, he must by all means abstract himself from words, and this not only when he wishes to attend to the thoughts of his own mind, but also when he tries to gather some fruit calmly from the writings of others. For since they sometimes signify two different thoughts by one word, or one thought by different words, it often seems that the same matter is opposed when they contend only about words; and so one must attend not so much to the words as to the thoughts which they probably have, though not aptly expressed. And in general it is almost certain that those who disagree about first notions, ideas and differences disagree only in words, which would most easily appear if definitions were sought of the words they use, fit to arouse a clear idea in the mind. For example: Hobbes says that there is no incorporeal substance; we, on the contrary, say there is. Let us grant him his words, but let us attend to what each has in his mind. He understands by substance a body, an extended thing: so, I grant you there is no incorporeal body. But by those words I mean that there is something, or some thing, which is conscious of the things that are in itself, which you do not deny exists. You say that this very thing (which I call mind) does not differ really from body; another affirms it. Do you wish that the idea, or concept, or attention, cannot be had of thought without its being had at the same time of extension, and conversely, so that the one cannot be conceived without the other, so that to be conscious of either is by that very fact to be conscious of both? He does not say so. Good: this is what we call differing in thing and substance; and unless you are unteachable, you ought not to refuse this way of speaking, once you have first been instructed in its meaning. But if you wish to designate body, or the extended, by the word mind, you express well-conceived things badly or in an unusual way. And so it is with the rest, which in dictionaries ought to be set out in such a way that they serve to distinguish thoughts, and not hardly teach anything beyond the pronunciation and substitution of words.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Tertiæ opinionis de notitia spiritualium per sensus acquirenda, ejusque sequelarum absurditas. 2. Sensus non sunt exemplaris vel efficiens causa notitiæ. 3. Nec occasio necessaria. 4. Eorum hac in re usus & incommodum.
units.tr: 1. The absurdity of the third opinion, that knowledge of spiritual things is acquired through the senses, and of its consequences. 2. The senses are neither the exemplary nor the efficient cause of knowledge. 3. Nor is the occasion necessary. 4. Their use in this matter and its inconvenience.

units.la: I. CUm verba, de quibus modo, sensus non absolvant, etiamsi ad eos referantur, ulterius inquirendum, an in sensibus, quos externos vocant, sit rerum spiritualium notitia? De tactu, gustu & olfactu, (ut populari hac divisione utamur) non est, credo, quod disceptetur: at de alteris duobus audias, unum esse sensum disciplinæ, alterum experientiæ, nil esse in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu: Ideam Dei ex sermonibus aliorum, ex rerum corporalium inspectione posse efformari. Hinc plurimi Dei & cæterarum mentium ideas, easdem esse putant cum apparitionibus corporeis & visis illis extraordinariis quæ de Deo aut de Angelis in Sacris facta fuisse dicuntur. Quærunt an Deus sit visibilis in altera vita? & hanc optime sibi repræsentare putant si splendida, si pulcra, si exquisitissime sensibus accommodata, concipiant. Quare multi mentis suae erga Deum regimen, hoc est, Religionem, in apparentibus statuunt, & vel aurium titillationi, vel oculorum delectationi, coloribus, figuris, motibus, materiae cujusdam praesentiae, usui, vel etiam visioni, aut tactioni, toti occupantur. quae inter omnes nationes diverse obtinentia, mortales ad odium & caedes mutuas divisere, & a vero Dei regno, cujus subjectum primum praecipuumque non norunt, elongavere, ex ignorantia eorum quae menti utrique increatae & creatae sunt propria, & substitutione sensibilium, quae impossibile est non esse multiplicia & diversa, pro intellectualibus.
units.tr: I. Since the words I have just discussed do not exhaust the senses, even when they are referred to them, we must inquire further whether there is knowledge of spiritual things in those senses which they call external. I believe there is no point in disputing about touch, taste and smell, to use this popular division; but on the other two you will hear it said that one sense belongs to instruction and the other to experience, and that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses; that the idea of God can be formed from the words of others and from the observation of bodily things. Hence most people think that the ideas of God and of other minds are the same as the bodily appearances and those extraordinary visions which are said in the Sacred Books to have been granted concerning God or the angels. They ask whether God is visible in the other life, and they think they represent him best to themselves if they imagine him splendid, beautiful and most exquisitely suited to the senses. Therefore many people place the government of their mind toward God, that is, their religion, in visible things, and devote themselves wholly to the tickling of the ears, the delight of the eyes, colors, shapes, motions, the use of some material presence, or even to seeing or touching. These things, which prevail in different ways among all nations, have set mortals against one another in hatred and mutual slaughter, and have removed them far from the true kingdom of God, whose first and chief subject they do not know, through ignorance of what is proper to both the uncreated and the created mind, and through the substitution of sensible things, which cannot help being manifold and diverse, for intellectual ones.

units.la: II. Ut autem hac in re aliquid certi & clari determinari possit, sensum consideramus quatenus est in corpore, ut deinde videamus quid ex illo ad mentem resultet; & an mentium notitia sit a sensibus. Res una potest dici ab alia esse, vel tanquam ab efficiente causa, vel tanquam ab exemplari, vel tanquam ab occasione: quibus modis potest peti, an Mentium de se vel de aliis notitia a sensibus procedat? At cum sensus in corpore nil sint praeter motum materiae seu organorum, motus autem nil possit efficere praeter motum ejusdem naturae (quae separatio superficierum est) mens vero sit incapax istius recipiendi; patet non modo notitiam non posse ullam in mente a sensibus effici, sed & nil prorsus, utut quamminimum fingi possit. Quod etiam in mente, illa ipsa, aut aliud efficiens, nil producat depromptum ex sensibus corporeis tanquam si hi exemplaris vices sustinerent, facile est animadvertere: nam ipsa sensio, seu perceptio, non est in corporeis. Imo ideae extensionis, motus, figurarum, quae per sensus corporeos venire putantur ut corporum notitiam habeamus, tales sunt, ut si exacte quod res est dicere velimus, debeamus judicare rem se plane aliter habere in corporibus: alioqui, quia sola superficies idea[?] sensuali (ut sic dicam) fingitur, solam superficiem corporibus tribuere debemus, nullam vero profunditatem, nullum quoque motum nisi crassa Minerva, nullam figuram vere regularem: nam vera motus instrumenta & vehicula, exactae corporum figurae, omnino occultantur. Quod si nec aliunde nec prius alias multo puriores & ordinatiores haberemus in mente corporum, figurarum, motuum ideas, nil vere de corporibus cognoscere possemus. Quanto minus existimandum est, perceptiones quae in mente sunt Lucis, colorum, sonorum, & similes, ut & caloris, doloris, & ejusmodi, habere inter corporea suum exemplar ad cujus similitudinem nem sint formatæ ? Igitur nil in mente à sensibus, quatenus in corpore spectantur, efficitur, nil illorum repræsentatur unde possit dici, notitiam, ne illam quidem de corporibus, duobus hisce modis ab illis provenire. Quod si nec corporum notitia, qua ratione notitia de mente ab illis efficeretur, vel ad illorum similitudinem esset accom-modata ?
units.tr: II. But so that something certain and clear may be determined in this matter, let us consider the sense as it is in the body, so that we may then see what results from it in the mind, and whether the knowledge of minds comes from the senses. One thing may be said to be from another either as from an efficient cause, or as from an exemplar, or as from an occasion; in these ways it can be asked whether the knowledge of minds, of themselves or of others, proceeds from the senses. But since the senses in the body are nothing but the motion of matter or of organs, and motion can produce nothing except motion of the same nature (which is a separation of surfaces), while the mind is incapable of receiving such motion, it is plain that not only can no knowledge be produced in the mind by the senses, but nothing at all, however small it may be imagined. That the mind itself, or some other efficient cause, produces nothing drawn from the bodily senses, as if these stood in the place of an exemplar, is easy to see: for sensation itself, or perception, is not in bodily things. Indeed, the ideas of extension, motion and figures, which are thought to come through the bodily senses so that we may have knowledge of bodies, are such that, if we wish to say exactly what the thing is, we must judge that the matter is entirely otherwise in bodies. Otherwise, since the idea is feigned by the sensible alone (so to speak), we must attribute to bodies only a surface and no depth, no motion either except by coarse wisdom, and no truly regular figure; for the true instruments and vehicles of motion and the exact shapes of bodies are wholly hidden. And if we did not have in the mind, from elsewhere and earlier, far purer and more orderly ideas of bodies, figures and motions, we could know nothing truly about bodies. How much less should we think that the perceptions in the mind of light, colors, sounds, and likewise of heat, pain and the like, have among bodily things their own exemplar, to whose likeness they were formed? Therefore nothing is produced in the mind by the senses, insofar as they are regarded in the body; nothing of them is represented from which it could be said that knowledge, not even that of bodies, comes from them in these two ways. And if the knowledge of bodies is not produced by them, by what reasoning would the knowledge of the mind be produced by them, or be adapted to their likeness?

units.la: III. Restat ut videamus an sensus sint occasio notitiæ quam mens de spiritualibus acquirit. Notandum duplicis generis ideas in mente ex occasione sensuum excitari: Unas vocabimus primarias, seu immediatas, quoniam illæ non ex interventu voluntatis nostræ formantur, & præcipue spectant ad statum corporis nostri illas excitantis, quatenus id ad sui conservationem quibusdam corporibus, quibus circumcingi-tur, jungendum est, & ab aliis quibusdam removendum, quod præcipuum illarum est officium. Non enim dati sunt sensus corporei, ut patet in brutis, ad veritatis rerum cognitionem, quæ intellectus, non sensuum, est objectum: sed ut organorum corporeorum systema integrum servaretur. Hinc ideæ illæ primariæ quæ ab ipsis immediate in mente excitantur, non putandæ sunt schematismi rerum: confusæ & tumultuariæ sunt perceptiones, quæ pro diversitate graduum jucunditatis vel molestiæ, diversum arguunt habitum objectorum externo-rum, alimentorum, sanguinis, & spirituum animalium ad corporis totius compagem, dum externis, lux & colores, soni, odores, sapo-res, & tactiles, quas vocant, qualitates, melius ideæ; alimentis, si-tis & fames; sanguini, passiones; & spiritibus animalibus, eorumve vasculis, dolores & titillationes vehementiores ut plurimum respon-dent. Horum omnium cum sensus corporei nec efficientes, nec exemplares sint causæ, sed mera occasio, nil extra quam quod simul cum illis ponantur, commune cum illis habentes; cum ea, etsi in mente sint, non tamen sint in omni, nec ex arbitrio, neque prorsus in mente divina; patet, ex iis occasionem noscendarum mentium haberi non posse nisi imperfectissime, quatenus inde noscere est mentem esse rem videntem, audientem, famem percipientem, dolentem, lætantem, & si quæ ejusmodi. quam inadæquatissimam, non naturæ mentis, sed modorum ejus quorumdam accidentariorum cognitionem, non omnium, sed quarumdam mentium creatarum, ipsa attentio mentis ad se ex corporis occasione efficit. Nil igitur in his quod ad notitiam naturæ mentis in se spectatæ, maxime vero increatæ mentis, conferat. Sunt & aliæ ideæ quæ ex occasione harum priorum, & consequenter sensensuum corporeorum, in mente excitantur, quas idcirco mediatas vel secundarias vocare possumus: ut cum lumen ex hac charta reflexum oculos diversimode movens, excitansque in mente ideas colorum quibus characteres varie repræsentantur, postmodum sequitur idea seu cogitatio de Deo, de anima, de aliis: vel cum, sono quodam audito, mentem subit cogitatio, indeque notitia multarum, ut sæpe fit, rerum: vel cum famem sentiens cogito consequenter de mentis meæ inopia, Deinque amplissima copia: vel cum tristis aut dolens, attendo ad Dei sapientissimam in omnia providentiam. Et ob has quæri potest, quia eæ revera pertinent ad notitiam mentium, & experimur eas sequi ex coloris vel soni perceptione, vel ex alio affectu, cui sensus corporeus occasionem præbuit, num spiritualium rerum notitia eousque sensibus alligata sit, ut hi sint ejus, non causa quidem, vel exemplar, sed occasio, quæ poni debeat ut sequens ponatur notitia, quemadmodum de prioribus ideis dictum est? Respondetur rem omnino se aliter habere cum his ultimis ac cum primis. Etenim primæ statim vel invita voluntate, ponuntur positis sensuum motibus: non ita ultimæ positis primis. Quot infantes, plebei, tardi, barbari, verba hæcce, aut similia, audire vel videre possunt, in quibus tamen nulla perceptio juste respondeat? Unde confidenter asseverare licet, si nil magis perfectum quam quod est in sensibus, earumque ideis, aliunde accedat, neminem unquam posse ex his incidere in Dei, mentiumve notitiam: essetque verisimilius nos, si audiendi facultate essemus destituti, ex sola colorum visione in sonorum notitiam devenire, siquidem plus analogiæ sive paritatis fingi possit inter colores & sonos, quam inter res corporeas (vel earum sensibiles ideas) & Deum. Aliunde adsint oportet rerum spiritualium ideæ, quas attente mens contempletur, multa studio multo in iis detegens, quæ demum labore & industria coloribus, characteribus, verbis, sonis alliget, ut cum per corporea à spiritualibus sit sæpe evocata & impedita, per ipsa etiam aliquando minus quam per alia impediatur, meminerit que hoc modo sui ad se reditus. Id ni foret, in legendo vel audiendo, omnis luderetur opera: verborum externorum plaustra non inferunt sua positione verba interna, quæ demum vere verba sunt, quæque nemo hominum alteri loquendo insinuare aptus est, sed impressit solus mentium author Deus, ad quæ capienda collecta mente, cæteris relictis, serio est attendendum.
units.tr: III. It remains for us to see whether the senses are the occasion of the knowledge which the mind acquires of spiritual things. It must be noted that two kinds of ideas are excited in the mind on the occasion of the senses. We shall call the first primary, or immediate, since they are not formed through the intervention of our will, and they chiefly concern the state of our body which excites them, insofar as this must be joined to some bodies for its preservation, by which it is surrounded, and separated from certain others; this is their chief office. For bodily senses have not been given, as is clear in the case of the brutes, for the knowledge of the truth of things, which is the object of the intellect, not of the senses, but so that the whole system of bodily organs might be preserved. Hence those primary ideas which are excited in the mind immediately by the senses are not to be thought of as representations of things: they are confused and tumultuous perceptions, which, according to the diversity of degrees of pleasantness or unpleasantness, indicate a different state of external objects, of food, of blood, and of the animal spirits, for the constitution of the whole body. While light and colors, sounds, odors, flavors, and what they call tactile qualities correspond better to external things as ideas; hunger and thirst to food; passions to blood; and pains and more vehement titillations, for the most part, to the animal spirits or their vessels. Since bodily senses are neither efficient nor exemplar causes of all these things, but merely an occasion, having in common with them nothing beyond their being posited together; and since these ideas, although they are in the mind, are not in every mind, nor at its own choice, nor wholly in the divine mind, it is plain that from them an occasion of knowing minds can be had only most imperfectly, insofar as from them one knows that the mind is a thing that sees, hears, perceives hunger, grieves, rejoices, and such like. This most inadequate knowledge, not of the nature of the mind but of certain accidental modes of it, and not of all minds but of certain created minds, the very attention of the mind to itself produces on the occasion of the body. Nothing in these things therefore contributes to knowledge of the nature of the mind as it is in itself, and most of all of the uncreated mind. There are also other ideas which are excited in the mind on the occasion of these former ones, and consequently of the bodily senses, and which we may therefore call mediate or secondary: as when light reflected from this paper, moving the eyes in different ways and exciting in the mind ideas of colors by which characters are variously represented, there afterwards follows an idea or thought of God, of the soul, of other things; or when, on hearing a certain sound, a thought comes into the mind and with it knowledge of many things, as often happens; or when, feeling hunger, I then think of the poverty of my mind and of the most abundant plenty of God; or when, sad or grieving, I attend to God's most wise providence over all things. And on account of these, it may be asked, since they truly pertain to the knowledge of minds, and we find that they follow from the perception of a color or sound, or from some other affection which the bodily sense has given occasion for, whether the knowledge of spiritual things is so bound to the senses that these are its cause, not indeed as efficient or exemplar, but as occasion, which must be posited so that the following knowledge may be posited, just as has been said of the former ideas? The answer is that the matter stands altogether otherwise with these last than with the first. For the first are posited immediately, even against the will, when the motions of the senses are posited; not so the last when the first are posited. How many infants, common people, slow-witted persons, and barbarians can hear or see these words, or similar ones, in which yet no perception rightly corresponds?
