Whence we may confidently assert that, if nothing more perfect than what is in the senses and their ideas comes from elsewhere, no one could ever arrive from these at the knowledge of God or of minds; and it would be more probable that, if we were deprived of the faculty of hearing, we would arrive at the knowledge of sounds from the mere vision of colors, since more analogy or parity can be imagined between colors and sounds than between bodily things (or their sensible ideas) and God. Ideas of spiritual things must be present from elsewhere, which the mind contemplates attentively, discovering many things in them by much study, which at length, by labor and industry, it binds to colors, characters, words and sounds; so that, since it is often called forth and hindered by bodily things from spiritual ones, it is sometimes hindered even less by these than by others, and in this way it remembers its return to itself. If this were not so, all effort in reading or hearing would be wasted: the carts of external words do not bring in by their arrangement the internal words, which are in truth the words, and which no man is able to insinuate to another by speaking, but which the sole author of minds, God, impresses; and to receive these, with the mind gathered in and other things set aside, one must attend seriously.

units.la: IV. Ex quibus patet, sensus primo & præcipue nos à rebus spiritua-libus abducere: mentem tamen sibi attentam posse ita illis uti, ut quæ in ea fine illorum vi sunt impressa & cogitata, possit eorum occasione, non naturali, sed studio multo acquisita, iterum in cogitationem revocare. Attendamus igitur principio ad ea quae in mente sunt. quod si facere datur, multis, iisque tantis impedimentis liberabimur, ut quae emolumenta ab iisdem nos habere credimus, ullius vix fuerint consideratio-nis: ut vere Cartesius quinto opponenti dixerit: Quia tam ingenue interrogas quas putem mentem meam habituram fuisse Dei & sui ideas, si ex quo infusa est in corpus manssiset[?] huc usque in eo clausis oculis, & absque ullo aliorum sensuum usu: ingenue & candide respondeo, me non dubitare (modo ipsam in cogitando non impeditam a corpore, ut neque etiam adjutam supponamus) quin easdem, quas nunc habet, Dei & sui ideas fuisset habitura, nisi tantum quod multo puriores & clariores habuisset: sensus enim ipsam in multis impediunt, ac in nullis ad illas percipiendas juvant: & nihil obstat, quominus omnes homines eadem se habere aeque animadvertant, quam quia in rerum corporearum imaginibus percipiendis nimium occupantur. Illas igitur semoveamus, seu imaginatione, ut mox dicetur, seu sensu, ut jam dictum, sistantur; atque obiter animadvertamus, quod si nec corporum notitia fit a sensibus, multo minus spiritualis & divina veri & boni cognitio, imo fruitio, cum illorum crassaminibus nectitur: ut proinde multum abest quin illis cum exuviis corporis depositis, jacturam momentosam patiamur.
units.tr: IV. From these things it is clear that the senses first and above all draw us away from spiritual things; yet a mind that is attentive to itself can make use of them in such a way that, on the occasion of those things, it can recall to thought what has been impressed and thought in it by their force, not by natural means but acquired through great effort. Let us therefore first attend to the things that are in the mind. If this can be done, we shall be freed from many and such great hindrances that the advantages we believe we have from them will hardly be worth considering at all. Truly, as Descartes said to his fifth opponent: "Since you ask so frankly what ideas of God and of itself I think my mind would have had, if from the moment it was infused into the body it had remained there with closed eyes and without any use of the other senses up to now, I answer frankly and candidly that I do not doubt (provided we suppose it is not hindered in thinking by the body, nor helped by it either) that it would have had the same ideas of God and of itself that it now has, except that it would have had them much purer and clearer. For the senses hinder the mind in many ways and help it in none in perceiving those ideas; and nothing prevents all men from noticing that they have the same, were they not so occupied with perceiving the images of corporeal things." Let us therefore set those aside, whether they are held back by imagination, as will be said shortly, or by sense, as has already been said; and let us observe in passing that if the knowledge of bodies does not come from the senses, much less does the spiritual and divine knowledge, indeed the enjoyment, of truth and good, which is bound up with their grossness; so that far from suffering a serious loss, we are, once those things are laid down along with the body's outer husk, very far from it.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 1. 2. Quarta opinio, quae est Imaginationis duplici nomine se omnibus conceptibus immiscentis, & omnia, etiam divina, conspurcantis. 3. Consuetudini imaginandi an ex Cartesianis meditationibus obviam iri possit? 4. 5. 6. Deducuntur inde imperfectiones imaginationis & perfectiones purioris cogitationis. 7. Imaginabilia paucis remota.
units.tr: 1. 2. The fourth opinion, which is that the imagination, under a double title, intrudes into all concepts and defiles everything, even divine things. 3. Can we be met by the habit of imagining, from the Cartesian meditations? 4. 5. 6. From this are deduced the imperfections of the imagination and the perfections of purer thought. 7. Things imaginable are set aside in a few words.

units.la: I. HActenus repulimus tum eos qui rerum spiritualium notitiam ideasve dari negant; tum eos qui illorum corticem seu signa, nempe mera verba, amplectuntur, eos denique qui ad ideas quidem, sed alienas, nempe sensibiles, convertuntur. Superest ut imaginabiles, utpote quae plane etiam alienae sunt, ab hac tribu abdicemus. Duplici nomine eae in omnibus nostris conceptibus ordinarie hospitantur: Primo consuetudine, quae eis locum & ortum; secundo praejudiciis quibusdam falso pro axiomatis habitis, quae eisdem nutrimentum & robur sup-peditarunt.
units.tr: I. Hitherto we have rejected both those who deny that any knowledge or ideas of spiritual things are given, and those who embrace the bark or signs of them, namely mere words, and finally those who turn to ideas indeed, but alien ones, namely sensible ideas. It remains that we banish from this company the imaginable things, since they too are plainly alien. In two ways these ordinarily find lodging in all our concepts: first, by custom, which gives them their place and origin; second, by certain prejudices falsely held as axioms, which have supplied them with nourishment and strength.

units.la: II. Impossibile est ut Dei vel mentis creatae habeatur notitia, idea-ve distincta, quamdiu mens non liberabitur ab ideis imaginariis sive corporeis, quae eam ita pertinaciter ab ortu tenent, ut ex consuetudi-ne, nil reale, nilque perfectum sine illis concipi posse sibi persuadeat. Ubivis, in rebus ipsis quas spirituales recte aut secus arbitratur, exten-sionem, spatium, saepissime motum, aliasque corporeas proprietates admiscet: qua mixtura omnia corrumpuntur. Quapropter operae pre-tium est, ut quilibet conatu summo, & rationibus undique conquisitis renitatur tam pertinaci versus corporea inclinationi, quae non tantum speculationes philosophicas, sed & Divinam notitiam, & cultum reli-giosum, alieni intrusione conspurcat & deperdit. Externa idololatria qua statuae materiales ut ad Deum relatae coluntur,non aliunde est quam ex eo quod in Deo & in mentibus concipiendis, hominis animus se ad imaginabilia converterit, inde quas intus finxit imagines non dubitavit externo typo exprimere, sine quo nihilominus interna fuerit idololatria Deum imaginandi facultate percipere velle, sive Deum sub specie humana, aut sub idea nescio cujus extensi subtilis omnia permeantis, & sine nullo terminum habentis effingas. quem errorem inter suos confi-tetur Augustinus, quique revera est mutatio incorruptibilis Dei in spe-ciem corruptibilis creaturae: &, si eum ad creatam mentem referas, eam repraesentare instar tenuis cujusdam rei spatio definitae, est naturae ejus, veraeque adeo Divinae imaginis, abnegatio.
units.tr: II. It is impossible that a knowledge or distinct idea of God, or of any created mind, should be had as long as the mind is not freed from imaginary or corporeal ideas, which hold it so stubbornly from its origin that, by habit, it persuades itself that nothing real and nothing perfect can be conceived without them. Everywhere, in the very things which it judges to be spiritual, rightly or wrongly, it mixes in extension, space, very often motion, and other corporeal properties; by this mixture all things are corrupted. Therefore it is worth the effort that anyone, with the greatest exertion and with arguments gathered from every side, should resist so stubborn an inclination toward the corporeal, which defiles and destroys not only philosophical speculations but also the divine knowledge and religious worship, by the intrusion of what is alien. External idolatry, in which material statues are worshipped as related to God, arises from nothing other than this: that in conceiving God and minds, the human spirit has turned to the imaginable, and then has not hesitated to express in an external form the images it had fashioned within. Without this, internal idolatry would nevertheless be present, namely the wish to perceive God by the faculty of imagining, whether you picture God under the appearance of a man, or under the idea of I know not what subtle extended thing permeating all things and having no bound. This is the error which Augustine confesses among his own people, and which is truly a change of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible creature; and if you refer it to a created mind, to represent that mind as some thin thing defined by space is a denial of its nature, and indeed of the true divine image.

units.la: III. Utile esset ad mali hujus expulsionem ut Cartesianarum Meditationum Prima cum parte secundae, attente evolveretur. Nam cum ibi objectiones omnes Scepticorum proponantur iis qui adhuc earum solvendarum sunt nescii, inde habitum contrahunt priori contrarium, omnes imagines corporum, extensionis, figurae, motus, spatii, a conceptibus suis removendi, ut facilius tutiusque mentem concipiant extra periculum alieni in ejus idea admiscendi: quippe qui ne aliena admittant, eo deducentur, ut ad tempus supponant nil corporei, nil extensi, nil spatium occupantis, nil moti, verbo, nil ejus quod imaginatione offertur, existere; imo, nullum locum, nullum spatium, quo melius importuna phantasmata in illis volitantia recedant, & mentem sibi ipsi permittant.
units.tr: III. It would be useful, for the expelling of this evil, to read attentively through the First of the Cartesian Meditations together with the part of the Second. For since all the objections of the Sceptics are there set forth for those who are not yet aware of how they are to be solved, they contract a habit contrary to the former: that of removing from their concepts all images of bodies, extension, figure, motion, and space, so that they may conceive the mind more easily and safely, outside the danger of mixing in what is alien to its idea. Indeed, lest they admit alien things, they will be led to suppose, for a time, that nothing corporeal, nothing extended, nothing occupying space, nothing moved exists; in a word, nothing of what is presented to the imagination; indeed, no place and no space, so that the troublesome phantasms flitting about in them may withdraw more easily and leave the mind to itself.

units.la: IV. Porro, si haec attente meditentur ex iis patebit, primo, Omnia quae imaginatione repraesentantur, esse dubia & incerta, ob rationes ibi expressas, & quamdiu sola imaginatione uti volumus ad eorum notitiam. Assero, nullam veritatem, de re ulla, de mente, de corpore, ejusque existentia vel essentia, demonstrari posse ab ullo quamdiu sola imaginatione utitur. Tentet id qui volet. Sed & probare seu tentare velle, jam aliquid est imaginatione superius. Imagines corporeas in phantasia contemplans illarum quidem conscius est, sed nec certus esse, nec alios certos facere potest, eas non esse vana somnia & figmenta quibus deludatur, nisi ultra illas mentem evehat, & certitudinis suæ aliud quærat fundamentum quam nudam illarum in imaginatione præsentiam.
units.tr: IV. Furthermore, if these matters are attentively pondered, it will become clear from them, first, that all things which are represented by the imagination are doubtful and uncertain, for the reasons expressed there, and as long as we wish to use the imagination alone for their knowledge. I assert that no truth concerning any thing, concerning mind or body, or their existence or essence, can be demonstrated by anyone as long as he uses the imagination alone. Let whoever wishes try it. But even to wish to prove or attempt this is already something above the imagination. Contemplating corporeal images in the fancy, one is indeed conscious of them, but one can be neither certain nor make others certain that they are not empty dreams and fictions by which one is deceived, unless the mind raises itself above them and seeks for its certainty a foundation other than the bare presence of those things in the imagination.

units.la: V. Deducetur inde, secundo, esse in nobis facultatem cognoscendi imaginatione superiorem. Si imaginatio esset facultas suprema, non quæreremus ultra illam assurgere: nam unde hoc nobis in mentem veniret, ut, tanquam superioris conscii, illam deserere cogitaremus, nosque ad sublimiorem cogitandi modum, qui nec figuras, nec spatia, similiaque intueatur, elevare? Sed & velle istud negare, aut de illo dubitare, actus istius, quam dicimus, facultatis est. qua enim figura, quo spatio, voluntatem illam cujus es conscius, quæque infinitis aliis modis variari potest, concipis, & tibi præsentem notamque sistis? Nobilem hunc concipiendi modum, ab omni extensione remotum, non dubium est accommodari debere objectis nobilissimis, quæ nisi ipsæ mentes fuerint, nulla merentur hoc nomine compellari.
units.tr: V. It follows from this, secondly, that there is in us a faculty of knowing that is superior to the imagination. If the imagination were the highest faculty, we would not seek to rise above it; for from where would it come into our mind to think of abandoning it, as if conscious of something higher, and to raise ourselves to a more sublime mode of thinking, one which regards neither figures nor spaces nor the like? But even to wish to deny this, or to doubt it, is an act of that faculty which we call the faculty of knowing. For by what figure, by what space, do you conceive that will of which you are conscious, which can be varied in infinitely many other ways, and set it present and known before you? This noble mode of conceiving, removed from all extension, ought undoubtedly to be adapted to the most noble objects, which, unless they are minds themselves, deserve no name by which they might be called such.

units.la: VI. Nec difficile est & illud tertium hinc colligere: Dari objecta, eorumque notitiam talem, quæ cum imaginatione, ejusque objectis, extensione, spatio, motu, nil plane habeant commercii. Facultatem nobilissimam illam objecto destitui & agere non posse, (hoc est, nihil quod omnino corporeum fit posse, prætermissis imaginabilibus, cognoscere) axiomatibus innatis adversatur. Sit potius illa ipsa sui objectum, & hoc ipsum noscat. Objecta quod concernit, notandum est, plerosque homines sibi imponere, putantes se concipere aliquid, cum sæpe nihil concipiant, tametsi verbo aliquid esse dicant: verbi causa, cum prætendunt materiam sine quantitate, aut mentem sine cogitatione cognoscere, objectum quod illis superest, nihil est. At non ita, cum in concipienda mente quantitatem, extensionem, spatium, motum, & similia, removemus; non sic tollimus omne reale, superest aliquid quod non est nihil, sed quam maxime positivum & perfectum, nempe aliquid cogitans, dubitans, volens, affirmans, negans, sciens, amans, gaudens, ecquis omnia sublimia, præ quibus imaginabilia vix quicquicquam sunt, incerta sunt, obscura sunt, enumeret? Sed hæc ad i-psam notitiam: de qua, ut de facultate & objectis factum est, aliquid quo-que est annotandum: nempe eam non esse completæ certitudinis, ubi concipi potest objectum ejus non existere; nec summæ evidentiæ, ubi in ipsis quæ prætenduntur clarissima esse, superest obscuritas: quibus duobus incommodis quæ imaginationi omni adhærent, intellectualis mentium notitia liberatur. Qua enim absurditate assereretur dari trian-gulum absque figura vel extensione, pari contenderetur me dum cogito vel non existere, vel non habere facultates volendi, & similes, easque cognoscendi: cum, si hæc negarem, eo ipso faterer me velle negare, & me nosse quid negem: adeo ut notitia intellectualis quam habeo de me cogitante, ab omni imaginatione remotissima, sit ultimæ certitudinis. Non ita de notitia corporum, maxime de illa quæ imaginatione fieri prætenditur. possibile enim est mihi concipere, me cogitante nulla exi-stere corpora, spatia, & similia, vel posse ea non existere; ita ut mei de me cogitante cognitio non idcirco fiat incertior: quæ suppositio nec im-possibilis conceptu, nec absurda, ut mox præcedentes, est dicenda. Præterea in imaginatione in se spectata, semper involvitur obscuritas & confusio: nam cum prætendat sibi quasi præsentia sistere omnia quæ in extensione, figuris, motibus; ea vero, quamquam vel unius corpu-sculi, sint indefinita; necessariò conatu excidit, & si quid amplecti putet, massæ sunt confusæ quæ illam defatigant & deludunt: cujus exemplum ipse Hobbes de se ipso præbet in rebus corporeis alioquin clarissimis & omnium facillimis cognitu, unde patet quam importunum sit vel in rebus materialibus imaginatione uti & niti. vir enim ille imaginosus, quia ut cætera, sic & principia Geometriæ imaginatione voluit metiri, in libello quem de principiis & ratiocinatione geometrarum conscripsit, statim in ipso limine lapsus est, dum punctum, lineam, superficiem, imaginatione capere volens, tribuit illi partes, isti latitudinem, & huic profunditatem, unde & plura alia absurda imaginatur. De intellectuali notitia non ita est, præsertim cum illa circa mentes versatur: quæ concipit, ea vere suo modo attingit qualia sunt, & ut distincta sunt ab aliis quæ non sunt id ipsum, ut exemplis de re cogitante allatis attendenti cuivis liquet. Neque ad id opus est ut omnia quæ in suo objecto sunt capiat, sufficit si quæ pauca attingit, vere qualia in se sunt, & qualiter se revera habent, suo modo attingat. Quomodo igitur, ut ad rem præcipuam redeamus, id quod parum realitatis possidet, quod non est plane certum, quod negari potest, quod est obscurum, nempe omne imaginatum, fuerit fundamentum cognoscendi id quod maxime reale seu perfectum, quod certum, quod inconcussum, quod evidens, & distinctum ? Quomodo imaginata extensio cum annexis, fuerit notitiæ intellectualium causa, medium, vel notitia ipsa ?
units.tr: VI. Nor is it difficult to draw from this a third point: that there are objects, and a knowledge of them, which have absolutely no commerce with the imagination and its objects, extension, space, and motion. That this most noble faculty should be deprived of an object and be unable to act, (that is, be unable to know anything that is wholly corporeal, the imaginables apart), is contrary to innate axioms. Rather, let it be its own object, and let it know this very thing. As for objects, it must be noted that most men deceive themselves, thinking they conceive something when often they conceive nothing, even though they say in words that something is. For example, when they profess to know matter without quantity, or mind without thought, the object that remains to them is nothing. But it is not so when, in conceiving the mind, we remove quantity, extension, space, motion, and the like; we do not thus take away all that is real; something remains which is not nothing, but most positive and perfect, namely something thinking, doubting, willing, affirming, denying, knowing, loving, rejoicing. Who could enumerate all the sublime things, in comparison with which the imaginables are scarcely anything at all, and which are uncertain, obscure? But these matters concern the knowledge itself, and about it, as about the faculty and the objects, something must also be noted: namely that it is not of complete certainty when its object can be conceived as not existing, nor of the highest evidence when, in the very things which are claimed to be clearest, obscurity remains. By these two inconveniences, which cling to all imagination, the intellectual knowledge of minds is freed. For with what absurdity would it be asserted that there is a triangle without figure or extension; by the same reasoning it would be contended that while I think I either do not exist, or do not have the faculties of willing, and the like, and of knowing them; whereas, if I were to deny these things, I would by that very act confess that I will to deny, and that I know what I deny; so that the intellectual knowledge I have of myself thinking, being most remote from all imagination, is of the highest certainty. It is not so with the knowledge of bodies, especially that which is claimed to be gained by imagination. For it is possible for me to conceive that, while I think, no bodies, spaces, or the like exist, or that they may not exist; so that my knowledge of myself thinking is not made any less certain on that account. This supposition is neither impossible to conceive nor absurd, as the preceding ones are to be called. Moreover, in the imagination considered in itself, obscurity and confusion are always involved; for since it claims to set before itself, as if present, all the things that are in extension, figures, and motions, which, even of a single small body, are indefinite, it necessarily falls short in the attempt; and if it thinks it grasps anything, there are confused masses which wear it out and deceive it. Hobbes himself provides an example of this in his own case, in corporeal things otherwise very clear and the easiest of all to know; whence it is evident how troublesome it is to use and rely upon the imagination even in material things. For that man of great imagination, because, like the other things, he wished to measure the principles of geometry by the imagination, in the little book which he wrote on the principles and reasoning of geometers, slipped at once on the very threshold, while wanting to grasp point, line, and surface by the imagination; he assigned parts to the point, breadth to the line, and depth to the surface, whence he also imagines many other absurdities. It is not so with intellectual knowledge, especially when it is concerned with minds: what it conceives, it truly attains in its own way as they are, and as they are distinct from others which are not the same thing, as is clear to anyone who attends to the examples given about a thinking thing. Nor is it necessary for this that it should grasp all that is in its object; it is enough if it attains a few things, truly as they are in themselves, and in the way they really are. How, then, to return to our main point, could that which possesses little reality, which is not plainly certain, which can be denied, which is obscure, namely everything imagined, be the foundation of knowing that which is most real or perfect, that which is certain, unshaken, evident, and distinct? How could imagined extension, with its attachments, be the cause, the means, or the knowledge itself of intellectual things?

units.la: VII. Quæ omnia si bene animadvertantur, non munient tantum viam ad notitiam mentium ; sed & earum naturam ab omni imagina-bili alienam demonstrare apta sunt, quod hic loci non persequemur ul-terius, cum sufficecerit ea proposuisse quæ à consuetudine nos ad imagi-nabilia vertendi revocarent ad sublimiora. Quod si quis palpabili modo & paucis ab ea declinare velit, consideret omnem extensionem partes involvere, partes vero figuras & mensuras, spatium autem nullum esse quin extensione præditum sit, & consequenter partibus, & mensura, in longitudine, latitudine & profunditate : omnem motum fieri in spa-tio, cujus pars deseritur acquirendæ alius ergo, & consequenter omnem rem motam simul quoque extensam esse : insuper, si animadvertat tum id omne esse corporeum & materiale, tum impertinens esse menti tri-buere partes, figuram, & mensuram, facile convincetur eo ipso omnem spatii occupationem, motum, & omnia imaginabilia à conceptu de men-tibus esse exterminanda.
units.tr: VII. If all these things are carefully considered, they not only pave the way to knowledge of minds, but also serve to show that their nature is wholly foreign to anything imaginable. We will not pursue this further here, since it is enough to have set out those points which might call us back from the habit of turning to imaginable things and lead us to higher matters. But if someone wishes to turn aside from this in a tangible way and briefly, let him consider that all extension involves parts, that the parts involve figures and measures, that there is no space which is not endowed with extension, and consequently with parts and measure in length, breadth and depth; that every motion takes place in space, one part of which is left behind while another is acquired, and consequently that every moved thing is also extended. Moreover, if he notices both that all this is corporeal and material, and that it is out of place to attribute parts, figure and measure to the mind, he will easily be convinced by this very fact that every occupation of space, motion, and all imaginable things must be banished from the concept of minds.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. Imaginationis quæ in rebus spiritualibus miscetur fulcra quatuor. 2. Exponitur primum, Quod nusquam est, neque est. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Destruitur multis, & ejus contrarium evincitur.
units.tr: 1. Of the imagination that mixes itself into spiritual things, four supports. 2. First it is set out: What is nowhere, is not. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. It is overturned in many ways, and its contrary is proved.

units.la: I. Hujus mali, conceptuum videlicet crassorum ubi de intellectua-libus agitur, radix est in habitu corporea unice contemplandi : sed alimentum & succus quo fovetur, à præjudiciis inde natis submini-stratur, quia illa veritatum, imo axiomatum nomen apud omnes primo obtinuerunt, & apud multos etiamnum obtinet. Inter præcipua hæc sunt : Quod nusquam est, id neque esse. Deum ubique esse non operatione tantum, neque sola potentia, sed & essentia, qua etiam replet terram & cœlos. Mentem humanam jungi corporis totius, vel saltem cerebri, extensioni. Eam cum corpore transferri, & sic cum illo moveri, quod & cum Angelis interdum commune fiat. Quamvis autem quæ hisce responsiones debentur & fient, videri possint digressiones à præcipuo scopo, & quidem longiores, tædiosæ, & non necessariæ, cum objectum intellectuale, quale nostrum est, possit absque corporeorum mentione tractari; attamen si reputetur, nil in tabula mentis pure scribi posse, nisi male scripta prius deleantur, absque quo, confusio fieret major; si advertatur, Medicos, etiamsi eorum scopus præcipuus & ultimus sit corpus ægrum nobili succo & vigore implere,nihilominus multum laboris & temporis impendere evacuandis humoribus pravis qui debilitatem & morbum causantur; non culpabitur adeo sequens opera, siquidem iis offeratur qui debiles, & ad imaginabilia valde propensi sunt. Cæteri meliora quærant vel proponant.
units.tr: I. The root of this evil, namely the gross notions that arise when we deal with intellectual things, lies in the habit of contemplating only corporeal things. But the nourishment and sap by which it is fostered is supplied by the prejudices that arise from this habit, because those propositions, indeed axioms, first gained acceptance among everyone and still hold sway among many. The chief of these are: What is nowhere, that is not. God is everywhere not only by operation and by power alone, but also by essence, by which he also fills the earth and the heavens. The human mind is joined to the extension of the whole body, or at least of the brain. It is carried along with the body, and so moves with it, which at times becomes common even with the Angels. Although the replies that are owed to these, and will be given, may seem to be digressions from the main aim, and indeed long, tedious and unnecessary ones, since an intellectual object such as ours can be treated without mention of corporeal things; nevertheless, if it is considered that nothing can be written purely on the tablet of the mind unless the badly written things are first erased, without which the confusion would become greater; and if it is noted that physicians, even though their chief and final aim is to fill the sick body with noble juice and vigour, nonetheless spend much labour and time in draining off the bad humours that cause weakness and disease, then the one who follows this work will not be blamed too much, since it is offered to those who are weak and very prone to imaginable things. Others may seek or propose better things.

units.la: II. Redeamus igitur ad prædicta axiomata, (sic enim ea ex consuetudine, quanquam immerito, vocabimus) quæ cum universalem inducant confusionem ita profligare animus est, ut non supersit, ubi in iis quæ mentes concernunt possint subsistere. Primum, cum cæterorum sit basis, etiam primo patietur examen. Vult illud nobis persuadere, id non esse, sive non existere, quod in nullo spatio existit. Hoc schola sic sua lingua effert: Quod nusquam est, id neque est. Quod de præsentia quæ sit per motum extensionis seu expansionis in spatio vult intelligi. Hinc est quod ejusmodi opinionis defensores multum impendant operæ in construendis quibusdam spatiis imaginariis quæ infinita sint, & ultra mundi limites extendantur,ne cæteroqui Dei præsentia terminetur spatiis mundi limitatis, sitque ipse limitatus Deus. Nec minus laborant de spatio per quod mens in corpore diffundatur. quærunt an illa sit tota in toto & tota in singulis partibus? vel an in una tantum ex illis? Et concesso, illam esse in omnibus & singulis, quo deveniat, si ex corporis partibus una resecetur, anima, quæ prius tota erat inibi? Quod ut solverent, imaginati sunt quandam contractionem, quasi limax ad se in testa contraheretur. Sed ut crassa istiusmodi imaginata pulvere subtilitatis suæ condirent, ea in tres seorsim divisere classes quas verborum involucris seorsim texerunt. Dixerunt nempe præsentiam, quam & ubietatem vocant, aliam esse circumscriptivam, quam corporibus; aliam definitivam, quam creatis mentibus, sive animabus; aliam repletivam, quam Deo soli tribuunt. nec vero opus est ut teramus tempus in commentis & quæstionibus eorum referendis, cujusmodi sunt, An Angelus possit contrahi in punctum? An Spiritus in momento possit moveri? An ab uno extremo ad aliud possit se conferre non eundo per medium? Ubi erat v. g. anima Lazari postea suscitati, dum in sepulcro corpus ejus adhuc latebat? num forte illa in digito delitescebat? & similes nugæ. Omnia hæc cusa sunt ex falsa illa hypothesi, quod non est nihil id debere esse alicubi, hoc est, in spatio extendi. Hanc autem interpretationem illis non attribui gratis, sed esse juxta illorum sensum, satis patet ex allegatis quæstionibus: vel si quod tibi tempus terere placet, consule ipsos. Nonnullus {a} qui pro eorum spinis sterilibus utilitatem facilem repositsse dicitur, Spatium, quod & Ubietatem vocat, inter communes entis affectiones recenset, & dividit ut supra, idque tribuit mentibus & Deo, etiam imaginarium cum reali, addita Regula, alicubi esse est omnium entium existentium universale attributum. Quod nusquam est, non est. Quem etiam errorem fatetur se erraße Augustinus, & per eum à Dei notitia remotum fuisse, ut videre est passim in suis confessionibus, ubi, inter alia, luctam suam adversus imaginabilia sic describit. {b} Clamabat violenter cor meum adversus omnia phantasmata mea, & hoc uno ictu conabar abigere circumvolitantem turbam immunditiæ ab acie mentis meæ: & vix dimota in ictu oculi, ecce conglobata rursus aderat, & irruebat in aspectum meum, & obnubilabat eum: ut quamvis non forma humani corporis, corporeum tamen aliquid cogitare cogerer per spatia locorum, sive infusum mundo, sive etiam extra mundum per infinita diffusum; etiam ipsum incorruptibile, & inviolabile & incommutabile, quod corruptibili, & violabili & commutabili præponebam. Quoniam quicquid privabam spatiis talibus, nil mihi esse videbatur. Et paulo post: Ego itaque incrassatus corde, nec mihimet ipsi vel ipse conspicuus, quicquid non per aliquanta spatia tenderetur, vel diffunderetur, vel conglobaretur, vel tumeret, vel tale quid caperet aut capere posset, nihil prorsus esse arbitrabar: per quales enim formas ire solent oculi mei, (hæc radix est præjudicii, nempe corporeorum contemplandi & imaginandi consuetudo) per tales imagines ibat cor meum: nec videbam hanc eandem intentionem, qua illas ipsas imagines formabam, non esse tale aliquid; quæ tamen ipsas non formaret; nisi esset magnum aliquid.
units.tr: II. Let us then return to the aforesaid axioms (for so we shall call them by custom, though undeservedly), which, since they introduce a universal confusion, I intend to strike down so thoroughly that nothing is left by which they could stand in matters concerning minds. The first, since it is the basis of the rest, will also be examined first. It wants to persuade us that what does not exist in any space, that is, does not exist, is not. The school expresses this in its own language: What is nowhere, that is not. This it wishes to be understood of a presence that exists through motion of extension or expansion in space. Hence the defenders of this opinion spend much effort in constructing certain imaginary spaces that are infinite and extend beyond the limits of the world, lest otherwise the presence of God be bounded by the limited spaces of the world, and God himself be limited. Nor do they labour less over the space through which the mind is diffused in the body. They ask whether it is wholly in the whole and wholly in each of the parts, or only in one of them? And, granting that it is in all and each, what happens if one of the parts of the body is cut away: does the soul, which was previously whole there, go too? To solve this they imagined a certain contraction, as if a snail were drawn into itself within its shell. But to season these crude imaginings with the dust of subtlety, they divided them into three separate classes, which they covered separately with wrappings of words. For they called one presence, which they also call ubiety, circumscriptive, which belongs to bodies; another definitive, which belongs to created minds or souls; and another repletive, which they assign to God alone. Nor indeed is there any need to waste time in recounting their fancies and questions, such as: Can an Angel be contracted into a point? Can a spirit be moved in a moment? Can it transport itself from one extremity to another without passing through the middle? Where was the soul of Lazarus, afterwards raised, while his body still lay hidden in the tomb? Perhaps it was lurking in a finger? And similar trifles. All these have been devised from that false hypothesis, that what is not nothing must be somewhere, that is, must be extended in space. That this interpretation is not ascribed to them without reason, but is in accordance with their meaning, is sufficiently clear from the questions cited; or, if you are pleased to waste some time, consult them yourself. Some [a] who is said to have drawn easy usefulness from their sterile thorns, reckons space, which he also calls ubiety, among the common affections of being, and divides it as above, and assigns it to minds and to God, imaginary space together with real, adding the rule: To be somewhere is a universal attribute of all existing beings. What is nowhere, is not. Augustine also confesses that he himself erred in this, and was thereby kept far from the knowledge of God, as may be seen throughout his Confessions, where, among other things, he describes his struggle against imaginable things thus. [b] My heart violently cried out against all my phantasms, and with this one blow I tried to drive off the swarm of uncleanness flying around the edge of my mind; and scarcely had it been brushed away in the twinkling of an eye, behold, it gathered together again and rushed into my sight and clouded it: so that, although not in the form of a human body, I was nonetheless compelled to think of something corporeal, spread through spaces of places, whether poured into the world or even diffused through infinity outside the world; even that which is incorruptible, inviolable and unchangeable, which I set above the corruptible, violable and changeable. For whatever I deprived of such spaces seemed to me to be nothing. And a little later: I, therefore, thickened in heart, and not even visible to myself, thought that whatever was not extended, or diffused, or gathered together, or swollen, or did not take or could not take some such thing through some spaces, was altogether nothing: for through such forms as my eyes are wont to pass, through such images my heart went; nor did I see that this very intention by which I formed those very images is not something of this kind; and yet it would not form them unless it were something great.

units.la: III. Jam, dictum axioma excutiamus. Concedimus valere illud in omni corpore, qualecunque id sit vel fingatur: si nusquam est, si in spatio non est, neque est: spatium enim ab essentia corporum inseparabile est, neque ipsa ab illo distinguitur, cum ea consistat in extensione longa, lata & profunda, quæ ipsissima spatii idea est. At si ad substantias incorporeas referatur axioma, fallit profecto: salsissimum enim est, mentem, si nusquam seu in nullo spatio sit, non existere. neque opus est ad ejus falsitatem detegendam, veritatemque ei oppositam agnoscendam, ut multum exacta & exquisita mentium notitia prius imbuamur: sufficit vel communissima omnibus mortalibus notio, qua intelli-gimus, gimus, Mentem sive Spiritum non posse mensurari vel pede, vel spitha-ma, vel ulna : neque posse dici hanc mentem, exempli causa, esse lon-gam aut latam ulnas tres, vel pauciores, pluresve, vel etiam infinitas. Suppone ergo, prout petit falsus canon refellendus, Spiritum seu men-tem esse in spatio aliquo pro lubitu accepto ; spatium illud præditum erit extensione nonnulla, cui mensura quædam, parva aut magna, palmus vel pertica, poterit applicari, eaque applicata semel aut multoties, ab uno extremo ad aliud perveniet, quo modo illud una, denis, aut centenis absolvetur mensuris ; vel primæ quæ se sistit spatii parti eadem applicata, & quaquaversum in infinitum reduplicata, undiquaque ex-tremum non inveniet : quale concipiunt spatium in quo Deum esse sin-gunt. Utraque hypotheseos suæ necessaria sequela absurda est, & ulti-ma Deum non decet, ex qua quippe sequeretur Dei essentiam spatio coëxtensam vel decempeda mensurabilem fore, hac solum cum excep-tione, non posse eam dum mensuraretur ita emetiri, ut ad finem per-veniatur, quippe quæ eo carere intelligitur, quam etiam ob causam infinita spatia sibi esse imaginatos non diffitentur. Imo quidam {a}eo devenerunt, ut sibi persuaderent spatium quod in se omnia recipit, quodque omnium rerum locus est, etiam æternum esse, & esse ipsum Deum quatenus est immensus, sive ipsam Divinam immensitatem, quæ habeat diversas partes virtuales, quibus diversæ applicentur & insint corpora locata (quod sane est valere vel posse mensurari & dividi), quæque cum neque sit punctum, neque in puncto, habeat extensionem virtualem infinitam. Sed omittamus in posterum exemplum illud de Deo, ne illo cum tantis absurdis composito ludere videamur : quamquam absurda ejusmodi cogitata non proferamus alio fine, quam ut, iis expulsis, quæ Deo digniora & decentiora sint substituantur. Pergamus igitur, supposita in spatio mente creata. Ergo spatium tale, certa mensura definitum, à mente creata, cujus substantia ibi præsens prætenditur, replebitur aut totum, aut quoad partem, aut ita plene ut etiam se ulterius diffundat substantia spiritus ad certos usque termi-nos, quos ultra non consistet, sed præcise aliquo usque se extendet, tantum extensionis, vel, si mavis, coextensionis habebit : itaque cum spatio commensurabitur, dividetur cum eo in partes, duas, quaternas & sic consequenter : quod cum absurdissimum merito habeatur, fatendum est, illud, unde necessario fluit, axioma, de spatii necessitate ad Entium & Mentium existentiam ne sint nihil, etiam absurdissimum esse. Nec est quod verbis dicant, mentis substantiam in spatio esse, neque tamen extendi aut mensurari cum eo: nam & in ipsis verbis est repugnantia, & nova absurditate priorem cumulant. etenim fatentur, τὸ[?] in spatio esse, vel spatium ipsum, esse de essentia & natura rei spiritualis, (certe (extra genus causae efficientis,) id absque quo aliquid non est Ens, vel cessat esse Ens, est maxime de ejus essentia) vel dicant, si malint, esse proprietatem inseparabilem. agnoscunt iidem esse spatio sive essentiale, sive proprium, ut sit extensum, mensurabile, divisi-bile, in partes binas, ternas, & similes. Unde sequitur, siquidem spatium a substantia spirituali sit indivulsum, ipsam rem spiritualem, seu Mentem, extendi, mensurabilem, divisibilem in partes binas, ternas, plures, esse: nam quod necessario & naturaliter cujusdam rei est particeps, hoc ipso omnium eorum quae rei illi sunt essentialia & propria particeps devenit. nisi absurde hoc primum cognitum in prioris absurditatis gratiam inficientur. Sed & quae superius de illis sunt allata, ut quae spirituum contractionem & similia concernunt, ipsorum hac de re cogitata satis superque recludunt, quanquam ea verbis conantur utcunque dissimulare.
units.tr: III. Now let us examine the said axiom. We grant that it holds for every body, whatever it may be or be imagined to be: if it is nowhere, if it is not in space, it is not. For space is inseparable from the essence of bodies, nor is it distinguished from them, since it consists in extension in length, breadth and depth, which is the very idea of space itself. But if the axiom is referred to incorporeal substances, it certainly fails: for it is most absurd that a mind, if it is nowhere or in no space, does not exist. Nor, to detect its falsity and recognise the truth opposed to it, is it necessary that we be first imbued with a very exact and refined knowledge of minds: the most common notion, shared by all mortals, is enough, by which we understand that a mind or spirit cannot be measured either by a foot, or a span, or an ell; nor can it be said that this mind, for example, is three ells long or broad, or fewer, or more, or even infinite. Suppose, then, as the false canon we are refuting requires, that a spirit or mind is in some space taken at will; that space will be endowed with some extension, to which some measure, small or large, a palm or a rod, can be applied; and when this is applied once or many times, it will go from one extremity to the other, so that it is completed by one, ten or a hundred measures; or, applied to the first part of space that presents itself and repeated in every direction to infinity, it will find no extremity anywhere: such as they conceive the space in which they imagine God to be. Each of the two consequences necessarily following from their hypothesis is absurd, and the last is unbecoming to God, for it would follow that the essence of God would be co-extended with space, or measurable by a ten-cubit rod, with this one exception, that while it was being measured it could not be measured so as to reach an end, since it is understood to lack one; and for this reason they do not deny that they have imagined infinite spaces. Indeed, some [a] have come to such a point that they persuaded themselves that space, which receives all things in itself and is the place of all things, is eternal, and is God himself insofar as he is immense, or the very divine immensity, which has diverse virtual parts, to which diverse bodies are applied and placed within (which is surely to be capable of being measured and divided), and which, since it is neither a point nor in a point, has infinite virtual extension. But let us henceforth omit that example concerning God, lest we seem to be playing with it, composed as it is with so many absurdities; although we do not bring forward such absurd thoughts for any other end than that, once they are driven out, things more worthy and more fitting to God may be substituted. Let us therefore proceed, supposing a created mind to be in space. Then such a space, defined by a certain measure, will be filled by the created mind, whose substance is present there and stretched out, either wholly, or as to a part, or so fully that the substance of the spirit also diffuses itself further, up to certain limits beyond which it will not remain, but will extend itself precisely up to a certain point, and will have only so much extension, or, if you prefer, co-extension; and so it will be measured with space, will be divided with it into parts, two, four, and so on consequently. Since this is rightly considered most absurd, it must be admitted that the axiom from which it necessarily flows, namely that the existence of beings and minds depends on space, lest they be nothing, is itself most absurd. Nor is there any point in their saying in words that the substance of the mind is in space, yet is not extended or measured together with it: for there is a contradiction in the very words, and they pile up a new absurdity on the former one. For they admit that to be in space, or space itself, belongs to the essence and nature of a spiritual thing (certainly, outside the genus of efficient cause, that without which a thing is not a being, or ceases to be a being, is most of its essence), or, if they prefer, they say it is an inseparable property. The same people acknowledge that space, whether essential or proper, makes a thing extended, measurable, divisible into two, three and similar parts. Whence it follows that, if space is not separated from a spiritual substance, the spiritual thing itself, or the mind, must be extended, measurable, divisible into two, three, or more parts: for whatever necessarily and naturally partakes of some thing, by that very fact comes to partake of all the things that are essential and proper to that thing, unless they absurdly deny this first point, in favour of the earlier absurdity. But also what was said above about these matters, concerning the contraction of spirits and similar things, abundantly reveals their thinking on this subject, although they try in words to disguise it somehow.

units.la: IV. Praeterea non solum mentis in spatio praesentia, de qua hactenus, sed etiam praesentiae illius initium, seu ingressus in aliquod spatium per alterius desertionem, & ipsius praesentiae duratio, falsi convincere possunt & absurdi axioma illud cui innituntur haec imaginata. Si enim supponam mentem nondum esse in hoc certo spatio, sed in contiguo, unde velit exire ut se ad hoc sequens conferat; quomodo quaeso exitum & ingressum hunc concipies, nisi tribuendo Spiritui partes simul cum extensione divisibili? Dicas velim in quo fit spatio in illo tempore, vel si recusas, momento, dum mutat ille spatium prius ut aliud repleat ubi? Tunc enim, aut erat in nullo: quod suppositum destruit; aut totus erat in priori, vel totus in posteriori: quod non est mutare, sed manere, & jam antea mutasse; restat ut concipiant, (etiamsi id verbis negent, quia id crassius est quam ut aperte dicatur) illam mentem partim esse in uno, partim in altero spatio, & quasi successive ab uno ad aliud promoveri. Et hoc ipsum est tribuere partes menti, saltem in conceptu, sive concipere mentem divisibilem; quod aperte absurdum est.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, not only the presence of the mind in space, of which we have spoken so far, but also the beginning of that presence, or its entry into some space through the leaving of another, and the duration of the presence itself, can prove false and absurd the axiom on which these imaginings rest. For if I suppose that the mind is not yet in this certain space, but in an adjoining one, from which it wishes to go out in order to betake itself to this next one, then how, I ask, will you conceive this exit and entry, unless you attribute parts to the Spirit together with divisible extension? Tell me, I beg, in which space it is at that time, or, if you object to "time," at that moment, while it changes the former space so as to fill another one where? For then either it was in nothing, which supposition destroys the point; or it was wholly in the former, or wholly in the latter, which is not to change but to remain, and to have already changed before. It remains that they conceive (even if they deny it in words, because this is too crude to be stated openly) that that mind is partly in one space and partly in another, and is moved, as it were successively, from one to another. And this itself is to attribute parts to the mind, at least in conception, or to conceive the mind as divisible; which is plainly absurd.

units.la: V. Idem de duratione ejus in spatio dici potest, eo quod nullius sit usus. Ad quid, amabo, spatium pro Mente? quod vinculum, quae necessitas, hanc illi alligat, sive ejus operationes, sive naturam spectes? Num per spatium subsistunt operationes mentis? Num quid spatium, ejusque extensio earum sunt vel objectum necessarium, vel subjectum, vel principium, vel confervans causa? Quod si naturam illius spectes, quid est in illa, plane spiritualis & incorporea ut est, quod spatium requirat ad hoc ut incipiat vel continuet existere? Quid est illud in toto mentis apparatu, quod necessariam, vel aliam omnino involvat relationem ad spatii occupationem? Quin potius, quid magis adversum notitiis quae omnibus de natura mentium sunt communes, quam effata similia, mentes esse divisibiles in parte, esse extensas & mensurabiles vel palmo, vel pede, aliave extensa mensura? Quae conclusiones necessario fluunt ex axiomate, Omne quod est, alicubi sive in spatio est: quod in falsa ducens ipsum falsum est.
units.tr: V. The same can be said of its duration in space, on the ground that it serves no purpose. To what end, I ask you, space for the Mind? What bond, what necessity binds it to this, whether you look to its operations or to its nature? Do the operations of the mind subsist through space? Are space and its extension a necessary object, subject, principle, or conserving cause of them? But if you look to its nature, what is there in it, which is plainly spiritual and incorporeal as it is, that requires space in order to begin or continue to exist? What is there in the whole apparatus of the mind that involves a necessary, or any other, relation to the occupation of space? Nay rather, what is more contrary to the notions that are common to all about the nature of minds than such sayings as that minds are divisible in part, are extended, and are measured by a span, a foot, or some other extended measure? These conclusions flow necessarily from the axiom, Whatever is, is somewhere or in space; which, by leading into falsehood, is itself false.

units.la: VI. Peti etiam potest, an Cogitatio, meditatio, judicia affirmantia aut negantia, amor, cupiditas, odium, & si quae similia, sint nihil? Si non sunt nihil, in quo igitur sunt ubi? quod spatium, & quantum tenent? Et cum omne spatium sit divisibile cum eo quod in illo est, ut probatum, possitne serio dici aut concipi, judicium aliquod, exempli gratia, esse longum aut latum tot mensuras? amorem occupantem tantum spatii altum esse mille pedes; divisum autem cum spatio in partes duas, restare utrinque quingentos, & plura ejusmodi? Non igitur, cum haec a ratione sint aliena, in spatio ea sunt: neque tamen sunt nihil. Nec est quod objicias, esse ea facultates, operationes, & accidentia mentis, non autem substantiam ipsam: Axioma vero de substantia loqui, non de illis. Nam primo, ipsa cogitatio, mentisque facultates intellectus & voluntas, ab ea realiter non distinguuntur, sed sunt ipsa ejus substantia, quod infra pluribus ostendetur: si igitur hae non sunt in spatio, nec etiam ipsa mens. Secundo, non potest sane concipi operationes, quas actus secundos vocant, alicujus rei quae per naturam suam in spatio est, ipsas non esse in spatio, praesertim cum in re agente subsistunt, & sunt immanentes, quales superius recensitae. quomodo quaeso operationes quae subsistunt in re cujus natura vult ut sit in spatio, ipsae spatium cum eis quae spatio sunt competentia, non requirent, non involvent? Denique de omnibus accidentibus, modis & variationibus quae rem aliquam afficiunt, affirmatur, ea quorum subjectum est in spatio non posse absque spatio concipi, nec sine divisibilitate: atque ita est de omnibus quae corpori accidunt; & in universum, est de natura omnis modi & accidentis ut non possit concipi absque eo quod est ita de essentia ejus subjecti, ut hoc nihil esset sine illo, nam accidens est ipsius entis, sive naturae, sive ejus quod rei est essentiale, mutatio quaedam, vel, si mavis, variatio quaedam substantiae.
units.tr: VI. It may also be asked whether thought, meditation, judgements affirming or denying, love, desire, hatred, and whatever such things are, are nothing. If they are not nothing, where then are they, and what space do they occupy and how much of it? And since every space is divisible along with what is in it, as has been proved, can it seriously be said or conceived that some judgement, for example, is so many measures long or broad, or that love occupying so much space is a thousand feet high, and, divided with the space into two parts, leaves five hundred on each side, and many more things of this kind? Therefore, since these things are alien to reason, they are not in space; yet neither are they nothing. Nor is there any point in your objecting that these are faculties, operations and accidents of the mind, and not its substance itself, and that the axiom speaks of substance, not of them. For first, thought itself and the mind's faculties of understanding and will are not really distinct from it, but are its very substance, as will be shown at greater length below; if therefore these are not in space, neither is the mind itself. Second, it cannot surely be conceived that the operations which they call second acts of a thing that by its nature is in space are not themselves in space, especially since they subsist in the acting thing and are immanent, of the kind enumerated above. How, I ask, will operations that subsist in a thing whose nature requires that it be in space not require space, and not involve along with it those things that belong to space? Finally, it is affirmed of all accidents, modes and variations that affect any thing, that those whose subject is in space cannot be conceived without space, nor without divisibility; and so it is with all that befalls a body; and in general it is the nature of every mode and accident that it cannot be conceived without that which belongs to the essence of its subject, so that without it this would be nothing; for an accident is a certain change, or, if you prefer, a certain variation, of the being itself, whether of its nature or of what is essential to the thing.

units.la: VII. Essent vero fortasse nonnulli qui modos vel accidentia rei spa-tiosæ, dicerent spatiosa & divisibilia esse quidem, verum per accidens, non per se. De quibus nugis, siquidem eis sit respondendum, dici potest, eas, si ad præsens negotium applicentur, nimis absurdas videri; nam judicium, amorem, aliaque, esse spatiosa vel in partes divisibilia per accidens, durius est quam ut dicatur; & præterea, loquela est secum dupliciter pugnans, aliquid esse spatiosum & divisibile per accidens. Idem enim est ac si dicerent, Rei ejus positionem & existentiam posse esse sine spatio ex natura sua, quod pugnat cum iis quæ supposuere prius: sed & contradicens est, dari divisibile per accidens: nam cui accidit ut dividi possit, id talis fuit naturæ ut ei potuerit accidere divisio: fuit igitur ex natura divisibile. potest equidem sine pugna quid dici per accidens divisum, sed non divisibile. Itaque, quod concludimus, cum mentis plurima sine spatio & divisibilitate concipiantur, quæ ita con-cipi non possent, nisi eorum subjectum imaginario isto spatio careret, corruit salsissimum axioma de omnium Entium spatio.
units.tr: VII. There would perhaps be some who, when speaking of the modes or accidents of a spatial thing, would say that they are indeed spatial and divisible, but only by accident, not in themselves. To such trifles, if they are to be answered, it may be said that these, if applied to the present business, seem far too absurd; for to say that judgement, love and other such things are spatial or divisible into parts by accident is harsher than it can be stated; and moreover, the expression is doubly self-contradictory, to say that something is spatial and divisible by accident. For it is the same as if they said that the position and existence of such a thing can be without space by its own nature, which conflicts with what they supposed before; but it is also contradictory that there should be something divisible by accident: for that to which it happens that it can be divided was of such a nature that division could happen to it; it was therefore divisible by nature. One may indeed say without contradiction that something is divided by accident, but not that it is divisible by accident. Therefore, what we conclude is this: since many things of the mind are conceived without space and divisibility, which could not be conceived thus unless their subject lacked that imaginary space, the most false axiom about the space of all beings falls to the ground.

units.la: VIII. Addemus & illud à consideratione existentiæ spatii desum-ptum. Quæro, an spatium, quale tribuunt Menti Increatæ & creatæ, sit merum nihil, an vero aliquid reale in se? Nihil esse dici non potest, cum sit extensum, divisibile, mensurabile, multis modis terminan-dum, & tale, ut de illo infinita demonstrari possint, atque etiam circa figuras in eo possibiles. Sane de nihilo non possunt talia affirmari quæ maxime sunt positiva. Adde quod, si spatium nihil esset, etiam non existeret, non esset: meliori enim jure dixeris, quod nihil est, neque est; quam, quod nusquam est, neque est. Mens igitur nulla in eo esset, eo quod id non daretur. Igitur esse aliquid fatendum est: de quo iterum quæro, an illud à Deo sit creatum? an vero existat à se, & independens sit, & initio carens? Certe posterius hoc afferet nemo qui Deum ut par est venerari conabitur: restat igitur prius, illud nimirum à Deo esse creatum. At, quod spatium occupabat Deus, mens æterna, antequam creatum ef-set ab illa spatium? Ubi erat? Itane erat nihil cum in spatio nondum existente & creato non erat, siquidem, quod nusquam est, neque est? Sed cum maxime fuerit, & nullibi fuerit, num quid præterea potuit creare, nempe mentes ponere, (res cum ipsius natura convenientes, saltem eatenus ut sint sine spatio) cum spatia nulla essent? Nonne nunc corpora spatiaque cuncta, servatis tamen mentibus, in nihilum redigere potest? Quod autem hic potentiæ divinæ medio utamur, id nil impedit quo-minus res distinguantur: si enim res una absque alia seorsim poni potest, à quacunque potentia id fiat, omnino ab illa diversa est, nec ullo nexu necessario cum ejus existentia nectitur. Et hactenus quidem contrarium axiomati prætenso, multa esse, omnes nempe mentes, quæ spatio non egeant, demonstratum est. Omnia vere perfecta, & realia in spatiis ponere, quærere, nec ultra spatiosa omnia scandere, quasi nil præterea esset, mentis est in materia demersæ, divinioris mundi multum nescia. Mirari interim subit quam circumspecte cudat vulgus axiomata, dum mentibus spatia tribuit, aufert vero tempus: cum contrarium, ubi de mentis statu in quo jam illa est, agitur, sit prorsus veritati congruum.
units.tr: VIII. We shall add also what is drawn from a consideration of the existence of space. I ask whether space, such as they attribute to the uncreated and created Mind, is mere nothing, or rather something real in itself. It cannot be said to be nothing, since it is extended, divisible, measurable, bounded in many ways, and such that infinite things can be demonstrated of it, and also concerning the figures possible in it. Certainly such most positive properties cannot be affirmed of nothing. Add that if space were nothing, it would also not exist and would not be: for one may more rightly say, what is nothing neither is, than, what is nowhere neither is. Therefore no mind would be in it, since it would not be given. So it must be granted that something is: about which again I ask, whether it was created by God, or whether it exists of itself, and is independent and without beginning? Certainly no one who tries to revere God as is fitting will assert the latter; the former therefore remains, namely that it was created by God. But what space did God, the eternal Mind, occupy before space was created by Him? Where was He? Was He then nothing, since He was not in a space not yet existing and created, if indeed what is nowhere neither is? But since He was most fully and yet nowhere, could He moreover create anything, namely, could He place minds (things agreeing with His own nature, at least so far as they may exist without space), when there were no spaces at all? Can He not now reduce to nothing all bodies and all spaces, the minds being preserved? But that we here use the means of the divine power does nothing to prevent things from being distinguished; for if one thing can be posited separately without another, by whatever power this is done, it is entirely distinct from that other and is not bound to its existence by any necessary connection. And so far indeed, against the supposed axiom that there are many things, namely all minds, which do not need space, has been demonstrated. But to seek all things that are perfect and real in spaces, and to climb no higher than spatial things, as if nothing else existed, is the mark of one sunk in matter and very ignorant of the more divine world. Meanwhile it is worth wondering how carelessly the common people coin axioms, when they assign spaces to minds but take away time; whereas the opposite, where the state in which the mind already is comes into question, is entirely consistent with the truth.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: I. Secundum Imaginationis in spiritualibus mixtæ fulcrum, scilicet obscura phrasis, quod Deus creaturis etiam corporeis sit præsens ratione essentiæ. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. Quid de ea exproprietate vocum sit sentiendum? exemptis scrupulis quatuor.
units.tr: I. The second prop of imagination in spiritual matters, namely the obscure phrase, that God is present to creatures, even corporeal ones, by reason of his essence. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. What is to be thought of this impropriety of words? Four scruples removed.

units.la: I. CUm axiomata cætera, quæ initio præcedentis capitis sunt propositá, huic, quod modo deductum est, innitantur, jam eo fulcro remoto, prostata videntur, & revera sunt. Quoniam tamen modis diversis, quique magis urgere & vigere putantur, sunt allata; cumque non videatur rationi congruum negare mentes corporibus, saltem quasdam quibusdam esse præsentes, unde idea spatii, quod à corpore est divulsum, iterum cum mente miscetur; utile fortassis erit, si sequentibus confusionem eam conemur evitare. Secundum proponebatur his similibusve verbis: Deum ubique esse præsentem, hoc est in omni spatio, non ratione operationis tantum, neque sola potentia, sed & ratione essentiæ suæ. Quam sententiam omnes quidem quoad verba videntur amplecti: hinc celebris apud omnes versiculus Enter præsenter Deus est & ubique potenter, at de sensu litigant. Qui saniori Philosophia sunt imbuti verbis illis sensum jungunt nobiliorem, & omni spatiosa præsentia superiorem. Cæteri essentiæ per omnia præsentiam nescio quam, quasi per diffusionem seu expansionem immensam, omnia permeantem, terram & cœlos replentem, & ultra sese diffundentem, imaginantur; voluntque Deum debere omni spatio extenso, locatoque, prius præsentem ratione essentiæ suæ concipi, quam ratione suæ operationis. Nos axioma illud obscurum & improprium esse putamus quoad verba; quoad sensum quem hi posteposteriores ei annectunt, ipsum falsum esse ostendetur. Nec est cur quis hic offendatur in limine, ac si à rebus tolleretur Dei præsentia: absit ut Dei præsentiam, qua omnibus adest, vel ejus verum modum, negemus. reputare debes aliud esse ipsam rei veritatem, aliud opiniones quas de illa ex præjudiciis foves, quasque ausit forte aliquis examinare, & recusare sine temeritate vel crimine. Interim, ne quis fervore Zeli, quasi Deus impeteretur, patiatur prius se abripi, quam lumine qualicunque affundi, ei assideat æstum hunc suis lacrymis temperaturus Augustinus, qui errorem communem, olimque suum, sic deplorat mox post ultima verba quæ in capite præcedenti sunt relata ({a}) Ita etiam Te, vita vitæ meæ (Deus) grandem per infinita spatia undique cogitabam penetrare totam mundi molem; & extra eam quaquaversum, per immensa sine termino, ut haberet te terra, haberet cœlum, haberent omnia, & illa finirentur in te, tu autem nusquam. Sicut autem luci solis non obsisteret corpus aëris hujus, qui supra terram est, quominus per eum trajiceretur, penetrans eum non dirumpendo, aut concidendo, sed implendo eum totum; sic tibi putabam non solum cœli, & aëris, & maris, sed etiam terræ corpus pervium, & ex omnibus maximis, minimisque partibus penetrabile, ad capiendam præsentiam tuam, occulta inspiratione intrinsecus & extrinsecus administrantem omnia quæ creasti. Ita suspicabar, quia cogitare aliud non poteram, nam falsum erat: illo enim modo major pars terræ majorem tui partem haberet, & minor minorem. Et interpositis paucis hæc diluens, addit: non autem es ita. Sed nondum illuminaveras tenebras meas.
units.tr: I. Although the other axioms set out at the beginning of the preceding chapter rest upon this one, which has just been deduced, once that prop is removed they seem to collapse, and indeed they do. Since, however, they have been advanced in various ways, and those which are thought to press and carry the most weight, and since it does not seem reasonable to deny that minds are present to bodies, at least some minds to some bodies, whence the idea of space, which has been torn away from body, is mixed again with the mind, it will perhaps be useful, in what follows, to try to avoid that confusion. The second axiom was put forward in these or similar words: God is present everywhere, that is, in every space, not merely by reason of operation, nor by power alone, but also by reason of his essence. All people seem indeed to embrace this statement as far as the words go; hence the well-known little verse, God is present by essence and powerful everywhere; but they dispute about the meaning. Those who are steeped in a sounder philosophy attach to those words a nobler sense, one superior to all spatial presence. Others imagine some presence of essence through all things, as it were a vast diffusion or expansion, permeating all things, filling earth and heavens, and spreading beyond itself; and they want God, in every extended and located space, to be conceived as present by reason of his essence before he is present by reason of his operation. We judge that axiom obscure and improper as to its words; as to the sense which these later writers attach to it, it will be shown to be false. Nor is there any reason for anyone to take offence at the threshold, as if the presence of God were being removed from things: far be it from us to deny the presence of God, by which he is present to all things, or its true mode. You ought to consider that one thing is the truth of the matter itself, and another the opinions which a person cherishes about it from prejudices, and which someone may dare to examine and reject without rashness or crime. Meanwhile, lest anyone, in a burst of zeal, as if God were being attacked, should first be carried away before being lit by any light at all, let Augustine sit beside him, to temper this heat with his tears, he who laments the common error, and once his own, just after the last words reported in the preceding chapter ({a}): Thus also, O Thou life of my life, I thought of Thee as penetrating through infinite spaces the whole vast mass of the world, and outside it on every side, through immeasurable regions without limit, so that earth should have Thee, heaven should have Thee, all things should have Thee, and they should be bounded in Thee, but Thou nowhere. And just as the body of this air, which is above the earth, does not hinder the light of the sun from passing through it, penetrating it not by breaking or cutting it but by filling it entirely, so I thought that Thy presence was not only in the body of heaven, air and sea, but even in the body of earth, permeable and penetrable through all its largest and smallest parts, to receive Thy presence, which by hidden inspiration governs from within and without all the things Thou hast created. So I supposed, because I could think of nothing else, for it was false: for in that way the greater part of the earth would have a greater part of Thee, and the lesser a lesser. And, after a few words interposed, refuting these things, he adds: But Thou art not so. But Thou hadst not yet enlightened my darkness.

units.la: Et alio in loco ({b}): Constituebam in conspectu spiritus mei universam creaturam, quicquid in ea cernere possumus, sicut est terra, & mare, & aër, & sydera, & arbores, & animalia mortalia, & quicquid in ea non videmus, sicut firmamentum cœli, insuper & omnes Angelos, & cuncta spiritualia ejus; sed etiam ipsa, quasi corpora essent, locis & locis ordinavit imaginatio mea: & feci unam massam grandem distinctam generibus corporum creaturam tuam, sive quæ revera corpus erant, sive quæ ipse pro spiritibus finxeram. Et eam feci grandem, non quantum erat, quod scire non poteram, sed quantum libuit, undique versum sane finitam. Te autem Domine, ex omni parte ambientem & penetrantem eam; sed usquequaque infinitum: tanquam si mare esset ubique & undique per immensum infinitum solum mare, & haberet infra se spongiam quamlibet magnam, sed finitam tamen; plena esset undique spongia illa ex omni sua parte ex immenso mari: Sic creaturam tuam finitam te infinito plenam putabam, & dicebam: Ecce Deus, & ecce quæ creavit, & bonus est Deus atque his validissime longissimeque præstantior; sed tamen bonus bona creavit, & ecce quomodo ambit atque implet ea. Paucisque de malo interjectis, de iis omnibus addit: addit: Talia vol vebam pectore misero, ingravidato curis mordacissimis de timo-re mortis: & non inventa veritate, &c. Similia sunt cogitata quibus vulgo Dei præsentiam sibi repræsentant, nisi quod dicant, Deum quoad essen-tiam esse totum in toto, & totum in qualibet parte spatii, mundi, cor-porum. At, quid hoc aliud est quam multiplicatio Dei, etsi unus es-sentia dicatur? Plane quemadmodum spatii, & materiæ, sive corporis essentia, quæ una est & numeratur, concipitur tamen tota in toto, & tota in qualibet parte spatii & materiæ sive corporis: ut etiam tota aquæ maris natura, quæ non nisi una est, concipiebatur ab Augustino in toto mari illo, & in tota spongia, eademque tota in singulis spongiæ parti-bus. Hanc sequelam negaverint licet, non libet tamen eos in quosque spatiorum suorum angulos insequi. Imaginationi in quæstione de præ-sentia Dei januam, quam nostrum secundum axioma refutandum pan-dit, claudere satis esto.
units.tr: And in another place ({b}): I set before the eyes of my spirit the whole creation, whatever we can see in it, such as earth, and sea, and air, and stars, and trees, and mortal animals, and whatever we do not see in it, such as the firmament of heaven, and moreover all the Angels and all their spiritual things; but my imagination arranged these, as though they were bodies, in places and locations; and I made one great mass of your creation, distinguished by kinds of bodies, whether those that really were bodies, or those which I had myself fashioned in place of spirits. And I made it large, not as large as it was, which I could not know, but as large as I pleased, certainly finite on every side. But you, O Lord, surrounding and penetrating it on every part, yet infinite on every side: as if there were a sea everywhere and on all sides through immeasurable infinite space, a sea alone, and it had within it some sponge, however large, yet finite; that sponge would be full on every part from the immense sea. Thus I thought of your finite creation as full of your infinite self, and I said: Behold God, and behold what he has created, and God is good and far more excellent than these most mightily and most greatly; yet, being good, he created good things, and behold how he surrounds and fills them. And, after interposing a few words about evil, he adds concerning all these things: I turned such thoughts over in my wretched heart, burdened with the most biting cares about the fear of death, and without having found the truth, etc. Similar are the thoughts by which the common people picture to themselves the presence of God, except that they say that God is wholly in the whole, in essence, and wholly in every part of space, of the world, of bodies. But what is this other than a multiplication of God, even though he is said to be one in essence? Just as the essence of space, or of matter, or of body, which is one and is counted as one, is nonetheless conceived as whole in the whole, and whole in every part of space and matter or body; just as the whole nature of sea water, which is only one, was conceived by Augustine as being in the whole of that sea, and in the whole sponge, and that same whole in each single part of the sponge. They may deny this consequence, but I do not care to pursue them into every corner of their spaces. It is enough to close the door to imagination in the question of God's presence, which our second axiom sets out to refute.

units.la: II. Patet ex demonstratis in capite præcedenti Deum fuisse cum nul-la essent spatia, & sic ejus essentiam nusquam fuisse præsentem nisi in se ipsa, absque omni spatio.
units.tr: II. It is clear from what was demonstrated in the preceding chapter that God existed when there were no spaces, and so his essence was nowhere present except in itself, apart from any space.

units.la: Igitur præsentia in spatio non est ipsi essentia-lis, seu, non est de ratione essentiæ ejus ut sit in spatio: Ergo in illo plane neque est, neque esse potest, quia nihil est nec esse potest in essentia Dei præter ipsam puram essentiam. Nil quoque de novo accidere potest Deo ratione essentiæ: nam quæ accidere Deo concipiuntur sunt tantum denominationes ab operationibus externis, sive iis quæ non sunt in essen-tia sua. Itaque extra respectum ad operationes, (quod quis hoc sensu di-xerit, non nisi operative,) Deus quibusdam à se diversis præsens non potest dici: neque id (esse præsentem) dicendum est Deo proprie ratio-ne suæ essentiæ accidere, sive eum, qui priusratione suæ essentiæ nulli rei à se diversæ (cum esset nulla) erat præsens, omni rei demum factum esse præsentem essentiæ suæ ratione. Quod erat demonstrandum.
units.tr: Therefore presence in space is not essential to him; that is, it does not belong to the nature of his essence that he should be in space. Hence he is plainly not in it, and cannot be, because nothing is or can be in the essence of God except the pure essence itself. Nor can anything new happen to God by reason of his essence. For what are conceived as accidents in God are only denominations taken from external operations, that is, from those things which are not in his essence. Thus, apart from his relation to operations (which one might call "present" only in an operative sense), God cannot be said to be present to certain things distinct from himself. Nor is it to be said that being present is an accident of God by reason of his essence, so that he who previously, by reason of his essence, was present to no thing distinct from himself (since there was none), has finally come to be present to every thing by reason of his essence. This was to be demonstrated.

units.la: III. Sed quoniam ex alienæ sententiæ confutatione, non idcirco affulget lux ad conceptum veritatis oppositæ, tota res hic paucis est ex-ponenda. Notandum igitur, primo, Utrinque subesse fundamentum omnium consensu solidum, nempe, Deum, cum creaverit omnia quæ in universo sunt spatia, & quæ eis continentur, cumque cuncta conser-vet, regat, gubernet, eis omnibus maxime adesse. Hoc ratum est. Sed ne huic stramineum quid superædificetur, notandum est, secundo, quid vocibus, præsentia, ubi, essentia, possit designari. 1. Potest aliquis adesse alicui rei ea tantum ratione ut hæc sit effectus & operatio externa illius, qui tunc præsens esse operative dicetur: & hoc in moralibus sæpe occur-rit rit cum quibus divina maxime congruunt. Quod si quis ita rei adsit, ut hæc sit objectum ejus cogitationis, intelligentiæ voluntatisque, vel ipse etiam ab illa re noscatur, consideretur, aut ei aliquo simili modo resera-tur, dicetur ille esse rei præsens objective, sed distinctionis ergo, ille acti-ve, quatenus scilicet is de re illa cogitat, res vero quæ vicissim præsens, aut etiam ille ipse quatenus ab ista re cogitatur, vel alio aliquo modo repræsentatur, passive. Denique potest aliquid ita dici præsens cuidam rei, ut non habeatur respectus ad præcedentia, sed ut concipiatur nexus ejus cum re cui præsens dicitur, & quasi immeatio in illam. hoc ultimum præsentiam subjectivam vocare licet, cui præcipue attenditur in quæ-stione, ubi res est? 2. Sed & illud ubi quæri potest respectu subjecti simpliciter, absque connotatione spatii, ut si quæratur, ubi est negatio, vel dissensus? & respondeatur, in voluntate; vel respectu subjecti spatium connotantis, quod idem erit ac si quæreretur, in quo spatio res est? 3. De essentia autem, hic sufficiet notare, rei essentiam, rei attributa essentialia omnia, omnes perfectiones essentiales, naturam rei, unum & idem esse. Quæ omnia si quis bene complicet, quid de cu-jusque rei præsentia, sive illa res sit corpus, sive mens, ejusve operatio interna aut externa, (de his enim omnibus quæri potest, ubi sint?) fa-cile poterit determinare, modo secundum distincta hanc quæstionem, ubi res sit, qualibet de re variare tentet. quod uno aut altero exemplo, quatenus ad scopum hunc utile est, declarabitur.
units.tr: III. But since light does not shine on the concept of the opposite truth merely from the refutation of another's opinion, the whole matter must here be set out briefly. It should be noted, then, first, that both sides rest on a foundation that all agree is solid: namely, that God, having created all the spaces that are in the universe and the things contained in them, and preserving, ruling and governing all of them, is most of all present to all of them. This is settled. But so that nothing straw-like be built upon this, it should be noted, second, what the words presence, where, essence may signify.
