(1) One may be present to a thing merely in the sense that the thing is an effect and external operation of that person, who in that case is said to be present operatively; this often occurs in moral matters, with which divine things agree most closely. If someone is present to a thing in such a way that the thing is the object of his thought, understanding and will, or he himself is known or considered by that thing, or is represented to it in some similar way, he is said to be present to the thing objectively; but, for the sake of distinction, he is said to be present actively, insofar as he thinks of that thing, while the thing, in turn, is present passively, or the person himself, insofar as he is thought of by that thing or represented in some other way. Finally, something may be said to be present to a thing in such a way that no reference is made to what precedes, but its connection with the thing to which it is said to be present is conceived, as it were an immanence in it. This last we may call subjective presence, and it is chiefly this that is in view in the question: where is the thing? (2) But the word where may also be asked with respect to the subject simply, without any connotation of space, as when one asks: where is denial or dissent? and the answer is: in the will. Or with respect to a subject connoting space, which would be the same as asking: in what space is the thing? (3) As for essence, here it will suffice to note that the essence of a thing, all its essential attributes, all its essential perfections, and its nature are one and the same. If anyone carefully folds these together, he will easily be able to determine what is to be said of the presence of any thing, whether that thing is a body or a mind, or whether it is its internal or external operation (for of all these one may ask where they are), provided he keeps distinct the question where the thing is and tries to vary it for any thing whatever. This will be illustrated by one or another example, insofar as it is useful for this purpose.

units.la: IV. De corporibus non est quod dicamus, cum ea, fatentibus omnibus sint in spatio, id est, secundum rei veritatem, in se ipsis: spatium enim est ipsamet corporis essentia, ut bene demonstravit Carte-sius in Principiorum Philosophiæ Parte secunda: siquidem demptis ab omni corpore eis quæ ipsi accidentalia sunt, sola remanet idea spatii, quæ proinde sola ei essentialis est. Quæ cum ita sint, videntur illi qui quærunt, An Mens sive spiritus sit in spatio, idem velle quasi peterent, an mentis essentia sit in corporis essentia, sive, an perfectiones mentis essentiales, ejusque attributa, sint in natura, inque attributis essentialibus corporum? an hæc sint illorum subjectum? Quod sua absurditate sese conficit. Igitur, ut ad res spirituales, & quæ Deum concernunt, accedamus, ubi difficultates non parvæ ob præjudicia & phantasmata corporea, si quis quærat, ubi sit Deus? Et in hac quæ-stione respiciat ad spatium, ac si quæreret, in quo spatio sit Deus, ejus-ve essentia? an in omni, vel solum in aliquo? quæstio perab-surda est, ut ex hoc & præcedenti capite visum. Cum idem sit ac si quæreretur, cui spatio jungatur vel insit essentia, seu natura, seu omnes perfectiones & attributa Dei ? vel an Spatium nectatur cum essentia, attributisve divinis ? quod demum idem est ac, an Spatium sit ipsa Divina essentia ? Absurde quaeritur de subjecto quaestionis, ut scholastice dicam, praedicatum toto genere diversum. perinde quaeras de Mente, in qua sit figura, vel in quo sapore ? Si vero quaestio, ubi sit Deus ratione essentiae, vel ubi sit ejus essentia ? habeat respectum simpliciter ad subjectum, sive ad illud in quo sit ipsa essentia, responderi debet eam esse in Deo solo : quod & de omnibus ejus attributis, utpote ab ejus essentia non distinctis, & de operationibus ejusdem internis, asserendum est. Hoc sensu nulli in toto universo creaturae praesens est, sed sibi ipsi Soli, Filio, Spirituique aeterno. Profecto si Deus ratione essentiae suae, quae omnes ejus divinas perfectiones, internasque operationes complectitur, ulli creaturae praesens esset, sive spirituali, sive corporeae, caperetur Deus a creatura, haecque possideret & in se haberet omne id quod Deus in sua essentia possidet, esset enim essentia Dei in illa. Neque locum hic habet distinctio de adaequato & inadaequato, quippe quae cogitationis creatae conceptui, non autem ipsi Divinae essentiae applicari potest. Ergo abeant dicta de praesentia Dei ratione essentiae totius in toto mundo, & totius in qualibet parte, & similes perabsurdae voces de illo, quem sensu allato, nec ulla creatura, nec omnes simul, nec coeli coelorum, capiunt. Credibile est homines, si quid Deus sit recte nossent, non ausuros, ne Deum dedecore afficerent, talia proponere : at illi in cognoscendo Numine Summo ita sunt securi & supini, ut eis nosse suffecerit ipsum esse id, (ut cum Philosopho loquar) qui Latine Deus Gallice Dieu dicitur, & ab hominibus colitur : nil multum curantes, an quae ejus Summam deceant Majestatem ipsi attribuantur ?
units.tr: IV. Concerning bodies there is nothing we need say, since, as all admit, they are in space, that is, according to the truth of the matter, in themselves; for space is itself the essence of body, as Descartes well demonstrated in the second part of his Principles of Philosophy. For when everything accidental to body is removed, the idea of space alone remains, and this alone is therefore essential to it. Since these things are so, those who ask whether mind or spirit is in space seem to want to ask whether the essence of mind is in the essence of body, or whether the essential perfections of mind and its attributes are in the nature and essential attributes of bodies, or whether these are its subject. This refutes itself by its own absurdity. So, to come to spiritual things and those which concern God, where difficulties are not small because of prejudices and bodily phantasms: if someone asks, where is God? and in this question looks to space, as if he were asking in what space God or his essence is, whether in every space or only in some? The question is absurdly put, as has been seen from this and the preceding chapter. It is the same as asking to which space the essence or nature, or all the perfections and attributes of God, are joined or inhere; or whether space is bound up with the essence or divine attributes; which in the end is the same as asking whether space is the divine essence itself. The question is absurd about the subject of the question, as the Schoolmen would say: a predicate wholly of a different kind. It is like asking of a mind what shape it has, or what flavour. But if the question where is God by reason of his essence, or where his essence is, is taken simply with respect to the subject, that is, to that in which the essence itself is, it must be answered that it is in God alone; and this must be asserted of all his attributes, as not distinct from his essence, and of his internal operations. In this sense he is present to no creature in the whole universe, but to himself alone, the Son, and the eternal Spirit. Indeed, if God by reason of his essence, which embraces all his divine perfections and internal operations, were present to any creature, whether spiritual or corporeal, God would be contained by the creature, and that creature would possess and have within itself everything that God possesses in his essence; for the essence of God would then be in it. Nor does the distinction between adequate and inadequate have any place here, since it can be applied to the created concept of thought, not to the divine essence itself. Therefore let there be done with the statements about the presence of God by reason of his essence, as a whole in the whole world, and as a whole in every part, and similar utterly absurd expressions about him whom, in the sense set out, no creature, nor all together, nor the heaven of heavens, can contain. It is credible that men, if they rightly knew what God is, would not dare to put forward such things, lest they bring dishonour upon God; but they are so careless and remiss in knowing the Supreme Deity that it is enough for them to know that he is the being (to speak with the Philosopher) which in Latin is called Deus, in French Dieu, and is worshipped by men; caring little whether the things attributed to him are fitting for his supreme Majesty.

units.la: V. Sin quaestio, Ubi Deus sit praesens ? intelligatur ita, quasi quaeretur ; Quanquam Deus ex ratione essentiae sive suorum attributorum nullibi sit nisi in se, ejusque natura & essentia, qua talis, non requirat ut ullum aliud ens vel ubi existat, imo non necessario objectum a se aliud contempletur, velit, operetur ; quaero tamen, an placuerit ipsi ex liberrima voluntate de aliis cogitare, alia velle, & ponere, & ipse ab illis cogitari & repraesentari ? (quod ad operationem ejus reducitur, cum & hoc ultimum efficiat.) Quaestioni huic, quae rationi valde consentanea est, & quaerit Dei praesentiam objective, utroque modo, activo & passivo, perspicue responderi potest ex consideratione rerum quas posuit existentes : Idem enim est, ac si, seposita Dei essentia, & operationibus ejus quæ internæ vocantur, de externis quæreretur, an den-tur tales à Deo placitæ, cognitæ, productæ, sustentatæ, gubernatæ, quibus Deus repræsentetur? & an illæ sint in spatio? Quibus nemo non videt respondendum esse, omnino tales dari, easque Deum tanquam imagine referre; verum quasdam ex iis plane carere spatiis, ut mentes, quasdam autem, ut corpora omnia, à spatiis non sejungi. Atque hoc modo Deus præsens est creaturis, nempe ratione liberrimæ operationis, & repræsentationis, quæ & ipsa Dei opus est, simul cum omnibus quæ existunt. Neque requirit aliam sui præsentiam ipse Deus, vel ejus opera; Non Deus, sive ejus essentia & operationes internæ, ut visum supra; non Dei opera, sufficerit enim ipsis si ea voluerit Deus, si ab illo sint cognita, si producta, si gubernata, si vel in partium sua-rum extensione aut motu, vel in cogitationis natura aut variatione re-ferant quamoptime fieri datur, divinas ejus perfectiones. Istis autem magis aut minus præsens dicitur Deus, prout ibidem plura vel pauciora producit, quæ plus minusve divinas ejus perfectiones tanquam in tabula vel imagine, depingunt: ita corporibus minus est præsens quam men-tibus: etsi enim in illis numerus partium, qui definiri nequit, & mo-tuum regimen varium, quod à constantissimis regulis non discedit, alia-que, luculentæ satis sint imagines infinitarum Dei perfectionum, ejus-que constantiæ; cum tamen non constet ullum materiale de novo crea-ri, nec in primariis materiæ modis augeri, (nam motus, à quo omnis diversitas, non augetur in universo, nec incipit aliquod corpus ex oc-casione alterius moveri, quin hoc tantundem perdat motus) videtur sic Deus præsens esse seque communicare corporibus modo determina-to, cum mensura, absque novæ operationis novo additamento: Non ita mentibus, quæ ejus operatione indies novæ creantur, quarum mo-di & perfectiones ita augentur eo operante, ut si ex occasione scientiæ vel cæterarum dotum unius scientiam aliasque perfectiones altera ac-quirat, non tamen idcirco de doctrina sua suisque donis quicquam de-perdat prior: quæ certe major potentiæ & bonitatis divinæ imago est & effectus, adeoque præsentia: Sed ejus gradus summus elucet in men-tibus perspicacibus, sanctis, pacificis, tranquillis, quales beatæ cre-duntur; nec majus de illis dicit sacra pagina cum earum prærogativas summas recenset, quam quod Dei imago, non essentialis, quæ ipse Deus est, sed producta, creata, renovata, in illis sit operante Deo: dicit vero nunquam in illis esse Dei essentiam, seu quod idem est, ipsum Deum ratione suæ essentiæ. Scio quosdam sanctos viros, rerumque dividivinarum expertos, interdum dicere, debere hominem eousque devenire ut sit in Deo, inque divina essentia: At hisce formulis nil aliud designant, quam non debere hominem ullis Dei operationibus particularibus adhærere, verum tum se Deo operanti indeterminate subjicere, tum operationem Dei immediatam, intimam, & plenariam experiri. prout quoque cum ab iisdem dicitur, quod divina essentia sit rerum omnium essentia, nil aliud denotatur, nisi quod omnis rerum realitas sit à Deo qui est essentia sufficientissima, & causa omnium. Quæ omnia ad operationes Dei, earumve modos spectantia, à dictis non discedunt, sed eis potius illustrantur. Deus itaque creaturis adest, cœlum terramque replet, quatenus cœlum, terra, & omnia, replentur operibus voluntatis, sapientiæ, potentiæ, bonitatis, sanctitatis, gaudii, felicitatis, aliarumque divinarum perfectionum. Opera ejus ipsæ sunt creaturæ diversimode Dei præsentia fruentes, pro diversa operationis & repræsentationis divinæ mensura. Quod si in creaturis detur quid quod à Deo non sit productum, neque eum referat, id non est aliquid, sed nihil, vel malum sive peccatum, à quo Deus longissime abesse dicitur, quia cum ejus præsentia sit externa operatio, id ejus operatio nequaquam est.
units.tr: V. But if the question "Where is God present?" is understood as though it were asked in this way: although God, by the nature of his essence or of his attributes, is nowhere except in himself, and his nature and essence, as such, do not require that any other being exist somewhere, indeed he does not necessarily contemplate, will, or work on any object other than himself; nevertheless I ask whether it has pleased him, by his most free will, to think of other things, to will and to establish them, and to be thought of and represented by them (which is reduced to his operation, since this last also effects it). This question, which is very consonant with reason and asks about God's presence objectively, in both ways, active and passive, can clearly be answered from a consideration of the things he has posited as existing. For it is the same as if, setting aside God's essence and his so-called internal operations, one asked about the external ones: whether there are such things, pleased, known, produced, sustained and governed by God, by which God is represented, and whether these are in space. To these questions everyone sees that the answer must be that such things certainly exist, and that they refer to God as to an image; but that some of them plainly lack space, such as minds, while others, such as all bodies, are not separated from space. And in this way God is present to creatures, namely by reason of his most free operation and representation, which is itself God's work, together with all things that exist. Nor does God himself, or his works, require any other presence of himself: not God, or his essence and internal operations, as was seen above; nor God's works, for it is enough for them that God has willed them, that they are known by him, produced, and governed, and that they refer God's divine perfections as well as possible, whether in the extension or motion of their parts, or in the nature or variation of thought. God is said to be more or less present to these, according as he produces more or fewer things in them which depict more or less his divine perfections, as in a tablet or image. Thus God is less present to bodies than to minds: for although in bodies the number of parts, which cannot be defined, and the varied governance of motions, which does not depart from most constant rules, and other things, are sufficiently clear images of God's infinite perfections and of his constancy; yet since it is not established that any matter is newly created, nor that it increases in its primary modes (for motion, from which all diversity comes, does not increase in the universe, nor does one body begin to be moved on the occasion of another without that body losing just as much motion), it seems that God is present to bodies and communicates himself to them in a determined mode, with measure, without any new addition of new operation. It is not so with minds, which are newly created daily by his operation, and whose modes and perfections are so increased by his working that, if on the occasion of knowledge or other gifts one acquires knowledge and other perfections, the former nevertheless does not on that account lose anything of his learning or of his gifts. This is certainly a greater image and effect of divine power and goodness, and so of presence. But its highest degree shines forth in minds that are perceptive, holy, peaceful and tranquil, such as are believed to be the blessed; nor does Sacred Scripture say anything greater of them when it recounts their supreme prerogatives, than that the image of God, not essential (which is God himself), but produced, created and renewed, is in them by God's working; but it never says that God's essence is in them, or what is the same, God himself by reason of his essence. I know that certain holy men, experienced in divine things, sometimes say that a man ought to attain to such a point that he is in God, and in the divine essence. But by these formulas they mean nothing other than that a man ought not to cling to any particular operations of God, but rather to submit himself to God working indeterminately, and to experience God's operation as immediate, intimate and full. In the same way, when they say that the divine essence is the essence of all things, nothing else is signified than that all the reality of things is from God, who is the most sufficient essence and the cause of all. All these things, which concern God's operations or their modes, do not depart from what has been said, but are rather illustrated by it. Thus God is present to creatures, fills heaven and earth, in so far as heaven, earth and all things are filled with the works of his will, wisdom, power, goodness, holiness, joy, happiness and other divine perfections. His works are themselves creatures enjoying the presence of God in various ways, according to the diverse measure of divine operation and representation. But if there is in creatures anything which was not produced by God, and does not refer to him, that is not something, but nothing, or evil or sin, from which God is said to be far away, because since his presence is an external operation, that thing is by no means his operation.

units.la: V I. Supersunt adhuc nonnullæ difficultates particulares, quas auferre æquum est conari, cum etiam viris qui magni habentur, importunæ fuerint, & quarundam causa vocibus maxime impropriis & deceptricibus hi sint usi. Ipse Cartesius {a} cum nollet admittere, Deum esse ubique ac si ejus essentia ubique existeret, diceretque eum ratione potentiæ suæ ubique esse, non autem ratione essentiæ; cum videret Dei potentiam & ejus essentiam esse unum & idem, primo satius esse putavit in talibus de mente creata quam de Deo ratiocinari: sed cum urgeret opponens Deum non posse esse ubique ratione potentiæ, quin ibidem sit ratione essentiæ, eo quod potentia Dei non sit extra Deum sita, sive extra Dei essentiam, neque ab eadem essentia distinguatur; Respondit, concedendo Dei essentiam debere ubique præsentem esse ut ejus potentia ibi se exercere posset, sed non per modum rei extensæ. Hunc loquendi modum sequitur & excedit Forgeus in suo de Mente sive Spiritu hominis tractatu, asserens, {b} Deum rebus omnibus esse præsentem omnipotentia, essentia, & subsistantia sua; imo omnes creaturas respondere certæ cuidam parti immensitatis divinæ, in qua omnes includuntur. quæ quamvis sano sensu explicet, quis tamen non videt ea verba aliquid obscuri secum in mentem invehere, quod eam ad spatium imaginandum disponat ? Alius Author Clarissimus (²) utens itidem (quamquam sensu sano) vocibus impropriis, quæ aliud ex instituto communi significant, adeoque obscuritatem conceptuum fovent, dicit quoque Deum præsentem esse omnibus, essentia, essentialiter, ratione essentiæ, id omnes quos vocant Cartesianos, asserere, nec posse contrarium evinci vel ex Cartesio, vel ex eorum scriptis qui recte ipsum Philosophantem sequuntur. Ego equidem conor ipsum recte Philosophantem sequi, verum id non impedit quominus credam verbis illis, Deum esse creaturis præsentem essentia, vel ratione essentiæ, si ex usu ordinario interpretentur ea, non significari verum; & quamvis veritatem eis substituant, id non fit ex usu verborum communi, sed à dispositione mentis ipsi verborum significationi, quam ordinarie obtinere deberent, reluctantis. Satis patet ex eis quæ supra, numeris 2. & 4. voces illas non esse proprie verum significantes: sed & hoc magis videbitur si advertamus verba illa, essentia, ratione essentiæ, ex usu omnium non adhiberi, nisi ad significandum aliquid quod rei internum est, naturale, proprium, ab illa inseparabile, & cum ea, ut ita loquar, identificatum: ubi vero est quæstio de externis relationibus, vel de modis, qui rei essentiam non constituunt, neminem illis uti solere. Exempli causa, nemo dicit corpus esse quadratum vel sensibile essentia, sive ratione essentiæ, neque ea essentia dicitur quadrata, sensata, sed extensa, corpus extensum ratione essentiæ, dicitur tamen ipsum corpus esse quadratum, & sensum sive sensu perceptum, quia illa vox, corpus, talis est, ut in usu communi non excludat respectum ad particulares modos & accidentia, cum vox essentia eum plane excludat: Sic, ubi de divinis, quamvis Deus & essentia Dei sint unum & idem, attamen cum volumus exprimere conceptum ubi Deus involvitur non tanquam rei prædicandæ subjectum in quo sit illa res, sed tanquam efficiens, operans, disponens, cui nova relatio externa accedat, non permittit usus ut voce essentiæ utamur, nec dicimus Deum ratione essentiæ esse Creatorem, esse locutum, incarnatum, passum, mortuum, &c. ut ut illis magis adfuerit quam ullis aliis creaturis: de Deo talia dicimus, quia sub illa voce inclusit usus etiam respectum ad externa, non autem sub voce essentia, quo verbo expresse omnes voluere exclusa quæcunque cum ipso Deo non sunt unum & idem ens ejusdem naturæ. Ergo non exacte dicitur Deus ulli rei præterquam sibi, ratione essentiæ præsens. At, quid argumento supra allato respondendum est, Cum Deus potentia sua creatoris sit præsens, sequi & proprie essentia, quæ ipsa potentia est, præpræsentem eis esse dicendum? Negandum est exacte dici Deum esse creatis præsentem ratione essentialis potentiæ, sive, quod idem est, essentialem Dei potentiam in creaturis esse, eo sensu & iisdem de causis quibus id supra, numeris 2. 3. 4. est negatum. Potentiam divinam concipimus quidem producere aliquid, non autem ipsam esse in re producta, sed ejus effectum. Adest Deus, sed effectu & operatione potentiæ illius quæ in ipso solo est, & cujus nomen si ipsis operationibus detur, ad rhetoricum tropum satius est recurrere, quam concludere, præsentiam operationis, quæ est in creatura esse ipsam Dei potentiam, imo essentiam & naturam, cum ejus perfectionibus cunctis, quippe quæ tantum sit aliquarum satis imperfecta tabula simul & effectus. Neque aliter est statuendum, nisi libeat creaturam pro Creatore amplecti, & huic elogium illud sacrum denegare, quod inhabitet lucem inaccessam. Imo, quod verbo sit dictum, quæcunque de pluribus modis præsentiæ divinæ dicuntur, ea in operationem ejus debent resolvi, ut cum sapientia, providentia, cura, consilio suo cunctis præsens affirmatur, non hisce asseritur, sapientiam, providentiam, curam & consilia Dei esse in creaturis: in solo Deo æterno sunt, in creatis vero operationes hoc vel illo tempore, his aut illis circumstantiis circumcinctæ, prout Deo placitum est; & hæc ipsa operationum, rerumve positio præsentia Dei illa est quæ per concursum fieri dicitur.
units.tr: VI. There remain some particular difficulties, which it is fitting to try to remove, since they have troubled even men who are held in great esteem, and some of them have used words that are most improper and deceptive in explaining these matters. Descartes himself, when he did not want to admit that God is everywhere as if his essence existed everywhere, and said that he is everywhere by reason of his power and not by reason of his essence; since he saw that God's power and his essence are one and the same, first thought it better in such matters to reason about a created mind than about God. But when an objector pressed that God cannot be everywhere by reason of his power without being there also by reason of his essence, since the power of God is not located outside God, or outside God's essence, nor is it distinguished from that same essence, he replied by conceding that God's essence must be present everywhere so that his power could exercise itself there, but not in the manner of an extended thing. Forgeus follows and goes beyond this manner of speaking in his treatise on the mind or spirit of man, asserting that God is present to all things by his omnipotence, essence and subsistence; indeed, that all creatures correspond to a certain part of the divine immensity, in which all are included. Although he explains this in a sound sense, who does not see that these words bring into the mind something obscure, which disposes it to imagine space? Another most distinguished author, using likewise (though in a sound sense) improper words, which in common usage signify something else, and so foster obscurity of concepts, also says that God is present to all things by essence, essentially, by reason of his essence; and he asserts that all whom they call Cartesians hold this, nor can the contrary be proved either from Descartes or from those who rightly follow him as a philosopher. I for my part try to follow him rightly as a philosopher; but this does not prevent me from believing that those words, that God is present to creatures by essence or by reason of essence, if they are interpreted according to ordinary usage, do not signify the truth; and although they may substitute the truth for them, this is not from the common usage of the words, but from a disposition of mind resisting the meaning which the words ought ordinarily to have. It is sufficiently clear from what was said above, in sections 2 and 4, that those expressions do not properly signify the truth. This will appear still more if we notice that the words "essence" and "by reason of essence" are, in everyone's usage, employed only to signify something which is internal to a thing, natural, proper to it, inseparable from it, and, so to speak, identified with it; but where the question concerns external relations, or modes which do not constitute the essence of a thing, no one is accustomed to use them. For example, no one says that a body is square or sensible by essence, or by reason of essence; nor is that essence called square or sensed, but extended; a body is extended by reason of its essence; yet the body itself is said to be square, and sensed or perceived by sense, because the word "body" is such that in common usage it does not exclude reference to particular modes and accidents, whereas the word "essence" plainly excludes such reference. So, in speaking of divine things, although God and the essence of God are one and the same, yet when we wish to express a concept in which God is involved, not as the subject of a predicate in which that thing is, but as an efficient cause, operating, disposing, to whom a new external relation is added, usage does not allow us to use the word "essence"; nor do we say that God is by reason of his essence the Creator, has spoken, has become incarnate, has suffered, has died, etc., although he was more present to these things than to any other creatures. We say such things of God, because under that word usage also includes reference to external things; but not under the word "essence", which everyone has expressly wished to exclude from whatever is not one and the same being of the same nature as God himself. Therefore it is not strictly said that God is present to any thing other than himself by reason of his essence. But what must be answered to the argument brought forward above, namely: since God is present to his creatures by his creative power, it follows that, properly speaking, he must be said to be present to them by his essence, which is that very power? It must be denied that God is strictly said to be present to creatures by reason of an essential power, or, what is the same, that the essential power of God is in creatures, in the sense and for the same reasons for which this was denied above in sections 2, 3 and 4. We indeed conceive that the divine power produces something, but that it is not itself in the thing produced, but its effect. God is present, but by the effect and operation of that power which is in him alone; and if the name of that power is given to its operations themselves, it is better to have recourse to a rhetorical trope than to conclude that the presence of the operation which is in the creature is the very power of God, indeed his essence and nature with all his perfections, since it would be merely a sufficiently imperfect tablet and effect of some of them. Nor is it to be determined otherwise, unless one is willing to embrace the creature in place of the Creator, and to deny to him that sacred description, that he dwells in unapproachable light. Indeed, to put it in a word, whatever is said of several modes of the divine presence must be resolved into his operation; so that when he is affirmed to be present to all things by wisdom, providence, care, counsel, this does not assert that the wisdom, providence, care and counsel of God are in creatures: they are in God alone, eternally; but in creatures they are operations at this or that time, surrounded by these or those circumstances, as it has pleased God; and this very positioning of operations and things is that presence of God which is said to take place through concurrence.

units.la: VII. Accedit alia difficultas ex eo quod non videatur rationi consentaneum asserere Deum, ejusve potentiam, ibi operari ubi non est. Deus, inquiunt, operatur præsens aut absens: non absens, est igitur præsens ratione essentiæ in illo ubi in quo operatur. Quid vero hoc est? An illud, Dei essentia, Dei potentia, debet esse in illo subjecto ubi est ejus operatio? Sive, Deus non potest operari in illa re ubi vel in qua non est Dei natura vel quæ non habet Dei essentiam? sive, Non datur operatio Dei externa, nisi in Dei natura & essentia? (nam hæc omnia eodem recidunt). An hic sensus verborum, Deus, ejusve potentia non potest operari ubi non est? Hæc omnia non vera sunt apertissime. Quid illud, Deus non operatur absens, sed præsens? Voluntne Dei naturam & perfectiones esse præsentes in illa re ubi operatio ejus externa est? næ, quantum fallerentur! Contrarium verum est: nam quæ res est operatio, seu subjectum operationis Dei externæ, illa non habet in se essentiam & naturam divinam. Instas, ubi quis operatur ibi præsens est, non enim datur actio in distans, absurdum est aliquem alicubi operari seu esse operantem, nec tamen ibi esse (quoad essentiam scilicet, alias nil objicitur.) Resp. ut quis se his extricet, examinet tantum voces secundum superius distincta. Ecquid illud ubi? An hoc: In quo sub-jecto vel spatio aliquis operatur, in illo subjecto vel spatio est ejus natu-ra? Hoc dici non potest, nequidem de corporibus, quae in alia agunt ea externe tangendo, non vero eorum spatium penetrando, & de his solis, ob contactum, dictum est, non dari operationem in distans: Sed de Mentibus res plane se habet aliter. Ratiocinatio sic procedit: In qua re, sive illa sit extensa, sive non sit in spatio, quis (si is sit Deus) operatur, in illa est ejus operatio, imo est illa objectum ejus cognitio-nis, voluntatis, potentiae, & ab hujus efficacia omnia quae in re illa sunt omnino dependent: bene. Cavendum est ab hoc sophismate: Qui in ubi operatur sive est operans, utique est in ubi: nam operan-tem esse dicit esse, igitur in ubi operantem esse dicit in ubi esse. Resp. Operantem esse non infert primo esse in ubi, deinde agere in illo: Sed, de Deo qui operans est, dicit, primo aliquid velle, & secundo, poni aliquid extra illum, vel extra ejus essentiam. Clarius. esse operan-tem non significat nexum (seu praesentiam) essentiae operantis cum opere aut cum ejus natura, sed nexum positionis voluntatis in operante potente, cum positione operis extra illum. quo sensu abest ut extenue-tur praesentia Dei, quin contra, patet inde Deum esse magis praesen-tem creaturae, quam creatura sibi ipsi, cum creatura non sit ob se ipsam, sive quia est, non habeat secum nexum necessarium; sed ideo sit, quia voluntas ut sit in Deo est, habeatque in omnibus nexum ita necessarium cum voluntate Dei efficaci, ut hac posita illa demum adsit. Sed haec ad Dominium & potentiam Dei, de quibus suo loco, sunt referenda. Nullae in his difficultatibus, etsi alia objici possint, re-manent, modo omnia in simplicissima verba resolvantur. Est interim cur quis miretur, quod non potius omnes creaturas dixerint esse in Deo ratione essentiae suae spectato, aut esse in essentia divina, quod magis cum idea imaginaria immensitatis extensae conveniret; quam Deum ratione essentiae suae in illis esse: quod imperfectius quid vide-tur inferre.
units.tr: VII. A further difficulty arises from the fact that it does not seem reasonable to assert that God, or his power, operates where he is not. God, they say, operates either present or absent; he is not absent, therefore he is present by reason of his essence in that place where he operates. But what does this mean? Does it mean that the essence of God, the power of God, must be in that subject where his operation is? Or does it mean that God cannot operate in that thing where or in which the nature of God is not, or which does not have the essence of God? Or that there is no external operation of God unless in the nature and essence of God? (For all these amount to the same thing.) Or is this the sense of the words: God, or his power, cannot operate where he is not? None of these is plainly true. What of the statement: God does not operate absent but present? Do they want the nature and perfections of God to be present in that thing where his external operation is? No indeed, how greatly they would be mistaken! The opposite is true: for the thing which is the operation, or the subject of God's external operation, does not have in itself the divine essence and nature. You insist: wherever someone operates, there he is present, for there is no action at a distance; it is absurd for someone to operate somewhere, or to be operating there, and yet not be there (as to essence, of course; otherwise nothing is objected). I answer: so that one may extricate oneself from these matters, one need only examine the words according to the distinctions drawn above. What then of the word "where"? Does it mean this: in what subject or space someone operates, in that subject or space is his nature? This cannot be said, not even of bodies, which act on others by touching them externally, not by penetrating their space; and only of these, on account of contact, has it been said that there is no operation at a distance. But with minds the matter is plainly otherwise. The reasoning proceeds thus: in whatever thing, whether it is extended or is not in space, someone (if that someone is God) operates, in that thing is his operation; indeed that thing is the object of his knowledge, will and power, and all the things that are in that thing depend entirely on his efficacy: good. We must beware of this sophism: whoever operates in a where, or is an operator, is certainly in a where; for to say "operating" is to say "being," therefore to say "operating in a where" is to say "being in a where." I answer: to be operating does not imply, first, being in a where, and then acting in it; but of God, who is operating, it is said that first he wills something, and second, that something is placed outside him, or outside his essence. More clearly: "being operating" does not signify a connection (or presence) of the operating essence with the work or with its nature, but a connection of the positing of the will in the powerful operator with the positing of the work outside him. In this sense, far from the presence of God being diminished, it is clear from this that God is more present to the creature than the creature is to itself, since the creature is not on account of itself, that is, because it is, it does not have within itself a necessary connection; rather it is because the will, insofar as it is in God, has a connection with the efficacious will of God in all things so necessary that, this being posited, the creature is then present. But these matters are to be referred to the dominion and power of God, of which in its place. No difficulties remain in these matters, though other objections can be raised, provided that everything is resolved into the simplest words. Meanwhile there is reason for someone to wonder why they have not rather said that all creatures are in God with respect to his essence, or are in the divine essence, which would agree better with the imaginary idea of an extended immensity, than that God is in them by reason of his essence, which seems to imply something more imperfect.

units.la: VIII. Si obtendat aliquis, notitiam communem, & consequenter veram, apud omnes agnosci hanc, Deum videlicet in coelis, in altissi-mis, esse, simul cum sanctis mentibus à corpore liberis. Is consideret rerum creaturarum compages esse duas, & quasi duplicem mundum, intel-lectualem spiritualium, & materialem corporarum: in hoc ultimo statum rerum ita distingui, ut quae inferius, ignobiliores; quae supra, digniodigniores; quæ superius adhuc, vel quæ omnium summæ putantur, di-gnissimæ omnium in tota mole habeantur: desumptum autem esse à materiali mundo modum loquendi de intellectuali, in quo cum dentur mentes quarum status vilis & ignobilis, ignorantes nempe, errantes, & in vitiis constitutæ; aliæ utcunque istis sordibus clutæ; aliæ quarum statum veri bonique fruitio digniorem reddit; sed super omnibus omnium purissima, sanctissima, perfectissima mens Dei; Num per cœ-lum altissimum in quo Deus esse dicitur, ipsissimum ejus perfectionum statum, ejus puritatem, Sapientiam, dignitatem, lucem quam inhabi-tat inaccessam, intelligere fuerit iniquum? Imo etiam mentium Creata-rum ipse Deus, qui eas in sua cognitione, cura, amoreque vult gerere, in quem etiam unum cogitationes illæ suas refundunt, cœlum hoc sen-su possit haberi. Aut si de cœlo non ita sublimi, sed creato sit quæstio, Nonne ipsæ puræ & sanctæ mentes, quæ imagine Dei donatæ eum con-templantur & amant, recte id cœlum nominarentur in quo sit ipse Deus, quantum quidem in creaturis esse potest; in quod etiam ipsæ mentes di-cantur ingredi cum in statum ita purum & pure spiritualem, perfectissi-mumque, quanquam non absolute, transeunt? Contra vero ea quæ veritate & virtute privantur, diverse, pro sua quæque turpitudine & ærumna, ideo in luto, in infimis, jacere & deprimi dicantur? Sta-tus mentium, non locus seu spatium, quo carent, sic designatur. Interim non negaverim in cœlo corporeo dici Deum esse ob gloriæ & potentiæ in illo per effectus speciales patefactionem: Sed hoc non suf-ficere, mentemque hoc sensu non impleri, quilibet sibi intentus ipse animadvertere potest. Cur in interpretando magnalia Dei corporeis re-bus acquiescamus? Ne quis tamen putet corporum mentibus unitorum commercium cum corporeis cœlis hic negari, cum sola mens ut ab omni corpore libera hic spectetur, in qua cæteroquin est Deo facile absque corpore ideas, sensibilium instar, excitare, quibus ea quæ in loco glorio-fis corporibus destinato existunt, repræsententur eo modo, vel nobiliori, quo quæ circa nos in terris sunt medio corporeo nobis repræsentantur. Id autem menti, quamdiu soluta est corpore non ita certum est accidere, ac illud quod de spirituali statu est prolatum. Sed excurrimus longius.
units.tr: VIII. If anyone objects that it is a common notion, and consequently a true one, acknowledged by all, that God is in heaven, in the highest places, together with holy minds freed from the body, let him consider that the structure of created things is twofold, as it were a double world: the intellectual world of spiritual beings, and the material world of bodies. In the latter, the state of things is so distinguished that the things below are less noble, those above more noble, and those higher still, or those thought to be the highest of all, are regarded as the most noble of all in the whole mass. Moreover, the manner of speaking about the intellectual world has been borrowed from the material world, in which there are minds whose state is base and ignoble, namely ignorant, erring, and established in vices; others somehow besmirched by those filths; others whose enjoyment of truth and good renders their state more worthy; but above all, the purest, holiest, most perfect mind of God. Would it be unjust to understand by the highest heaven, in which God is said to be, his very own state of perfections, his purity, wisdom, dignity, and the light which he inhabits, inaccessible? Indeed, God himself may be held to be heaven in this sense, even of created minds, whom he wills to bear in his knowledge, care and love, and into whom alone those thoughts of theirs pour back. Or if the question concerns not so lofty a heaven but a created one, are not the pure and holy minds themselves, which, endowed with the image of God, contemplate and love him, rightly called that heaven in which God himself is, as far as indeed it can be in creatures; into which the minds themselves are said to enter when they pass over into a state so pure, purely spiritual and most perfect, although not absolutely? On the contrary, are those things which are deprived of truth and virtue said to lie and be cast down in the mire, in the lowest places, each according to its own baseness and misery? In this way the state of minds, not a place or space, which they lack, is designated. Meanwhile I would not deny that God is said to be in the corporeal heaven, on account of the manifestation of his glory and power in it through special effects; but that this is not enough, and that the mind is not fulfilled in this sense, anyone attentive to himself can notice. Why should we rest content in interpreting the wonders of God by corporeal things? Yet lest anyone think that the intercourse of minds united to bodies with the corporeal heavens is here denied, since only the mind, free from every body, is considered here, in which it is otherwise easy for God, without a body, to excite ideas, like those of sensible things, by which those things which exist in the place destined for glorified bodies are represented in the same way, or in a nobler way, as those things which are around us on earth are represented to us through the bodily medium. But that this happens to the mind, as long as it is loosed from the body, is not so certain as that which has been stated about the spiritual state. But we have wandered on too far.

units.la: IX. Animadverti velim, ne ullus sit suspicioni locus, hanc doctri-nam, quæ ex eo venit quod omnis imperfectio à Deo sit removenda, nil plane habere commune cum hæresi quorumdam, qui ideo docent Deum ratione essentiæ suæ non esse ubique, sed operatione tantum, quia ei imperfectiones tribuunt: Nempe finxerunt Deum tanquam ens aliquod corporeum certo loco & spatio in coelis definitum, & respectu essentiae suae sic limitatum, unde ipse immediate quidem in coelis, quibus essentia ejus includitur, agat: at quae in terris sunt non possint ei accepta referri nisi per interventum eorum quae sunt inter coelum & terram, quibus opus habeat, ut in objecta a se loco remota agat, nempe per coelum in sublunaria, per haec in terram, & per terram in animalia & homines, quorum omnia non existant ex sola efficacia Divinae potentiae, sed opus fit interventu mediorum, ac si absque iis nil posset Deus in ultimis efficere: quemadmodum homo machinae plurium rotarum admotus, ultimam a qua abesset non posset movere nisi per primam quam tangeret, unde motum in ultima, hac & caeteris interpositis, operaretur. Qui Deum sic operatione adesse, essentia vero ob ejus localem terminum abesse imaginantur, absurdum & blasphemum proferunt. Sed id in praecedentibus cum omni relatione praesentiae essentialis ad quantumcunque spatium, ita repulsum est, ut Dei ideam inde minui, aut obscurari, conqueri possit nemo, si insuper velit ea quae de Deo in Libro tertio dicentur, inspicere.
units.tr: IX. I would have it noted, so that there may be no room for suspicion, that this doctrine, which arises from the fact that every imperfection must be removed from God, has nothing at all in common with the heresy of certain persons, who therefore teach that God is not everywhere by reason of his essence, but only by operation, because they attribute imperfections to him. Namely, they imagined God as some corporeal being defined in heaven in a certain place and space, and thus limited with respect to his essence, so that he indeed acts immediately in the heavens, in which his essence is contained, but the things that are on earth can be referred to him only through the intervention of the things that lie between heaven and earth, which he needs in order to act upon objects remote from himself in place: namely, through heaven upon the sublunary things, through these upon the earth, and through the earth upon animals and men; all of which exist not from the sole efficacy of the divine power, but the work is done by the intervention of means, as if God could effect nothing in the ultimate things without them; just as a man applied to a machine of several wheels, unable to move the last wheel, from which he is distant, except through the first which he touches, would thereby work motion in the last, through this and the other intervening wheels. Those who imagine that God is thus present by operation, but absent in essence on account of his local limit, utter something absurd and blasphemous. But in the preceding discussion this has been so refuted, together with every relation of essential presence to any space whatever, that no one can complain that the idea of God is thereby diminished or obscured, if he will moreover look at what will be said about God in the third Book.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: I. 2. 3. Tertium & quartum imaginationis fulcrum corruunt. Mens corpori praesens est absque extensione. eoque moto, non movetur ipsa.
units.tr: I. 2. 3. The third and fourth props of the imagination fall. The mind is present to the body without extension, and when the body is moved, the mind itself is not moved.

units.la: I. Reliqua duo quae imaginationi favent axiomata supra enumerata, de Mentium cum corporibus copulatione, quae motum, rem imaginabilem, cum iisdem communem inferre videntur, nullius roboris erunt nescientibus vel praecedentia, vel saltem eatenus sapientibus, ut sciant Mentis naturam intellectu & voluntate absolvi & contineri. Inde enim nullo negotio concluditur, Mentem, cum illa modo naturae suae congruo, non vero adversante, fit cum corpore unienda, eique praesens sistenda non posse aliter adesse praesentem, quam ipsum corpus vel aliquid quod fit corporis percipiendo seu intelligendo, & volendo: ut non sit opus naturam vel essentiam intellectus & voluntatis inesse substantiae corporis, (alioqui corpus esset mens) sed sufficiat si mens concipiat & velit quaedam quae corpus concernunt (quae est objectiva praesentia) unde sequantur in corpore quaedam operationes. (quod praesentiam ratione operationis dixeris.) Potest & nexus inter haec dari strictior, siquisiquidem non tantum in corpore agatur aliquid ex occasione mentis, verum etiam si in ipsa mente ob motum in corpore varium, aliquid accidat & percipiatur: quo modo mens unum quid cum corpore dicetur esse, non naturæ transmutatione aut mixtione, sed positione simultanea quarumdam operationum in utroque, ut si certa fiat cogitatio in mente, fiat & certus quidam motus in corpore, & vicissim, quæ innumeris modis variari possunt. At cum hæc connexa non sint eatenus de natura utriusque extremi, sed ex liberrimo supremæ causæ placito uno occurrant, perperam cum mentis natura seorsim spectanda est, recurritur ad corpus, ac si illius natura naturæ hujus spatiosæ & mobilis particeps esset.
units.tr: I. The remaining two axioms listed above, which favour the imagination, concerning the coupling of minds with bodies, which seem to imply that motion, an imaginable thing, is common to both, will have no force for those who do not know the earlier points, or at least are not wise enough to know that the nature of the mind is comprehended and contained within intellect and will. For it is easily concluded from this that the mind, when it is to be united with a body and set present to it, cannot be present in any other way than by perceiving, understanding and willing the body itself, or something that belongs to the body, in a manner congruent with its own nature and not opposed to it. So there is no need for the nature or essence of intellect and will to inhere in the substance of the body (otherwise the body would be a mind); it is enough that the mind conceives and wills certain things that concern the body (this is objective presence), whence certain operations follow in the body (which you may call presence by way of operation). The connection between these can also be stricter: not only does something happen in the body on the occasion of the mind, but also something happens and is perceived in the mind itself because of the varied motion in the body. In this way the mind may be said to be one thing with the body, not by any change or mixing of natures, but by the simultaneous positing of certain operations in both, so that when a certain thought arises in the mind, a certain motion arises in the body, and conversely; and these can be varied in countless ways. But since these connected things are not, on that account, of the nature of either extreme, but occur together by the most free decree of the supreme cause, it is wrong to consider them apart from the nature of the mind and to have recourse to the body, as if the mind's nature shared in the nature of this extended and mobile thing.

units.la: II. Præter operationes mentis internas circa ideas suas, quæ sua sponte ipsi præsto sunt, versantes, habet mens nullas alias ex ratione naturæ suæ necessarias; nil igitur extra se necessario operatur. Imo cum quicquid Deus præter creatam mentem produxit non sit notum creatæ menti ex vi naturæ ejus seorsim spectatæ, sive cum non sit de natura ejus ut sit conscia aliarum rerum præter ipsam creatarum, prout neque harum natura postulat ut menti sint notæ, nunquam accideret ut in illis, utpote ignotis & non perceptis, operaretur mens: verum cum placuerit causæ supremæ ut mentium cum corporibus, quoad operationes, sit nexus, voluit ut certis materiæ cujusdam, ex: gr: corporis humani, aut cerebri, positis motibus, certa quædam idea sensatiove in mente ut hæc de corpore moneretur, excitata esset, quæ operatio corporis in mentem dicitur; & vicissim ut posita quadam in mente voluntate, motus corporis cujusdam certo modo determinaretur. Non vero sequitur ex harum corporis & mentis actionum passionumque concursu simultaneo, mentem naturæ vel proprietatum corporis esse participem, easque in se recipere, certo situ gaudere, extendi, stare vel decumbere, currere, sal-tare, loco moveri, spatio certo detineri, & quæ his similia: cum tan-tum debeat inferri, mentem quidem tales mutationes in corporis motu & situ velle, eas autem operationes externas ideo statim poni. Quamvis, ut quod proprie res est, dicatur, ea omnia non operetur mens creata, ut neque sensus à corpore in mente efficiantur, sed una Dei voluntas cun-cta producat, cum mutuo utrorumque nexu, ita ut creata mens corpo-ri non sit præsens nisi mediante Dei præsentia, quatenus nempe is opera-tiones suas in mente & corpore ita voluit nectere. Sic vitam, motum & existentiam in ipso habemus.
units.tr: II. Apart from the internal operations of the mind concerning its own ideas, which are present to it of their own accord, the mind has no other operations necessary from the nature of its being; therefore it does nothing necessarily outside itself. Indeed, since whatever God has produced apart from the created mind is not known to the created mind from the power of its nature considered in isolation (that is, it is not of the nature of the mind to be conscious of other created things besides itself, just as the nature of those things does not require that they be known to the mind), it would never happen that the mind operated upon those things, as unknown and unperceived. But since it has pleased the supreme cause that there be a connection between minds and bodies with respect to operations, it willed that, when certain motions of some matter, for example of the human body or the brain, were posited, a certain idea or sensation should be aroused in the mind, so that the body would be made known to the mind; this is said to be the operation of the body upon the mind. And conversely, that when a certain volition is posited in the mind, a motion of a certain body should be determined in a certain manner. Yet it does not follow from this simultaneous concurrence of the actions and passions of body and mind that the mind shares in the nature or properties of the body, receives them into itself, has a certain position, is extended, stands or lies down, runs, leaps, is moved from place to place, is held in a certain space, and things like these. Only this should be inferred: that the mind does will such changes in the motion and position of the body, and that those external operations are therefore immediately posited. Although, to speak as the thing really is, the created mind does not produce all these things, just as sensations are not effected in the mind from the body; rather, the one will of God produces all things, together with the mutual connection of the two, so that the created mind is not present to the body except through the presence of God, insofar as He willed to link their operations in mind and body in this way. Thus "in him we live, and move, and have our being."

units.la: III. Cæterum si quis adhuc imaginarium illum mentium motum vix à se possit removere, eo quod, cum mens sua sit juncta corpori, quocumque illud moveatur, etiam hæc cum illo moveri, si quidem illi ad- sit semper, videatur esse concipienda; nihil est quod præterea ei dicatur, nisi ut semota ad tempus ipsius mentis cum corpore suo conjunctionis consideratione, suam cogitationem in alias mentes corporibus non ita mancipatas deflectat, nempe in Angelos, qui cum materia interdum aliquo junguntur nexu, non ita quidem stricto ut ille est qui mentes humanas corporibus annectit, attamen eousque cum illo conveniente, ut uterque non sit de essentia Mentium. Primo igitur, concipe, uti potes, Angelum aliquem nullum plane ex natura sua nexum cum materia habentem, ita ut hæc ne quidem sit objectum ejus cogitationis, neque nos- cat is, an detur ullum corpus. Suppone insuper velle Deum Angelo illi existentiæ corporum notitiam aliquam dare, idque Eum exequi effi- ciendo ut positis molis corporeæ cujusdam diversis motibus, figuris aliisque variationibus multiplicibus, ponantur in mente Angeli cogitationes perceptionesve quæ eis respondeant, & quales illæ sunt quas vigilantes, vel etiam interdum dormientes, de lumine, coloribus, figuris, motibus, & aliis, experimur, vel aliæ. Quis inde concludat naturam Angelicæ illius mentis similem ideo esse istis externis! esse igitur lumen, habere figuram, rotundam, triangularem, aliam, quia percipit ista? habere motum & extensionem, quoniam istorum ideæ in illa sunt? Vix certe unus aliquis eo absurditatis hac conclusione deveniret. Cogita tertio, Deum non tantummodo voluisse ut mens illa afficeretur ex occasione molis istius corporeæ, verum etiam ut ista moles diversimode moveretur & afficeretur ex occasione diversarum cogitationum & placiti Spiritus Angelici; ita ut si hic præditus sit ea voluntate ut moles horsum vel aliorsum moveatur, sequatur is motus; si ut moles talem figuram & situm assumat, id ea occasione statim fiat, hicne opus est ut ipsam Angeli naturam moveri, & diversimode figuris indui, quis sibi imaginetur? Nonne sufficit si concipiam, omnes quidem illas corporeas affectiones in mole corporis esse; in mente vero Angeli præter illarum perceptionem & voluntatem nil omnino de illis esse? Atque his modis movent Angeli corpora, & ipsi dicuntur in terram descendere, ascendere in cœlum corporeum, celerrimo eoque diverso motu moveri, non ratione essentiæ suæ nec in illa, quasi esset horum subjectum, sed tum respectu istarum operationum externarum quæ in corporibus quibus- dam fiunt ex occasione voluntatis Angelicæ; tum etiam objective, quatenus modo quæ in supremis, modo quæ in infimis, hæc illave, objecta sunt Cogitationis Angelicæ. Cogita tandem mentem tuam cum mente Angeli ejusdem naturæ esse creatam, & ei talia ex voluntate Dei accidere quæ jam diximus; molemque illam materiæ esse tuum corpus, nec tibi difficile consequenter fuerit concipere mentem sic corpori adesse, ut neque illa extendatur, neque moveatur, neque sit in spatio, idve mutet, utut hæc omnia corpori ipsa volente & percipiente eveniant. Equidem eatenus mens nostra cum Angelis in corporum assumptione convenit: quanquam deinde in multis, in hoc vero præcipue differat, quod mentis nostræ perceptiones quas ex occasione corporis habet, multæ sint, vividæ sint, potentes & valde urgentes sint; cum quas corpus recipit impressiones ex mentis voluntate sint pauciores, debiliores, & parvo limite contineantur; ita ut plus corpus in Mentem, quam Mens in corpus, polleat: At in Angelis contra fit, & plus illi valent in corpora, quam corpora in illos.
units.tr: III. Moreover, if anyone still can scarcely remove from himself that imaginary motion of minds, because, since his mind is joined to the body, it seems that wherever the body is moved, the mind must also be moved with it, if indeed it is always present to it, nothing more can be said to him than this: setting aside for the time being the consideration of the mind's own union with its body, let him turn his thought to other minds not so bound to bodies, namely to the Angels, who sometimes are joined to matter by some connection, not indeed as strict as that which binds human minds to bodies, yet agreeing with it to such a degree that neither is of the essence of minds. First, then, conceive, as you can, some Angel having no connection whatever with matter by its nature, so that matter is not even the object of its thought, and it does not know whether any body exists. Suppose further that God wishes to give that Angel some knowledge of the existence of bodies, and carries this out by effecting that, when certain bodily masses undergo various motions, figures and other manifold variations, there arise in the mind of the Angel thoughts or perceptions corresponding to them, such as those we experience, waking or even sometimes sleeping, of light, colours, figures, motions and other things, or others. Who would conclude from this that the nature of that Angelic mind is therefore similar to those external things? That it is light, has a figure, round or triangular or otherwise, because it perceives these? That it has motion and extension, since the ideas of these are in it? Scarcely anyone would reach such an absurd conclusion. Think, third, that God has willed not only that that mind should be affected on the occasion of that corporeal mass, but also that this mass should be moved and affected in various ways on the occasion of various thoughts and the decision of the Angelic spirit; so that if the spirit is endowed with the will that the mass be moved hither or thither, that motion follows; if that the mass assume such a figure and position, this happens immediately on that occasion. Who would imagine that the Angel's own nature must here be moved and clothed in different figures? Is it not enough if I conceive that all those corporeal affections are in the mass of the body, while in the mind of the Angel there is nothing of them at all except the perception and will of them? And in these ways Angels move bodies, and are said to descend to the earth, ascend to the corporeal heaven, and be moved with very swift and varied motion; not by reason of their essence, nor as if they were the subject of these in it, but partly with respect to those external operations which take place in certain bodies on the occasion of the Angelic will, and partly also objectively, insofar as this or that is the object of the Angelic thought, now the highest things, now the lowest. Finally, think of your mind as created of the same nature as the mind of an Angel, and that such things befall it by the will of God as we have just said; and let that mass of matter be your body. It will then not be difficult for you to conceive that the mind is present to the body in such a way that it is neither extended, nor moved, nor in space, nor changed, although all these things happen to the body, which itself wills and perceives them. Indeed, in this respect our mind agrees with the Angels in the assumption of bodies; although afterwards it differs from them in many things, and especially in this: that the perceptions our mind has on the occasion of the body are many, vivid, powerful and very urgent, whereas the impressions the body receives from the will of the mind are fewer, weaker and confined within narrow limits; so that the body prevails over the mind more than the mind over the body. But in Angels it is the reverse: they prevail over bodies more than bodies over them.

units.la: Hactenus falsas de Mentium generaliori notitia opiniones cum earum causis conati sumus removere, & ostendere dari notitiam intellectualem de re intellectuali, sine spatio & extensione: quod tum in genere, de omnibus spiritibus; tum specialius, de Deo, & de Mente creata, à qua etiam motus est remotus, demonstratum est, ut deinceps sequentia iis non contaminarentur. Quod si quibusdam longior videatur fuisse dis-cursus, reputent ii vel infirmissimis scrupulos præcipuos eximere inibi fuisse intentum: his enim, si qui sint, datur discursus iste, quibusdam forte brevior, si eo non possint à materialibus ad nobiliora etiamnum abstrahi: quibus nil est utilius quam ut similia animo sæpe revolvant.
units.tr: Hitherto we have tried to remove the false opinions about our general knowledge of minds, together with their causes, and to show that there is an intellectual knowledge of an intellectual thing, without space or extension. This has been demonstrated in general, for all spirits, and more particularly for God and for created mind, from which motion has also been removed, so that what follows should not be contaminated by them. If anyone thinks the discussion was rather long, let them consider that its chief aim was to remove the main scruples even from the weakest readers: for this discussion is given to such people, if there are any, and perhaps it will seem too short to some, if they cannot yet be drawn from material things up to the nobler ones. Nothing is more useful to such people than to turn these things over often in their minds.

units.la: Corruptibile corpus animam aggravat, & terrena inhabitatio mentem de pluribus sollicitam deprimit. Sap. cap. IX. v. 15.
units.tr: A corruptible body weighs down the soul, and an earthly dwelling presses down the mind that is anxious about many things. Wisdom, chapter 9, verse 15.

units.la: LIBER SECUNDUS UBI De Mente Increata & Creata, Earumque Perfectionibus & hujus imperfectionibus, in genere agitur. CAPUT I.
units.tr: BOOK TWO, WHERE the Uncreated and Created Mind, their Perfections and the Imperfections of the latter, are treated in general. CHAPTER I.

units.la: 1. Omnibus corporeis sepositis, 2. superest Cogitatio utrique Menti tribuenda. 3. In illa una, est essentia Mentis creatæ. 4. Proponuntur difficultates sex in posterum resolvendæ.
units.tr: 1. With all corporeal things set aside, 2. Thought remains to be ascribed to each Mind. 3. In that one thing lies the essence of the created Mind. 4. Six difficulties are set out to be resolved in what follows.

units.la: I. CUm supra ab initio diversæ de rerum spiritualium notitia referrentur opiniones, quintum inter illas occupabat locum ea quæ puriori cogitatione & intellectu res mentis vult indagari posse. Quam sententiam, utpote verissimam, ita amplectimur & sequi conabimur, ut non modo omne corporeum, imaginabile, sensibile exulet ab idea Mentis; verum ut nequidem occasionem de spiritualibus loquendi sumpturi simus, (nisi forte rarissime & ex incidenti,) ab existentia, vel à consideratione rerum corporearum: sed tanquam istis omnibus exuti, à contemplatione Mentis creatæ ad increatam simus annixuri. Quamvis enim quæ inter opera Dei sunt corporea, multis, iisque insignibus characteribus sint insignita, quibus Artificis sui Summi perfectiones summæ significanter manifestentur: attamen, quia his cum Dei essentia nihil communius intercedit, siquidem nil corporeum prout corporeum est, tribui possit Enti summe Perfecto; cum præterea, etiamsi quis ex corporum inspectione Deum cognoscere prætendat, mentem nihilominus intercedere est necessarium; cumque Mens plures, eosque insigniores Divinitatis gerat characteres; nil utilius ab illa fieri potest, quam si materialia quæcunque sibi quasi in nihilum redigat, neque ea magis spectet ac si nulla existerent: Semoveat etiam illorum quas habet ideas, quo melius & sincerius ex sui solius inspectione ad Deum tentet assurgere. Hoc propositum à Cartesio cum utilitate adhibitum, multis displicuisse dolendum est: Cum tamen non tantum ad notitiam, sed & ad verum amorem Dei, simili via, imo etiam strictiori, qua omnia creata, etiam nos ipsi, nihil nobis fiant, ut solus Deus fiat omnia, progrediendum esse sancti viri dixerint.
units.tr: I. Although at the beginning various opinions concerning the knowledge of spiritual things were reported, the fifth place among them was held by the view that the nature of the mind can be investigated by purer thought and understanding. We embrace this opinion, as the truest, and shall endeavour to follow it, so that not only is everything corporeal, imaginable and sensible banished from the idea of the Mind, but we shall not even take occasion to speak of spiritual things (except perhaps very rarely and incidentally) from existence or from the consideration of corporeal things. Rather, stripped of all these, we shall strive to rise from the contemplation of the created Mind to the uncreated. For although the corporeal things among God's works are marked with many and notable characters, by which the supreme perfections of their Supreme Maker are significantly made manifest, yet, since nothing is more remote from the essence of God than these, inasmuch as nothing corporeal, as corporeal, can be ascribed to the Being most perfect; and since, moreover, even if someone claims to know God from the inspection of bodies, the mind must nonetheless intervene; and since the Mind bears many and more remarkable characters of the Divinity, nothing can be more useful to it than to reduce to nothing, as it were, all material things, and to regard them no more than if they did not exist. Let it also set aside the ideas of them which it has, so that it may try to rise to God better and more sincerely from the inspection of itself alone. It is to be regretted that this method, employed with profit by Descartes, has displeased many; yet holy men have said that we must proceed not only to the knowledge but to the true love of God by a similar way, indeed by a stricter one, in which all created things, even ourselves, become nothing to us, so that God alone becomes all things.

units.la: II. Mens hoc in statu posita, quæcunque in ipsa restant circumspiciens, nil præter cogitationem invenit, quod sibi, & Enti alteri de cujus existentia certa fit, tribuat: ut enucleate rem proposuit Cartesius in Meditatione secunda, & tertia. Cogitatio igitur sola superest absque imaginatione indaganda, ut per eam & in ea naturam Mentis tum Increatæ cum creatæ agnoscamus. Quod eo fiet ordine, ut primo videamus naturam utriusque Mentis eatenus convenire, ut in cogitatione sita sit. Ne tamen creaturam cum Deo misceri quis inde sequi putet, ostendetur secundo, at generalius, quomodo Cogitatio seu Mens utraque disconveniat, una perfectionum excellentia, altera earumdem limite & imperfectionum mixtura. Ne vero quis dicit perfectiones immensas quæ Deo tribuuntur, vel limites perfectionum quæ Menti humanæ dantur, quæ forsan ad divinas, utpote earum scopum, cum tempore eo tendentes perventuræ præsumi possent, esse omnia figmenta libera humanæ cogitationis; proponetur, tertio, via certa qua perfectiones Dei, perfectiones item & imperfectiones mentis creatæ, harumque limites, mensura & regula, tuto possint agnosci. Atque his tribus Secundus hic Liber absolvetur.
units.tr: II. The Mind, placed in this state, looking around at whatever remains within itself, finds nothing except thought, which it may ascribe to itself and to another Being, of whose existence it becomes certain. Descartes set out the matter clearly in his Second and Third Meditations. Thought alone therefore remains to be investigated without imagination, so that through it and in it we may recognise the nature of the Mind, both uncreated and created. This will be done in the following order: first, we shall see how the nature of each Mind agrees, insofar as it consists in thought. Lest anyone suppose from this that the creature is mixed with God, it will be shown secondly, and more generally, how the Thought or Mind of each differs: the one by the excellence of perfections, the other by the limit of the same and a mixture of imperfections. Moreover, lest anyone say that the immense perfections ascribed to God, or the limits of the perfections given to the human mind, which may perhaps be presumed to attain the divine perfections as their goal in time, are all free fictions of human thought, a sure way will be set out, thirdly, by which the perfections of God, the perfections and imperfections of the created mind, and their limits, measure and rule, can be safely known. With these three things this Second Book will be completed.

units.la: III. Mentis utriusque, Increatæ & Creatæ, notio magis generalis & evidens dari non potest, quam si tanquam Cogitatio utraque concipiatur. Hæc enim utriusque Essentia seu natura est, quod facile de utraque, remotis apparenter adversantibus, demonstrari potest. Et primo quidem, ut de creata Mente agatur, (nam hæc ut occasio de altera loquendi præcedere debet) certum est, Cujuscunque rei essentiam seu naturam consistere in eo, quod ita concipitur in re, ut etiamsi omnia cætera in nihilum redigerentur, id tamen ut nihilominus existens clare concipi posset, & quidem ita concipi, ut eo solo posito sequatur series attributorum rei, modorumque plurimorum, quorum illud ipsum sit immediatum subjectum. Nisi hoc sit concipere rei alicujus essentiam, id ipsum quod res est, & quidem ita proprie, ut ille conceptus tum ab omni conceptu alieno separetur, tum etiam amplectatur id quod est primum & fundamentale in re de qua quæstio est; fateor me scire non posse, quid dici mereatur conceptus essentiæ rei cujusquam. Atqui omnibus corporeis remotis, deprehendo in Me, sive in Mente mea, (quod enim in me est præter corpus, Mentem voco) concipio, inquam, in me etiamsi omnia corpora cum meo, omnia inquam quæ in mundo sunt, tollerentur, me tamen dum cogito sufficienter existere, sive, satis esse mihi ad conscientiam existentiæ meæ cogitationem, ita ut ad evidentem hujus veritatis, sum res, notitiam, non opus sit ad alia quæcunque præter cogitationem attendam, & me convertam. Video ea posita involvi, indeque sequi plurima attributa quæ in nihilo esse non possunt, absque cogitatione concipi non possunt, ei immediate insunt, quæque agnoscunt omnes ad rem spiritualem pertinere. Cogitatio igitur est mei, sive mentis meæ, sive ejus quod in me est præter corpus, essentia & natura. Quod si cogitatio à me tollatur, nil plane mihi superest unde conscius sim vel percipiam me non esse nihil, superest forte brutissimum quid extensum cujus aliquis alius forsitan est conscius: sed quid hoc ad Mentem. Quo negato negatur directe quicquid est in me præter brutissimam molem, negatur omnis perceptio, voluntas, judicandi, amandi, imo imaginandi & sentiendi fundamentum & actus; id certe est essentia ejus rei quæ præter molem corpoream in me est. Talem esse Cogitationem cuilibet attendenti est evidentissimum. Quo fit, ut ex hac & præcedenti ratione sit concludendum, in hoc uno consistere essentiam Mentis creatæ ut cogitet: Sive illam esse uno verbo Cogitationem: quod unum si ei dederit ejus Author, de cætero nil illa opus habet ad hoc ut sit quod est.
units.tr: III. A notion of the Mind, both uncreated and created, more general and evident cannot be given than if each is conceived as Thought. For this is the essence or nature of each, which can easily be demonstrated of each, once apparently opposing things are removed. And first, to speak of the created Mind (for this must come first, as the occasion for speaking of the other), it is certain that the essence or nature of any thing consists in that which is conceived in the thing in such a way that, even if all other things were reduced to nothing, it could nonetheless be clearly conceived as existing, and indeed conceived in such a way that, with it alone posited, there follows a series of attributes of the thing and of many modes, of which it is itself the immediate subject. Unless this is to conceive the essence of some thing, namely that which the thing is, and indeed so properly that this concept is both separated from every alien concept and also embraces what is first and fundamental in the thing under question, I confess I do not know what should be deemed worthy to be called the concept of the essence of any thing. But with all corporeal things removed, I find in Me, or in my Mind (for what is in me besides the body I call Mind), I conceive, I say, that in me, even if all bodies were taken away together with mine, all bodies, I say, which are in the world, I nonetheless exist sufficiently while I think; or, thought is enough for me for the consciousness of my existence, so that for the evident knowledge of this truth, that I am a thing, there is no need to attend to anything whatever other than thought, and to turn myself to it. I see that, these being posited, there are involved and follow from them very many attributes which cannot be in nothing, which cannot be conceived without thought, which are immediately in it, and which all acknowledge to pertain to a spiritual thing. Thought, therefore, is the essence and nature of me, or of my mind, or of that which is in me besides the body. But if thought were taken away from me, nothing at all would remain to me by which I might be conscious of, or perceive, that I am not nothing; perhaps some very brutish extended thing would remain, of which someone else may perhaps be conscious; but what is this to the Mind? With this denied, whatever is in me besides a brutish mass is directly denied: every perception, will, power of judging, loving, and indeed the foundation and act of imagining and sensing, is denied. That certainly is the essence of that thing which is in me besides the corporeal mass. That Thought is such is most evident to anyone who attends to it. Hence it follows, from this and the preceding argument, that the essence of the created Mind consists in this one thing, that it thinks; in one word, that it is Thought. If its Author has given it this one thing, it has no need of anything else for the rest to be what it is.

units.la: IV. Conclusionem hanc à multis æque admitti ob sequentes difficultates est animadversum.
units.tr: IV. That this conclusion is equally admitted by many people, on account of the following difficulties, has been noticed.

units.la: Causantur nonnulli. 1. Cogitationem non esse aliquid satis reale, ut in ea Mentis natura consistat. 2. Quemlibet habere plures cogitationes, quas sæpissime mutat, ac proinde multæ cuilibet essent assignandæ mentes diversæ & mutabiles. 3. Cogitationem esse actionem, quæ præsupponit aliquod agens. 4. Cogitationem esse attributum, quod requirit subjectum aut substantiam ubi sit: quamvis enim Mens sit res seu substantia cogitans, non tamen quæri, quid illa cogitatio sit, sed quid sit illa res seu illa substantia, in qua est cogitatio? 5. Mentem debuisse ergo semper cogitare necessario à quo tempore est creata, ante nativitatem ejus cui inest corporis, etiamque in somno, siquidem cogitatio sit ejus essentia: at de priori nemo est conscius; de posteriori nec omnes, nec semper. 6. Denique cogitationem esse posse modum aut temperamentum corporis, ut in brutis, nec ab illo realiter differre, verum corpus cogitare posse. Quæ omnia si ita removeantur, ut sequentium hisce adversantium patescat veritas, nempe, Cogitationem esse rerum omnium realissimam; esse unum quid fixum & subsistens; Esse principium in suo genere agens & primum; Esse ipsam Mentis substantiam & subjectum omnium quae in Mente; Esse à Mente inseparabilem; Denique esse quid diversum & incommunicabile omni corpori, nilque in sua natura includere quod corporeum sit: arbitror nil adeo posse aliunde obsistere, quominus ut vera admittatur conclusio inferens, Mentem esse ipsissimam Cogitationem.
units.tr: Some raise objections. 1. Thought is not something real enough for the nature of the mind to consist in it. 2. Each person has several thoughts, which he very often changes, and therefore many different and changeable minds would have to be assigned to each person. 3. Thought is an action, which presupposes some agent. 4. Thought is an attribute, which requires a subject or substance where it is; for although the mind is a thinking thing or substance, it is not asked what that thought is, but what that thing or substance is in which the thought is. 5. The mind must therefore always have been thinking of necessity from the time it was created, even before the birth of the body in which it is, and even in sleep, if thought is indeed its essence; but no one is conscious of the former, and of the latter not everyone, nor always. 6. Finally, thought may be a mode or temperament of the body, as in the brutes, and not really differ from it, and the body may be able to think. If all these objections are so removed that the truth of the following points, opposed to these, becomes clear, namely that thought is the most real of all things; that it is something fixed and subsistent; that it is the principle, first and active in its own kind; that it is the very substance of the mind and the subject of all that is in the mind; that it is inseparable from the mind; and finally that it is something different from, and not shareable with, any body, and that its nature includes nothing corporeal: I judge that nothing can otherwise stand in the way of admitting as true the conclusion that the mind is thought itself.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Inter res omnes cogitatio est quam maxime realis. 2. Una est, fixa & persistens. 3. Est principium omnium quae in Mente sunt.
units.tr: 1. Among all things, thought is by far the most real. 2. It is one, fixed and persisting. 3. It is the principle of all the things that are in the Mind.

units.la: I. Qui Mentem omnium rerum maxime realem esse, ut revera est, fatentur, impediuntur quo minus eam putent esse ipsam Cogitationem, quia haec aliquod non ita reale videtur indigitare.
