At ii facile sibi satisfieri patientur, si, ubi explicuerint quid per reale intelligant, observare velint, quocunque sensu aliquid reale dicatur, eo cogitationem omnia ab ipsa diversa, in realitate vincere. Vis per reale id designare quod certum est & inconcussum, quod negari nequit, quod chymaerico & plane ficto opponitur? Quid hoc sensu magis reale est quam cogitatio? Omnia corpora negari, & nihil esse, possunt à me supponi: & quoties, ea quae tanquam à me diversa mihi repraesentantur, nihil sunt praeter figmenta, chymaeras, & somniorum lusus? At, vel in ipsis somniis me cogitare, mihi certum est: Me, quamdiu vivit Mens, & potest dicere se esse, ita certum est cogitare, ut id negare sine contradictione non possim. An reale tibi idem est quod evidens & clarum? Certe inter haec primas tenet cogitatio. quis clare percipiat omnia quae sunt actu in aliqua re corporea quoad numerum partium, vel exactam motus aut figurae mensuram? at omnia quae jam actu sunt in mea cogitatione (quod de se quilibet asseverare potest) clare video, nec negare possum, quin eo ipso affirmem me evidenter percipere quid in mea cogitatione non sit, quidve sit. Quod si tibi reale sit idem atque id quod permanens est, nec tenues evanescit in auras: hoc quidem sensu humanum corpus non multum fuerit reale, utpote cujus substantia ita continuo fluit, ut in corpore senis aut adulti ne forte unica superfsit particula ejus quod in illo erat cum infans nasceretur; cum post aliquantulum temporis spatium desinat esse id quod fuit, & ejus cujus fuit: nil etiam minus reale est Mente, si illa ut aura quaedam tenuis, vel vapor, aut halitus concipienda sit.
units.tr: I. Those who admit that the Mind is the most real of all things, as indeed it is, are prevented from thinking it is thought itself, because thought seems to indicate something not so real. But they will easily be satisfied if, once they have explained what they mean by real, they are willing to observe that, in whatever sense something is called real, thought surpasses in reality all things that are different from it. Do you wish by "real" to designate what is certain and unshaken, what cannot be denied, what is opposed to the chimerical and the purely fictitious? What is more real than thought in this sense? All bodies can be supposed by me to be denied and to be nothing; and however often those things that are represented to me as different from myself are nothing but figments, chimeras and the play of dreams, yet even in the dreams themselves I am certain that I think. As long as the Mind lives and can say that it exists, I am as certain that I think as I cannot deny it without contradiction. Or is "real" the same for you as "evident" and "clear"? Certainly thought holds the first place among these. Who clearly perceives all the things that actually exist in some corporeal thing with respect to the number of its parts, or the exact measure of its motion or figure? But all the things that now actually exist in my thought (which anyone can assert of himself) I see clearly, and I cannot deny that, by that very fact, I affirm that I evidently perceive what is not in my thought, or what it is. But if "real" for you is the same as what is permanent and does not vanish into thin air like a tenuous breath: in this sense the human body would not be very real, since its substance flows so continually that in the body of an old man or an adult perhaps not a single particle remains of what was in it when the infant was born; since after a certain span of time it ceases to be what it was and to be of the one whose it was. Nothing is less real than the Mind, if it is to be conceived as some thin breeze, or vapour, or breath.

units.la: At cogitatio constanter Cogitatio est, non evanescit ut fiat aliud quid, vel alterius cujusdam. Si denique, qui sensus praecipuus est, reale & perfectum tibi Synonyma sint, cogitationis realitatem maximam inde agnoscs. Vere definienda est realitas perfectione. quod nihil est, realitatem vere non habet, quia perfectionem habet nullam. pulvisculus reale quid est, quia perfectione nonnulla praeditus est. Deus maxime realis est, quia maxime perfectus. Ergo, si res creatas spectemus, quid perfectius est, brutane extensio, aut vivida cogitatio? moveri, habere partes; aut intelligere, velle, & quam plurimas nobilissimas facultates possidere? Si modos, major-ne perfectio in certis particularum corporearum dispositionibus, quibus diverse quae in diversis corporibus miramur, constant, quam in sublimi cogitationis dispositione, quae omnia sibi vivide sistit praesentia, circa illa solide judicat, recte ratiocinatur, sponte approbat aut improbat, amanter amplectitur, jucunde gaudet, placide acquiescit, & quae similia fere infinita sunt? Haec certe perfecta ita sunt, ita realem nobis sistunt cogitationem, ut cetera diversi ab illa generis vix prae illa realia videantur. Sed & ipse Deus quanti prae omnibus cogitationes humanas facit? siquidem illas solus velit possidere, & ab illis quantum potest, possideri, si illas cum Zelotypia ambiat, & quia illae ab eo deviae fuerant, mirabilia patraverit ut eas sibi reduceret, si ejus magnalia in iis maxime excellentissimo modo operetur; si denique omne praeceptum & sacrum in bene cogitando incluserit! Est igitur inter omnia creata realissimum.
units.tr: But thought is constantly thought; it does not vanish so as to become something else or something of another kind. Finally, if you take as synonyms "real" and "perfect" (which is the chief sense), you will thereby recognise the greatest reality of thought. Reality is rightly defined by perfection: what is nothing does not truly have reality, because it has no perfection. Dust is something real because it is endowed with some perfection. God is most real because he is most perfect. So, if we consider created things, what is more perfect: brute extension, or lively thought? To move and have parts; or to understand, to will, and to possess very many most noble faculties? If we consider modes, is there greater perfection in certain dispositions of corporeal particles, in which we marvel at the various qualities found in various bodies, than in the lofty disposition of thought, which vividly presents to itself all things as present, judges soundly about them, reasons rightly, spontaneously approves or disapproves, lovingly embraces, joyfully rejoices, calmly rests, and things like these, which are nearly infinite? These are certainly perfect things, and they present to us thought as so real that the other things of a kind different from it seem scarcely real in comparison with it. But how highly does God himself value human thoughts above all things? Since he alone wishes to possess them, and to be possessed by them as far as he can; if he embraces them with jealous love, and when they have strayed from him has worked wonders to bring them back to himself; if he works his great deeds in them in a most excellent manner; if, finally, he has included every precept and every holy thing in right thinking! Therefore it is the most real of all created things.

units.la: II. Quod secundo loco est oppositum, ab ambiguo vocis cogitationis sensu qui modo generalior, modo specialior est, ortum ducit. Etenim si ea voce variam perceptionis nostrae ad varia objecta, puta modo ad corporea, modo ad spiritualia, ad terram, ad coelum, ad Deum, ad nos ipsos, applicationem intelligere velimus, tunc quidem multas cogitationes, easque interruptas, in qualibet mente esse verum est: at hoc sensu nequaquam prolatum est Mentis naturam cogitationem esse: neque enim est de ejus essentia in genere & confusius spectata ut certo alicui objecto, percipiendo prae alio, applicetur, etsi illa cum naturae sit finitae, & omnia simul percipere impotentis, necessario applicetur alicui ex omnibus illis, imo determinatius (quod ad formam specialiorem infra referemus) in certum unum prae aliis tendat. Quapropter ut per vocem cogitationis Mentis natura non ambigue notetur, intelligenda est Cogitatio, ut limitata quidem, quia omnia simul percipere non potest; at non ut determinata ad certum quid, quia nullum habet in quovis actu, ut res simpliciter conscia, cum ullo objecto specialiori, imo ne quidem secum, quatenus in seipsam reflectere posset, necessarium nexum. Et hoc sensu Cogitatio generalius quid est quam priori, & unica in Mente dici debet, est enim perceptio intima eorum, quæcunque ea sint, quæ in illa sunt: nam ut objecta diversa sint, ut etiam diversimoda percipiantur applicatione, ad hoc unum tamen redeunt, quod sint perceptio, hoc est, cogitatio una, diversis modis variata. Res similis perfacile compre-hendetur, nempe certum, exempli gratia, ceræ fructulum quamplu-rimis figuris variari potest, naturam autem suam unam idcirco mutare dici non potest: fiat ex triangulari rotundum, quadratum, aut interno calore aliam quamlibet assumat figuram, eadem natura tamen permanet ac persistit. Eadem prorsus ratione una fixa manet Mentis natura Cogi-tatio, diversitate objectorum, & applicatione sui ad ea subinde mu-tabilis.
units.tr: II. The second objection arises from the ambiguous sense of the word thought, which is sometimes more general and sometimes more specific. For if by that word we wish to understand the various application of our perception to various objects, say sometimes to corporeal things, sometimes to spiritual, to earth, to heaven, to God, to ourselves, then it is indeed true that in any mind there are many thoughts, and these interrupted; but in this sense it has by no means been asserted that the nature of the Mind is thought. For it is not of its essence, considered in general and more confusedly, that it should be applied to some definite object in preference to another by perceiving; although, since it is of a finite nature and unable to perceive all things at once, it is necessarily applied to some one of all those objects, or rather (which we shall refer to a more specific form below) tends toward a certain one in preference to others. Therefore, so that the nature of the Mind may be unambiguously designated by the word thought, it must be understood as Thought, limited indeed, because it cannot perceive all things at once; but not as determined to some particular thing, because in any act it has no necessary connection, as simply conscious being, with any more specific object, or even with itself, insofar as it could reflect upon itself. And in this sense Thought is something more general than in the former sense, and ought to be called one in the Mind; for it is the inner perception of whatever those things are that are in it: for although the objects are different, and they are perceived in differing ways by application, yet they come back to this one thing, that they are perception, that is, one thought varied in diverse modes. A similar matter is very easily understood: for example, a certain piece of wax-fruit can be varied in very many shapes, yet it cannot be said that its nature is therefore changed in one way: whether it is made round from triangular, square, or by internal heat takes on any other shape whatever, its nature nonetheless remains and persists. In exactly the same way the one fixed nature of the Mind, Thought, remains, though it is from time to time changeable by the diversity of objects and by its application to them.

units.la: III. Pari modo solvi potest tertia difficultas, qua Mentis natura Cogitatio ideo esse negabatur, quod hæc actio esset, non Res agens. Nam, (ne jam immoremur in eo quod non omnis cogitatio actio sit, sed sint etiam multæ illic passiones) notandum est, vocem actionis certam applicationem rei ad singulare aliquod objectum communiter designa-re. quo sensu dici nequit cogitationem late sumptam, ut mox monitum est, notantemque mentis naturam, esse actionem: cum potius sit, tum principium agens, tum etiam subjectum passiones admittens. Hoc cæ-teroquin non impedit quominus Cogitatio, quatenus consideratur ut applicatio specialis ad aliquod objectum, actio fit vocanda: at tunc ea, ut visum, non est de essentia Mentis sive Cogitationis fundamentalis: non enim idcirco est in nobis perceptio seu conscientia, quia ad tale quid objectum est applicatio, sed contra. Igitur hoc sensu natura Cogitatio-nis non est actio. Cæterum quemadmodum verba ex semetipsis valde sunt indifferentia, nihilque consideratu dignum præter voluntariam, quæ eis assignatur, significationem obtinent, si quis præter usum com-munem velit Cogitationem, ut ea hic asseritur esse Mentis natura, actio-nem vocare, vocet quantum libuerit: at tunc negandum est id, quod ita actionem appellabit, deposcere aliam rem diversam unde tanquam à principio actio ea emanare concipiatur.
units.tr: III. In the same way the third difficulty can be solved, by which it was denied that the nature of the Mind is Thought, on the ground that this is an action and not an acting thing. For (not to dwell further on the point that not every thought is an action, but there are also many passions in it), it must be noted that the word action commonly designates the definite application of a thing to some single object. In this sense it cannot be said that thought, taken broadly, as has just been noted, and indicating the nature of the mind, is an action: since it is rather both an active principle and also a subject that admits of passions. Nevertheless this does not prevent Thought, insofar as it is considered as a specific application to some object, from being rightly called an action; but then, as seems clear, this is not of the essence of the Mind or of Thought as fundamental. For we do not have perception or consciousness in us because there is an application to such an object, but on the contrary. Therefore in this sense the nature of Thought is not an action. Moreover, just as words in themselves are very indifferent and obtain no meaning worth considering except the meaning voluntarily assigned to them, so if anyone, contrary to common usage, wishes to call Thought, as it is here asserted to be the nature of the Mind, an action, let him call it as he pleases; but then it must be denied that whoever calls it an action in this way requires another, different thing from which that action is conceived to emanate as from a principle.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. 2. 3. 4. Cogitatio est Mentis ipsius substantia, natura, essentia. 5. 6. Eaque ab omni Mente inseparabilis.
units.tr: 1. 2. 3. 4. Thought is the very substance, nature and essence of the Mind. 5. 6. And this is inseparable from every Mind.

units.la: I. UBi Mens materialibus Phantasmatibus libera est, quarta difficultate, quæ dicta est, non præpedietur. Sit cogitatio attributum substantiæ cogitantis, non tamen inde inferendum est eam esse in re quid diversi ab ea cui tribuitur re, sive substantia. Quinimo tanquam ipsamet res & substantia concipi debet: non enim requiritur in omni attributione ut inter id quod tribuitur, & id cui attribuitur, diversitas intercedat, ut videre est in attributis divinis quæ non sunt diversum quid ab ipso Deo: cum detur quoque attributio identitatis, ut sic loquar, id est, talis modus loquendi quo ostendamus id quod duobus pluribusve verbis intelligitur, esse rem unam & eandem. qualis modus est in hoc negotio, ubi Mens dicitur Res cogitans, vel substantia quæ cogitat.
units.tr: I. When the Mind is free from material phantasms, it will not be hindered by the fourth difficulty, which has been stated. Let thought be an attribute of a thinking substance; yet it does not follow from this that it is something in the thing different from the thing to which it is attributed, or from the substance. Indeed, it ought to be conceived as the very thing and substance itself. For it is not required in every attribution that there be a difference between that which is attributed and that to which it is attributed, as may be seen in the divine attributes, which are not something different from God himself. For there is also an attribution of identity, if I may so speak, that is, a mode of speaking by which we show that what is understood by two or more words is one and the same thing. Such a mode occurs in this matter, where the Mind is called a thinking thing, or a substance that thinks.

units.la: II. Difficultas in eo est, quod homines cum velint concipere substantiam præcise & in genere, nihilominus quia conceptus ille incompletus est, vel inviti eo delabuntur, ut ad substantiam in specie attendant, cui cum postea cogitationem superaddere velint, constat conceptum illius substantiæ ante attributionem cogitationis consideratæ, fuisse conceptum corporis: non enim datur substantia specialis, seu revera existens, à cogitatione diversa præter corpus. Atque ad hoc spectant absurda illa postulata, ut explicetur natura non Cogitationis, sed substantiæ hoc est trunci seu stipitis illius à cogitatione diversi, in quo est cogitatio. Notandum igitur, ne quis his verborum tricis implicetur, nomen substantiæ diversimode usurpari, interdum denotare conceptum de re incompletum, aliquando completum, seu rem ipsam prout existit extra conceptum: quæ ne in nimias subtilitates evaporent, facilius iis exemplis capientur, unde omni logomachiæ finis imponatur. Si mihi dicatur, Deum creaturum vel creasse rem quandam, quæ, etiamsi omnes cæteræ præter illam in nihilum redigerentur, subsisteret tamen: conceptus quem habeo ex hac occasione est conceptus substantiæ, sed tamen non possum inde certo scire, an illa res sit corpus, vel mens, extensa vel cogitans, non concipio ideo cogitationem, vel extensionem à Deo productam, conceptus meus de illa re est indifferens ad recipiendum pro sui complemento ideam cogitationis, vel ideam extensionis, & eatenus ad neutram est determinatus. Et substantia dicitur incompleta hoc sensu, qui non respicit rem in se, nulla enim res à Deo producta est extra conceptum meum, quæ existens, sit indeterminata ad cogitatio-nem vel extensionem, & quæ neutram involvat, quæque conceptui illi meo generali respondeat; sed ad conceptum solum, eumque imperfe-ctum, refertur. Cum vero dico, Mens est substantia, substantiæ voce aliud jam significo quam me concipere Mentem esse quid indifferens ad recipiendum extensionem vel cogitationem, & neutram involvere: sed voce ea designo aliquid reipsa existens extra conceptum, atque cogita-tione præditum. In priori sensu cogitatio differt à substantia, sed hoc in conceptu, non in re ipsa, hoc est, quando attendo ad cogitationem, alio modo cogito quam quando attendo ad substantiam priori modo sumptam: conceptus sunt differentes & diversi: plus concipitur in uno quam in altero. In posteriori vero, Cogitatio est substantia, hoc est, in ipsa re non est ulla diversitas inter illam rem cogitantem quæ cæteris rebus deficientibus subsistere potest, & Cogitationem. Illa res est ipsis-sima cogitatio. adeo ut absurdum sit quærere aliud quid subsistens, & quidem diversi generis. Quod autem dicitur, substantiam per se non cognosci, sed per attributa, imo sola accidentia nosci, ut quidam volunt, unde concludunt Cogitationem non esse Substantiam ipsam, utpote quæ facile noscatur; facile solvi potest si ad jam dicta attendatur: verum est cum quis substantiam in priori & generali sensu concipit, eum non ideo cognoscere esse extra se rem determinatæ naturæ, cogitantis vel extensæ, ut exemplo visum est; verum etiam est, cogitationem non esse talem substantiam generalem & abstractam, adeoque hoc modo sub-stantiam (Specialem) non cognosci per se (per generalem substantiæ conceptum) : At cum cogitatio sit substantia certa, & determinata, in sensu posteriori, omnino falsum est talem substantiam per se non cognosci, sed sola accidentia: idem enim est acsi diceres, mentem seu Cogitatio-nem (simile de corpore dixeris) ut talem, ut substantiam specialem & certam non cognosci, non cognosci per conceptum de se; vel tanquam accidens cognosci. Quin potius accidentia, utpote indefinita, non ita facile ut suæ substantiæ cognoscuntur, neque per se cognoscuntur, sed in omni accidentis conceptu necessario conceptus substantiæ, etsi indirecte, involvitur, ut in conceptu figuræ vel motus subest notio extensionis. Hinc nova ratione potest evinci cogitationem esse Mentis substantiam, si nempe in percipiendis modis sive accidentibus Mentis, ut judicare, negare, tristari, sperare, metuere, ratiocinari de quibusvis, quæratur conceptus subjecti cui hi insunt modi, quique hisce conceptis ne-cessario adest: nam præter Cogitationem nullum invenietur; estque proinde illa Mentis Substantia.
units.tr: II. The difficulty lies in this: when men wish to conceive substance precisely and in general, nevertheless, because that concept is incomplete, they either unwillingly slip into attending to substance in its species, to which they then wish to add thought; it is evident that the concept of that substance, considered before the attribution of thought, was the concept of body. For there is no special substance, or one really existing, distinct from thought, apart from body. And to this pertain those absurd demands that the nature not of thought but of substance be explained, that is, of that trunk or stock distinct from thought in which thought is. It must therefore be noted, lest anyone become entangled in these snares of words, that the name substance is used in different ways: sometimes it denotes a concept of a thing that is incomplete, and sometimes a complete one, or the thing itself as it exists outside the concept. So that these matters may not evaporate into excessive subtleties, they will be grasped more easily by examples, by which an end may be put to all verbal wrangling. If it is said to me that God will create or has created some thing which, even if all the others besides it were reduced to nothing, would nevertheless subsist: the concept I have from this occasion is the concept of substance, but I cannot therefore know with certainty whether that thing is a body or a mind, extended or thinking. I do not conceive thought, or extension, to have been produced by God; my concept of that thing is indifferent to receiving, as its complement, the idea of thought or the idea of extension, and to that extent it is determined to neither. And substance is said to be incomplete in this sense, which does not regard the thing in itself, for no thing produced by God exists outside my concept which, existing, is undetermined to thought or extension, and which involves neither, and which corresponds to that general concept of mine; rather it is referred only to the concept, and that imperfect. But when I say, the Mind is a substance, by the word substance I now signify something other than my conceiving the Mind to be something indifferent to receiving extension or thought, and involving neither; rather by that word I designate something really existing outside the concept and endowed with thought. In the former sense thought differs from substance, but this is in the concept, not in the thing itself; that is, when I attend to thought, I think in a different way than when I attend to substance taken in the former way: the concepts are different and diverse; more is conceived in one than in the other. In the latter sense, however, thought is substance; that is, in the thing itself there is no diversity between that thinking thing, which can subsist when all other things are wanting, and thought. That thing is most truly thought itself, so that it is absurd to seek some other subsisting thing, and indeed of a different kind. As for the claim that substance is not known through itself but through its attributes, or indeed only through its accidents, as some wish, whence they conclude that thought is not substance itself, inasmuch as it is easily known; this can easily be resolved if attention is paid to what has already been said. It is true that when someone conceives substance in the former and general sense, he does not thereby know that there is outside himself a thing of determinate nature, thinking or extended, as was shown by the example; it is also true that thought is not such a general and abstract substance, and so in this way substance (specific) is not known through itself (through the general concept of substance). But since thought is a certain and determinate substance, in the latter sense, it is wholly false that such a substance is not known through itself, but only through accidents: for it is the same as if you were to say that the mind or thought (you may say the same of body) is not known as such, as a specific and certain substance, is not known through its concept of itself; or is known only as an accident. Rather, accidents, being indefinite, are not so easily known as their substance is, nor are they known through themselves; but in every concept of an accident the concept of substance is necessarily involved, though indirectly, as in the concept of figure or motion there underlies the notion of extension. Hence it can be proved by a new method that thought is the substance of the Mind, namely if, in perceiving the modes or accidents of the Mind, such as judging, denying, being saddened, hoping, fearing, reasoning about anything whatever, the concept of the subject in which these modes inhere is sought, and this concept necessarily involves the concept of thought: for besides thought no other will be found; and that is therefore the substance of the Mind.

units.la: III. E dictis clarum est, quomodo intelligendum sit illud quod dif-ficultatem pariebat, scilicet, Cogitatio est in substantia, nempe ita: Conceptui generali substantiæ debet addi conceptus cogitationis ad re-præsentationem naturæ Mentis, vel, ut conceptus iste sit conformis rei (Menti) extra conceptum existenti: non vero ita quasi putare debere-mus, rem seu substantiam primo existere, deinde superindui cogitatione tanquam aliquo ab ea diverso, cum cogitatio sit ipsissima illa substantia, quæ solo concursu Dei & nulla plane re creata, eget ad existendum; quæque cum per se subsistat, nullo, præter se, subjecto in quo sit, indiget.
units.tr: III. From what has been said it is clear how that which caused the difficulty is to be understood, namely, thought is in substance; that is, to the general concept of substance there must be added the concept of thought, as a representation of the nature of the Mind, or so that this concept may conform to the thing (the Mind) existing outside the concept. It is not, however, that we should think, as if the thing or substance first existed and then were clothed with thought as with something distinct from it; since thought is that very substance itself, which needs nothing but the concurrence of God and no created thing at all in order to exist; and which, since it subsists through itself, needs no subject in which it is, apart from itself.

units.la: IV. Igitur ridiculus fuerit, qui quasi hanc sententiam de cogitatione quæ sit ipsa substantia, ludibrio expositurus, has voces, substantia quæ cogitat, hac paraphrasi, Cogitatio quæ cogitat, inverteret: Cum, si habeatur respectus ad conceptum substantiæ indeterminatum, ut primo monitum, hoc sit idem ac, conceptus substantiæ indeterminatus ex se cui superadditur conceptus cogitationis ad ejus complementum & determinationem; si vero ad rem ipsam extra conceptum, tunc unum & idem eæ voces significent, ita ut non sit opus unius reduplicatione; Si denique ad utrumque, perinde sit ac, res quæ cogitat, vel, Cogitatio, non debet concipi ut accidens sive modus qui non subsistat nisi in alia re creata, sed ut ens ab omni alia creatura in existendo independens. In quibus omnibus nil absurdi. Taceo posse etiam cum ratione dici, Cogitationem cogitare, per id intelligendo, perceptionem, quæ ex natura sua non est determinata ad certa objecta, sese ad illa determinare, adeoque singulares perceptiones producere; nec non cogitationem esse in cogitatione, hoc est, cogitationem quamlibet particularem non alia de causa in nobis esse, quam quia una in nobis est perceptio in qua omnes subsistunt. Sed de verbis satis hactenus.
units.tr: IV. Therefore he would be ridiculous who, as if to make mockery of this opinion that thought is substance itself, would invert the words "substance which thinks" into this paraphrase, "thought which thinks". For if regard is had to the concept of indeterminate substance, as was first noted, this would mean: an indeterminate concept of substance in itself, to which the concept of thought is added for its completion and determination; if however regard is had to the thing itself outside the concept, then these words would signify one and the same thing, so that there is no need for the one to be repeated; and if finally regard is had to both, it would amount to: the thing which thinks, or thought, must not be conceived as an accident or mode which does not subsist except in another created thing, but as a being independent in existence from every other creature. In all of which there is nothing absurd. I pass over that it can also be rightly said that thought thinks, understanding by this a perception which, by its nature, is not determined to certain objects, determines itself to them, and so produces particular perceptions; and also that thought is in thought, that is, that any particular thought is in us for no other reason than that there is in us one perception in which all subsist. But enough has been said about words so far.

units.la: V. Scrupulus quintus rem ipsam tangit, non voces solas. Certum enim est, Mentis rem sive substantiam, sive naturam, non esse Cogitationem si vel per momentum Mens sine Cogitatione exstitit. Sed negamus Mentem à[?] quo est creata unquam fuisse non-cogitantem, etenim cum non sit nihil, cogitationem si tollas, nil superest quod de ea affirmes, adeoque hoc ipso eam in nihilum redigis. Quid enim cogitatione sublata restat quod menti assignes? in primis tanquam ejus essentiam? Facultas cogitandi, dices. Bene, si per facultatem illam intelligas potentiam determinandæ Cogitationis existentis ad varia objecta: sed hoc ipsum dicit cogitationem actu esse, quod enim non est, determinari nequit à se aut ab alio. At si eo velis mentem cogitatione actuali destitui, posse vero certo tempore, aliquave occasione eam recuperare, insignificantia loqueris. Nam quodlibet existens aliquid actu possidet, aut ipsum est nihil: nec satis est potentia possidere, cum illud nil reipsa possideat quod sola potentia, quæ actum excludit, aliquid possidere dicitur. Asserere vero Mentem actu possidere ipsam cogitandi facultatem, idem ef-set, ac si de corpore affirmaretur, id extensionis facultate, non autem extensione ipsa, esse præditum. Quippe notandum est omnem facultatem supponere aliquid reale & existens actu, in quo illa resideat, nisi libeat ipsi nihilo facultates tribuere: & quid aliud est facultas si in re ipsa extra conceptum spectetur, nisi ipsa res variabilis? quid est in corpore facultas recipiendi figuras, nisi ipsa extensio, quatenus varie terminari apta est? quid facultas cogitandi, nisi ipsa cogitatio, quatenus ad varia objecta, & variis modis, potest applicari? An aliud in re ipsa concipi potest? aut illud si concipias, effer iis verbis quæ aliquid certi & clari significent: certum enim est nil diversi sine nugis allegari posse.
units.tr: V. The fifth scruple touches the thing itself, not merely the words. For it is certain that the thing or substance of the mind, or its nature, is not thought if the mind existed without thought even for a moment. But we deny that the mind, from the moment it was created, was ever non-thinking. For since it is not nothing, if you take away thought, nothing remains of which you could affirm anything; and so by this very act you reduce it to nothing. For once thought is removed, what is left that you could assign to the mind? Above all, as its essence? "The faculty of thinking," you will say. Well, if by that faculty you mean the power of determining an existing thought to various objects, then this very thing says that thought is actual, for what does not exist cannot be determined either by itself or by another. But if by this you mean that the mind is deprived of actual thought, yet can recover it at a certain time or on some occasion, you are speaking meaninglessly. For whatever exists either actually possesses something, or it is nothing. Nor is it enough to possess something potentially, since that which possesses nothing in reality is not said to possess anything by mere potency, which excludes actuality. Moreover, to assert that the mind actually possesses the faculty of thinking would be the same as if it were affirmed of a body that it is endowed with the faculty of extension, but not with extension itself. Indeed it must be noted that every faculty presupposes something real and actually existing in which it resides, unless one is pleased to attribute faculties to nothing. And what else is a faculty, if it is viewed in the thing itself apart from our concept, than the thing itself as variable? What is the faculty of receiving figures in a body, except extension itself, insofar as it is apt to be variously bounded? What is the faculty of thinking, except thought itself, insofar as it can be applied to various objects and in various ways? Can anything else be conceived in the thing itself? Or, if you conceive something else, express it in words that signify something certain and clear; for it is certain that nothing different can be alleged without trifling.

units.la: VI. Fortassis vero contingeret, ut quidam ex iis qui mentis naturam in Cogitatione, quæ semper adsit, poni audirent, sibi imaginarentur hoc esse interpretandum de sublimibus meditationibus, aut discursibus, res hujus mundi, aut forte etiam spirituales, spectantibus: quibus cum destituantur infantes, etiam Mentis natura sic privarentur. Verum enim vero nil opus est ut cogitatio ad hæc objecta & hos modos adstringatur, cum perceptio immediata eorum quæ sunt in nobis non magis denotet meditationes ratiocinationesque exquisitas, quam sensus doloris, voluptatis, gaudii, tristitiæ, amoris, aversationis, colorum, sonorum, saporum & similes, qui omnes in infantulis recens natis, & ex parte in nondum natis, ex occasione corporis ejusque alimenti, oriri possunt. Neque necesse est ad hanc veritatem, ut Mens meminerit se semper cogitasse, sive ut omnium quas unquam habuit cogitationum sit memor: cum nec intellectualium ipsa meminerit, nisi & vivide & diu sese eis applicuerit. nam quod ad eas attinet quæ cum corpore aliquem nexum habent, requiritur ad earum reminiscentiam, ut dum Mens percipit aliquid, advertitque reflectendo super hoc pure & attente id sibi novum esse, utatur cerebro bene parato, firmo & tranquillo, ut vestigia hujus facile impressa constanter serventur. Quapropter non mirum est, si non infantes modo, sed & ipsi viri priorum cogitationum omnium non recordentur, Cum nemo unquam possit omnes unius hebdomatis aut diei, enumerare, etsi certus sit tempus illud cogitando impensum fuisse. Ex his ergo sequitur, actum quidem reminiscentiæ omnium actuum cogitandi non esse Mentis naturam: at eam esse ipsissimam cogitationem manet hactenus inconcussum.
units.tr: VI. It might perhaps happen that some of those who heard that the nature of the mind is placed in thought, which is always present, would imagine that this is to be interpreted as referring to lofty meditations or reasonings about the things of this world, or perhaps even spiritual things; and that since infants lack these, the nature of the mind would be denied to them in the same way. But in truth there is no need for thought to be confined to these objects and these modes, since the immediate perception of what is within us denotes no more exquisite meditations and reasonings than the sensations of pain, pleasure, joy, sadness, love, aversion, colours, sounds, tastes and the like, all of which can arise in newborn infants, and in part even in those not yet born, on the occasion of the body and its nourishment. Nor is it necessary for this truth that the mind remember that it has always thought, or that it be mindful of all the thoughts it has ever had; for it does not even remember intellectual thoughts unless it has applied itself to them both vividly and for a long time. As for those thoughts which have some connection with the body, their recollection requires that, while the mind perceives something and, by reflecting purely and attentively upon it, notices that this is new to it, it make use of a well-prepared, firm and tranquil brain, so that the traces of this impression are easily and constantly preserved. Therefore it is no wonder if not only infants but even adults do not remember all their earlier thoughts, since no one can ever enumerate all the thoughts of a single week or day, even though he is certain that time was spent in thinking. From these things it therefore follows that the act of remembering all the acts of thinking is not the nature of the mind; but that thought itself is its very essence remains so far unshaken.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 1.--13. Demonstratur Cogitationem, sive mentem, & corpus quam maxime inter se distingui. 14.--17. Nullum corpus posse cogitare, etsi ex mente & corpore unum compositum fiat. 18. Usus horum.
units.tr: 1.–13. It is demonstrated that thought, or mind, and body are distinguished as far as possible from one another. 14.–17. No body can think, even if a single composite is made from mind and body. 18. The use of these.

units.la: I. CUm fit demonstratum Cogitationem absque corpore concipi & esse posse, eamque esse substantiam, ultimus evanescit scrupulus, quo dubitabatur, num forte cogitatio à corpore realiter differret, essetve ejus modus aut temperamentum? Num corpus posset cogitare? Sequitur enim ex dictis, Cogitationem substantiam esse quæ non sit corpus, nec corporis modus; & consequenter, inter omnes corporis modos non reperiri cogitationem, hoc est, corpus non posse cogitare. Quia tamen res momentosa est, quæque nonnullos satis molestę exercet, non pigebit id ex professo demonstrare, & differentiæ inter cogitationem sive Mentem, & corpus, limites quasi designare.
units.tr: I. Since it has been demonstrated that thought can be conceived and can exist without body, and that it is a substance, the last doubt vanishes, by which it was questioned whether perhaps thought really differs from body, or whether it is a mode or temperament of body. Could body think? For it follows from what has been said that thought is a substance which is not body, nor a mode of body; and consequently that thought is not found among all the modes of body, that is, that body cannot think. Yet because the matter is weighty, and troubles some people quite a lot, I shall not hesitate to demonstrate this expressly and, as it were, to mark out the limits of the difference between thought or mind and body.

units.la: II. Ut in verborum cum rebus confusione non ludatur. Primo, postulamus ut præter Mentem nil creati existere supponatur, interimque attendatur ad rerum creabilium exemplaria seu ideas in mente existentes: adsunt ideæ conscientiæ intimæ, perceptionis, judicii, affectuum, quæ multis modis variari possunt, sed quæ tamen omnes ad unam reducuntur cogitationem: adsunt ideæ extensionis partibus constantis, quæ si diverse adhærere secundum longitudinem, latitudinem aut profunditatem concipiuntur, figuras varias repræsentant; si vero separari, ortum omnis generis varietatis ostendunt, sed hæc etiam sub una extensionis idea comprehenduntur omnia: Denique sunt & ideæ aliæ quæ ex his duabus, extensionis & cogitationis, videntur ita compositæ, ut neutra separari ab illis possit: exempli causa, idea albedinis (etiamsi extra mentem nil simile existat, ut cum adest in somniis, ac-cidit) cidit) involvit perceptionem, sed & extensionem etiam, quis enim percipiat albedinem sine extensione ? Sic de omnibus coloribus, & sensibus, v.g. de ideis soni, doloris, & similium, quæ percipiuntur non sine relatione ad certum locum seu spatium, remotum aut proxi-mum, ut experiri licet. Et hæ sunt tres generalissimæ omnium de rebus idearum classes.
units.tr: II. So that we are not playing with confusion between words and things, first we ask that nothing created be supposed to exist besides mind, and meanwhile that attention be paid to the exemplars or ideas of creatable things existing in the mind. There are the ideas of inner consciousness, of perception, of judgement, and of the affections, which can be varied in many ways, but which are all reduced to the one thought. There are the ideas of extension consisting of parts, which, if they are conceived as adhering variously in length, breadth or depth, represent various figures; but if they are separated, they show the origin of every kind of variety, yet all these are also comprehended under the one idea of extension. Finally, there are also other ideas which seem to be so composed of these two, extension and thought, that neither can be separated from them. For example, the idea of whiteness (even though nothing similar exists outside the mind, as happens when it is present in dreams) involves perception, but also extension as well; for who could perceive whiteness without extension? So too with all colours and sensations, for instance the ideas of sound, of pain, and of similar things, which are perceived only in relation to a certain place or space, distant or near, as one may experience. These are the three most general classes of all ideas of things.

units.la: III. Secundo, supponamus generalius nos sine ulla specialiori designatione moneri quædam independenter à se invicem è nihilo emer-gere. Cum omnis cognitio rei fiat per ideam propriam reique singula-rem, hic vero ad ideam nullam talem possit præ alia recurri, (nil enim certi determinatur) patet, cognitionem quam hac occasione sumus habituri, redditum iri à nobis incompletam, dum ab omnibus ideis specialibus abstrahemus: quomodo, ut jam dictum, concipiemus non-nihil per se subsistens, hoc est, habebimus substantiæ conceptum, sed ab omnibus ideis recensitis ita abstractum ut nullam involvat, quamvis deinceps, ubi videbimus res ideis repræsentatas existere, conceptus iste omnibus fiat communis: quo sensu poterit dici, plures res, etiam na-turæ diversæ, in unam substantiam, vel potius in unum substantiæ generalem conceptum, convenire, hoc est, ut substantiam concipi. Sed de illa substantiæ unitate inter Cogitationem & extensum non quæri-tur, nec res in se ideo unæ sunt quia uno generalissimo modo conci-piuntur, nihil enim quod incepit esse, est & manet merum esse, sive nil existere potest quod præcise conceptui isti generali respondeat, neque habeat aliquid singularius quo ejus natura constituatur. Quod si quia res conveniunt in uno generali concipiendi modo, ideo unum quid essent dicendæ, multo magis sequeretur, ob diversitatem conceptus res etiam in se debere esse diversas; adeoque cum concipitur de una re, primo quod sit nonnihil, secundo quod sit substantia, tertio quod habeat talem aut talem naturam, quarto quod jam existat, quinto quod duret in existentia, sequeretur inquam, rem unam in tot res secari, & esse à se diversam: quod omnes qui hanc differentiam distinctionem rationis, eo quod sit in solo conceptu, appellant, inficias eunt. Ex his igitur, nil ad rerum unitatem vel diversitatem concludere est.
units.tr: III. Second, let us suppose more generally, without any more particular designation, that certain things are admonished to emerge from nothing, independently of one another. Since every knowledge of a thing comes about through its own idea and the single thing, but here no such idea can be had in preference to another (for nothing certain is determined), it is clear that the knowledge we shall have on this occasion will be rendered by us incomplete, while we abstract from all the special ideas. In this way, as already said, we shall conceive something subsisting through itself, that is, we shall have the concept of substance, but abstracted from all the ideas recounted so that it involves none of them; although afterwards, when we see things existing which are represented by ideas, this concept will become common to all. In this sense it may be said that several things, even of diverse natures, agree in one substance, or rather in one general concept of substance, that is, that they are conceived as substance. But the question is not about that unity of substance between thought and the extended, nor are things on that account one in themselves because they are conceived in one most general mode; for nothing which has begun to be is, and remains, mere being, or nothing can exist which corresponds precisely to that general concept and has nothing more singular by which its nature is constituted. But if, because things agree in one general mode of conceiving, they were therefore to be called one thing, it would follow much more that, on account of the diversity of concepts, things must also be diverse in themselves; and so, when of one thing it is conceived first that it is something, second that it is a substance, third that it has such or such a nature, fourth that it now exists, fifth that it endures in existence, it would follow, I say, that one thing is cut into so many things and is diverse from itself: which all who call this difference a distinction of reason, because it is only in the concept, deny. From these things, therefore, nothing can be concluded concerning the unity or diversity of things.

units.la: IV. Jam tertio supponatur, ut res ipsa est, nos moneri existere revera res in se & extra nos respondentes omnibus istis nostris ideis, quod etiam infantes credidimus, ideis inquam illis quas ante in nobis animadvertimus. Hic quæri debet, nisi ut infantes ab er-rore abripi velimus, An singulis ideis singulæ res respondeant, quæ inter se ita differant, ut quælibet seorsim existat independenter ab alia?
units.tr: IV. Now, third, let it be supposed, as the matter itself is, that we are admonished that there really exist things in themselves and outside us corresponding to all these our ideas, which even infants believed, namely those ideas which we previously notice in ourselves. Here it must be asked, unless we wish to be carried away into error like infants, whether single things correspond to single ideas, which differ among themselves in such a way that each exists separately, independently of the other?

units.la: V. Cui quæstioni ut satisfiat, idearum convenientia & disconvenientia curiosius est advertenda: Deinde videndum, an ex illis de rebus ipsis sit judicandum?
units.tr: V. In order to satisfy this question, the agreement and disagreement of the ideas must be noticed more carefully; then it must be seen whether judgement is to be made from them concerning the things themselves.

units.la: VI. Attendenti ad plures ideas, v. g. cognitionis, dubitationis, affirmationis, negationis, amoris, & similes, omnes eatenus convenire inter se ut sint cogitatio, clarissimum est; ut & disconvenientiam ex eo esse, quod illa una cogitatio diversis tantum modis variata esse concipiatur, nam etsi illa concipi possit absque hoc vel illo modo, tamen non potest de ea negari potentia illos recipiendi, &, si supponatur ut existens, non potest non actu ab aliquo affici, & illa omnibus subest, hinc illam necessario involvunt. Unde, si, (quod deinceps ponetur) de rebus existentibus è conceptu nostro sit judicandum, cum contemplor ideas cognitionis, dubitationis, affirmationis, & cæteras, non inde concludere debeo esse in re ipsa id quod dubitat, id quod cognoscit, id quod affirmat, id quod negat, diversas res existentes, sed unam esse cogitationem, sic diversimode se habentem; ita ut ista non differant in re ipsa inter se & à cogitatione, ut neque etiam in conceptu solo quem de illis habeo, sed in modorum varietate: quæ differentia modalis dicitur, à reali, & ab ea quæ rationis est, distincta. Idem de ideis extensionem involventibus dici potest, de motu, figuris, corporibus singularibus: omnes unius extensionis varie se habentis sunt, nec inter se, & ab illa in re, sed bene in modo, differunt.
units.tr: VI. That all the ideas, for instance of knowledge, doubt, affirmation, negation, love, and the like, when attended to, agree among themselves so far as they are thought, is most clear; and that their disagreement consists in this, that this one thought is conceived as varied only in different modes. For although it can be conceived without this or that mode, yet it cannot be denied of it that it has the power of receiving them, and, if it is supposed to exist, it cannot but actually be affected by something; and this underlies all of them, hence they necessarily involve it. Whence, if (as will be posited further on) judgement is to be made about existing things from our concept, when I contemplate the ideas of knowledge, doubt, affirmation and the rest, I ought not to conclude from this that there are in the thing itself that which doubts, that which knows, that which affirms, that which denies, as diverse existing things, but that there is one thought, variously disposed in this way; so that these do not differ in the thing itself among themselves and from thought, nor even in the concept alone which I have of them, but in the variety of modes: which is called a modal difference, and is distinct from the real and from that which belongs to reason. The same can be said of ideas involving extension, of motion, figures, and individual bodies: they are all of one extension variously disposed, and they differ not among themselves and from it in the thing, but well in mode.

units.la: VII. Præterea, cum attendo ad unam cogitationis variabilis ideam, concipio non modo unam cogitationem posse existere quæ ad hujus exemplar sit, sed etiam ita multiplicari posse, ut plures numero Mentes, sive res cogitantes, existant, quarum cum quamlibet per eandem Cogitationis ideam (quæ essentia substantiæ ejus dicitur) concipiam, non puto quidem eas essentia, sive idea naturæ, inter se differre: attamen, quia concipio unamquamque ex numeratis exstituram etiamsi cæteræ reliquæ in nihilum redigerentur, moneor illas res esse inter se diversas res, quapropter illas inter se realiter, non vero essentialiter dif-ferre, concludere debeo.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, when I attend to one idea of a variable thought, I conceive that not only can one thought exist which corresponds to this exemplar, but also that it can be multiplied so that several minds, or thinking things, in number exist; and though I conceive each of them through the same idea of thought (which is said to be the essence of its substance), I do not indeed think that they differ among themselves in essence, or idea of nature; yet, because I conceive that each one of those counted would exist even if the rest were reduced to nothing, I am warned that they are things diverse among themselves, and therefore I ought to conclude that they differ among themselves really, but not essentially.

units.la: VIII. Denique cum duas prædictas[?] ideas, ad quas omnes ultimo reducuntur, cogitationis scilicet & extensionis, ad unam ita reducere tento, ut quælibet id quod in ea præcipuum concipitur, retineat, quemadmodum factum est cum ideam cognitionis, aut affirmationis, reduxi ad Cogitationem nihil ei detrahendo, aut cum ideam cognitionis cum idea dubitationis eatenus vidi convenire ut retineret utraque id quod in illis est præcipuum, nempe cogitationem; plane id deprehendo esse impossibile. Si abstraho à cogitatione & extensione, fit quidem conceptus communis utriusque incompletus, & qui nil in re quod sibi præcise respondeat notare potest: at quod cogitatio qua talis cum extensione qua tali conveniat, non capio. Concipio seorsim cogitationem absque extensione, & viceversa: concipio utramque diversam ab altera, imo ea negata: concipio eas ut modificatas, v. g. Cogitationem de Deo, reflexionem super meam perceptionem; extensionem mille ulnarum, motum circularem, & sic de cæteris, non solum tanquam diversas, verum etiam oppositas & contrarias, ut in risum subitum fere solvar cum talia unum quid esse fingi posse puto. Hinc judico, si tales res, cogitatio nempe & extensio, extra conceptum meum existentes, putandæ sint esse ideis perceptis similes, non tantum eas differre realiter, ut modo de duabus pluribusve mentibus inter se dixi, quia nempe sunt res plures; sed etiam, quæ omnium maxima est distinctio, eas essentialiter, essentia substantiæ suæ, distingui, cum utraque per diver-sam & oppositam plane ideam, adeoque essentiam, debeat concipi. Adverto tamen fieri posse, ut cogitatio & extensio, quæ essentia & re, in se & in modis suis differunt, ita conveniant, ut posita quadam variatione in cogitatione, eodem tempore sequatur variatio in extensione, & vicissim; ita ut simul earum modi certi varientur, ponantur, cessent: imo, concipio facile esse Cogitationum sive Mentium Authori, ut velit nullam de novo Cogitationem vel Mentem ponere, nisi certum quoddam extensum certis modis disponatur. Quæ si fiant, nihilominus percipiam res eas semper realiter & essentialiter manere distinctas, quanquam tunc sint unum quid compositione, hoc est, unum compositum, quia simul ponentur, simulque ponent variationes, ut unius variatio sit ponenda cum alterius variatione, quod rerum essentiam non mutat. Atqui horum omnium claras ideas in me habeo, hæc clarissime & valde distincte omnia percipere & concipere mihi sum conscius.
units.tr: VIII. Finally, when I try to reduce the two aforesaid ideas, to which all are at last reduced, namely thought and extension, to one, so that each retains what is conceived in it as chief, as was done when I reduced the idea of knowledge or of affirmation to thought, taking nothing away from it, or when I saw the idea of knowledge agree with the idea of doubt so far that each retained what is chief in them, namely thought; I plainly find this to be impossible. If I abstract from thought and extension, there results indeed an incomplete common concept of both, which can denote nothing in the thing that precisely corresponds to it; but I do not grasp how thought as such agrees with extension as such. I conceive thought separately without extension, and conversely; I conceive each as different from the other, indeed as negated by it; I conceive them as modified, for example, thought of God, reflection upon my own perception; extension of a thousand ells, circular motion, and so on for the rest, not only as diverse, but also as opposed and contrary, so that I am almost moved to sudden laughter when I think that such things can be feigned to be one thing. Hence I judge that if such things, thought and extension, are to be thought of as existing outside my concept, and similar to the perceived ideas, they differ not only really, as I just said of two or more minds among themselves, because they are plainly several things; but also, which is the greatest distinction of all, they differ essentially, in the essence of their substance, since each must be conceived through a completely diverse and opposed idea, and therefore through a diverse essence. I observe, however, that it may happen that thought and extension, which differ in essence and in reality, both in themselves and in their modes, so agree that, when a certain variation is posited in thought, at the same time a variation follows in extension, and conversely; so that at once certain modes of them are varied, posited, or cease. Indeed, I conceive it to be easy for the Author of thoughts or minds to will not to posit any new thought or mind, unless a certain extended thing is disposed in certain modes. If these things come about, nevertheless I shall perceive that those things always remain really and essentially distinct, although they are then one thing in composition, that is, one composite, because they are posited together and together they posit variations, so that the variation of one is to be posited together with the variation of the other; which does not change the essence of things. And yet I have clear ideas of all these things in me; I am conscious that I perceive and conceive all these most clearly and very distinctly.

units.la: I X. Jam ubi suppono me moneri res ideis respondentes existere, debeone de illarum inter sese distinctionibus & convenientiis judicare secundum illa quæ mox in illarum idearum differentiis & convenientiis clare percepi? At quis de hoc dubitet? cum sit notio omnium intima, prima, certissima, qua negata, omnia quæ de me, de Deo, de mundo, de fide & revelatis tenentur, indiscriminatim negantur. ideo enim te-nentur, quoniam illorum ideae clare, vivide, distincte, concipiun-tur. Unde scio cogitationem non esse laternam? unde demonstravero Deum mundumque existere; putabo coelum ingens non esse aquae gut-tulam; si illud audiendum sit, haec quidem in intellectu bene ita se habere, at non in re ipsa? Imo, unde scio in me revera esse cogitatio-nem quam percipio? Si res aliter esse potest quam percipitur eviden-ter, ergo ego percipiens me cogitare possum tamen re ipsa in hoc ipso esse non cogitans: quod strenue falsum se prodit: nam eo ipso quo negarem in me esse cogitationem, etsi eam percipiam, actus cogitatio-nis, nempe ipsa negatio, in me poneretur. Sed cum omnes omnino homines intime persuasi sint possibile esse, ut de rerum differentiis, sal-tem generalioribus recte judicetur; velim scire, an illud fieri debeat sine perceptione, vel contra perceptionem, vel secundum illam? Primum est ignorantia & temeritas; secundum, error & absurdum; restat igi-tur tertium, ut ipsa rerum differentia mihi eo perspecta fit. Atqui illa ipsa quibus res inter se differunt non sunt formaliter in mea cogitatione, sed in rebus ipsis; & nihil de rebus doceor nisi per ideas, quae rerum vices gerunt: etiam quae in sensibus (unde aliqui rerum distinctionem hauriunt) Mentem meam proxime feriunt, ideae sunt: remittor igitur ad idearum perceptiones, inter quas quin clarae & distinctae obscuris & confusis sint praeponendae ubi judicandum est, nullum dubium me-rito esse potest.
units.tr: IX. Now, supposing that I am warned that things corresponding to the ideas exist, ought I to judge of the distinctions and agreements between those things according to what I have just clearly perceived in the differences and agreements of those ideas? But who could doubt it? For this is the most intimate, first and most certain notion, and if it is denied, everything that is held concerning myself, God, the world, faith and the things revealed is denied indiscriminately. They are held for this very reason: that their ideas are conceived clearly, vividly and distinctly. Hence how do I know that thought is not a dream? How shall I demonstrate that God and the world exist? Shall I think that the vast heaven is not a drop of water? If one must listen to that, these things are indeed well arranged in the intellect, but not in reality itself? Indeed, how do I know that the thought which I perceive really exists in me? If a thing can be otherwise than it is clearly perceived, then I, perceiving that I think, could nevertheless in reality not be thinking in this very act. That is plainly shown to be false, for by the very act by which I should deny that thought exists in me, although I perceive it, the act of thinking, namely the denial itself, would be posited in me. But since all men have been thoroughly persuaded that it is possible to judge rightly of the differences of things, at least of the more general ones, I should like to know whether this ought to be done without perception, or against perception, or according to it? The first is ignorance and rashness; the second, error and absurdity; there remains therefore the third, that the very difference of things be made plain to me by that perception. But those very features by which things differ from one another are not formally in my thought, but in the things themselves; and I am taught nothing about things except through ideas, which take the place of things. Even those things which strike my mind most closely through the senses (from which some draw their notion of the distinction of things) are ideas; I am therefore referred back to the perceptions of ideas, and among these there can be no reasonable doubt that clear and distinct ideas are to be preferred to obscure and confused ones when judgment is to be made.

units.la: X. Itaque redeo ad idearum mearum contemplationem & comparationem: & cum illas satis diuque expendi, animadverto, quaecunque de distinctione modali inter cogitationem & suos modos, item quae de reali inter plures Cogitationes sive Mentes, quaeque similiter itidem de extensione dicta sunt, ita plane esse debere in rebus ipsis: & de his non est magna difficultas. At ut, quod praecipuum est, sciam quae sit di-stinctio inter Cogitationem, seu Mentem, & Extensionem, sive cor-pus (voces has nobis unum esse, dictum saepe, quae si cuidam displi-ceant, cum aliis permutentur) diligentius utriusque ideas intueor, quas sive comparem, sive separem, sive ad unam tantum attendam altera semota, vel etiam, si fieri posset, deleta; tamen non minus bene clare & complete utramvis concipio. Ita, ex una parte contemplor ideam cogitationis ejusque modorum seu variationum secundum ob-jecta varia, ut sunt, conceptus de Deo, de se, de aliis quamplurimis; & secundum facilitatem aut difficultatem sese cum objectis jungendi, quod ad voluntatem aut habitus spectat, ad amorem, odium, & similia. His dimissis, clare inspicio extensionem, inque ea variationes in-numeras, prout partes quæ in ea diversimode adhærent vel separantur (quod cum extensione Principium Physicæ est, seu causa diversitatum omnium quæ in omnibus sunt corporibus). Deinde hæc comparo: Sed tum, quanta dissimilitudo! Cogitatio non est extensio. Cogitare non est extendi vel moveri, seu separare partes. Cogitatio Mentis meæ imperfectæ de Deo perfecto, vel de alio præstantissimo objecto, non est motus celer extensionis parvæ ad extensionem magnam. attentio defixa in objectum, & adhæsio rei extensæ ad aliquam rem extensam, plane diversa sunt. Amor, odium, &c. non sunt admotio vel separatio variarum extensionum: subjectum quod illis modis variatur, cogitatio est, (Phantasma vocet Hobbius, vel aliud quid si velit) non extensio. Sic, extendi, esse parvum, crassum, hoc vel illo modo figuratum, moveri per hos vel illos meatus, concipio plane aliud esse quam cogitare, idque hoc vel illo modo, esse hujus vel istius ideæ conscium. Hæc, & ejusmodi quamplurima, plus toto cœlo differentia concipiuntur: adeoque de rebus quæ per illas repræsentantur sequentia concludo.
units.tr: X. I therefore return to the contemplation and comparison of my ideas; and when I have weighed them sufficiently and long, I notice that whatever has been said about the modal distinction between thought and its modes, likewise about the real distinction between several thoughts or minds, and similarly about extension, must plainly be so in the things themselves; and about these there is no great difficulty. But in order that I may know, which is the chief point, what the distinction is between thought, or mind, and extension, or body (these terms, as has often been said, are for us one and the same; if they displease anyone, let them be exchanged for others), I look more carefully at the ideas of each; whether I compare them, or separate them, or attend to one alone with the other set aside, or even, if it were possible, destroyed, I conceive each no less clearly and completely. Thus, on the one hand, I contemplate the idea of thought and its modes or variations according to its various objects, such as the concept of God, of self, and of very many others; and, according to the ease or difficulty of joining itself to objects, which pertains to the will or to habits, to love, hatred and the like. Setting these aside, I clearly inspect extension, and in it innumerable variations, according as the parts that adhere in it in different ways are joined or separated (which, together with extension, is the principle of physics, or the cause of all the diversities that are in all bodies). Then I compare these things: but then, what a dissimilarity! Thought is not extension. To think is not to be extended or moved, or to separate parts. The thought of my imperfect mind about the perfect God, or about another most excellent object, is not a swift motion of a small extension to a large extension. Attention fixed upon an object, and the adhesion of an extended thing to some other extended thing, are plainly different. Love, hatred, etc. are not the approach or separation of various extensions: the subject which is varied in those modes is thought (let Hobbes call it phantasm, or anything else he likes), not extension. So, I conceive that to be extended, to be small, thick, shaped in this or that way, to be moved through these or those passages, is plainly something other than to think, and to be aware of this or that idea in this or that way. These and very many similar things are conceived as differing by far more than the whole heaven; and therefore I conclude the following about the things that are represented through these ideas.

units.la: XI. Primo, Cogitatio sive Mentis substantia est essentiæ ab exten-sione vel materia maxime distinctæ, atque adeo, quod illuc redit, non est materialis, sed immaterialis. Quid enim in illarum ideis commune? an repugnat unam sine altera concipere, vel etiam concipere alterutram existere sine socia? Certe minus absurde judicaveris cœlum esse terram, & ignem aquam, & corpus hominis vitreum, & arborem urbem Ro-mam, & triangulum circulum esse, quam cogitationem esse materialis naturæ. Ista enim jam in instantiam allata, re ipsa distingui dicuntur, nec tamen alia de causa quam quod unum sine aliis concipiatur, & utro-bique aliquid sit quod commune non est, utut quamplurima communia habeant, exempli gratia, quod sint extensa, sint mobilia, sint figura prædita, aliaque ejusmodi. Quid ergo de cogitatione & de corpore, in quorum ideis omnia plane sunt diversa, & nihil omnino commu-ne est?
units.tr: XI. First, thought or the substance of mind is of an essence most widely distinct from extension or matter, and therefore, which comes to the same thing, it is not material but immaterial. For what is common to their ideas? Is it contradictory to conceive one without the other, or even to conceive either of them existing without its companion? Certainly you would judge with less absurdity that heaven is earth, and fire water, and the body of a man glass, and a tree the city of Rome, and a triangle a circle, than that thought is of a material nature. For those things, once brought forward as examples, are said to be really distinct, and yet for no other reason than that one is conceived without the others, and in each there is something that is not common, although they have very many things in common: for instance, that they are extended, that they are movable, that they are endowed with figure, and other things of this kind. What then of thought and body, in whose ideas all things are plainly different, and nothing at all is common?

units.la: XII. Secundo, sequitur cogitationem distingui ab extensione ejus-ve modis, magis quam una Mens ab alia numero Mente distincta sit: sive, magis abesse a Mente mea ut sit materialis vel sit aliquid corporis mei, quam abest ab anima Johannis ut sit Anima Pauli. Patet ex dictis duas mentes realiter distingui, seu esse duas numero res, nec tamen essentia differre, cum etsi una sine altera possit concipi & existere, tamen utraque concipi non possit nisi per unam eandemque cogitationis ideam: at res cogitans & res extensa non tantum seorsim concipiuntur ut exi-stentes; sed etiam si utramque velim concipere prout in se est, necessa-rio ideae diversae naturae adhibendae sunt, nec una id complete effici potest. Est igitur major distinctio inter quodcunque corpus & mentem meam, quam solum inter duas aliquas res.
units.tr: XII. Second, it follows that thought is distinguished from extension and its modes more than one mind is distinct from another mind in number; or, that my mind is further from being material or being any part of my body than it is from the soul of John being the soul of Paul. It is clear from what has been said that two minds are really distinct, or are two things in number, and yet do not differ in essence, since although one can be conceived and exist without the other, yet neither can be conceived except through one and the same idea of thought. But a thinking thing and an extended thing are conceived not merely separately as existing; and even if I wish to conceive each as it is in itself, ideas of diverse nature must necessarily be employed, and one cannot accomplish this completely. There is therefore a greater distinction between any body whatever and my mind than there is merely between any two things whatever.

units.la: XIII. Sequitur tertio, Cogitationem magis à corpore differre quam ab ipso nihilo: Sive, magis abesse à Mente ut sit materialis, quam ut sit nihil; & extensionem sive naturam corpoream magis quam ipsum nihil ab ejus natura esse removendam. Respectu quidem substantiae genera-lissime conceptae non magis differt cogitatio à corpore quam à nihilo: hoc est; convenientius asseritur cogitationem habere id commune cum corpore, quod sit aliquid per se subsistens, quam ut ea dicatur esse nihil. At si respiciatur ad res ipsas quatenus una est Cogitatio, altera vero ex-tensio, illa ab hac magis abest quam à nihilo, & haec magis de cogitatio-ne neganda est quam ipsum nihil. Olim Cogitatio creata omnis fuit ni-hil, jam ejus essentia cum nihilo eatenus stat sive de nihilo participat, quatenus non est summum Ens, estque de Ejus essentia, utpote crea-ta, ut in illa imperfectiones, quae sunt nihil, quamplurimae involvan-tur: impossibile enim est ut habeatur Mentis creatae idea, quin nihil, hoc est imperfectio, ei essentialiter involvatur. At quis ferat dicentem extensionis, materiei, corporis ideam, ideae cogitationis ejusque va-riationum ita involvi, ut hanc sine illa concipere sit impossibile? Quin potius, contrarium est attendenti verissimum. Magis igitur cogitatio à materia quam à nihilo differt, quemadmodum aliquid magis ab oppo-sito distinguitur quam à diverso, scientia magis ab errore quam ab igno-rantia, via vera magis à contraria quam à statione quieta vel à via sim-pliciter deviante, denique ut virtus magis à vitio remota est quam ab in-fania, vel stupiditate, aut somnolentiae statu.
units.tr: XIII. It follows, third, that thought differs from body more than it differs from nothing itself; that is, my mind is further from being material than from being nothing; and extension, or the corporeal nature, must be removed from its nature more than nothing itself is. Indeed, with respect to substance conceived most generally, thought does not differ from body more than from nothing: that is, it is more fittingly asserted that thought has this in common with body, that it is something subsisting through itself, than that it is said to be nothing. But if one looks at the things themselves, insofar as one is thought and the other is extension, the former is further from the latter than from nothing, and the latter must be denied of thought more than nothing itself is. Formerly every created thought was nothing; now its essence stands with nothing, or partakes of nothing, insofar as it is not the highest Being, and in its essence, as created, many imperfections, which are nothing, are involved: for it is impossible that an idea of a created mind be had without nothing, that is imperfection, being essentially involved in it. But who would tolerate someone saying that the idea of extension, of matter, of body is so involved in the idea of thought and its variations that it is impossible to conceive the one without the other? Rather, the contrary is most true to one who attends to it. Therefore thought differs from matter more than from nothing, just as something is distinguished more from its opposite than from what is merely different, science more from error than from ignorance, the true way more from the contrary than from a quiet standing still or from a way that simply goes astray; and finally, as virtue is further removed from vice than from insanity, or stupidity, or the state of drowsiness.

units.la: XIV. Concluditur quarto, Nullum corpus posse cogitare; hoc est, quaecunque intelliguntur per corpus & per ea quae sunt in illo, qualia sunt, extensio, quantitas, figura, motus, quies, situs partium, & quaecunque ex his complicatis diversimode oriuntur, non habent in se, in sua essentia, sive natura, quicquam ejus quod ut cogitatio concipitur: nam in sua idea nihil tale continent. Sola attentione opus est. Da extensioni quaslibet figuras & partes, coacerva, compinge, move, divide, comminue, & ut dicam, subtilisa, ideone cogitationem adesse concipiendum est? Si crassam sumas materiae massam, eique figuram ali-quam quam, veluti rotundam, aliamve assignes, an hujus gratia cogitabit ? Negas. Quod si des aliam mixtam magis, si figuram humani corporis ejusque membrorum & vasorum omnium extus & intus ei dare tibi esset concessum, concipis ne idcirco illam molem esse cogitaturam ? Vel, si ad subtiliorem materiam recurrere placet, si moles æque crassa ac prior, dividatur deinde in partes decem, vel viginti, hacne de causa eam cogitare opinaberis ? si in mille, in myriadas innumeras, quantumvis subtiles, figura motuque ad placitum præditas; si omnia hæc subtilissima agillimaque in vasa massæ prioris infundas, ita ut per ea, per cerebri anfractus & vias, hoc vel illo modo, in rectum, in obliquum, inter hæc corpora, hos parietes, potius quam inter alia insinuentur, & motitentur, unde motus membrorum externe sequatur, an jam hoc ipso aderit cogitatio ? Eccur quæso infinitæ partes istius materiæ, spirituum nempe animalium, quæ ex corpore continuo evaporant, ut fit, & in aëra disperguntur, non cogitabunt etiam ? nempe quia forte inter extensum alio modo dispositum (aërem videlicet) & motu forte magis recto aguntur, cæteræ autem quæ inibi manent partes, quia inter aliud extensum (cerebrum scilicet) alia via, & motu magis forsitan obliquo moventur, ideo cogitabunt, conscia erunt sui, Dei, rerum quamplurimarum, judicabunt, amabunt, sperabunt, virtutibus vitiisve pollebunt ! Quis unquam Deum, cum is injungit ut se contemplemur, noscamus, laudemus, amamus, arbitretur hisce nos jubere ut sanguis noster, ejusve subtilissima portio tali vel alio temperamento sit præditus, tenuis sit aut crassior, agilis aut lentus, multus vel paucus, & ut hoc vel alio modo moveatur aut quiescat ? Id de omnibus cogitationibus, cum omnes sint ejusdem naturæ quæri etiam potest. Ecce, quam obnoxiæ sint stultitiæ hominum mentes, cum fere omnes à teneris talia spectra cudant, & adultæ foveant, vixque magno cum labore tandem dimittant.
units.tr: XIV. We conclude fourthly that no body can think; that is, whatever is understood through body, and through those things that are in it, such as extension, quantity, figure, motion, rest, the situation of parts, and whatever arises in various ways from these combined, does not have in itself, in its essence or nature, anything of that which is conceived as thought. For in their idea they contain nothing of the kind. Only attention is needed. Give extension whatever figures and parts you like; heap them together, join them, move, divide, grind, and, so to speak, refine them: is it therefore to be conceived that thought is present? If you take a thick mass of matter and assign to it some figure, say round, or another, will it think on that account? You deny it. But if you grant another, more mixed, and it were allowed you to give it the figure of the human body and all its members and vessels outside and inside, do you conceive that the mass would therefore think? Or, if you prefer to have recourse to a finer matter: if a mass as thick as the former is then divided into ten or twenty parts, will you suppose on that account that it thinks? If into a thousand, or into countless myriads, however fine, endowed with figure and motion at will; if you pour all these most subtle and most agile things into the vessels of the former mass, so that through them, through the windings and passages of the brain, they are insinuated and moved in this or that way, straight or oblique, between these bodies, these walls, rather than between others, and from this the external motion of the limbs follows: will thought then be present by this very fact? Why, I ask, should the infinite parts of that matter, namely the animal spirits, which evaporate continually from the body, as happens, and are dispersed into the air, not think as well? Namely, because perhaps they are moved by a rather straight motion among the extended thing disposed in another way (namely the air), while the other parts which remain there, because they are moved in another way and perhaps with a rather oblique motion among another extended thing (namely the brain), therefore they will think, will be aware of themselves, of God, of very many things, will judge, will love, will hope, and will be endowed with virtues or vices! Who ever supposes that God, when he enjoins us to contemplate, know, praise and love him, is commanding us in these things that our blood, or some most subtle portion of it, be endowed with this or that temperament, be thin or thicker, agile or sluggish, abundant or scant, and be moved or at rest in this or that way? This question can also be asked about all thoughts, since all are of the same nature. Behold how liable the minds of men are to folly, since almost all from their tender years forge such phantoms, cherish them when grown, and scarcely with great labour at last let them go.

units.la: XV. Atqui, dices, notatum est supra quasdam in Mente esse ideas quæ cogitationem & extensionem ita involvant, ut neutra à socia divelli possit, ut cum dolorem, cum colorem, cæterasque sensuum ideas sentio, aut etiam imaginor, occurrit perceptio quædam cum extensionis confusa designatione. Cur igitur non judicaremus in re ipsa existere aliquid isti ideæ simile, id est, extensum simul & cogitans ? Nonne præterea videmus animalia quæ sola materia constant, his sensibus esse præ-dita ? eaque ex illis in quibus sanguis est nobilior, & vasa concinnius elaborata, ita industria esse, ut puriori forte cogitatione imbuantur ? Quid, quod & inter homines ii minus bene cogitent quorum cerebella contumax vapor ex atra bile labefactat, vel humor nimius emollit, quorum sanguis solito crassior vel tenuior, lentior vel concitatior, abundantior vel parcior est? Nonne haec arguere videntur, vel cogitationem à materia pendere, vel in multis esse unum quid cum illa? Respondeo, ideas sensuum non esse datas ut sint exemplaria naturae rerum, ut mille experimentis evinci potest, sed ideas intellectus: tametsi sensuum ideis sua, ut videbitur, respondeat veritas. Intellectu autem clare percipimus cogitationem solam, & corpus solum, seorsim; unde distinctas esse res conclusimus: concipimus evidenter motum cum extensione necti, atque adeo, non esse res diversas, quod pariter de amore cum cogitatione valet: at, quod cogitatio & extensio sint inseparabiles & unum quid, non intelligimus. Secundo, intelligimus fieri posse ab authore omnium, ut in Mentis perceptione variationes dentur certo & simul cum certa aliqua massa diversimode variabitur: attamen quamvis illae variationes simul occurrant, & simul illarum sim conscius, percipio nihilominus rerum variatarum essentiam diversam, ut prius, non vero unam fore idcirco, siquidem ideae cogitationis & extensionis semper diversae sint.
