Jam tertio intelligo, doctus sensuum experimentis, id fieri non modo posse sed & ita se habere: nam cum simul variationis cogitationis & extensionis sensus in me ponatur talis, qui nil clare mihi proponens, confusissime etsi vivide, subindicat commodum vel incommodum commune rei extensae & cogitantis ex alterutrius dispositione; cum videam talem tamque vividam perceptionem in cogitatione mea non esse nisi simul cum tali extensionis sensu & perceptione; denique cum sciam me ex ideis de rebus debere judicare, atque Authorem mei non esse fallacem, qui posuerit in me frustra illarum idearum nexum, utut confusum; concludo, ita etiam rem se habere extra conceptum meum, ut quaedam massa revera ponatur cujus dispositio commoda vel incommoda cum cogitationis sensu commodo vel incommodo nectatur, id est, scio me habere corpus; uti & alia dari judico, sed quae mecum non ita arcte uniantur, quia habeo perceptiones extensionem involventes quas ut extra molem meam sentio; ac denique cum corpus meum somno subsidere, & tamen perceptiones eas, utut dilutiores, & minus similitudinis nexusve cum illis quae vivide & ordinarie mihi obversantur (quod vigiliam à somniis discriminat) me habere attendo, animadverto id, ex cujus immediata variatione variatur perceptio mea, non esse ex eorum numero quae externa sunt, neque id tam totam corporis mei esse molem, quam ejus partem, quae ut in Capite à me percipitur.
units.tr: XV. But, you will say, it has been noted above that certain ideas in the Mind so involve thought and extension that neither can be separated from its companion: when I feel, or even imagine, pain, colour, and the other ideas of the senses, a certain perception occurs together with a confused designation of extension. Why then should we not judge that something similar to that idea exists in the thing itself, that is, something extended and at the same time thinking? Do we not moreover see that animals which consist of matter alone are endowed with these senses, and that those in whom the blood is nobler and the vessels more elegantly wrought are so industrious that they are perhaps imbued with a purer thought? What of the fact that among men those think less well whose little brains are weakened by a stubborn vapour from black bile, or softened by excess of humour, whose blood is thicker or thinner than usual, slower or more agitated, more abundant or scarcer? Do not these things seem to prove either that thought depends on matter, or that in many cases it is one thing with it? I reply that the ideas of the senses are not given so that they may be patterns of the nature of things, as can be shown by a thousand experiments, but the ideas of the intellect; although the truth of the sensory ideas corresponds to them, as will be seen. Now by the intellect we clearly perceive thought alone and body alone, separately; whence we have concluded that the things are distinct. We evidently conceive that motion is bound up with extension, and so they are not different things; the same holds equally of love and thought. But that thought and extension are inseparable and one thing, we do not understand. Second, we understand that it can be brought about by the author of all things that variations are given in the perception of the Mind and are varied in a certain way together with a certain mass; yet although those variations occur together, and I am conscious of them together, I nevertheless perceive that the essence of the varied things is different, as before, and that they will not for this reason be one, since the ideas of thought and extension are always different. Now thirdly, I understand, taught by the experiments of the senses, that this not only can be so but also is so: for since in me there is set up a sense of the variation of thought and extension together, which, presenting nothing clearly to me, but very confusedly though vividly, indicates the common advantage or disadvantage of the extended and thinking thing from the disposition of one or the other; since I see that such a vivid perception in my thought is not present except together with such a sense and perception of extension; and finally, since I know that I ought to judge of things from ideas, and that my Author is not deceptive, who would have placed in me in vain a connection of those ideas, however confused: I conclude that it is also so outside my conception, that some mass is really set up whose advantageous or disadvantageous disposition is bound up with an advantageous or disadvantageous sense of thought; that is, I know that I have a body; and I judge that others are also given, but which are not so closely united with me, because I have perceptions involving extension which I feel as outside my mass; and finally, since I attend to the fact that my body sinks into sleep, and yet I have those perceptions, however fainter and with less likeness or connection to those which present themselves vividly and ordinarily to me (which distinguishes waking from dreams), I notice that that thing, from whose immediate variation my perception varies, is not among those that are external, nor is it so much the whole mass of my body as that part of it which is perceived by me in the head.

units.la: XVI. Atque adeo conclusio, quæ quinta est, ex præcedentibus hæc sequitur, Cogitationem & extensionem unum esse, non re & essentia quæ diversissime intelliguntur, sed compositione, existentia simultanea, & quatenus ponuntur simul extensionis & cogitationis quædam variationes, quæ simul & uno actu sentiuntur, & imaginatione etiam capiuntur. Et hoc ipsum est quod nos docent ideæ illæ sensuum, imo & imaginationis, in quibus perceptio & extensio confuse, sed & indivulse complicantur. Sic igitur judicium de rebus illis fit conformiter cum ideis quas sensu percipimus, & nihilominus cogitationis essentia ab omnis corporis natura quam remotissima est. De brutis autem, quod in iis ad-vertimus non cogitationes sunt, sed motus, nec hi illis similes quos à cogitatione imperatos in nostro & aliorum corpore animadvertimus esse certissima cogitationis indicia; sed omnino brutos, sine ullius ideæ per-ceptione à sola materiæ dispositione oriundos, ut evidentissime Carte-sius de Homine, & Forgeus in suis ad illum notis, demonstrarunt.
units.tr: XVI. And so the conclusion, which is the fifth, follows from what precedes: that thought and extension are one, not in thing and essence, which are understood as most diverse, but in composition, simultaneous existence, and insofar as certain variations of extension and thought are posited together, which are felt together in one act and are also grasped by imagination. And this very thing is what those ideas of the senses, indeed of the imagination, teach us, in which perception and extension are confusedly, yet inseparably, combined. Thus the judgement about those things is made in conformity with the ideas we perceive by sense, and nevertheless the essence of thought is as remote as possible from the nature of every body. Concerning brutes, however, what we notice in them are not thoughts but motions, nor are these like those motions which, commanded by thought, we notice in our own and others' bodies, which are most certain indications of thought; but brutes altogether, without the perception of any idea, arise from the mere disposition of matter, as Descartes most evidently demonstrated concerning Man, and Forgeus in his notes on him.

units.la: Quod si maxime contendas in brutis cogitationem dari, vel perceptio-nem, idque tibi concederetur, nil tamen pro cogitationis materialitate, ut sic loquar, concluderes, sed omnino sequeretur, vi præcedentium, eam cogitationem fore substantiam essentia à corpore distinctam: quale principium nec adesse, nec debere adesse brutis, probatu est facillimum. Instantia de hominibus pro diverso corporis temperamento diverse co-gitantibus, nil aliud evincit, quam diversimode variari cogitationem pro corporis variationibus multiplicibus, ita ut si hæ in corpore ejusve humoribus sint lentæ, crassæ, confusæ, turbulentæ, vel contra, ordi-natæ, faciles, agiles; mentis cogitationes etiam varientur modo len-to, confuso, stupido, inordinato, aliisque, qui cum mutatione corpo-rea habeant nexum: quemadmodum ex varia dispositione characterum quorumdam externorum, varie in nobis cogitationes sequuntur, veræ, falsæ, dubiæ, sublimes, leves, lætæ, tristes, nec tamen characteribus istis facultatem cogitandi inesse judicamus; ita de corpore judicandum est. nec refert si characteres dicantur à cogitatione sic esse dispositi: nam ut manet nihilominus cogitatio ab illis distincta, sic & à corpore; ut ne dicam Cogitationem Divinam sic corpora quævis ordinasse, & præterea leges tulisse de nexu cogitationis cum illorum diversis motibus variandæ.
units.tr: But even if you strongly insist that thought, or perception, is found in brutes, and that were granted to you, you would still not conclude anything for the materiality of thought, so to speak. Rather, it would follow, by the force of what has gone before, that this thought would be a substance essentially distinct from the body. It is very easy to prove that such a principle neither is nor ought to be present in brutes. The instance of men who think differently according to the different temperament of their bodies proves nothing more than that thought varies in various ways as the body undergoes its manifold changes: if the humours of the body, or of its fluids, are sluggish, thick, confused and turbulent, or on the contrary orderly, easy and nimble, then the thoughts of the mind also vary, becoming slow, confused, dull, disordered and so on, which have a connection with the bodily change. Just as, from the varied arrangement of certain external signs, various thoughts follow in us, true, false, doubtful, lofty, light, joyful, sad, yet we do not judge that these signs possess the faculty of thinking, so the same judgement must be made of the body. It makes no difference if it is said that the signs are so arranged by thought: for thought remains nonetheless distinct from them, and likewise from the body; not to mention that the divine Thought has so ordered all bodies and, moreover, has laid down the laws by which thought is to vary in connection with their different motions.

units.la: XVII. Diutius immorati sumus huic materiæ de distinctione rei cogitantis à re extensa, quod cum magni momenti esse videatur, etiam evidenter sit asserenda, ut factum arbitror. Quod si nonnullis placet ulterius verbis contendere, his unum adhuc considerandum est, nempe non multum esse verbis attendendum in hoc negotio, sed ideis, praesertim simplicioribus, completioribus & primariis, circa quas attendat an res sub harum una vel pluribus concipiat? Si quis enim dicat, Cogitationem esse cum corpore unam substantiam, differre autem ab illo modaliter; isque per substantiam intelligat conceptum istum generalem entis per se existentis, qui ad Mentem & ad corpus referri potest, placeat vero illi, contra usum communem, modum appellare cogitationem qua conceptus ille impletur ut mentem repraesentet, non adeo repugnandum est, dummodo sola nomina ex usu recepto deturbet, nec ipsas res ideo confundat. Etenim nihilominus sequetur, illud, quod vocat modum, cogitationem scilicet, & ex parte altera extensionem, inter se non convenire, nisi quatenus sunt aliquid per se, differre autem ita, ut concipiatur utrumque, & cognoscatur, plane diversum ab altero, illo etiam sepposito, & negato. unde concluditur illa duo, quocunque insignian-tur nomine, tantum inter se distingui, quantum ulla res ab alia distincta esse concipi possit. Appellet, si lubet, cogitationem materialem: si dicat se hac nova nomenclatura exprimere pro materiae cujusdam variatione cogitationem variari multis modis, efficiatque ut alii hanc vocem admittant, gratulandum ipsi; sin vero ideas rei cogitantis & extensae necessario & essentialiter unam esse sic velit prodere, proprio conceptui repugnat.
units.tr: XVII. We have dwelt rather long on this matter, the distinction of the thinking thing from the extended thing, which, since it seems to be of great moment, I think has been asserted clearly enough, as indeed it has. But if some are pleased to contend further about words, one thing more must be considered: namely, that in this business we ought not to attend much to words, but to ideas, especially the simpler, fuller and primary ones, on which we should fix our attention, asking whether a thing is conceived under one or several of these. For if someone says that thought and body are one substance, but differ from it modally, and by substance he understands that general concept of a being existing through itself, which can be referred both to the Mind and to the body, and if he is pleased, contrary to common usage, to call modus that thought by which that concept is filled up so as to represent the mind, we need not greatly object, provided he only overturns the names from accepted usage and does not on that account confound the things themselves. For nonetheless it will follow that what he calls the mode, namely thought, and on the other side extension, do not agree with each other except insofar as they are something in themselves, and they differ in such a way that each is conceived and known to be plainly diverse from the other, even when the other is set aside and denied. Hence it is concluded that those two, however they are marked by name, are distinguished from each other only as much as any thing can be conceived as distinct from another. Let him call it, if he likes, material thought; if he says that by this new nomenclature he expresses that thought varies in many ways according to the variation of some matter, and brings it about that others admit this term, he is to be congratulated; but if he wishes thereby to declare that the ideas of the thinking thing and the extended thing are necessarily and essentially one, he contradicts the proper concept.

units.la: XVIII. Nil ad complementum capitis hujus adderetur, nisi quod cum antehac sit notatum, ex substitutione corporalium sive per sensum sive per imaginationem, pro intellectualibus, sequi in praxi, in Mentis erga Deum regimine, in modo quo Deum colere plurimi putant, foedam depravationem, videretur jam uno verbo monendum, quomodo possit ostendi ex observato inter Cogitationem & corpora omnia discrimine, id esse evitandum. Nam quod de rei cogitantis a rei extensae differentia dictum est, id, caeteris paribus, de modorum utriusque rei inter se distinctione est dicendum: certum autem est Mentes & corpora cum ad Deum referuntur naturam seu essentiam suam non deponere, sed ea retenta, alio modo se habere, vel modos novos acquirere, quos cum essentia sua congruere verum est. Igitur cum superstitiosus vel forte infirmus aliquis, corporea & externa, motus, verba, & similia, pro divinis internis & spiritualibus amplectitur, deviat: Nam quemadmodum Mens a corpore quammaxime distincta est, ita mentis modi (inter quos ea sunt quae vere spiritualia & interna sunt) a corporis modis, ab externis omnibus, etiam quamlongissime differunt: & quemadmodum Mens magis differt à corpore quam ab alia Mente, ita etiam vere spiritualia magis ab externis corporeis differunt quam à Scientia Mathematica, hæc enim eatenus cum spiritualibus convenit quod sit in cogitatione: sed non ita est de externis, quæ re & essentia differunt. Imo, prout Mens magis differt à corpore quam à nihilo, ita & spiritualia magis à corporeis quam à pura externorum ignorantia & non-observantia. Cumque corpora nulla cogitare possint, ita nulla externa si sola & in se spectentur, unquam eo/devenient ut pro eis quæ vere & proprie spiritualia sunt & in se divina, possint haberi: nam quod Deo, in genere rerum spiritualium, gratum esse potest, ab alio est quam ab externo. Attamen, qua ratione Mentem non vult ponere Author omnium nisi corpus certum ponatur prius, nempe ob placitum suum, non vero quod utriusque rei natura hoc secum inferat; eadem is ordinarie disponit, ne divina interna, ne spirituales operationes ponantur, nisi adsint externa, neque tamen vi eorum ponuntur internæ spiritua-lesque operationes, nec cum illis necessarium & in rebus ipsis funda-tum nexum habent, sed omnis efficacia nexus in Dei placito est. Præ-terea, sicuti posita Mente, tum demum corporea ab illa percipiuntur, iisque Mens utitur dum se & alios docet, adhibendo illa tanquam si-gna & monitoria quibus cogitata in se & in aliis excitentur, imo dispo-nendo de illis ita sapienter, ut facile judicatur ab aliis qui simile quid ex-periuntur, Mentem cum illis externis eorumve principio materiali, cor-pore nempe, unum quid componere, etsi utrumque naturam suam non-confusam seorsim retineat; idem plane est de spiritualibus inter-nisque operationibus cum intus adsunt, tunc enim prosunt externa, ju-vant, monent & signant; nec fieri potest quin mens de omnibus ex-ternis in quæ valet, ita disponat, ut facile futurum sit, non quidem terrestribus brutisque mentibus, sed spiritualibus, judicare, vere adesse spirituale principium externo isti regimini, ita ut hoc cum illo unum quid constituat, unum nempe verum cultum, non obstante separatio-ne seu distinctione quæ est equidem in natura extremorum, non vero in positione eorum simultanea quamdiu mentes pure spirituales non eri-mus. Plura, eaque egregia deduci hinc possunt ab iis qui rem cum præ-dictis considerabunt attentius.
units.tr: XVIII. Nothing would be added to the completion of this chapter, except that, since it has been noted above that the substitution of bodily things, whether through sense or through imagination, for intellectual things, leads in practice, in the government of the mind towards God, and in the manner in which most people think God should be worshipped, to a foul depravation, it seems now that it should be advised in a single word how, from the observed distinction between thought and all bodies, this may be shown to be avoided. For what has been said of the difference between the thinking thing and the extended thing is, other things being equal, to be said of the distinction between the modes of each thing: and it is certain that minds and bodies, when they are referred to God, do not lay aside their nature or essence, but, retaining it, are disposed in another way or acquire new modes, which indeed agree with their essence. Therefore, when some superstitious or perhaps weak person embraces bodily and external motions, words, and the like, in place of divine, inward and spiritual things, he goes astray. For just as the Mind is most widely distinct from the body, so the modes of the mind (among which are those things that are truly spiritual and inward) differ far more widely from the modes of the body, from all external things. And just as the Mind differs more from the body than from another Mind, so truly spiritual things also differ more from external bodily things than from the science of mathematics; for the latter agrees with spiritual things in this, that it is in thought; but it is not so with external things, which differ in thing and in essence. Indeed, as the Mind differs more from the body than from nothing, so spiritual things differ more from corporeal things than from the mere ignorance and non-observance of external things. And since bodies cannot think anything, so no external things, if they are considered alone and in themselves, will ever come to be held as those things which are truly and properly spiritual and divine in themselves: for what can be pleasing to God in the genus of spiritual things is from something other than the external. Yet, by the same reasoning by which the Author of all things does not wish to place the Mind unless a certain body is placed first, namely on account of his good pleasure, and not because the nature of each thing brings this with it, he likewise ordinarily arranges that the divine inward things and spiritual operations are not placed unless external things are present; nor, however, are the inward and spiritual operations brought about by the force of those external things, nor do they have with them a necessary connection grounded in the things themselves, but all the efficacy of the connection lies in God's good pleasure. Moreover, just as, the Mind being placed, bodily things are then perceived by it, and the Mind uses them while it teaches itself and others, employing them as signs and reminders by which thoughts are stirred up in itself and in others, indeed disposing of them so wisely that it is easily judged by others who experience something similar that the Mind together with those external things, or with their material principle, namely the body, makes up one thing, although each keeps its own unconfused nature separately; the very same is plainly true of spiritual and inward operations when they are present within: for then the external things profit, help, admonish and signify; nor can it be that the mind, in all the external things over which it has power, so disposes them that it will easily come to pass that, not indeed by earthly and brutish minds but by spiritual ones, it is judged that a spiritual principle truly is present in that external government, so that the one together with the other constitutes one thing, namely one true worship, notwithstanding the separation or distinction which indeed lies in the nature of the extremes, but not in their simultaneous position, as long as we are not purely spiritual minds. Many excellent things can be deduced from this by those who consider the matter more attentively with the aforesaid points in mind.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. 2. 3. In Deo est aliquid Analogum nobiscum, idque est Cogitatio. 4. Refellitur Hobbes negans nos aliquid quod in Deo sit percipere. 5. 6. Demonstratur Essentiam Dei in Cogitatione, verbis specia-lioribus deinceps exprimenda, consistere.
units.tr: 1. 2. 3. There is in God something analogous to us, and this is Cogitation. 4. Hobbes is refuted, who denies that we can perceive anything in God. 5. 6. It is shown that the essence of God consists in Cogitation, to be expressed hereafter in more special terms.

units.la: I. POstquam hucusque Mentis humanæ essentiam esse ipsam Cogitationem ostendimus, restat ut & de Dei essentia probetur, eam esse etiam ipsissimam Cogitationem: quod neminem primo aspectu terrere debet, quasi assereremus hoc modo, vel Mentem creatam Ef-sentia Divina gaudere, vel Deum essentiam cum creata Mente eandem possidere. quod ut à veritate, ita à sensu nostro est alienissimum. Nil aliud verbis istis significari intenditur, præter id ipsum quod omnium ore circumfertur aliis vocibus, dum asserunt omnes Animam humanam Spiritum esse, sive Spiritus natura essentiaque frui; Deum quoque essentia sua Spiritum esse: unde nunquam ab ullo conclusum est, voluisse omnes vel naturam animæ humanæ in Deum mutare, aut Deum in illam. Sic substituta voce Cogitatio pro voce Spiritus, nil aliud hic asseritur, nisi omnia quæ in Mente humana sunt ad cogitationem esse referenda, & Mentem esse illam ipsam cogitationem; omnia etiam quæ in Deo sunt, Cogitationem esse, Deumque id ipsum esse, Cogitationem nempé, sive Perceptionem. At, & ille longe alia alioque modo in se quam in aliis Mentibus percipit, & nos Cogitationem Divinam altioris infinite generis esse percipimus quam nostras: unde infinita noscitur inter illas distantia, quæ post hæc ex sequentibus ita patebit, ut futurum sit, neminem inde conqueri posse Deum cum creatura misceri.
units.tr: I. Now that we have shown so far that the essence of the human mind is cogitation itself, it remains to prove that the essence of God is also most truly cogitation. No one should be alarmed at this at first sight, as if we were asserting either that the created mind shares in the divine essence, or that God possesses the same essence as the created mind. That is as far from the truth as it is from our understanding. Nothing else is intended to be signified by these words beyond what is repeated on everyone's lips in other words, when all affirm that the human soul is spirit, or enjoys the nature and essence of spirit, and that God too is spirit in his essence. From this no one has ever concluded that they meant to change the nature of the human soul into God, or God into it. So, by substituting the word cogitation for the word spirit, nothing else is asserted here than that everything in the human mind is to be referred to cogitation, and that the mind is that very cogitation; and that everything in God is cogitation, and that God himself is that same thing, namely cogitation or perception. But God perceives himself in a manner quite different from other minds, and we perceive the divine cogitation to be of a higher, infinitely different kind than our own. Hence an infinite distance is known to lie between them, which will become so plain from what follows that no one will be able to complain that God is confused with the creature.

units.la: II. Parum refert, ut mihi quidem videtur, multa opera disceptare, an dentur conceptus à Deo & à Creatura ita abstracti, ut possint esse utrique communes, seu de utroque prædicari. Quæ de his multum disputantur obscura sunt, & ob nimiam abstractionem & subtilitatem evanescunt fere. Clarius & firmius res tenebitur, si advertatur, conceptus ipsos non esse rebus communes vel proprios, sed res conceptibus repræsentatas: In conceptuum autem actibus omnibus res non repræsentari ex toto ut sunt, id est, complete. Hinc intellectus noster, qui ob infirmitatem actu uno completum rei statum bene apprehendere nequit, divisis actibus rei illi sese applicat, & , si erga duas res eodem modo versetur, quamvis res illæ diversissimæ sint, tamen ob istam similitudinem, quæ est in modo quo res diversas concipit, dicitur conceptus ille communis, resque dicuntur eodem conceptu apprehendi: atque sic significatur convenientia in modis cogitandi vel percipiendi res diversas. Itaque huc redit tota quæstio, An in modo quo conceptus finitus versatur circa Deum, non sit aliqua similitudo cum modo quo circa res creatas versatur? Quod evidentius est quam ut negari possit. At id, siquidem conceptum ipsum respiciat, nil de re concludit, nisi aliunde in rebus ipsis sit positivum similitudinis fundamentum, sine quo, ipsi conceptus generales qui communes dicuntur, falsi fuerint: nam si nulla plane intercedit similitudo inter objecta, ut inter Deum & nihil, non potest conceptus communis utrisque competere. Igitur ad rerum ipsarum convenientiam redeundum est, unde probetur, quod Dei essentia significanti nomine cum creata mente communi, Cogitatione nempe, non male designata sit.
units.tr: II. It matters little, as it seems to me, whether we spend much effort disputing whether there are concepts so abstracted from God and from the creature that they can be common to both, or predicated of both. What is much disputed on this point is obscure, and almost vanishes on account of its excessive abstraction and subtlety. The matter will be held more clearly and firmly if we notice that concepts themselves are not common or proper to things, but that things are represented by concepts. Now in all acts of conceiving, the thing is not represented from the whole, as it is, that is, completely. Hence our intellect, which on account of its weakness cannot grasp the complete state of a thing in a single act, applies itself to the thing by divided acts; and if it deals with two things in the same way, although those things are very diverse, yet on account of that similarity which lies in the mode in which it conceives diverse things, that concept is called common, and the things are said to be apprehended by the same concept; and thus agreement is signified in the modes of thinking or perceiving diverse things. Therefore the whole question comes down to this: whether in the mode in which a finite concept is directed toward God there is not some likeness to the mode in which it is directed toward created things? This is more evident than that it can be denied. But this, so far as it concerns the concept itself, concludes nothing about the thing, unless there is elsewhere in the things themselves a positive ground of similarity, without which the general concepts which are called common would be false: for if no similarity at all lies between the objects, as between God and nothing, a common concept cannot apply to both. Therefore we must return to the agreement of the things themselves, whereby it is proved that the essence of God is not badly designated by a term common with the created mind, namely Cogitation.

units.la: III. Nam etiamsi, ut deinceps specialius videbitur, nihil de Deo & de creaturis univoce dici possit, sive, quamvis verum sit nihil esse in Deo eo modo quo est in creatura, & vicissim, creaturam nihil possidere eodem modo & sensu quo Deus ipse, est tamen hos inter aliquid analogiæ, seu similitudinis, seu convenientiæ, qualis est inter typum & rem repræsentatam. Nam primo, quæ realia in Mente creata sunt formaliter, ea in Deo sunt non quidem formaliter, hoc est, eadem forma eodemve modo, sunt tamen eminentiori & perfectiori. Secundo, (quod prioris assertionis probationem involvit) quod est in mente creata non formaliter, sed objective, hoc est, quod repræsentatur per perfectissimam perceptionum Mentis specialium sive idearum quas creata contemplatur, id vero in Deo est non modo objective, sed & formaliter, hoc est, Deus revera possidet illas perfectiones quarum ideæ sunt objectum nostræ cogitationis. Atqui quæ realia in nobis sunt formaliter, ea, ut probatum est, sunt cogitatio, perceptio, voluntas: quæ vero realissima in nostris ideis sunt repræsentative, sunt ipsa Cogitatio perfectissima, perceptio voluntasque nullis defectibus obnoxiæ. Inter Deum igitur & inter Mentem creatam non obstante infinita disquiparantia ea est similitudo quæ non potest non iisdem verbis, Cogitationis scilicet, sive perceptionis spontaneæ , efferri ab eo qui Deo omnes perfectiones tribuit. Dicat aliquis, unde scis illa quæ concipis perfectissima de Cogitatione, de Perceptione voluntaria, & si quæ sunt similia, in Deo esse, non autem alia quae tu plane non nosti? Respondeo id probari cum existere probatur: nam per Deum non solet intelligi aliquid quod plane non cognoscitur, sed hoc ipsum quod per ideam de perfectissima cogitatione repraesentatur; aut, si nomen Cogitationis recusas, Res perfectissima, sive omnia perfecta perfectissime possidens, ea est quae per vocem Deus denotatur. Verum illud quod omnia perfectissima possideret, seipsum autem aliquo modo non possideret, perfectissimum non esset: id vero quod se non percipit, suique non est conscium, se plene non possidet: debes igitur necessario concipere, id ipsum, siquidem perfectissimum sit, habere cogitationem, & quidem perfectissimam: qui conceptus cum non potuisset in te poni ab illo qui re illa destitueretur, cumque involvat existentiam, siquidem concipere perfectissimam cogitationem sit concipere existentem cogitationem, determinat te ut judices illam existere. Atqui res esse similes conceptibus & judiciis clarissimis & distinctissimis, primum est cognitum, quo negato, possis concludere te non esse, etiamsi concipias & judices te esse: Datur igitur cum Deo & in Deo Cogitatio quae ipse Deus est.
units.tr: III. For even if, as will be seen more particularly hereafter, nothing can be said univocally of God and of creatures; or, although it is true that nothing in God is in the same way in which it is in the creature, and conversely that the creature possesses nothing in the same way and sense in which God himself does, there is nonetheless between them something of analogy, or likeness, or agreement, such as exists between a type and the thing it represents. For, first, what is really present in the created mind formally, that is in God not indeed formally, that is, in the same form or in the same way, but in a more eminent and more perfect manner. Second (which involves the proof of the former assertion), what is in the created mind not formally but objectively, that is, what is represented through the most perfect perception of the special perceptions or ideas of the mind which the creature contemplates, this in God is present not only objectively but also formally, that is, God truly possesses those perfections whose ideas are the object of our thought. But what is really in us formally is, as has been proved, cogitation, perception, and will; and what are most real in our ideas representatively are cogitation itself in its most perfect form, perception and will free from all defects. Between God and the created mind, therefore, notwithstanding their infinite inequality, there is that likeness which cannot but be expressed by the same words, namely of cogitation, or spontaneous perception, by one who attributes all perfections to God. Someone may say: how do you know that the things you conceive as most perfect of cogitation, of voluntary perception, and whatever else is similar, are in God, and not other things which you do not know at all? I reply that this is proved when existence is proved: for by God we do not usually understand something which is not known at all, but this very thing which is represented through the idea of most perfect cogitation; or, if you reject the name of cogitation, the most perfect thing, or the one possessing all perfect things in the most perfect way, is that which is denoted by the word God. But that which possessed all most perfect things, yet did not in some way possess itself, would not be most perfect; and that which does not perceive itself and is not conscious of itself does not fully possess itself. You must therefore necessarily conceive that this very thing, if it is most perfect, has cogitation, and indeed most perfect cogitation. This concept, since it could not have been placed in you by one who lacked that reality, and since it involves existence (for to conceive most perfect cogitation is to conceive an existing cogitation), determines you to judge that it exists. Now that things are like the most clear and distinct concepts and judgments is the first thing known, and if this were denied, you could conclude that you do not exist, even though you conceive and judge that you do. There is therefore with God, and in God, a cogitation which is God himself.

units.la: IV. Proinde à vero aliena sunt quae periculose, ut fere omnia, docet Hobbius, Nos cum Deo attribuimus ea quae de illo concipimus, non debere putare illis quid sit significari; sed tantum sic nostram admirationem & obedientiam, & humilitatem denotari: Non dari ideam & conceptum Dei, & similia, ex quibus homines à Dei, ut qui non modo ignotus, sed & qui incognoscibilis habeatur, notitia & studio revocantur. Omnia quae absurdis inmixta hinc inde conjicit, saepe refutantur per ea quae ipse iisdem in locis proponit. Exempli gratia, locus unus inter multa, in quo omnes sui hac de re errores breviter recolliguntur, consideretur obiter, qui exstat Cap. xv. §. 14. de Cive. Ibi absurda sunt, quod per Deum intelligi velit id quod concipi non potest; quod per intellectum intelligat tumultum animi suscitatum ab organis externis; per ideam vel conceptum, phantasma imaginarium. Contradicentia his sunt, in Deo esse aliquid voluntati nostrae analogum, nam hoc destruit praecedentia, & adversatur ei quod addit, nos tamen id concipere non posse, cum potius impossibile sit judicare de analogia rerum nisi prius eae concipiantur, tum seorsim, tum junctim, ut quid differant, quidve non, judicetur. Huc spectant quae addit, quando (inquit) dicimus aliquid (Deum scilicet) esse infinitum, non aliquid in re significamus, sed impotentiam in animo nostro, tanquam si diceremus, nescire nos, an & ubi terminetur. Egregia analysis ! Dico Deum esse infinitum ; idem est ac non dico Deum esse infinitum, nescio an sit infinitus, dubito an habeat terminos, & ubi sint, volo hoc respectu esse ignorans. An putat, uti equidem praetendit, sic Deum digne honorari ? Denique se ipsum refutat, 1. Cum de Deo dicit ibidem ea ex quibus sequitur Deum esse Creatorem, Æ-ternum, Omniscium, Rectorem omnium, Omnipotentem, Infini-tum, Immaterialem, Unum, Felicem. 2. Cum ait nos debere eum admirari, eique obedire cum humilitate : nam quid admiraberis sum-mopere id quod non possis affirmare non esse in se rem brutam, sed cogitatione revera præditam ? imo, quæ admiratio Dei hæc est, admiror Deum æternum, maximum, justum, dubito tamen, imo (ut loquitur) nolo dicere eum talem esse, ne limitibus phantasiæ meæ illum circumscribam ? Atqui si Deus non est talis, tunc propria tua fi-gmenta, & te ipsum qui illa cudis, admiraris. Sed & obedientia ex ani-mo, qualem intelligit, non præstatur, nisi ubi sunt leges, leges vero cogitationis signa & effecta sunt : neque etiam coram aliquo humiliter ex animo nos gerimus, nisi judicemus esse eum conscium (cogitantem) suæ Potentiæ & nostræ imbecillitatis. 3. Postremo, cum fatetur unum nomen Naturæ Dei esse significativum, cujus significatum proprie & reipsa in Deo sit, nempe Existens sive Esse vel Est simpliciter, omnia quæ dixit resorbet. Nam nomine hoc, quo Deus ipse suam designat Essen-tiam, omnia includuntur quæ Deo possunt attribui : etenim qui est simplex & merum esse, ei deest nullum esse, nullum purum esse; igitur is non deest sibi ipsi, hoc est, is sui est conscius, sive cogitat. Sic de cæ-teris attributis perfectissimis, quæ hic recensere non est opus, si ipsi ea deessent, non esset utique esse simplex, sed esse imperfectum, compo-situm ex esse & non esse.
units.tr: IV. Accordingly, those things are far from the truth which Hobbes teaches, as he does almost everywhere, dangerously: that when we attribute to God what we conceive of him, we ought not to think that what he is is thereby signified, but only that our admiration, obedience and humility are thereby denoted; that there is no idea or concept of God, and similar things, by which men are called back from the knowledge and zeal of God, as one who is held not only unknown but unknowable. Everything which he mixes in with absurdities here and there is often refuted by the things which he himself sets forth in the same places. For example, let one passage be considered in passing, among many, in which all his errors on this matter are briefly gathered together, which stands in Chapter xv, §14 of De Cive. There the absurdities are these: that by God he wishes to be understood what cannot be conceived; that by intellect he understands a tumult of the mind stirred up by external organs; by idea or concept, an imaginary phantasm. Contradictory to these are the statements that there is in God something analogous to our will, for this destroys what precedes, and conflicts with what he adds, that we nevertheless cannot conceive it, since it is rather impossible to judge of the analogy of things unless they are first conceived, both separately and together, so that it may be judged how they differ and how they do not. To this belong his words: when (he says) we say that something (namely God) is infinite, we do not signify something in the thing, but an incapacity in our mind, as if we said that we do not know whether, or where, it ends. A remarkable analysis! I say that God is infinite; this is the same as not saying that God is infinite, not knowing whether he is infinite, doubting whether he has limits, and where they are, wishing in this respect to be ignorant. Does he think, as he indeed pretends, that God is thus worthily honoured? Finally, he refutes himself: (1) when he says in the same place those things from which it follows that God is Creator, Eternal, Omniscient, Ruler of all, Omnipotent, Infinite, Immaterial, One, Blessed. (2) When he says that we ought to admire him and obey him with humility: for what will you admire greatly, if you cannot affirm that it is not in itself a brute thing, but truly endowed with cogitation? Indeed, what admiration of God is this, "I admire God as eternal, greatest, just, yet I doubt, or rather (as he puts it) I am unwilling to say that he is such, lest I circumscribe him by the limits of my imagination"? But if God is not such, then you admire your own fictions, and yourself who forges them. Moreover, obedience from the heart, such as he understands it, is not rendered unless there are laws, and laws are indeed signs and effects of cogitation; nor do we conduct ourselves humbly from the heart before anyone unless we judge that he is conscious (thinking) of his power and our weakness. (3) Lastly, when he admits that one name of God's nature is significative, whose signification is properly and really in God, namely Existing or Being, or simply Is, he swallows up everything he has said. For in this name, by which God himself designates his essence, all things are included that can be attributed to God; for he who is simple and pure being lacks no being, no pure being; therefore he does not lack himself, that is, he is conscious of himself, or thinks. So too with the other most perfect attributes, which it is not necessary to list here: if these were lacking to him, he would not be simple being, but imperfect being, compounded of being and non-being.

units.la: V. Probatum igitur est, quia id negantes exstiterunt, in Deo esse aliquid conceptibus nostris consonum, idque idea de cogitatione dignissima repræsentari. Unde facile deducitur, Essentiam Dei, atque conceptum quem de Deo possumus habere quam amplissimum, omnia complectentem, ad quem omnia reducantur, ex quo fluant, sine quo non possit concipi Deus, (qui conceptus sane essentiæ conceptus est,) in una Cogitatione Divina quæ à nobis pro modulo nostro concipitur, consistere. Perfectissimæ Cogitationi nihil deest, ergo omnia complectitur, est igitur una Cogitatio omnia. Hinc simplicitas, quæ hoc ipsum est, quamque aliqui ultimum attributum in Deo considerandum esse dicunt, revera primum est, namque ejus cognitio præsupponi debet ante specialem cæterorum cognitionem, & in cujuslibet conceptu involvi, absque quo nullum attributum Deo dignum concipies: quanquam post perlustrationem omnium, denuo possis ad illam attentius & clarius reflectere, quo sensu ultimum attributum eam dixeris. Sed pergimus. Id quod est in Deo omnia, proculdubio est Essentia Dei, Cogitatio igitur est essentia Dei. Ad hanc quæcunque in Deo sunt reducuntur, nulla enim res in Deo est cujus Deus non sit conscius per illam ipsam rem: alioqui darentur in Deo res perceptione destitutæ quas Deus cogitatione ab illis diversa perciperet, res brutæ igitur, & incogitantes, quod blasphemum est, & non Deo, sed imperfecto idolo dignus conceptus. Ex illa etiam cætera fluunt attributa omnia. Posita Cogitatione perfectissima, sequitur eam se ipsam nosse, Intelligentia; se ipsam simul possidere, Æternitas; se ipsa subsistere, sive se ipsam sufficere sibi, Sufficientia, sive Independentia; sibi ipsi acquiescere, Felicitas; se ipsam probare, Justitia, Sanctitas; non frustra aliquid velle seu cogitare, Potentia; & sic de cæteris omnibus. Nega de Deo quæcunque voles, modo unam cogitationem Divinam sive perfectissimam concedas, manent omnia, superest omnium Dei attributorum sufficientissimum fundamentum: at sine illa, non potest ullum concipi Dei attributum, neque ipse Deus. Possum concipere Deum potuisse esse non Creatorem, non Redemptorem, & similia; possum ita concipere unum Dei attributum sine alio attributo, ut in ejus conceptu non insit formaliter conceptus alterius: at impossibile est ut Deum qui sit sine Cogitatione cogitem; impossibile est ut ejus aliquod attributum concipiam in cujus conceptu non sit formaliter cogitatio, cujus basis & fundamentum, ratio positiva, &, si ita loqui liceat, subjectum immediatum, non sit ipsa Cogitatio Perfectissima. Nec video quid ultra requiri possit, ut concludatur, Naturam & Essentiam Dei esse ipsam Cogitationem.
units.tr: V. It has therefore been proved that those who deny this have stood up, since there is in God something agreeing with our concepts, and this is represented by an idea most worthy of thought. From this it is easily deduced that the essence of God, and the concept we can have of God as fullest of all, embracing all things, to which all things are referred, from which they flow, and without which God cannot be conceived (which concept is certainly the concept of essence), consists in one Divine Thought, which is conceived by us according to our measure. A most perfect Thought lacks nothing; therefore it embraces all things; therefore one Thought is all things. Hence simplicity, which is this very thing, and which some say is the last attribute to be considered in God, is in truth the first. For its knowledge must be presupposed before the special knowledge of the others, and it must be involved in the concept of anything, without which no attribute worthy of God can be conceived. Yet after surveying all of them, you may again reflect on it more attentively and clearly, in what sense you may call it the last attribute. But let us go on. That which in God is all things is undoubtedly the essence of God; therefore Thought is the essence of God. To this all the things that are in God are referred, for there is no thing in God of which God is not conscious through that very thing; otherwise there would be in God things destitute of perception, which God would perceive by a thought different from them, therefore brute and unthinking things, which is blasphemous, and a concept worthy not of God but of an imperfect idol. From it also all the other attributes flow. Given a most perfect Thought, it follows that it knows itself, which is Intelligence; that it possesses itself all at once, which is Eternity; that it subsists by itself, or suffices to itself, which is Sufficiency, or Independence; that it rests in itself, which is Happiness; that it approves itself, which is Justice, Holiness; that it does not will or think anything in vain, which is Power; and so on for all the rest. Deny of God whatever you please, provided you grant one Divine or most perfect Thought: all remains, and the most sufficient foundation of all the attributes of God survives. But without it, no attribute of God can be conceived, nor God himself. I can conceive that God could have been not Creator, not Redeemer, and the like; I can conceive one attribute of God apart from another attribute, so that the concept of the other does not formally inhere in its concept. But it is impossible for me to think of God who is without Thought; it is impossible for me to conceive any attribute of his in whose concept there is not formally thought, whose basis and foundation, positive ground, and, if I may so speak, immediate subject, is not the Most Perfect Thought itself. Nor do I see what more can be required in order to conclude that the Nature and Essence of God is Thought itself.

units.la: VI. Abunde monitum est, Cogitationem, cum de Mente Increata & creata prædicatur, in sensu eodem acsi ea utriusque Genus esset, non sumi: verum similitudinem aliqualem sic notari inter res quarum una eminentissimo, altera diminutissimo sensu, voce notantur eadem. Ne vero ob vocis unitatem res ipsæ confundantur, addendæ sunt aliæ voces, non quidem ut per eas, tanquam per differentias, Cogitatio, acsi genus esset, in Deum & creatam Mentem, ut in species quasdam restringitur: Sed ut quod in utraque Mente diversum est, id explicite cum voce quæ ob analogiam communis est, significetur. Est igitur quomodo modo differant inquirendum, vel potius, utriusque natura penitius est inspicienda, & deinde comparanda.
units.tr: VI. It has been sufficiently pointed out that Thought, when it is predicated of the uncreated and the created mind, is not taken in the same sense as if it were a genus common to both. Rather, the same word is used to mark a certain likeness between things of which the one has it in the most eminent sense and the other in the most diminished sense. Yet lest the things themselves be confused because of the unity of the word, other words must be added. These are not meant to restrict Thought, as if it were a genus, into God and the created mind as into certain species, by means of them as differences. Rather, what differs in each mind is to be expressed explicitly, along with the word that is common by analogy. It remains, then, to inquire how the two differ, or rather, the nature of each must be examined more closely and then compared.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: I. 2. Prima inter Cogitationem Creatam & Increatam differentia, cum utriusque definitione & sequelis nonnullis. 3. 4. Secunda itidem proponitur. 5. 6. Tertia: sed omnes generalius.
units.tr: The first difference between created and uncreated Thought, with its definition and some consequences. 3. 4. A second is likewise set out. 5. 6. A third; but all more generally.

units.la: I. PRimo, cum Mentem sive cogitationem meam intueor, deprehendo quidem illam quoad subjectum seu conscientiam ipsam immediatam quae est in nobis, quam liceat appellare materiam sive materiale cogitationis, unam esse; at unam illam esse variabilissimam quoad formas quas successive induit, in percipiendis objectis innumerabilibus, in judiciis, inque passionibus quamplurimis: quae omnia nec simul nec eodem modo percipio, quaeque si ad differentiam cogitationis creatae singulatim essent recensenda, suo numero me obruerent. Adverto tamen omnia illa in hoc unum reduci, ut sint variabilitas cogitandi; ita ut prima notio quam distincte de mente mea, qualis jam est hoc in statu, efformo, haec sit, quod sim Cogitatio variabilis multiplicitate & reduplicatione actuum Cogitandi. Haec est forma prima generalis Mentis creatae, susceptibilitas nempe innumerabilium formarum, sive modorum cogitandi quoad numerum, tempus, & modum. Haec imperfectio omni Menti creatae essentialis est eatenus, ut quanquam in futurum gratia Increatae Mentis fieri possit ut creata mens actu fixetur, ut sic dicam, cum uno objecto, idque uniformiter & constantissime, maneat tamen, tum ejusdem actus repetitio seu successio, vel ejus fundamentum, tum capacitas variationis inconstantis. Ulterius, cum quaero, unde illa in mea Cogitatione variabilitas? Video eam inde esse, quod Cogitatio mea sit limitata, & non omne cogitabile, sed quoddam tantum, una vice complectatur, ita ut si ad aliud attendere velim, prius cessat mente percipi. Hinc quae secundo occurrit notio qua creatam Mentem distinctius novi, est limitatio in Cogitando. Quapropter, quod Mens Creata sit Cogitatio mutabilis & limitata, prima generalissimaque ejus definitio est, & plus negat realitatis quam ponit: neque enim aliter esse potest quin illud quod non est Ens Summum, involvat necessario in natura sua, & proinde in definitione, defectus quamplurimos, quos ei essentiales esse inde patet, quod iis in Cogitatione positis, ponatur eam creatam esse, id vero negetur si ii adesse non posse concipiantur; quodque ab eorum mixtura omnis formarum seu modorum multiplicitas, quos humana mens induere possit, oriatur.
units.tr: I. First, when I look upon my mind or thought, I perceive that, as to its subject, that is, the immediate consciousness itself which is in us, which may be called the matter or material of thought, it is one; but that this one is most variable as to the forms it successively takes on, in perceiving innumerable objects, in judgments, and in very many passions. I do not perceive all of these at once, nor in the same way; and if they were to be recounted one by one in order to distinguish created thought, they would overwhelm me by their number. I notice, however, that all of these reduce to this one thing, that they are the variability of thinking; so that the first notion which I form distinctly of my mind, as it now is in this state, is this: that I am a variable thought, by the multiplicity and repetition of acts of thinking. This is the first general form of created mind, namely the susceptibility to innumerable forms, or modes of thinking, as to number, time and manner. This imperfection is so essential to every created mind that, although in the future, by the grace of the uncreated Mind, it may come about that the created mind is fixed in act, so to speak, upon one object, and that uniformly and most constantly, there nevertheless remains both the repetition or succession of the same act, or its foundation, and the capacity for inconstant variation. Further, when I ask whence this variability in my thought comes, I see that it is because my thought is limited, and does not embrace every thinkable thing at once, but only a certain thing; so that if I wish to attend to something else, the first ceases to be perceived by the mind. Hence the second notion which occurs to me, by which I know the created mind more distinctly, is limitation in thinking. Therefore, that the created mind is a changeable and limited thought is its first and most general definition, and it denies more reality than it posits; for it cannot be otherwise than that what is not the Supreme Being should necessarily involve in its nature, and therefore in its definition, very many defects, which it is plain are essential to it, because when these are posited in thought, it is posited that it is created, and this is denied if they cannot be conceived as present; and from their mixture arises all the multiplicity of forms or modes which the human mind can take on.

units.la: At res aliter se habet in ea Cogitatione quæ Deus est: non enim illa formarum, actuum, successionis, multiplicitate variatur, sed uniformis est, sui ipsius constans forma est (qua voce liceat cum sacris uti), sive mera est Cogitatio omne cogitabile semel & simul complectens, vel, ut opposite ad id quod de creata Mente dictum est definiatur, sive, (ne quis ob vocem definitionis pueriliter rixandi occasionem sumat) notetur, est Cogitatio simplex & infinita. quæ etiam, siquidem illa duo quæ in Mente creata mox notata sunt, in hoc unum conveniant, quod sint defectus, vel non-realitas, ex opposito possit dici una voce, perfectissima, sive realissima Cogitatio.
units.tr: But it is otherwise in that Thought which is God: for it does not vary by a multiplicity of forms, acts, or succession, but is uniform; it is a constant form of itself (a word which we may use with the sacred writers), or it is pure Thought embracing everything thinkable once and at the same time; or, to define it in opposition to what has been said of the created mind, (lest anyone, on account of the word "definition", take a childish occasion for quarrelling), let it be noted that it is simple and infinite Thought. Which also, since those two things just noted in the created mind agree in this one thing, that they are defects or non-reality, can be called by one word, from the opposite, most perfect, or most real Thought.

units.la: II. Ex his patet, in substantia increata omnia esse ipsam substantiam, sive rem ipsam simpliciter: at in Substantia creata, esse quidem aliquid fixum & unum, per quod substantia fixe & constanter à nihilo, & ab alia, si detur, substantia, distinguatur; verum illud fixum, quod est ipsa substantia, cum simpliciter perfectum non sit, debere esse mobile seu variable. quæ varietates modi appellantur. Sic in mente, Cogitatio est illud fixum, quod semper & constanter adest; at illa quot modis variatur & limitatur? In corpore itidem est extensio fixa, sed innumerabilibus modis variata. Patet etiam faciliorem esse Dei Cognitionem, quam creatæ Mentis: nam ut Deus unus noscatur sufficit contemplatio Cogitationis quæ simpliciter, sine ulla limitatione, discriminatione, adjectione, restrictione, est Cogitatio. Cogitatio mera omnia novit simul, omnia complectitur, omnia etiam quæ vult extra se ponit, nam Cogitatio mera cogitat se esse efficacissimam, alioqui hac cogitatione destitueretur, & sic esset in illa non-Cogitatio, nec esset mera Cogitatio; etiam cogitat res esse ut ipsi placet cogitare: nam si aliter essent, determinaretur & variaretur Cogitatio ab externis, & sic non amplius esset merum quid; si vero plane non essent, limitaretur, nam non posset id quod vellet cum veritate cogitare: quod alienum est à Cogitatione mera. (Hoc de Potentia specialius hic monitum est, quia de aliis attributis facilius videre est quod omnia sub Cogitatione una, absolute sic dicta, comprehendantur: & forsan id alibi ostendetur.) At in una Mente creata, hac illave, cognoscenda, quantum difficultatis! studio cavendum est ne quid nimis, vel non satis, ei tribuatur; in limitando & restringendo sudandum est; & cum in Deo noscendo cogitata nostra ruptis omnibus repagulis intrepide effun-dere possimus, hic parce stillandum est: nec etiam quemadmodum in-dividualem Dei cognitionem, cum ille unus sit, dant quæ generalius dicta sunt, ita ad individualem Mentis cujusdam creatæ notitiam, suf-ficit ut habeatur notio Cogitationis variabilis & limitatæ: quamvis enim scias in genere ex ejus limitatione sequi in ea multarum rerum ignorantiam & inconsiderantiam, paucarum vero scientiam; facultates, quæ ipsi tribuuntur, esse, non quid ab illa diversum, sed illam ipsam quatenus consideratur ut à multis causis variabilis vel varianda; actum ei tribuere, nil aliud esse quam eam ut variantem vel dum variatur spectare; habitum, ut jam variatam, & aptam ad actum repetendum: (nam id omne quod his verbis cum ratione designari potest, est ipsa cogitatio sic considerata, unde sequitur id à Deo hoc sensu esse remo-vendum, quod in antecessum ad omnia quæ de Deo dicentur, hic notasse juvet) tamen animus hic non acquiescit ubi de aliqua mente in particulari est quæstio. Iterum limitanda ignorantia, scientia, alia, secundum objecta, aliaque fere infinita; quænam facultates per actus in habitus transfiere; ex actibus & habitibus bonis malisve, qui innu-merabiles sunt, quosque simul habere potest nemo, designandum est quos ex omnibus habeat, ad quem usque gradum, nam variationes eunt quasi in infinitum. Quæ omnia vix ex longissima experientia & familiaritate nota sunt (ut neque etiam requiruntur in vita cum aliis degenda, cum tunc de Mentibus aliorum præsumendum sit, nisi con-trarium pateat, Deum æque in illis ac in nobis bona, vel forte meliora, esse operatum, quod ab amore, non autem à scientia procedit.) Hæc si cum Divinis comparentur, evidentissime evincent, Deum facillime omnium rerum, ipsaque adeo Mente mea, quæ omni corpore notior est, nosci posse.
units.tr: II. From these things it is plain that in the uncreated substance, all is the substance itself, or the thing itself simply; but in created substance there is indeed something fixed and one, through which the substance is fixedly and constantly distinguished from nothing and from another substance, if there is one; yet that fixed element, which is the substance itself, since it is not simply perfect, must be mobile or variable, and these variations are called modes. Thus in the mind, Thought is that fixed element which is always and constantly present; but in how many modes is it varied and limited? In body likewise there is fixed extension, but varied in innumerable modes. It is also plain that the knowledge of God is easier than that of the created mind: for in order to know the one God it is enough to contemplate Thought which is simply, without any limitation, distinction, addition, or restriction, Thought. Pure Thought knows all things at once, embraces all things, and posits outside itself all that it wills; for pure Thought thinks itself to be most efficacious, otherwise it would be destitute of this thought, and so there would be in it non-Thought, and it would not be pure Thought; it also thinks things to be as it pleases to think them: for if they were otherwise, Thought would be determined and varied by external things, and so would no longer be a pure thing; and if they were not at all, it would be limited, for it could not think what it wished with truth, which is foreign to pure Thought. (This has been noted here more specifically concerning Power, because concerning the other attributes it is easier to see that all are comprehended under one Thought, absolutely so called; and perhaps this will be shown elsewhere.) But in one created mind, this or that, to be known, how great is the difficulty! With care one must avoid attributing to it either too much or too little; one must labour in limiting and restricting; and whereas in knowing God we can pour out our thoughts fearlessly, with all barriers broken, here we must drip them out sparingly. Nor, as the things said more generally give the individual knowledge of God, since he is one, so does it suffice for the individual knowledge of some created mind that there be a notion of variable and limited Thought; for although you know in general that from its limitation there follow in it ignorance and inconsiderateness of many things, and knowledge of few; the faculties which are ascribed to it are not something different from it, but it itself, insofar as it is considered as variable, or to be varied, by many causes; to ascribe to it an act is nothing other than to regard it as varying, or while it varies; a habit is to regard it as already varied and apt to repeat the act (for all that can be rightly designated by these words is Thought itself so considered, whence it follows that this must be removed from God in this sense, which it is helpful to have noted here in advance for all that will be said about God). Yet the mind does not rest here when the question concerns some particular mind. Ignorance, knowledge, and other things must again be limited according to their objects, and by many almost infinite things; which faculties pass over from acts into habits; from good and evil acts and habits, which are innumerable, and which no one can have at once, it must be determined which ones one has, and to what degree, for the variations go on as if to infinity. All of these are scarcely known from very long experience and familiarity (nor are they even required in living a life with others, since then one must presume concerning the minds of others, unless the contrary is plain, that God has worked in them as well as in us good things, or perhaps better ones, which proceed from love, not from knowledge). If these are compared with the divine things, they will most evidently show that God can be known most easily of all things, and indeed even my mind, which is better known than any body.

units.la: III. Secundo, ut non tantum generalius Cogitationem meam no-scam per modum negationis quæ est in ejus limitationibus & variationi-bus; sed etiam specialius, per modum affirmationis eorum quæ tan-quam positivum quid in Mente variabili ita sunt, ut cum ejus statu arctius quam cætera omnia nectantur, conabor me omnibus, quantum potero, cogitandi formis exuere, & quamminimum mihi tribuere, ut tandem id realitatis remaneat, quod mihi ex natura status mei creati est intime innatum. Exuo igitur eos cogitandi modos qui sensus externi vocantur, cum dolore, voluptate, & passionibus turbidis cunctis: nam hæc sunt ab alieno, ab extrinseco, ex occasione corporum; corpora vero vel plane non esse, vel saltem me non spectare possunt. Ima-ginationem item semoveo, easdem ob causas. Depono praeterea cogitationes de omni re creata a me realiter diversa, sive Mens ea sit, sive corpus: nam possent illae res non esse, ego vero illarum ideis, prout a me diversae sunt, carere, me nihilominus subsistente. Etiam aversationem, tristitiam, odium, similesque passiones, etsi ut plane spirituales spectatas, sepono: fieri enim potuisset ut nihil exstitisset a quo aversari, ob quod tristari, odisse, opus esset. His dimissis, remanet tamen Cogitatio tendens ad aliquam formam qua impleatur, ad aliquod ubi acquiescat, quae Cogitatio nec sensus, nec imaginatio, nec turbida passio est; id est, supersunt Intellectus & Amor, sive, Quæstio intelligens acquiescentiae: remansit quidem mea etiam Cogitatio ut est objectum sui ipsius, at hoc ipso quo se inspicit, imperfecta ut est, sistitur ei maximum aliud objectum per ideam cogitationis absolute perfectissimæ, Deus nempe, quem non potest non concipere ut existentem, summe potentem, a cujus placito omnia, ipsaque proinde, pendeant: ex cujus comparatione ipsa suæ imperfectionis, quod a se nihil sit, nihil habeat, nihil omnino possit, magis magisque convincitur: Unde si ejus Intellectus & Amor id quod in se est, quatenus a se procedit, velint amplecti, frustrantur, nihil enim a me in me est; si vero in id feruntur quod est a Deo in me, cum hoc se ipso non sit nec subsistat, ducit id hoc ipso ad Deum, perfectissimam potentissimamque Cogitationem, quæ Intellectus & Amoris unum, proprium, realissimum objectum est, quo Intellectus & Amor implentur cum acquiescentia. Exutis igitur, quantum fieri potuit, omnibus formis, remanet in Cogitatione creata, sui quidem forma non considerabilis & æstimabilis; quod nempe ex se sit prorsus nihil; Dei vero forma, seu imago, intellectum & amorem postulans & implens. Atqui hæc est Mentis creatæ dos, qua quid ei vel intimum magis, vel convenientius? ita ut in culpa sint, & contra naturam agant, qui alienis formis cogitationem implendo, hanc, quæ propria est, seponunt: cum hæc tamen necessario involvatur in ea Mentis creatæ definitione, qua quid in ipsa omnium maxime positivum & intimum sit, exprimitur. Scilicet, Mens Creata est Cogitatio intellectu & amore ad Deum tendens cum sui despectu. Ne quis tamen putet tendentem esse denotare hic actum, sed, ut in definitionibus fieri debet, positivam & inseparabilem ab omni creata mente facultatem: nam vel in damnatis, capacitas illa Dei, sed inexpleta, manet, cum fundamento non-acquiescentiae in se, absque quibus nec miserae essent. Nec despectus hic est Mentis improbatio & contemptus quatenus illa opus Dei est, sed est praetermissio, imo rejectio sui ipsius quatenus quaeritur, an ipsa sit objectum cui intellectu & amore acquiescere possit? Non est etiam quod quis definitionem hanc spectet ut Theologicum aliquod consectarium. certe, si quod confidenter pro-ponere ausim [?], illud maxime est, hanc Creatae Mentis (sine relatione ad corpus spectatae) definitionem talem esse, ut magis positiva, simplex, naturalis, adeoque vere Philosophica dari non possit; quod at-tendenti ad modum quo inventa est, fiet evidens, nam profecto haec res, si ulla alia, attentionem meretur.
units.tr: III. Second, so that I may know my thinking not only more generally, by way of negation, in its limitations and variations, but also more specifically, by way of affirmation, I will try to strip myself of all forms of thinking, as far as I can, and to attribute as little as possible to myself, so that in the end there remains that reality which is inwardly innate to me from the nature of my created state. I therefore strip away those modes of thinking which are called the external senses, together with all pain, pleasure and turbid passions: for these come from what is other and external, on the occasion of bodies, and bodies either may not exist at all or at least cannot concern me. I likewise set aside imagination, for the same reasons. I further put aside thoughts of every created thing really distinct from me, whether it be mind or body: for those things might not exist, and I could nonetheless exist while lacking their ideas, insofar as they are distinct from me. I also set aside aversion, sadness, hatred and similar passions, even though they are regarded as purely spiritual: for it might have happened that nothing existed toward which there was need to feel aversion, to be saddened or to hate. With these dismissed, there nonetheless remains a thought tending toward some form by which it may be filled, toward some object in which it may rest; this thought is neither sense, nor imagination, nor turbid passion. That is, there remain the Intellect and Love, or, an intelligent Question of acquiescence. Indeed my thought also remains as the object of itself; but in the very act by which it inspects itself, being imperfect as it is, there is set before it another, greatest object, through the idea of a thought absolutely most perfect, namely God, whom it cannot but conceive as existing, supremely powerful, on whose pleasure all things, and therefore it too, depend. From the comparison with him, it is more and more convinced of its own imperfection, that it is nothing of itself, has nothing, and can do nothing at all. Hence, if its Intellect and Love wish to embrace what is in itself, insofar as it proceeds from itself, they are frustrated, for nothing from me is in me; but if they are carried toward what is in me from God, since this is not and does not subsist by itself, it thereby leads it to God, the most perfect and most powerful Thought, who is the one, proper, most real object of Intellect and Love, by which Intellect and Love are filled with acquiescence. Therefore, with all forms stripped away as far as could be done, there remains in created thought a form of itself which is not considerable or estimable, namely that it is of itself altogether nothing; but the form, or image, of God, demanding and filling the intellect and love. Yet this is the endowment of the created mind: what could be more inward or more fitting to it? So that those are at fault and act against nature who, by filling their thought with alien forms, set aside that which is proper to it, although this is necessarily involved in that definition of the created mind by which is expressed what in it is most positive and most inward of all. Namely: The created mind is a thought tending by intellect and love toward God, with a contempt of itself. Yet let no one think that tending here denotes an act; rather, as must be done in definitions, it denotes a positive faculty, inseparable from every created mind: for even in the damned that capacity for God remains, but unfulfilled, together with the ground of non-acquiescence in themselves, without which they would not be wretched. Nor is this contempt the disapproval and scorn of the mind insofar as it is a work of God; it is rather an omission, indeed a rejection of itself, insofar as it is asked whether it can itself be the object in which intellect and love could rest? Nor should anyone regard this definition as some theological corollary. Certainly, if I may venture to put forward something with confidence, it is chiefly this: that this definition of the created mind (considered without relation to body) is such that a more positive, simple, natural, and therefore truly philosophical definition cannot be given; this will become evident to one who attends to the manner in which it was discovered, for surely this matter, if any other, deserves attention.

units.la: Jam si modo simili Cogitationem quae Deus est, contradistincte ad hanc noscere tento, ipsam etiam concipere possum ut exutam multis formis quae relationem ad externa habent, quales sunt, esse decernentem, Creatorem, Conservatorem, Miseratorem, Redemptorem, Ju-dicem, & similes: nam potuisset fieri ut nulla essent creata & creanda, ad quae haec referuntur; & quamvis adsint, non tamen ei essentialia sunt. At remanet suae ipsius Cogitationis Forma, seu Imago, invariabilis & uniformis, quam Cogitet, & in se esse probet, velit, hoc est, cui per amorem acquiescat; ita ut bene dicatur Cogitatio in notitia suae Formae Amore acquiescens. Quomodo quantum fieri potest complete, genuine & distincte Deum designare datur.
units.tr: Now if, in a similar way, I try to know the Thought which is God, in contrast to this, I can also conceive it as stripped of the many forms that have relation to external things, such as deciding, Creator, Preserver, Merciful, Redeemer, Judge, and the like: for it could have happened that no created or creatable things existed to which these relate; and although they are present, they are not essential to it. But there remains the form, or image, of its own Thought, invariable and uniform, which it thinks, and which it proves, wills, to be in itself, that is, in which it rests by love; so that it may rightly be said: Thought, resting by love in the knowledge of its own Form. In this way it is given to designate God as completely, genuinely and distinctly as possible.

units.la: I V. Certe in his quae de utraque Mente jam dicta sunt, latent quamplurima quae nullius non sunt momenti, e quibus unum aut alterum advertere non fuerit plane fruftraneum: In primis autem Logicam veram in hac denudatione & sejunctione formarum cogitandi, ut eo melius postea unaquaeque valore justo aestimetur, ordine debito reponatur, eique pro merito incumbatur, consistere, ne in nugis & indebitis teratur vita. Non enim est Logice, sive cum ratione agere, primam cogitandi formam quae vel occurrit, vel placet, v. g. de angulis aut circulis, de numeris, de sonis, de sensibilibus, aliisve vitam brutam terrestremque spectantibus, arripere, totamque in istis cogitationem, quanquam cum ordine aliquo, impendere. At omnes primo removere, ut deinde eam quae restat, Dei, tanquam dignissimam amplectamur, & porro ex caeteris quasdam ut accessorium resumere quatenus in dignissima illa fundantur, cum ea nectuntur, ad eam referuntur, ea demum vera & Sacra Logica est quam cum homine Deus condidit. Calamitosum est, homines consumere secula in detegendis, disponendis demonstrandisque corporum formis & proprietatibus, unde naturalem scientiam educerent, ut à Mathematicis aliisque factum est; neminem autem simile quid de formis Cogitationis aggredi, quamvis inde Ethicæ veræ fundamenta, omnisque qui cæterum ab historiis solidior fructus exspectatur, dependeant. Sistitur & illa formarum denudatione species nonnulla nobilis illius abstractionis tantopere à Sanctis commendatæ eis qui ad Deum tendunt. Patet etiam inde quid sit Lex Dei, & quo-modo fundetur illa in natura status Cogitationis creatæ. Quodnam of-ficium Mentis creatæ, Qui nexus mentis cum Deo. Deum in Mente esse quærendum, externaque, ubi illis adhæretur, impedimenta esse. Nexus mentis cum corpore rationem dari non posse ex consideratione Mentis ipsius, vel corporis, sed eam esse à principio alio libere de his disponente. Libertatem Mentis corpore destructo majorem fore quam eo integro: etenim vere tunc, si se antea assuefecerit in Dei contemplatione & amore, in libertatem asseretur[?]. Sed hæc pluraque alia mittimus. Hic certe, si ullibi, ea inveniuntur Dei invisibilia, quæ ab ipso manifestata, ab omnibus videntur qui ea mente perpendunt, ut ait au-thor sacer. Quinimo Mysterium Sanctæ Trinitatis verbis quibus Deus designatus est connotari satis explicite, agnoscent illi qui ea quæ non modo Augustinus, atque post eum plurimi, veluti Mornæus, aliique de hoc mysterio dixere, sed etiam quæ Sacri Authores reliquere, attentius meditabuntur.
units.tr: IV. Certainly, in what has now been said of each Mind, there lie hidden very many things of no small importance, of which it will not be altogether useless to note one or another. Above all, true Logic consists in this stripping and separation of the forms of thinking, so that afterwards each may be more easily valued at its just worth, placed in its due order, and given its proper weight, lest life be wasted on trifles and things out of place. For it is not logical, or acting with reason, to seize upon whatever first form of thought occurs or pleases, for example concerning angles or circles, numbers, sounds, sensible things, or other matters pertaining to brute and earthly life, and to spend all one's thought on these, however orderly. Rather, to remove all forms first, so that then we may embrace that which remains, God, as most worthy, and afterwards to take up certain others from the rest as accessory, insofar as they are grounded in that most worthy one, are bound up with it, and are referred to it: this is the true and sacred Logic which God established together with man. It is a calamity for men to spend centuries in uncovering, arranging and demonstrating the forms and properties of bodies, from which they might derive natural science, as the Mathematicians and others have done; yet no one attempts anything similar concerning the forms of thought, although on these depend the foundations of true Ethics, and whatever more solid fruit is expected from the other studies. By this stripping of forms there is also presented a certain noble kind of that abstraction so greatly commended by the Saints to those who strive toward God. It is also evident from this what the Law of God is, and how it is founded in the nature of the state of created thought. What is the office of the created mind, and what the bond of the mind with God. That God is to be sought in the Mind, and that external hindrances are present where people cling to them. That the bond of the mind with the body cannot be explained from consideration of the mind itself or of the body, but that it is from another principle which freely disposes of these things. That the freedom of the mind will be greater when the body is destroyed than while it is whole: for truly then, if it has previously accustomed itself to the contemplation and love of God, it will be asserted into liberty. But we pass over these and many other things. Here certainly, if anywhere, are found those invisible things of God which, being made manifest by him, are seen by all who consider them with their mind, as the sacred author says. Moreover, those who will meditate more attentively, not only on what Augustine, and after him very many, such as Mornaeus and others, have said about this mystery, but also on what the Sacred Authors have left, will acknowledge that the Mystery of the Holy Trinity is sufficiently explicitly connoted in the words by which God is designated.

units.la: V. Tertio, ut ad propositum redeatur, si specto, unde accidant Cogitationi meæ talia quæ ita limitantur? unde tot formæ? Cur in se non acquiescens ultra se tendit? Video id inde esse, quod à me non sim, nec per me, nec ob me, acsi mihimet essem scopus, nil solidi sim, nec mei ipsius repræsentativum, alioqui quæ in me essent omnia perfecta essent, siquidem non haberent aliud exemplar, alium scopum, quam se, nec à se discederent: Sed quod è contra sim ab alio, per alium, ob alium, umbra quasi & imago alium referens. Ista, quæ-cunque in me sunt permeant, &, ut sic loquar transcendunt, discrimi-nantque Cogitationem meam ab illa Cogitatione quæ talis est qualem dixi, quia à se ipsa est, per se, ob se, solide subsistens, & sui repræsentativa; unde est etiam quod quicquid illa cogitat, bonum sit & perse-ctum, nam ad aliud non tendit à cujus scopo aberret.
units.tr: V. Thirdly, to return to the point: if I consider where such limited thoughts in my mind come from, where so many forms come from, why does my thought not rest in itself but reaches beyond itself? I see that this is because I am not from myself, nor through myself, nor for myself, as if I were my own end; I am nothing solid, nor a representation of myself. Otherwise, everything in me would be perfect, since it would have no other model and no other end than itself, and would not depart from itself. But on the contrary, I am from another, through another, for another, a shadow and image, as it were, referring to another. Whatever is in me pervades and, so to speak, transcends, and distinguishes my thought from that thought which is such as I have described, because it is from itself, through itself, for itself, subsisting solidly and representing itself. Hence it also follows that whatever that thought thinks is good and perfect, for it does not tend toward anything else, so as to stray from its end.

units.la: VI. Et hæ quidem sunt Generaliores Cogitationis creatæ ab increa-ta differentiæ, cæterarum magis particularium scaturigines: quæ cum sufficiant ad ostendendum Deum cum creatura non ideo permistum fuisse etsi eodem Cogitationis nomine sit expressus, hic non deducentur latius.
