Sed tamen de via qua ad illas certo cognoscendas, hoc est ad mentis utriusque perfectiones imperfectionesve oppositas aut inhærentes disterminandas pervenitur, quædam necesse est addere, quibus omnes scrupuli, quantum fieri potest, è medio tollantur.
units.tr: VI. These are indeed the more general differences between created and uncreated thought, the springs from which the more particular ones flow. Since they are sufficient to show that God was not thereby mingled with creature, even though both are expressed by the same name of thought, they will not be pursued at greater length here. Yet it is necessary to add some points about the way by which we come to know these with certainty, that is, to determine the perfections and imperfections of either mind, whether opposed or inherent, and by these means to remove, as far as possible, all doubts.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: 1. Viæ tres noscendi Dei perfectiones. 2. Sola causalitatis demonstrativa est. 3. Probatur ipsam esse in via eminentiæ, novumque Existentiæ Dei argumentum proponitur. 4. 5. 6. 7. Via negationis aut nulla est, aut ad causalem referenda. 8. Proprietates perfectionum Dei essentialium.
units.tr: 1. The three ways of knowing the perfections of God. 2. Only the way of causality is demonstrative. 3. It is shown that it is the way of eminence, and a new argument for the existence of God is proposed. 4. 5. 6. 7. The way of negation is either nothing, or must be referred to the causal way. 8. The properties of the essential perfections of God.

units.la: I. Aiunt passim Dei notitiam tum generaliorem, tum quæ specialior sit, viis tribus acquiri, è quibus primam nominant causa-litatis viam, cum à consideratione effectuum qui in mundo prostant, devenitur ad eorum causæ primæ, quæ Deus est, cognitionem. Viam eminentiæ appellant alteram, cum nempe postquam creata aliqua per-sectio perspecta est, ea deinceps Deo tribuitur, Sed in gradu eminentis-simo & summo. Tertia, negationis via dicitur, quæ est cum visæ in creaturis imperfectiones à Deo removentur.
units.tr: I. They say that the knowledge of God, both the more general and the more special, is acquired by three ways. Of these they name the first the way of causality, by which, from the consideration of the effects that exist in the world, one arrives at the knowledge of their first cause, which is God. They call the second the way of eminence, when some created perfection has been perceived and is then attributed to God, but in the most eminent and supreme degree. The third is called the way of negation, which is when the imperfections seen in creatures are removed from God.

units.la: II. Fatendum est, si de occasione qua ad cogitandum de Deo exci-temur, quæstio fit, tunc omnia esse vias ad notitiam ejus: atque adeo cum omnia possint considerari vel ut effecta quædam, vel ut habentia perfectiones, vel ut limitata in suis perfectionibus seu habentia imperfectiones, quemadmodum mox mentem meam, sed inverso ordine consideravi 1. ut limitatam & variabilem, 2. ut intelligenter quæren-tem acquiescere, 3. ut non à se, sed ab alio, quorum trium, 1. est viæ negationis, 2. viæ eminentiæ, 3. viæ causalitatis, sic omnes vias ad tres illas causalitatis, eminentiæ & negationis posse reduci: quomodo etiam in libro sequenti ex inspectione eorum quæ in nobis sunt effecto-rum utcunque perfectorum, vel imperfectionibus nonnullis prædito-rum, occasionem sumemus de Deo cogitandi specialius. At si sit quæstio de modo demonstrandi certitudinem eorum quæ Deo attribuuntur, sive, si quæratur, qua via aliquis ita cogitabit de Deo ejusque attribu-tis, ut certus sit suam quam de illis habebit notitiam esse veram, tunc illa trium viarum enumeratio superflua & vitiosa est: Nam postremæ duæ in quantum non possunt ad viam causalitatis referri, nullius sunt roboris ad certam notitiam ingenerandam. Etenim quicquid in creatis, præsertim vero in Mentibus, effectus operatioque Dei non est, id omne vel merum nihil, vel error, vel peccatum est: & vicissim, quicquid neque error, neque peccatum, neque nihil est, id Dei operatio & effectus est à causa illa summa procedens. Atqui indubium est, id omne unde notitia Dei in nos derivatur, non esse nihil, vel errorem, sed opus aliquod: quod cum non nisi à Deo procedat, evidenter concluditur, Deum agnosci solummodo per ea quæ ipse operatus est, hoc est per viam solius causalitatis. & cavendum est ne quis per opera Dei hic sola intelligat opera corporea, quin potius his dimissis, ad ea quæ alterius sunt ordinis, ad cogitationem nempe, ideasque ejus immutabiles, quibus nil addere possumus, nil detrahere, in primis vero ad ideam Cogitationis summæ perfectæ, est attendendum: hæ enim operationes Dei sunt, à quibus notitiam ejus acquirimus, quatenus nempe eæ soli Deo tanquam earum Authori & Causæ possunt referri. quales demonstrationes de Deo solidas proposuit in Meditationibus suis Cartesius. Et quamvis in quinta videatur Philosophus ille alia via quam Causalitatis & effectuum, Dei existentiam demonstrare, attamen attendenti bene ad rerum ordinem & ad res ipsas, manifeste patebit inibi demonstrata certitudinem suam summam à præcedentibus desumere, nec posse omnes difficultates repelli, quin ad causam efficientem recurratur. quod pluribus ostendi posset, nisi à commentando in aliorum scripta locus hic esset alienus.
units.tr: II. It must be admitted that, if the question concerns the occasion by which we are stirred to think about God, then all things are ways to the knowledge of him. And since all things can be considered either as certain effects, or as having perfections, or as limited in their perfections, that is, as having imperfections, just as I considered my own mind a little while ago (though in reverse order): (1) as limited and changeable, (2) as intelligently seeking rest, (3) as not from itself but from another. Of these three, the first belongs to the way of negation, the second to the way of eminence, and the third to the way of causality. In this way all the ways can be reduced to those three: causality, eminence and negation. In the same manner, in the following book, from the inspection of those effects in us which are in some measure perfect, or of those which have some imperfections, we shall take occasion to think of God more particularly. But if the question is about the manner of demonstrating the certainty of what is attributed to God, or, if one asks by what way someone will think of God and his attributes so as to be certain that the knowledge he has of them is true, then that enumeration of three ways is superfluous and faulty. For the last two, insofar as they cannot be referred to the way of causality, have no strength to produce certain knowledge. Indeed, whatever in created things, and especially in minds, is not the effect and operation of God, that is either mere nothing, or error, or sin; and conversely, whatever is neither error, nor sin, nor nothing, is an operation and effect of God proceeding from that supreme cause. But it is beyond doubt that all that from which the knowledge of God is derived into us is not nothing, nor error, but some work; and since this proceeds only from God, it is evidently concluded that God is known only through what he himself has done, that is, through the way of causality alone. And care must be taken that no one understands by the works of God here only bodily works. Rather, setting these aside, attention must be given to those that belong to another order, namely to thought and to his immutable ideas, to which we can add nothing and from which we can take nothing away, and above all to the idea of supreme and perfect Thought. For these are operations of God by which we acquire knowledge of him, insofar as they can be referred to God alone as their author and cause. Such are the solid demonstrations about God which Descartes has put forward in his Meditations. And although in the fifth Meditation that philosopher seems to demonstrate the existence of God by another way than that of causality and effects, yet anyone who attends well to the order of the matters and to the matters themselves will clearly see that the supreme certainty demonstrated there is derived from what precedes, and that its difficulties cannot all be repelled without recourse to the efficient cause. This could be shown at greater length, were this place not out of place for commenting on the writings of others.

units.la: III. Imo de tribus istis quas enumerant alii, viis, omnino fuisset tacitum, nisi necessitas ostendendi Dei notitiam ideamque non esse quid ficti & negativi, sed aliquid veri & maxime positivi, id requisiisset. Etenim viæ hæ duæ, eminentiæ & negationis, prout à causalitatis via distinguuntur, rem obscurant: nam etsi certam perfectionem quam in creaturis agnoscis, plurimis adaugeas gradibus ut eam quam eminentissime Deo tribuas, unde scies[?] tamen exinde sequi perfectionem illam adauctam dari in aliquo, nempe in Deo, nisi id per viam causæ consequaris, ab ea edoctus, perfectiones quæ in te & in tuis ideis sunt, debere esse à Sustentatore tui tantas ad minimum revera possidente? vel, generalius loquendo, debere dari causam tantis perfectionibus in re ipsa præditam, quantas in repræsentatione habes? Sic igitur, cum in nobis detegentes perfectionem aliquam, eam, postquam ampliata fuerit, attribuemus Deo, erimus certissimi attributionem fictam non fore, quæque sit cum variis mentis nostræ figmentis cassa reputanda; sed judicium esse solidum, lidum, ex eorum genere quæ ab effectu ad causam remeant. atqui nihil magis est necessarium judicio fundato in necessitate concludendi esse-ctum à causa procedere, non vero à nihilo, perfectumque ab imperfecto ut à causa non venire. Et notandum est effectum hic dici, non Cogita-tionem solum in se & materialiter spectatam, neque tantum ut in gene-re limitatam & variabilem, sed maxime ut suis formis seu ideis, saltem quibusdam, indutam. Quæritur causa formarum, sive modorum co-gitandi, & specialius formæ sive modi cogitandi de Ente summo, seu, quod idem est, ideæ Dei. Certum est ejus causam non esse Cogitatio-nem meam generalissime & ut materialiter consideratam: nam si cogita-re, seu conscium esse, inferret Dei ideam, hæc idea deberet esse in omni-bus meis, etiam imperfectissimis, cogitandi modis, siquidem Cogita-tio in illis est. Præterea, si cogitatio mea, seu conceptus meæ cogitatio-nis, sufficeret completè ad conceptum Cogitationis perfectissimæ, non possem me ipsum non concipere ut cogitationem perfectissimam cum concipio me cogitare. Neque etiam quæsita causa in aliis meis cogitandi modis & formis, Dei forma seu idea minus perfectis, latere credi potest, quasi imperfecti forma haberet in se (non dico comparatè) formam per-secti. Quicquid autem in me est, Cogitatio est cum ejus modis: igi-tur non in me, sed extra me, postulata causa quærenda est, quæren-da inquam, sed in re de qua eadem incommoda quæ de me non possim allegare, ob quæ vidi me causam illam non esse. Ergo causa danda est Cogitatio, in cujus cogitandi modis omnibus involvatur Cogitatio perfectissima, quæque se ipsam non posset non vere concipere perfectis-simam Cogitationem, hoc est, quæ sit Deus. unde invictissime Deum esse concluditur. Quod etiam clarius conficietur, si non solum meo-rum modorum Cogitandi, sed & simul substantiæ cogitantis, ejusque præsentis durationis, quæratur causa. Imo, quæstio causæ Cogitatio-nis meæ materialiter sive substantialiter spectatæ, ducit me ad Dei exi-stentiam, ut dicetur ubi de sufficientia Dei agetur. Denique ausim di-cere, sequendo viam Causalitatis, omnium optime de Dei existentia certos reddi nos posse, si attendatur ad illam acquiescentiam in eo qui per ideam perfectissimam repræsentatur: Nam certitudo illa de Deo quæ ex eo venit quod in nostra cogitatione intellectuve sit idea Dei, est qui-dem firmissima, sed fatendum est eam non raro esse infructuosam inuti-lemque, vel talem quæ nil nisi vanos pariat discursus, relinquatque sui possessores practice Atheos. At dum datur ut videam & sentiam me ha-bere in Illa re quæ per ideam de cogitatione summa repræsentatur, ubi plenissime & absolutissime jam & in æternum acquiescam, non possum non determinari potentissime ad confitendum ex toto animo meoCogitationem illamSummam sibi sufficientem & acquiescentem: etenim sentio & video, etsi non complete, tamen evidentissime, nil magis positivum & perfectum in me esse illa, non modo tendentia, sed & acquiescentia in Deo agnito, quæ certe non potest esse ab ulla alia re quam ab illo, nam ubi superiori capite cogitandi formis me quantum poteram exuebam; omnia præter me & Deum evanescebant, nec in istis quiescere dabatur; etiam in me nil intellexi, nec etiamnum intelligo quod non fit (in respectu ad acquiescentiam) despectu vel prætermissione dignum, & incapax fundandæ acquiescentiæ. Restat igitur pro causa Deus, sive cogitatio, quam concipio suæ ipsius de se notitiæ acquiescere, quamque ut ultimum tendentiæ & acquiescentiæ scopum & fundamentum amplexor. Si non existeret Ille, cur non potius in me, qui sum res vere existens, quam in figmento mero, quale est id quod non existit, quiescere daretur? Quanquam ubi quis se ipsum prætermittens in Deo vere acquiescit, non opus sit multis ejusmodi ratiocinationibus: nam certitudo splendida & inconcussa immediate ei acquiescentiæ jungitur. Hinc est quod probi, qui scientias humanas edocti non sunt, de Deo verius & solidius certiores sint quam Doctores Theoretici; idque non ex eo quod ab aliis audiverint, vel ex libro legerint, sed quia fundamenti cui acquiescunt soliditatem potentissime, efficacissime & vividissime sentiunt, etiamsi exprimere non possint humana scientiarum methodo sensa animi, nec verbis compositis argutias oppositas refellere omnes, utpote Metaphysicis reflexionibus non assueti. Sed id omnibus commune est cum de Dei existentia & perfectionibus certiores fiunt ex consideratione Cogitationis, sive illa spectetur ut indeterminata substantia, sive ut modificata in intellectu per ideam Dei, aut in voluntate per acquiescentiam in re ab idea repræsentata, ut omnes per viam Causalitatis gradiantur.
units.tr: III. Indeed, of those three ways which others enumerate, I would have said nothing at all, unless the necessity of showing that the knowledge and idea of God is not something feigned and negative, but something true and most positive, had required it. For these two ways, eminence and negation, insofar as they are distinguished from the way of causality, obscure the matter. For although, having recognised a certain perfection in creatures, you increase it by many degrees so as to attribute it to God in the most eminent way, yet from this you will not know whether that increased perfection is given in something, namely in God, unless you attain this through the way of cause: being taught by it that the perfections which are in you and in your ideas must come from a sustainer of yours who really possesses them at least to such a degree? Or, speaking more generally, that there must be a cause which has in reality as many perfections as you have in your representation? Thus, when in ourselves we discover some perfection and, after it has been enlarged, we attribute it to God, we shall be most certain that the attribution is not feigned and is not to be reckoned empty, like the various figments of our mind; rather that the judgment is solid, being of the kind which goes back from effect to cause. And nothing is more necessary to a judgment founded on the necessity of concluding that an effect proceeds from a cause, and not from nothing, and that the perfect does not come from the imperfect as from a cause. And it must be noted that here the effect is taken to mean not only thought considered in itself and materially, nor only as thought in general, limited and changeable, but chiefly as clothed with its forms, or ideas, at least some of them. The cause of these forms, or modes of thinking, is sought, and more specifically the form or mode of thinking about the supreme Being, or, which is the same, the idea of God. It is certain that its cause is not my thinking considered most generally and materially. For if to think, or to be conscious, implied the idea of God, this idea would have to be in all my modes of thinking, even the most imperfect, since thought is present in them. Moreover, if my thinking, or the concept of my thinking, were sufficient completely for the concept of the most perfect Thought, I could not fail to conceive myself as most perfect Thought whenever I conceive myself thinking. Nor can it be believed that the cause sought lies hidden in my other modes and forms of thinking, in which the form or idea of God is less perfect, as if the form of the imperfect had in itself (I do not say comparatively) the form of the perfect. But whatever is in me is thought together with its modes; therefore the cause must be sought not in me but outside me, and sought in a thing about which I cannot allege the same inconveniences as about myself, on account of which I have seen that I am not that cause. Therefore the cause must be given as a Thought in whose modes of thinking the most perfect Thought is involved, and which cannot fail to conceive truly the most perfect Thought, that is, which is God. From this it is most invincibly concluded that God exists. This will be made even clearer if the cause is sought not only of my modes of thinking but at the same time of the thinking substance and of its present duration. Indeed, the question about the cause of my thinking, considered materially or substantially, leads me to the existence of God, as will be said where we treat of the sufficiency of God. Finally, I venture to say that, by following the way of causality, we can be made certain of the existence of God in the best possible manner, if attention is paid to that acquiescence in him who is represented through the most perfect idea. For that certainty about God which comes from the fact that in our thought or intellect there is an idea of God is indeed most firm; but it must be admitted that it is not rarely fruitless and useless, or such that it produces nothing but vain reasonings and leaves its possessors practically atheists. But while I see and feel that I have, in that thing which is represented through the idea of supreme thought, a place where I may now and for eternity rest most fully and absolutely, I cannot but be most powerfully determined to confess with my whole soul that this Supreme Thought is sufficient to itself and at rest. For I feel and see, though not completely yet most evidently, that nothing more positive and perfect is in me than that tendency, and indeed that rest, in the known God, which certainly cannot come from any other thing than from him. For when in the preceding chapter I was stripping myself as far as I could of the forms of thinking, all things except myself and God were vanishing, and it was not possible to rest in them; nor in myself did I understand, nor do I yet understand, anything which is not (with respect to rest) worthy of contempt or neglect, and incapable of founding rest. There remains, therefore, God as the cause, or as the thought which I conceive to rest in its own knowledge of itself, and which I embrace as the ultimate goal and foundation of my tendency and rest. If he did not exist, why would rest be given in me, who am a really existing thing, rather than in a mere figment, such as that which does not exist? Yet when someone, leaving himself aside, truly rests in God, there is no need for many such reasonings: for a splendid and unshaken certainty is joined immediately to that acquiescence. Hence it is that the godly, who have not been taught human sciences, are more truly and solidly certain about God than the theoretical teachers; and this not because they have heard it from others or read it in a book, but because they feel most powerfully, most effectively and most vividly the solidity of the foundation on which they rest, even if they cannot express the feelings of their mind by the method of the human sciences, nor refute all opposing subtleties with composed words, being unaccustomed to metaphysical reflections. But this is common to all, when they become more certain of the existence and perfections of God from the consideration of Thought, whether it is viewed as an undetermined substance, or as modified in the intellect through the idea of God, or in the will through acquiescence in the thing represented by the idea, so that all proceed by the way of causality.

units.la: IV. De via negationis idem dici potest, oftendidque eam sine causalitatis inclusione nequicquam probare de Deo quæcunque de illo concludit. Constanter redeundum est ad positivam operationem. Et quamvis ad negandum de Deo imperfectiones quasvis non videatur causa positiva opus esse, in hoc tamen ipso maxime falluntur, errantque errorem ita communem, simulque notitiæ rerum spiritualium ita adversantem, ut non possit ejus falsitatis detectio hic prætermitti.
units.tr: IV. The same can be said of the way of negation: it has been shown that, without including causality, it proves nothing whatever about God that it concludes about him. We must keep returning to the positive operation. And although, in denying imperfections of any kind of God, there does not seem to be any need for a positive cause, people are most mistaken precisely in this point, and they err with an error so common, and so opposed to the knowledge of spiritual things, that the exposure of this falsehood cannot be passed over here.

units.la: V. Peperit hunc ista negationis via, quam qui secuti, cum imperfectiones quas in se animadvertebant, à Deo removerent negando eas de illo, nomina etiam illi negativa, qualia sunt immortalis, immutabilis, incomprehensibilis, independens, infinitus, & si quæ similia, tribuerunt. Idque inde primo processit, quod homines qui ista nomina primi adhibuerunt, cum prius ad creaturas quam ad Deum attenderent & reflecterent, magisque eis adhærere, iisque frui cuperent & quærerent quam Deo; ipsis quoque, earumque modis, utut imperfectis, prius nomina simplicia & positiva imposuere: Cumque postea Deus eis in mentem venisset, notassentque talia in eo non esse qualia in creatis, sed omnino alia, iisdem nominibus, præposita negatione, perfectiones ejus, ab illis, quæ creaturarum sunt, diversas, designaverunt. Simili opera erga mentem creatam, quatenus cum corporibus comparatur, sunt usi: hæc enim, ultimum studiorum curarumque suarum fuit objectum. Corporea prius optata & quæsita positivis nominibus appellarunt, sed tandem advertentes se etiam esse præditos re aliqua, quæ aliud quam corpus erat, & cujus proprietates nil corporibus simile involverent, eam à rebus corporeis, sed negatione præfixa, denominaverunt incorpoream, immaterialem, invisibilem, immortalem, &c. Quod si eorum Mentes Deum & sese omnium primo essent contemplatæ, credendum est eos alio modo de illorum denominationibus disposituros fuisse, nominaque corporum magis negativa fuisse futura quam mentium; magisque ea Mentium creatarum, quam Increatæ Mentis.
units.tr: V. This way of negation gave rise to the following practice. Those who followed it, when they removed from God the imperfections they observed in themselves by denying them of him, also ascribed to him negative names, such as immortal, immutable, incomprehensible, independent, infinite, and others of the same kind. This first came about because the men who first used these names attended and reflected on creatures before God, and they were more attached to creatures, and wanted to enjoy them and seek them more than God. So they first gave simple and positive names to the creatures and to their modes, however imperfect these were. Afterwards, when God came into their minds, they noticed that such things were not in him as they were in created things, but altogether different. So they used the same names, with a negation placed before them, to designate his perfections, which differ from those that belong to creatures. They did the same with the created mind, insofar as it is compared with bodies, for this was the final object of their studies and cares. At first they called bodily things, which they desired and sought, by positive names. But at last, realising that they too were endowed with some reality which was other than body, and whose properties involved nothing like bodies, they named it, with a negation prefixed, by its difference from bodily things: incorporeal, immaterial, invisible, immortal, and so on. If they had first contemplated God and themselves before all else, it must be believed that they would have arranged the names of these things in a different way, so that the names for bodies would have been more negative than those for minds, and those names would apply more to created minds than to the uncreated Mind.

units.la: VI. Atqui parum esset si de solis ageretur nominibus: Sed cum ex eo quod nomen negativum est, concludere prætendunt, conceptum illi nomini respondentem etiam in se negativum esse, hoc est, nil realitatis, nil positivi complectentem, id jam non leve quiddam est. Et hoc ipsum est quod multi prætendunt, dum nempe ex negativis quæ Deo tribuuntur nominibus, inferunt Deum à nobis nosci per viam negationis, eum itaque, ut quoque Mentem nostram, à nobis nosci non positive, sed negative, hoc est, nosci à nobis quid non sint, non vero quid sint. Tales si de notitia Dei aliarumque Mentium alloquaris, continuo te ridiculum, tuumque propositum impossibile clamitabunt: etenim, inquient, nosse quid non sit Deus, quid non sit Mens, veluti, nosse eos non esse mortales, corporeos, materiales, visibiles, id vero non est nosse quid sint; tum tribuere negationes, non est eisdem tribuere perfectiones & realitates, quæ positivæ sint; neque ideam infiniti, quæ ad Deum refertur, cum negativa sit, requirere causam positivam quæ eam in me posuerit; ut neque etiam Deum idcirco positive perfectiorem per illam dici. His similibusque ratiocinationibus, Dei, rerumque spiritualium notitiam destruere volunt homines isti, eamque habere magis pro negatione & ignorantia, quam pro vera scientia, quo deinceps rebus corporeis, quæ, vel ipsis judicibus omnium facillime, perfectissime, & maxime positive cognoscuntur, possint immergi.
units.tr: VI. But it would be a small matter if the question concerned only names. However, they claim that from the fact that a term is negative they may conclude that the concept corresponding to that name is also negative in itself, that is, contains nothing of reality or of the positive. This is no slight matter, and it is exactly what many people maintain: from the negative names attributed to God they infer that God is known by us through the way of negation, and therefore that he, like our own mind, is known by us not positively but negatively, that is, we know what he is not, not what he is. If you speak to such people about the knowledge of God and of other minds, they will at once cry out that you are ridiculous and that your proposal is impossible. For, they will say, to know what God is not, or what a mind is not, is like knowing that they are not mortal, corporeal, material, or visible; but that is not knowing what they are. Further, to ascribe negations is not to ascribe perfections and realities, which are positive. Nor does the idea of the infinite, which refers to God, since it is negative, require a positive cause that placed it in me; nor is God on that account said to be positively more perfect through it. By such and similar arguments these people want to destroy the knowledge of God and of spiritual things, and to hold it to be more a negation and an ignorance than true science, so that they may then be immersed in corporeal things, which, as even their own judges agree, are known most easily, most perfectly and most positively of all.

units.la: VII. At contrarium ab initio hucusque manifeste, ni fallor, est ostensum. Addendum tamen ex occasione hujus negativæ notitiæ, Primo, non posse sine contradicentia asseri aliquid negative cognosci. Equidem potest de aliquo nosci, quod in natura sua multas perfectionum negationes includat: sed notitia in hoc non subsistit, verum ad ea quæ in re positiva sunt pergit. Notitia mere negativa est proprie notitia de nihilo, nam non alia est in nobis nihili idea, quam per rerum negationem. Neque est quod regerant se ideo non concipere nihil, cum id ipsum quod negative nosci ajunt, præsupponant esse rem aliquam: nam non adeo novum est absurda præsupponere. ea alicujus rei præsuppositio tanquam suppositio nihili habebitur, donec aliquid positivi in ea agnoscatur. Possit quidem res generalius concipi ut de ea nihil particularius affirmetur: sed hic agitur, non de conceptu rei abstracto & generali, verum de re particulari, à corpore, &, cum de Deo quæritur, ab omnibus rebus quæ non sunt Summæ, distincta, à qua non possis omne positivum particulare tollere, quin ipsam rem tolles ita ut remaneat nihil. Præterea, nil crassius est eo errore qui quod in verbis positivum est confundit cum eo quod est in rebus & conceptibus positivum; qui grammaticam, usumque verborum iniquum cum Philosophia & ratione perturbat. Ecquis ignorat, id vere positivum esse, quod infert & ponit realitatem perfectionemque? Contra vero, id esse negativum quod perfectionem negat, asseritve imperfectionem? Atque adeo, si imperfectio denotetur nomine, Grammaticam si spectes, positivo, ejus nihilominus assertio in re & in conceptu negativa est; ejus vero negatio, positiva & affirmativa: nam imperfectionis positio est perfectionis negatio; & imperfectionis negatio, vera perfectionis & realitatis positio est. Respectus igitur est habendus ad id quod per verba sive negantia, sive affirmantia, in conceptu repræsentatur, ut ex perfectione quam hæc attribuunt, vel imperfectione quam removent, vel secus, judicetur utrum de positivis nec ne sit quæstio. Hoc modo examinandum est, an id quod verbis de Deo exprimitur, sit positivum, nec ne? Profecto, vocabula, mortalis, comprehensibilis, mutabilis, finitus, imperfectiones connotant, quapropter negativa sunt, tollunt enim reali-tates tates quasdam à subjectis quibus tribuuntur. Cum econtra, voces immortalis, incomprehensibilis, immutabilis, infinitus, removentes illas imperfectiones, secum involvant inferantque manifeste oppositas perfectiones, quapropter maxime positivæ sunt, veluti etiam omnia quæ in idea Dei comprehenduntur. Certe idea Dei ita positive perfecta est, ut ea sit sola notio positiva quam habemus, ex cujus inspectione judicare possimus, quid Dei vel nostri respectu perfectum aut imperfectum esse dici possit.
units.tr: VII. But I think that the opposite has been clearly shown from the beginning up to this point. Yet, on the occasion of this negative knowledge, the following must be added. First, something cannot be asserted to be known negatively without contradiction. Indeed, something may be known which in its nature includes many negations of perfections; but the knowledge does not rest there, but proceeds to what is positive in the thing. Purely negative knowledge is properly knowledge of nothing, for we have no idea of nothing except through the negation of things. Nor is there reason for them to say that they do not conceive nothing, since what they say is known negatively they themselves presuppose to be some thing. For it is not so new to presuppose absurd things. Such a presupposition of a thing is to be regarded as the supposition of nothing until something positive is acknowledged in it. A thing may indeed be conceived in general terms, so that nothing more particular is affirmed of it; but here we are concerned not with an abstract and general concept of a thing, but with a particular thing, distinct from body and, when we inquire about God, from all things that are not the Supreme. From it you cannot remove every particular positive quality without removing the thing itself, so that nothing remains. Moreover, nothing is grosser than the error that confuses what is positive in words with what is positive in things and concepts; it disturbs grammar and the usage of words, which is unfair, with philosophy and reason. Who does not know that the positive is truly that which implies and posits reality and perfection? On the contrary, that is negative which denies perfection and asserts imperfection? So, if an imperfection is denoted by a term that is positive in grammar, its assertion is nonetheless negative in the thing and in the concept, while its denial is positive and affirmative; for the positing of an imperfection is the negation of a perfection, and the negation of an imperfection is in truth the positing of perfection and reality. Regard must therefore be had to what is represented in the concept by words, whether negating or affirming, so that it may be judged, from the perfection they ascribe or the imperfection they remove, or the reverse, whether the question concerns positive things or not. In this way it must be examined whether what is expressed of God in words is positive or not. Indeed, the words mortal, comprehensible, mutable, and finite connote imperfections, and therefore they are negative, for they remove certain realities from the subjects to which they are attributed. On the other hand, the words immortal, incomprehensible, immutable, and infinite, which remove those imperfections, involve and manifestly imply opposed perfections, and therefore they are most positive, as are also all the things that are contained in the idea of God. Certainly the idea of God is so positively perfect that it is the only positive notion we have, from the inspection of which we can judge what can be said to be perfect or imperfect with respect to God or to ourselves.

units.la: VIII. Ergo de Deo concludimus, omnia quidem occasionaliter ad ejus perfectionum, quæ omnes positivæ sunt, notitiam ducere; viam autem causæ demonstrare eas revera in ipso existere. Quales illæ sint, generaliter ex præcedenti capite colligendum, nempe, non variabiles & limitatæ, sed uniformes, infinitæ; non ad aliud tendentes, sed sibi acquiescentes; non desumptæ à creaturis, sed à se ipsis exstantes. unde sequitur, omne quod formaliter in creatura est, id inquam omne, sic spectatum, si ad naturam Dei referatur, involvere imperfectionem, & consequenter ab illa removeri debere. Sequitur & ex hoc, essentiales perfectiones Dei non consistere in externis sive decernendis, sive agnoscendis, sive efficiendis: Sed Deum ex necessitate perfectionis suæ esse Indifferentem omnibus ponendis vel decernendis, aut secus. Si quæ in his difficilia occurrunt, ea suis locis in Libro sequenti, ubi de Dei attributis in particulari, reservantur. Sed videamus prius nonnihil penitius de Mentis creatæ perfectionibus & imperfectionibus, ne harum regulis ignoratis, plus minusve tribuamus illi.
units.tr: VIII. Therefore we conclude about God that all things lead, on occasion, to the knowledge of his perfections, which are all positive; but the way of cause shows that they really exist in him. What they are may generally be gathered from the preceding chapter: namely, they are not variable and limited, but uniform and infinite; they do not tend towards another, but rest in themselves; they are not derived from creatures, but exist from themselves. Hence it follows that everything that is formally in a creature, all of it, I say, when considered in this way, if it is referred to the nature of God, involves imperfection and consequently must be removed from him. It also follows from this that the essential perfections of God do not consist in external things, whether in decreeing, acknowledging, or effecting them; but that God, by the necessity of his perfection, is indifferent to positing or decreeing all things, or not. If any difficulties arise in these matters, they are reserved for their proper places in the following book, where the attributes of God are treated in particular. But let us first look somewhat more deeply into the perfections and imperfections of the created mind, lest, if we are ignorant of the rules for these, we attribute to it more or less than is due.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Cautelæ quinque de Modo cognoscendi Perfectiones Mentis creatæ. 6. 7. Ubi non sint quærendæ. 8. Ubi sint. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13. Earum limites & complementum probatur. 14. Certiores notæ de earum existentia. 15. De imperfectionibus unde judicandum.

Their limits and completeness are proved. 14. More certain marks of their existence. 15. From what the imperfections are to be judged.

units.la: I. NE Creator & Creatura confundantur, neve ulla superfit occasio eos confundendi, quasi creaturæ imperfectiones possent ita in ipsa augeri, ut illa tandem deveniret in Deum; & quasi ad hoc ipsum homini datus sit amor, ut eo aspiraret; necesse est creatæ Mentis perfectiones, earumque mensuram, & à Divinis differentiam, distinctius ctius proponere. Statuamus itaque, Primo, notionem fundamentalem ad quam verae & solidae perfectiones exigendae sunt, esse id quod simpliciter & absolute τὸ[?] nihil excludit, hoc est, id quod per ideam Summae Cogitationis, sive Entis maximi, significatur: nam non datur esse simplicius, est merum esse, quod simplicissime nihilo opponitur, sine ulla restrictione, ulloque adjecto. Hinc noscimus quae perfectiones Deo sint tribuendae, & quae de illo negandae imperfectiones, veluti, dependentia, ignorantia, dubitatio, scientia incerta, vel incompleta, habere alium scopum quam se, esse alterius rei imaginem, & similia.
units.tr: I. LEST the Creator and the creature be confused, and lest any occasion remain for confusing them, as if the imperfections of the creature could be so increased in it that it would at last become God, and as if love had been given to man for this very purpose, that he might aspire to it, it is necessary to set out more distinctly the perfections of the created mind, their measure, and their difference from the divine. Let us therefore establish, first, that the fundamental notion to which true and solid perfections must be referred is that which simply and absolutely excludes nothing, that is, what is signified by the idea of the highest Thought, or the greatest Being. For there is no simpler being than this: it is pure being, which is opposed most simply to nothing, without any restriction and without any addition. Hence we know which perfections are to be attributed to God, and which imperfections are to be denied of him: for example, dependence, ignorance, doubt, uncertain or incomplete knowledge, having an aim other than itself, being the image of another thing, and the like.

units.la: II. Secundo, notemus Perfectiones Dei non esse regulam secundum quam de Perfectionibus Mentium Creatarum earumque imperfectionibus ita judicetur, acsi Mentes eae perfectiores essent quae de natura seu essentia Divinarum perfectionum magis essent participes; imperfectiores vero quae minus. Nam contra, omnes creatae mentes infinite & aequaliter distant a reali possessione essentialium Dei attributorum: adeoque, quod illis careant ostendit quidem illas non esse perfectas, perfectione scilicet Entis summi, at non sequitur ideo eas non esse perfectas perfectione sibi convenienti: nam ultimae hae perfectiones generis sunt ab aliis diversi. Ergo, non possidere perfectiones Dei, quod esset imperfectio Deum dedecens, non est dedecens Creaturas. Igitur quae respectu Dei imperfectiones essent, pendere ab alio, ad aliud referri, non omnia nosse perfectissime, caeteraque similia, ea in creaturis habenda non sunt pro imperfectionibus, saltem pro imperfectionibus creaturae indecoris: Sed siquidem imperfectiones sint, eas vocabimus imperfectiones vel necessarias, vel stabiles, vel decentes, pro diversitate eas concipiendi: quibus opponendae sunt imperfectiones emendandae, abjiciendae, vel etiam indecorae.
units.tr: II. Second, let us note that the perfections of God are not the rule by which the perfections of created minds and their imperfections are to be judged, as if those minds were more perfect which were more partakers in the nature or essence of the divine perfections, and more imperfect those which were less so. For on the contrary, all created minds are infinitely and equally distant from the real possession of the essential attributes of God. Therefore, that they lack these shows indeed that they are not perfect with the perfection of the highest Being, but it does not follow that they are not perfect with the perfection that belongs to them, for these last perfections are of a different kind. Thus, not possessing the perfections of God, which would be an imperfection unbefitting God, is not unbefitting the creatures. Accordingly, those things which would be imperfections with respect to God, such as depending on another, being referred to another, not knowing all things most perfectly, and other similar things, are not to be held in creatures as imperfections, at least not as imperfections unbecoming to the creature. But if they are imperfections, we shall call them either necessary, or stable, or becoming, according to the way in which we conceive them. Opposed to these are the imperfections to be corrected, to be cast off, or even unbecoming.

units.la: III. Tertio, notandum est, etsi natura Dei non sit absolute regula omnium perfectionum & imperfectionum, ut dictum, quia esse Dei nullo modo est esse aliarum rerum, attamen cum placuerit Deo, ut vellet esse aliquid praeter se, quod sit quasi umbra vel speculum, vel tabula, ubi ejus perfectiones adumbrarentur per aliquam similitudinem, non sibi cum illis essentialem, sed umbratilem; hinc, istam voluntatem, quae Deo non necessaria est, sed ad quam ille indifferentissimus fuit, hoc placitum ut repraesentaretur, esse normam perfectionum creaturas decentium, earumque imperfectionum deponendarum, quatenus nempe eae cum illa conformantur, aut secus. Nec datur alia via ad perfectiones Dei, quae omnis perfectionis, etsi diverso modo, regula sunt, accedendi, quam ista. Nam via participationis cum essentia est impervia: putare autem ea quae in creaturis sunt, easve concernunt, repraesentare Deum immediate, non intercedente voluntate Dei quae prius non fuerit ad hoc indifferens, quasi creaturarum essentiae, ideae, regulae, essent necessario nexae cum intelligentia Divina simplici, talesque quales sunt essent sine decreto ullo, placitoque Dei liberrimo; id ipsum falsum esse, plenius, ubi de Dei Dominio agendum, demonstrabitur. Restat ergo solum placitum Dei, quo voluit utcunque, & per modum umbrae vel picturae, à creatis repraesentari.
units.tr: III. Third, it must be noted that although the nature of God is not absolutely the rule of all perfections and imperfections, as has been said, because the being of God is in no way the being of other things, nevertheless, since it pleased God to will that there should be something besides himself which would be, as it were, a shadow, or a mirror, or a tablet, in which his perfections might be shadowed forth by some likeness, not essential to them but shadowy, hence that will, which was not necessary to God, but to which he was most indifferent, and by which he chose to be represented, is the norm of the perfections fitting for creatures, and of the imperfections to be laid aside, insofar as they conform to that norm, or otherwise. Nor is there any other way of approaching the perfections of God, which are the rule of every perfection, though in a different manner, than this one. For the way of participation with the essence is impassable. To suppose, however, that the things which are in creatures, or concern them, represent God immediately, without the intervention of the will of God, which was not previously indifferent to this, as if the essences, ideas and rules of creatures were necessarily bound up with the simple divine understanding, and were such as they are without any decree or most free pleasure of God: that this is itself false will be shown more fully when we treat of the dominion of God. There remains therefore only the pleasure of God, by which he willed that in some way and by way of a shadow or picture he should be represented by the created things.

units.la: IV. Quarto, antequam hæc specialius mentibus applicentur, est etiam advertendum perfectiones esse vel substantiales vel modales, seu modum quo substantia disponitur spectantes; hasque, etsi sine illis esse non possint, illis tamen multo digniores & magis considerables esse. Ratio, quia τὸ esse illius rei umbratilis sive umbrae, non est suum esse, sibi esse, ad se referri, (solius Dei est tale esse) sed est esse respectivum & ad aliud; non absolute esse, sed hoc vel illo modo esse: adeoque ejus perfectio maxima non in simplici esse, sed in modis τῶ[?] esse quaerenda est. Patet hoc vel ex ipsius Dei judicio, asserentis satius esse aliquem non existere, cum de illius perfectionis statu agitur, quam pessimo quodam modo disponi; vel ex ipsarum rerum inspectione, e. g. Extensionis sive corporis quoad materiae essentiam perfectio est, ut sit longitudine, latitudine & profunditate constans: At hoc solum, chaos quoddam est. Perfectiones autem quae ex diverso dispositionis materiae modo oriuntur, & unde ordinatur pulcherrimum & admirabile mundi systema ejusque partes, tam egregie in vastitate coelorum, in expansis aërum, in aquarum profundis terraeque meditullio, visceribus, superficie, quae innumeris plantarum, animalium, aliorumque mirabilium speciebus condecorata est, variatæ, quae omnia nexibus tam arctis aptisque adhaerent & conservantur; nonne extensum sine ordine chaos, & eximii ordinis dissolutionem multis parasangis praecedunt? Quo fit etiam ut Philosophi istis, quae ex modis materiae pendent, perfectionibus cognoscendis omne fere tempus studiumque impendant, essentialem materiae perfectionem non sic, utpote quae non praecipua sit, curantes. Cur in Mente agnoscenda non ita ageretur? Certe in ejus perfectionibus conquirendis non est quod uni ejus substantiae,&,ut ita dicam,materiae perfectioni, quae est cogitatio,conscientia, conscium esse,quaeque in miserrimis imperfectissimisque exstat mentibus, unice haereamus. de hac jam non esto quaestio: Sed de perfectionibus quae spectantur in modis formisque cogicogitandi, quæ consideratu dignissimæ sunt, & veræ Philosophiæ præci-puam partem revera constituunt.
units.tr: IV. Fourth, before these things are applied more particularly to minds, it must also be noted that perfections are either substantial or modal, that is, concerning the mode by which a substance is disposed; and although these cannot exist without substances, they are nevertheless far more worthy and more considerable than they. The reason is that the being of that shadowy thing, or shadow, is not its own being, being in itself or referred to itself (such being belongs to God alone), but is a relative being, a being in relation to another; not absolutely being, but being in this or that way. Therefore its greatest perfection is to be sought not in simple being, but in the modes of being. This is clear both from the judgment of God himself, who affirms that it is better for someone not to exist than to be disposed in some very bad way, when the question concerns the state of perfection; and from the inspection of things themselves. For example, the perfection of extension, or body, as regards the essence of matter, is that it should consist of length, breadth and depth; but this alone is a kind of chaos. The perfections, however, which arise from the different disposition of matter, and from which the most beautiful and admirable system of the world and its parts is ordered, so splendidly in the vastness of the heavens, in the expanse of the airs, in the depths of the waters and in the middle of the earth, its bowels and surface, which is adorned and varied with countless species of plants, animals and other marvels, all of which cohere and are preserved by such close and fitting bonds: do not extension without order and chaos precede the dissolution of an excellent order by many leagues? Hence it also happens that philosophers spend almost all their time and study in knowing those perfections which depend on the modes of matter, while not caring for the essential perfection of matter, as being not the principal one. Why should it not be done in the same way in recognising the mind? Certainly, in seeking out its perfections there is no reason for us to cling solely to its one substance and, as I may say, its matter-perfection, which is thought, consciousness, being conscious, and which exists even in the most wretched and most imperfect minds. Let there be no question of this now. But the question concerns the perfections which are regarded in the modes and forms of thinking, which are most worthy of consideration and in truth constitute the principal part of true philosophy.

units.la: V. Advertendum denique est, nihil hic quæri de perfectionibus Co-gitationis sive Mentis Creatæ, prout inter se possent complicari, unæque in aliis fundarentur: Sed prout quælibet seorsim se habet. Nam cæte-roqui, quemadmodum in prognosticis productio aliquarum plantarum vel animalium, etsi in sese valde vilium, si tamen ex bona aëris, tellu-risque temperie procedat, magna perfectio reputanda est; Sic modus Cogitandi sensualis, audire, videre, vel imaginari, quatenus ex nobi-lissimo amoris Dei principio venit, & cum eo involvitur, perfectio ma-gna est, quamvis si solus sit, vel spectetur, non ita sit reputandus. De simplicioribus autem & verioribus modorum cogitandi in mente creata perfectionibus, non vero de complicatis & nonnunquam æquivocis, quæstio hic est, eaque generalior.
units.tr: V. Finally, it must be noted that nothing is sought here about the perfections of Thought or of the created mind as they might be combined with one another and founded in one another, but as each one stands by itself. For otherwise, just as in prognostics the production of some plants or animals, although in themselves very worthless, if it proceeds from a good temperature of the air and earth, is to be reckoned a great perfection; so the sensual mode of thinking, to hear, to see, or to imagine, insofar as it comes from the most noble principle of the love of God and is involved with it, is a great perfection, although if it is alone, or is considered alone, it is not to be reckoned so. The question here concerns the simpler and truer perfections of the modes of thinking in the created mind, not the complicated and sometimes equivocal ones, and it is a more general question.

units.la: VI. Hisce in antecessum animadversis dicimus, & quidem primo (quod facile ex eis quæ hic & cap. vi. dicta sunt elicitur) Perfectiones Mentis non consistere in modis cogitandi quibus materialia repræsentantur, non in hoc ut Mens quæcunque sunt aut esse possunt videat, audiat, gustet, tangat, non ut voluptuetur, vel ut imaginetur. Externa hæc sunt, nec Dei placitum de sui perfectionibus mente repræsentandis referunt. Adeoque non dedatur illis ea Mens quæ perfectione vera cupit indui. Quin imo his crassaminibus non raro studeat subduci parata præ excellentiori bono, vel omnibus istis exspoliari, planeque iis exui quæ visu, auditu sensibusque cæteris, cum affectibus & imaginatione, proprie usurpantur. Nobile hoc studium mortificationis veram Philosophiam non quidem facit, etsi hoc sensu afferat Plato mortis meditationem Philosophiam esse, sed ad veram Philosophiam disponit: sic enim itur ad veras Mentis perfectiones, quarum unum studium vera Philosophia meretur dici.
units.tr: VI. Having made these observations beforehand, we say, and first of all (which is easily drawn from what has been said here and in chapter vi.), that the perfections of the mind do not consist in the modes of thinking by which material things are represented, nor in this, that the mind should see, hear, taste, touch whatever things there are or can be, nor that it should delight, or that it should imagine. These are external matters, and they do not relate to the pleasure of God that the perfections of himself should be represented in the mind. Therefore that mind which desires to be clothed with true perfection is not to be given over to them. Indeed, it is often ready to withdraw from these gross things for the sake of a more excellent good, or to be stripped of all of them, and to be quite divested of those things which are properly employed by sight, hearing and the other senses, together with the affections and the imagination. This noble study of mortification does not indeed make true philosophy, although in this sense Plato asserts that the meditation of death is philosophy, but it disposes one towards true philosophy: for in this way one goes to the true perfections of the mind, the one study of which deserves to be called true philosophy.

units.la: VII. Porro, & hoc manifestum est, perfectiones mentis cui, omnibus imperfectionibus exutis, supereret intelligentia & amor, sive quæstio intelligens acquiescentiæ, non in hoc jacere, ut illa sui consideratione & complacentia, sive placito, impleatur, sibique acquiescat. Nam cum illa à se sit nihil, nec sibi sufficiat conservandæ, nec sui sit scopus, suique repræsentativa, perfectio illa salsissime fundata, adeoque imperfectissima esset; hoc est, perfectio non esset. Hinc patet, ad veram perfectionem adspiranti necessario dissolvendam esse sui sibimet ipsi adhæsionem per omnimodam prætermissionem sui.
units.tr: VII. Furthermore, and this is clear, the perfection of a mind from which all imperfections have been stripped, in which understanding and love, that is, an intelligent questing for acquiescence, abound, does not consist in this: that the mind be filled and satisfied by its own consideration and self-satisfaction, or by its own pleasure, and rest in itself. For since that mind is nothing of itself, is not sufficient for its own preservation, and is not its own goal, and is representative only of itself, that perfection would be founded on the most salty ground and would therefore be most imperfect; that is, it would not be a perfection at all. Hence it is plain that the one who aspires to true perfection must necessarily dissolve the adherence of self to itself through the complete setting aside of self.

units.la: VIII. At vero Mentis perfectiones sunt in illis cogitandi modis, actibus, & habitibus, qui ad Deum tendunt, dicunturque intelligen-tia & amor Dei, sive acquiescentia in Deo; qui cum sint innumeri, re-censeri facile non possunt, sed nec ubi sese offerunt, ignorari. Effati hu-jus probatio in capite mox citato reperitur, ubi visum est, nil magis po-sitivum, hoc est perfectum, in Mente esse Dei notitia & amore: cum-que ibidem dictum sit inter imperfectiones mentis, easque non inde-coras, diversitatem sive reiterationem actuum quoad numerum, (quod est ab habitu & eum facit) inveniri, haec, quam jam dicimus Mentis creatae perfectio, eo ipso extensa est ad actus habitusque innumeros. Sed nonnulla hic addenda sunt, ut complementum & limites harumce perfectionum designentur.
units.tr: VIII. But the perfections of the mind lie in those modes of thinking, acts and habits which tend toward God, and which are called the understanding and love of God, or acquiescence in God. Since these are innumerable, they cannot easily be listed, yet neither can they be unknown when they present themselves. The proof of this statement is found in the chapter cited just above, where it was shown that nothing in the mind is more positive, that is, more perfect, than the knowledge and love of God. And since it was said in the same place that among the imperfections of the mind, and those not unbecoming, there is found a diversity or repetition of acts as to number (which comes from a habit and makes it what it is), this perfection of the created mind, which we are now speaking of, is by that very fact extended to innumerable acts and habits. But some things must be added here, so that the completion and limits of these perfections may be marked out.

units.la: IX. In Modo cogitandi de Deo est quidem perfectio mentis vera, at non quatenus Mens super illius modi possessionem reflectens, ei ad-haeret, sese considerat ut intelligentem, ut in Divinis doctam, & in idea Dei noscenda peritam; sibi placet quod sit talis & tanta, in se exul-tat, sibi applaudit, & intime sibi de se ipsa testimonium optimum largitur liberaliter: Hoc enim esset propriae suam ipsius de Deo Cogitatio-nem, vel seipsum quemque, quatenus Deum quisque cogitat, admi-rari, adorare, sibique ipsi acquiescere. Idea Dei quae in nobis est, non est Deus ipse, sed modus mentis nostrae; & amor ille noster, sive acquiescen-tia, non est ens summum, adeoque horrendum esset in illis quiescere, illaque sic adorare. Haec pessima & subtilissima omnium superbia & idololatria. Notandum igitur, ideas perceptionesque rerum non ducere ad semetipsas, nec repraesentare se ipsas ut sunt modi cogitandi in co-gitante; sed res ipsas quas imitantur repraesentare, atque ad eas ducere: nec enim tabula picta seipsam, sed aliud quid exhibet; nec visio significat se esse modum cogitandi in Mente, aut etiam se ex certo motu par-tium cerebri enasci; sed fert cogitationem ad rem quae extra se est. Sic modum ipsum Cogitandi de Deo per notitiam & amorem non debet Mens amplecti quatenus in Mente est, sed extra sese efferri in objectum modo isto repraesentatum. Deus me fecit talis naturae, ut quod optan-dum est, quod amplectendum tanquam bonum, debeat 1. a me nosci, 2. ut ejus notitia excitet sensum gratum, allicientem, pellentem me ad id. Illa notitia & sensus iste non debent quidem rejici, sed quaeri & assumi, verum quatenus sunt vehicula ad scopum Deum, non vero ob illa ipsa & ut iis haereatur.
units.tr: IX. In the mode of thinking about God there is indeed a true perfection of the mind, but not insofar as the mind, reflecting upon its possession of that mode, clings to it, considers itself as intelligent, as learned in divine matters and skilled in knowing the idea of God; insofar as it takes pleasure that it is such and so great, exults in itself, applauds itself, and inwardly grants itself the best testimony about itself with generosity. For this would be to admire and adore one's own thought of God, or oneself insofar as one thinks of God, and to rest in oneself. The idea of God that is in us is not God himself, but a mode of our mind; and that love of ours, or acquiescence, is not the supreme being, so that it would be dreadful to rest in those things and so adore them. This is the worst and most subtle of all pride and idolatry. It must therefore be noted that ideas and perceptions of things do not lead back to themselves, nor do they represent themselves as they are, as modes of thinking in the thinker; rather they represent the things themselves which they imitate, and lead to those things. For a painted picture does not show itself but shows something else; nor does a vision signify that it is a mode of thinking in the mind, or even that it arises from a certain motion of the parts of the brain; rather it carries the thought to a thing that lies outside itself. Thus the mind must not embrace the very mode of thinking about God through knowledge and love insofar as it is in the mind, but must be carried outward to the object represented in that mode. God has made me of such a nature that what is to be desired, what is to be embraced as good, must (1) be known by me, and (2) its knowledge must stir in me a pleasing, alluring sense that drives me toward it. That knowledge and that sense ought indeed not to be rejected, but sought and taken up, insofar as they are vehicles toward God as goal, and not for their own sake or so that one may cling to them.

units.la: X. Et hoc satis aperte designatum est cum omnia illa ad Deum ten-dere dere dicta sunt. Quid vero hoc est, ad Deum tendere? An quod debea-mus Deum concipere ut in scopo, sive in uno extremo, nos vero in alio, a quo nobis sit discedendum, & progrediendum per medium ma-gis ac magis, ut tandem ad eas perfectiones, quae in Deo sunt, possi-dendas perveniamus? Hoc esset cupere fieri Deum, & solio suo Deum velle deturbare, quo nihil non modo magis impium, sed etiam magis absurdum fingi potest. In mente creata imperfectio naturalis est & sta-bilis pendere ab alio, nempe a Deo, a qua si discedere cuperem, mihi ipsi contradicerem: Cuperem me perfectum esse, hoc est, me saltem aliquid esse; & tamen optarem ut non penderem a Deo, ut me non sustentaret Deus, hoc est, cuperem me esse nihil: quod contradicto-rium est: nam quod a Deo non pendet est nihil. At qui revera imper-sectio decens est, &, si ita dicere liceat, perfecta, fundamentumque cae-terarum in creatura perfectionum, ut a Deo absolutissime pendeat crea-tura. adeoque non decet ab imperfectionibus stabilibus deficere velle, & ad independentiam, omnipotentiam, aliasque Deo essentiales per-sectiones tendere: nam, ut monitum est, hae scopus & mensura nostra-rum perfectionum non sunt: nec repraesentatio Dei in hoc consistit ut imago ejus umbratilis, & picta, omnia quae sunt in originali possideat, ut neque id in rerum aliarum imaginibus etiam requiritur, alioquin ipsa imago esset originale illud; Sed sufficit si ductus tales, lineamentaque talia in illa sint, ex quibus quale originale sit possit agnosci. talis autem in imagine independentia originale, ipsamque adeo imaginem, deforma-ret, tolleret, nec repraesentaret. Praeterea, iste progrediendi modus absurdus est: quamvis enim in infinitum perfectiones tuas augeas, nun-quam eo devenient ut cum Divinis eadem sint essentialiter. Perfectio-nem creatam quot velis gradibus amplifices, nunquam idcirco Divina fuerit. Ut neque putandum est, illam viam eminentiae, qua ad Deum per creaturarum perfectiones venitur, talem esse, ut perfectio creata quae ampliari dicitur, maneat tanquam fundamentum cui gradus sine numero superexstruas, ut digna evadat quae postea Deo tribuatur: Sed omnino gradatione illa nil conficitur, nisi saltetur, ut ita dicam, saltu infinito una vice ad aliud quid a perfectione creata prius posita diversum prorsus, in quo illa non substernatur ut fundamentum, sed cui occasio solum cogitandi fuerit. Tendentia igitur illa alia esse nequit nisi ad hoc, ut intelligentia & amor Mentis impleantur & occupentur, non a se ipsis, vel ab ipsa Mente, sed ab alio objecto, a Deo nempe. quo sensu accipienda sunt, ut vera sint, quae in Meditatione tertia Cartesius sic effert: Dum in me ipsum Mentis aciem converto, non modo intelligo me esse rem incom-pletam, & ab alio dependentem, remque ad majora & majora sive meliora in-definite aspirantem, sed simul etiam intelligo illum à quo pendeo, majora ista omnia non indefinite & potentia tantum, sed re ipsa infinite in se habere, atque ita Deum esse. Incommodæ alioqui locutiones.
units.tr: X. And this has been indicated quite plainly when all those things were said to tend toward God. But what is it, to tend toward God? Is it that we ought to conceive God as the goal, or as one extreme, and ourselves at the other, from which we must depart and advance through the middle ever more and more, so that at last we arrive at possessing the perfections that are in God? To wish this would be to desire to become God, and to want to hurl God from his throne, than which nothing can be imagined that is not only more impious but also more absurd. In the created mind, imperfection is natural and stable: to depend on another, namely on God. If I wished to depart from him, I would contradict myself: I would wish to be perfect, that is, to be at least something; and yet I would wish not to depend on God, not to be sustained by God, that is, I would wish to be nothing. This is contradictory, for what does not depend on God is nothing. But in truth this imperfection is fitting, and, if I may so speak, perfect, and the foundation of all the other perfections in the creature: that the creature depend most absolutely on God. Therefore it is not fitting to wish to fall away from stable imperfections and to strive toward independence, omnipotence, and the other perfections essential to God. For, as has been warned, these are not our goal and measure of perfections; nor does the representation of God consist in this, that its shadowy and painted image possess everything that is in the original, just as this is not required even in the images of other things; otherwise the image itself would be that original. Rather it is enough if there are such outlines and such features in it from which it may be recognized what sort of original it is. But such independence in an image would deform the original, and thus the image itself, and would abolish it rather than represent it. Moreover, this way of progressing is absurd: for however much you increase your perfections to infinity, you will never arrive at the point of being essentially the same as the divine perfections. However many degrees you add to created perfection, it will never on that account become divine. Nor should we think that the way of eminence, by which we come to God through the perfections of creatures, is such that the created perfection which is said to be enlarged remains as a foundation on which you may build degrees without number, so that it becomes worthy to be afterwards ascribed to God. Rather, nothing at all is accomplished by such gradation unless, so to speak, one leaps at a single bound, by an infinite leap, to something entirely different from the created perfection first posed, in which that perfection is not laid down as foundation, but serves only as an occasion for thought. That tending therefore cannot be other than toward this: that the understanding and love of the mind be filled and occupied, not by themselves or by the mind itself, but by another object, namely God. In this sense the words that Descartes expresses in the third Meditation must be taken, so that they are true: While I turn the eye of my mind upon myself, I understand not only that I am an incomplete thing, and dependent on another, and aspiring indefinitely to greater and greater or better things, but at the same time I also understand that he on whom I depend has in himself all those greater things not indefinitely and merely potentially, but actually and infinitely, and thus that he is God. Otherwise these expressions are inconvenient.

units.la: XI. Hic iterum limitibus & cautela opus est: non enim ad hoc ten-dendum est, ut omnia quæ sunt in Deo pernoscam, quod curiositatis, temeritatis & superbiæ esset, non modo si ad ipsam Dei naturam respi-ciatur, sed etiam cum quæcunque Deus de aliis decrevit, disposuit & noscit, ego nosse & intelligere optarem. Ut neque etiam amor hicce est Mentis unitio cum Natura Dei quam possidere Mens creata judicaret naturæ suæ esse conveniens: Nam cum iste amor non sit cæcus affectus, impetusve brutus, sed maxime sit intellectualis, perspicit naturæ suæ non competere permixtionem cum Dei perfectionibus, intelligitque notitiam omnium quæ in Deo sunt, vel quæ Deus vult de aliis sibi non convenire, ideoque ad illa isto modo non fertur: At possim illum Amo-rem Intellectualem, si in me sit, dicere, esse mei traditionem ipsi Deo de me quicquid ei placet statuenti, qua acquiesco & delector in eo quod Deus sit id quod est, quodque de se ipso manifestavit, & volo ut ille repræsentetur & noscatur in me & in cæteris prout ei placitum est. Etiam hic locum non habet ea speculatio qua amans cum objecto amato sese ut unum aliquod totum considerat cujus ipse sit pars nonnulla, quæ si minor sit reliquo, huic etiam, tunc magis amando, sit postponen-da. Non enim Mentem meam spectare debeo ut Divinæ auræ particu-lam portionemve nonnullam Dei maximi, & ex hoc figmento imagi-nario in Deum magis quam in me ferri: Sed, si aliquis ad me respectus sit habendus, considerandus sum ut minima particula objectorum in-numerabilium sui placiti, immensorumque suorum operum, quæ ta-men omnia sunt ejus tantum umbra, nil ex se solidi, nil subsistentis, nil realiter proprii habens. Magnæ hujus umbræ sum ego tenue punctu-lum, cujus omnis realitas est in illo Dei placito, quo sic ipse voluit ad-umbrari quia ipsi placuit ita velle, nam est Dominus. Ita ut tandem ad ipsum Deum sit deveniendum, ibique acquiescendum.
units.tr: XI. Here again limits and caution are needed. For we must not strive to know thoroughly all that is in God, which would be curiosity, rashness and pride, not only if one looks to the very nature of God, but also if I should wish to know and understand whatever God has decreed, arranged and knows concerning others. Nor is this love the union of the mind with the nature of God, which a created mind would judge to be fitting for its own nature. For since this love is not a blind affection or brute impulse, but is especially intellectual, it perceives that mixing with the perfections of God does not befit its nature, and understands that knowledge of all that is in God, or of what God wills concerning others, is not becoming to it, and therefore it is not carried toward those things in that way. But if it is in me, I could call that Intellectual Love the handing over of myself to God, who determines whatever pleases him concerning me, by which I acquiesce and delight in the fact that God is what he is, and what he has made known of himself, and I wish that he be represented and known in me and in others as it pleases him. Here too the speculation has no place by which the lover, considering himself together with the beloved object as one whole of which he is some part, which if smaller than the rest is to be set aside for that whole, the more he loves it. For I ought not to regard my mind as a particle or some portion of the divine breath of the greatest God, and on the basis of this imaginary fiction be carried more toward God than toward myself. Rather, if any regard to myself is to be had, I must be considered as the very smallest particle of the countless objects of his pleasure and his immense works, which are yet all only his shadow, having nothing solid of their own, nothing that subsists, nothing that is really proper to them. I am a thin little point of this great shadow, whose whole reality lies in that pleasure of God by which he has thus willed to be shadowed forth, because it pleased him so to will, for he is Lord. So that in the end one must arrive at God himself and there acquiesce.

units.la: XII. De qua acquiescentia notetur, eam non terminari & quiesce-re in placiti Dei effectu, qui res creata est, & sæpe à nobis non diversa, sed in ipso placito quatenus à Deo est, sive in Deo volente, quicunque sit ejus in me effectus sive terminus. Adeoque, etiamsi, ut fieri posset, se plane aliter erga me haberet, & alia quævis in me operaretur, vel operari desineret, quia tamen id à Dei placito esset, etiam ei esset ob hunc respectum, non vero ob respectum ad me, acquiescendum. Ea qui-dem quæ placitum Dei noluit à nobis ut indifferentia spectari, indiffe-renter ob placitum idem spectare non debemus, verum potius, quia sibi ea placere Deus testatus est, ea etiam ob Deum amplecti, ut ejus pla-cito sic conformemur: at quæ ut indifferentia ex se voluit spectari, ut (certo modo) quæ nexum mei cum corpore,ejusque durationem anxiam aut levem, gratam aut ingratam, longam aut brevem; modum quo cæ-teri mecum agere possunt durum mollemve, aliaque innumera quæ mi-hi accidere possunt, ea ita indifferenter spectanda sunt, atque, cum placitum Dei decretumque esse constat, ita excipienda, ut ne velimus quidem, etsi possemus, cupere quicquam mutare, eisve, quæcun-que sint, vel minimum resistere: quod esset nostrum placitum præ Di-vino amplecti: quamvis paratos nos esse deceat contrarium quoque ex-periri, si Deo id videretur.
units.tr: XII. This acquiescence should be noted: it does not stop and rest in the effect of God's will, which is a created thing and often not different from us, but in the will itself insofar as it comes from God, or in God willing, whatever its effect or outcome in me may be. So even if God were to treat me altogether otherwise, and work something else in me, or cease working at all, we should still acquiesce in it, and he would be pleasing to us for this reason, not for any regard to me. Indeed, those things which God has not wished us to regard as indifferent, we must not regard as indifferent for the sake of that same will; rather, because God has declared that they please him, we ought also to embrace them for God's sake, so that we may be conformed to his will in this way. But those things which he has willed to be regarded as indifferent in themselves, such as (in a certain sense) the bond between me and my body and its duration, whether troubled or light, pleasant or unpleasant, long or short; the manner in which others can deal with me, whether harshly or gently; and countless other things that can happen to me, these are to be regarded as indifferent in this way, and, since it is certain that they are God's will and decree, they are to be received so that we do not wish, even if we could, to change anything, nor offer the slightest resistance to them, whatever they may be; for that would be to embrace our own will in preference to the divine. Nevertheless, it becomes us to be ready to experience the opposite too, if it should seem good to God.

units.la: XIII. Hanc acquiescentiam perfectionem esse Mentis summam & fundamentalem inde patet, quod ea optime Deum repræsentet. Nam non dubium est quin placitum Dei quo voluit Deus à creaturis repræ-sentari, ipsum optime repræsentet. nec dubium est quin in illius placi-ti repræsentatione sit summa creaturæ perfectio: at talis acquiescentia intelligens optime placitum Dei repræsentat, id refert, id probat qualiter Deo placet: quæ Summa imitatio Dei est.
units.tr: XIII. That this acquiescence is the highest and fundamental perfection of the mind is clear from the fact that it represents God best. For there is no doubt that God's will, by which he willed to be represented by creatures, represents him best; nor is there any doubt that the highest perfection of a creature lies in representing that will. But such an acquiescence, being intelligent, represents God's will best: it refers and proves in what manner it pleases God, and this is the highest imitation of God.

units.la: XIV. Summa illa perfectio cæteras omnes Mentis, etiam diminu-tissimas, etiam sensuales, permeare potest, & in illis inveniri. At sæpe in eo falluntur homines quod illam ibi adesse credant unde tamen abest. Certior ejus nota probatioque est, non ubi arridet omnia, ubi sensus nullo tanguntur incommodo, ubi corpori deest nihil, ubi imaginatio demulcetur, ubi socii cæteriqve[?] vel adulantur, vel non adversantur, ubi Mens super se reflectens cogitat se intelligentem, se amantem Dei esse, se ei acquiescentem cum gratissimo sensu, unde delectatio & ingens gaudium. Nam in illis ipsis quæ vult Deus, quæque Mentem dulcedine afficiunt, timendum est, ne Mens ea amplectens, id ob se agat, adeoque, contra superius demonstrata, se ut sui scopum suique repræsentativam consideret. At ubi omnia ista ei adversissima accidunt, ipsaque velut arida languet sine gaudio quod ex sensu amoris Dei, tunc suf-penso, enascitur, & tamen isti Dei placito, utut duranti, quia à Deo est, acquiescit Mens, sine affectatione, parata cæteroqui vel jucundissi-mum, vel qualemcunque Deo placuerit statum ob ejus placitum, sive ob Deum volentem, ingredi, ibi demum Summæ perfectionis, cujus quidem creatura sit capax, probationem adesse, utique agnoscendum est: ibi enim patet placitum Dei purissime, sine ulla alieni mixtura, repræsentari.
units.tr: XIV. That highest perfection can pass through all the other faculties of the mind, even the most diminished and even the sensual ones, and be found in them. Yet people are often deceived in this, in that they believe it is present there when it is in fact absent. A surer mark and proof of it is not where everything smiles, where the senses are touched by no discomfort, where the body lacks nothing, where the imagination is soothed, where companions and others either flatter or do not oppose us, where the mind, reflecting upon itself, thinks that it is understanding, loving God, and acquiescing in him with a most pleasing sense, whence comes delight and great joy. For in those very things which God wills, and which affect the mind with sweetness, we must beware lest the mind, embracing them, does so for its own sake, and so, contrary to what was demonstrated above, regards itself as its own goal and its own representation. But where all those things fall out most adversely for it, and it languishes as if dry, without the joy which arises from the sense of the love of God, then, in suspension, the mind acquiesces in that will of God, however lasting it may be, because it comes from God, without affectation, and is otherwise ready to enter, for God's will and for God's sake, either the most joyful state or whatever state has pleased God. Then at last it must surely be acknowledged that there is present the proof of that highest perfection of which a creature is capable: for there the will of God is seen to be represented most purely, without any admixture of what is alien.

units.la: XV. Atque hæc de perfectionibus Mentis creatæ generaliora ex principiis internis deducta huc usque, satis sunto: unde patet quam longe, quantaque cum certitudine eas à Divinis distare, non obstante earum cum placito Dei conformitate, asseri possit. Quod de ejusdem imperfectionibus sit censendum paucis etiam apertum est, idque amplius potest deduci ex regulis oppositorum. Sed hoc ipsum ex professo deinceps tractabitur.
units.tr: XV. These things, concerning the more general perfections of the created mind, deduced thus far from internal principles, are enough. From this it is clear how far, and with how great certainty, it can be asserted that they differ from divine things, notwithstanding their conformity with the will of God. What is to be judged concerning its imperfections is also made plain in a few words, and this can be deduced further from the rules of opposites. But this very matter will be treated deliberately hereafter.

units.la: Ipsius invisibilia à condito mundo ex effectis mente perpensa conspiciuntur. Rom. I. v. 20.
units.tr: His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. Rom. 1. v. 20.

units.la: LIBER TERTIUS IN QUO De Deo & de Mente Creata, sive Anima, specialius tractatur. CAPUT I.
units.tr: BOOK THREE, IN WHICH God and the created mind, or soul, are treated more specifically. CHAPTER I.

units.la: 1. Quomodo de Dei attributis specialius sit tractandum. 2. Considerationes nonnullæ de Cogitatione creata ex quibus occasio agendi de Deo desumetur. 3. Attributa Dei ex his conside-randa.
units.tr: 1. How the attributes of God are to be treated more specifically. 2. Some considerations on the created thought, from which an occasion of acting concerning God will be taken. 3. The attributes of God to be considered from these.

units.la: JAm de iis specialius agendum est quæ in Dei Idea veniunt observanda, quæque respectum ad particularem præsentemque creaturarum statum, earumdemque regimen particulare, non involvunt, etsi nonnulla ad earum essentiam, nonnulla ad generalem existentiam, earumque nexum respiciant.
