Ut autem ordine nonnullo procedamus, & simul quæ de Deo dicenda sunt illustrentur, ad mentem nostram reflectere debemus, ut ex iis quæ in illa contemplabimur, ad Dei perfectiones considerandas deducamus. nam cum uno conspectu quicquid à nobis de Deo sciri potest attingere non possimus, non dubium est quin nobis liceat id pluribus, qui diversis nominibus designentur, tentare & utcunque exequi; cumque si Deum solum intueamur, is adeo Simplex & uniformis Cogitatio nobis appareat, ut, præter id quod in ejus definitione fuit expressum, nullus in eo ordo, nulla distinctio, nullum prius & posterius reperiatur, non immerito, cæteris rebus prætermissis, ex mentis nostræ inspectione occasionem nostrarum de illo Cogitationum ordine nonnullo disponendarum, depromemus. Distributiones attributorum Dei in negativa, positiva, communicabilia, incommunicabilia, aliasque ejusmodi, quoniam difficultatibus non carent, & controvertuntur, nec etiam quæ de Deo sunt dicenda, ita illustrant ut ea quæ ex consideratione Mentis veniunt, prætermittimus, alias forsan in fine allaturi. Cæterum ex iis, quas in Mente nostra animadvertemus, sive perfectionibus, sive imperfectionibus stabilibus aut indecoris, sive imperfectionibus deponendis emendandisve, ad Dei perfectiones recurremus, non quasi multis probaturi ex his principiis illas in Deo esse, sed illustraturi, ut dictum, ex hac occasione: nam via qua Deum illis praeditum esse demonstretur, jam supra ostensa est. tametsi nulla Deo perfectio sine sua demonstratione, sed ea brevi, in posterum tribuetur. Rem igitur ipsam aggrediamur.
units.tr: Now we must treat more particularly those things which are to be observed in the Idea of God, and which do not involve a respect to the particular and present state of creatures or their particular government, although some of them relate to their essence, some to their general existence and their connection. But so that we may proceed in some order, and at the same time so that what is to be said of God may be made clear, we must turn back to our own mind, so that from what we contemplate in it we may deduce the consideration of God's perfections. For since we cannot take in at one glance whatever can be known of God, there is no doubt that we are permitted to attempt this in several parts, designated by different names, and to carry it out in whatever way we can. And since, if we look at God alone, He appears to us as so simple and uniform a thought that, apart from what was expressed in His definition, no order, no distinction, and no before and after can be found in Him, we shall not unreasonably, setting other things aside, draw from the inspection of our own mind an occasion for arranging our thoughts about Him in some order. We pass over the divisions of God's attributes into negative and positive, communicable and incommunicable, and others of that kind, since they are not free from difficulties and are disputed, and since they do not illuminate what is to be said of God in the way that those things which come from the consideration of the mind do; perhaps we shall bring them forward at the end. Moreover, from those things which we notice in our mind, whether perfections, or imperfections that are lasting or unbecoming, or imperfections that are to be laid aside or corrected, we shall have recourse to the perfections of God; not as though we intended to prove by these principles that those perfections are in God, but to illustrate them, as has been said, on this occasion. For the way by which God is shown to possess them has already been set out above, although no perfection of God is to be granted without its own demonstration, which will be given shortly in its place. Let us therefore come to the matter itself.

units.la: II. Quod ut fiat, terminis multa subtilitate conquisitis valedicens, rebus corporeis caeterisque creatis non conspectis (quanquam ex inci-denti earum ideas in Mente mea contemplabor) ad Mentem meam me converto, in ejus cogitationibus ea animadversurus quae sponte sua jam sese offerent, ex quibus ad Deum fiat reditus. Animadverto igitur (1) me cogitare: (2) me, qua talem, praeter cogitationem nihil habere: (3) me illud ipsum a me non possidere: (4) in me esse tam multiplices dispositiones seu aptitudines ad diversimode cogitandum, (5) ut omnes enumerare, imo concipere non possim, ita ut eatenus egomet mihi sim incognitus; (6) quamvis omnium cogitationis meae objectorum ego sim proximum, (7) me facile concipere res a me dif-ferentes quamplurimas, quarum quaedam pares mihi aequalesque sint: (8) adverto etiam inter eas dari posse quasdam majores me, quasdam etiam inferiores, (9) at me non posse illarum omnium ideis & pro-prietatibus quicquam addere, vel detrahere: (10) idque me incassum tentaturum: unde patet mei respectu caeterorum sterilitas: (11) Imo scio ne a voluntate quidem mea esse, ut res illas, praesertim me majo-res, modo convenientiori in me ponam, ita ut illis fruar decenter, & sicut cum ratione opto; (12) nec ab eadem voluntate mea pendere ut extra me existant; (13) nec quot sint, quae earum natura, quod regimen, aliaque de illis ejusmodi, me perfecte cognitione tenere: (14) Animadverto tamen licere mihi cogitationes illas meas de istis eo quo placet ordine disponere, quamvis primarum cum ultimis concatenatio decens, & ultimarum a primis deductio, sit perdifficilis, & saepe in illis ita disponendis, inopinata & inexpectata oboriantur, nec sequatur quod erat intentum. (15) Deprehendo quoque, quantum quidem contendam, impossibile mihi esse, omnes uno aspectu intueri, sed debere ut defectui isti succurratur, cogitationem meam prolon-gari, (16) & consequenter variari, hoc est, successive objectis di-versis mox huic, mox illi, & quidem modis saepe diversis, applicari, (17) meque nec adhuc eis omnibus praeditum esse, ad quae mea ferri possét cogitatio. (18) In cogitationibus illis meis quæ verum & bo-num noscendum possidendumque spectant, non adverto coactionem ullam, nulla enim in me, me reluctante, ab extraneo impetu poni-tur: (19) at idem dicere non sustineo de modis cogitandi quibusdam, qui sensus vel doloris, vel voluptatis, vel aliis nominibus appellantur, quosque tanquam à rebus à me diversis vel præter voluntatem recipio. (20) Novi denique libertate mea me posse abuti, eadem me negando, quæ in me esse vel fuisse vere percepero, (21) aut vera fore voluero & promisero; (22) vel etiam res viles & me indignas, amore prose-quendo. Quæ omnia cum Mente recolo, adverto ita imperfecta esse, (23) ut eis semper perfectionis novus gradus addi possit; (24) aut aliquis, imo omnes detrahi, quia nempe nil in me est quod impediat, quo minus author meus in pristinum nihilum me, (si voluisset) redu-cat: (25) Ita ut nil sit cur adeo de me ipso bene opiner, meque mihi ipsi spectandum commendem. Possent proculdubio plures aliæ hisce si-miles addi considerationes, & ordine ab hoc diverso componi: est enim cuilibet id juris in suas cogitationes,& ob id ipsum mihi persuadeo in nu-merum & ordinem mearum hic positarum neminem infensum fore, cum liceat cuivis eas non probanti, proprias suas numerosiores & ordi-natiores proponere.
units.tr: II. In order to do this, bidding farewell to a multitude of terms sought out with great subtlety, and with corporeal things and other created things set aside (although I shall contemplate their ideas in my mind incidentally), I turn myself toward my own mind, to observe in its thoughts those things which will already present themselves of their own accord, from which a return to God may be made. I observe, therefore: (1) that I think; (2) that I, as such, have nothing besides thought; (3) that I do not possess that very thing from myself; (4) that in me there are so many manifold dispositions or aptitudes for thinking in diverse ways, (5) that I cannot enumerate them all, nay, cannot even conceive them all, so that to this extent I am unknown to myself; (6) although I am the nearest to all the objects of my thought; (7) that I can easily conceive very many things different from me, some of which are equal and like to me; (8) I observe also that among them there can be some greater than I, and some also lesser; (9) but that I cannot add anything to, or take anything from, the ideas and properties of all of them; (10) and that I would attempt this in vain; whence the barrenness of my own powers in relation to other things is evident; (11) indeed I know that it is not even in my will to place those things, especially those greater than I, in me in a more suitable way, so that I may enjoy them becomingly and as I rightly wish; (12) nor do they exist outside me by any will of mine; (13) nor do I hold perfect knowledge of how many they are, what their nature is, what their government is, and other things of this kind concerning them; (14) I observe, however, that it is lawful for me to arrange those thoughts of mine about them in whatever order I please, although a fitting connection of the first with the last, and the deduction of the last from the first, is very difficult, and often in arranging them there arise unexpected and unforeseen things, and what was intended does not follow. (15) I perceive also, as far as I can strive, that it is impossible for me to take in all of them at one glance; but that, so that this defect may be remedied, my thought must be prolonged, (16) and consequently varied, that is, applied successively, now to this object, now to that, and often in diverse ways; (17) and that I am not yet endowed with all those things to which my thought could be directed. (18) In those thoughts of mine which concern the knowing and possessing of the true and the good, I notice no constraint at all; for no compulsion is placed in me by any outside force against my resistance. (19) But I cannot say the same of certain modes of thinking which are called by the names of sense, or of pain, or of pleasure, or by other names, and which I receive as from things different from myself, or apart from my will. (20) Lastly, I know that by my freedom I can abuse myself, by denying those things which I have truly perceived to be in me or to have been in me, (21) or by wishing and promising that they will be true; (22) or even by loving and pursuing vile things that are unworthy of me. When I recall all these things with my mind, I notice that they are so imperfect (23) that a new degree of perfection can always be added to them; (24) or indeed some, nay all, can be taken away, because surely there is nothing in me that prevents my author from reducing me, if he willed, to my former nothingness: (25) so that there is no reason why I should think so highly of myself, or commend myself to my own regard. Doubtless several other considerations similar to these could be added, and arranged in an order different from this one; for everyone has the right to his own thoughts, and for that very reason I am persuaded that no one will be hostile to the number and order of mine set down here, since anyone who does not approve of them is free to put forward his own, more numerous and better ordered.

units.la: III. Cæterum, quamvis ea quæ de Deo concipi possunt ex rela-tione vel occasione quæ à creaturis aut vero à mente sola est, non possint numero astringi, sintque indefinita; Præcipua tamen Dei attributa, &, ut sic efferam, Primitiva, ex singulis hisce notatis proponentur & disponentur, Nempe 1. Dei Vita, 2. Spiritualitas, 3. Sufficientia, 4. Activitas, 5. Incomprehensibilitas, 6. Intelligentia, 7. Unitas, 8. Altitudo, 9. Dominium, 10. Bonitas, 11. Felicitas, 12. Poten-tia, 13. Cognitio vel Scientia, 14. Sapientia, 15. Æternitas, 16. Con-stantia, 17. Simplicitas, 18. Libertas, 19. Impassibilitas, 20. Justi-tia, 21. Veracitas, 22. Sanctitas, 23. Infinitas, 24. Immortalitas, 25. & Gloria. Literæ A & D interpositæ, ea quæ de Mente creata, sive Anima, (perinde enim est qua voce utamur, cum quid ea significatur fit satis evidenter expressum) & illa quæ de Deo dicentur, dister-minabunt.
units.tr: III. Moreover, although those things which can be conceived of God from the relation or occasion which comes from creatures, or from the mind alone, cannot be restricted to a number and are indefinite, nevertheless the chief attributes of God, and, so to speak, the primitive ones, will be set forth and arranged from each of these noted points, namely: 1. the Life of God, 2. Spirituality, 3. Sufficiency, 4. Activity, 5. Incomprehensibility, 6. Intelligence, 7. Unity, 8. Height, 9. Dominion, 10. Goodness, 11. Blessedness, 12. Power, 13. Cognition or Knowledge, 14. Wisdom, 15. Eternity, 16. Constancy, 17. Simplicity, 18. Liberty, 19. Impassibility, 20. Justice, 21. Veracity, 22. Holiness, 23. Infinity, 24. Immortality, 25. and Glory. The letters A and D, interposed, will determine what is said of the created mind, or soul (for it makes no difference which word we use, since what is signified by it is expressed clearly enough), and what will be said of God.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: (I) VITA.
units.tr: (I) LIFE.

units.la: §. A. I. Vita Animae naturalis.
units.tr: §. A. I. The natural life of the soul.

units.la: I. OMnium primum quod mihi de me occurrit illud est, Me Cogitare, ut supra etiam animadverti: videoque cogitationem mihi ita annecti, ut sine illa esse non possim id quod de me novi, at posita intima illa conscientia, posito me esse conscium, sufficiens hac ex parte existere fundamentum cur credam, sciam, sentiam, me esse, vigere, magis ac magis perfici posse. Hoc ipsum est quod proprie appellare possum Vitam Mentis meae naturalem, & ideo affirmare, Mentem ex naturae suae conditione esse rem viventem. Alias vocis hujus, vitae nempe, significationes, praesertim quae in rebus corporeis obtinent, relinquo: nec jam ad illam nobilissimam attendo quae est cum cogitatio mea ad gradum perfectionis suae summum adducetur: Sed de illa ago quae Menti est naturalis, nec aliud per eam video posse designari quam Cogitationem, sive, actu esse Conscium, ad quam cetera quae illa carent si comparentur, mortua dici possunt. Hinc de eo quod supra adduxi, nempe Mentem semper cogitare, magis magisque persuadeor: nam cum Mentis natura vivens sit, ergo natura sua est actualiter agens, (latiori sensu, qui passionem vividam includit), cum viventem esse, sit agere, & vita non sit facultas, sed actus. Quid autem est, praeterquam cogitare, ob quod agere dici possit. Ad facultatem quod attinet, quod sola facultate sive potentia vivit, id actu mortuum est, nec vivens dicitur: neque etiam facultas pro vita sumi potest, nec distingui a Mente quatenus haec est & existit, nisi Mentem fatearis rem esse in se mortuam & brutam. Quae de animalculorum quorumdam vita sopita allegari possent ad hanc rem nihil attinent.
units.tr: I. The first thing that occurs to me about myself is that I think, as I have also noted above. I see that thought is so bound up with me that without it I could not be what I know myself to be; and, given that inner consciousness, given that I am conscious of myself, I have, so far as this goes, a sufficient foundation for believing, knowing and feeling that I exist, that I am alive, and that I can be made more and more perfect. This very thing is what I can properly call the natural life of my Mind, and so I affirm that by the condition of its nature the Mind is a living thing. I leave aside the other meanings of this word, life, especially those which hold for corporeal things; nor do I now look to that most noble life which my thought will attain when it has been raised to the highest degree of its perfection. I am speaking of that life which is natural to the Mind, and through it I see that nothing else can be designated than thinking, or, in other words, being actually conscious; compared with which, things that lack it may be called dead. Hence I am more and more persuaded of what I adduced above, namely that the Mind always thinks: for since the nature of the Mind is living, its nature is therefore actually active (in the broader sense, which includes a vivid passion), since to be living is to act, and life is not a faculty but an act. Moreover, what is there, apart from thinking, on account of which it could be said to act? As for faculty: whatever lives only by faculty or power is actually dead, and is not called living; nor can faculty be taken for life, nor be distinguished from the Mind insofar as it is and exists, unless you were to admit that the Mind is in itself a dead and brutish thing. What may be alleged about the life of certain tiny animals lying dormant has nothing to do with this matter.

units.la: 2. Vita Dei, fundamentum attributorum. 3. Jurare per vitam Animae vel Dei. 4. Vitae Mentis creatae inimica. mortua. Bona vita.
units.tr: 2. The life of God, the foundation of the attributes. 3. Swearing by the life of the Soul or of God. 4. Life is hostile to the created Mind; death; good life.

units.la: II. Deum etiam, ad quem me converto, non possumnon concipere Cogitantem ut jam supra vidi. neque dubium est quin cogitare, si modo cogitationis objectum præcipuum & ipse cogitandi modus non limitentur, vera sit perfectio: igitur ea non destituitur qui ut perfectis-simus concipitur. Est ergo Deus cogitans, sui & omnium si quæ sunt conscius, nec ab ejus natura cogitatio est separabilis. Hoc ipsum est, quod attributum Vitæ dicitur, de cujus excellentia hic nil specialius addetur, cum dicta & dicenda ad eam pertineant. Addo tamen, quemadmodum in mente creata, imo in omnibus viventibus, vita est fundamentum quo stant omnia cætera, & quo diruto corruunt; ita etiam Vitam Dei omnibus ejus attributis substerni, & in omnibus inveniri debere, omnia enim vitam involvunt, nec concipi possunt nisi in conceptu illo expresse includatur quod sint viventia. At quid illud est, quod ut primum & quasi fundamentum omnium assignari possit, præter cogitationem simpliciter consideratam? Merito igitur hæc Dei Vita appellari debet.
units.tr: II. God also, to whom I turn, I cannot but conceive as thinking, as I have already seen above. Nor is there any doubt that thinking, provided that the principal object of thought and the very mode of thinking are not limited, is a true perfection; therefore he who is conceived as most perfect is not deprived of it. God is therefore thinking, aware of himself and of all things that are; nor is thought separable from his nature. This very thing is what is called the attribute of Life, about whose excellence nothing more particular will be added here, since the things said and to be said pertain to it. I add, however, that just as in the created mind, indeed in all living things, life is the foundation on which all other things stand, and on whose collapse they fall, so the life of God must underlie all his attributes and must be found in all of them; for all things involve life, nor can they be conceived unless it is expressly included in that concept that they are living. But what is it that can be assigned as first and, as it were, the foundation of all, apart from thought simply considered? Rightly, therefore, this must be called the Life of God.

units.la: III. Velim notari, ut nonnullus horum fit fructus, id ipsum bene intelligi posse ubi in Sacris de Vita Dei vel de Deo vivente, mentio fit: nam quamvis nonnullibi forte ad id attendendum sit, quod Deus non possit deficere seu desinere, vel sit potentissimum agens (quod ad immortalitatem & potentiam post hæc referetur) illud tamen, quod Deus sit conscius sui, suarum perfectionum, potentiæ & bonitatis, &c. Imo conscius omnium quæ fiunt, ut plurimum spectatur. Hinc maxime introducitur Deus ut, vivens ubi agitur de hominibus vel qui non attendunt ad hoc quod Deus sit conscius tum suæ justitiæ & potentiæ, tum eorum quæ ipsi agunt, dicuntve, vel qui ad id ipsum attendunt aut attendere debent; unde formula jurandi, Deus vivit & anima tua vivit, &c. quasi dicerent, Deus qui suæ potentiæ ad vindicandum malum conscius est, scit me hoc vel illud (de quo agitur) sincere cogitare, hujusque esto ita persuasus ac tuæ ipsius cogitationis conscius es. Sed & ibi interponitur Deus ut vivens cum certiores vult reddere homines de eo quod ipse revera cogitat, & cujus conscius est, exempli causa, in illustri illa protestatione, Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur & vivat, &c. Ne peccator peccatis suis territus apud se cogitet, si quidem Dei amore non sum dignus, sed contra, ejus desertione, sequitur ut ille cogitet de me non reformando, sed potius de me, ut mereor, in peccatis meis relinquendo & deserendo; est quod ego cogitem sive conscius sim eum mihi bene non velle, non sibi de me bene conscire, vel saltem an bene velit, dubito & nescio: Opponit Deus Ego Vivo nolo mortem peccatoris. Quæ ita sumi possunt acsi diceret, Quis novit Mentem Domini, aut ejus præ Domino conscius est? Atqui ego vivo: Ego conscius sum & mei, & eorum quæ in me sunt, adeoque scio & conscius sum illud in me non esse, nempe velle mortem peccatoris, sed conscius sum quod velim ego ut vivat, hæc est mea mens & cogitatio; & quam certum est illud prius, me mentis meæ conscium esse, tam certum est hoc posterius. Atque hoc est summum certitudinis nostræ de Dei placito erga nos fundamentum, Protestatio per vitam Dei.
units.tr: III. I would like it to be noted, as some fruit of this, that the same thing can well be understood wherever in the Sacred Writings mention is made of the Life of God or of the living God. For although in some places perhaps attention is to be paid to the fact that God cannot fail or cease, or is the most powerful agent (which will be referred later to immortality and power), nevertheless that God is conscious of himself, of his perfections, power and goodness, etc., is what is chiefly regarded. Indeed, he is most often set forth as conscious of all things that happen. Hence God is principally introduced as living where the discussion concerns men who either do not attend to the fact that God is conscious both of his justice and power and of what they themselves do or say, or who do attend, or ought to attend, to this very thing; whence the formula of swearing, God lives and your soul lives, etc., as if they said: God, who is conscious of his power to avenge evil, knows that I think this or that (about which the matter is in question) sincerely, and be assured of this just as you are conscious of your own thought. But God is also introduced there as living when he wishes to make men more certain of what he himself really thinks and of which he is conscious; for example, in that illustrious protestation, As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live, etc. Lest the sinner, terrified by his sins, think within himself that, indeed, he is not worthy of the love of God, but on the contrary, by his desertion, it follows that God thinks of him not in reforming him but rather, as he deserves, in leaving and forsaking him in his sins; there is something that I think or am conscious of, namely that he does not wish me well, that he is not conscious of good toward me; or at least I doubt and do not know whether he wishes well. God answers: I live; I do not desire the death of the sinner. These words can be taken as if he said: Who knows the mind of the Lord, or is conscious of it before the Lord? But I live: I am conscious both of myself and of what is in me, and therefore I know and am conscious that this is not in me, namely to desire the death of the sinner, but I am conscious that I desire that he may live; this is my mind and my thought; and as certain as it is that the former, that I am conscious of my mind, so certain is this latter. And this is the highest foundation of our certainty concerning God's good pleasure toward us: a protestation through the life of God.

units.la: IV. De se ipsa, Mens creata reputet omnia quæ cogitationem, quæ vita ejus est, obtundunt, ut vitæ inimica esse evitanda. Omnia quæ cogitatio non sunt, ei spectanda esse ut in se mortua, etiam litera quæ sacra dicitur mortua est, solus Spiritus, sive cogitatio quæ à Deo est & Deum refert, vitam infert. Denique siquidem in cogitando vivit, cum cogitans cupiat vivere bene, ut bene cogitet danda est opera; & in hoc totum artificium consistit, ut bonis formis induatur Cogitatio.
units.tr: IV. As for the created Mind itself, let it reckon as hostile to its life all things that dull its thinking, which is its life, and let it avoid them as things to be shunned. Everything that is not thought must be regarded by it as dead in itself; even the letter which is called sacred is dead; the Spirit alone, or the thought which is from God and refers to God, brings life. Finally, since it lives by thinking, and since the thinking mind desires to live well, care must be given so that it thinks well; and in this lies the whole art, that thought be clothed in good forms.

units.la: CAPUT III. (2) SPIRITUALITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. (2) SPIRITUALITY.

units.la: 1. Spiritualitas. 2. Spiritualis vita.
units.tr: 1. Spirituality. 2. Spiritual life.

units.la: I. NOn jam hic iterum, nisi animo, recolam ea quæ superiori libro fuse demonstrata sunt, Cogitationem nempe ita in me esse, ut præter illam nihil sit, quod ad mei, qualem jam me considero, essen-tiam naturamque pertineat, ita ut in illa sola tota mea natura includatur exclusis omnibus cæteris. Completa hæc notio rei sive naturæ cujusdam quæ cogitatione absolvitur, Spiritualitas proprie dicenda est, ob quam assero mentem meam Spiritum esse.
units.tr: I. Here I shall not again go over, except in outline, what was demonstrated at length in the previous book: namely, that thought is in me in such a way that nothing else belongs to the essence and nature of me, as I now consider myself, apart from it, so that my whole nature is contained in it alone, all else being excluded. This complete notion of a thing or nature which is comprised in thought is properly called Spirituality, and on account of it I maintain that my mind is a spirit.

units.la: II. Inter plurima quæ hinc colligi possunt, illud in primis notetur, eam mentem dicendam omnino spirituali vita vivere cujus omnes cogi-tationes ad cogitationem ita feruntur, ut illæ hac ultimo terminentur, in ea omnia inveniant, eique acquiescant.
units.tr: II. Among the many things that may be gathered from this, let this be noted above all: that a mind is rightly said to live altogether a spiritual life when all its thoughts are so directed toward thought that they end in it, find everything in it, and rest in it.

units.la: §. D. 3.4. Mera Cogitatio Dei Spiritualitas.
units.tr: §. D. 3.4. Pure Thought is Spirituality.

units.la: III. In Deo, cum ad illum ex hac occasione attendo, ita etiam cogitationem esse animadverto, ut tota ejus Natura in illa sola consistat, exclusis omnibus caeteris, quae praeter cogitationem possunt concipi. Id ni esset, in Deo darentur plurima quae essentia inter se differrent, nam quicquid cogitatio non est, id essentiam à Cogitatione diversam obtinet: atque Deus ita componeretur ex partibus, quarum una alteram excluderet, uniusque realitas & perfectio in alia non inveniretur: quo modo Deus conciperetur ut imperfectus & non simplex. Sed contrarium superius demonstratum est, ubi etiam hoc ipsum quod jam de Deo asserimus, cum nempe praeter cogitationem nihil habere in sua natura, firmis, ut puto, argumentis probatum est, quae labore idem hic demonstrandi nos levabunt. Notetur idcirco, omnia quae in sequentibus Deo attribuentur, nil esse praeter meram Cogitationem.
units.tr: III. In God, when I attend to him on this occasion, I likewise observe that he is thought in such a way that his whole nature consists in that alone, all else that can be conceived apart from thought being excluded. If it were otherwise, there would be in God many things differing from one another in essence, for whatever thought is not, has an essence different from thought; and God would thus be composed of parts, one of which excluded the other, and the reality and perfection of the one would not be found in the other; so God would be conceived as imperfect and not simple. But the contrary has been demonstrated above, where it was also proved, by arguments which I believe are firm, that what we now assert of God, namely that he has nothing in his nature beyond pure thought, and these arguments will spare us the labour of demonstrating it again here. Let it therefore be noted that all the things that will be attributed to God in what follows are nothing but pure Thought.

units.la: IV. Ex hisce facile est concipere, quid sit Dei Spiritualitas, nimirum quod non tantum cogitet Deus, sed quod omnia quae in ejus natura sunt cogitatio mera sint. Sic Deus est Spiritus.
units.tr: IV. From these things it is easy to grasp what God's Spirituality is, namely that God not only thinks, but that all things which are in his nature are pure thought. Thus God is Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: (3) SUFFICIENTIA.
units.tr: (3) SUFFICIENCY.

units.la: 1. 2. Quaestiones de existentia rerum. Ratio, causa, causa efficiens, esse à se positive. 3. De re positiva quaeritur absurde an sit à se negative, & an sit sui causa efficiens? 4. Mens humana non est à se positive. 5. Nec ulla alia res, nisi sit perfectissima.
units.tr: 1. 2. Questions about the existence of things. Reason, cause, efficient cause, to be from oneself positively. 3. It is absurdly asked of a positive thing whether it is from itself negatively, and whether it is its own efficient cause. 4. The human mind is not from itself positively. 5. Nor is any other thing, unless it is most perfect.

units.la: I. NIl magis naturale & obvium est quam ubi quid esse percipitur, ejus causam sive rationem postulare. quapropter, cum cogitans existem, occurrit consequenter menti meae ut quaeram, unde hoc? quae ratio, quae causa? At, priusquam quaesito satisfiat, & ad Deum ex hujus occasione ascendamus, nonnullae voces quibus utendum est, ut sunt causa, ratio, causa efficiens, esse à se positive vel negative, sunt explicandae, ne, quod aliquando est immerito factum à rixandi cupidis, absurditatem & falsitatem nonnulli impingant verissimis sententiis.
units.tr: I. Nothing is more natural and obvious than to demand the cause or reason of a thing when we perceive that it exists. Hence, since I think and therefore exist, the question naturally arises in my mind: whence is this? What is the reason, what is the cause? But before this question is answered, and before we ascend to God on the occasion of it, some terms that we must use, such as cause, reason, efficient cause, and to be from oneself positively or negatively, must be explained. This is so that some people, eager to quarrel, may not charge the most true opinions with absurdity and falsehood, as they have sometimes unjustly done.

units.la: II. Cum aliqua res existit, vel noscitur ut existens, de ejus existentia duae possunt quaestiones proponi; altera quae habeat respectum ad cognitionem nostram de ea, ut si quaeratur, Cur asseris te nosse quod haec res, v. g. Deus, aut Mens finita, existat? Cui non difficulter respondeti potest, De mente finita quidem ex mei experientia; De infinita vero ex rationibus quibus ejus existentia demonstratur. Quaestio altera quae de rei existentia formari potest, non tam respicit cognitionem nostram, sive assertionem qua dicimus nos nosse rem existere, quam rem ipsam in se consideratam: ut si petatur, Quare res illa non tantum est possibilis, sed est etiam existens? Cur extra possibilitatis terminos existentiam actualem habet, vel in eam devenit? Quae causa, quae ratio, quae perfectio allegabitur? Cui quaestioni non nisi duobus modis respondeti potest: vel enim extra Rem ipsam non ibitur; vel ad aliam oportebit converti. Primum fit, ubi ratio existentiae rei redditur ex natura rei ipsius quae ita perfecta perspicitur, ut non opus habeat existentiam aliunde mutuare, cum ejus naturae perfectiones ad hoc sufficiant, illam secum inferant, adeoque sint ratio, causa, realitas, perfectio illa, quae rei existentiae, & quaestioni de illa, satisfaciunt. Et nota hic vocabulo ratio, causa, non designari rem ab illa de qua quaeritur diversam, sed ipsammet eandem, quatenus tales sunt ejus perfectiones ut absque alterius interventu existere sufficiant. Hocce modo existere, id est quod dicitur esse a se, cujus loquendi formulae significatio est maxime positiva, quoniam ponit sive affirmat perfectiones maximas. Modus alter quo ultimae isti quaestioni respondetur, in hoc consistit, ut ad assignandam rationem, sive causam, cur res sit existens, nec solum possibilis, ad rem aliam a quaesita diversam nos converti oporteat, quod tunc fit, cum postquam animadversum est rei quaesitae perfectiones non tantas esse ut natura earum existentiam inferat, ut illarum conceptus a conceptu existentiae sit inseparabilis, vel illis necessario junctus, asseritur, nexum illum naturae rei possibilis cum existentia actuali, quando adest, ideo adesse, quod a re alia, quae non simpliciter causa, sed causa efficiens dicitur, positus sit. & istarum vocum prima, causa videlicet, indigitat existentiae quaesitae rationem a re assignata cui nomen causae tribuitur, deduci; altera, nempe efficiens, denotat rem assignatam ita inferre existentiam quaesitam, ut tamen illa (causa nempe) non fit cum hac (de cujus existentia quaeritur) unum & idem quid, sed fit diversa a re existente, quæ ejus opus externum, non vero una eademque res cum illa ipsa est. Adeoque, quamvis res quæ est à se positive, existen-tiæ suæ causa seu ratio in sensu jam allato dici possit, nequaquam tamen sui causa efficiens est dicenda, quoniam voces istæ si ex usu recepto usur-pandæ sunt, tantum adhibendæ sunt ubi à re aliqua alia res natura diversa existentiam habere significatur.
units.tr: II. When some thing exists, or is known to exist, two questions about its existence can be raised. One concerns our knowledge of it, as when someone asks: Why do you assert that you know that this thing, for example God or a finite mind, exists? To this one may easily reply: of a finite mind, indeed, from my own experience; of the infinite, from the arguments by which its existence is demonstrated. The other question that can be raised about a thing's existence does not so much concern our knowledge, or the assertion by which we say that we know the thing exists, as the thing itself considered in itself: for example, if it is asked: Why is that thing not only possible but also existing? Why does it have actual existence outside the limits of possibility, or come to it? What cause, what reason, what perfection will be alleged? To this question there is only one of two ways to reply: either one will not go outside the thing itself, or one will have to turn to another. The first happens when the reason for a thing's existence is given from the nature of the thing itself, which is seen to be so perfect that it has no need to borrow existence from elsewhere, since the perfections of its nature are sufficient for this, bring it along with them, and therefore are the reason, cause, reality and perfection that satisfy both the existence of the thing and the question about it. And note here that by the words reason and cause is designated not a thing different from the one asked about, but that very same thing, insofar as its perfections are such that they suffice to exist without the intervention of another. In this way to exist is what is called to be from oneself, whose form of speech has the meaning most positive, since it posits, or affirms, the greatest perfections. The other way in which this last question is answered consists in this: in order to assign the reason, or cause, why a thing exists and not merely is possible, we must turn to another thing different from the one sought. This happens when, after it has been noticed that the perfections of the thing sought are not so great that their nature brings existence with them, so that their concept is inseparable from, or necessarily joined to, the concept of existence, it is asserted that the connection of the nature of a possible thing with actual existence, when the latter is present, is present because it has been posited by another thing, which is called not simply a cause but an efficient cause. And of these terms, the first, namely cause, indicates that the reason for the existence sought is derived from the thing assigned, to which the name of cause is given; the second, namely efficient, denotes that the assigned thing so brings about the existence sought that yet that thing (the cause, namely) is not one and the same thing with this (whose existence is asked about), but is different from the existing thing, and is its external work, not truly one and the same thing with it. Accordingly, although a thing that is from itself positively can be said to be the cause or reason of its own existence in the sense already stated, it must nevertheless by no means be called its own efficient cause, since these words, if they are to be used according to accepted usage, are to be employed only where it is signified that a thing of a different nature has existence from another thing.

units.la: III. Hisce præsuppositis, &, cum evidentia sint, concessis, ad me redeo qui cogitans existo, & peto, non quamobrem judicem me exi-stere cogitantem, sed, cur existam? Quid judicem esse causæ cur ex-istam? Sumne ego à me? Certe, si quispiam suggereret mihi me à me esse, illudque à me esse, intellectum negative oportere, nempe ita, ut nihil aliud significetur, quam me nec nosse, nec assignare posse in me & extra me ullam existentiæ meæ causam, ineptissima esset talis sugge-stio, esset enim loco rationis, ignorantiæ solius productio. Non novi ego in me, neque extra me, causam ullam realem meæ existentiæ, ergo non datur, vel non quærenda est, adeoque sum à me negative, absurdum fuerit ratiocinium de nulla re quicquam concludens præter ignorantiam ejus qui ita de re quacunque ratiocinaretur: at ignorantia nostra non est regula veritatis rerum. Sed neque ignorantiæ tantum no-ta est sensus iste negativus istius formulæ esse à se, cum per eam respon-detur quæstioni de re aliqua positiva, verum etiam absurditatum scatu-rigo: nam cum ipsum nihil ideo fit nihil, quia nec in se nec extra se causam existentiæ habet, sive causam cur existat, neque, quamdiu est nihil, habere concipi possit, non modo dici poterit juxta doctrinam illam lepidam ipsum nihil esse à se, at negative, (de quo loquendi mo-do non est adeo contendendum;) verum sic non impedictur quin τ̈ [?] nihil habendum sit pro re positiva, utpote de quo in ratione existentiæ eadem causa quæ de re positiva sit alleganda. Commodius ergo quæram, an Ego sim à me positive? Qua in quæstione adverto etiam notionem ef-ficientis causæ locum non obtinere. Absurde quærerem,an Ego sim cau-sa efficiens mei ipsius? Nam sic supponerem me à me ipso posse differre, meque non esse memet ipsum: non enim proprie nominatur efficiens causa, nisi ubi res ab effectu differt, & vicissim ubi effectus à causa supponitur diversus: efficiens dicit ex rebus duabus alteram possidere prius quam det, alteram nil habere priusquam recipiat, sed demum incipere aliquid habere cum causa diversa, prius existens, determinatur ad hoc, ut det. quæ quidem omnia non possunt concipi vel de me vel de ulla re cum ratione quæri posse, cum neque ullo modo concipi possint. Restat itaque significatio positiva existendi à se, cujus respectu petam, an sim à me, positive nempe, sive, An quæ in natura mea sunt perfectiones sint tales, ut mei, vel, quod idem est, sui, existentiam inferant?
units.tr: III. With these things presupposed, and granted since they are evident, I return to myself, who think and exist, and I ask not why I judge that I exist thinking, but why I exist. What do I judge to be the cause why I exist? Am I from myself? Certainly, if someone were to suggest to me that I am from myself, and that this being from myself must be understood negatively, namely in such a way that nothing else is meant than that I neither know nor can assign any cause of my existence in me or outside me, such a suggestion would be most inept, for it would be the production of mere ignorance in place of a reason. I know of no real cause of my existence in me or outside me; therefore there is none, or it is not to be sought; and so I am from myself negatively. That reasoning would be absurd, concluding nothing about any thing except the ignorance of the one who reasoned in this way about any thing whatever. But our ignorance is not the rule of the truth of things. Moreover, this negative sense of the formula to be from oneself carries not only the mark of ignorance, when it is used to answer a question about some positive thing, but also a flood of absurdities: for since nothing becomes nothing because it has in itself and outside itself no cause of existence, or cause why it exists, nor, as long as it is nothing, can it be conceived to have one, then not only can it be said, according to that witty doctrine, that nothing itself is from itself, negatively (about which mode of speaking there is no need to contend greatly); but in this way it is not prevented that nothing must be counted as a positive thing, since in the reason for its existence the same cause must be alleged as for a positive thing. It is more convenient, therefore, to ask whether I am from myself positively. In this question I notice that the notion of an efficient cause does not apply either. I would ask absurdly whether I am the efficient cause of myself. For in that way I would suppose that I could differ from myself, and that I am not myself: for a thing is properly named an efficient cause only where the thing differs from the effect, and conversely where the effect is supposed to be different from the cause; the efficient cause implies that of two things one possesses something before it gives it, the other has nothing before it receives it, but only begins to have something from a different cause, existing previously, which is determined to give. All these things cannot be conceived either of me or of any thing, so as to be asked about with reason, since they cannot be conceived in any way. There remains, therefore, the positive meaning of existing from oneself, with respect to which I shall ask whether I am from myself, positively, namely, or: Are the perfections that are in my nature of such a kind that they bring with them the existence of me, or, which is the same, of myself?

units.la: IV. Id vero nequicquam asseverare queo, si attente perspexero, quod esse à se sit habere necessariam existentiam; perfectiones ita completas & reales possidere, ut absque contradictione non possit negari, cum attente considerantur, eas existere; includere existentiam in essentia & conceptu ejus; talem esse, ut quærenti cur existat res? solide ex solius rei consideratione, cæteris prætermissis, responderi possit; denique esse conscium (nam de re cogitante agitur, & de actuali existentia) se sibi sufficere, & re ipsa sibi acquiescere, imo sponte sua habere sive in se, sive extra se, omne quodcunque placet. Quæ si singulatim discutio, ut videam, an in me sint, omnia experior à me aliena. Existentia mea non necessario juncta est essentiæ meæ, sive, ut cum schola loquar, non est de essentia mea; vel, ut clarius dicam, idea seu conceptus quem de mei natura quispiam posset habere, (qui essentia in creatis rebus dicitur) non est talis, ut cum eo necesse sit concipere & judicare rem existere extra conceptum qualis in conceptu intelligitur. etenim, antequam existerem fieri facile potuit ut ego tanquam possibilis, nec tamen tanquam existens, si quidem re ipsa nondum eram, conciperer: quare non ea est natura mea ut ab existentia sit inseparabilis, eamque inferat, cum fuerit olim actu ab illa separata. Neque etiam quæ in me sunt perfectiones tantæ sunt, ut negari nullo modo possint, aut etiam ut si vere concipi debeant, statuendum sit eas existere: nam ego innumeras ejusdem mecum naturæ & conditionis mentes ita mihi repræsento, ut conceptus de illis à me tamen non exigat ut statuam illas existentia frui, quam ab illis sine contradictione removeo, cum liceat mihi eas ut non existentes, sed tantum possibiles, clare, distincte, absque ulla in conceptu repugnantia & sine contradictione considerare. Præterea cum plurima in me sint quæ à me realiter non distinguuntur, sed, quatenus modi sunt mei, modali distinctione, & quorum tamen ratio à mei solius consideratione nunquam reddi potest, ut notio entis me majoris, cupiditas perfectionum meas superantium, quæstio acquiescentiæ extra illa quæ jam in natura mea possideo, ad quorum causam ad aliquid præter me respiciendum est; multo magis ad meæ existentiæ causam assignandam recurrendum est ad rei à me diversæ considerationem: si enim ipse modus cogitationis à me non est, multo minus ipsa substantia, ipsa cogitatio. Denique si à me essem, si jam ponerem mei existentiam, cum illud sit actus, & ego res conscia eorum quæ in me actu sunt, ejus rei essem conscius. Atqui ego ad me quam accuratissime possum attendens non tantum hu-jus non sum conscius, sed contra percipio evidenter & experior, meam existentiam, imo, ut alicubi fusius videbitur, omnia quæ in me sunt, in quibus vel minima realitas reperitur, non esse opus mei, &, ut sic dicam, ea se ipsa in existentia non posuisse, sed omnium omnino causam atque rationem extra ipsa esse requirendam, adeoque extra me, qui semper alterius opus sum, ab aliena potentia & voluntate, non vero à mea, plane dependens. Quæ enim potentia illa mea qua me existentem ponerem? Si cogitatio spontanea non esset illa, mea non esset, sed alie-na. Cogitare autem sponte & volens, me non ponit. Equidem existo volens, sed in quæstione cur existam non possum acquiescere voluntati meæ, nam illa non satis realis est ut eam concipiens, judicem existen-tiam ab ipsa esse inseparabilem, ut jam animadversum; nec illa me po-nit qualem vellem respectu modorum, ut dictum. Sum quidem me attendente quod velim esse, sed sum etiam me id non cogitante: imo experiri possum me si ob angores animi evitandos esse non vellem, ideo tamen non desiturum esse, quod fieret, si absurda fictio, quod à mea vo-luntate essem, locum habere nonnullum dici posset. Unde sequitur me esse ab alio, qui is est quem voco Deum.
units.tr: IV. I cannot possibly assert this, if I attentively consider what it means for something to have its necessary existence from itself: to possess perfections so complete and real that, when they are attentively considered, it cannot be denied without contradiction that they exist; to include existence in its essence and concept; to be such that, when someone asks why the thing exists, a solid answer can be given from the consideration of the thing alone, with everything else set aside; and finally to be aware (for we are speaking of a thinking thing and of actual existence) that it is sufficient for itself, rests in the thing itself, and indeed of its own accord has, whether in itself or outside itself, whatever it pleases. When I examine these things one by one, to see whether they are in me, I find that all of them are foreign to me. My existence is not necessarily joined to my essence, or, as the Schools put it, it is not part of my essence; or, to speak more plainly, the idea or concept that anyone could have of my nature (which is called essence in created things) is not such that, with it, it is necessary to conceive and judge that the thing exists outside the concept in the way it is understood in the concept. For before I existed, I could easily have been conceived as possible, but not as existing, since in fact I was not yet. Therefore my nature is not such that existence is inseparable from it and implies it, since at one time it was actually separated from it. Nor are the perfections that are in me so great that they cannot be denied in any way, or that, even if they must be conceived truly, it must be held that they exist. For I represent to myself countless minds of the same nature and condition as mine, and my concept of them does not require me to hold that they enjoy the existence which I remove from them without contradiction, since I may consider them clearly and distinctly, without any repugnance in the concept and without contradiction, as not existing but merely possible. Moreover, since there are many things in me that are not really distinct from me, but are distinct by a modal distinction, insofar as they are modes of me, and whose reason can never be given from the consideration of myself alone, such as the notion of a being greater than myself, the desire that exceeds my perfections, and the question of rest outside those things which I already possess in my nature, for whose cause one must look to something beyond me: much more, to assign the cause of my existence, one must have recourse to the consideration of a thing different from me. For if the mode of thinking is not from me, much less is the substance itself, the thought itself, from me. Finally, if I were from myself, if I already posited my existence, since that would be an act, and I am a thing conscious of what is actually in me, I would be conscious of that act. But I, attending to myself as carefully as I can, am not only not conscious of this, but on the contrary I perceive and experience evidently that my existence, and indeed, as will be seen more fully elsewhere, that all the things in me in which even the smallest reality is found, are not my work, and, so to speak, did not place themselves in existence; rather, the cause and reason of all of them must be sought entirely outside themselves, and therefore outside me, who am always the work of another, plainly dependent on an alien power and will, and not on my own. For what power is that of mine by which I would posit myself as existing? If that spontaneous thought were not, it would not be mine but another's. But to think spontaneously and willingly does not posit me. Indeed I exist willingly, but in the question why I exist, I cannot rest on my will, for it is not real enough that, conceiving it, I could judge existence to be inseparable from it, as already noted; nor does it posit me as I would wish with respect to the modes, as said. I am indeed, while attending to myself, what I wish to be; but I am also what I am while not thinking of it. Indeed I can experience that, if I did not wish to be, in order to avoid anguish of mind, I would nevertheless not cease to be, which would happen if the absurd fiction could be said to have any place, namely that I am from my will. Hence it follows that I am from another, who is the one I call God.

units.la: V. Antequam vero ad illum transeam id notabo quod ex mox dictis in omnia defluit: scilicet (1) hinc manifestum esse me non solum, sed etiam omnia in quibus est vel minima imperfectio, non esse à se: nam si essentia illorum non excludit eam quantumlibet parvam quam habent imperfectionem, nec includit illi minimæ imperfectioni oppositam, quæ valde parva debet esse, realitatem, quomodo excluderet maximam illam imperfectionem τὸ non esse, includeretque omnium primam & præcipuam realitatem esse? Quomodo illud quod in genere Entis id quod maximum est includeret, excluderet (ut fiat) id quod minimum est, & naturæ suæ conveniens, & cujus defectus illi est imperfectio? Sic aliquid esset respectu sui potentissimum & impotentissimum, nam ma-ximam perfectionem ponere posset in se, minimam autem ponere non posset, quæ contradictoria sunt. (2) Ergo si quid est à se, illud nul-lam, ne minimam quidem, imperfectionem habet, & consequenter omnes perfectiones cogitabiles habet, quibus nulla major est ea quæ existentiam per se infert. (3) Ergo etiam absurdum est fingere, id, quod prius nihil fuit, incepisse postea esse à se, sive se ponere; & præterea id quod se ponit, non esse perfectissimum: nam prius dicit quod ipsum nihil sit adeo perfectum ut rerum existentia ab illo sit petenda, quod stultum est; posterius vero asserit, ei quod maximam habet perfectionem, siquidem sit à se, deesse maximam perfectionem, siquidem negetur esse perfectissimum: quæ contradicentia sunt. Assuescat ex his Mens in positione omnium sibi non hærere, sed ad aliud semper respicere: nec solidam ullius rei existentis causam rationemque se habere putet, donec ad Ens Perfectissimum devenerit.
units.tr: V. Before I pass to him, I will note what flows from what has just been said into all things: namely, (1) that it is manifest from this that not only I, but also all things in which there is even the smallest imperfection, are not from themselves. For if the essence of those things does not exclude the imperfection they have, however small it may be, nor include the reality opposed to that smallest imperfection, which must be very small, how would it exclude that greatest imperfection, the not-being [τὸ non esse], and include the first and chief reality, being [esse], of all? How would that which includes what is greatest in the genus of being exclude (so that it may come to be) what is least, and agreeable to its nature, and whose lack is an imperfection for it? Thus something would be most powerful and most powerless with respect to itself, for it could posit in itself the greatest perfection but could not posit the least, which are contradictories. (2) Therefore, if anything is from itself, it has no imperfection, not even the smallest, and consequently has all conceivable perfections, than which none is greater than that which infers existence through itself. (3) Therefore it is also absurd to imagine that what previously was nothing began afterward to be from itself, or to posit itself; and moreover that what posits itself is not most perfect. For first it says that it is so imperfect that the existence of things must be sought from it, which is foolish; and afterward it asserts that what has the greatest perfection, if it is from itself, lacks the greatest perfection, if it is denied to be most perfect: which are contradictions. Let the mind become accustomed from these things not to rest in the positing of all things, but always to look to something else; and let it not think that it has a solid cause and reason of any existing thing until it has arrived at the Most Perfect Being.

units.la: 6. 7. Deum esse à se positive, quæ ejus Sufficientia est. Causæ duæ à Metaphysicis omissæ. 8. Sufficientia Dei ut in literis sacris expressa.
units.tr: 6. 7. That God is from himself positively, which is his Sufficiency. Two causes omitted by the Metaphysicians. 8. The Sufficiency of God as expressed in the sacred letters.

units.la: VI. Nunc ex horum consideratione ad Deum, Cogitationem illam summam, transiens, non modo novi eum esse existentiæ meæ rationem & causam, quam efficientem appellare possum, cum sim ejus opus ab illo differens, & extra ejus naturam positum; verum etiam, Divinam illam ejus naturam perfectionesque intuens, percipio illum esse à se, non negative, quasi ratio cui ens summum existat, hæc esset, quod non noverim aliquid diversum unde is esset, aut quasi ejus ratio seu causa, esset res negativa, sive imperfectio quædam; sed quam maxime omnium positive. Hoc est, ratio, causa, vis, efficacia, virtus, quæ in Deo concipitur & quæ intelligitur existere, est res omnium maxime positiva, realis, perfecta, adeo ut existere dicendus sit ille vi & efficacia naturæ suæ, sive perfectionum, quæ tantæ, tam abundantes realitate, ita plenæ, ita completæ sunt, ut earum, adeoque Dei, existentia, non aliunde sit accersenda, cum nihil eis aliunde superaddi possit. Cum igitur cætera omnia per causam à se ipsis diversam existant, quæ eam ob rem efficiens appellatur, Deus solus existit per se & propter se suasque perfectiones, id est, quoniam est Ens perfectissimum. Et ista causæ notio, cum nempe non itur ultra rem propositam in qua tantas perfectiones reperire est ut eæ ad existentiam rei sufficiant, prior est notione causæ efficientis, imo ejus fundamentum est: nam qui ille cujus existentia esset desumenda aliunde quam à naturæ suæ consideratione & virtute, origo existentiæ aliorum à se diversorum esse posset? Ergo Deus ita est à se, ut ratio sive causa qua existit, sit causa omnes alias antecedens, prima & radicalis, unde etiam omnes rerum aliarum existentiæ, etsi mediante alia causa, quæ est placiti, pullulant. Et hinc patet quam jejune Metaphysici vulgo de causis, etsi omnia transcendere prætendant, philosophentur, cum de hac omnium nobilissima & prima, quæque si insolita voce efferenda esset, causa Identitatis vel Suitatis (qua voce, alia quidem in re, illustris Baconus usus est) posset vocari, nihil dixerint; ut neque de causa ab hac nobilitate secunda, quam prorsus nescierunt, qua tamen rerum veritates & essentiæ, non dicam efficiuntur (eo quod ad existentiam id soleat referri) sed statuuntur, quæque idcirco causa statuens est dicenda, de qua inferius ad Dominium Dei.
units.tr: VI. Now, passing from these considerations to God, that highest Thought, I not only know that he is the reason and cause of my existence, which I can call efficient, since I am his work, differing from him and placed outside his nature; but also, looking upon that divine nature of his and his perfections, I perceive that he is from himself, not negatively, as if the reason on account of which the highest being exists were this, that I know of nothing different from which it is, or as if its reason or cause were a negative thing, or some kind of imperfection; but, above all things, positively. That is, the reason, cause, power, efficacy and virtue which is conceived in God and which is understood to exist, is the most positive, real and perfect of all things, so that he is rightly said to exist by the force and efficacy of his nature, or of his perfections, which are so great, so abundant in reality, so full and so complete, that their existence, and therefore God's, is not to be sought from elsewhere, since nothing can be added to them from elsewhere. Since therefore all other things exist through a cause different from themselves, which for that reason is called efficient, God alone exists through himself and on account of himself and his perfections, that is, because he is the most perfect Being. And this notion of cause, since, namely, one does not go beyond the thing proposed, in which such great perfections are to be found that they suffice for the existence of the thing, is prior to the notion of efficient cause; indeed it is its foundation. For how could that being, whose existence were to be derived from elsewhere than from the consideration and power of its own nature, be the origin of the existence of other things different from itself? Therefore God is from himself in such a way that the reason or cause by which he exists is the cause preceding all others, first and radical, from which indeed the existence of all other things sprouts, even though through another cause, which is that of decree. And hence it is plain how meagrely the Metaphysicians generally philosophise about causes, although they profess to transcend all things, since about this most noble and first cause, which, if it had to be expressed by an unusual word, could be called the cause of Identity or of Aseity (a word the illustrious Bacon used, though in another matter), they have said nothing; nor about the second cause of this nobility, which they utterly did not know, by which nevertheless the truths and essences of things are, I will not say brought into being (since that is usually referred to existence), but established; and which for that reason is to be called the establishing cause, of which more below, concerning the Dominion of God.

units.la: VII. Quod autem (ut in viam redeamus, & supra assumpta Deo applicentur) quod inquam Dei natura & perfectiones existentiam inferant, ut non possint non existentes concipi, quod de illis existentia negari nequeat absque contradictione, quod Deus à se, se ipsum solum requirens, & se ipso sufficiens sit affirmandus, id ex attentione ad illum atque ad ea quæ in illo sunt, fiet evidentissimum. Consideretur is ut merum esse, sive ut mera Cogitatio, & omnia patebunt. Mera Cogitatio est Cogitatio sine ulla limitatione, Cogitatio sine ulla limitatione in se habet existentiam, alioqui si hæc extra illam esset quærenda, limitaretur illa, siquidem extra illam aliquid, quo opus habet, & quo in se destituretur, existeret. Idem conficietur si terminis Entis summi, sive perfectissimi utamur, nam contradicens est concipere velle tale Ens ut non existens; aut judicare, repugnando conceptui, id non existere. Plura non addam. videatur Cartesii Meditatio Quinta, cum primis responsionibus, ubi rem pluribus persequitur, quæ non libet hic resumere.
units.tr: VII. But that (to return to the path, and that the things assumed above be applied to God), that, I say, the nature and perfections of God imply existence, so that they cannot be conceived as not existing, that existence cannot be denied of them without contradiction, and that God is to be affirmed as from himself, requiring himself alone and sufficient in himself, this will become most evident from attention to him and to those things which are in him. Let him be considered as pure being, or as pure Thought, and all things will become plain. Pure Thought is Thought without any limitation; Thought without any limitation has existence in itself; otherwise, if existence were to be sought outside it, it would be limited, since something outside it would exist which it needs, and in which it would be deprived of itself. The same will be concluded if we use the terms of the highest, or most perfect, Being; for it is contradictory to wish to conceive such a Being as not existing, or, by judging against the concept, to judge that it does not exist. I will add no more. Let the Fifth Meditation of Descartes be consulted, together with the first replies, where he pursues the matter at greater length, which I do not wish to resume here.

units.la: VIII. Atque ad hanc Dei prærogativam perfectionemque respicitur, cum ei tribuitur Sufficientia, sive independentia in existendo. quo sensu Sacræ literæ dicunt, præter illum nil esse, ut significent à nulla re ab illo diversa existentiam ejus desumi; sed eum sibi ipsi sufficere, ut & aliis rebus, quæ sine illo nihil sunt. Et huc præter nomen שׁדִי[?], quod sciunt omnes sufficientiam designare, referri potest apprime illa Dei responsio, qua Mosi quærenti, quis vel quid Deus sit? Respondet se ipsum notificans, Sum qui sum. Sum, hoc est, mea essentia, qui sum, id est, est ut existam, est mea existentia, est illa quæ ab existentia est inseparabilis: Sum ita perfectus ut existentiæ meæ ratio sit ego ipse, non diversa, non separabilis à me ipso. quo etiam nomen tetragrammaton, quod esse & existere significat, revocari potest.
units.tr: VIII. And to this prerogative and perfection of God regard is had when Sufficiency is attributed to him, that is, independence in existing. In this sense the sacred letters say that there is nothing besides him, to signify that his existence is derived from no thing different from him; but that he suffices to himself, as also for other things, which without him are nothing. And to this, besides the name שׁדִי[?], which everyone knows to signify sufficiency, can be referred especially that answer of God, by which, when Moses asked who or what God is, he replies, making himself known: I am who I am. I am, that is, my essence; who I am, that is, it is that I exist, it is my existence, it is that which is inseparable from existence: I am so perfect that the reason of my existence is myself, not different from, not separable from myself. By which also the name Tetragrammaton, which signifies to be and to exist, can be recalled.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: (4) ACTIVITAS.
units.tr: (4) ACTIVITY.

units.la: 1. Facultates Mentis plures. 2. An in mala mente sint facultates ad bonum? 3. Facultates obsunt activitati merae. Memoria Spiritualis. Habitus.
units.tr: 1. The faculties of the Mind are many. 2. Do faculties for the good remain in a bad mind? 3. Faculties are an obstacle to pure activity. Spiritual memory. Habits.

units.la: I. Post praecedentes de me observationes quae mihi advenit quarta haec est, quod cum mihi ipsi me notum magis & familiarem red-dere conor, ut sciam quis sim, & simul omnia quae in me esse possunt specialiora colligam & amplectar, tum capacitas adeo immensa cogi-tandi innumera innumeris modis occurrit, ut certos limites ipsi praefi-gere cum ratione non ausim: nam non potest cogitatio mea tam multi-pliciter variari, quin facile concipiam illam pluribus posse variari modis ab eo à quo ego sum, qui cum novas novasque sine termino in me ex-citare queat cogitationes, video me esse variabilem indefinite, sive me innumeris esse praeditum facultatibus; est enim hoc ipsum facultas in mente creata, nempe aptitudo sive capacitas ad variationem quandam, quarum ingentem numerum ab illa haberi antea probatum est, ubi af-fertum fuit esse de Mentis natura ut indefinite sit variabilis, utut va-riatio ipsa actualis sive actus facultatis, non adsit idcirco nisi praesente causa.
units.tr: I. Following my earlier observations about myself, this fourth one occurs to me: when I try to make myself more known and familiar to myself, so that I may know who I am and at the same time gather and embrace all the more particular things that can be in me, the capacity for thinking appears so immense, and capable of countless thoughts in countless ways, that I do not dare to set fixed limits to it by reason. For my thinking cannot be varied in so many ways without my easily conceiving that it can be varied in more ways still by him from whom I am, who, since he can stir up in me new and ever new thoughts without end, I see that I am variable without definite limit, or that I am endowed with countless faculties. For this itself is a faculty in a created mind, namely a fitness or capacity for a certain variation, of which an immense number was previously shown to be possessed by it, when it was asserted that it is of the nature of the Mind to be variable without definite limit; although the variation itself, as an actual act of the faculty, is not present except when its cause is present.

units.la: II. Ad haecce, (ut hoc obiter dicam) attendentibus, non diffi-cile erit se quibusdam difficultatibus quae nonnullos importune exer-cent, extricare: Exempli causa, disputatur, an homo lapsus habeat facultates resipiscendi, credendi, & similes? facultas est variabilitas, Mens autem non est invariabilis, quod solius Dei est. Sed, an forma illa cogitationis quae constituit resipiscentiam, fidem, &c. potest acci-dere cogitationi sive Menti? an cum illa congruit, an vero repugnat illi, aut destruit illam? Nequaquam. Hoc sensu, quidni has habeat facultates? Si vero ad actum, sive ad ipsam Mentis variationem respi-ciatur, quaestio fuerit, vel, An tales variationes possint accidere Menti sine causa sufficiente? quod absurdum esset asserere; vel, an possit Mens ita mutari, si nempe causa adsit sufficiens? Quo sensu iterum omnes Mentes & illas & plures alias habent facultates, hoc est, à causa sufficiente ita mutari & poni possunt. Sed si jam quaeratur, An illa mutationis causa sit non-Deus, an hujus positionis ratio reddi possit ex consideratione naturæ rei quæ Deus non sit? Ex præcedenti capite, & ex sequentibus, manifestum est quid ad hoc sit respondendum. In his itaque, ut & in infinitis fere aliis, nulla est expensis terminis difficultas. Quod si in hisce nonnulli per facultatem se intelligere causam cujus vi res variatur profiteantur, cum ea vis sit in Deo, nil vero quod in Deo est sit subjective in creaturis, ut demonstratum, consequitur omnes ea destitui. Sed nobis facultas est id quod diximus.
units.tr: II. Here, (to mention this in passing), if one attends to these matters, it will not be difficult to extricate oneself from certain difficulties that trouble some people unduly. For example, it is disputed whether fallen man has faculties of repentance, of believing, and the like. A faculty is a capacity for variation, but the Mind is not invariable, which belongs to God alone. But can that form of thought which constitutes repentance, faith, etc. happen to a thought or Mind? Does it agree with it, or does it instead conflict with it or destroy it? By no means. In this sense, why should it not have these faculties? If, however, one looks to the act, or to the very variation of the Mind, the question would be either: Can such variations happen to the Mind without a sufficient cause? This would be absurd to assert. Or: Can the Mind be so changed, namely if a sufficient cause is present? In this sense again, all Minds, both those and many others, have faculties, that is, they can be so changed and placed by a sufficient cause. But if it is now asked whether that cause of change is a non-God, or whether the reason for this positing can be given from the consideration of the nature of a thing that is not God, the preceding chapter and the following ones make clear what is to be answered to this. In these matters, therefore, as in almost endless others, there is no difficulty once the terms are weighed. But if some in these matters profess to understand by faculty the cause by whose power a thing is varied, since that power is in God, and nothing that is in God is subjectively in creatures, as has been demonstrated, it follows that all creatures are deprived of it. But for us a faculty is what we have said.

units.la: III. Cum animadverti supra me, sive Cogitationem meam à se non esse, sed à Deo, concludendum reliqui me esse ex natura mea rem vere passivam, sive aliunde recipientem: at jam id luculenter patet ex istis, quæ in me sunt facultatibus, numero indefinitis, quæ omnes sunt capacitates recipiendi id quod nondum actu in me est. An id venturum sit per modum actionis, an vero ut passio, jam non examino: sed, quicquid sit, me non esse rem mere activam inde infero, idem illaturus ex iis quæ ex facultatibus istis postquam in actum fuere deductæ, in Mente resultant, qualia sunt, memoria spiritualis, quæ est in mente, capacitas cogitandi se olim attente & pure de nonnullis cogitasse, & habitus spirituales, qui sunt aptitudo cogitationis ad recipiendam facile præ omnibus aliis formis formam eam quæ repetitis vicibus illi adfuit. qui, quamquam sæpe verbo, non tamen conceptu confundendi sunt cum facultatibus, quas semper præsupponunt, simulque cum illis capacitatem recipiendi.
units.tr: III. When I observed above that I am not my own thought, but that my thought is from God, I concluded that I am by my nature something truly passive, that is, receiving from elsewhere. But now this is clearly evident from those faculties in me, which are indefinite in number and are all capacities for receiving what is not yet actually in me. Whether this will come about by way of action or as a passion, I do not now examine; but whatever the case, I infer from this that I am not a purely active thing, and I shall infer the same from those things which result in the Mind once these faculties have been brought into act, such as spiritual memory, which is in the mind, the capacity of thought to recall that it once thought attentively and purely about certain things, and spiritual habits, which are the fitness of thought to receive more readily, before all other forms, that form which has been present to it again and again. These, although they are often confused in word, must not be confused in concept with the faculties, which they always presuppose, and along with them the capacity for receiving.

units.la: 4. Dei natura & placitum nil aliunde recipere possunt. Activitas Dei ut ab Impassibilitate distincta concipiatur.
units.tr: 4. The nature and the good pleasure of God cannot receive anything from elsewhere. The activity of God is to be conceived as distinct from impassibility.

units.la: IV. Ad Deum quod attinet, nil tale in eo percipio; non facultates, non memoriam intellectualem qualem dixi, non habitus, non recipiendi in se capacitatem ullam: Sed ut purus actus à me concipitur, quod ipsum, dum illi Activitatem tribuo, indigitare volo. Cogitatio mera omnia sibi convenientia actu includit & à se habet; si quid recipiendi foret capax, ejus non cogitatio actualis seu incogitantia, prius in illa fuisset, quod conceptui puræ Cogitationis repugnat. Sed quid illud esset quod conciperem eam recipere posse, & unde? Certe non ab alio id venire posset. hoc crassius est quam ut expresse refutetur; ergo à se ipso posset recipere Deus: quid vero? se ipsum? atqui jam se ipsum habere concipitur : aliud ipso deterius ? non admittere potest : aliud ipso excellentius ? non datur. sed & unde Cogitatio quæ pure est à se haberet notionem rei se melioris ? Certe cum talis notio è consideratione rei à pura cogitatione diversæ foret desumpta, non potest eo in Cogitatione quæ purissime à se est ullo modo fingi esse. Abest ergo à natura Dei aptitudo quidvis recipiendi. A placito ejus id etiam abest, cum immutabilis sit cogitatio : & quamvis alio modo id se habere potuisset, si Deo visum fuisset, ea tamen non est receptio à creatura, nec ejusmodi diversitatis aptitudo, Dei naturam respicit, sed res creatas vel statutas. Sed hæc ipsa ex aliis attributis, Unitatis nempe, Dominii, Simplicitatis, Libertatis, Impassibilitatis, qua actus recipiendi, ut hic per Activitatem potentia sive facultas, removetur, luculentius patebunt.
units.tr: IV. As for God, I perceive nothing of this kind in him: no faculties, no intellectual memory such as I have described, no habits, no capacity whatever for receiving into himself. Rather, he is conceived by me as pure act, which I wish to indicate by ascribing to him Activity. Pure thought includes actually, and has from itself, all things that belong to it; if it were capable of receiving anything, its actual thinking, or non-thinking, would have been in it before, which is repugnant to the concept of pure thought. But what would that be which I might conceive it could receive, and from where? Certainly it could not come from another. This is too crude to need express refutation; therefore God could receive from himself. But what? Himself? Yet he is already conceived as having himself. Something worse than himself? He cannot admit that. Something more excellent than himself? None exists. But also, whence would a Thought which is purely from itself have the notion of a thing better than itself? Certainly, since such a notion would have been drawn from the consideration of a thing different from pure thought, it cannot in any way be imagined to be in that Thought which is most purely from itself. Therefore the capacity for receiving anything is absent from the nature of God. It is also absent from his good pleasure, since his thought is unchangeable; and although it could have been otherwise, if it had seemed good to God, nevertheless that is not a reception from a creature, nor does such a capacity for diversity regard the nature of God, but created or appointed things. But these matters will be made clearer from the other attributes, namely Unity, Dominion, Simplicity, Liberty, Impassibility, by which the act of receiving, which here is removed by Activity as potency or faculty, will be more clearly shown.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: (5) INCOMPREHENSIBILITAS.
units.tr: (5) INCOMPREHENSIBILITY.

units.la: 1. Anima Incomprehensibilis. Incomprehensibilitas absoluta, sive objectiva & subjectiva simul, magna imperfectio: sed stabilis nec culpanda. Culpanda opposita curiositas.
units.tr: 1. The soul is incomprehensible. Absolute incomprehensibility, that is, objective and subjective at once, is a great imperfection, but a stable one and not blameworthy. What is blameworthy is the opposite, curiosity.

units.la: I. Cum autem, ut ad me redeam, istarum facultatum quæ in me sunt, numerum cognitione assequi non possim (impossibile enim est ut determinem quot modis variari possit Cogitatio mea) inde convincor, non modo eatenus me mihi esse incognitum, verum etiam me ne posse quidem à me cognosci, adeoque hoc sensu me mihi incomprehensibilem esse. Et noto attributum illud incomprehensibilitatis si absolute spectetur, sive, si non referatur ad aliud subjectum quam ad illud de quo dicitur, ita ut illud sibi ipsi sit incomprehensibile, imperfectionem non parvam involvere: est enim defectus Cogitationis magnus & ignorantia, sibi ipsi notum nec esse, nec esse posse. quamobrem materialia maxime infra Mentes imperfecta sunt, quoniam nullo modo, ne minima quidem ex parte, se nosse, se capere, multo minus se comprehendere queunt, adeoque absolutissime sibi incomprehensibilia sunt. Adverto etiam imperfectionem illam in me stabilem esse, non rejectaneam: nam me ipsum comprehendere, nil aliud est quam complete nosse omnia quæ Deus placito & potentia sua in me ponere potest: quod ut noscam, natura mea nec requirit, nec admittit, ut amplius dicetur. Ex quo principio improbatur & damnatur cupiditas illa curiosa, qua quæ mihi evenire possunt aut eventura sunt, quæque me Author meus celavit, mihi quocunque modo prædici velle possem.
units.tr: I. Since, to return to myself, I cannot grasp by knowledge the number of those faculties which are in me (for it is impossible for me to determine in how many ways my thought can be varied), I am convinced from this that I am not only unknown to myself to that extent, but that I cannot even be known by myself, and so in this sense I am incomprehensible to myself. And I note that this attribute of incomprehensibility, if it is regarded absolutely, or if it is not referred to any subject other than that of which it is said, so that the thing is incomprehensible to itself, involves no small imperfection: for it is a great defect and ignorance of thought not to be known to itself, nor to be able to be known. For this reason material things, which are far below minds, are most imperfect, since in no way, not even in the smallest part, can they know themselves, grasp themselves, much less comprehend themselves, and so they are absolutely incomprehensible to themselves. I also observe that this imperfection in me is stable, not something to be rejected: for to comprehend myself is nothing other than to know completely all that God by his pleasure and power can place in me; and that I do not require or admit to know, as will be said more fully. From this principle is disapproved and condemned that curious desire by which I might wish to have foretold to me, in whatever way, the things that can happen to me or are about to happen, and that my Author has hidden from me.

units.la: 2. Deus incomprehensibilis. 3. 4. Non potest complete, sive adæquate repræsentari per rem diversæ ab illo naturæ; neque etiam ulla res. 5. Incomprehensibilitatis Dei usus.
units.tr: 2. God is incomprehensible. 3. 4. He cannot be completely, or adequately, represented by a thing of a nature different from his; nor indeed by any thing. 5. The use of God's incomprehensibility.

units.la: II. Quanto magis ergo Deus Incomprehensibilis putandus est, non quidem sibi, cum hoc à Cogitatione mera & activissima exulet, sed mihi, & aliis quibuscunque ab illo diversis fortisque[?] meæ creatæ ab illo participibus? Ut mirari subeat quædam de illo, de ejus potentia, de placito, à nonnullis ideo esse negata, quod ea cogitationibus suis comprehendere non possent. Atqui cum vidi modo me mihi esse incomprehensibilem, id in eo fundatum erat quod Dei potentiam & placitum, unde quamplurima mihi eventura aut evenire capacia ponere valet, à me non comprehendebantur. Igitur quanto magis illius natura, essentia, & quæ in ea sunt omnia, mihi sunt incomprehensibilia?
