Certe, siquidem comprehendere sit adæquate omnia mente complecti, aut Deus esset Cogitatio imperfecta, si à me, Cogitatione imperfecta, sic caperetur; aut ego essem Cogitatio mera, si illum, vel unum ex illis quæ in eo sunt in quo omnia unum sunt, comprehenderem, atque ita, & ego essem Deus, ille vero, siquidem à me qui tunc Cogitatio mera essem, ut diversus comprehenderetur, tanquam finitus conciperetur: nam nihil à Cogitatione mera, quæ infinita est, diversum est, quin finitum sit. Hac igitur assertione, Deum esse mihi comprehensibilem, absurde Deo eos limites tribuerem quos à mente mea removissem prius. Deus itaque est omnino à me Incomprehensibilis.
units.tr: II. How much more, then, must God be thought incomprehensible, not indeed to himself, since this is far removed from pure and most active thought, but to me, and to all others who are different from him and to my created sharers in him? So that it is a wonder that certain things about him, about his power and his pleasure, have been denied by some for the reason that they could not comprehend them by their thoughts. But indeed, when I saw just now that I am incomprehensible to myself, this was founded on the fact that the power and pleasure of God, from which he can bring about very many things that are going to happen to me or are capable of happening, were not comprehended by me. Therefore, how much more are his nature, essence, and all that is in him incomprehensible to me? Certainly, if to comprehend means to embrace all things adequately with the mind, then either God would be an imperfect thought, if he were grasped in this way by me, who am an imperfect thought; or I would be pure thought, if I comprehended him, or even one of those things which are in him, in whom all things are one; and thus I would be God, and he, provided that he was comprehended by me, who would then be pure thought, as something different, would be conceived as finite: for nothing that is different from pure thought, which is infinite, fails to be finite. By this assertion, then, that God is comprehensible to me, I would absurdly attribute to God those limits which I had previously removed from my mind. God is therefore wholly incomprehensible to me.

units.la: III. Quamvis autem hoc attributum sit relativum, nec sit in subjecto respectu sui, sitque verbo negativum, attamen ejus fundamentum est maxime in Deo, maximeque positivum, est enim ipsa Dei natura, sive mera & perfecta Cogitatio, quæ ideo à Cogitatione deficiente non potest adæquate repræsentari. Imo, ut id addam, repræsentatio adæquata per aliquid quod sit naturæ à repræsentato diversæ, est quid contradictorium: nam repræsentatio per rem naturæ diversæ siquidem non habeat omnia prout in repræsentato sunt, est inadæquata ; quod si vero omnia habeat, tunc non differt à re ipsa: quomodo Deus repræsen-tatur per ideam seu imaginem à se de se conceptam, sibique naturalem, quæ adeo ab ipsa natura non differt; aut denique si res quæ aliquid adæquate repræsentare vere dicitur, sit diversa à repræsentato, tunc proprie non repræsentat, sive non recipit similitudinem rei, sed est ejus causa efficiens vel statuens: quomodo Deus omnia quæ ab ipso sunt diversa, non proprie repræsentat, sed statuit, vel efficit, cum earum ideas concipit. Ultra hæc non potest repræsentatio extendi, nec ea qua Deus à nobis repræsentatur vel concipitur, est ultimi vel medii generis recensiti, sed primi, adeoque non potest ea non esse inadæquata, & Deus Incomprehensibilis.
units.tr: III. Although this attribute is relative, and is not in the subject with respect to itself, and is negative in word, nevertheless its foundation lies chiefly in God, and is most positive, for it is the very nature of God, that is, pure and perfect thought, which therefore cannot be adequately represented by deficient thought. Indeed, to add this too: an adequate representation by something of a nature different from what is represented is a contradiction in terms: for a representation by a thing of a different nature, if it does not have all things as they are in what is represented, is inadequate; but if it has all of them, then it does not differ from the thing itself. So God is represented through an idea or image conceived by himself of himself, and natural to himself, which therefore does not differ from his very nature. Or finally, if a thing which is said truly to represent something adequately is different from what is represented, then it does not properly represent, that is, it does not receive the likeness of the thing, but is its efficient or establishing cause: so God, when he conceives the ideas of all things that are different from himself, does not properly represent them, but establishes or brings them about. Representation cannot be extended beyond these; and that representation by which God is represented or conceived by us is not of the last or middle kind listed, but of the first, and so it cannot be other than inadequate, and God is incomprehensible.

units.la: IV. Quæri posset, Annon quemadmodum Deus effecit ut repræsentaretur in me utcunque per ideam quæ ipsa non est Deus, nec formaliter habet ea quæ in Deo, sed objectivè ; sic posset etiam quoad omnia quæ in illo sunt, per ideam in me adæquate repræsentari, quæ non ideo tamen inferret me infinitum esse, vel me omnia quæ in Deo sunt, adæquate possidere formaliter, sed idealiter & objectivè tantum? Resp. Quid de quæstionibus, quæ circa id quod Deus facere posset proponuntur, censeri debeat, alibi dicetur. Sed ad rem ipsam respondeo, esse in terminis contradictionem. Hic conceptus absurdissimus est, repræsentare Deum complete & adæquate, nec tamen formaliter, sed objectivè: cum ista repræsentatio Dei completa sit de forma, de natura, de essentia Dei, adeoque inseparabilis ab illo, nec extra illum possibilis. Objecti illius summi notitia adæquata est ipsum illud objectum, alias Deus se ipsum adæquate noscens, haberet notitiam sive Cogitationem, quæ non esset ille ipse, quod absurdi convictum est. Verbo, non dari adæquatam repræsentationem per rem naturæ diversæ, notio communis est, quæ cuilibet attendenti meditatione perpendenda, & exemplis omnium quæ in mundo sunt illustranda relinquitur.
units.tr: IV. It might be asked: just as God has brought it about that he is represented in me in some way through an idea which is not itself God, and does not formally have the things which are in God, but only objectively, might he not also be adequately represented in me, as regards all the things that are in him, through an idea, which would not, however, imply that I am infinite, or that I formally possess adequately all the things that are in God, but only ideally and objectively? Reply: what ought to be judged about questions which are put concerning what God could do will be said elsewhere. But to the matter itself I reply that there is a contradiction in the terms. This concept is most absurd, to represent God completely and adequately, and yet not formally but objectively: since such a complete representation of God is of the form, of the nature, of the essence of God, and so is inseparable from him, nor is it possible outside him. The adequate knowledge of that highest object is that very object itself; otherwise God, knowing himself adequately, would have a knowledge or thought which was not he himself, which has been proved to be absurd. In a word, that there is no adequate representation through a thing of a different nature is a common notion, which is left to be weighed by anyone who attends to it with meditation, and to be illustrated by examples from all the things that are in the world.

units.la: V. Hæc Dei Incomprehensibilitas maximè confert ad Fidem tum persuasivam, tum operativam, sive Theoriæ, & Praxeos, in iis quæ Deus revelat, seu ipsum ejusve naturam, seu ejus placitum, aut ea quæ ab eo efficienda vel facta sunt, concernunt. Nam cum Deus ea de se concipiat quæ ab hominibus concipi non possunt, hoc ipsum potest hominibus iis verbis declarare ex quibus illi ea utcunque attingant, non autem comprehendant. Præterea, potest illi placere ut velit, imo effecturus sit, vel efficiat quædam quæ cogitationis humanæ limites excedant, hinc judicia sive placita Dei incomprehensibilia exclamat sanctus vir. Hæc igitur fide persuasiva recipienda sunt, (quod etiam pessimi quique fa-ciunt, & ipsi quoque Dæmones) attamen, ubi demum ea revelata esse constat: nam quod quædam quæ non modo concipi nequeunt, sed & conceptui repugnant, nec revelata sunt, hac via obtrudantur, omnino ridiculum est. Sed & fidei vere efficaci hic est suus locus: cum nempe Deus hominem ducit per avia, quorum sequela, eventus & ratio non cernuntur, cum jubet ingredi ea, qualia sunt, in hoc patientiæ suæ re-gno, amare inimicos, beneficum esse in persequentes, vim vi non re-pellere, pati, fugere laudes & honores, non quærere delectationes, sed contraria amplecti, imo se ipsum odisse, & quod æterni est exercitii, se ipsum non spectare, pluraque ejusmodi: quæ etsi Menti bene meditanti clarissime instar notitiarum ingenitarum conspiciantur, sunt tamen cogitationi sibi adhærenti & adhuc carnali, absurda & stulta, ei vero quæ valde attente non meditatur incomprehensibilia; tunc homini ea non comprehendenti & vere fidere volenti volupe erit juxta principium allatum, Deum suum clausis oculis, prudentia & ratiocinatione carnali spreta, sequi secure: Si enim Deum & ejus placitum intellectu puro non comprehendi posse constat, multo minus à Mente adhuc in-crassata, & concupiscentiis gravata, aut in deducendis & concipiendis ordine veritatibus ab una aliqua prima dependentibus non exercitata, comprehendi poterunt.
units.tr: V. This incomprehensibility of God contributes most to faith, both persuasive and operative, that is, to theory and practice, in those things which God reveals, whether they concern himself and his nature, or his pleasure, or the things which are to be or have been done by him. For since God conceives of himself things which cannot be conceived by men, he can declare this very thing to men in those words by which they somehow reach these things, but do not comprehend them. Moreover, it may please him to will, indeed he will bring about or does bring about certain things which exceed the limits of human thought; hence the holy man cries out: "God's judgments or pleasures are incomprehensible." These things, therefore, are to be received by persuasive faith (which even the worst people do, and the demons themselves too); yet, when it is established that they have been revealed. For it is wholly ridiculous that certain things, which not only cannot be conceived but even contradict conception, and have not been revealed, should be forced upon us in this way. But truly effective faith also has its place here: namely, when God leads a man through pathless ways, whose sequel, outcome and reason are not discerned, when he commands him to enter such things as these in the kingdom of his patience: to love enemies, to be kind to persecutors, not to repel force with force, to suffer, to flee praises and honours, not to seek pleasures but to embrace their opposites, indeed to hate oneself, and, which is of eternal practice, not to regard oneself, and many things of this kind. Although these, to a mind meditating well, appear most clearly like innate notions, yet to thought that clings to itself and is still fleshly they are absurd and foolish, and to one who does not meditate very attentively they are incomprehensible. Then, for the man who does not comprehend them but wishes to trust truly, it will be pleasant, according to the principle stated, to follow his God securely with eyes closed, with prudence and fleshly reasoning set aside. For if it is established that God and his pleasure cannot be comprehended by pure intellect, much less will they be able to be comprehended by a mind still thickened, and weighed down by desires, or not exercised in deducing and conceiving truths in their order, which depend on some one first truth.

units.la: CAPUT VII. (6) INTELLIGENTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. (6) UNDERSTANDING.

units.la: 1.2.3. Mens intelligit se primum, sed confuse, nec distincte, nisi Deum prius noscat.
units.tr: 1.2.3. The mind understands itself first, but confusedly and not distinctly, unless it first knows God.

units.la: I. ETiamsi sensu mox explicito egomet mihi sim incognitus, novi tamen me generalius, quatenus existo cogitans: quare hoc re-spectu ex omnibus objectis & formis quæ cogitationi meæ accidere pos-sint, quæ à me confusius noscantur, de quorum existentia sim certus, objectum primum & proximum sum Ego ipse, proximaque forma ea est quæ me ipsum mihimet, sed generalius, repræsentat. Id ne prave detorqueatur, vel immerito sine notitia traducatur, nonnulla eget explicatione: fieri enim forte posset, ut maligne inde concluderetur, me Creaturæ præ Creatore primum locum assignare, illiusque existentiam Dei ipsius existentia certiorem proponere. quæ vero à Cogitatione mea valde sunt aliena. Nam, ut ne dicam contrarium exinde concludendum esse, non hic loci quæritur, quid respectu perfectionis prius sit? neque, quid in re ipsa sit certius, constantius, necessarium magis & existens? quod jam supra visum est: Sed petitur, quid prius sit cognitione, & quidem confusa? & quid confuso illo modo prius cognoscatur existere? Certe cognoscentem cognito esse ratione & conceptu prius, extra dubium est. Igitur Cogitatio creata, quæ cognoscens est, & cujus natura in hoc est ut sit sui existentis conscia, hoc sensu prior est eo quod postea novit, nempe Deo: nam ea revera cogitare concipitur, & hujus conscia esse, priusquam concipiatur ut de re à se diversa cogitans.
units.tr: I. Even though, by an explicit sense, I am myself unknown to myself at once, I nevertheless know myself more generally, insofar as I exist as a thinking being. Therefore, in this respect, of all the objects and forms that can occur to my thought, those which are known to me more confusedly, and of whose existence I am certain, the first and nearest object is I myself, and the nearest form is that which represents me to myself, but more generally. Lest this be twisted wrongly or ascribed to me without warrant, it needs some explanation. For it might perhaps be maliciously concluded from this that I assign the creature the first place before the Creator, and propose its existence as more certain than the existence of God himself. These things are far removed from my thinking. For, not to say that the contrary must be concluded from it, the question here is not what is prior with respect to perfection, nor what is more certain, more constant, and more necessarily existent in the thing itself; this has already been considered above. Rather, the question is what is prior in knowledge, and indeed in confused knowledge, and what is known to exist earlier in that confused manner? Surely it is beyond doubt that the knower is prior to the known in reason and concept. Therefore the created thought, which knows, and whose nature is such that it is conscious of its own existence, is prior in this sense to what it afterwards knows, namely God. For it is indeed conceived to think and to be conscious of this, before it is conceived as thinking about a thing diverse from itself.

units.la: Quod vero objectaretur, nempe sic existentiam Dei ut dependentem ab existentiæ creatæ mentis statui, vel illius certitudinem huic postponi, & hac statuminari, unde sequeretur Mente creata deficiente vel remota, existentiæ Dei certitudinem commoveri & concuti, si non plane prosterni; quam absurde illud opponeretur, inde patet, quod hic neque de ipsa Dei existentia, neque de ejus certitudine subjectiva sive vi qua illa in se stat, plane agatur, sed de notitia quam ego de me vel de illa habere possum, deque hujus mea notitiæ certitudine cujus objectum est illius existentia in se certissima. Profecto certitudo notitiæ meæ de illius existentia omnino corruit si non existo, eamque habere nequeo nisi prius ponatur me esse, me præditum esse perceptionibus quæ immediate sui sensum certitudinemque inferant. At si, quid prius sit dignitate aut etiam cognitione distincta, quæratur, tantum abest ut ego ipse vel mei ipsius notitia præcedat, quin potius plane non nosfem quousque perfectus aut imperfectus sim, nisi prius oculos in Deum Authorem perfectissimum conjicerem, unde colligerem me magis vel minus perfectum prout ejus perfectiones magis vel minus repræsento.
units.tr: As for the objection that I would thus establish the existence of God as dependent on the existence of a created mind, or would place its certainty after this and prop it up on this, so that, if the created mind were deficient or remote, the certainty of God's existence would be shaken and shattered, if not utterly overthrown: how absurd this objection is becomes clear from the fact that here we are not dealing plainly with God's existence itself, nor with its subjective certainty, that is, the power by which it stands in itself, but with the knowledge that I can have of myself or of him, and with the certainty of this my knowledge, whose object is his existence, most certain in itself. Certainly the certainty of my knowledge of his existence wholly collapses if I do not exist, and I cannot have it unless it is first posited that I am, endowed with perceptions that immediately yield a sense of self and certainty of self. But if the question is what is prior in dignity or even in distinct knowledge, then far from my own self or knowledge of myself coming first, I would not even know whether I am perfect or imperfect, unless I first turned my eyes to God, the most perfect Author, from whom I would gather that I am more or less perfect according as I represent his perfections more or less.

units.la: II. Et hæc omnia in superiori libro demonstrata sunt: nam ubi me omnibus alienis exuebam, remanebat primo conscientia seu notio mei sive meæ intelligentiæ, at illa informis, se sola nec se intelligere, nec implere valens, ad aliud, nempe ad summum Ens, tendebat, quod prius contemplata, & ad se reversa, se postmodum suasque perfectiones novit distinctius.
units.tr: II. All these things have been demonstrated in the preceding book. For when I stripped myself of all foreign things, there remained first the consciousness or notion of myself, or of my understanding; but this, being formless, and unable to understand or complete itself by itself alone, tended towards another, namely the highest Being, which, having first contemplated it and then returned to itself, it afterwards knew more distinctly, together with itself and its perfections.

units.la: III. Ergo Cogitationis intelligentiæque meæ objectum primum Ego ipse sum, sed obscure: ut autem lux affulgeat, ut quid meum sit, quid non sit, distincte sciam, deficit in se intelligentia mea, & in theoria, haut secus ac in praxi (ubi etiam intellectus mei objectum primum tenebrae meae sunt) alterius objecti poscit opem; Itaque mei ipsius intelligentia se sola, eo quo compleri posset modo, incompleta est.
units.tr: III. Therefore the first object of my thought and understanding is I myself, but obscurely. Yet so that light may shine on me and I may know distinctly what is mine and what is not mine, my understanding is deficient in itself, and both in theory and in practice (where my own shadows are also the first object of my intellect) it requires the help of another object. Thus the understanding of myself, by itself alone, is incomplete in such a way that it could not be made complete.

units.la: 4. Intelligentia Dei de se, primo, complete, est ipsemet ille, in illo solo, de illo solo. 5. Scientiæ simplicis Intelligentiæ objectum solus Deus, non res creabiles aut possibiles.
units.tr: 4. The understanding of God concerning himself is, first and completely, himself, in him alone, and of him alone. 5. The object of the simple understanding is God alone, not creatable or possible things.

units.la: IV. Demonstrata jam superius Re vivente, & pure quidem, sibi sufficiente, activa, à se ipsa sola comprehensa, facile est percipere id quod ex sexta hac de mente mea consideratione occasione in Deo est animadvertendum. Nempe primo, Eum ita cogitare sive intelligere, ut primum proximumque suum objectum sibi ille sit, nam est res cogitans, in qua primum omnium est, ut sit sui conscia: Deinde, Illam sui cognitionem esse perfectam, clarissimam, completam se ipsa, ut non ad aliud ab ipso diversum sit attendendum, cum cogitatio sit mera, sibique sufficiens: Adeoque tertio Intellectionem sive Intelligentiam ab ipso sive ab ejus Essentia non differre, siquidem perfectissima cogitatio sit: Unde & hoc sequitur, eam ita esse Deo naturalem ut nullis sit communicabilis creaturis, quippe quæ perfectissima intellectione capaces non sint; sed id omne esse Deum quod Deum complete intelligit; Et illud denique, notitiam illam Dei de se, solam esse, quæ ei sit essentialis & immutabilis. Quod si alia præter se noscat, non necessario illa noscit, sed ex placito, cum potuerit ea non nosse uti jam novit; ut tamen inde concludi nequeat sic in illo futuram fuisse ignorantiam, mutationemve, nam tunc ista nec existentia, nec vera, nec etiam possibilia dici potuissent, ut postmodum demonstrabitur.
units.tr: IV. Now that the living Being has been demonstrated above, and that being purely active, self-sufficient, and comprehended by itself alone, it is easy to perceive what must be noted about God from this sixth consideration of my mind. Namely, first, that he thinks or understands in such a way that he himself is his first and nearest object, for he is a thinking thing, in which the first thing of all is that it is conscious of itself. Then, second, that this self-knowledge is perfect, most clear, and complete in itself, so that no attention need be paid to anything diverse from himself, since thought is pure and sufficient to itself. And thus, third, that his intellection or understanding does not differ from himself or from his essence, since it is the most perfect thought. Whence it also follows that it is so natural to God that it cannot be communicated to creatures, since they are not capable of the most perfect intellection; and that everything is God which understands God completely. And finally, that this knowledge of God concerning himself alone is the only knowledge which is essential and immutable to him. But if he knows other things besides himself, he does not know them necessarily, but by choice, since he could have not known them, as he now knows them; yet it cannot thence be concluded that there would have been ignorance or change in him, for then those things could not be called existent, true, or even possible, as will be demonstrated afterwards.

units.la: V. Hæc Dei notitia de se solo, completa, quæ in ipso solo est, & ipsemet est, sola ei essentialis, naturalis, necessaria, immutabilis, ea est, quæ voce Intelligentia, etiam in literis Sacris, denotatur: eadem sola Simplicis Intelligentiæ, vel simpliciter intelligens Scientia est appellanda, neque, pace aliter sentientium, ulla creabilia, ullas rerum essentias vel abstractas veritates, respicit. Nam Deus simpliciter intelligens sibi ipsi sufficit, neque est necesse ad complementum Intelligentiæ suæ ut ad alia respiciat, quamvis si ex abundanti ipsi placet ut aliquid præter se sit verum, si velit aliquid fingere, sequatur illud esse verum, illudque ab illo cognosci & videri: sed id ad scientiam visionis, quam vocant, refero, non vero ad Intelligentiam, quod nomen Notitiae Dei de se ipso significandae esto sacratum, altera de caeteris quibuscunque rebus notitia nomine Cognitionis vel scientiae insignita. Haec & similia conferre licet cum eis quae de Filio Dei, qui ipsa illa Intelligentia apud Sacros Authores cluet, dicuntur, ut à nonnullis factum, & à nemine cassa opera, si modo debite fiat, faciendum.
units.tr: V. This knowledge of God concerning himself alone, complete, which is in himself alone and is himself, the only one essential, natural, necessary, and immutable to him, is what is denoted by the word Understanding, also in the Sacred Letters; this alone is to be called the Simple Understanding, or simply the understanding Science, and, with due respect to those who think otherwise, it regards no creatable things, no essences of things or abstract truths. For God, understanding simply, is sufficient to himself, nor is it necessary for the completion of his understanding that he look to other things; although, if out of abundance it pleases him that something besides himself be true, or if he wishes to feign something, it follows that that is true, and is known and seen by him. But this I refer to the so-called knowledge of vision, not to the Understanding; the name Understanding should be reserved for the knowledge by which God knows himself, while the other knowledge of all other things is marked with the name of cognition or science. These and similar matters may be compared with what is said of the Son of God, who in the Sacred Authors is celebrated as that very Understanding, as has been done by some, and which should be done by everyone, provided it is done properly and not in vain.

units.la: CAPUT VIII. (7) UNITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. (7) UNITY.

units.la: 1. Anima ex natura sua non est unica, sed multiplicabilis. 2. demonstratur. 3. Maxima Mentium inter se unitas. Non impedit quin sint plures numero mentes. 4. Sequelae notabiles. De principio individuationis & multiplicitatis. Individuum perfectissimum tantum unicum numero esse potest. Ab individuorum cognitione est incipiendum. Scientia est de individuis.
units.tr: 1. The soul by its nature is not unique, but capable of being multiplied. 2. This is demonstrated. 3. The very great unity of minds among themselves. It does not prevent there being several minds in number. 4. Notable consequences. On the principle of individuation and of multiplicity. A most perfect individual can be only one in number. One must begin from the knowledge of individuals. Science is of individuals.

units.la: I. POstquam objectum meae Cogitationis primum memetipsum esse deprehendi, ita tamen ut, si distincte sim mihi agnoscendus, praecedere debeat notitia Dei, qui hoc modo etiam primum proximumque mei objectum dici potest, imo mihi praesentius evidentiusque quam egomet mihi; jam quasi extra me vadens (quod minus necessarium, & semper, nisi de primis bene prospectum sit, noxium) libet secundaria quaedam objecta quaerere, non quidem ut praecipue examinem, an praeter Deum & me existant? Sed ut ea contempler inter Mentis ideas tanquam à me diversa, & existendi capacia. Incipiam ab illis quae mecum quammaximam similitudinem nexumque habere possent. Animadverto igitur me habere ideas aliarum Mentium ejusdem mecum naturae, sive, me concipere objecta aeque perfecta & earumdem mecum realitatum, quae tamen non sunt Ego ipse; sive, quae concipiuntur ut à me diversa, etsi quae ego habeo, ipsa similiter habeant.
units.tr: I. Having found that the first object of my thought is myself, yet in such a way that, if I am to be known distinctly, the knowledge of God must come first (who in this way can also be called my first and nearest object, indeed more present and more evident to me than I am to myself), now, as it were going outside myself (which is less necessary and always harmful unless the primary matters have first been well considered), I am pleased to seek some secondary objects, not chiefly to examine whether they exist beside God and me, but to consider them among the ideas of the mind as different from me and capable of existing. I shall begin with those which could have the greatest likeness and connection with me. I notice, then, that I have ideas of other minds of the same nature as mine, that is, I conceive objects equally perfect and sharing the same realities as mine, which yet are not myself; or, those which are conceived as different from me, although the ones I have themselves have similar ones.

units.la: II. Neque dici potest pluralitatem illam objectorum diversorum, ejusdem mecum naturae participum, esse tantum figmentum Mentis meae, quae cum ideam numerorum habeat ex eo quod quasdam sui variationes sentiat & numeret, simulque idea sui praedita sit, numerum pluralitatis & ideam sui per figmentum componat, adeoque plures Men-tes concipiat, ut tamen conceptus in natura possibilitatis plurium Men-tium non fundetur, cum sit fictio: Nam contra, non tantum est ex nu-meris modorum Mentis cum Mente mea conflatus, sed ex natura ipsa Ideæ Mentis creatæ, quæ omnia non complectitur, fluit conceptus iste. Etenim positio Cogitationis qualis Ego sum, non excludit positionem alterius cogitationis meæ similis; nec perceptio sive conscientia ejus quod in me est, impedit quominus alter aliquis habeat etiam perceptio-nem ejus quod in se est eodem prorsus modo; nec prohibet quin hæ duæ perceptiones omnino differant, non solum quoniam, utut perfectæ sint æqualiter, nonnulla inter eas diversitas esse potest in modis quibus ad objecta vel diversa, vel etiam eadem applicabuntur, ubi tam stupenda multiplicitas & differentia est, ut si exempli causa, mille myriadibus hominum incumbat cogitare, verbi gratia, de Deo, ne duo quidem suas eadem de re cogitationes, eodem modo sint disposituri; sed etiam quia quæ ab alio percipiuntur, non ideo, & eo ipso, in me & a me perci-piuntur; nec, pari modo, quæ percipio, ideo quia in me sunt alius mihi similis percipit.
units.tr: II. Nor can it be said that this plurality of diverse objects, sharing my own nature, is merely a fiction of my mind. My mind, since it has the idea of number from the fact that it perceives and counts certain variations of itself, and since it is also endowed with an idea of itself, might compose the number of plurality and the idea of itself by fiction, and so conceive several minds; yet the concept does not rest on the nature of the possibility of several minds, since it would be a fiction. On the contrary, this concept flows not merely from the numbers of the modes of the mind joined with my mind, but from the very nature of the idea of a created mind, which does not embrace all things. For the positing of a thought such as I am does not exclude the positing of another thought of mine that is similar; nor does the perception or consciousness of what is in me prevent another from having also the perception of what is in himself in exactly the same way; nor does it forbid these two perceptions from differing altogether. This is so not only because, though equally perfect, there can be some diversity between them in the modes by which they are applied to objects, either different or even the same, where there is such an astonishing multiplicity and difference that if, for example, a thousand myriads of men were to set themselves to think, say, of God, not even two of them would arrange their thoughts about the same matter in the same way. It is also because what is perceived by another is not, for that reason and by that very fact, perceived in me and by me; nor, likewise, what I perceive is perceived by another like me merely because it is in me.

units.la: III. Fieri quidem potest ut quæ in me percipiuntur eadem etiam ab alio mihi simili percipiantur similiter: sed hæc unitas non est perceptio-nis ipsius, nec ab ipsa petenda est, sed ab alia causa. Potest ille a quo Ego & cæteri (si qui) sumus, velle, ut cum aliquid percipio aliquis alius sit ejusdem perceptionis conscius, vel etiam plures, idque vel mediante solo Dei placito, vel ita ut cum illo consensus quoque meus intercedat, adeoque fiant unius cogitationes tanquam omnium, & omnium tanquam unius: (quæ admiranda unitas & communio in Sanctis mentibus corpore solutis esse possit, quæ omnes, quantum fieri potest, prorsus admirabiliter unum quid inter se fiant.) Attamen, quemadmodum Corpus & Mens unum arctissimo nexu constituentia, nihilominus reipsa sunt duæ numero res; ita etiam hic est, nam hoc non obstante, manet distinctionis & pluralitatis fundamentum, cum omnes possint separari, & seorsim quantum sufficit complete concipi. neque enim necesse est ut dum præcise concipio Deum ponere in me cogitationem, concipiam ideo & hoc ipso ejus conscientiam in alio poni, vel alium dari qui ejus conscius sit: quia, cum ego non sim omne perfectum, ne quidem omne perfectum creaturam decens, positio cogitationis meæ non ponit in al-tero cogitationem, quasi alter ille, ut pars, in me, toto omnia comprehendente, contineretur; nec alterius cogitationis positio meæ Cogitationis positionem infert, acsi alter ut pars extra me ut totum non exi-steret: Ego, sive, opus Dei in me, Ego inquam cogitans, sum quidem aliquid, sum non nihil, sed non sum omne, non omne creabile, non omne Dei repræsentativum, ut ex potentia Dei facile demonstrare est, adeoque non excludo infinita alia mihi similia ejusdem mecum naturæ, nil repugnat quin eorum pluralitatem innumeram evidenter concipiam.
units.tr: III. It can indeed happen that what is perceived in me is also perceived in the same way by another like me; but this unity does not belong to the perception itself, nor is it to be sought from the perception itself, but from another cause. He from whom I and the others (if there are any) come may will that, when I perceive something, some other person, or even several, should be conscious of the same perception, and this either through the mere pleasure of God alone, or in such a way that my own consent also intervenes with his; and so the thoughts of one become as those of all, and of all as of one (a wonderful unity and communion, which can exist among holy minds once loosed from the body, who, so far as is possible, become one thing among themselves in a wonderfully admirable way). Yet, just as body and mind, constituting one thing by the closest bond, are nevertheless in reality two things in number, so it is here too; for notwithstanding this, the foundation of distinction and plurality remains, since all can be separated and, separately, conceived completely enough. For it is not necessary that, while I conceive precisely that God places a thought in me, I should therefore and by that very fact conceive that its consciousness is placed in another, or that another exists who is conscious of it; because, since I am not all perfection, nor even all perfection befitting a creature, the positing of my thought does not posit a thought in another, as if that other, as a part, were contained in me, who comprehend everything as a whole; nor does the positing of another's thought imply the positing of my thought, as if the other, as a part, did not exist outside me as a whole. I, that is, the work of God in me, I who think, am indeed something, I am not nothing, but I am not everything, not every creatable thing, not every representation of God, as may easily be demonstrated from the power of God; and therefore I do not exclude the infinite other beings like me, of the same nature as mine; nothing prevents me from clearly conceiving their innumerable plurality.

units.la: IV. Non jam deducam specialius quæcunque ex istis, quæ nonnullis sterilia, vel forte inepta videri possint, (ad quid enim probem me non esse alium, vel posse dari à me alios qui non sint ego?) sequuntur, & momentosa quidem. In illis omnis unitatis communionisque in quibuscunque rebus, imo & diversitatis, fundamenta, cum exemplo evidentissimo ad quod omnia componi possunt, continentur. Quid sit principium individuationis, ut vocant, de quo dant tot sine mente sonos, & pluralitatis, sive multiplicitatis, ex his patet. Exemplo quoque patet, essentiam individualem prius nosci quam abstractus habeatur conceptus, sive quam noscantur essentia generalis, quæ inde venit quod individuum non habeat omne perfectum, quare de perfectissimo individuo non concipitur essentia generalis, sed individualis tantum, cum individuum illud omnem solidam realitatem exhaurire (ut sic dicam) concipiatur, secus quam in creatis, ubi realitas quæ in ipsis concipitur, ejusque causa, Dei placitum, ad alia, non obstante unius ex illis positione essentiaque, extendi, potest percipi (qui conceptus essentia abstracta vel universalis dicitur.) Inde etiam manifestum est, falsum esse tritum illud, A cognitione universalium, non autem particularium, in detectione veritatis esse incipiendum: particularium non dari scientiam, sed universalium. Quin contra, ab individuis (& utinam in spiritualibus atque praxi quilibet à sui ipsius individui inspectione!) exordiendum est, eorumque propria, &, quantum fieri potest, completa datur scientia: At quia unum aliquod individuum non est omne, sive non exhaurit omnem realitatem, sed reduplicari & multiplicari potest, sive, similia dari possunt, hinc quam de uno scientiam habeo ad alia ista extendere queo, at non ita amplam, sed magis restrictam, quia plures de uno circumstantias, quæ sunt variabiles, novi, quam de cæteris, unde de Mente mea habeo scientiam magis completam, quam de idea mentis à me abstracta. Hoc est malum nostrum, quod in omnibus, in divinis etiam rebus, omnia à nobis abstrahamus, contemplemur eorum ideas tanquam phantasmata extra nos in aëre, ut sic dicam, volitantia, tantia, nec ea in individuo quisque suo requirat, cum tamen vera omnis scientia incipiat ab individuo, ab individuali experientia, & in ea fundetur. Nimia abstractio omnia in omnibus fere corrupit. Sed, ut ad metam redeam, horum usus praecipuus est, ut inserviant unitati Dei dilucide percipiendae.
units.tr: IV. I shall not now deduce in more detail whatever follows from these points, which may seem barren or perhaps foolish to some (for why should I prove that I am not another, or that there can be given others by me who are not myself?), yet they are indeed of weight. In these are contained the foundations of all unity and communion in whatever things, and even of diversity, together with a most evident example to which everything can be reduced. What the principle of individuation is, as they call it, about which they make so many empty sounds without understanding, and of plurality or multiplicity, is clear from these things. It is also clear from the example that the individual essence is known before the abstract concept is had, or before the general essence is known. This comes about because an individual does not have every perfection; hence no general essence is conceived of the most perfect individual, but only an individual essence, since that individual is conceived as exhausting, so to speak, all solid reality; this is unlike created things, where the reality conceived in them, and its cause, God's pleasure, can be perceived as extending to others, notwithstanding the positing and essence of one of them (this concept is called abstract or universal essence). Hence it is also plain that the hackneyed saying is false, that one must begin in the discovery of truth from the knowledge of universals and not of particulars: there is no science of particulars, but of universals. On the contrary, one must begin from individuals (and would that everyone in spiritual matters and in practice began from the examination of his own individual self!), and science of their proper and, so far as possible, complete kind is given. But because one individual is not everything, that is, does not exhaust all reality, but can be repeated and multiplied, that is, similar things can be given, the knowledge I have of one can be extended to those others, but not so widely, rather more narrowly, because I know more of the variable circumstances concerning the one than concerning the rest; whence I have a more complete knowledge of my own mind than of the idea of the mind abstracted by me. This is our evil: that in all things, even divine ones, we abstract everything, and contemplate their ideas as phantasms flitting outside us, so to speak, in the air, and do not seek them in each individual; yet all true science begins from the individual, from individual experience, and is founded upon it. Excessive abstraction corrupts almost everything in everything. But, to return to my goal, the chief use of these things is that they serve to make the unity of God clearly perceived.

units.la: 5. Conceptus plurium Deorum fictio absurda & contradictoria. 5.6.7.8. Demonstrationes de Dei unitate. 8.9. Polytheismus, Atheismus, Deismus, Trinitas, Unitas.
units.tr: 5. The notion of several Gods is an absurd and self-contradictory fiction. 5, 6, 7, 8. Demonstrations of the unity of God. 8, 9. Polytheism, Atheism, Deism, Trinity, Unity.

units.la: V. Quodsi jam tentem similia eis quae modo de me dixi applicare Deo, ut videam, num posset aliquis ejusdem cum illo naturae, ei aequalis, & tamen ab illo ut Ego ab alia Mente ejusdem mecum naturae, differens dari; tunc omnia quae de me dixi ejus respectu prorsus corruunt, & se aliter habent. Si plures Deos concipere vellem, fictio esset, & quidem absurda ex parte rei, hoc est, ideam pluralis numeri cum Idea Dei ita jungerem, ut ipsius ideae Dei consideratio absurdi me convinceret, & judicii mei figmentum refutaret, tanquam naturae rei conceptae repugnans. Dico judicium illud fore figmentum: nam omnes rationes quae me determinant ad judicandum existere Deum, non nisi unius Dei existentiam postulant & inferunt; qua agnita, difficultates quibus nisi notus fuisset Deus angebar, plane sedantur omnes, ita ut unius Dei existentiae solide acquiescere detur: unde sequitur praeter necessitatem & sine causa & ratione alios quaeri vel statui; nec id fieri posse nisi ex mera mentis petulantia & fictione quae nullius rei fictae existentiam demonstrare potest. Sed dico insuper illam fictionem esse absurdam & contradictoriam: nam cum per Deum intelligatur ens perfectissimum, cum Deus sit omne perfectum in genere perfectionis absolutae, cum omnia quae realissima sunt ipse sit, ex ejus definitione, sequitur eo solo concepto, atque existente, concipi & poni omne perfectum cogitabile, omne reale absolutum quod esse posse dici posset: adeoque ejus conceptus & essentia omne perfectissimum extra & praeter ipsum formaliter excludunt. Quod est omne absolute id excludit aliud omne absolute, alioqui quod est absolute omne, non esset absolute omne. Ergo Deus unicus est.
units.tr: V. If I now try to apply to God things similar to those I have just said about myself, to see whether there could be someone of the same nature as him, equal to him, and yet distinct from him, as I am distinct from another mind of the same nature as mine, then everything I have said about myself collapses entirely in relation to him and stands otherwise. If I wished to conceive several Gods, it would be a fiction, and an absurd one on the side of the thing itself: that is, I would join the idea of plurality with the idea of God in such a way that the consideration of the idea of God itself would convince me of absurdity, and would refute the figment of my judgment as repugnant to the nature of the thing conceived. I say that this judgment would be a figment: for all the reasons which determine me to judge that God exists demand and imply only the existence of one God; once this is acknowledged, all the difficulties which troubled me while God was unknown to me are wholly calmed, so that one may rest securely in the existence of the one God alone. From this it follows that to seek or posit others beyond what is necessary, and without cause or reason, can happen only from the mere wantonness and fancy of the mind, which cannot demonstrate the existence of any thing it fancies. But I say further that that fiction is absurd and self-contradictory: for since by God is understood the most perfect being, since God is all perfection in the kind of absolute perfection, since he himself is, by his definition, all things that are most real, it follows that by the mere conception and existence of him alone, every conceivable perfection and every absolute reality that could be said to be possible is conceived and posited; and therefore his concept and essence formally exclude every most perfect thing outside of and beside himself. What is absolutely all excludes every other thing absolutely; otherwise what is absolutely all would not be absolutely all. Therefore God is one.

units.la: VI. Idipsum sic quoque conficitur. Si plures darentur Dii, tunc vel convenirent in una Essentia, vel in ea non convenirent: Si in Essentia una Divina non convenire dicantur, non sunt igitur omnes vere Dii; si dicantur convenire in una essentia, Ergo & in una existentia, adeo- que unum existunt, seu unus Deus est: nam in Perfectissimo Ente Es- sentia est existentia, (quod patet ex Simplicitate lib. II. cap. v. & vi. de- monstrata, & deinceps pluribus illustranda) & existentia (ex supradictis) est individualis, cum unius existentia exhauriat & complectatur totam & omnem realitatem seu perfectionem.
units.tr: VI. The same is also proved in this way. If several Gods were given, then either they would agree in one essence, or they would not agree in it. If they are said not to agree in one divine essence, then not all of them are truly Gods; if they are said to agree in one essence, then also in one existence, and so they exist as one, or there is one God: for in the most perfect being essence is existence (which is evident from the simplicity demonstrated in book II, chapters v and vi, and to be further illustrated hereafter), and existence (from what has been said above) is individual, since the existence of the one exhausts and embraces the whole and every reality or perfection.

units.la: VI. Idem etiam demonstratur ex aliis quæ generalius de Deo demonstrata sunt, exempli causa, ex eo quod Deus sit Cogitatio mera: si autem daretur alius Deus, tunc uterque esset individuum illius speciei Deus, sic neuter esset Deus, neuter esset non-pars, vel totum, vel merum quid. Cogitatio mera præter se nil simile novit, (ex Intelli- gentia) Ergo præter se nil simile, nempe quoad essentiam, exstat, nam si exstaret, illaque id non nosset, tunc mera cogitatio non esset mera cogitatio, siquidem in illa esset ignorantia sive non Cogitatio, adeoque Deus non esset Deus, quod sese destruit. Vel, ut clarius res proponatur, suppone Deos esse duos, dico, aut illos sese mutuo nosse ex necessitate, aut secus: si se non necessario norunt, non sunt perfecti necessario, atque ignorantes sunt vel esse possunt, nec igitur sunt Dii, nec plures Dii; si se norunt necessario, tunc Cogitatio unius de altero est Cogitatio de altero alteri necessaria, quod Cogitationi meræ repugnat, cum illa se ipsa sola compleatur. Illa autem, ut pergam, alterius de altero necessaria cogitatio, vel ab altero illo dependebit & veniet, quod iterum Deo vero non competit; vel ab illo ipso dependebit qui de altero cogitat, adeoque ille cogitans de altero ita apud se reputabit, Ego me contemplans concipio me non esse omne perfectum, sed præter me dari æque perfectum, quod à Deo alienum est. Sed nec posset unius cognitio de altero æque perfecto venire nisi ab altero: ut nec ego, Mens creata, nosem alias Mentes mihi similes esse posse, nisi id haberem à notitia alterius, potentiæ nempe Dei. Quod si unus se ipsum percipiens eo ipso alterum percipere fingatur, & vicissim, ita ut unius cogitatio, cognitio, adeoque perfectio, sit alterius cogitatio & perfectio, tunc non ut duo, sed ut unus percipientur. Itaque ad Unitatem veniendum est ex consideratione Intelligentiæ Dei.
units.tr: VI. The same is also demonstrated from other things that have been demonstrated more generally about God: for example, from the fact that God is pure thought. For if another God were given, then each would be an individual of that species God; thus neither would be God, neither would be a non-part, or a whole, or a mere something. Pure thought knows nothing like itself apart from itself (from intelligence), therefore nothing like itself, namely in essence, exists apart from it; for if it existed, and that thought did not know it, then pure thought would not be pure thought, since in it there would be ignorance or non-thought, and thus God would not be God, which destroys itself. Or, to set the matter out more clearly, suppose there are two Gods. I say that either they know each other necessarily, or not. If they do not know each other necessarily, they are not necessarily perfect, and they are or may be ignorant, and so they are not Gods, nor are there several Gods. If they know each other necessarily, then one's thought of the other is a thought of the other which is necessary to the other, which is repugnant to pure thought, since that is complete in itself alone. Moreover, to continue, that necessary thought of one about the other will either depend on and come from that other, which again does not belong to the true God; or it will depend on the very one who thinks of the other, and so that thinking one will reflect within himself thus: I, contemplating myself, conceive that I am not all perfection, but that there exists beside me an equally perfect being, which is alien to God. But neither could one's knowledge of another equally perfect being come except from the other: just as I, a created mind, could not know that other minds like me could exist, unless I had this from knowledge of another, namely of the power of God. But if one, perceiving himself, is feigned by that very act to perceive the other, and conversely, so that the thought, knowledge and therefore perfection of one is the thought and perfection of the other, then they will be perceived not as two, but as one. Thus we must arrive at Unity from consideration of the intelligence of God.

units.la: VII. Eo nos revocat ejusdem acquiescentia in se, sine qua Cogitationis meræ conceptus destruitur. Mera Cogitatio sibi acquiescit: quod sibi acquiescit non requirit necessario alterius rei à se diversæ notitiam nec præsentiam: Ergo excludit necessitatem alterius entis; igitur non datur, nec dari potest Deus alter, alioqui necessario daretur, cum Deus sit ens necessarium. Eadem Unitas Dei ex ejus sufficientia, aliisque attributis demonstranda relinquitur, cum, quæ hactenus, sufficiant.
units.tr: VII. The acquiescence of God in himself, without which the concept of pure thought is destroyed, calls us back to the same point. Pure thought acquiesces in itself; that which acquiesces in itself does not necessarily require the knowledge or presence of any other thing distinct from itself: therefore it excludes the necessity of another being. Hence another God does not exist, nor can he exist; otherwise he would necessarily exist, since God is a necessary being. The same unity of God is left to be demonstrated from his self-sufficiency and his other attributes, since those that have been set out so far are sufficient.

units.la: IX. Non potest concipi major in Deo distinctio quam quæ in Cogitatione una & eadem, eaque perfectissima, alioqui Polytheismus introducitur qui Deismo pejor est hæresis. Nam, ut ex dictis patet, positio plurium Deorum non tantum est Mentis fictio, unde qui plures colunt Deos, idololatræ, sui ipsorum vel fictionum suarum Mentium cultores dicuntur: Sed etiam est Dei abnegatio, conceptus de Deo destructio, negatio veritatis hujus: Deus est Res seu Cogitatio perfectissima & mera; sive Deus est Deus. Unde coinquinati Polytheismo vere Atheismi rei sunt, quod de Deistis iisque qui Unitarios se vocant, ita dici nequit. Sed nec hi ex unitate habent unde suum propugnent errorem, non enim quæ concipitur in Deo distinctio talis est quæ Unitati ejus sit opposita, sed ea est quæ cum illa optime concordet. Ipse Deus ob sui Summam Perfectionem se ipsum summe amans & quærens, conatus (humano more loquendo) se ipsum quantum posset multiplicare ut se ipsum amabilissimum, quantum posset inveniret, amaret; id quidem extra se executus est ponendo sui umbras, tabulas, imagines, quarum cum una non sufficeret admirabilibus ejus perfectionibus adumbrandis, innumeras, easque omnimoda varietate diversas produxit: at dum in se ipso per adorandam quæ in Trinitate est, generationem se multiplicavit, quia perfectissime sic expressus est, extra unitatem naturæ individuæ non abiit, siquidem extra unum perfectissimum nullum aliud sit. Et qui notabunt eam unam Cogitationem includere acquiescentiam in sui Intelligentia per tendentiam sive amorem perfectissimum, eaque simul cum illis quæ de Incomprehensibilitate Dei dicta sunt, meditabuntur, non sument ex Unitate Dei occasionem de Trinitate dubitandi, sed potius ex illa de hac certiores fient. quod cuivis attendenti animadvertere est.
units.tr: IX. A greater distinction cannot be conceived in God than that which is in one and the same thought, and that most perfect; otherwise Polytheism is introduced, which is a heresy worse than Deism. For, as is clear from what has been said, the assertion of several Gods is not merely a fiction of the mind; hence those who worship several Gods are called idolaters, worshippers of themselves or of their own mental fictions. But it is also a denial of God, a destruction of the concept of God, a denial of this truth: God is a Thing or Thought most perfect and pure; or, God is God. Hence those tainted with Polytheism are truly guilty of Atheism, which cannot be said of the Deists and of those who call themselves Unitarians. But neither do these have from unity anything from which they might defend their error; for the distinction conceived in God is not of such a kind as to be opposed to his unity, but is one that agrees very well with it. God himself, on account of his supreme perfection, loving and seeking himself supremely, strove (speaking in human manner) to multiply himself as far as he could, so that he might love himself as most lovable as far as he could find. Indeed he carried this out outside himself by positing his shadows, tablets, images; and since one alone would not suffice to shadow forth his admirable perfections, he produced innumerable ones, and these in every kind of variety. But while within himself he multiplied himself by generation, which is in the adorable Trinity, because he was thus most perfectly expressed, he did not go beyond the unity of the individual nature, since outside the one most perfect there is nothing else. And those who will note that this one thought includes acquiescence in his own intelligence through the most perfect tendency or love, and who will meditate on this together with what has been said about the incomprehensibility of God, will not take from the unity of God an occasion to doubt the Trinity, but will rather be made more certain of it from that unity. This is easy for anyone attending to it to notice.

units.la: X. Tandem notetur, Deum ita esse unum, ut strictior sit in illo unitas quam in Mente mea individua, separatiorque suo sensu in me sit pluralitas & diversitas, quam in Deo. Sunt in Mente mea plures diversifique cogitandi actus à se separabiles, sæpe mea Mens ad se non attendit, à se quodammodo abest, sibi incognita, interrupta in suis cogitandi modis maxime intimis, aliud à se postulans, quamvis illa numero una sit: At hæc omnia à Deo qui numero, essentia, conceptu unicus est, plane sunt remota.
units.tr: X. Finally let it be noted that God is one in such a way that unity in him is stricter than in my individual mind, and plurality and diversity in me are more separate in their sense than in God. In my mind there are several and diverse acts of thinking, separable from one another; often my mind does not attend to itself, is in some measure absent from itself, unknown to itself, interrupted in its most inward modes of thinking, and requiring something other than itself, although it is one in number. But all these things are wholly remote from God, who is unique in number, in essence and in concept.

units.la: CAPUT IX. (8) ALTITUDO.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. (8) HEIGHT.

units.la: 1. 3. Mens quibusdam rebus superior, quibusdam inferior. 2. Ejus dejectio summa cum subjicitur corpusculo quod ad cetera proportionem puncto minorem habet.
units.tr: 1. 3. The mind is superior to some things and inferior to others. 2. Its lowering is at its greatest when it is subjected to a little body which, in proportion to the rest, is less than a point.

units.la: I. Porro, inter res quae mihi tanquam à me differentes repraesentantur, sunt & aliae quas tanquam me minores, aliae quas tanquam me majores adverto: nec opus est ad hujus evidentiorem probationem, ut Deum, ad cujus essentiam omnia quae ejus placitum in me contulit evanescunt, in exemplum adducam, cum inter illa quae ab illo diversa concipiuntur, Mentes creatas concipiam mea Mente multo perfectiores, vividius, purius, extensius cogitantes, magis activas, sibi ipsis notiores, & omnibus quae in me vel jam notavi, vel notabo deinceps, me quam longissime superantes, placiti Divini exactiores imagines, in quibus indefinite excellentiora quam in me Deus efficere voluerit; neque adeo inter res ejusdem mecum generis, creatas nempe, ex mediis, vel fere etiam ex infimis, esse.
units.tr: I. Further, among the things that present themselves to me as different from myself, some I perceive as smaller than me and others as greater. Nor, to prove this more clearly, is there any need to take God as an example, before whose essence all the things that his pleasure has bestowed on me vanish. Among those things conceived as different from him, I can conceive created minds far more perfect than my own, thinking more vividly, purely and extensively, more active, better known to themselves, and surpassing me by far in everything that I have already noted or will note hereafter: more exact images of the divine pleasure, in which God has willed to produce things indefinitely more excellent than in me. Nor, indeed, are they among things of my own kind, namely created things, from the middling or almost even from the lowest.

units.la: II. Et quamvis perfectiones meae, si meo libuerit Authori plura melioraque in me operari prae iis quae ipse in quibusdam agit, nonnullas quae aliis insunt, hocce modo praecedere possint; imo, quamvis jam corpore omni (ne me cum aliis mentibus temere comparem) quamvis inquam omni re extensa (cujus ideam jam aliquatenus contemplabor) sim perfectior, cum res quae sui, Dei, mirabilium ejus attributorum operumque conscia est, omni re extensa, mobili, figurata, quae bruta omnis est, sit augustior; attamen si has ipsas res mecum, quatenus illis utcunque jam alligatus sum & subjectus, confero, summae tenuitatis meae per illas ipsas quoque convincor. Cogito, ut illuc parumper excurram, extensionem universi immensam cui limites finesque sine absurditate & repugnantia in meo conceptu assignare non possum; ita ut stellatum, quod apparet coelum, in quo innumerae, ut in lactea, quae dicitur, via, stellarum myriades utcunque deteguntur, prae immenso illo universitatis spatio quod ultra & quaquaversum sine ullius finis conceptu, extendi concipitur, sit revera instar puncti concipiendum, quanquam spatium à Sole, nobis hujus puncti centro, ad Saturnum (quod diametrorum terræ millibus quinque aut sex constare ajunt) non immerito à peritioribus decuplandum esse putetur si ad proximarum nobis stellarum distantiam commensurandam sit aptandum, idemque centupliciter repetendum, imo millecuplex substituendum si ad remotiores inter apparentes applicandum sit. Cogito præterea, apparentis illius cœli hoc nostrum, quod ad firmamentum extenditur, iterum punctum esse, hujusque puncti spatium illud quod à tellure annuatim circa Solem delata describitur (veritas, sine animo rixandi, si quæ est in tota Physica, necessaria, clara, & demonstrabilis). iterum punctum esse, quod patet ex horizontis æqualitate apparente, & defectu parallaxeos in stellis. Porro, cogito istius puncti, sive sphæræ quam terræ circa Solem circulus in duas secare partes concipitur, ipsam terram iterum punctum esse, quippe quæ se non habeat ad illam quantum se habet unum ad ter millies millena millia. (Nam posito, diametrum eclypticæ continere 1500 terræ diametros, ratio triplicata, quæ est solidi terræ ad solidum spatii sphærae quam illa circa Solem ambit, exurgit 3375000000. si vero pro maximo diametro sumantur telluris 1550, ut exactiores circiter numerant, tunc exurget proportione unius ex his punctis ad alterum proportio 1--ad 3723875000.)
units.tr: II. And although my perfections, if it had pleased my Author to work more and better things in me than he does in certain others, could surpass some that belong to others in this way; indeed, although I am already more perfect than all body (lest I rashly compare myself with other minds), than every extended thing (whose idea I will now consider to some extent), since the thing which is conscious of God, of his wonderful attributes and works, is more august than every extended, mobile, figured thing, which is entirely brute; yet if I compare these very things with myself, insofar as I am in some way already bound and subject to them, I am convinced of my own extreme slightness by these very things as well. I think, to digress briefly, of the immense extension of the universe, to which, in my conception, I cannot assign limits or ends without absurdity and contradiction; so that the starry heaven that appears, in which the countless myriads of stars that are in some measure discovered, as in the so-called Milky Way, when compared with that immense space of the universe which is conceived to extend beyond and in every direction without any conception of an end, must truly be conceived as like a point. Although the distance from the Sun, the centre of this point for us, to Saturn (which they say is five or six thousand times the diameter of the earth) is not unreasonably thought by the more skilled to be increased tenfold if it is to be measured against the distance of the nearest stars, and the same must be repeated a hundredfold, or indeed a thousandfold substituted, if it is to be applied to the more remote among the visible stars. I think, moreover, that this heaven of ours, which extends to the firmament of the visible heaven, is again a point; and that the space described by the earth carried yearly around the Sun is again a point (a truth, without any desire to quarrel, which if there is any in the whole of physics, is necessary, clear and demonstrable), again a point, as is evident from the apparent equality of the horizon and the absence of parallax in the stars. Further, I think that the circle which the earth is conceived to trace around the Sun, cutting into two parts the sphere of this point, is itself again a point, since it bears to that sphere no greater proportion than one bears to three thousand million times a thousand million. (For, supposing the diameter of the ecliptic contains 1500 diameters of the earth, the tripled ratio, which is that of the solid earth to the solid of the space of the sphere which that circle encloses around the Sun, comes out as 3,375,000,000. But if for the greatest diameter one takes 1550 of the earth's, as the more exact calculators roughly count, then the proportion of one of these points to the other comes out as 1 to 3,723,875,000.)

units.la: Quid igitur ad hæc portio superficiei terræ? quid regio? quid urbs? quid domus? nisi particulæ particularum punctuli? quid ipsaque adeo glebula luti exigua, pulvisculusve quo detenta Mens est (ut notum) quasi captiva atque vincta, atque ita vincta, imo ita depressa, ut sæpissime, quoties dormitur, vel ægrotatur violentius, ipsa cum omnibus ejus facultatibus quasi deglutita & absorpta reperiatur, idque invita, sæpissime etiam, quæ omnium vilissima est dejectio, ipsa volens, pulvisculi sui onere, cura, cultu uno, sese obruens, etsi sciat glebulæ evanidæ stabilitatem momentis, quorum unum non infert sequens, mensurari, omniaque vix duratura usque dum punctum illud in cujus superficiei punctiuncula recumbimus ex suis gyris absolverit nonnullos, qui & ipsi universi cæterorum respectu paucissimi sunt, quemadmodum terræ status præ cœlorum statu non putatur durabilis, nec hic ultimus quicquam ad veram æternitatem, vel æternitatis, quantum in Mente creata dari potest, expressam imaginem sit comparandus? Et tamen, quæ tua homo insania est, hæc tenuissima vana, maxima maximeque seria esse putas, ob quæ ridiculo simul & execrando ausu, Deus tibi relinquendus, contemnendus, omnia turbanda & violanda, tuque ipsi tibi magnifice æstimandus videris homo, parve culex, vermiculæ instar scarabei in stercore puncti punctuli ex majoris umbræ puncto de-sumpti, pulvisculi evanidi rasuram cumulans & versans, atque illic agens cuniculos, thronos & triumphos, mox inibi conculcande! Certe, cum talem mentis cum corpore statum sic tacitus & serio apud me intueor, vix eo vilius quid & abjectum magis occurrit, ut ad stupo-rem admirandum veniat, unde illa his tota occupari, adhærere, iisque deliciari possit.
units.tr: What then of this portion of the earth's surface? What of a region? What of a city? What of a house? Are they not but particles of particles of a little point? What of even that small clod of mud or speck of dust by which the mind is held (as is well known), as if captive and bound, and so bound, indeed so depressed, that very often, whenever it sleeps or is more violently ill, it is found, together with all its faculties, as if swallowed up and absorbed, and this against its will; and very often, which is the basest of all degradations, it is willing itself, burying itself under the one burden, care and cultivation of its speck of dust, although it knows that the stability of that vanishing clod is measured by moments, of which one does not bring about the next, and that everything is scarcely going to last until that point on whose surface we lie as a tiny speck has completed some of its revolutions, which are themselves very few in comparison with the rest of the universe? Just as the state of the earth is not thought durable in comparison with the state of the heavens, is not this last thing to be compared with eternity itself, or with the expressed image of eternity, so far as it can be given in a created mind? And yet, what madness is yours, O man, that you think these most slight and vain things to be the greatest and most serious, on account of which, in a ridiculous and detestable audacity, God is to be abandoned by you, despised, all things to be thrown into confusion and violated, and you yourself seem to yourself a man to be esteemed greatly, a little gnat, like a little beetle in the dung of a point of a point, taken from the point of a greater shadow, heaping up and turning over the scraping of a vanishing speck of dust, and there making tunnels, thrones and triumphs, soon to be trampled underfoot there! Certainly, when I silently and seriously contemplate within myself such a state of mind with the body, scarcely anything viler or more abject occurs to me, so as to come to a wondering stupor, whence that mind could be wholly occupied with these things, cling to them, and take delight in them.

units.la: III. Respiro nonnihil cum ad meas quæ Deum concernunt cogitationes recurro, præ quibus evanescunt cætera, licet infirmæ & valde paucæ illæ sint, &, ut dixi, superari possint ab aliis quas in quibusdam posuerit perfectiores Deus, unde vidi medium me inter duo quasi constitutum, & corporeis quidem suo sensu superiorem: sed non esse cur me cæteris (quæ esse possunt) mentibus, præferam, aut etiam omnino æqualem iis reputem, cum superiores me esse, possint à me concipi.
units.tr: III. I breathe a little when I return to my thoughts which concern God, in comparison with which other things vanish; although those thoughts are weak and very few, and, as I said, can be surpassed by others which God has willed to place in certain beings as more perfect. Whence I have seen myself as placed in a kind of middle between two, superior to corporeal things by my own sense; but there is no reason why I should prefer myself to other minds (which may exist), or consider myself altogether equal to them, since I can conceive others to be superior to me.

units.la: 4. 5. Deus est absolutissime summus. 6. Atheorum absurda ratiocinatio. 7. 8. 9. Exploditur. Infinitum Ens quomodo nec includit nec excludit cate-ra entia. 10. Obmurmuratio; sed repulsa, & deinceps magis repellenda.
units.tr: 4. 5. God is absolutely the highest. 6. The absurd reasoning of the atheists. 7. 8. 9. It is refuted. How an infinite Being neither includes nor excludes other beings. 10. Muttered objection; but it is repelled, and is to be repelled still more hereafter.

units.la: IV. De Deo autem non ita est: non modo enim nil majus eo absque contradictione dicere ausim me concipere; verum etiam illum se ipso neminem majorem percipere evidenter intelligo. Nam cum nil sit majus Cogitatione absolutissima, perfectissimaque, cum se talem esse intelligat, sequitur eum nil se majus concipere. Præterea, is qui omnia sua possidet à se ipso, nullam etiam habet notitiam nisi à se ipso: Ergo nil nosse potest quod ab ipso non sit, estque ille suarum notitiarum mensura, ut sic dicam: nil igitur se ipso majus novit, alioquin ea notio rei majoris à re à se diversa proveniret, atque in illo esset aliam ob causam quam ob ipsum, sive ob ejus naturam, nempe vel ob rem quæ major agnita esset, vel ob nihil; quæ omnia de Deo dici nequeunt. Huc faciunt quæ mox de Dei unitate dicta sunt, nam quibus modis Deum alterum ab ipso nec esse nec concipi posse ostensum est, eisdem nec ipso majorem posse fingi demonstrabitur.
units.tr: IV. With God, however, it is not so: for I would not only dare to say that I conceive nothing greater than him without contradiction, but I also clearly understand that he perceives no one greater than himself. For since nothing is greater than the most absolute and most perfect thought, and since he understands himself to be such, it follows that he conceives nothing greater than himself. Moreover, he who possesses all that is his from himself has no knowledge except from himself: therefore he can know nothing that is not from himself, and he is, so to speak, the measure of his own knowledge. Therefore he knows nothing greater than himself; otherwise that notion of a greater thing would arise from a thing different from himself, and would be in him for some other cause than himself, or on account of his nature; namely either on account of a greater thing being known, or on account of nothing; all of which cannot be said of God. What is said shortly about the unity of God bears on this, for in the same ways in which it has been shown that another than himself neither is nor can be conceived, in those same ways it will be demonstrated that no one can be imagined greater than himself.

units.la: V. Ergo omnibus quæ Deus tanquam à se diversa concipit, ipse major est, adeoque inter ejus attributa Altitudo est agnoscenda, ipseque dicendus cum Scripturis Altissimus sive primus, vel cum Scholis Ens Summum, non aliquo respectu tantum, ut in genere rerum creatarum, sed absolutissime, super omnibus quae ab ullo concipi queant, quippe quae nec minimum quid univoce cum illo commune habeant, ut alibi demonstratum est: cum tamen minimae inter creatas res nonnihil cum majoribus commune possideant.
units.tr: V. Therefore, to all the things that God conceives as diverse from himself, he himself is greater; and so Height [Altitudo] must be acknowledged among his attributes, and he must be called, with the Scriptures, the Most High or First, or, with the Schools, the Supreme Being [Ens Summum]: not in some respect only, as among the genera of created things, but absolutely, above all things that anyone can conceive; for these have not even the smallest thing in common with him univocally, as has been demonstrated elsewhere, although the smallest of created things do possess something in common with the greater ones.

units.la: VI. Occurrit hic difficultas, quae quoniam ab Atheis videtur pro-ficisci, &, si diluatur, ad sequentia sex attributa, nec non ad praecedentia illustranda, confert, hic examinanda est. Quandoquidem, inquiunt illi, res quaedam non modo concipiuntur, sed & existere dicuntur Deo minores, ut quilibet de se existente affirmat, videtur inde concludendum nullum esse Deum, sive Ens perfectissimum, summum & Infinitum. Etenim quemadmodum plures Deos existere non posse inde concluditur, quod unus, cum infinitus sit, jam omne capiat quicquid est existentiae & perfectionum, excludatque omnem alium ab ipso diversum; ita etiam, inquiunt, non posset unus existere qui infinitus & perfectissimus sit, nisi quicquid esse potest perfectionis & existentiae ab ipso differentis possideat ita ipse, ut extra se illud plane neget & excludat: nam infinitum & perfectissimum in genere Entis excludit aliud Ens, alioqui dici posset id non omnia comprehendere, neque omnia esse, si praeter ipsum aliquid daretur quod non esset ipsum: adeoque non esset infinitum & perfectissimum. Unde sic concludunt; Si Ens infinitum existit, nulla ab ipso diversa existunt: Sed multa ab ipso diversa, nos nempe, existunt: non igitur existit Ens infinitum.
units.tr: VI. A difficulty arises here, which seems to come from the Atheists, and which, if it is resolved, contributes to illustrating the six attributes that follow as well as those that precede; so it must be examined here. Since, they say, certain things are not only conceived but are also said to exist, lesser than God, as anyone who affirms something about himself as existing would do, it seems to follow that there is no God, that is, no most perfect, supreme and infinite Being. For just as it is concluded that several Gods cannot exist, because the one, being infinite, already contains all that exists and all perfections and excludes every other thing different from himself, so, they say, one who is infinite and most perfect could not exist unless he possessed in himself every perfection and existence that can be different from him, in such a way that he plainly denies and excludes it outside himself. For the infinite and most perfect in the genus of Being excludes another Being; otherwise it could be said that it does not comprehend all things, nor is all things, if something were given besides it which was not itself; and so it would not be infinite and most perfect. Hence they conclude thus: If an infinite Being exists, no things different from it exist; but many things different from it, namely we, exist; therefore an infinite Being does not exist.

units.la: VII. Ne jam repetam responsiones quibus ineptum hoc Sophisma confutavit Cartesius in responsionibus ad secundas objectiones; notabo hic, salsissimum, imo contradictorium esse afferere Ens infinitum, summum, perfectissimumque, debere in se suaque natura & essentia omnis generis perfectiones, realitates & existentias a se diversas, quae sibi inferiores, comprehendere formaliter, hoc est, qualiter se habent, & quales concipiuntur: cum enim in se & in respectu ad ens infinitum sint imperfectae, si infinitum illas possideret in se tales, imperfectiones in se contineret, adeoque infinitum non esset infinitum, nec perfectissimum esset perfectissimum, summumque haberet non summa, quod contradicens est. Cum igitur natura infiniti istas res non comprehendat in se & formaliter, sequitur existentiam sive positionem Naturae Entis infiniti, summi, perfectissimique non tolli positione seu existentia, nec etiam conceptu rerum ab ipso diversarum. Ergo sic erat concludendum, Non dari Ens infinitum, perfectissimum & summum quod perfectiones creatas vel finitas formaliter in se includat, vel formaliter extra se excludat: quod conceditur libenter. etenim quemadmodum Ens perfectissimum, quia in natura sua complectitur omnem perfectionem infinitam, ideo extra & praeter suam essentiam omnem perfectionem infinitam excludit; sic quia in eadem sua essentia & existentia nullam capit finitam perfectionem, nullam igitur ejus essentia & existentia extra se excludit, sive impedit necessario quominus extra se existat finita perfectio.
units.tr: VII. Not to repeat now the answers by which Descartes refuted this foolish sophism in his replies to the Second Objections, I will note here that it is most absurd, indeed contradictory, to assert that the infinite, supreme and most perfect Being must comprehend in itself and in its nature and essence all perfections, realities and existences of every kind that are different from it and inferior to it, formally, that is, in the way they are and as they are conceived. For since they are imperfect in themselves and in relation to the infinite Being, if the infinite Being possessed them in itself as such, it would contain imperfections in itself, and so it would not be infinite, nor would the most perfect be most perfect, and it would have the highest things, not the highest, which is a contradiction. Since, therefore, the nature of the infinite does not comprehend those things in itself and formally, it follows that the existence or positing of the nature of the infinite, supreme and most perfect Being is not removed by the positing or existence, nor even by the concept, of things different from it. Therefore it had to be concluded thus: there is no infinite, most perfect and supreme Being which formally includes in itself created or finite perfections or formally excludes them from itself; this we readily grant. For just as the most perfect Being, because in its nature it embraces every infinite perfection, therefore excludes from itself and beside its essence every infinite perfection, so, because in that same essence and existence it contains no finite perfection, its essence and existence does not exclude outside itself, or necessarily hinder, that a finite perfection exists outside it.

units.la: VIII. Ergo absurdum est dicere, Deum non fore Summum & Omnia, si quaedam realitas seu perfectio existeret, quae ipse non esset, quia nempe sic aliquid, haec scilicet perfectio, ei addi posset: Neque enim Deus dicitur Summus vel Omnia, quod ejus essentia habeat subjective omnia finita & creata, vel haec sit ipsa, alioquin esset imperfectus, & finitae res essent Deus, quemadmodum etiam dictum est eum non dici ubique quod ejus essentia sit ubique: sed in se & subjective est omnia, nempe omnia quae absolutissime perfecta sunt, & sic sibi soli est omnia, ut etiam sibi soli praesentem esse dictum est; respectu vero rerum creatarum & finitarum omnia dicitur operative (ut supra de Ubi & eandem ob causam, nam esse Dei, & ubi esse, unum sunt) & representative, (ut, si placet, hic & alibi interdum cum Scholis loquamur:) sive, ideo omnia dicitur quia rerum omnium perfectiones ab illo solo desumuntur, eumque ita referunt, ut infinite majores in eo designentur. Non itaque dicendum est, Deum fore imperfectum & non-Summum, si perfectionibus creatis ipse in se & formaliter destituatur, tunc etenim illum earum additione perfectiorem majoremque evadere posse: Sed contra, ipsius perfectionis & verae Altitudinis conceptus destruitur si cum ipso hae perfectiones misceri fingantur. Hinc patet quid de effato illo, Infinitum in genere Entis sive Perfectionis excludit quodlibet aliud Ens, sit censendum: quod vel figmentum est, nempe si fiat abstractus conceptus ab omni Ente, qui genus vocetur, & tribuatur postmodum omni Enti & in specie Deo addita voce Infiniti qua fingatur Deum omnia complecti ad quae iste conceptus abstractus extendi posset: at tale Ens, tale spectrum non est Deus. Quod si per genus Entis seu perfectionis intelligatur aliquid omnes perfectiones tum finitas tum infinitas involvens, iterum est figmentum, nil enim tale esse ibi demonstratum est ubi probatum fuit finitum & infinitum, sive Deum & creaturam nil univoce habere commune.
