Verum autem est effatum si sic intelligatur, Ens infinitum non patitur ut in se fit infinitum quod sit a se aliud, neque ut extra & praeter se sit infinitum aliud, aliud Ens Summum, à se, vere-que per se solidum: omne tale revera negat & excludit: praeter Deum enim nil dari quod sit vere solidum, subsistens à se, vere reale, ἀρχέτυ-πον[?], verissimum est, omnia praeter ipsum non sunt à seipsis & ob se, sed vestigia, umbrae, figurae, tabulae realitatis solidae, non ipsa realitas. Item hoc sensu axioma verum est; Ens infinitum non patitur esse in se, in sua natura, quodlibet ens finitum & imperfectum, omne tale excludit ab essentia sua, essetque contradicens si tale quid ex illo non excludi fingeretur. Sed si effati pars prior de Ente Summo, maxime ut potente extra se operari spectato, posterior de infimo Ente extra Deum considerato, efferatur, tunc fallit: falsum enim est Infinitum Summum in perfectione summa excludere sive non pati extra se esse aliud ens in genere perfectionis limitatae, atque adeo sui ipsius imaginem vel picturam umbratilem & ab ipso effectam.
units.tr: VIII. Therefore it is absurd to say that God would not be the Highest and All if some reality or perfection existed which he himself was not, because then something, namely this perfection, could be added to him. For God is not called the Highest or All because his essence subjectively has all finite and created things, or because it is them itself; otherwise he would be imperfect, and finite things would be God, just as it has also been said that he is not called everywhere because his essence is everywhere. Rather, in himself and subjectively he is all things, namely all things that are absolutely perfect, and thus he is all things to himself alone, just as it has been said that he is present to himself alone; but with respect to created and finite things he is called all things operatively (as above concerning Where, and for the same reason, for God's being and being where are one) and representatively (as, if you please, we sometimes speak here and elsewhere with the Schools); that is, he is called all things because the perfections of all things are derived from him alone, and they so refer to him that they are designated in him infinitely greater. It is therefore not to be said that God would be imperfect and not the Highest, if he himself in himself and formally lacked created perfections; for then he could become more perfect and greater by their addition. But on the contrary, the concept of perfection and of true Height is destroyed if these perfections are imagined to be mixed with him. Hence it is clear what is to be thought of that saying, "The infinite in the genus of Being or perfection excludes any other Being." This is either a fiction, namely if an abstract concept is formed from every Being, which is called a genus, and afterwards is attributed to every Being, and in the species of God the word "infinite" is added, so that God is feigned to embrace all things to which this abstract concept could be extended: but such a Being, such a phantom, is not God. But if by the genus of Being or perfection is understood something involving all perfections, both finite and infinite, again it is a fiction; for nothing of that kind has been demonstrated there where it was proved that the finite and the infinite, that is God and creature, have nothing univocally in common. But the saying is true if it is understood thus: the infinite Being does not allow that another thing which is different from it should become infinite in itself, nor that another infinite Being, a supreme Being from itself and truly solid through itself, should exist outside and beside itself; for it truly denies and excludes every such thing. For besides God there is nothing that is truly solid, subsisting from itself, truly real, [archetype]; it is most true that all things besides him are not from themselves and for themselves, but are traces, shadows, figures, copies of solid reality, not the reality itself. Likewise, in this sense the axiom is true: the infinite Being does not allow any finite and imperfect being to be in itself, in its own nature; it excludes every such thing from its essence, and it would be a contradiction if such a thing were imagined not to be excluded from it. But if the first part of the saying is pronounced of the Supreme Being, especially as it is regarded as able to act outside itself, and the latter part of the lowest Being considered outside God, then it is false: for it is false that the Infinite Supreme, in supreme perfection, excludes or does not allow another being in the genus of limited perfection to exist outside itself, and thus its own image or shadowy picture effected by itself.

units.la: IX. Inde emerserunt tenebrae istae, quod opificis perfectiones cum perfectionibus opificii male sint confusae. Sed si quae supra dicta sunt de differentia creatarum perfectionum ab increatis teneantur, dissipabitur omnis obscuritas, patebitque de Essentia perfectissimi Authoris omnium esse, ut operis sui perfectiones, utpote quae dependentes, finitae, passivae, quaedam etiam extensae, formaliter non possideat, nedum ille eo sit negandus quod produxerit talia à se diversa opera. Uno verbo, nil naturae summae, Enti perfectissimo infinitoque tribuendum est, ei nil addi posse supponendum est, praeter perfectissimas perfectiones, quas cum jam possideat, sequitur nil ei addendum posse supponi, neque igitur perfectiones imperfectas finitarum rerum. Infinito quoque, ut hoc addam, existente, finita poni nequeunt, ab alio nempe quod non sit ens summum: At asserere Id operationes externas producere non posse, & quidem quia infinitum habetur, atque ita potentiam impotentem in illo concipere, aut etiam Id negare quia operationes externae existunt, insania est eam excedens istorum quorum est elogium, Stultus dicit in corde suo, non est Deus.
units.tr: IX. From this those shadows have arisen, namely that the perfections of the Maker have been wrongly confused with the perfections of the work. But if what has been said above about the difference between created and uncreated perfections is held, all obscurity will be dispelled, and it will be clear that the essence of the most perfect Author of all things does not formally possess the perfections of his work, since these are dependent, finite, passive, and some even extended; much less is he to be denied on the ground that he has produced such works different from himself. In a word, nothing of supreme nature is to be attributed to the most perfect and infinite Being; it is to be supposed that nothing can be added to him, except the most perfect perfections, which, since he already possesses them, it follows that nothing can be supposed to be addable to him, nor therefore imperfect perfections of finite things. Also, since the infinite exists, finite things cannot be posited, namely from something else which is not the supreme Being. But to assert that it cannot produce external operations, and indeed because it is held to be infinite, and thus to conceive an impotent power in it, or even to deny it because external operations exist, is madness, exceeding that of those of whom the saying is: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God."

units.la: X. Instari tamen murmure sic posse animadverto: Ens summum si existat, nulla cognoscere se inferiora, adeoque multo magis illa omnia, si existat, excludere debere. Quod autem nulla quae ipso sint inferiora, adeoque finita, percipere possit & debeat, inde patere, quod perceptio perfectissima & mera non requirat alterius quam sui ipsius perceptionem: nam si necessario aliud praeter se percipit & noscit, sequitur eam solam suae intelligentiae non sufficere, siquidem sine alterius à se diversi perceptione esse non possit: quae autem perceptio alterius perceptione absente non est perfecta, ea perceptio non est summa seu summe perfecta, nec est Entis summi. Cui difficultati non video qui satisfieri queat ab illis, qui rerum creatarum ideas necessario in Deo esse, ab illo concipi scientia simplicis intelligentiae, independentesque esse ab ejus voluntate, sibi persuadent: At nos eam facile, ut superiorem, eodemque modo, solvimus; dicimus enim: quemadmodum nullas perfectiones finitas in se complectitur natura Dei, sic ejus Cogitationem sive perceptionem essentialem, vel intelligentiam simplicem & naturalem, nil complecti, quod ut a seipsa, ab ente summo, diversum repraesentetur; & quemadmodum non est necesse Deo ut ponat extra se finita quaedam, sic non esse necesse ut Deus concipiat & noscat quaedam a se diversa; utque potuisset Deus nil a se diversum ponere, sic potuisset nil a se diversum concipere & nosse; denique quemadmodum si placet ipsi ex lubitu quaedam ponere, ea non ex necessitate ponit, quasi ipse sine illis indigeret, vel non aliter posset facere, aut omnino abstinere, ita si ipsi placuit quaedam statuere, adeoque concipere, (nam τὸ[?] concipere Dei de rebus ab illo diversis est statuere) ea concipit quidem, sed non ex necessitate, quasi absque illorum conceptu ejus Cogitatio deficeret, vel quasi non aliter nosse posset, aut omnino nil praeter se solum nosse. Quae cum nonnullis forte insolentia videri possint, erunt sequentis capitis argumentum, post quod quae de Potentia, quae hisce implicatur, dicenda sunt, non longe amandabuntur.
units.tr: Yet I notice that the following objection may be raised: if the supreme Being exists, it must not know any inferior things, and so it must much more exclude all those things, if they exist. That it cannot and ought not to perceive anything inferior to itself, and therefore finite, is shown by this: the most perfect and pure perception requires no perception other than of itself. For if it necessarily perceives and knows something other than itself, it follows that this perception alone is not sufficient for its understanding, since it could not exist without the perception of something different from itself. But a perception that is not perfect without the perception of something else is not a supreme perception, or a perception that is supremely perfect, and it is not the perception of the supreme Being. I do not see how this difficulty can be met by those who persuade themselves that the ideas of created things are necessarily in God, conceived by him through the knowledge of simple understanding, and independent of his will. We, however, resolve it easily, as we did the earlier one, and in the same way. For we say: just as the nature of God embraces no finite perfections within itself, so his thought or essential perception, or his simple and natural understanding, embraces nothing that is represented as different from itself, from the supreme Being. And just as it is not necessary for God to place outside himself certain finite things, so it is not necessary that God conceive and know certain things different from himself. And just as God could have placed nothing different from himself, so he could have conceived and known nothing different from himself. Finally, just as, if it pleases him, he places certain things by his free choice, and does not place them out of necessity, as though he lacked them or could not act otherwise, or could refrain altogether, so, if it has pleased him to establish certain things, and hence to conceive them (for God's conceiving of things different from himself is the same as establishing them), he indeed conceives them, but not out of necessity, as though his thought would be deficient without the conception of them, or as though he could not know otherwise, or could know nothing at all beyond himself alone. Although these points may perhaps seem strange to some, they will be the subject of the following chapter, after which what must be said about the power implicated in these matters will not be deferred for long.

units.la: CAPUT X. (9) DOMINIUM sive AUTHORITAS. vel, Jus absolutum in Omnia.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. (9) DOMINION, or AUTHORITY; or, Absolute Right over All Things.

units.la: 1.2. Mens creata, etsi quibusdam superior, non habet jus in ullas veritates, nullasque ponit.
units.tr: 1.2. The created mind, though superior to some things, has no right over any truths and posits none.

units.la: I. NOvi me Cogitantem, cogitantem de rebus me majoribus, mihi aequalibus, meque inferioribus: Me quatenus cogito non esse a me, vidi: modum cogitationis de re me majore a me non esse perspexi quoque, idem etiam visurus de modis cogitandi qui res mihi aequales vel me minores repræsentant, sive, de ideis rerum quarumcunque creata-rum, creabiliumve, quas, cum nil eis demere nilque superaddere pos-sim, à me video nequaquam pendere. Nam quamvis cogitando, ex-empli gratia, de materialibus, figuras multifarias mihi fingere videar ad lubitum, hæ tamen non sunt à me proprie, nec figmenta mea dici de-bent, cum earum sit nulla, quæ, si in conceptu solo spectetur, quam-plurimas & mei respectu immutabiles veritates non includat, quæque adeo non sit ab alio quam à me: Et quamvis modo hanc, modo illam, modo aliam quam forsan in me nondum animadverti imaginem, etiam-si chymericam dixeris, mihi actu concipere liceat, hoc tamen nequa-quam est fingere, sed variare conceptum, & applicare alternatim ad ideas quarum veritates & proprietates à me non pendent. Figmentum esset, si judicarem extra me simile aliquid existere, eo quod illas ita concipio: at id non asseritur, sed contra, quemadmodum nil habet juris, nil do-minii, nil authoritatis Mens creata in ullas rerum ideas, formas, natu-ras, essentias, proprietates, veritates, ut mox ostendetur, sic nec in earum existentiam, ut demonstrabitur in posterum. Quodcunque positivi creata Mens judicat in rebus esse quod ab alio quam ab ipsa non sit inibi antea positum, id figmentum falsum est, nec vere positivum. Non est conceptus creatus ita efficax, potens, & perfectus ut ullius realitatis sit verus fictor, nam omnis realitas quæ Deus non est à Dei placito non potest non esse.
units.tr: I. I have seen that I, thinking, think about things greater than myself, things equal to me, and things lesser than me. As far as I think, I have seen that I am not from myself; I have also perceived that my mode of thinking about a greater thing is not from myself, and I shall see the same about the modes of thinking that represent things equal to me or lesser than me, that is, about the ideas of all created or creatable things, which, since I can neither take anything from them nor add anything to them, I see by no means depend on me. For although, when I think, for example, about material things, I seem to myself to form many figures at will, these are nevertheless not properly from me, nor ought they to be called my fictions, since there is none of them which, if considered in the concept alone, does not include very many truths that are unchangeable with respect to me, and which therefore is not from anyone other than me. And although I may be able actually to conceive now this, now that, now another image which perhaps I have not yet noticed in myself, even if you call it chimerical, this is by no means to fabricate, but to vary the concept and apply it in turn to ideas whose truths and properties do not depend on me. It would be a fiction if I judged that something similar existed outside me because I conceive them thus; but this is not asserted. On the contrary, just as the created mind has no right, no dominion, no authority over any ideas, forms, natures, essences, properties, or truths of things, as will soon be shown, so neither has it over their existence, as will be demonstrated hereafter. Whatever positive thing the created mind judges to be in things, which was not previously posited there by another than itself, that is a false fiction and not truly positive. A created concept is not so effective, powerful, and perfect as to be the true maker of any reality, for every reality which is not God cannot fail to be from the pleasure of God.

units.la: II. De me quidem experior mentem meam rerum ideas, sive essen-tias, sive naturas, earumque proprietates & veritates, seu res illæ sint spirituales, seu extensæ, ita intueri, ut ea in illas sponte feratur, cum il-lis congruat, illis consentiat, eas approbet tanquam verissimas: at non illæ ideo ita se habent, non ideo veræ sunt quia illis assentior, illas con-cipio, easque esse veras approbo. Quæcunque de creata Mente hacte-nus demonstravi, & detegam deinceps, à me non pendent, ut neque pen-dent à me quæcunque de corporum natura sive essentia, de motibus, eorumque regulis, vera possunt prædicari. De numeris figurisque cun-ctis veritates omnes tales sunt quales se habent, ut nequicquam eis con-tulerim, talesque permanebunt, cum omni eo quod recte veri nomen habet, certaque natura & essentia est præditum, me sive volente, sive invito: nam nihil mutationis veritatibus illis possum introducere, ut ne-que eis statuendis quicquam contuli. Adeoque præpollentia illa Men-tium præ rebus extensis, vel quarumdam Mentium creatarum præ me, vel mei præ quibusdam aliis, ista inquam præpollentia quam supra dixi me advertere cum concipio ideas rerum (præter Deum) me superan-tium, vel me inferiorum, non alia esse potest, quam quod concipiam Deum secundum ejus placitum magis à quarumdam natura & regimine, minus vero ab aliis, repræsentari: non autem quod à Cogitatione finita procedat ut quædam, utut minima, concipiat, quorum veritatem magis vel minus ponat vel inferat. Ad hoc requiritur ut quis sit sui repræsentativus & sui scopus: sic enim omne ejus figmentum recte placitum sive lubitum suum repræsentabit, & à sui scopo non aberrabit, adeoque verum erit. Sed præter Deum, nullam mentem talem esse vidimus.
units.tr: II. Indeed, I find in myself that my mind intuits the ideas, or essences, of things, or their natures, and their properties and truths, whether those things are spiritual or extended, in such a way that it is spontaneously carried toward them, agrees with them, assents to them, and approves them as most true. Yet they are not thus constituted because of this, they are not true because I assent to them, conceive them, and approve them as true. Whatever I have hitherto demonstrated about the created mind, and shall afterwards uncover, does not depend on me, just as whatever can truly be predicated about the nature or essence of bodies, about motions and their rules, does not depend on me. All truths about numbers and figures are such as they are; I have contributed nothing to them in vain, and they will remain such, with everything that rightly has the name of truth and is endowed with a certain nature and essence, whether I will it or am unwilling: for I can introduce no change into those truths, nor have I contributed anything to establishing them. Therefore that pre-eminence of minds over extended things, or of some created minds over me, or of me over certain others, this pre-eminence, I say, which I noted above when I conceive the ideas of things (other than God) that surpass me or are inferior to me, can be nothing other than that I conceive God, according to his pleasure, to be represented more by the nature and governance of some things, and less by others; not that a finite thinking proceeds to conceive some things, however minute, whose truth it posits or infers more or less. For this it is required that someone be his own representative and his own goal: for thus every fiction of his will rightly represent his pleasure or his will, and will not stray from its goal, and so will be true. But apart from God, we have seen that there is no such mind.

units.la: 3. Metaphysica de transcendentalibus, falsa. 4. 5. Omnes rerum ideæ, naturæ, veritates, non sunt tales ex natura sua sive ex se ipsis, sed ex Dei placito, quod antecedenter liberrimum & ad illas indifferens considerari debet, statuta. 6. 7. 8. Demonstratur ex natura & attributis Dei. 9. Ea nihilominus Menti sunt innata. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. Difficultates. Ex consideratione Dei quinque orta, resolvuntur. 16. Veritates & essentiæ rerum ut sint immutabiles & æternæ, aut secus. 17. Nulla quæ in rebus veritas fluit proprie ex Dei natura. 18. 19. 20. 21. Considerationes ex quibus omnes difficultates à respectu rerumortæ possunt dissolvi. 22. 23. Concluditur evidenti hujus doctrinæ expositione. 24. Horum utilitas.
units.tr: 3. The metaphysics of the transcendentals is false. 4. 5. All ideas, natures, and truths of things are not such from their own nature or from themselves, but are established by the pleasure of God, which must be considered antecedently most free and indifferent to them. 6. 7. 8. It is demonstrated from the nature and attributes of God. 9. Nevertheless, these are innate to the mind. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. Difficulties. Five arising from the consideration of God are resolved. 16. Whether the truths and essences of things are immutable and eternal, or otherwise. 17. No truth which flows in things flows properly from the nature of God. 18. 19. 20. 21. Considerations by which all difficulties arising from the respect of things can be dissolved. 22. 23. It is concluded by a clear exposition of this doctrine. 24. The usefulness of these.

units.la: III. Deum hoc respectu in eandem cum creatis mentibus classem fere ab omnibus reponi dolendum est, dum nempe docent, quod ille rerum ideas, essentias, veritates, concipiat adæquate quidem, sed tamen ita, ut necessario eas concipiat, ut ejus neque conceptus, neque voluntas, sit causa veritatum earum, quippe quæ aliter esse non potuerint, quæque dicantur esse à se immutabiles, veræ & æternæ, & ita cum Deo connexæ, ut si non omnes, saltem quædam, eæque præcipuæ non possint negari, (hoc est, ut interpretor, affirmari non posse quod illæ potuissent aliter se habere,) quin Dei natura negetur atque veritas. Quasi vero fluerent illæ immediate & absque interventu decreti sive placiti ex ipsa Dei essentia! cum hoc modo Solus Filius & Spiritus Dei ex illo procedant. Emanarunt illæ tenebræ à vana Philosophia otiosorum & fabulosorum Scholasticorum, qui cum Deum ejusque opera pro objectis suarum cogitationum despicarentur, figmentis suis inhiantes, nobis cuderunt horribilem scientiam quam Metaphysicam vocarunt: non eam quiquidem quæ in Cognitione Dei & præcipuarum realitatum, sive veri-tatum & operationum ab ipso positarum consistens, verissima haberi debet, ad quam etiam quæ hic exstant referri posse confido; sed non-nullam aliam quæ sit de Ente universalissimo, de Essentia, de attribu-tis transcendentalibus, Uno, Vero, Bono, &c. ita ut hæc scientia præ-scindat à Cognitione Dei & rerum cæterarum, imo eam præcedat: un-de quæ concludit attribui possint omni enti sive creato sive increato, in-fimo & summo. Quasi scilicet cognosci posset aliqua, sive veritas, sive bonitas, sive essentia, cujus fundamentum essentiale & ratio vera atque solida non esset Dei placitum! Quasi veritas ut positive independens esset consideranda, aut contradistingui posset à Dei dependentia & vo-luntate; cum hoc ipsum sit! Horribile est, quod doceatur aliquid veri de creaturis postea prædicandi, esse considerandum ut transcendens re-spectum ad Dei dependentiam & voluntatem sive placitum. Tenebræ transcendentales sunt isthæc, noxiumque figmentum dari talem noti-tiam vere fundatam de re vera, sive talem scientiam, eamque omnium primam, de Ente, Vero, Bono, &c. quo sic homines magis magisque assuescerent omnia spectare ut non dependentia à Deo: Cum tamen omne verum sit à Deo, omnisque ejus certitudo & demonstratio in Dei notitia fundata. Obtestor quosvis cordatos, An ex nugis istis trans-scendentalibus aliquid luminis, fructus, usus, extra rixas & tenebras, in ea quæ Deum vel homines concernunt redundans, unquam reporta-verint? Miscet illa falso nominata scientia in antecessum omnium Crea-torem cum creatura, acsi univoce haberent quædam entitatis, veritatis, bonitatis, causalitatis, &c. communia, quod salsissimum esse undique mox patebit amplius: aut vero fateantur prætensas suas definitiones, enuntiationesque scientificas de Ente, uno, vero, &c. cum Enti creato & Increato non competant univoce, (etenim omnino nil reale vel sub-jective, vel causaliter, vel effective Deo & creaturis commune est sensu univoco) esse tantum distinctiones & definitiones nominis æquivoci, & eas (siquidem relinquant æquivocationem) ineptissimas: nominalia autem nullam pariunt scientiam. Exemplo lubet has tenebras discutere. Cum ajunt, Ens est id quod est, aut nomen Entis, quod est æquivocum ut-pote Summo increatoque & infimo seu dependenti commune, explica-re volunt per voces minus æquivocas, ne maneat ambiguum, quasi dice-rent, Per vocem Ens notamus id quod est suum esse, sive cujus essentia & veritatis ratio in se ipso est, nec ultra se quæri debet: quomodo ostendent se Deum designare, & aliud membrum, ens nempe dependens, excludere: quod tamen ne semel quidem monere, ut neque etiam hæc eorum Mens fuit; Aut (quod intenderunt) rem definire volent, quasi dicerent, Ens est, hoc est, datur vel concipitur aliqua realitas, eaque univoce communis omnibus (creatis nempe & increatis) quæ est id quod est, hoc est, cujus communis realitatis natura, idea, essentia, veritas, est & concipitur in ipsa independenter ab omni re, quæque ipsa est sibi suum esse, sua veritas, &c. quod effatum est improbum. Idem est de suæ transcendentalis veritatis definitione, Veritas est conformitas rei cum se ipsa. Hæc Deo soli, non vero, ut volunt, sensu eodem creatis rebus competit. Sola Divinæ naturæ veritas est, cujus essentia sive natura consistit in hoc, ut secum sit uniformis, suæque perfectionis mensura: at in creatis, vel quæ circa creata sunt id absurdum est, nam hæc absoluta non sunt, nec sui repræsentativa. Absurdus esset qui de imagine cujus essentia & veritas in eo consisteret, ut alicujus placitum repræsentaret, causaretur in ea esse veritatem, eo quod illa sibi ipsi esset conformis, & spectaretur ut independens à quavis alia re, ab omnibusque præscinderetur.
units.tr: III. It is to be lamented that God is almost by everyone placed in this respect in the same class as created minds, when they teach that he conceives the ideas, essences, and truths of things adequately, yet in such a way that he conceives them necessarily, so that neither his concept nor his will is the cause of those truths, since they could not have been otherwise, and they are said to be immutable, true, and eternal from themselves, and so connected with God that, if not all, at least certain, and those the principal, cannot be denied (that is, as I interpret it, it cannot be affirmed that they could have been otherwise) without the nature and truth of God being denied. As if indeed they flowed immediately and without the intervention of a decree or pleasure from the very essence of God! Since in this way only the Son and the Spirit of God proceed from him. Those darknesses emanated from the vain philosophy of idle and fabulous Scholastics, who, while they regarded God and his works as objects of their thoughts, gaping after their own fictions, forged for us that horrible science which they called Metaphysics: not indeed that which consists in the knowledge of God and of the chief realities, or truths and operations posited by him, which ought to be held the truest, and to which I trust that what is set forth here may also be referred; but some other science concerning the most universal Being, concerning Essence, concerning the transcendental attributes, One, True, Good, etc., so that this science abstracts from the knowledge of God and of other things, and even precedes it: whence it concludes that they can be attributed to every being, whether created or uncreated, lowest and highest. As if, forsooth, anything could be known, whether truth, or goodness, or essence, whose essential foundation and true and solid reason were not the pleasure of God! As if truth were to be considered as positively independent, or could be distinguished from the dependence and will of God; when this very thing is! It is dreadful that it be taught that something true to be afterwards predicated of creatures should be considered as transcending the respect to God's dependence and will or pleasure. These are transcendental darknesses, and it is a harmful fiction that there should be such a truly grounded notion of a real thing, or such a science, and the first of all, of Being, Truth, Good, etc., by which men would become ever more accustomed to regard all things as not dependent on God: when yet every truth is from God, and all his certainty and demonstration are founded in the knowledge of God. I beseech any men of sound judgment: have they ever gathered from these transcendental trifles any light, fruit, or use, outside of strife and darkness, bearing on what concerns God or men? That falsely named science mixes the Creator with the creature in advance of all things, as if they had certain things in common univocally, of entity, truth, goodness, causality, etc., which will soon be shown everywhere to be most false; or else let them confess that their pretended definitions and scientific statements about Being, One, True, etc., do not apply univocally to created and uncreated being (for absolutely nothing real is common to God and creatures in a univocal sense, either subjectively, or causally, or effectively), and that they are only distinctions and definitions of an equivocal name, and (if they keep the equivocation) most inept; but nominal things produce no science. It is pleasing to dispel these darknesses by an example. When they say, "Being is that which is," or the name of Being, which is equivocal, as it is common to the highest uncreated and to the lowest or dependent, they wish to explain it by less equivocal words, lest it remain ambiguous, as if they said: "By the word Being we mark that which is its own being, or whose essence and reason of truth is in itself, nor ought to be sought beyond itself": how will they show that they designate God and exclude the other member, namely dependent being? Yet they did not once think to warn of this, nor was this their intention. Or (what they intended) they will wish to define the thing, as if they said, "Being is," that is, "some reality is given or conceived, and it is univocally common to all (created and uncreated), which is that which is, that is, whose nature, idea, essence, and truth of the common reality is and is conceived in itself independently of every thing, and which itself is its own being, its own truth, etc."; which statement is improper. The same is true of the definition of their transcendental truth: "Truth is the conformity of a thing with itself." This in the same sense belongs to created things, as they claim, not to God alone. The truth of the divine nature alone is such, whose essence or nature consists in this, that it be uniform with itself and the measure of its own perfection; but in created things, or in those which concern created things, this is absurd, for these are not absolute, nor representative of themselves. He would be absurd who, concerning an image whose essence and truth consisted in this, that it represented the pleasure of someone, should claim that the truth is in it because it is conformed to itself, and should regard it as independent of every other thing, and abstract it from all.

units.la: IV. Primus quo tenebræ illæ hoc sæculo ex Philosophia, unde in Theologiam Scholasticam & omnia transcenderant, utcunque sunt discussæ, Celebris Cartesius fuit. Sed cum hæc paucis ex occasione & obiter tantum, nec ita exacte sint proposita {a} ab illo, nec, quod sciam ab ullo exactius, quæ tamen dignissima sunt, & maxime conferunt ad Majestatem Dei Summam super omnibus infinite elevatam & Dominantem agnoscendam & celebrandam; operæ pretium est ea diligentius exponere. Sic dedidicemus tribuere Deo imperfectiones nostras, qui volumus eum veritates concipere quas prius non determinaverit ipse tales, sed jam ut determinatas invenerit; cum tamen nos ipsi in praxi nos ita geramus, acsi voluntates sive affectus nostri erga objectum aliquod importarent in objectum illud veritates & qualitates quas inibi esse volumus: quomodo in theoria quod est nostri Deo damus, in praxi quod est Dei affectamus.
units.tr: IV. The first person to dispel, to some extent, those shadows which in this century had spread from philosophy into Scholastic theology and into everything else was the famous Descartes. But since he set these things out only briefly and in passing, on occasion, and not so exactly, and since, as far as I know, no one has done so more exactly, although they are most worthy and contribute greatly to acknowledging and celebrating the majesty of God, supreme and infinitely elevated above all things and ruling over them, it is worth the effort to expound them more carefully. Thus we have unlearned to ascribe our own imperfections to God, when we wish him to conceive truths which he had not previously determined to be such, but which he found already determined; yet in practice we conduct ourselves as though our wills or affections towards some object carried into that object the truths and qualities we want to be there. In theory we give God what is ours; in practice we attribute to ourselves what is God's. ## [2]

units.la: V. Dico igitur, Deum concipere necessario, necessitate naturæ suæ, veritates illas quæ de illo sunt, quæque ejus naturam, essentiam, attributa, immediate spectant, & illum nunquam fuisse ad has indifferentem. At non item de veritatibus quæ ideas, essentias, proprietates omnium eorum quæ ipse Deus non sunt, concernunt, sive existant, aut solum concipiantur, sive ad Mentium naturam aut ad corpora, eorumve motus, regulas, ad figuras, aut ad numeros, aut alia quævis, referantur. Nam ideo eas tales concipit & cogitat Deus, non quod eæ ex sese sint tales immutabilesque, sed quod ipsi placuerit eas tales statuere: adeo ut veritates illæ sint dependentes à Dei placito, & veræ, quia Deo eas placuit sic statuere. Atque placitum istud, (sive voluntas) quo hæccce statuit Deus, concipiendum est ut indifferentissimum ex natura sua ad hæc statuenda vel plane omittenda, vel diversa decernenda. Quomodo vel nullæ, præter illas quæ ipsam Dei essentiam concernunt, fuissent veritates, vel omnino aliæ fuissent quam quæ sunt hodie. Imo, quod plus est, ita Deus horum omnium respectu concipiendus est, ut postquam veritates illæ ideales, essentiales, propriæ, &c. ad tempus usque præsens duraverunt, potuerint deinceps immutari, aliæque vel nullæ prorsus, statui, si hoc ei placuisset; adeo ut quæ jam sunt, non sint in se & ex se immutabiles, tametsi possint esse, ut revera sunt, immutabiles ex placito Dei: nec enim habemus causam suspicandi Deum illas statuentem ad tempus statuisse, cum placeat ei suum placitum, & tanquam bona probet quæcunque vel fecit, vel statuit; nec sit quod is illas destruat hac de causa, ut scilicet omnia à placito suo pendere ostendat illis, qui eum hac gloria spoliant: nam & hi cum omnes mutatæ fuissent veritates, etiam ipsi fuissent mutati, neque eorum cognitiones mansissent; & id ipsum, quod in causam allegatum est, jam ostendit Deus luculentissimis in omnium Mentibus testimoniis, quæ facile est agnoscere si ad sequentes demonstrationes bene attendatur: nam eæ in hoc principium resolvuntur, quod Deus non sit confundendus cum illis quæ non sunt Deus, sive, quod solus Deus sit Deus; & effata assumpta ex supra demonstratis sunt.
units.tr: V. I say, therefore, that God necessarily conceives, by the necessity of his nature, those truths which concern him, which relate immediately to his nature, essence and attributes, and that he was never indifferent to these. But it is not so with truths which concern the ideas, essences and properties of all those things that are not God himself, whether they exist or are merely conceived, whether they relate to the nature of minds or to bodies, to their motions and laws, to figures, to numbers, or to any other thing. For God conceives and thinks them to be such not because they are by their own nature such and immutable, but because it has pleased him to establish them as such; so that those truths depend on God's pleasure, and are true because it pleased God to establish them so. And this pleasure (or will) by which God has established these things must be conceived as, by its very nature, wholly indifferent to establishing them, or to omitting them altogether, or to decreeing them otherwise. In that case there would either have been no truths except those which concern the very essence of God, or they would have been altogether different from what they are today. Indeed, what is more, God must be conceived with respect to all these things in such a way that, after those ideal, essential, proper truths, and so on, have lasted up to the present time, they could afterwards be changed, and others, or none at all, established, if this had pleased him. So that the things which now are are not immutable in themselves and of themselves, although they can be, and indeed are, immutable by God's pleasure. For we have no reason to suspect that God, having established them for a time, established them for a time only, since his pleasure pleases him, and he approves whatever he has done or decreed as good. Nor is there any reason why he should destroy them for this cause, namely to show that everything depends on his pleasure, to those who deprive him of this glory. For even if all truths had been changed, they themselves would also have been changed, and their cognitions would not have remained. And this very thing which has been alleged as a cause God already shows by the clearest testimonies in the minds of all, which are easy to recognise if one attends carefully to the following demonstrations. For these are resolved into this principle, that God is not to be confused with those things which are not God, or that God alone is God; and the propositions assumed are drawn from what has been demonstrated above. ## [3]

units.la: VI. Deus est unus. Non esset Deus unus si conciperet aliquid à se diversum & tamen sibi univocum, seu habens secum similem radicitus & essentialiter proprietatem. Ergo præter se nullum concipit verum necessarium, nullum immutabile per se.
units.tr: VI. God is one. God would not be one if he conceived something different from himself yet univocal with himself, that is, having a property similar to himself and essentially the same. Therefore, beside himself he conceives no truth as necessary, nothing immutable through itself. ## [4]

units.la: VII. Solus Deus est perfectissimus. Ergo sola ejus Essentia est summe & absolute necessaria: nam absoluta simpliciter necessitas summa est perfectio. Necessitas absoluta Cogitationis de objecto perfectissimo excludit necessitatem absolutam Cogitationis de objecto imperfecto, nam ea opus non habet, essetque imperfecta si ea opus haberet. Præterea, absoluta necessitas essentiis & veritatibus finitis sive non perfectissimis tribui nequit, quin tribuatur eis una ex perfectionibus summis, & consequenter omnes: quod in Deum peccat. Unde sequitur eas omnes, finitas nempe, non esse summe & absolute necessarias, id est, non esse absolute & necessario id quod sunt, adeoque absolute loquendo, de iis aliter esse potuisse.
units.tr: VII. God alone is most perfect. Therefore his essence alone is supremely and absolutely necessary; for absolute necessity simply is the highest perfection. The absolute necessity of the cognition of a most perfect object excludes the absolute necessity of the cognition of an imperfect object, for the latter has no need of it, and it would be imperfect if it had need of it. Moreover, absolute necessity cannot be ascribed to finite essences and truths, or to those that are not most perfect, without ascribing to them one of the highest perfections, and consequently all of them; and this is an offence against God. Hence it follows that all these finite things are not supremely and absolutely necessary, that is, they are not absolutely and necessarily what they are, and so, speaking absolutely, they could have been otherwise. ## [5]

units.la: VIII. Solus Deus est à se positive, id est, Solus ille est, qui talem habet naturam, essentiam, tales proprietates veritatesque, quarum ra-tio reddi possit ex consideratione rei ipsius, ut non sit opus ad aliud objectum se conferre & ulterius provocare. Atqui hoc attributum ab eo ad aliud raperetur, si praeter ipsum fingeremus quasdam essentias, veritates, naturas, &c. tales esse, ut si de illis quaereretur, cur essent tales? cur verae? ex harum unarum inspectione posset responderi, ideo tales esse, quia talis est earum natura; tales esse à se ipsis ab aeterno; Deum non aliam ob causam illas tales concipere, quam quoniam ipsae tales sunt. Perinde dixeris dari essentias, naturas, veritates, à Deo independentes, à se ipsis autem dependentes, vel sibi ipsis sufficientes, quod ita Deo injurium est ut non putem ullum haec percipientem ea deinceps probaturum, nam haec important Dei dependentiam à rebus ab ipso independentibus. 1. Cogitationis Dei complementum non penderet sive non esset à sui solius intelligentia, siquidem aliud esset quod Deus praeter notitiam sui necessario requireret, ideae nempe rerum & veritates quae necessariae dicuntur. Illud autem quod non haberet id quod est necessario requisitum, completum non esset, atque ita complementum cogitationis Divinae penderet à quibusdam quae Dei natura non sunt, quae ab ejus voluntate independentia finguntur, & quibus ille carere non posset. 2. Non esset Ens sibi acquiescens, se solo gaudens, si aliud praeter ipsum esset verum quo necessario ille frui deberet. 3. Non esset independens à scopo vel motivo à se diverso, si aliquid nosset & vellet tanquam verum & bonum, ea de causa quod illud jam antea tale fuisset. 4. Denique notitia & perceptio Dei, cum ejus Natura, penderet ab illis quae non sunt Deus. unde enim Deus, qui has novit essentias & veritates, notitiam illarum habet? an ab illis, aut vero à se ipso? Quis dicat Deum ab illis cognitionem earum habere? Ad Deum ipsum recurrendum esse patet. At in eandem incidemus absurditatem, imo in majorem ita quam evitare conabamur, nisi ad Deum recurramus tanquam ad causam earum rerum liberrimam, & plane ad eas prius indifferentem; afferere enim Deum res istas concipere necessario, quia suam ipsius naturam concipit, adeo ut illae necessario conceptui ipsius naturae sic sint connexae ut in eo includantur, idem esset acsi quis afferet, non posse Dei naturam sine illis concipi, unde qui eas negaret, naturam essentiamque Divinam etiam tolleret, quemadmodum una perfectione Dei negata, etiam negantur caeterae. Igitur natura Dei ab illis penderet eo sensu quo dici potest eam à suis perfectionibus pendere, hoc est, in illis & per illas existere. Quæ cum manifeste falsa sint, necessario fatendum est, aut notitiam Dei de illis rebus aliunde quam à Deo procedere, adeoque aliquid esse reale, essentiale, verum, bonum, quod non sit ipse Deus, quodque tum intellectum Divinum ad sui cognitionem ita determinaverit, ut hic non aliter potuerit id concipere, quippe quod ab illo non pendeat, tum voluntatem Divinam inclinaverit ad id independenter ab ipsa approbandum: quod jam falsi convictum est; aut concludendum est, ut vere, omnia illa à placito & lubitu Dei tanquam prius indifferenti spectato pendere, eaque talia esse qualia sunt, essentialia nempe, propria, vera, bona in ideis (neque enim de actuali existentia hic sermo est) quia placuit Deo velle hoc ita esse; Deumque illa concipere talia, quia novit suum placitum de illis, scitque se indifferentem prius fuisse, & aliter potuisse suum placitum determinare. Sic Summus Dominus est, à nullo ullatenus ullo sensu pendens, à cujus arbitrio liberrimo omnis quæ ipse non est veritatis Authoritas pendeat. Aliæ hujus demonstrationes ex aliis attributis prætermittuntur, cum hæ sufficiant.
units.tr: VIII. God alone is from himself positively, that is, he alone is the one who has such a nature, essence, properties and truths that the reason for them can be rendered from consideration of the thing itself, so that there is no need to turn to another object and appeal further. Yet this attribute would be snatched away from him and transferred to another if we imagined that certain essences, truths, natures and so on were such apart from him, that if one asked of them, why are they such? why are they true? the answer could be given from inspecting these very things: they are such because their nature is such; they are such from themselves from eternity; and God conceives them as such for no other reason than because they themselves are such. In the same way you might say that there are essences, natures and truths independent of God, but dependent on themselves, or sufficient to themselves; and this is so injurious to God that I do not think anyone perceiving these things will afterwards prove them, for these imply a dependence of God on things which are independent of him. (1) The completeness of God's cognition would not depend on, or would not be derived from, his own understanding alone, if there were something besides which God necessarily required in addition to the knowledge of himself, namely the ideas of things and the truths which are called necessary. But that which lacked what was necessarily required would not be complete; and so the completeness of divine cognition would depend on certain things which are not the nature of God, which are feigned to be independent of his will, and without which he could not be. (2) He would not be a Being resting in himself, rejoicing in himself alone, if something other than himself were true, which he would necessarily have to enjoy. (3) He would not be independent of an aim or motive different from himself, if he knew and willed something as true and good for the reason that it had already been such before. (4) Finally, the knowledge and perception of God, together with his nature, would depend on those things which are not God. For whence does God, who knows these essences and truths, have knowledge of them? From them, or from himself? Who would say that God has the cognition of them from them? It is plain that we must have recourse to God himself. But we would fall into the same absurdity, indeed into a greater one than the one we were trying to avoid, unless we had recourse to God as the most free cause of those things, and entirely indifferent to them beforehand. For to assert that God conceives these things necessarily because he conceives his own nature, so that they are so connected with the necessary conception of his nature that they are included in it, would be the same as if someone asserted that the nature of God cannot be conceived without them; whence whoever denied them would also take away the divine nature and essence, just as when one perfection of God is denied, the others are denied too. Therefore the nature of God would depend on those things in the sense in which it can be said to depend on its perfections, that is, to exist in them and through them. Since these are manifestly false, it must necessarily be admitted either that the knowledge of God concerning those things proceeds from some other source than God, and so that there is something real, essential, true, good, which is not God himself, and which has determined the divine intellect for the knowledge of itself in such a way that it could not conceive it otherwise, since it does not depend on him, and has inclined the divine will to approve it independently of itself: which has already been proved false; or it must be concluded, as is true, that all those things depend on the pleasure and will of God, regarded as previously indifferent, and that they are such as they are, namely essential, proper, true, good, in ideas (for the discussion here is not about actual existence), because it has pleased God to will that this should be so; and that God conceives them as such because he knows his own pleasure concerning them, and knows that he was previously indifferent and could have determined his pleasure otherwise. Thus the Supreme Lord is dependent on nothing, in no way and in no sense, and from his most free decision all the authority of truth, other than himself, depends. The other demonstrations of this from other attributes are omitted, since these are sufficient.

units.la: IX. Atque hæ sunt origines idearum & veritatum omnium à natura Dei differentium, sive materialia, sive spiritualia spectent. quæ quamquam respectu Dei proprie innatæ & naturaliter ejus conceptui impressæ dici non possint, sunt nihilominus innatæ cuivis creatæ Menti, eique naturaliter ita insculptæ, ut diversum ab illis nullatenus concipere possit. Et quemadmodum Rex aliquis monetam novam excogitare, vel novas leges statuere valet, quas, si posset, in animis subditorum ita imprimeret, ut per se notæ innatæque haberentur; ita quoque nil impedit quin Deus ideas veritatesque omnes cum earum legibus finxerit & excogitaverit ex lubitu, easque inscripserit ita mentibus, ut non possint concipi non veræ notitiæ innatæ, earumque contrarium ab ullo bene attendente non possit non haberi ut falsum, id est, ut non statutum à Deo. Utque peritus Pictor nonnunquam figmenta non contemnenda gratis effingit delectabundus; sic visum est Beatissimæ Menti sibique Soli secum sufficientissimæ ex libero & superabundanti placiti lubitu ludere, (ut illa de se in Sacris Scripturis ait) & ludibundæ instar fingere quæ delectabunda in conceptu suo contemplaretur, exhibituræ postea extra se per potentiam specimina nonnulla lusorum figmentorumque suorum, sed talia, quæ Mentem perfectissimam, sufficientissimam, summe intelligentem, summe sapientem, cujus stultitia omni sapientia imaginabili celsior est, non male decerent. Ita etiam lusit in humanis divina placentia rebus.
units.tr: IX. These, then, are the origins of all ideas and truths that differ from the nature of God, whether they concern material or spiritual things. Although with respect to God they cannot properly be called innate, or naturally impressed on his concept, they are nonetheless innate to every created mind and so naturally engraved on it that it cannot conceive anything different from them. Just as a king can devise a new coinage or enact new laws, and would, if he could, impress them on the minds of his subjects so that they were held to be known and innate in themselves, so too nothing prevents God from having fashioned and devised all ideas and truths, together with their laws, at his pleasure, and from having inscribed them on minds in such a way that they cannot be conceived otherwise than as true innate notions, and that no one who attends carefully can help holding their contrary to be false, that is, not decreed by God. And just as a skilled painter sometimes freely sketches, with delight, figures that are not to be despised, so it pleased the most blessed Mind, self-sufficient in himself alone, to play, from the free and overflowing pleasure of his will (as he says of himself in the Holy Scriptures), and, playing like a child, to fashion in his thought things which he might contemplate with delight, and afterwards to display outside himself, by his power, some specimens of his playful creations. Yet these are such as fittingly befit a most perfect, most self-sufficient, most intelligent and most wise Mind, whose foolishness is loftier than every imaginable wisdom. So too in human affairs the divine will has played as it pleased.

units.la: X. Difficultates forte non paucæ occurrent illis qui hæc nondum penitius sunt scrutati, quæ ex consideratione tum Dei concipientis & statuentis, tum rerum ab eo conceptarum & statutarum, possent emergere. Harum præcipuas conabimur è medio tollere. Ex respectu ad Deum hæ oriuntur.
units.tr: X. Not a few difficulties will perhaps occur to those who have not yet searched these matters more deeply, which could arise from considering both God as conceiving and decreeing, and the things conceived and decreed by him. We shall try to remove the chief of these. They arise from the relation to God.

units.la: XI. Primo, negandum esse non videtur Deum scire quid possit vel velit statuere, aut secus; adeoque scientia vel conceptus præcedit statutum. Sed qui hoc dicunt, præsupponunt esse quid diversum à Deo quod ante Dei arbitrium seu placitum, habeat veritatem & possibilitatem à parte sui. quod est πρῶτον ψεῦδος. Deus, inquiunt, sit quid, &c. quid est illud quid? Non datur nec concipitur ullum quid ante Dei placitum. Absurdum est dicere, Deum concipere vel scire id quod pendet ab ejus decreto priusquam pendeat sive pendere concipiatur, vel quasi non penderet ab illo: nosse id ut antecedens ejus placitum, cujus idea est placiti consequens.
units.tr: XI. First, it does not seem that we must deny that God knows what he can or wills to decree, or otherwise; and so knowledge or conception precedes the decree. But those who say this presuppose that there is something distinct from God which, prior to the will or pleasure of God, has truth and possibility on its own side. This is a first falsehood (πρῶτον ψεῦδος). "God," they say, "is something, etc." What is that something? No "something" is given or conceived prior to the pleasure of God. It is absurd to say that God conceives or knows that which depends on his decree before it exists, or before it is conceived to depend, or as if it did not depend on him: to know it as antecedent to his pleasure, whose idea is the consequent of the pleasure.

units.la: XII. Secundo, ex eo quod dictum est Deum ad has veritates indifferentissimum potuisse eas plane non statuere, adeoque nec concipere, nec scire, videtur sequi in Deo, siquidem potuisset veritates omnes quæ jam præter ipsum sunt, nescire, ignorantiam sic dari potuisse: cujus absurdi removendi gratia, antecedens, unde fluxit, tollendum fuerit. At, qui hoc putarent, nescirent ipsi quid esset ignorantia. Ignorantia supponit esse objectum scibile & verum, eaque non datur ubi nil tale est: atqui nil tale est ante statutum Dei, ut demonstratum est. Ille à cujus statuto omnis veritas pendet, & qui non novit quæ non statuit, non est dicendus ignorans: non magis quam dici possit in Deo esse ignorantiam, quia non novit muscas esse homines, ut neque novit omnes homines fore æternum beatos.
units.tr: XII. Second, from what has been said, that God, being most indifferent towards these truths, could have not decreed them at all, and so neither conceived nor known them, it seems to follow that there could have been ignorance in God, since he could have been ignorant of all the truths that exist apart from himself. In order to remove this absurdity, the antecedent from which it flows must be taken away. But those who think this would not know what ignorance is. Ignorance presupposes an object that is knowable and true, and it does not exist where there is nothing of the kind; yet there is nothing of the kind before the decree of God, as has been shown. He from whose decree all truth depends, and who does not know what he has not decreed, is not to be called ignorant: no more than it can be said that there is ignorance in God because he does not know that flies are men, or because he does not know that all men will be eternally blessed.

units.la: XIII. Tertia difficultas hæc est. Si ideæ & veritates potuissent aliter à Deo statui & concipi, Dei conceptus esset mutabilis, vel potuisset aliter se habere quam se jam habet, & sic in illo esset possibilitas varietatis: quod offendit in superiorem demonstrationem de activitate Dei. Hæc objectio omnium speciosissima & validissima primo adspectu videtur, quæ tamen omnium debilissima & absurdissima deprehendetur, si animadvertas (1) non hic sermonem esse de conceptu quem de se ipso habet Deus, quemque ad Intelligentiam supra retulimus. Ille Dei de se conceptus non potuit nec potest aliter se habere, quia Dei naturæ sive essentiæ nil vel à se vel ab alio de novo accidit vel accidere potuit: at (2) de conceptu quem habet Deus de illis quæ ipse non sunt, idem judicandum non est, cum sit conceptus placiti sui indifferentissimi, alia spectantis, non autem naturae suae absolute necessariae ad se ipsam relatae. Equidem nequaquam puto Dei scientiae sive conceptui aliquid diversitatis aliunde posse accidere: quod activitati repugnaret; neque in illo vel contraria, vel diversa per modum successionis esse posse: qua in re cum mutabilitas sive variabilitas proprie consistat, eam etiam rejeci: Sed assero, non esse in Dei natura neque in ejus placito ea de causa imperfectionem, quod potuerit aliter statuere, decernere, velle, adeoque aliter concipere statutum, decretum, placitum fuisse. Quin contrarium destruit tum activitatem Divini conceptus, conceptus enim qui formam & veritatem aliquam a se diversam concipit cujus ipse causa non est, quamque absolute aliter concipere non potest, non est activus, sed passivus; tum Dei libertatem in rebus producendis: nam illas non potuisset alio modo efficere existentes, nisi potuisset illas aliquo saltem modo diversas concipere: quae diversitas si Dei conceptum non dedeceat, neque etiam illa quam asserimus. Est equidem potentia aliter se habendi imperfectionis nota in creatis rebus, quia receptionem & dependentiam dicit: sed in Dei, non dico natura, at, placito, sive conceptu de omnibus quae ipse non sunt, est mera activitas & perfectio, qua Deus concipit se nulli praeter se ex necessitate esse alligatum. Radix erroris in eo est, quod ut nostrum concipimus, sic Dei conceptum velimus considerare, nempe ut rem recipientem: cum tamen sit principium summe activum, sive placitum liberrimum, de quo omnium respectu hoc Augustini dixeris, Quia vides (sive concipis) ea sunt: vel, quia placet, ea sunt. Et cum nemo dubitet potuisse Dei voluntatem placitumque de rebus, saltem nonnullis, v. g. de me existente, &c. aliter se habere, adeoque Deum potuisse aliter concipere suam voluntatem determinationemque placiti sui, neque tamen ea sequi quae mox objiciebantur; non video cur hoc ad omnia quae diximus non extenderint, nisi quia omnia non spectarunt ut a Summo Domino dependentia.
units.tr: XIII. The third difficulty is this. If ideas and truths could have been decreed and conceived by God otherwise, the conception of God would be mutable, or could be otherwise than it now is, and thus there would be in him a possibility of variety; this offends against our earlier demonstration of God's activity. This objection seems at first sight the most specious and most powerful of all, yet it will be found the weakest and most absurd of all, if you consider (1) that we are not speaking here of the concept which God has of himself, which we referred above to his Understanding. That concept of God concerning himself could not be, and cannot be, otherwise, because nothing new has happened or could happen to the nature or essence of God, either from himself or from another. But (2) the same judgment does not hold for the concept which God has of those things which are not himself, since it is the concept of his most indifferent pleasure, looking to other things, and not of his absolutely necessary nature, related to itself. Indeed, I by no means think that any diversity can arise in the knowledge or concept of God from elsewhere, since this would be repugnant to his activity; nor can contrary or different things exist in him by way of succession; and since mutability or variability properly consists in this, I have rejected it too. But I assert that there is no imperfection in the nature of God, nor in his pleasure, for this reason: that he could have decreed, determined, willed otherwise, and so conceived the decree, determination and pleasure otherwise. Indeed, the contrary destroys both the activity of the divine conception (for a conception that conceives a form and truth distinct from itself, of which it is not the cause, and which it cannot absolutely conceive otherwise, is not active but passive) and God's freedom in producing things: for he could not have brought those things into existence in any other way unless he could have conceived them in some way at least different; and if this diversity does not disgrace the divine conception, neither does the diversity we assert. Indeed, the power of being otherwise is a mark of imperfection in created things, because it implies receptivity and dependence; but in God, I do not say his nature, but his pleasure or concept concerning all things that are not himself, it is pure activity and perfection, by which God conceives that he is bound to nothing outside himself by necessity. The root of the error lies in this: that we wish to consider the concept of God as we consider our own, namely as something receiving; whereas it is a supremely active principle, or most free pleasure, of which, with respect to all things, one may say what Augustine said: "Because you see" (or conceive) "they are, therefore they are"; or, "because it pleases, they are." And since no one doubts that the will and pleasure of God concerning some things at least, for example concerning my existence, could have been otherwise, and so that God could have conceived otherwise his will and the determination of his pleasure, without the consequences that were just now objected; I do not see why they did not extend this to all that we have said, unless because they did not regard all things as dependent on the Supreme Lord.

units.la: XIV. Quarto objici posset, si hanc veritatem, ternarius numerus est major binario & non continet bis duo -- mutare vel non-ponere fuisset Deo indifferens, Ergo in Mysterio Trinitatis, quae ipse Deus est, alia veritas esse potuisset: aut vero numerorum veritates absolute sunt necessariae, & immutabiles simpliciter. Respondeo, de veritatibus quae non sunt ipsissimus Deus esse hic quaestionem, non de iis quae Deus ipse sunt: Praeterea, numeros qui in Deo sunt, non esse univocos cum illis qui in creatis concipiuntur, non ejusdem realitatis, non veritatis cum illis univocæ: adeoque non licere ex unorum veritate & proprietate de aliis judicare. Umbra sunt hi ultimi, eaque non habens immediatam relationem ad priores, sed ex arbitrio Dei aliter disponere potentis.
units.tr: XIV. Fourthly, it could be objected: if this truth, that the number three is greater than two and does not contain twice two, were indifferent to God, to change it or not to posit it, then in the mystery of the Trinity, which is God himself, another truth could have been possible; or else truths about numbers are absolutely necessary and simply immutable. I reply: the question here concerns truths which are not God himself, not those which God himself is. Moreover, the numbers which are in God are not univocal with those conceived in created things, nor of the same reality, nor univocal in truth with them; and so it is not permitted to judge of others from the truth and property of the one. The latter are a shadow, and not having an immediate relation to the former, but able to be arranged otherwise by the arbitrary will of God.

units.la: XV. Denique difficultas oriri posset, ex eo quod Deus justus & verax prædicetur, quo significatur, Deum salva sua justitia & veritate non posse aliter disponere, judicare, statuere, quam facit & facturus est, saltem de plurimis. At, Justitia Dei dicit quidem quæ statuit ea modo ipsum decenti statuta esse; Veracitas vero, Eum illa quæ statuit certo modo se habitura & duratura, non esse mutaturum: Sed non inferunt eum non fuisse prius causam horum liberrimam, neque fuisse indifferentem vel ad nulla statuenda, vel ad alia stabilienda quæ æque eum decuissent, quæque si illi placuisset, vel certo, vel nullo tempore fuissent limitata. XVI. Aliæ sunt difficultates quæ vel ex consideratione rerum, vel ex præjudiciis circa ipsas veritates procedunt, vel ex axiomatibus ambiguis & in sequiorem partem vulgo intellectis. Ultimæ hujus classis hoc effatum in exemplum esto: Rerum natura, sive essentia, sive forma, sunt immutabiles & æterna, ab ipso etiam Cartesio propositum in quinta Meditatione & defensum in responsionibus quintis: quod tamen videtur hactenus assertis opponi. Respondeo, axioma verum esse si de immutabilitate loquatur quam Deus statuerit, dum nempe ei placuit quaedam non esse mutanda: item sensu vulgari æterna dici posse quorum positionem nullum antecessit tempus, vel potius quæ Deus æternus concipit sine successione, quæque nunquam desinent esse: sed hæc non destruere ea quæ prius dicta sunt. Nam quamvis Deus ab æterno quid conceperit, statueritque id mutandum non fore, non sequitur tamen eum id necessario concepisse & statuisse, neque diversum potuisse. Me v. g. ab æterno, qualis sum, concipit, Mentem immortalem statuit: quis ideo dicat eum non aliter potuisse? Nil igitur se ipso valet simile ratiocinium, adeoque nec rerum non modo existentiæ, sed & essentiæ, est applicandum. Quod si de immutabilitate independenti absolutaque, & de æternitate proprie sic dicta axioma intellectum velint, falsum est omnino. Sola Dei natura proprie æterna est exclusive ad omnia, ut plenius demonstrabitur, ubi suus accesserit locus, apposita hujus difficultatis luculentiori discussione: Sola etiam Divina essentia est immutabilis absolute, nec est de ratione veritatis ab ipsa diversæ ut sit immutabilis. Cogito de Mente, scribo, lego, veritates sunt (etsi de existentia rerum) quas Deus voluit mutabiles & cessaturas, sunt tamen veritates. tates. Atqui si res cæteræ, earumque veritates & Essentiæ absolute spectentur, id est, sine respectu ad positionem determinationis placiti Divini, rerumque inter se connexionem, (quæ ejus effectus est) non majori nexu Deus cum quibusvis de quibuscunque rebus, formisque præter ipsum adhæret, quam cum hac veritate, Ego de Mente cogi-to, vel lego. nam ad omne quod ipsius natura non est, is ex natura sua est indifferens.
units.tr: XV. Finally, a difficulty could arise from the fact that God is called just and truthful, which signifies that God, while his justice and truth remain intact, cannot dispose, judge, or decree otherwise than he does and will do, at least in most matters. But the justice of God says only that what he has decreed has been decreed in a manner fitting for him; and his truthfulness says only that he will not change what he has decreed, which will be and endure in a certain way. Yet they do not infer that he was not previously the most free cause of these things, nor that he was indifferent either to decreeing nothing, or to establishing other things which would have been equally fitting for him, and which, had it pleased him, would have been limited either with certainty or at no time. XVI. There are other difficulties which proceed either from the consideration of things, or from prejudices about the truths themselves, or from ambiguous axioms understood in the commonly accepted worse sense. Let this saying serve as an example of the last class: The nature, or essence, or form of things is immutable and eternal, which Descartes himself put forward in his Fifth Meditation and defended in his Fifth Replies, yet which seems to be opposed to what has been asserted so far. I answer that the axiom is true if it speaks of the immutability that God has decreed, namely, since it has pleased him that certain things should not be changed; likewise, in the common sense, things can be called eternal whose existence no time preceded, or rather, which the eternal God conceives without succession, and which will never cease to be. But these do not destroy what was said before. For although God, from eternity, conceived something and decreed that it would not be changed, it does not follow that he necessarily conceived and decreed it, nor that he could not have done otherwise. For example, from eternity he conceives me as I am and decrees that I have an immortal mind: who would therefore say that he could not have done otherwise? Therefore such reasoning has no force at all, and so it must not be applied to the existence of things, nor indeed to their essence. But if they wish the axiom to be understood of an independent and absolute immutability, and of eternity properly so called, it is wholly false. Only the nature of God is properly eternal, exclusively with respect to all things, as will be demonstrated more fully when its own place arrives, with a clearer discussion of this difficulty set out. Also, only the divine essence is absolutely immutable, and it is not part of the nature of truth, distinct from that essence, that it be immutable. I think about the mind, I write, I read; these are truths (even if concerning the existence of things) which God willed to be mutable and to cease; they are nonetheless truths. But if other things, and their truths and essences, are viewed absolutely, that is, without respect to the positing of the determination of the divine pleasure, and to the connection of things among themselves (which is his effect), God is attached to any things whatever, and to forms apart from himself, by no greater bond than to this truth: I think or read about the mind. For with regard to everything that is not his own nature, he is by his nature indifferent.

units.la: XVII. Adeoque ex præjudicio est quod in adversum instar legis adferatur, veritates multas fluere ex Dei natura; repræsentare ita Dei naturam, ut non possint mutari vel negari quin eo ipso negetur vel mutari concipiatur Dei natura, earum imaginum originale & exemplar. Ex Dei natura nil præter ipsum Deum, Filium nempe & Spiritum Sanctum, fluit. Placitum, idque antecedenter indifferens, non vero natura, est origo & vita cæterorum omnium. Quæ repræsentant Deum, repræsentant mediante placiti libera determinatione. Nulla materia ex se apta est, nil ex se capax est repræsentandi Deum: nam extra Dei na-turam necessariam, universalissimum nihil est. Deus mullam habet ima-ginem umbratilem (non loquor de solida, quæ ipse Deus est) umbra-tilem inquam imaginem non habet ex necessitate naturæ suæ, sed ea imago, ejus natura & essentia, est ex abundanti & gratuita indifferen-tissimi liberrimique placiti sui liberalitate & bonitate. Eam si noluisset statuere Deus, sequeretur tantum, solam suam naturam sibi voluisse placere, non autem se ipsum sibi displicere: quia contra, si imaginem ex necessitate statuisset, ostendisset se aliqua re à se diversa carere non posse, se aliqua re opus habere, sequeque adeo non plane sibi acquiescere, neque se, ut solus est, sibi omnino placere. Si quæ creatura negaret jam illas, quæ Dei sunt, imagines, non quidem directe & immediate negaret Dei naturam, negaret tamen Deum quatenus ipsi placuit sic se re-præsentare: nam etsi Deus non habeat nexum cum alterius rei veritate, natura, &c. habet tamen nexum cum se ipso & cum placito suo, quatenus ipsi placuit se determinare, & velle aliquid tale, verum, bonum, essentiale, esse & fore. Id jam concipi nequit aliter esse nunc posse vel debere: non quidem ob rem ipsam, sed quia non potest concipi, Deum aliter velle quam vult, voluisse quam voluit: non potest concipi Deum placiti sui consensui non consentire, ab eo dissolvi, res aliter effectu-rum & positurum quam statuere voluit, & si libere voluit, & potuit non velle. ex hypothesi autem quod voluerit, quia à se ipso statuente non separatur, contrarium concipi non potest. Sed extra hanc hypothesin, coram ejus Essentia Summa omnis omnium essentia, forma, natura, veritas, bonitas, &c. universaliter & absolute in merum Nihil evanescunt. Et huc forte respexerunt Theologi nonnulli ex veteribus, dum dicerent, Dei essentiam esse supra omnem essentiam, ejus Bonitatem esse super-essentialiter Bonam, Eum super-essentialiter verum, unum, &c. vel plusquam unum esse, plusquam verum, & similia.
units.tr: XVII. Therefore it is a prejudice when, as a law against the opposing view, it is brought forward that many truths flow from the nature of God; that is, to represent the nature of God in such a way that they cannot be changed or denied without thereby denying or conceiving the nature of God, the original and exemplar of those images, to be changed. Nothing flows from the nature of God except God himself, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit. The divine pleasure, which is antecedently indifferent and not nature, is the origin and life of all else. Those things which represent God, represent him through the free determination of the pleasure. No matter is by itself fit, nothing by itself is capable of representing God: for outside the necessary nature of God there is the most universal nothing. God does not have any shadowy image (I am not speaking of the solid image, which is God himself); he does not have a shadowy image, I say, from the necessity of his nature, but that image, its nature and essence, is from the abundant and gratuitous liberality and goodness of his most indifferent and freest pleasure. If God had not willed to establish it, it would follow only that he willed his nature alone to please him, but not that he displeased himself: because on the contrary, if he had established the image from necessity, he would have shown that he cannot be without something different from himself, that he has need of something, and it would follow that he does not fully rest in himself, nor, as he is alone, wholly please himself. If any creature were now to deny those images which belong to God, it would not indeed directly and immediately deny the nature of God, but it would deny God insofar as it pleased him to represent himself thus: for although God has no bond with the truth, nature, etc. of another thing, he does have a bond with himself and with his pleasure, insofar as it has pleased him to determine himself, and to will that something be such, true, good, essential, and to be and to remain so. This cannot now be conceived to be otherwise, nor to be able or ought to be otherwise: not indeed on account of the thing itself, but because it cannot be conceived that God wills otherwise than he wills, or has willed otherwise than he willed; it cannot be conceived that God does not consent to the consent of his pleasure, that he is dissolved from it, that he will effect and posit things otherwise than he decided to, if he willed freely, and was able not to will. But on the hypothesis that he has willed, since he is not separated from himself as the one decreeing, the contrary cannot be conceived. But outside this hypothesis, in the presence of his supreme Essence, all essence, form, nature, truth, goodness, etc. of all things vanish universally and absolutely into mere Nothing. And perhaps some of the older theologians had this in view when they said that the essence of God is above every essence, that his Goodness is supra-essentially good, that he is supra-essentially true, one, etc., or more than one, more than true, and similar things.

units.la: XVIII. Quia vero ex consideratione rerum singularum infinita possent objici ut ad absurdum ducentia quæ invicta viderentur, v. g. si quæreretur, An Deus ex Dominio illo Summo, summaque indifferentia ponere posset circulum quadratum, triangulum rotundum, creaturam à Creatore independentem? An odium Dei posset bonum fieri, ejusque amor quoad naturam suam mutari, & malus devenire? An mens sine Cogitatione esse posset? aliaque quæ singulatim recenseri & refelli non possent; commodum erit, nonnullas hic observationes conji-cere, ex quibus minus attenti sese difficultatibus quibusvis liberare valeant, nam cæteroquin attendentibus constare potest, omnium objectionum crypticas refutationes in præcedentibus latere.
units.tr: XVIII. But because from the consideration of individual things infinite objections could be raised which lead to absurdities and would seem invincible, for example, if it were asked, whether God, from that supreme Dominion and supreme indifference, could posit a square circle, a round triangle, a creature independent of the Creator? Could the hatred of God become good, and his love be changed as to its nature and become evil? Could a mind exist without thought? And other things which could not be enumerated and refuted one by one: it will be useful here to set down some observations, by which less attentive readers may be able to free themselves from any difficulties; for otherwise, to attentive readers it can be clear that the cryptic refutations of all objections lie hidden in what has gone before.

units.la: XIX. Observetur primo, sub prætextu hujus Dominii absolutissimi in omnia, multa objici posse, quæ, etsi videantur doctrinam hanc impugnare, eam tamen plane non concernunt. Ex. gr. cum Dei placitum, quod prius indifferens, tandem determinatum est, absurdum est quærere, an cum est determinatum possit esse non-determinatum in sensu composito? vel, an determinatum qua tale, sit etiamnum indifferens? Ejusmodi absurdum, quod sic impugnari creditur, nemo, quod sciam, protulit. Atqui id præsupponunt qui petunt, an Deus ex absoluto Dominio possit facere, ut quod factum vel statutum est, non fuerit factum; & ut quod per aliquod tempus verum fuit, de eo verum sit postea, id nunquam plane verum fuisse? Hoc est ipsum Deum concipere ut à se determinatum & non-determinatum, statuentem & non statuentem, volentem & non volentem, sustentantem & non sustentantem simul, probantem & non probantem, ponentem & non ponentem eandem operationem. Idem esset acsi quæreretur, An possimus concipiendo Deum esse actu positorem rei alicujus, eo ipso concipere eum esse non-positorem hujusdem rei, sive, an Deus sit non statuens dum statuit? Absurda hæc sunt, quibus objiciendis ne minimam quidem occasionem dederunt quæ supra sunt dicta. (ut neque quæ infra de potentia, ad quam possis omnes referre difficultates quatenus existentiam spestant, deducentur.) Nemo Dei Dominium Potentiamque concepit un-quam, tanquam si extenderetur ad quid agendum & non agendum si-mul. Atqui hoc statuere oportuisset ut hisce objectionibus occasio suis-set data. etenim ad hoc ut verum sit id quod fuit non fuisse non obstan-te quod fuerit, vel ut creatura sit à Creatore independens, concipien-dus est Deus tanquam si simul statuisset & non statuisset, utque simul creans, sustentans, & non creans, non sustentans. Equidem Domi-nium Dei absolutum bene & vere concipitur sub notione indifferentiae ad infinita captum meum superantia statuenda diversimode pro placito; at non sub notione agendi & non agendi simul. adeoque nullos feriunt objectiones similes praeter eos qui absurda haec proposuisset. Libet vero prae caeteris mirari, quam apposite per modum objectionis quae-ratur, an veritas haec, Creatura pendet à Creatore, posset à Deo mutari? Docent alii, creaturas, respectu scilicet essentiae, ideae, veritatumque ibi contentarum, à Dei voluntate non dependere: quae autem hactenus dicta sunt, eo redeunt, ut ostendant non modo existentias, sed & es-sentias, & veritates creaturarum, nulla excepta, à sola Dei voluntate ab-solutissime pendere, ut sine ejus placito nil plane sint. Jam obmurmu-ratur, utrum inde non sequi posset creaturas ab illo non pendere? Recte & convenienter admodum! Sic suos subtiliter & circumspecte ducit con-tradicendi studium.
units.tr: XIX. Let it be observed first that under the pretext of this absolute Dominion over all things, many objections can be raised which, although they seem to attack this doctrine, do not in fact touch it at all. For example, since God's pleasure, which was previously indifferent, has at last been determined, it is absurd to ask whether, once it has been determined, it can be non-determined in a composite sense? Or whether the determined, as such, is still indifferent? As far as I know, no one has put forward this absurdity as if it were thereby being attacked.
