Yet those who ask whether God, from absolute Dominion, could bring it about that what has been done or decreed had not been done, and that what for some time was true should afterwards be true of it, and that it had never been plainly true, presuppose exactly this? This is to conceive God as at once determined and non-determined, decreeing and not decreeing, willing and not willing, sustaining and not sustaining, approving and not approving, positing and not positing the same operation. It would be the same as if one asked whether, by conceiving God to be actually the positor of some thing, we thereby conceive him to be the non-positor of the same thing; or whether God is not decreeing while he decrees. These are absurdities, and what has been said above gave no occasion whatever for objecting to them (just as what is deduced below about power will not either, to which you may refer all difficulties insofar as they concern existence). No one has ever conceived the Dominion and Power of God as if it extended to doing and not doing the same thing at once. But this would have had to be asserted for such objections to have been given occasion. For in order that what was done may be true as not having been done, notwithstanding that it was done, or that a creature may be independent of its Creator, God must be conceived as if he had at once decreed and not decreed, and as at once creating, sustaining, and not creating, not sustaining. Indeed the absolute Dominion of God is rightly and truly conceived under the notion of an indifference to positing infinite things, which exceed my understanding, in diverse ways according to his pleasure; but not under the notion of doing and not doing at once. Therefore such objections strike only those who would have put forward these absurdities. But it is particularly worth wondering at how aptly it is asked, by way of objection, whether this truth, that a creature depends on its Creator, could be changed by God! Others teach that creatures, namely with respect to essence, idea, and the truths contained therein, do not depend on the will of God; but what has been said so far comes to this, that it shows not only the existences but also the essences and truths of creatures, none excepted, to depend most absolutely on the sole will of God, so that without his pleasure they are nothing at all. Now someone mutters: is it not then to be inferred that creatures do not depend on him? Rightly and most fittingly! Thus the zeal for contradicting leads its followers subtly and cautiously astray.

units.la: XX. Secundo, observandum est, omnes rerum sive idearum proprie-tates à rebus & ideis ipsis non esse diversa quaedam, sed res ideasque ipsissimas, quatenus non subsistitur eorum conceptui generali, sed particularius & penitius inspiciuntur. Unde absurdum esset per modum objectionis in praecedentia, quaerere, Utrum manente rei essentia, ejus proprietas mutari posset vel potuisset ex absoluto illo Dei Dominio? Exempli causa, utrum dari potuisset circulus quadratus, hoc est, figura cujus lineae à centro ad circumferentiam essent aequales, nec tamen (quod eodem recidit) radii vel diametri omnes essent aequales? Hoc recidit in absurditatem praecedenti observatione rejectam, cum idem sit, acsi quaereretur, an res sic posita dum ita ponitur sit non ita posita uti est? sive, an Deus sit simul quid ponens & non-ponens? quod cum ratione nobis objici nequit. Huc redit quaestio, an possint res à Deo statui quae ipsum non repraesentent ullo modo, quaeque ei repugnent? Est ipsa rerum essentia reconditissima & intima, quod scilicet sint effectus sive sequelae placiti Dei, adeoque ipsum praese ferant, ostendant, ejusque sint repraesentationes. Hoc est ipsum τὸ[?] esse rerum, ut cuivis ferio philosophanti patet. Sic igitur quæstio esset, an res possint esse non-res in sensu composito? sive, an Deus sit simul ponens & non-ponens? quæ inepte adferuntur.
units.tr: XX. Second, it should be noted that all the properties of things or of ideas are not something diverse from the things and ideas themselves, but are the very things and ideas themselves, insofar as we do not rest in their general concept but look at them more particularly and more deeply. Hence it would be absurd, by way of objection to what has gone before, to ask: whether, with the essence of a thing remaining, its property could be changed, or could have been changed, by that absolute dominion of God? For example, could a square circle have been given, that is, a figure whose lines from the centre to the circumference were equal, and yet (which comes to the same thing) not all its radii or diameters were equal? This comes down to the absurdity rejected in the preceding observation, since it is the same as if one asked whether a thing so posited, while it is being so posited, is not posited as it is; or whether God is at once positing and not positing. This cannot be objected to us with reason. The question comes down to this: whether things can be set up by God which in no way represent him and which are repugnant to him? The very essence of things is most hidden and intimate: namely, that they are effects or consequences of the purpose of God, and so they display him, show him forth, and are representations of him. This is the very being of things [τὸ εἶναι], as is plain to any thoughtful philosopher. Thus the question would be whether things could be non-things in a composite sense; or whether God is at once positing and not positing. These are brought forward foolishly.

units.la: XXI. Atque adeo notandum est tertio, (quod præcedentis observationis sequela est) ad doctrinam hancce rectè percipiendam, utendum esse abstractione universali ab omni re, idea, essentia, natura, forma, veritate, &c. quæ Deus ipse non sunt. Nam si quis ideam aliquam, præsertim generalem, retinens, quærere velit, an hac manente cæteræ particulares (illam proculdubio involventes) mutari possint? quicquam objiciendi erit incapax. Rediret enim prima absurditas objicientium, quasi dictum fuisset rem esse non rem in sensu composito. Igitur abstra-hendum est ita, ut cogitetur, Deum omnino veritates essentiasque alias quàm quas jam habemus, statuere ex indifferentia potuisse, quo suppo-sito, quæ jam sunt veritates omnino nihil essent, nec magis possent concipi quam quæ non statuit Dominus. Itaque corruunt quæ de numeris, figuris, &c. objiciuntur: nam qui in his difficultatem quærunt, præsupponunt ideam extensionis & numeri, & interim volunt illam, quam restantem considerant, exclusam à particularibus suis subjectis. Non itaque dicendum est, Deum statuere potuisse ut 2 & 3 non essent 5, vel numerus, impar, & similia: neque assentior Cartesio {a} dicen-ti, fieri potuisse ut contradictoria falsa non essent, nec trianguli tres anguli duobus rectis æquales: solutiones quoque similium difficulta-tum quas ibi proponit non puto esse omnes admittendas. perinde quasi numerorum vel linearum ideæ seorsim restarent, eorum vero combinationes aliter se habere possent: etenim ipsorum combinationes sunt ipsorum natura & ideæ simul conceptæ. Idem ergo esset acsi assereretur, figurarum numerorumque naturam manere, simulque non manere, quod in Dei placitum si resolvatur, ponit Deum statuentem & non-statuentem simul. Simplices linearum numerorumque ideæ etiam cum cæteris evanescunt coram Dei absoluto Dominio. Nec dici potest ex dictis sequi, extensionis idea remanente figurarum veritates posse mutari, cum de essentia materiæ non sint. non sunt quidem de ejus essentia si hæc generalius & indeterminata spectetur: sunt tamen de essentia materiæ ita determinatæ à suo Authore, qui non ideo hoc respectu summus Dominus dicitur quasi materiam hoc modo disponens, esset hoc ipso eam alio modo disponens; quod extravagatur. Ita etiam quæ de Dei amore vel odio sunt objecta, repulsanda sunt: talia enim objici non possunt quin præsupponatur natura, idea seu essentia Mentis, id est, placitum Dei de se ipso repraesentando per cogitationem umbratilem de cujus natura est ut ad Deum tendat, quemadmodum in lib. II. demon-stratum est. Ergo absurdum est si quis praesupponat hoc fieri & restare, & tamen simul velit concipere hoc non fieri, aut contrarium, sensu compo-sito, recte statui. Amor praesupponit Mentis naturam, haec voluntatem sive placitum Dei sese hoc modo adumbrandi, qua positione con-cepta & etiam subsistente absurdum est uti ad diruendam aliam, quae nisi per abstractionem ab hac ipsa non concipitur,quamque suppeditat confi-deratio Divinae Essentiae solius necessariae & independentis, ejusque erga caetera indifferentiae, qua per alia nescio quae, quam per naturas rerum o-mnium quales jam sunt, potuisset se ipsum repraesentare si voluisset Deus.
units.tr: XXI. And so a third point must be noted, which follows from the preceding observation: to grasp this doctrine rightly, we must use a universal abstraction from every thing, idea, essence, nature, form, truth, etc., which are not God himself. For if someone, retaining some idea, especially a general one, wishes to ask whether, with this remaining, the other particular ideas (undoubtedly involving it) could be changed, he will be incapable of raising any objection. For the first absurdity of the objectors would return, as if it had been said that a thing is a non-thing in a composite sense. We must therefore abstract in such a way that we think God could have established, out of indifference, truths and essences other than those we already have; given this supposition, the truths that now exist would be nothing at all, and could no more be conceived than those the Lord did not establish. Thus the objections raised about numbers, figures, etc. collapse: for those who seek difficulty in these presuppose the idea of extension and number, and at the same time want that idea, which they consider remaining, to be excluded from its particular subjects. So it should not be said that God could have established that 2 and 3 were not 5, or that a number is not odd, and similar things; nor do I agree with Descartes {a} when he says that it could have come about that contradictories were not false, nor that the three angles of a triangle were not equal to two right angles: I do not think that all the solutions of similar difficulties which he proposes there are to be admitted either. This would be as if the ideas of numbers or lines remained separately, while their combinations could be otherwise: for their combinations are indeed their nature and their ideas conceived together. It would therefore be the same as if it were asserted that the nature of figures and numbers both remains and does not remain at once; which, if it is resolved into the purpose of God, posits God as establishing and not establishing at the same time. The simple ideas of lines and numbers also vanish, along with the rest, before the absolute dominion of God. Nor can it be said that it follows from what has been said that the truths of figures could be changed while the idea of extension remains, since they are not of the essence of matter. They are indeed not of its essence if this is viewed in a more general and indeterminate way; yet they are of the essence of matter as determined by its Author, who is not for this reason called the supreme Lord in this respect, as though by disposing matter in this way he would by that very fact be disposing it in another way; which is absurd. So too the objections about God's love or hatred must be rejected: for such things cannot be objected to without presupposing the nature, idea or essence of Mind, that is, the purpose of God to represent himself through a shadowy thought whose nature is to tend towards God, as was demonstrated in book II. Therefore it is absurd if someone presupposes that this happens and remains, and yet at the same time wishes to conceive that it does not happen, or the contrary, in a composite sense, to be rightly established. Love presupposes the nature of Mind, and Mind presupposes the will or purpose of God to shadow himself in this way; when this position has been conceived and even remains in place, it is absurd to use it to overthrow another, which is not conceived except by abstraction from this very thing, and which is supplied by the consideration of the Divine Essence alone, necessary and independent, and of its indifference towards other things, by which God could have represented himself, if he had willed, through some other things I know not what, than through the natures of all things as they now are.

units.la: XXII. Inculcabo clarius, vel ad fastidium, ne nullus capiat. Inter illa quae de rebus praeter Deum concipimus, sunt, Primo, Ideae primi-tivae, v. g. nostrae Cogitationis, extensionis sive spatii, figurarum sim-pliciorum, numerorum & aliorum in theoreticis; in practicis vero, ideae boni, amoris, & similes. Secundo, principia prima seu axiomata, tum theoretica, qualia sunt ex. gr. geometrica axiomata; tum practica, qualia sunt, verbi causa, principia moralia sive syntheresios, ut vocantur: quae omnia dicuntur indemonstrabilia, quia per clariora demon-strari nequeunt; & innata, non modo quia cum natura Cogitationis no-strae certo modo nectuntur, sed etiam quia mentem sic disposuit Deus, ut si haec de illis cogitet, statim ea nullo intercedente ratiocinio, videat esse vera. Sunt, tertio, ideae ex illis compositae, & conclusiones speciali-ores, tum in theoreticis, quales sunt, v. g., geometricae propositio-nes; tum in practicis, ut conclusiones morales: quarum omnium ve-ritas non patet per se primo aspectu, quaeque ideo falsae vel obscurae a mente obscura possent haberi, non autem a mente attendente & ratio-cinante. Jam, quae hic de dependentia & mutabilitate veritatum omnium a Deo dixi, non ita capi debent, acsi solummodo de veritatibus tertiae hujus classis dicta essent, dum quae sunt primae & secundae supponerentur remanere: nam cum ultimae hae sint ipsae primae & secundae penitius consideratae, poneretur contradictio in ipsa una Dei determinatione, sive in Deo statuente & non statuente simul idem. Sed quae sunt dicta extendenda sunt ad omnes sine ulla exceptione etiam simpliciores primae & secundae classis ideas & veritates, a quibus est abstra-hendum, sive quas transcendere oportet, ut Divinae Authoritatis in omnia conceptus habeatur.
units.tr: XXII. I will repeat this more clearly, even to the point of tedium, lest anyone fail to grasp it. Among the things we conceive apart from God are, first, the primitive ideas, for example, of our thought, of extension or space, of the simpler figures, of numbers, and of others in theoretical matters; and in practical matters, the ideas of good, of love, and similar things. Second, the first principles or axioms, both theoretical, such as the geometrical axioms for example, and practical, such as, to give an instance, the moral principles or synderesis, as they are called. All of these are said to be indemonstrable, because they cannot be proved through things clearer than themselves; and innate, not only because they are bound up with the nature of our thought in a certain way, but also because God has so disposed the mind that, if it thinks of these things, it immediately sees them to be true without any intervening reasoning. Third, there are ideas composed of those, and more specific conclusions, both in theoretical matters, such as geometrical propositions, for example, and in practical matters, such as moral conclusions. The truth of all of these is not evident of itself at first glance, and so they might be held false or obscure by an unattentive mind, but not by a mind that attends and reasons. Now, what I have said here about the dependence and mutability of all truths on God should not be taken as though it had been said only of the truths of this third class, while those of the first and second were supposed to remain; for since these last are the first and second themselves considered more deeply, a contradiction would be posited in the one determination of God, that is, in God establishing and not establishing the same thing at once. Rather, what has been said must be extended to all, without any exception, including the simpler ideas and truths of the first and second class, from which we must abstract, or which we must go beyond, so that the concept of the Divine Authority over all things may be held.

units.la: XXIII. Quomodo autem aliae veritates esse potuissent, aut quaenam illæ, fateor me non concipere: nam jam essent si conciperentur. Ut ne dicam mentem meam à Deo esse determinatam ad eas quas is sta-tuere, & à me ex parte concipi voluit. Nec video quid hac in re possit ultra requiri ab illis qui Deum ut Summum omnium Arbitrum à quo omnia dependent, intuebuntur.
units.tr: XXIII. How other truths could have been, or what they would be, I confess I do not conceive: for they would already exist if they were conceived. Not to mention that my mind has been determined by God to those which he willed to establish and to be conceived by me in part. Nor do I see what more can be required in this matter from those who look upon God as the supreme Arbiter of all, on whom all things depend.

units.la: XXIV. Quid de hac doctrina judicaturi sint cæteri, nescio. Ego certe, si eam mente revolvo, non ut ex curiositate in Dei conceptus & Cogitationes inquiram, sed ex animo celebrandi summum ejus Dominium, & admirandi immensam super omnibus elevationem, omniumque coram eo tenuitatem, fateor mihi videri me inde habere unde impellar ad intimam & ineffabilem magnificentissimæ ejus Majestatis ve-nerationem, liberalitatis laudem, confidentiam in eis quæ sanxit & pro-misit, omniumque præ illo despectum. Majestatem inconfusam, ex naturæ suæ incomparabili excellentia ab omni re distinctissimam, separatissimam, verè lucem inaccessam, seu Veritatem talem, qualis præter ipsam nulla alia est, pro infirmitate mea secundum ejus placitum utcun-que intueor. Laudo Bonitatis liberalitatem, quæ eo est commendabi-lior, quo nullis prorsus rebus adstringitur, nullisque debet vel id quod in idea ipsæ sunt. In veritatem effatorum recumbo, quæ si cum is in-differens esset rata voluit esse, cur jam ea amplexus ille, eadem mutatu-rus à me concipertur? Denique deprehendo omnia in reconditissimis suis fundis & essentiis, Bonitate & Veritate, coram ejus Divina Essentia non pulverem modo esse, sed & absolutum & purum nihil. Si quæ præter Deum invenio in abundantia placiti mentis liberrimæ omnia inve-nio, extra nihil.
units.tr: XXIV. What others will judge of this doctrine, I do not know. I for my part, when I turn it over in my mind, not from curiosity to inquire into the conceptions and thoughts of God, but from a desire to celebrate his supreme dominion and to admire his immense elevation above all things and the lowliness of all things before him, confess that I seem to have from it that by which I am moved to an inward and ineffable veneration of his most magnificent Majesty, to praise of his liberality, to confidence in those things which he has decreed and promised, and to contempt of all things in comparison with him. I behold, as far as my weakness allows and according to his purpose, a Majesty unconfused, most distinct from every thing by the incomparable excellence of his nature, most separate, truly a light unapproachable, or a Truth such that no other is like it apart from itself. I praise the liberality of his Goodness, which is the more commendable in that it is bound by no things at all, and owes nothing to anything, not even to what exists in the idea itself. I rest in the truth of his declarations, which, if he, being indifferent, willed them to be valid, why should I conceive that he would change them, now that he has embraced them? Finally, I perceive that all things, in their most hidden foundations and essences, are before his Divine Essence, in Goodness and Truth, not merely dust but an absolute and pure nothing. If I find anything besides God, I find it all in the abundance of the purpose of his most free Mind; outside it, nothing.

units.la: Non est ergo quod extra Divinum placitum quiesce-re vel quæram vel optem. Omnium optima analysis & resolutio esto non natura rei, ad quam non bene tanquam ultimo multi provocant, sed, sine quo nulla est natura,Dei placitum,quod (nemo tamen hoc abu-tatur ad figmenta sua commendanda) non modo in mysteriis sacris, sed & in rebus naturalibus, etsi Philosophastri id solide non capiant, imo & in illis quæ falso transcendentales dictæ sunt veritates, ultima meta esto. Hoc enim axioma, quod primum vocant, Quodlibet est, aut non est, vel Impossibile est idem esse & non esse, in hoc resolvitur & fundatur; Deus ex placito hoc volens, & statuens, non est id ipsum non-volens, non-sta-tuens, non est negans suum placitum, non discrepans à se ipso volente. Adeo ut nil sit sui fundamentum & ratio, præter unum Deum, qui ex placito in omnibus unus ita viget ut ejus placitum sit vis omnium. Non libet plura dicere, sed de his meminerimus in posterum.
units.tr: There is therefore no reason for me to seek or wish to rest in anything outside the divine pleasure. The best analysis and resolution of all things is not, as many wrongly appeal to it as the final ground, the nature of a thing; rather, without which there is no nature, the pleasure of God. (No one, however, should abuse this to commend his own fictions.) This pleasure is the ultimate goal not only in sacred mysteries but also in natural things, although the petty philosophers do not grasp this soundly; indeed, it is so even in those things which are falsely called transcendental truths. For this axiom, which they call first, namely Whatever is, either is or is not, or It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be, is resolved into and grounded in this: God, by this pleasure, willing and decreeing, is not the same as not-willing and not-decreeing; he does not deny his own pleasure, nor does he dissent from himself willing. So that there is no foundation and reason of itself apart from the one God, who by his pleasure is one in all things and so holds sway that his pleasure is the power of all. I do not wish to say more, but let us remember these things hereafter.

units.la: CAPUT VII. (10) BONITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. (10) GOODNESS.

units.la: 1. Mens ex se sterilis cæteris nil veritatis realitatisque communicat.
units.tr: 1. The mind, barren in itself, communicates nothing of truth or reality to other things.

units.la: I. Cum itaque omnis veritatis realitatisque Idea pendeat à Deo, non est quod prætendam aliquid ex me fingere quod vim ullam in se habeat: & cum ut nihil mei, sic nihil alieni à me sit; natura ergo mea, placitumque res est erga alias ex se ipsa omnino sterilis. Et quanquam in fundo Mentis meæ veritatem investigem, & interdum inveniam, non est tamen quod putem eam de mea fabrica esse, aut à me constitutam: sed potius eam thesauri instar occulti, cujus detectio demum patefiat, non autem realitas à me fiat, latuisse. Nam & omnes quotquot sunt Mentes cæteræ veritates easdem, eodem modo, ubi debite in fundo suo quærunt, reperiunt, quod non accideret; si eæ à cujusque placito essent effictæ, siquidem ex millenis figmentis quæ à diversis fiunt Mentibus ex mero arbitrio, vix duo quidem conveniant. Et quamvis forte si Mentium natura non fuisset, cæteræ de aliis præter Deum rebus veritates non fuissent forte determinatæ, hoc nil aliud infert quam eas simul cum Mentibus, non autem per illas, fuisse statutas.
units.tr: I. Since, therefore, the whole idea of truth and reality depends on God, there is no reason for me to pretend that I fashion anything of my own accord that has any power in itself. And since nothing is mine any more than nothing is foreign to me, my nature, and my disposition toward other things, is therefore wholly barren of itself. And although I search for truth in the depths of my mind, and sometimes find it, there is no reason to think that it is of my own making or established by me. Rather, it is like a hidden treasure, which lay concealed until at last it is uncovered; its reality is not made by me. For all the other minds that exist also find the same truths, in the same way, when they seek them rightly in the depths of their own being, which would not happen if these truths were fashioned by each one's will. For out of a thousand fictions that different minds make by mere arbitrary choice, scarcely two would agree. And although, perhaps, if minds did not exist, the other truths about things besides God would perhaps not have been determined, this implies nothing more than that these truths were established together with minds, not through them.

units.la: 2. 3. Bonitas Dei fons omnium. Traducitur male si aliquid ei subducatur.
units.tr: 2. 3. The goodness of God is the source of all things. It is wrongly traduced if anything is subtracted from it.

units.la: 4. Bonitas Essentialis Dei. 5. Quomodo si nil præter Deum esset, Deus bonus esset?
units.tr: 4. The essential goodness of God. 5. How would God be good if nothing existed besides God?

units.la: II. Quid autem impedit quominus fingat Deus qualia placet, quæ ejus placitum repræsentantia, ideo vera & bona sint? Ipsa Dei natura tales ideas, etsi ab idea essentiæ suæ diversas, non impedit, neque ab illis obscuratur, cum illæ non-necessariæ & dependentes concipiantur. Ab ipsis quoque rerum ideis & veritatibus, cum antecedenter nihil sint, non potest impediri quominus Deus hic ex placito agat. Quemadmodum autem ejus placitum ut indifferens spectatum dedit nobis occasionem Dominium ejus Summum agnoscendi, sic idem placitum considera-deraderatum ut liberrime, ex nulla necessitate, ex nullo etiam externo motivo determinatum, id ipsum est, quod Bonitatem divinam appellare oportet, utpote quod sit fons fertilissimus, abundantissimus, liberri-musque, omnium, quæ quocunque modo præter Deum sunt, ex quo suas quæque hauriunt ideas, naturas, essentias, veritates, & si existant, existentiam atque durationem. Per Bonitatem illam Deus non suam quidem naturam, sed sui adumbrationem secundum suum placitum, per ejus liberam determinationem, communicavit iis quæ vel minimam veritatis umbram possident. Et hæc possessio ipsa communicatio sive donatio est.
units.tr: II. But what prevents God from forming whatever ideas he pleases, such that, representing his will, they are true and good? The very nature of God does not hinder such ideas, even though they differ from the idea of his own essence, nor is it obscured by them, since they are conceived as non-necessary and dependent. Nor can God be prevented from acting here by his will, by the ideas of things and truths themselves, since these are nothing prior to it. Just as his will, viewed as indifferent, gave us occasion to acknowledge his supreme dominion, so the same will, considered as most freely determined, by no necessity, and by no external motive whatever, is precisely what we ought to call the divine goodness. For it is the most fertile, most abundant and most generous source of all things that exist in any way apart from God, from which each draws its ideas, natures, essences, truths, and, if they exist, existence and duration. Through that goodness God has communicated, not his own nature indeed, but a shadowing forth of himself, according to his will, by his free determination, to those things which possess even the faintest shadow of truth. And this possession is itself a communication or gift.

units.la: III. Hanc Divinam Bonitatem indecenter traduci patet, cum asseritur, Deum ex necessitate consensum sive placitum suum quibusdam rerum veritatibus dare, aut eum non aliter potuisse, aut ipsi opus fuisse ut approbationem nonnullis daret, aut quædam ab illo suam naturam non derivare. Durum est dicere aliquid in rebus esse quod ejus Libera-litati suam formam, naturam, veritatem, suum esse, suum ortum, non debeat. Sed hæc jam destructa sunt. Bonitas coacta, Bonitas non à se mota, Bonitas ex parte, Bonitas limitata, Bonitas sine qua aliqua ab ipsa diversa est bonitas, à Divina Bonitate aliena est. Quin potius omnis omnium bonitas, quam passivam vocare possis, ab Divina illa est, quam idcirco activam, (soli Deo propriam,) dixeris. Quare, omne reale, omnis veritas statuta, omnis essentia, substantia, cogitans, extensa, omnis modus, motusque, sive in idea, sive in existentia atque duratione, ideo sunt bona, ut revera sunt, quia placitum Dei est de illis ut sint. Itaque omnia quæ sunt, & dici, & concipi possunt, Bonita-tis Dei sunt præcones, ut non sit opus multa hic de illa ex professo congerere, cujus sedes est ubique.
units.tr: III. It is plain that this divine goodness is improperly traduced when it is asserted that God gives his consent or will to certain truths of things out of necessity, or that he could not have done otherwise, or that he needed to give approval to some things, or that some things do not derive their nature from him. It is hard to say that anything in things owes its form, nature, truth, being and origin to something other than his liberality. But these points have already been refuted. A goodness that is compelled, a goodness not moved by itself, a goodness in part, a limited goodness, a goodness without which some goodness is different from it, is alien to the divine goodness. Indeed, all the goodness of all things, which you could call passive, is from that divine goodness, which you may therefore call active (proper to God alone). Wherefore, every reality, every established truth, every essence, substance, thinking or extended thing, every mode and motion, whether in idea or in existence and duration, is therefore good as it truly is, because it is God's will that they should be. Thus all things that are, and can be spoken of and conceived, are heralds of the goodness of God, so that there is no need to heap up here, in a formal treatment, much about it, whose seat is everywhere.

units.la: IV. Cæterum, est in Deo essentialis Bonitas, quæ est sine respectu ad illa quæ non sunt Deus, cum ille nempe non ex indifferentia, sed ex amore sui se in se ipso sibi abundantissime & perfectissime communicat. At hic de ea Bonitate actum est quæ est relativa, & habet terminum in illis quæ non sunt Deus. Prior ad creaturas non accedit.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, there is in God an essential goodness, which is without reference to those things that are not God, since he communicates himself to himself most abundantly and most perfectly within himself, out of love of himself, not out of indifference. But here we have treated of that goodness which is relative, and has its term in those things that are not God. The former does not extend to creatures.

units.la: V. Inde constat quid sit regerendum huic quæstioni, Quomodo Deus esset bonus si nulla essent creata? addo, si nulla essent omnino statuta? Respondetur, Dei Bonitatem essentialem mansuram integram: sed etsi nihil tunc actu secundum ejus placitum communicaret, esset tamen talis, ut si placeret ei, velle aliquid dare, id esset ideo eventurum. Hæc jam nominanda prout cuique placet. Lingua scholarum dixeris, Deum Bonitate seu communicatione interna & essentiali semper quidem Bonum esse: at respectu eorum quæ is ipse non sunt, si ea nil essent, esset ille bonus, si non quoad actum, tamen quoad potentiam. Animadverti etiam potest ex his, quo sensu Solus esse Bonus dicatur.
units.tr: V. From this it is clear what answer should be given to the question, How would God be good if no creatures existed? I add: if nothing whatever were established. The answer is that God's essential goodness would remain entire; yet, even if at that time he communicated nothing in actuality according to his will, he would nevertheless be such that, if it pleased him to will to give anything, this would therefore come about. These matters may now be named as each one pleases. In the language of the schools you might say that God is always good in his internal and essential goodness or communication; but with respect to those things which are not himself, if these were nothing, he would be good, if not as to act, yet as to power. It may also be noticed from these points in what sense he alone is said to be good.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: (11) FELICITAS. §. A.
units.tr: (11) HAPPINESS. §. A.

units.la: 1. Felicitatis obstacula. Acquiescentia & Felicitas ut differant.
units.tr: 1. Obstacles to happiness. Contentment and happiness, how they differ.

units.la: I. Cum ex consideratione mei & eorum quæ in me observare queo occasionem de Deo loquendi debeam desumere, ad me igitur redire pergo. Memini me ideas rerum me majorum, mihi æqualium, me minorum, in me animadvertisse, in quarum naturas veritatesque mihi jus non fuerit ut de illis ad lubitum meum disponerem, ut illas aliter, aut etiam novas, conciperem & statuerem. Jam insuper experior, me ne quidem eo attingere perfectionis, ut res istas, ab alio quam à me statutas, modo naturæ suæ meæque conveniente, nempe aut cognitionis claritate, aut attentione fixa, aut affectu vel fruitione, aliove modo, in me possim ponere, illisque adeo frui ut vellem. Novi etenim & sentio, cogitationem meam non sic Deo impleri, eoque frui uti equidem id fieri posset. Idem pronuntio de rebus cæteris, sive illæ me, seu ego illas dignitate excedam, seu utrinque simus pares: non pendet enim à me ut ego eas in mea Mente ponam quomodo vel quando placeret, iisque fruar prout judicarem mihi maxime esse conveniens, etsi id vehementer optarem. Quamvis autem non essem ideo felix reputandus etiamsi hisce ultimis, à Deo diversis, fruerer ut vellem, est tamen indubium, illum qui eas optaret & voto excideret, non felicem fore dicendum. Igitur multo minus felicitatem adeptus est qui Deo non fruitur modo sibi conveniente & à Deo non improbato. Absentia optati quod naturæ optantis conveniens est, nec Deo displicet, ita constanter obstat Felicitati, ut hæc obtineri nequeat, quin impedimentum illud omnino removeatur. Perfectio quidem est in acquiescentia super Dei placito, quamvis id velit nos ita vacuos esse uti sumus: quo enim jure non acquiesceremus super placito illius qui nulli astringitur? Verum est quoque Mentis acquiescentiam in Felicitate inveniri, ita ut hæc sine illa ne quidem possit concipi: Attamen, talem felicitatis nostræ ideam impressit Deus, ut non concipiatur tanquam acquiescentia in quocunque statu, sed in complemento ultimo illius placiti. Quo in statu omne optabile quod jam cum felicitate abest, demum erit ratum.
units.tr: I. Since I must take the occasion of speaking about God from the consideration of myself and of what I can observe in myself, I therefore go on returning to myself. I recall that in myself I have noticed ideas of things greater than me, equal to me, and less than me, over whose natures and truths I have had no right to dispose at my pleasure, so as to conceive and establish them differently, or even newly. Moreover, I now find that I do not even reach so far in perfection that I can place these things, established by another and not by me, in myself in a manner suited to their nature and to mine, whether by clarity of knowledge, by fixed attention, by affection or enjoyment, or in some other way, and so enjoy them as I wish. For I know and feel that my thought is not thus filled by God, nor do I enjoy him in the way that I would wish this could happen. I say the same of other things, whether they surpass me or I surpass them, or we are equal on both sides: for it does not depend on me to place them in my mind when or how I please, and to enjoy them as I judge most fitting for me, although I earnestly desire this. Yet although I would not on that account be counted happy, even if I enjoyed these latter things, distinct from God, as I wished, it is nonetheless certain that one who wished for them and was disappointed in his wish cannot be called happy. Therefore much less has attained happiness one who does not enjoy God in a manner suited to himself and not disapproved by God. The absence of what is desired, when it is suited to the nature of the one desiring and does not displease God, so constantly stands in the way of happiness that it cannot be obtained unless that hindrance is wholly removed. Perfection indeed lies in acquiescence in God's good pleasure, even though he wills us to be as empty as we are: for by what right should we not acquiesce in the pleasure of one who is bound to no one? It is true also that acquiescence of the mind is found within happiness, so that happiness cannot even be conceived without it. Yet God has impressed on us such an idea of our happiness that it is conceived not as acquiescence in any state whatever, but in the final completion of that good pleasure. In that state, every desirable thing which is now absent together with happiness will at last be fulfilled.

units.la: 2. Felicitas Deo essentialis, cæteris incommunicabilis. felicitas Mentis creatæ. via ad illam. 3. Felicitati Dei nil potest addi, ei Mentis creatæ aliquid.
units.tr: 2. Happiness is essential to God and incommunicable to others. The happiness of the created mind. The way to it. 3. Nothing can be added to God's happiness, but something can be added to the created mind's.

units.la: II. De Deo autem, cum ille sit Summus & Perfectissimus, & à quo omnia quæ ab ipso diversa, omni modo pendent, eoque inferiora sunt, agnosco nil obstare quominus is fruatur omni eo quod ipsi conveniens putari à quocunque posset, ipsumque adeo Felicissimum esse reputandum, & quidem ex natura sua: Primo quia Ens Summum & Maximum est, Dein quia quæcunque ab ipso diversa vel exstant vel concipiuntur, nullam perfectionem ejus naturæ addere, nullamque adeo ab illa, quamvis ea omnia in nihilum absolute evanescerent, detrahere queunt. Quapropter nullis prorsus præter se opus habet ut omnibus fruatur quæ ejus naturæ conveniunt. Recte igitur attributum Felicitatis essentialis sive Beatitudinis, quam etiam Scriptura Deo speciali modo assignat, in ejus Natura dicitur includi, cum sit per se notum, Summam Cogitationem supra omnem ideam, naturam, rem à se diversam, se ipsam velle, se ipsam possidere, seque ipsa ita frui, ut sibi acquiescat, quæ summa, & ulli præter Deum incommunicabilis Felicitas est. nullus enim ita natura Cogitationis summæ frui potest, quamvis quis illam secundum Dei placitum adumbret, adeoque quamvis & ipsam ejus Felicitatem repræsentare possit, &, si felix fieri velit, debeat: nam creatæ Mentis felicitas Divinæ felicitatis adumbratio est, qua gaudebit Mens, cum Dei placitum, vel potius Deum volentem se plene manifestare & complentem suum placitum, volet illa, fruetur eo, & in eo acquiescet supra omnem ideam, omnem naturam, & rem omnem à Deo diversam: quæ est creatæ Mentis futura felicitas, & cujus viam ingressa est ea Mens, quæ nil præter Deum secundum ejus placitum optans, exspectando Divini placiti complementum, id quod placitum idem de præsenti rerum statu disponit ob Deum amplectitur.
units.tr: II. As for God, since he is the Highest and Most Perfect, and since all things distinct from him depend on him in every way and are therefore inferior, I acknowledge that nothing prevents him from enjoying all that could be thought to suit him, and that he must therefore be reckoned most happy, and indeed from his own nature. First, because he is the Highest and Greatest Being; then, because whatever things distinct from him either exist or are conceived cannot add any perfection to his nature, nor can they take away anything from it, even if all of them were to vanish absolutely into nothing. Therefore he has no need whatever of anything besides himself in order to enjoy all that suits his nature. Rightly, then, the attribute of essential happiness or blessedness, which Scripture also assigns to God in a special way, is said to be included in his nature, since it is known in itself that the highest Thought, above every idea, nature, and thing distinct from itself, wills itself, possesses itself, and enjoys itself so as to acquiesce in itself. This highest happiness is incommunicable to anyone except God. For no one can enjoy the nature of the highest Thought in this way, although one may shadow it forth according to God's good pleasure, and so may be able to represent his happiness, and, if he wishes to be happy, ought to do so. For the happiness of the created mind is a shadow of the divine happiness, in which the mind will rejoice when it wills God's good pleasure, or rather God who wills to reveal himself fully and to fulfil his own pleasure; it will enjoy him, and acquiesce in him above every idea, every nature, and every thing distinct from God. This is the future happiness of the created mind, and the mind which, desiring nothing but God according to his good pleasure, has entered on its way to it: waiting for the completion of the divine good pleasure, it embraces for God's sake whatever that same pleasure arranges in the present state of things.

units.la: III. Quod autem secundo dixi, Deum ideo absolute Felicem esse reputandum, quod quæ ab eo diversa sunt nil ei addere, nilque ab eo detrahere valeant, ostendit porro singulare plane Felicitatis genus, quale præter ipsum nullum est exemplum. Omni felicitati ab externo vel ab alio incrementum, aliquando omne, accedit, ita ut qui inter homi-nes pro felicibus ob potentiam vel scientiam, aut aliud quid, reputan-tur, si soli omnibusque præter se destituti statuerentur, non adeo se fe-lices experientur, adverterentque facile aliquid grati ex aliorum Socie-tate, notitia, amore, aut laude, &c. illis accedere. Imo non dubium est quin Mentis Creatæ Felicitati veriori, quam mox diximus, si illam ea Solam frui supponimus, aliquid accedat ex Societate cum cæteris mentibus Sanctis, cum nempe scit & videt Deo placuisse ut etiam à mul-tis præter ipsam ametur. Sed non ita de Deo colligendum est: quamvis enim ab innumeris noscatur, ametur, laudetur, & decenti modo re-præsentetur, non tamen ideo Felicior in se est, quam si Solus esset; cæ-teraque illa vel prorsus cessarent, vel plane aliter essent. Si quædam vo-luit statuere, efficere, creare, redimere, beneficiis ornare, quæ ipsum amarent & laudarent, non ideo fecit ut esset Beatior, sed quia ei placitum est sic suam Felicitatem, quæ ei sufficit, ex lubitu adumbrare. Quæ satis ex sese & ex antedictis patent.
units.tr: III. Now, as for what I said second, that God must therefore be reckoned absolutely happy because the things distinct from him can add nothing to him nor take anything from him, this further shows a quite singular kind of happiness, of which there is no example besides himself. Every happiness is at some time increased from outside or from another; in every case something is added. So those who among men are counted happy because of power or knowledge or something else, if they were set alone and stripped of everything except themselves, would not find themselves so happy, and would easily notice that something pleasant is added to them from the company, knowledge, love, or praise of others, and so on. Indeed there is no doubt that to the truer happiness of the created mind, which we spoke of just now, if we suppose it enjoyed alone, something is added from fellowship with the other holy minds, since it knows and sees that it has pleased God that it should also be loved by many besides itself. But this should not be inferred about God. For although he is known, loved, and praised by countless beings, and is rightly represented, he is not on that account happier in himself than if he were alone; and those other things would either altogether cease or would be wholly different. If he chose to establish, effect, create, redeem, and adorn with benefits certain beings who would love and praise him, he did not do so in order to be more blessed, but because it pleased him to shadow forth his happiness, which suffices for him, at his own will. These things are sufficiently clear from what has been said and from themselves.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. (12) POTENTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. (12) POWER.

units.la: 1.2. Cogitationis creatæ vi nil extra illam poni existens, quanquam cum ea quædam existant. 3. Non ita de Cogitatione Summa.
units.tr: 1.2. Nothing outside a created thought's power is posited, though certain things exist along with it. 3. It is not so with the Supreme Thought.

units.la: I. SI Ego in illa quæ præter Deum & me concipio, quamvis sint me minora, nil possum, imo si ne quidem ea in mente mea modo mihi cum illis conveniente queam sistere, ut iis pro voluntate fruar, ut jam vidi; multo minus consequitur me esse eum qui illa extra me, sive extra cogitationem meam, existere faciam. Cogitatio mea non est ita efficax ut valeat se ipsam variare ad formas rerum sibi repræsentandas sive in se depingendas, iisque pro lubitu fruendum; itaque multo minus ita efficax erit ut ad ejus votum sequatur res ipsas incipere extra illam in se ipsis existere, seu illæ mihi similes, seu dissimiles, seu extensæ, seu Cogitantes concipiantur ; nec dubito quin quæ dantur Mentes ejusdem mecum classis , hoc est, finitæ & creatæ, idem de se ipsis, si attendant , fateantur. Saltem ego ut de me dixi , ita de illis certus sum , eas extra se nil ponere , nil facere posse vi Cogitationis suæ.
units.tr: I. IF I cannot do anything with those things which I conceive apart from God and myself, though they are less than me, nay, if I cannot even hold them in my mind in a way suited to them, so as to enjoy them at will (as I have already seen), then much less does it follow that I am the one who causes those things to exist outside me, that is, outside my thought. My thought is not so effective that it can vary itself into the forms of things to be represented to it, or depicted in itself, and enjoy them at its pleasure; and therefore it will be far less effective in making things begin to exist outside it, in themselves, at its wish, whether they are conceived as like or unlike it, extended or thinking. Nor do I doubt that the minds which are given, of the same class as mine, that is, finite and created, would confess the same about themselves, if they gave it thought. At least, as I have said of myself, so I am certain of them: that they can posit nothing outside themselves, and do nothing, by the power of their thought.

units.la: II. De me quidem convincor per experientiam rem ita se habere : Nam etiamsi intentissime peroptem res nonnullas, corporeas aut cogitantes, existere, earumve existentium modos aut qualitates, puta, motus, figuras, milleque similes corporis variationes, quod & de Mentium modis dictum sit pariter, in illis mutari, poni, aut ab iisdem removeri, nil tamen adeo inde in rebus ipsis extra cogitationem meam sequitur, ut ne quidem hujus corporis cui Mentem meam junctam puto, motus, motuumve determinationes, à vi meæ cogitationis ponantur, prout quam sæpissime animadvertere datur: & quamvis sæpe posita in me certa cogitatione ipsi ponantur, non tamen magis sequitur eos à mea Cogitatione poni sive effici, quam si quis in foro positam pecuniam videns merces sequi, concluderet mercium existentiam vel motum à pecunia effici; vel etiam eum qui sponte pecuniam exhibere jussisset, ejus fabricæ esse cuforem, sive ejus motus effectorem.
units.tr: II. I am indeed convinced by experience that the matter stands thus in my own case. For even if I most earnestly desire that certain things, corporeal or thinking, should exist, or the modes or qualities of those existing things, such as motions, figures, and a thousand similar variations of the body (and what is said of the modes of minds is likewise true), that they be changed in those things, or posited in them, or removed from them, nothing follows from this in the things themselves outside my thought; not even the motions of this body to which I believe my mind is joined, or the determinations of those motions, are posited by the power of my thought, as is very often observed. And although, when a certain thought is posited in me, those things are often posited along with it, it does not follow any more that they are posited or effected by my thought, than if someone, seeing money placed in the market, concluded that the goods which follow it, or their existence or motion, are effected by the money; or again, than if one who had of his own accord ordered money to be produced were thereby the maker of its mint, or the cause of its motion.

units.la: III. Quod si ad Deum , ( de quo mox inquiremus utrum sic, an vero secus , sit reputandus: ) Si inquam ad Deum atque ad ea quæ supra de ejus sufficientia & Dominio dicta sunt, & quæ statim de Potentia dicentur, attendere velimus,perfacile erit demonstrative judicare,Cujus Cogitationis vi quæcunque exstant & existere pergunt, ponantur.
units.tr: III. But if we wish to attend to God (whom we shall shortly inquire whether he is to be so reckoned, or otherwise), and to what has been said above of his sufficiency and dominion, and to what will be said immediately concerning power, it will be quite easy to judge by demonstration by the power of whose thought whatever things exist, and continue to exist, are posited.

units.la: 4. 5. 6. Res vi voluntatis Divinæ poni demonstratur. 7. Potentiæ Dei triplex consideratio. 8. Prima, Potentia absoluta, de qua nil determinandum. 9. Altera in respectu ad rerum essentiam. De hac propositiones quatuor. 10. Prima. 11. Secunda. 12. Tertia. 13. Quarta, ubi obiter de Potentia Dei in mysterio Transsubstantiationis secundum Principia Cartesiana agitur. 14. De Adoratione. 15. Ultima divinæ Potentiæ consideratio. Omnia existere quia Deus vult. 16. Quæ existunt in maximis & minimis, in substantiis & modis, ab illo effici. 17-30. Quæstiones - &c.
units.tr: 4. 5. 6. It is demonstrated that things are posited by the power of the Divine will. 7. A threefold consideration of the power of God. 8. The first, absolute power, about which nothing is to be determined. 9. The second, in respect to the essence of things. On this, four propositions. 10. The first. 11. The second. 12. The third. 13. The fourth, where in passing the power of God in the mystery of transubstantiation is treated according to Cartesian principles. 14. On Adoration. 15. The last consideration of divine power. All things exist because God wills them. 16. Things which exist in the greatest and least, in substances and modes, are effected by him. 17-30. Questions, etc.

units.la: IV. Nam cum ad illum me converto , visurus num quæ ille ipse vult concipere , valeat extra conceptum suum prout vult ita ponere, ut res eæ existant quales ab illo concipiuntur, & existere decernuntur, agnosco in eo tantam Cogitationis seu voluntatis efficaciam, ut omnino in hac conclusione acquiescam, res existere ex efficacia & vi placiti Dei, sive quia placuit Deo eas non tantum statuere veras, aut earum ideas concipere, sed & velle ut illæ haberent in se ipsis eam quam habent rea-litatem umbratilem sive repræsentativam sui placiti. Non jam Sacras Scripturas in medium afferam ad efficaciam Divinæ hujus Cogitationis seu voluntatis demonstrandam, nam hoc genere argumentorum uti hic nolo; nec soli experientiæ mei insistam, qui sentio me existere & scio hoc esse ab illo, ut jam vidi: Sed secundum rationem id ex ante probatis colligam evidenter.
units.tr: IV. For when I turn to him, to see whether what he himself wills to conceive can, outside its conception, so posit things as he wills, that those things exist as they are conceived by him and decreed to exist, I recognise in him so great an efficacy of thought or will that I fully acquiesce in this conclusion: that things exist from the efficacy and power of God's good pleasure, that is, because it pleased God not only to establish them as true, or to conceive their ideas, but also to will that they should have in themselves that reality, shadowy or representative of his pleasure, which they have. I will not now bring the Holy Scriptures forward to demonstrate the efficacy of this divine thought or will, for I am unwilling to use this kind of argument here; nor will I rely on the experience of myself alone, who feel that I exist and know this to be from him, as I have already seen. Rather, I shall clearly infer this by reason from what has been proved before.

units.la: V. Hæc Divinæ Cogitationis vis & perfectio quæ rerum existen-tiam, qualem ipsa vult, inferat, à nullo posset negari, quin affirmetur Deo aliquid deesse, sive Ens perfectissimum non esse Ens Perfectissi-mum. Nam quamvis rerum existentiæ & naturæ, imo conceptus sive placitum Dei de illis non sint de essentia Dei, adeoque eorum negatio non inferat ex se directe Divinæ essentiæ negationem; tamen ex hypo-thesi quod Deus Perfectissimus illas hoc modo esse velit, sequitur, aut eas ita esse, aut si non sint is negatur eas voluisse qui dicitur eas voluisse, quod est contra hypothesin; aut si voluit, perfectissimum esse Ens ne-gatur, primo, quia ei sic statueretur aliquid deesse, non quod ejus Na-turæ deessent res externæ, utpote quæ ad eam non spectant, sed Deo quatenus voluit ita se determinare, sive Dei voluntati, censeretur deesse efficacia ponendi ea quæ vellet esse posita extra se ut essent tum notæ suæ efficaciæ, tum adumbrationes vel tabulæ divinarum suarum perfectionum. Etenim, quomodo Perfectissimus esset censendus ille in se, in Natura, in voluntate, in cogitatione sua, qui ne quidem quæ valde imperfecta sunt extra se ponere posse diceretur? Secundo, sic statue-retur, Deum tendere in non-Ens, & sic à se esse alienum. Deus se ipsum deserere non potest, & cum ad ea quæ à se diversa sunt attendere vult, id maxime facit ob se ipsum, sui scopus est ipse, ad alia tendit ut se ipsum per illa secundum suum placitum repræsentet, adeoque ut ad se fiat re-ditus. Atqui nihil, imo tale nihil quod invito Deo manet nihil, non re-præsentat Dei perfectiones. Igitur quia Deus se ipsum non deserit, concludendum est, quando vult aliquid extra se existere, tale quid etiam existere in quo perfectiones Dei adumbrentur, & ex quo ad Deum reditus fiat, id igitur non manet nihil.
units.tr: V. This power and perfection of the divine thought, if it brings about the existence of things in the way it wills, could not be denied without affirming that something is lacking to God, or that the most perfect Being is not the most perfect Being. For although the existence and nature of things, indeed the concept or decree of God concerning them, are not of the essence of God, and so their denial does not by itself directly imply a denial of the divine essence; nevertheless, on the hypothesis that the most perfect God wills them to be in this way, it follows either that they are so, or, if they do not exist, that he is denied to have willed them, though he is said to have willed them, which is contrary to the hypothesis; or, if he willed them, then he is denied to be the most perfect Being. First, because it would thereby be asserted that something is lacking to him: not that his nature lacks external things, since these do not pertain to it, but that God, insofar as he willed to determine himself thus, or the will of God, would be deemed to lack the efficacy of positing outside himself those things which he willed to exist, so that they might be both the marks of his efficacy and the shadows or tablets of his divine perfections. For how could he be considered most perfect in himself, in his nature, in his will, in his thought, who would not even be said to be able to posit outside himself things that are very imperfect? Second, it would thereby be asserted that God tends toward non-being, and so is alienated from himself. God cannot desert himself; and when he wills to attend to things that are distinct from himself, he does this chiefly for his own sake: he is his own end, and he tends to other things so that he may represent himself through them according to his own decree, and thus that a return to himself may be made. But nothing, indeed such a nothing as remains nothing despite God's will, does not represent the perfections of God. Therefore, since God does not desert himself, it must be concluded that when he wills something to exist outside himself, that thing also exists, in which the perfections of God are shadowed forth and through which a return to God is made; that thing, therefore, does not remain nothing.

units.la: sive placitum qualecunque sit & quocunque feratur, non impletur; quod à Deo removendum est, cum infelix nullo modo sit dicendus. Etiam quæ de Deo hactenus dicta sunt, præsertim de ejus Altitudine & Dominio, non permittunt ut ea statuantur, ex quibus sequeretur, Majorem aliquem eo concipi posse, aut ejus conceptum vel eo invito ad nihil restringi. At si Cogitatio illa Summa non inferret existentiam eorum quæ ipsa vult ut existentia cogitare, Major Cogitatio conciperetur atque perfectior, nempe alia, ad cujus determinationem res existerent ut ei placeret: Cumque Deus vult se determinare ad concipiendum aliquid ut existens, si id non existeret, tunc determinaretur Deus ab ipso nihilo ad concipiendum contrarium ejus quod vellet; ejusque voluntas statueretur cogi ad hoc, ut scilicet esset contenta eo quod non vult, adeoque ipso nihilo repleri, terminari, & determinari, quæ omnia contradictoria sunt. Nec est quod dicat nonnullus, Deum multa velle ut existentia, quæ tamen non fiunt, ut sunt ea quæ mandatorum suorum observantiam concernunt, quæ etsi velit atque jubeat ab omnibus fieri non tamen existunt in illis. Nam certum est eam Dei voluntatem non esse absolutum aliquod ejus placitum quo statuerit ipse prorsus efficere secundum vires divinamque potentiam quicquid ad hujus effecti productionem conferre potest, alioqui procul dubio res ita existeret: sed est declaratio qua homines monet sibi placere ut à se ipsis secundum sua phantasmata non prætendant operari, neve in nihilum tendant, & abutantur dotibus quas in eos contulit, qui scopus est mandatorum Dei: Sed nequaquam ex istis est concludendum, Deum absolute & quam plenissime potuit statuisse ut non deesset ulli ulla perfectio quæ in illo esse posset. Hoc omnino destrueret Dei ideam, si Deus ita volens, quodcunque vult non efficeret.
units.tr: or whatever the placement may be, is not fulfilled; and this must be removed from God, since he cannot in any way be called unhappy. Moreover, what has been said so far about God, especially about his Height and Dominion, does not permit us to posit anything from which it would follow that someone greater than him could be conceived, or that his conception could be restricted to nothing even against his will. But if that Supreme Thought did not imply the existence of those things which it wills to exist, a greater and more perfect Thought would be conceived, namely another one, by whose determination things would exist so as to please it. And since God wills to determine himself to conceive something as existing, if it did not exist, then God would be determined by mere nothing to conceive the opposite of what he wills; and his will would be stated to be compelled to this, namely to be content with what he does not will, and thus to be filled, bounded and determined by nothing itself, all of which are contradictory. Nor is there anything in what some one may say, that God wills many things to exist which nevertheless do not come to be, such as those which concern the observance of his commandments, which, although he wills and commands that they be done by all, nonetheless do not exist in them. For it is certain that this will of God is not some absolute decree by which he has determined to bring about absolutely, according to his powers and divine potency, whatever can contribute to the production of this effect; otherwise, without doubt, the thing would so exist. Rather it is a declaration by which he warns men that it pleases him that they not presume to act by their own fancies, nor tend toward nothing and abuse the gifts which he has bestowed upon them, which is the aim of God's commandments. But by no means is it to be concluded from these things that God has absolutely and as fully as possible determined that no perfection which could be in him should be lacking in anything. This would altogether destroy the idea of God, if God, willing thus, did not bring about whatever he wills.

units.la: VII. Ergo ex dictis patet tantam esse Dei volentis vim & efficaciam, ut, posito eum velle res, has vel illas, hoc aliove modo existere, eo ipso quod id velit, sequatur res tales existentes poni, nec aliter. Quam Divinæ voluntatis virtutem nomine Potentiæ in Deo agnoscimus. Ut autem de ea specialius nonnulla dicamus, & noscamus, eam ad objecta diversa relatam considerabimus, non ad omnia quidem singularia, sunt enim innumera, sed ad generaliora. Spectatur Potentia Dei ut relata ad res quæ jam existunt: Spectatur & eadem ut respectum habens ad res eas quæ adhuc non existunt, nec forte existent unquam, dicuntur tamen possibiles: Spectatur denique absolute, ut non relata ad res ullas seu existentiam, seu essentiam, naturam, veritatemque idealem habentes, tes, sed ut ante omnia exstantia, imo decreta. Nam sive concipiam res existere; sive putem res non existere, sed tantum concipi vel à Deo esse quoad ideas suas tantum statutas; sive denique Cogitem potuisse Deum nil effecisse, nil statuisse, adeoque nil præter Dei naturam habere veritatem, nihilominus Deum ut Potentem concipere debeo. De his agemus ordine retrogrado, initio facto ab ultima consideratione.
units.tr: VII. From what has been said, it is clear that the power and efficacy of God's will are so great that, once it is posited that God wills things to exist in this or that way, the very fact that he wills it entails that such existing things are posited, and in no other way. We acknowledge this virtue of the divine will in God under the name of Power. In order to say something more particular about it, and to know it better, we shall consider it as related to various objects: not to every single object, for these are innumerable, but to the more general kinds. God's Power is viewed as related to things that already exist. It is also viewed as having reference to those things that do not yet exist, and perhaps never will, yet are called possible. Lastly, it is viewed absolutely, as not related to any things that have either existence, essence, nature, or ideal truth, but as prior to all existence, indeed as prior to any decree. For whether I conceive things as existing, or think they do not exist but are merely conceived, or are established by God only as to their ideas; or lastly, whether I think that God could have effected nothing and decreed nothing, and so had no truth beyond the nature of God, I must nonetheless conceive God as Powerful. We shall treat these in reverse order, beginning with the last consideration.

units.la: VIII. Potentia Dei ultimo sensu, quæ absoluta dici potest, non adeo diversa est à Summo Dei Dominio, & consideratur antequam concipiamus Deum ullam rem, essentiam, veritatemque statuisse. Abstrahendum est igitur, ad ejus notitiam, ab omni rerum existentia, essentia, idea, veritate, & cogitandum, quamvis nulla præter Deum essent, nullaque unquam præter Deum essent habitura existentiam, essentiam & veritatem, Dei tamen voluntatem tam perfectam fore & esse, ut si & placeret quædam statuere & existentia velle, sive essent his, quæ jam sunt, similia futura, seu naturarum, essentiarum, veritatum prorsus ab illis diversarum quæ jam exstant, adeoque nobis incognita & incogitabilia, ea revera darentur prout vellet. Hoc sensu igitur Deus absolute Potens est, nec ad hoc indifferens, ut quodcunque ei placeret velle id ita esset vel non esset, prout ei placeret: nam non ideo potest, quia voluit ipse se determinare ad hæc vel illa, sed necessario, ob rationes jam dictas, quia est perfectissimus, nec talem habet voluntatem quæ effectu intento destituatur. Non est ideo potens hæc voluntas quia antecedenter indifferens spectata deinde determinata est ad hoc vel illud; sed potens est, quia Dei est, potens est ante omnem determinationem. Adeoque sic plura potest Deus quam vult, imo alia & diversa potest ac voluit statuitque esse vera, & efficere existentia: nulloque modo limitanda est hæc ejus Potentia ex consideratione idearum, essentiarum, veritatum, naturæque rerum existentium, quasi quæ in illis non exstant, aut cum illis non congruunt, absolute non posset Deus ille, cui omnia præter ipsum ex se ipsis sunt indifferentia, cum ex se ipsis pariter nihil sint. Non igitur quicquam determinandum est de Absoluta Dei Potentia, ut illam limitemus. Mens nostra jam determinata est ad ea quæ sunt, concipienda, neque tamen, ut mox videbitur, ad omnia, unde non potest concipere ad quænam possit se extendere Potentia Dei. Nonnulla requiritur Mentis attentio ad hæc & sequentia bene capienda, quibus semel conceptis, facile erit perspicere quid de Potentia Dei sit cogitandum, necne. Cæterum, quia hæc coincidunt fere cum iis quæ supra de Dominio Dei dicta sunt, iisdem etiam difficultatibus sunt obnoxia : quas ne iterum hic repetamus cum additis responsionibus, suffecerit mo-nuisse eas in loco citato omnes exstare.
units.tr: VIII. The Power of God in its last sense, which may be called absolute, is not very different from the Supreme Dominion of God, and it is considered before we conceive that God has established any thing, essence, or truth. To come to know it, we must therefore abstract from all existence, essence, idea, and truth of things, and think that, even if nothing existed besides God, and nothing besides God were ever going to have existence, essence, and truth, God's will would nonetheless be so perfect that, if it pleased him to establish certain things and will their existence, whether they were to be like those that now are, or natures, essences, and truths wholly different from those that now exist, and so unknown and unthinkable to us, these things would in fact be given just as he willed. In this sense, then, God is absolutely Powerful, and he is not indifferent to this, so that whatever pleased him to will would be or would not be, as he pleased. For he is not able to do this because he chose to determine himself to this or that, but necessarily, for the reasons already stated, because he is most perfect, and he does not have a will that lacks the intended effect. This will is not powerful because, viewed as previously indifferent, it was afterwards determined to this or that; rather it is powerful because it is God's, and it is powerful before any determination. Thus God can do more than he wills, indeed he can do other and different things than he willed and decreed to be true, and bring them into existence. In no way is this Power to be limited by considering the ideas, essences, truths, and natures of existing things, as if God, to whom all things besides himself are indifferent from their own nature, since they are of themselves nothing, could not absolutely do what is not in those things or does not agree with them. Nothing, therefore, must be determined about the Absolute Power of God in order to limit it. Our mind is already determined to conceive those things that are, yet not, as will soon appear, all things; hence it cannot conceive how far the Power of God can extend. Some attention of the mind is required to grasp these and the following points well; once they have been grasped, it will be easy to see what must be thought about the Power of God, or not. Moreover, since these almost coincide with what was said above about the Dominion of God, they are subject to the same difficulties; rather than repeat them here with the added replies, it will suffice to have warned that all of them are found in the place cited.

units.la: IX. Venio ad secundam de Dei Potentia considerationem, videlicet; Cum Deus se determinavit ut conciperet quasdam ideas, essentias, veritates, &c. prout ipsi placuit, ubi volet, (si placet) ut vel omnes, vel nonnullae ex illis existant extra suum conceptum, rem ita exequi potest, sive Potens est ille[?] res quas voluit conceptas, ponere extra conceptum. Hoc respectu dicitur Deus posse ea quae vult & voluit; & voluntatem de existentia quorundam efficacem sive Potentiam, non praecedere voluntatem decernentem eorum essentiam & naturam. ridiculum esset hoc sensu asserere, Deum illa posse quae noluit, sive quae non statuit, hoc est, quod posset existentiam rei illi concedere cui tamen nullam statuere voluisset naturam essentiamque. Noto hanc esse ratio-nem & Originem potentiae sive possibilitatis rerum, ideo enim possibiles dicuntur, quia prius ex Dei liberrimo arbitrio quoad naturas, essen-tias, ideas, veritatesque suas stabilitæ & ordinatæ, si accederet Dei placitum de earum existentia, ea ob efficaciam ejus existentiam nancisci ap-tæ, existerent. Hæc Divinæ Potentiæ consideratio sequentium Proposi-tio num veritatem mihi commendat, quarum Prima est:
units.tr: IX. I come to the second consideration of God's Power: since God has determined himself to conceive certain ideas, essences, truths, and so on, as it pleased him, wherever and whenever he wills (if it pleases him) that all or some of them exist outside his conception, he can carry this out. For he is able to posit outside the conception the things that he willed to be conceived. In this respect God is said to be able to do what he wills and has willed; and his will concerning the existence of certain things, that is, his efficacious will or Power, does not precede his decreeing will concerning their essence and nature. It would be absurd in this sense to assert that God can do those things which he has not willed, or has not established, that is, that he could grant existence to a thing for which he had not willed any nature or essence. I note that this is the reason and origin of the potency or possibility of things; for they are called possible because, having first been established and ordered by God's most free choice as to their natures, essences, ideas, and truths, they would exist, if God's pleasure concerning their existence were added, since by his efficacy they would obtain the existence for which they are suited. This consideration of the divine Power commends to me the truth of the following propositions, the first of which is:

units.la: X. De Potentia Dei possumus affirmare omnia quae evidenter concipimus. Hoc patet si hæc assumamus quae facile ex dictis demonstrari possunt, & deinceps demonstrabuntur, nempe Deum concipere quae ego concipio, & meum conceptum esse repraesentationem nonnullam Divini conceptus. Unde sic arguo: Quae ego concipio evidenter, ea Deus concipit, ea sunt in ejus conceptu, imo sunt in eo clarius & evidentius quam in meo: quae autem Deus concipit, quaeque adeo ideam, essentiam, veritatemque in ejus conceptu habent, ea, ex dictis, per Potentiam Dei existere apta sunt: Ergo quaecunque concipio possunt existere per Potentiam Dei, sive Deus potest efficere quaecunque Ego cum evidentia concipio.
units.tr: X. Concerning the Power of God we can affirm all that we clearly conceive. This is evident if we assume what can easily be demonstrated from what has been said, and will be demonstrated hereafter, namely that God conceives what I conceive, and that my conception is some representation of the divine conception. Hence I argue thus: what I clearly conceive, God conceives; those things are in his conception, indeed they are in it more clearly and evidently than in mine. But what God conceives, and so has the idea, essence, and truth of in his conception, these, from what has been said, are fit to exist through the Power of God. Therefore whatever I conceive can exist through the Power of God, or God can effect whatever I conceive with evidence.

units.la: XI. Quae non concipio, ea non debeo negare de Po-tentia Dei. Non dico, quae repugnant conceptui meo & destruunt ejus evidentiam, sed quae transcendunt, quae absorbent, ut sic loquar, ea non sunt Potentiae Divinae subtrahenda. Quando Deus ex iis quae concepit quaedam extra se effecit, adeoque me etiam, quem concepit, existentem reddidit, impressit mihi conceptus quosdam suis similes, sed non omnes impressit. Unde possum quidem ex conceptu meo affirmativa argumenta depromere, sed non licet sic reputare, hoc non concipio, ergo nec Deus concipit, nec efficere potest. Temeritatis summae est ejusmodi judicium, cum fieri possit ut illud de quo ita judicatur, non modo sit a Deo statutum atque conceptum, sed etiam ut adsit placitum Dei de ejus existentia, imo ut illud jam actu sit impletum atque existens. Et revera tale quid exstat in extensione partium materiae, in universi quantitate, in gradibus motus quoad celeritatem & tarditatem ejus, imo in rerum omnium principiis extremisque ultimis, in quibus omnibus impossibile est humanae Menti quicquam determinare, & concipere, ut clarius patebit cum de Cognitione ejus agemus ex professo. At num illa ideo Potentiam Dei ita constringet, ut eam ad suae capacitatis mensuram redigat? Dicetne nil posse Deum de illis determinare, concipere, efficere quicquam, quia illa in iis neutram oppositarum propositionum partem capere & amplecti valet? Etenim, si ab illa quaeretur, v. g. de universo, sive mundo corporeo, an a Potente Deo extensio ejus facta sit finita? Responderi nequit affirmative quin conceptus qui de extensione, sive spatio, cujus finis nullus concipitur, eo ipso destruatur sive negetur: nil autem Menti turpius est quam judicia efformare quibus conceptus reclamet, quaeque ei sint contraria. Quod si alteram partem amplexus, dixeris, Potentiam Dei mundum quoad extensionem positive & in se infinitum fecisse, jam eopse negabis ei novam materiam praeter illam quae jam exstat a Deo addi posse, nam extensio quae in se & vere positive est infinita, possibilitatem additionis novae excludit, cum haec exclusio rei ejusdem naturae sit ipse conceptus infiniti, Quid ergo hic determinari potest a Mente nostra? Nil. Ergo de sua imbecillitate, mensuraeque suae terminis angustis hic persuadeatur: ne vero quippiam ex his concludat de Dei Potentia. Non possum id capere, Ergo vis cogitandi in me est finita: bene. non autem, Ergo non potest id Deus efficere. quae consequentia est plane extra praemissam propositionem.
units.tr: XI. What I do not conceive, I ought not to deny concerning the Power of God. I do not mean what is repugnant to my conception and destroys its evidence, but what transcends it and, so to speak, absorbs it: these must not be withdrawn from the Divine Power. When God has effected outside himself some of the things he conceived, and so has also made me, whom he conceived, to exist, he has impressed upon me certain concepts like his own, but he has not impressed all of them. Hence I may indeed draw affirmative arguments from my conception, but it is not right to reason thus: I do not conceive this, therefore neither does God conceive it, nor can he effect it. Such a judgement is of the highest rashness, since it may happen that that concerning which such a judgement is made has not only been decreed and conceived by God, but also that God's pleasure concerning its existence is present, indeed that it has already actually been fulfilled and exists. And truly something of this kind exists in the extension of the parts of matter, in the quantity of the universe, in the degrees of motion as to its speed and slowness, indeed in the first principles and ultimate extremes of all things; in all of these it is impossible for the human mind to determine or conceive anything, as will appear more clearly when we treat of his Knowledge professedly. But will these things on that account so constrain the Power of God that they reduce it to the measure of their capacity? Will one say that God can determine, conceive, or effect nothing concerning those things, because the mind is unable to grasp and embrace either of the opposed propositions concerning them? For if one were asked, for example, about the universe, or the corporeal world, whether its extension was made finite by the all-powerful God, no affirmative answer can be given without the concept of extension, or space, whose limit is not conceived, being thereby destroyed or denied. Yet nothing is more shameful for the mind than to form judgements against which its concept cries out and which are contrary to it. But if you embrace the other part and say that the Power of God made the world positively and in itself infinite as to extension, you will then deny that any new matter besides that which already exists can be added to it by God; for an extension that is in itself and truly positively infinite excludes the possibility of new addition, since this exclusion of the same kind of thing is itself the concept of the infinite. What, then, can be determined here by our mind? Nothing. Let it therefore be persuaded of its own weakness and the narrow limits of its measure, but let it not conclude anything from these concerning the Power of God. I cannot grasp this; therefore the power of thinking in me is finite: that is well. But not: therefore God cannot effect this. That inference is plainly outside the premise.

units.la: XII. Nunquam supponendum est, quae Tertia est Propositio, Divinam Potentiam a nobis comprehendi, vel posse comprehendi, ut ex hac hypothesi ratiocinemur. Scimus Deum esse Incomprehensibilem, eundemque esse unam Cogitationem simplicem, unde videmus ejus Potentiam a finita Mente non posse comprehendi. Periculose igitur saepe dici solet, ne Deum quidem hoc vel illud posse, quasi vero ejus Potentiae Sphaera sive mensura caperetur. Nonnulli hac cautela neglecta in stulta & absurda de Potentia Dei quaesita devenerunt, exempli gratia, petierunt, An Deus possit id omne facere & exequi quod potest? Respondentibus, imo posse; Suppone Ergo, regerent, Deum id omne effecisse quod potest; an non posset ulterius aliquid facere? Si non posset, igitur tunc potentia ejus limites sibi invenisset, &c. Discursus hi prorsus inepti & absurdi sunt: nam primo, similes garruli supponunt Potentiam Dei comprehendi tum ab ingenio suo, cum supponunt se concipere eam cum omnibus suis factis; tum a creatis sive factis ipsis, quasi ea exhaurire illam possent. Deinde sibi contradicunt, nam postquam supposuerunt se concipere omnia ad quae Potentia se extendit, eaque ut jam existentia, lepide quaerunt num quid praeterea possit? hoc est, num possit ultra id quod eam posse supposuerunt se capere? quae quidem quaestio destruit & absurditatis convincit suppositionem prius positam. Denique tales supponunt naturam possibilitatis independentem, quam Deus non statuerit ex arbitrio & placito suo, sed cujus ideam prius veram necessario concipiat eo per illam determinatus, & ad cujus mensuram Potentia sese accommodet. quod satis superque repulsum est supra. Quod possibile est tale est, quia tale voluit Deus. Addemus ad alia absurda praecavenda sequentem propositionem, quae.
units.tr: XII. It must never be assumed, which is the third proposition, that the divine power is comprehended by us, or can be comprehended, so that we might reason from this hypothesis. We know that God is incomprehensible and that he is one simple thought, whence we see that his power cannot be comprehended by a finite mind. It is therefore often said dangerously, that God cannot do this or that, as if the sphere or measure of his power could be grasped. Some, neglecting this caution, have arrived at foolish and absurd questions about the power of God; for example, they have asked: Can God do and carry out all that he can do? When the answer is given, Yes, indeed he can, they retort: Suppose then that God has done all that he can do; could he not do something further? If he could not, then his power would have found its limits for itself, and so on. These arguments are utterly silly and absurd.
