For first, such chattering men assume that the power of God is comprehended both by their own intellect, when they suppose they conceive it together with all its works, and by the created things or works themselves, as if these could exhaust it. Then they contradict themselves: for after supposing that they conceive all the things to which the power extends, and taking them as already existing, they wittily ask whether it can do anything besides; that is, whether it can go beyond what they supposed they grasped. This very question destroys the supposition laid down first and proves it absurd. Finally, such men assume a nature of possibility independent of God, which God has not established by his own will and pleasure, but whose true idea he must necessarily conceive, being determined by it, and to whose measure his power must conform. This has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently refuted above: what is possible is such because God willed it to be such. To guard against other absurdities we shall add the following proposition, which is

units.la: XIII. Quarta est: Postquam idea essentia & natura rerum concepta sunt ut a Deo statuta, absurdum est ad Potentiam Dei recurrere, ut ea dicantur per Potentiam Dei existentia vel possibilia, quae rerum statui, naturae, ideisque positis adversantur. Nam si de absoluta Potentia Dei (quae ut ejus absolutum Dominium spectatur) sermo sit, ea nullas supponit adhuc essentias, veritates, naturas, ideas, nec ulla quae possint concipi; nullosque adeo rerum conceptus, quales tamen supponunt ii qui petunt, Num haec aut illa, quae vident esse a rerum natura essentiaque, quam concipiunt, aliena, possint fieri? Statutis vero rerum ideis essentiisque, Potentia quae in Deo est, non est sui statuentis abnegatio dum concipitur manere statuens, sed est efficacia ponendi quae ideis a se conceptis, quas etiam in nobis impressit, concordent. Quaecunque eis repugnant, ea sunt abnegatio Dei statuentis, Dei volentis efficere quae statuit, & efficientis quae voluit, adeoque sunt abnegatio Potentiae Dei, non vero ejus statumina. Id non satis consideraverunt ii qui rerum naturas & ideas tales a Deo positas esse tenent, quales Cartesius proposuit, & nihilominus docent, Se non posse determinare, utrum per Potentiam Dei duo contradictoria possint simul esse? An corpus unum idemque (cujus naturam essentiamque in extensione sive spacio constitutam esse putant) totum simul in duobus distinctisque locis & spatiis possit ponere Deus? Imo id & alia aeque contradictoria, non modo eum posse efficere, sed & actum effecisse ajunt. Quas assertiones, vel juxta sua ipsorum prinprincipia, falsas esse dico, earumque negationes veras. At exclamabunt forte, me ita Potentiam Dei negare, vel saltem limitare, si ita crude dicatur, Deum hæc non posse. Respondeo, an Potentiam Dei negem vel limitem, judicabit ex præcedentibus mens quævis liberi & tranquilli judicii; sed ad hominem, dico me nequaquam eam negare.
units.tr: XIII. The fourth is: Once the ideas of the essence and nature of things have been conceived as established by God, it is absurd to appeal to the power of God so that things which are opposed to the established state, nature and ideas should be said to exist or be possible through the power of God. For if the discussion concerns the absolute power of God (which is viewed as his absolute dominion), this power does not yet presuppose any essences, truths, natures, ideas, or anything that can be conceived; and so it presupposes no concepts of things of the kind that those who ask, Can this or that come about, nevertheless presuppose, namely, whether things which they see to be alien to the nature and essence of things, as they conceive them, can come to be. But with the ideas and essences of things having been established, the power which is in God is not a denial of his establishing will, while it is conceived to remain the establishing power; rather it is the efficacy of positing those things which agree with the ideas he has conceived, which he has also impressed upon us. Whatever is repugnant to these is a denial of God as establisher, of God willing to effect what he has established and effecting what he has willed, and so it is a denial of the power of God, not indeed of his establishments. Those who hold that the natures and ideas of things were so posited by God as Descartes proposed them did not sufficiently consider this; and yet they teach that they cannot determine whether, by the power of God, two contradictories can exist at the same time; or whether God can place one and the same body (whose nature and essence they think consists in extension or space) wholly at once in two distinct places and spaces. Indeed they say that he not only can bring about this and other equally contradictory things, but has actually done so. I say that these assertions are false, even according to their own principles, and their negations are true. But perhaps they will cry out that I deny or at least limit the power of God, if it is put so crudely as: God cannot do these things. I answer that whether I deny or limit the power of God, any mind of free and calm judgment will decide from what has gone before; but to the man himself I say that I by no means deny it.

units.la: Nam si de verbis Deus non potest litem intendas, ea non involvunt semper Potentiæ Dei negationem, alioqui S. Scriptura Potentiam Dei negaret, dum illis utens ait, Deum non posse se ipsum abnegare. Vocibus his nil aliud designatur quam quod Deus imperfectioni non sit obnoxius, nec possit concipi tale quid ei esse attribuendum quod imperfectionem includat: quo sensu verba potest, posse, potentia, negativa sunt, nam denotant capacitatem imperfectionis non-nullius, itaque à Deo per negationem sunt removenda, non-potest, non-potentia, &c. Quomodo non negatur vera & positiva[?] Dei Potentia sive efficacia efficiendi quæ statuit, nec ei dantur limites ulli, nisi ipsa omnimoda perfectio pro limite habeatur: Sed ostenditur, efficacem voluntatem Dei de rebus ponendis à se ipsa statuente non dissentire. Tantum abest ut Divinam Potentiam negatione vel limite impugnem, quin contra, assero Deum potuisse omnium rerum essentias, veritates, existentias, in nihilo linquere, vel alias statuere & efficere, de quibus nil quicquam determinare vel concipere queo: At scio, stabilitis ideis, essentiis, naturis atque veritatibus rerum, v. g. extensionis sive materiæ, corporum particularium, figurarum, &c. me non posse dicere, forte Deus potest efficere triangulum rectilineum cujus anguli tres non sint duobus rectis æquales: forte potest efficere ut unum corpus (posito quod ejus natura sit in extensione sive spatiositate, ut multis persuasum est) sit totum simul in duobus locis; adeoque ut totum corpus humanum in extensione multo minori quam ea est de ejus essentia statuitur, sit contentum; vel ut extensio quæ habet figuras, dispositiones, motus, cæterasque modificationes panis aut vini, eorumque particularum, sit (illis qui statuunt panis aut vini naturas essentiasque in his consistere) aut sanguis aut caro, &c. quia Deus est omnipotens. Quidni etiam dixeris, posse etiam forte se ipsum abnegare Deum? posse fallere, posse efficere quæ efficiens non concipiet, aut ea velle quæ non volet eo modo quo volet, quia scilicet est omnipotens? Peto, quid per Potentiam Dei intelligatur? An per illam talem intelligemus voluntatis Divinæ perfectionem qua res tales ponantur quales vult, aut vero quales ipsa non vult? Ultimum hoc absurdum est. Ecquis unquam cogitavit per Potentiam Dei absurda talia esse concipienda & notanda? Atqui id ipsum fit ab illis quibuscum agimus, ab iis videlicet qui deserto veteri Philosophandi modo, novum amplectuntur, juxta quem sua, nisi per hæc absurda, nequeunt concordare. Nempe, ipsis fatentibus, ex voluntaria constitutione Dei, spatium, extensio actualis, materia, corpus, res una fuerint; & tamen secundum eosdem, innumera quædam spatia, extensaque numero diversa & dissita, non erunt diversa numero materia, sed una numero! Uni spatio alia addentur, & tamen nil addetur corpori! Spatia minuentur & tollentur & extensioni sive materiæ corporis nil decedet. Aderit initio parvum panis volumen, extensio manebit eadem, & tamen erit corpus magnum, hoc est extensio actu major millies! manebit sua extensio, nec tamen manebit sua (quæ eis idem est) materia, sive sua actualis extensio! Manebunt ejus extensionis figuræ eædem in particulis, in motu, in quiete, in dispositione; nec tamen manebit eadem natura particularis, quæ vel secundum eos in his ipsis particularum dispositionibus consistit! Aut suis novis de natura principiis, quæ tanquam in sana ratione fundata tenent, renuncient, hoc est, sanè (ut putant) rationi renuncient; aut fateantur se juxta ea sibi ipsis contradicere, hoc est sanam itidem rationem abnegare. Cui incommodo nil per Divinæ Potentiæ allegationem medentur. Etenim, An ut credant Deum Omnipotentem esse, debent judicare Deum ponentem & conservantem eandem extensionem, esse non-conservantem eandem extensionem, seu, quod iis idem est, eandem materiam? eum conservantem illam parvulam, esse in hoc ipso non-conservantem parvulam, sed maximam? Eum sustentantem figuras dispositionesque easdem, non esse sustentantem easdem sive (quod non differre statuunt) eandem, quæ prius erat, naturam corporis specialem? Vix sine risu ab intelligente Lectore possunt legi quæ bonus Cartesius in Responsionibus quartis operose desudat hac in re, unde tandem concludes, Deum conservantem eandem panis aut vini extensionem internam, eandemque externam, nempe terminos, limites, figuras, dispositionesque easdem, esse tamen non conservantem hæc ipsa, sive ipsum panem & vinum; & tamen ipsi extensio est materia, & illæ particularum dispositiones sunt ipsum principium ex quo essentia panis atque vini distinguitur a natura carnis & cæterorum corporum, quorum essentiæ, uti inter se distinguuntur, sunt (secundum illum & suos sequaces) istæ figurationes & modificationes. Quid igitur conservante Deo eandem extensionem cum omnibus ejus modis mutatum fuisse, quid ex his principiis (secundum quæ omnia quæ constituunt natu-ram invariata & immutata eadem manent) quid diversi præter nomen aliud, alium usum, alias relationes, accessisse judicabunt? Sed vi-deant quo sic eos sua principia deducent. Non est equidem animus de Religionis controversiis (quas præstaret ex toto supprimi) agere, aut de dogmate ipso hic ex professo tractare, nec examinare an per Veteris Philosophiæ scholasticæ principia (qualiacunque sint) explicari possit necne? Hoc viderint alii. Sed cum Author operis non incelebris Artis Cogitandi intempestive satis & jactanter cum adversariis hac de re juxta principia à se posita sibi triumphet, non putavi eum vel suos celari debere quam efficaciter juxta principia Cartesiana quæ passim proponit, contrarium asserto suo possint evincere sui, quos sua opinione belle debellat, adversarii; ut alias is & sui cautius procedant, vel in Scriptis Philosophicis ejusmodi controversias plane (non nimis suis novis speculationibus confisi) intermittant. Dicit ille ({a}) Sensus evidenter docere adesse rotunditatem & albedinem, sed non docere an has faciat apparere panis substantia. Quid vero secundum ejus principia respondebunt ejus adversarii? Nempe, ratio & sensus docent mansisse panis extensionem, mansisse extensionis particularum dispositionem, figurationem, motum, quietem, situm; & in his ipsis consistere naturam distinctionemque essentiæ corporum, tu ipse fateris. Qui ergo dices mutatam esse Panis substantiam? Quid est te judice illa substantia præter extensionem & modos (quæ tu fateris remanere) nisi nomen cassum, cujus nulla idea habetur? Cur posita idea, quam essentialem dicis, quæque & in sensu & intellectu evidenter invariata manet, substituas aliam rem quæ per ideam prorsus diversam debet percipi? Siccine dices Deum posuisse in me ideam qua me certum & unum quid voluerit concipere, & eadem idea non voluerit me ideam quod voluit, sed non-idem concipere, atque eum ita tendere positive in non-ens? Dicit Author, ratione constare nec corpus unum tempore eodem in locis duobus diversis, neque duo corpora in eodem loco esse posse: at vero id esse intelligendum de conditione naturali corporum: alioqui defectum fore rationis si putaremus mentem nostram, utpote finitam, comprehendere posse Dei Potentiam, quæ infinita est. At (inquiat nonnullus) an ergo tollam defectum rationis meæ, si putavero, Infinitatem Potentiæ Dei in hoc consistere, ut is agens & sustentans unum quid, mihique ejus essentiæ claram ideam exhibens, sit tamen id ipsum non-sustentans; & priori idea essentiali invariata, mihi non ejus ideam exhibens, sed alius cujuspiam, cujus ideam diversissimam fateris statuisse?
units.tr: For if you bring a dispute over the words God cannot, those words do not always imply a denial of God's power. Otherwise Holy Scripture would deny God's power when it uses them and says, God cannot deny himself. These words signify nothing other than that God is not subject to imperfection, and that nothing of the kind can be conceived as belonging to him which would involve imperfection. In this sense the words can, to be able and power are negative, for they denote a capacity for some imperfection; therefore they are to be removed from God by negation: cannot, non-power, and so on. It is not denied that God has a true and positive power, that is, an efficacy of effecting what he decides, nor is any limit given to him, unless perfection itself in every respect is taken as a limit. What is shown is that God's efficacious will does not dissent from itself in things that it decides to set in place. So far am I from attacking the divine power with a denial or a limit that, on the contrary, I affirm that God could have left the essences, truths and existences of all things in nothing, or could have established and effected other things, of which I can determine or conceive nothing at all. But I know that, once the ideas, essences, natures and truths of things are fixed, for example of extension or matter, of particular bodies, of figures, and so on, I cannot say that perhaps God can make a rectilinear triangle whose three angles are not equal to two right angles; perhaps he can make one body (granting that its nature consists in extension or spaciousness, as many have been persuaded) be wholly at the same time in two places; and so that the whole human body be contained in a much smaller extension than is laid down as belonging to its essence; or that the extension which has the figures, dispositions, motions and other modifications of bread or wine, and of their particles, be (for those who hold that the natures and essences of bread or wine consist in these) either blood or flesh, and so on, simply because God is omnipotent. Why, indeed, might you not also say that God perhaps can even deny himself, can deceive, can effect things which the efficient cause would not conceive, or will things which he would not will in the way he wills them, simply because he is omnipotent? I ask: what is understood by the power of God? Shall we understand by it a perfection of the divine will by which things are set in place as he wills, or rather as he does not will them? The latter is absurd. Has anyone ever thought that such absurdities are to be conceived and noted as belonging to God's power? And yet this very thing is done by those with whom we are dealing, namely by those who, having abandoned the old manner of philosophising, embrace a new one, according to which they cannot agree with their own tenets except through these absurdities. Indeed, by their own admission, from the voluntary constitution of God, space, actual extension, matter, body and thing were one; and yet, according to the same people, certain countless spaces, and extensions differing and dispersed in number, will not be diverse in number as matter, but one in number! Other space will be added to one space, and yet nothing will be added to the body! Spaces will be diminished and removed, and nothing will be lost from the extension or matter of the body. There will be at the beginning a small volume of bread, the extension will remain the same, and yet it will be a large body, that is, an extension actually a thousand times greater! Its extension will remain, and yet its matter (which to them is the same thing) or its actual extension will not remain its own! The figures of that extension will remain the same in the particles, in motion, in rest, in arrangement; and yet the particular nature, which according to them consists in these very dispositions of the particles, will not remain the same! Either they must renounce their new principles about nature, which they hold as founded in sound reason, that is, they must (as they think) renounce reason itself; or they must confess that by these principles they contradict themselves, that is, equally deny sound reason. The appeal to divine power does nothing to remedy this inconvenience. For, that they may believe God to be omnipotent, must they judge that God, positing and preserving the same extension, is not preserving the same extension, or, which is the same to them, the same matter? That in preserving that small extension he is, in this very act, not preserving a small extension but a very great one? That in sustaining the same figures and dispositions he is not sustaining the same, or (which they hold to differ in no way) the same specific nature of body that was there before? Hardly without laughter can an intelligent reader read what the good Cartesius laboriously sweats out on this matter in his Fourth Replies, whence you would finally conclude that God, preserving the same internal extension of bread or wine, and the same external extension, namely the same termini, limits, figures and dispositions, is nevertheless not preserving these very things, that is, the bread and wine itself; and yet extension is matter for him, and those dispositions of the particles are the very principle by which the essence of bread and wine is distinguished from the nature of flesh and of other bodies, whose essences, as they are distinguished from one another, are (according to him and his followers) those figurations and modifications. What then, when God preserves the same extension with all its modes, has been changed? What different thing, other than a name, a different use, and different relations, will they judge to have been added, when from these principles (according to which all things that constitute the nature remain unchanged and unaltered and the same) they arrive at such a conclusion? But let them see where their principles lead them. It is indeed not my intention to deal with the controversies of religion (which it would be better to suppress altogether), nor to treat the dogma itself here professedly, nor to examine whether or not it can be explained by the principles of the old scholastic philosophy (whatever they may be). Let others see to that. But since the author of the not unfamous Art of Thinking triumphs too unseasonably and boastfully over his adversaries on this matter according to the principles he has laid down, I did not think that he or his followers should be spared the demonstration of how effectively, according to the Cartesian principles which he everywhere proposes, his own adherents can prove the contrary of his assertion, those adversaries whom in his opinion he handsomely defeats; so that he and his followers may proceed more cautiously in future, or altogether refrain from such controversies in philosophical writings, not trusting too much in their new speculations. He says: The senses clearly teach that roundness and whiteness are present, but they do not teach whether the substance of bread causes these to appear. But what will his adversaries reply according to his principles? Namely, reason and the senses teach that the extension of the bread has remained, that the arrangement, figuration, motion, rest and position of the extension of the particles have remained; and that the nature and distinction of the essence of bodies consists in these very things, as you yourself confess. Why then will you say that the substance of the bread has been changed? What, in your judgement, is that substance apart from extension and modes (which you confess remain), other than an empty name of which no idea is had? Why, having posited the idea which you call essential, and which remains evidently unchanged both in sense and in intellect, would you substitute another thing which must be perceived through an idea wholly different? Will you say in this way that God has placed in me an idea by which he willed me to conceive something certain and one, and that the same God, by the same idea, did not will me to conceive what he willed, but something not the same, and so tends positively toward non-being? The author says: It is established by reason that neither one body can be at the same time in two different places, nor can two bodies be in the same place; but this must be understood of the natural condition of bodies; otherwise there would be a defect of reason if we thought that our mind, being finite, could comprehend the power of God, which is infinite. But (someone may object) shall I remove the defect of my reason if I think that the infinity of God's power consists in this: that he, acting and sustaining one thing, and presenting to me a clear idea of its essence, is nevertheless not sustaining that same thing; and, the earlier essential idea remaining unchanged, is presenting to me not its idea but the idea of some other thing, whose wholly different idea you confess he has established?

units.la: Sed obsecro, quid etiam Authori nostro est illa, quam is narrat, conditio naturalis corporum in genere, nisi eorum naturæ constitutio, nisi ipsa natura, nisi ipsa corpora, nisi statutum & effectus voluntatis Dei, quæ voluit corpora esse talis naturæ, sive eorum naturam esse talem qua-lem is Author concipit esse? Adeoque sibi contradicit asserendo corpus, manens corpus, conditionem naturalem, sive suam naturam corpo-ream, mutare: Sic enim diceretur id non amplius esse corpus; Deumque velle ut naturam haberet corporis, & non haberet eodem tempore dum eam haberet, sive dum, te fatente, esset & maneret corpus. Sed forte satius fuerit Authori nostro & illis qui cum eo ex iisdem principiis Philosophantur, concludere, Deum potius se ipsum ut aliquid ponen-tem, statuentem, volentem, approbaturum simul & improbaturum, Deique Potentiam in hoc consistere, quam ut ii in illis quæ admiserunt fallantur. Ego vero facilius crediderim posse dari in Authore nostro Potentiam idem dicendi & non dicendi, statuendi & non statuendi, hoc est, sibi contradicendi, quam in Deo Potentiam idem simul ponendi & non ponendi, statuendi (secundum nostrum Authorem) talem corporum naturam in genere & in specie, & tamen eam non conservan-di dum omnia quæ in his ipsis sunt & (secundum Authoris nostri phi-losophemata,) hæc ipsa sunt, eadem conservat. Qua contradictione splendidior dari nequit.
units.tr: But I beg you, what does our author's so-called natural condition of bodies in general amount to, except the constitution of their nature, except nature itself, except the bodies themselves, except the decree and effect of the will of God, who willed bodies to be of such a nature, or willed their nature to be of such a kind as this author conceives it? And so he contradicts himself in asserting that a body, while remaining a body, changes its natural condition, that is, its corporeal nature. For then it would be said that it is no longer a body; and God would be said to will that it have the nature of a body, and at the same time not to have it, while it had it, that is, while, as you admit, it is and remains a body. But perhaps it would be better for our author, and for those who philosophise with him from the same principles, to conclude that God, as one who posits, decrees, wills, approves and at the same time disapproves, and that the power of God consists in this, rather than that they should be deceived in those things they have admitted. Indeed I would more readily believe that there can be in our author a power of saying and not saying the same thing, of decreeing and not decreeing, that is, of contradicting himself, than that there is in God a power of simultaneously positing and not positing, decreeing (according to our author) such a nature of bodies in general and in particular, and yet not preserving it, while he preserves those very things that are in them and (according to the philosophical tenets of our author) are these very things. No greater contradiction can be found than this.

units.la: XIV. Et huc me impulit Authoris Artis Cogitandi intempestiva di-gressio, & securus nimis ex suis principiis triumphus. Sed quia bellorum plus satis, eaque ex hac doctrina abundantissime ad odia & cædes usque pullularunt, præsertim circa adorationem quæ in hoc Sacramento fit vel omittitur; operæ pretium fuerit, si obiter ostendatur quam leniter fuisset hic actum si tantum cum ratione & modo universi processissent. Dissentitur de præsentia Humanitatis Domini: Deinde de Adoratione. Omnis fere dissensus qui inter homines de doctrinis est, inde oritur, quod verba quibus utuntur neutri clare explicent sive definiant. Peto hic definitiones, Quid intelligant per Adorationem? Si per τὸ adorare intelligant agnoscere & amplecti aliquod Ens pro Ente Summo, Æterno, Auctore & Sustentatore omnium: hoc sensu, sola Divina Natura est adoranda, nam est tale Ens, & humana non est Ens ejusmodi, nec pro tali haberi potest. Quodsi per τὸ adorare intelligunt (sensu altero) agnoscere aliquod Ens (puta humanitatem J.Christi) pro nobilissima & exaltatissima creatura (utpote unita strictissime cum Divinitate) & hanc internam agnitionem testari signis quibusdam externis, puta prostratione corporis, &c. hoc sensu (qui in sacris Authoribus locum habet) Creatura quæ est in Christo, hoc est ejus humanitas, quæ strictissime juncta Divinitati, & omnium creaturarum caput, est adoranda, ut patet ex ipsa verborum Significatione data. Et hæc constant inter omnes. Constat & hoc, Deum sensu primo esse adorandum in præsentia vel absentia sui corporis, utut id absens vel præsens sit vel putetur.
units.tr: XIV. And the untimely digression of our author's Art of Thinking, and his overly confident triumph on the basis of his own principles, have driven me to this. But since wars have sprouted more than enough, and from this doctrine hatreds and slaughter have sprung up most abundantly, especially concerning the adoration that is or is not offered in this Sacrament, it will be worth the effort to show in passing how gently this matter would have been handled had men proceeded only with reason and moderation. They disagree about the presence of the Lord's humanity; then about adoration. Almost every disagreement that exists among men about doctrines arises from this, that neither side clearly explains or defines the words they use. I ask here for definitions: what do they understand by adoration? If by adorare they understand to acknowledge and embrace some being as the supreme, eternal, author and sustainer of all, then in this sense only the divine nature is to be adored, for it is such a being, and the human nature is not a being of this kind, nor can it be held to be one. But if by adorare they understand, in the other sense, to acknowledge some being (for example the humanity of Jesus Christ) as the most noble and most exalted creature (inasmuch as it is most closely united with the divinity), and to attest this inward acknowledgement by certain outward signs, for example prostration of the body, and so on, then in this sense (which has its place in the sacred authors) the creature that is in Christ, that is, his humanity, which is most closely joined to the divinity and is the head of all creatures, is to be adored, as is clear from the very meaning of the words given. And these points are agreed by all. It is also agreed that God is to be adored in the first sense, whether his body is present or absent, whether it is absent or present or is thought to be so.

units.la: Jam si quis putet corpus Domini non adesse, confiteatur tamen adorationem Divinam primo sensu, sed actum adorationis secundo sensu sumptæ exhibere nolit, sive, nolit mente & gestibus agnoscere aliquam creaturam (puta panem Eu-charisticum) esse illam nobilissimam creaturam quam Deus sibi univit, (quam si adesse putaret, sensu jam dicto, altero, adoraret, ut & adorandam confitetur) tunc is impietatis & rejectionis Dei, ut fit à cæce fer-vidis, accusari non posse patet: nam, quanquam erraret, ejus error non esset de rebus ipsis, nempe de ea adoratione quæ Divinitatem concernit; neque de ea quæ humanitatem respicit, quam sensu dicto admittit; Sed tantum de circumstantia rei circa locum humanitatis; An ea humanitas, quam si crederet adesse, utique (juxta secundam definitionem) adoraret; sit in hoc loco, necne? Eccur ideo tanta odia? Quod si quis putans humanitatem adesse, eam solam ut creaturam & sine Divinitate spectatam, adoraret juxta primum adorationis sensum, is quidem sub-stitueret sive agnosceret creaturam pro Creatore, sive erraret in objecto adorationis primæ (neque hoc excusare vellem;) At si quis ad Deum attendens, ei adorationem primam deferat in præsentia (etsi putativa solum) ejus humanitatis, quam quoque sua debita (altero sensu) adoratione veneretur, hanc omissurus si illam abesse putaret; is ab iis qui ipsum errare putant, non est de alio crimine incusandus, quam quod circa circumstantiam rei, nempe loci humanitatis, hallucinetur. Neque habent partes dissentientes majus quod sibi cum evidentia exprobrent; & quantum una errat opinione alterius, tantum & altera opinione prioris, ita ut reciprocum sit crimen, quod una in aliam nequit suo judicio opinionique gravius reddere, quin se ipsam opinioni alterius ut gravius errantem repræsentet; crimen autem est circa quæstionem de circumstantia externa. At quale crimen, si quis putans corpus Domini adesse, inde occasionem sumat amandi Deum, reputans illum eousque suæ infirmitati condescendere (ut sic dicam) & se accommodare; aut si quis putans Domini corpus abesse, cogitet id fieri ne externæ præsentiæ nimis adhæ-reat, adeoque ut quærat pure per amorem uniri cum Spiritu Christi? Ecce, quo deventum fuisset si moderamine & ratione essent usi! Nam hæc meridiana luce clariora sunt. Sed forte eis invisa qui partes amant, vellentque odiorum & rixarum prætextus æternum remanere: Quibus, in gratiam quorumvis cordatorum, non est quod eousque placeatur. Sed redeamus ad propositum, videlicet Potentiam Dei.
units.tr: Now if someone thinks that the body of the Lord is not present, yet confesses that divine adoration is due in the first sense, but refuses to perform the act of adoration in the second sense, that is, refuses in mind and gesture to acknowledge some creature (for example the Eucharistic bread) to be that most noble creature whom God has united to himself (which, if he thought it present, he would adore in the second sense, as he confesses it is to be adored), then it is clear that he cannot be accused of impiety or of rejecting God, as blindly fervent people do. For although he would be in error, his error would not concern the things themselves, namely that adoration which concerns the divinity, nor that which regards the humanity, which he admits in the sense stated; but only the circumstance of the thing with regard to the place of the humanity: whether that humanity, which if he believed it present he would certainly (according to the second definition) adore, is in this place or not. Why then such great hatreds? And if someone who thinks the humanity present adores it alone, as a creature and considered apart from the divinity, according to the first sense of adoration, then indeed he would be substituting, or acknowledging, a creature in place of the Creator, or would be in error about the object of the first adoration (nor would I wish to excuse this). But if someone, attending to God, offers him the first adoration in the presence (though only supposed) of that humanity, which he also venerates with its due adoration (in the second sense), and would give up this if he thought it absent, then those who think him in error are not to accuse him of any other crime than that he is mistaken about the circumstance of the thing, namely the place of the humanity. Nor do the dissenting parties have any greater charge to bring against each other with evidence; and as far as one errs in the opinion of the other, so far the other errs in the opinion of the first, so that the charge is reciprocal, and one party cannot, by its own judgment and opinion, make the other's opinion appear more grievous without at the same time representing its own opinion as the more grievously erring. The charge, moreover, concerns a question about an external circumstance. But what crime is there if someone who thinks the body of the Lord present takes from this an occasion to love God, reflecting that he so condescends (so to speak) to our weakness and accommodates himself to it; or if someone who thinks the Lord's body absent reflects that this is done lest we cling too closely to an external presence, and so seeks to be united purely through love with the Spirit of Christ? See how far things would have gone had they used moderation and reason! For these things are clearer than the noonday light. But perhaps they will be unwelcome to those who love factions and wish the pretext for hatreds and quarrels to remain forever. To them, for the sake of any sensible persons, there is no need to yield further. But let us return to our purpose, namely the power of God.

units.la: XV. Superest ut considerem Divinam Potentiam in respectu ad existentiam rerum. Quamvis Dei Potentia sit ejus Naturæ essentiale attributum & necessarium, non tamen putandum est, res quæ per illam existunt, absolute necessarias esse, sive necessario existere. Nam etiamsi de his cogitans necessario judicare debeam, posito Deum velle aliquid esse, voluntatis ejus efficaciam tantam esse, ut sufficiat ad existentiæ rei illius positionem; non tamen est necesse ut Deus tale quid potius quam aliud, vel plane nihil, voluerit. Ergo, quemadmodum supra de rerum essentia & veritate, sic jam de earum existentia dicimus, etiamsi nulla esset, nec futura esset unquam, Deum semper nihilominus Potentem fore, quoniam hæc perfectio & efficacia ab ejus voluntate est inseparabilis, ut, si velit, res futuræ sint. Nota in transitu, cum omnia quoad essentiam & existentiam potuerint in æternum esse nihil, solius Dei necessitatem & sufficientiam. Sicut autem ex ejus Potentia est, ut si velit res esse, futuræ ideo sint, ita quoque reciproce dico, Si res, quæcunque sint, existunt, (ut revera existunt multæ, quarum compages mundus dicitur,) omnes per hanc vim, rationem & causam existunt quod Deus eas sic voluerit: sive, Omnia quæ existunt, à Dei voluntate efficaci sive Potentia, efficiuntur. Quod ex demonstratis sic deducitur. Si Deus aliquid velit existere, ob hoc ipsum velle res existet: At Deus vult res omnes esse ut jam sunt: nam si vellet aliter esse, nec tamen essent, ejus voluntas non esset potens. Igitur quod Deus velit res omnes esse id quod jam sunt, id velle est causa & ratio & vis positionis sive existentiæ omnium istarum rerum. Præterea, Nullæ res præter Deum necessario existunt sive habent in se rationem existentiæ suæ, ut in loco de Sufficientia Dei visum est: Ergo omnes res alibi rationem existentiæ habent. At alibi, ultra omnes res, nulla est res nisi Deus: Et cum in Deo consideretur ejus Natura se sola contenta, à qua nil procedit præter ipsum Deum; dein ejus placitum indifferens in determinatione ad externa; sequitur, hoc placitum sive hanc voluntatem quatenus determinata est ut ei placuit, esse rationem & causam existentiæ rerum. Sine hac, res carentes causa, tum interna, nempe necessitate essentiæ & existentiæ, tum externa, scilicet efficiente, nullæ omnino essent. Plures non adferam hujus veritatis probationes quæ ex aliis Dei attributis desumi[?] possunt, siquidem hoc sit eorum vis, ut sese mutuo probent.
units.tr: XV. It remains for me to consider the divine power in relation to the existence of things. Although the power of God is an essential and necessary attribute of his nature, it is not to be thought that the things which exist through it are absolutely necessary, or exist necessarily. For even if, thinking about these things, I must judge necessarily, supposing that God wills something to be, his will is so efficacious that it suffices to bring that thing into existence; yet it is not necessary that God should have willed this rather than something else, or nothing at all. Therefore, just as above we have said of the essence and truth of things, so now we say of their existence, that even if none existed, and none ever would, God would nevertheless always be powerful, since this perfection and efficacy is inseparable from his will, so that, if he willed, things would come to be. Note in passing that, since all things could in eternity have been nothing, both in essence and in existence, this shows the necessity and sufficiency of God alone. But just as it lies in his power that, if he wills things to be, they will therefore be, so conversely I say: if things, whatever they are, do exist (as in fact many do exist, whose frame is called the world), they all exist through this force, reason and cause, that God has willed them so; that is, all things that exist are brought about by the efficacious or powerful will of God. This is deduced from what has been demonstrated as follows. If God wills something to exist, by that very willing the thing will exist. But God wills all things to be as they now are; for if he willed them to be otherwise, and yet they were not, his will would not be powerful. Therefore, that God wills all things to be what they now are, this willing is the cause, the reason and the power of the positing or existence of all those things. Moreover, no things other than God exist necessarily, or have within themselves the reason of their existence, as was shown in the place on the sufficiency of God; therefore all other things have the reason of their existence elsewhere. But beyond all things there is nothing but God. And since in God we consider his nature, which is sufficient in itself, from which nothing proceeds except God himself; then his pleasure, indifferent in its determination toward external things; it follows that this pleasure, or this will insofar as it is determined as it pleased him, is the reason and cause of the existence of things. Without this, things lacking cause, both internal, namely the necessity of essence and existence, and external, namely the efficient cause, would not exist at all. I shall not give more proofs of this truth, which can be drawn from the other attributes of God, if indeed this is their force, that they mutually prove one another.

units.la: XVI. Cum dixi res omnes existentes, quales jam sunt, à sola Divini placiti efficacia poni, satis intelligitur, primo, hoc ad errorem & peccatum non esse extendendum, nam non sunt res, sed defectus, nec sunt rerum seu perfectionum existentiae, nec quid positivi, adeoque non opus eis est positiva causa ut ponantur. Secundo, per hoc patet, omnia quae realitatem habent his includi, à maximis ad minima: ipsae res, substantiae, earum perfectiones, proprietates, modi, duratio, longa brevisve, verbo, omnia, talia sunt, durant, stant, diversificantur, nulla alia de causa, quam quia Deus vult. Atque hoc non modo est de substantia corporea quae terram, coelos, & omnia quae in eis sunt, constituit, de ejus omnibus particulis, earumque figuris, motibus, dispositionibus, motuum determinationibus, quae etsi consensui Cogitationis creatae jungantur, non minus tamen sola vi divina ponuntur; sed etiam id ad omnes Mentes, earumque modos, debet extendi.
units.tr: XVI. When I said that all existing things, in the state they now are, are established by the sole efficacy of the Divine pleasure, it is sufficiently clear, first, that this must not be extended to error and sin, for these are not things but defects, and they are neither things nor existences of perfections, nor anything positive; therefore they do not need a positive cause in order to be established. Second, from this it is evident that all things which have reality are included here, from the greatest to the least: the things themselves, substances, their perfections, properties, modes, duration, long or short; in a word, all things are such, endure, stand, and differ, for no other reason than because God wills it. And this holds not only of corporeal substance, which constitutes the earth, the heavens, and all that is in them, of all its particles, their figures, motions, dispositions, and the determinations of motions, which, although they are joined to the consent of created thought, are nonetheless established by divine power alone; but this must also be extended to all Minds and their modes.

units.la: Præjudicium est puerile, cogitandi modos, hanc illamve cogitationem, scientiam, judicia, affectus, consuetudines, determinationes ad has illasve ideas, actusque omnes internos, quatenus in illis est aliquid positivi & non-nihil, minus à Potentia Dei pendere & effici quam modos corporeos. Scilicet ubi corpus aliquod novos induet modos, ut si lutum induceret formam humani corporis, si mons ex loco transportaretur, si planetarum motus in contrarium determinaretur, tunc hæc ut maxime positiva spectata ad maximam causam referentur; nec tamen id fieret cum Mentis modi mutantur & novi accedunt, cum Mens ignorans fit cognoscens, cum Deum nosse, optare, amare, &c. incipit! id à Causa Summa vel non efficeretur, vel parum esset! Cum tamen in hoc sit millies plus realitatis sive perfectionis, quam in totius universi motibus eorumve mutationibus. Puerorum est ubi nil corporei occurrit, vel nil quod coactivo modo nos afficiat, ut in illis quae Menti cum ejus consensu accidunt, ibi nil magni effici, vel nil prorsus, judicare, quare etiam quidam se à Deo sustentari non capiebant, quia id violento modo in se agi non experiebantur. Sed ut quis animadvertat quantae sint in modis mentium perfectiones realitatesque, reputet apud se, totam totius universi materiam, utut perfecta sit, ne unius quidem ex suis perfectionibus vel imperfectionibus esse conscium, qua perfectione nullus cogitandi modus destituitur: advertat deinde, quanta sit inter stupidam, ignaram, vel vitiosam, improbamque, & inter solertem, diligengentem, atque probam Mentem differentia, etsi tantum modalis sit, non enim inter Sanctum Angelum & Diabolum differentia est quoad 'essentiam: consideret omnia quae fiunt in mentibus, in mundo, in Rebuspublicis,&c. ex occasione modorum mentis fieri: attendat ad dif-ferentias idearum quibus modificantur cogitationes, ad diversitatem modorum quibus Mens in ideata fertur, v. g. in Deum, creaturasve, aurum, lutum, &c. amore, odio, tristitia, negligentia, &c. quanta in positione quorumdam prae aliis perfectio & realitas! quanta graduum perfectionis diversitas! quanta in quorumdam absentia negatio, pri-vatio, imperfectio! De illis quae privativa sunt, alibi: at de positivis, omnes cogitationes, earumque modi, cognitionis, judiciorum, scien-tiae, affectuum, omnium facultatum extensio, termini, actus, nu-merus, via, circumstantiae, omnia, à Dei voluntate efficaci poni, ex vi demonstrationum praecedentium fatendum est. Cum enim omnis realitas à placiti Divini efficacia efficiatur, quomodo hae ei subtrahen-tur? Denique, tertio, de objecto Potentiae Dei existente est advertendum, id esse res quas dixi, corporeas & spirituales omnes, earumque modos, sive à natura sive à gratia procedere dicantur, seu naturales, seu supernaturales aut coelestes vocentur. Non vere dicitur, homi-nem aliquid positivi ex se posse in naturalibus, aut politicis, qui in su-pernaturalibus, sive spiritualibus, quae statum gratiae spectant, nil pos-sit. quasi vero natura magis esset independens quam gratia! quasi creatura in statu naturae minus penderet à Deo quam in statu gratiae, ma-gisque ex se conferret in uno quam in alio statu. Perperam hic distin-guitur ubi nil hoc sensu est distinguendum. Omne & quodcunque est extra & praeter Deum, ex se nihil est, neque id, nisi Deo volente, quia & quatenus vult, existere potest. An vel minimum positivum est praeter & ultra Dei voluntatem? An praeter Deum datur aliquid quod sit sui existentis causa & ratio; & quod dicere posset, Deus me non po-suit, sed Ego memet independenter ab illo? Certe, causam vel minimi positivi quaerere extra Deum abnegatio Dei est: Et, siquidem aliquid putetur posse concipi ut independens à Deo, miror cur id non magis sta-tuatur de rebus perfectioribus, de summa quae in hominibus esse possit cognitione, doctrina, felicitate, conservatione vitae, & similibus, quam de minoribus quae in iisdem, qualia sunt ire, loqui,aliaeque actiones natu-rales aut politicae, quibus minus perfectionis & Potentiae inesse est agno-scendum. Si esse à se alicui praeter Deum tribuere velis, probabilius id de perfectioribus quam de imperfectioribus censere deberes.
units.tr: It is a childish prejudice to think that modes of thinking, this or that thought, knowledge, judgments, affections, habits, determinations toward these or those ideas, and all internal acts, insofar as there is something positive and not a little in them, depend less upon the Power of God and are effected less than corporeal modes. For when some body takes on new modes, as if clay were to take on the form of a human body, if a mountain were moved from its place, if the motions of the planets were determined in the opposite direction, then these, regarded as most positive, are referred to the greatest cause; and yet this does not happen when the modes of a Mind change and new ones arise, when a Mind that was ignorant becomes knowing, when it begins to know God, to desire, to love God, and so on! Would this be effected by the Supreme Cause not at all, or only slightly? Yet in this there is a thousand times more reality or perfection than in the motions of the whole universe or their changes. It is a mark of children to judge that nothing great, or nothing at all, is effected where nothing bodily occurs, or nothing that affects us in a compulsive way, as in those things which happen to the Mind with its consent; and so some people did not understand that they were sustained by God, because they did not experience this being done in them in a violent manner. But so that someone may notice how great the perfections and realities are in the modes of minds, let him consider within himself the whole matter of the entire universe, however perfect it may be, which is not aware of even one of its perfections or imperfections, and which lacks no perfection that any mode of thinking lacks. Let him then notice how great is the difference between a stupid, ignorant, or vicious and wicked Mind and a skilful, diligent, and upright Mind, even though this difference is only modal; for there is no difference in essence between a Holy Angel and the Devil. Let him consider that all things which happen in minds, in the world, in commonwealths, etc., happen on the occasion of the modes of the mind; let him attend to the differences of ideas by which thoughts are modified, to the diversity of the modes by which the Mind is carried toward its object, for example toward God or creatures, gold, clay, etc., by love, hatred, sadness, negligence, etc.; how great is the perfection and reality in the positing of some over others! How great is the diversity of degrees of perfection! How great is the negation, privation, and imperfection in the absence of some! Concerning those things which are privative, [we speak] elsewhere; but concerning the positive ones, from the force of the preceding demonstrations, it must be admitted that all thoughts and their modes, of knowledge, judgments, science, affections, of all faculties, their extension, limits, acts, number, way, circumstances, all are established by the efficacious will of God. For since all reality is effected by the efficacy of the Divine pleasure, how could these be withdrawn from it? Finally, third, concerning the object of the Power of God, it must be noted that it is the things I have named, all corporeal and spiritual things, and their modes, whether they are said to proceed from nature or from grace, whether they are called natural, supernatural, or heavenly. It is not rightly said that man can do something positive of himself in natural or civil matters, but can do nothing in supernatural or spiritual matters, which concern the state of grace—as if nature were more independent than grace! As if a creature in the state of nature depended less upon God than in the state of grace, and as if it contributed more of itself in one state than in the other state. Here a distinction is wrongly drawn where, in this sense, nothing is to be distinguished. Everything and whatever is outside and apart from God is of itself nothing, and it can exist only if God wills it, and insofar as he wills it. Is there even the least positive thing apart from and beyond the will of God? Is there something apart from God which is the cause and reason of its own existence, and which could say: God did not place me, but I placed myself independently of him? Certainly, to seek the cause of even the least positive thing outside God is a denial of God. And if something is thought to be capable of being conceived as independent of God, I wonder why this is not rather asserted of the more perfect things, of the highest knowledge, learning, happiness, preservation of life, and the like, which may be in men, than of the lesser things which are in the same men, such as going, speaking, and other natural or civil actions, in which less perfection and power is to be acknowledged. If you are willing to attribute being from itself to anything apart from God, you ought to judge this more probable of the more perfect things than of the less perfect ones.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Agnita Dei in omnia quæ existunt Potentia, nonnulla specialius de illa quærenda sunt, nempe, Quomodo actu rem quamque ponat? An res absolute, an vero sub certa conditione existere efficiat? Tertio, cur res nonnullæ contingenter, aliæ vero necessario existere dicantur? Tandem verbum unum alterumve de creatione & conservatione faciendum erit. De prima quæstione superfluum esset aliquid dicere, post ea quæ de efficacia divinæ voluntatis dicta sunt, nisi essent nonnulli qui præjudicio importuno falsoque ratiocinio præoccupati, rem claram tenebris involverent, obscurisque vocibus, dum subtilitates proferri à se putant, implicarent. Nempe cum unusquisque attendit ad se dum vult res quasdam externas incipere fieri per ipsius interventum, animadvertere potest, ad effectum non sufficere potentiam suam, sive quod possit suo modo, neque etiam sufficere quod velit seu decreverit rem esse; sed oportere cum his singularem virium contentionem explicare atqueMentis conatum, quem alii actum imperatum vocant, & cujus differentiam à simplici efficiendi voluntate sensu satis metimur omnes. Unde est, quod forte nemo sit, qui non tale quid de Deo, res antea non existentes efficiente, aliquando cogitaverit, maxime in primis quæ post infantiam formata sunt de illo judiciis, quæ apud multos nunquam corriguntur. Memini me, ni fallor, tale alicubi præjudicium simili ratiocinatione firmatum, vidisse: Res non incipiunt existere sive poni quia Deus est Potens, nam semper talis fuit, nec res semper fuere, & hac ratione etiam res plures quam sunt esse deberent; nec ponuntur quia est volens, nam dicitur fuisse volens ab æterno, nec ideo tamen res existebant, imo multa vult, quæ nondum ideo exurgunt, sed demum post plura secula futura sunt: Igitur præter Potentiam cum voluntate ut res ex nihilo in existentiam veniant, aliquid insuper requisiverunt, quod, si bene memini, actualem efficaciam vocarunt; eamque cum Voluntate & Potentia junctam res ponere existentes, quæ prius possibi-les erant. Sed ejusmodi crassis subtilitatibus non est opus. Non est Deus similis nostri, qui conamina ejusmodi violenta & transeuntia in se experiatur & extra se explicet. Sola Dei Potentis voluntas sufficit ut res existere incipiant, non quidem simul, cum illa Voluntas in Deo esse concipitur; sed eo tempore, momento, iisque circumstantiis, in qui-bus Deus ante omne tempus voluit res tales & tales existere. Ultra hoc nil requiritur: nec absurda, quibus instabatur, vim habent, si dixe-ro, Deum ita perfectam Cogitationem esse, ut quæ ante tempus voluit cogitare tali tempore modoque fore, ideo, quia voluit, etiam eodem tem-pore, modo, loco, &c. quomodo voluit, existant.
units.tr: Having recognised God's power over all things that exist, some points about it need to be examined more particularly, namely: How does he actually bring each thing into being? Does he make a thing exist absolutely, or only under a certain condition? Thirdly, why are some things said to exist contingently and others necessarily? Finally, something must be said about creation and conservation. Of the first question it would be superfluous to say anything, after what has been said about the efficacy of the divine will, were it not that some people, preoccupied with an unseasonable prejudice and false reasoning, wrap a clear matter in darkness and, while they think they are putting forward subtleties, entangle it in obscure words. For when each person reflects on himself, while he wills that some external things begin to be made through his own agency, he can observe that his power is not enough for the effect, either because he can do it in his own way or because it is not enough that he wills or decrees the thing to be; but it is necessary to bring to bear a particular exertion of strength with these, and a striving of the mind, which others call the commanded act, and whose difference from the simple volition to effect we all sufficiently perceive by feeling. Hence it is that perhaps no one exists who has never thought something of this kind about God, bringing into being things that did not previously exist, especially those judgments about him formed after infancy, which in many people are never corrected. I remember, if I am not mistaken, having seen somewhere such a prejudice supported by similar reasoning: Things do not begin to exist or be set in place because God is powerful, for he has always been such, and things have not always been, and by this reasoning things ought to be more numerous than they are; nor are they set in place because he is willing, for he is said to have been willing from eternity, and yet things did not therefore exist; indeed he wills many things which do not therefore arise, but only come to be after many ages. Therefore, besides power and will, that things may come from nothing into existence, they have required something further, which, if I remember rightly, they called actual efficacy; and they held that this, joined with will and power, causes things to exist which were previously possible. But such crude subtleties are not needed. God is not like us, who experiences in himself such violent and transient efforts and expresses them outside himself. The mere will of the powerful God is enough for things to begin to exist; not indeed at the same time as that will is conceived to be in God, but at the time, moment, and in those circumstances in which God, before all time, willed such and such things to exist. Beyond this nothing is required; nor do the absurdities urged against this have any force, if I say that God's thought is so perfect that what he willed before time to be thought to happen at such a time and in such a manner, therefore exists precisely because he willed it, at the same time, in the same manner, place, and so on, as he willed.

units.la: XVIII. Ex his facile est ea deducere quæ quæstioni secundæ satis-faciant. Nempe si Deus velit res sub quadam conditione & talibus cir-cumstantiis fieri, sequitur res non absolute, sed sub conditione existere, qua posita res ponantur, absente vero, non existant. Atque id probatur ex omnibus quæcunque fiunt & existunt, corporeis & spiritualibus, naturalibus & moralibus. Corpus meum, exempli gratia, non movetur, sive, certo modo determinatur in motu suo, nisi sub conditione inter-ventus voluntatis meæ: Mens humana non incipit existere, nisi corpus quoddam ei uniendum disponatur: In eadem, scientiam virtutemque non ponit Deus, nisi sub conditione attentionis, precum, hortatio-num, &c. uti nec vivet corpus, nisi mediantibus cibis auxilioque homi-num; & ita de cæteris. Nec tamen sequitur ex dictis, Deum pendere à creatura, aut se illi subjicere, aut mutabilem concipi, cum asseritur his, similibusque verbis veritatem denotari, videlicet, si hoc non fuisset, neque illud secutum esset, si hoc accidisset, non fuisset hic vel ille mortuus, aut aliud quid, & quæ ejusmodi de quibusvis eventibus dici possunt, & vera sunt: Nam, hæ regulæ agendi, sive conditiones ut agat Deus, non sunt Deo à creaturis impositæ, sed Deus eas suis operationibus præscripsit, quatenus noluit nisi sub hisce conditionibus operari. unde eas constan-ter observat, idque non necessario, quasi aliter nec potuisset nec pos-set, sed quod ex arbitrii sui libertate præscriptas, easdem ei constan-ter placeat observare; nisi quod, ut ostendat se non ideo illis alligari, atque se à nullis pendere, interdum non nihil aliter efficiat, & tunc mi-racula dicitur operari, de quibus mox. Sed, quod ad hanc rem præci-puum est, non creaturæ talium conditionum existentiam & circumstantias ponunt, verum ipse Deus eas cum omnibus, ut probatum est, ponit omnes. Cum ergo dicitur, si tale quid non fuisset, neque illud, quod secutum est, fuisset factum, id sic resolvi debet: Si hoc non fuisset, id est, si hoc Deus noluisset & non posuisset, signum fuisset eum noluisse nec positurum fuisse id quod secutum est. Principium est, ille ponit antecedens, Consummator est, ponit consequens: & cum non ponit antecedens, eo ipso notat se non positurum consequens: nam modus quo agit ordinarius convincit nos de nexu operationum ejus, quem cum observet ille, nos quoque diligenter observare debemus. Nec dici potest, Deum, quo pluribus mediis operatur, eo magis quasi indigentem videri, minusque Potentem: quin contra, eo majoris Liberalitatis Potentiæque argumenta luculentiora proponit, quo majori mediorum apparatu res efficit: cum media etiam æque ac res cæteras efficiat. Sed hominem de egestate palpabili modo sic convincit, ejusque fastum reprimit, dum cum sub legibus quibusdam, tum materiæ, tum motus, tum agnitionis miseriæ defectusque, & petitionis auxilii alieni, subjecit, ut hac debeat ad scopum suum transitus fieri.
units.tr: XVIII. From these things it is easy to deduce what will satisfy the second question. Namely, if God wills that things should come to be under a certain condition and in such circumstances, it follows that things exist not absolutely but under a condition, so that when the condition is posited things are set in place, but when it is absent they do not exist. And this is proved from all things that are made and exist, bodily and spiritual, natural and moral. My body, for example, is not moved, or is not determined in its motion in a certain way, except under the condition of the intervention of my will. The human mind does not begin to exist unless some body is prepared to be united to it. In the same way God does not bestow knowledge and virtue except under the condition of attention, prayers, exhortations, and so on; just as a body will not live unless by means of food and the help of men; and so on for the rest. Nor does it follow from what has been said that God depends on creatures, or subjects himself to them, or is conceived as changeable, when it is asserted, in these and similar words, that a truth is indicated, namely: if this had not happened, that would not have followed; if this had happened, this or that man would not have died, or something else; and whatever can be said of such events, and is true. For these rules of acting, or conditions under which God acts, have not been imposed on God by creatures; rather God has prescribed them by his own operations, inasmuch as he was unwilling to act except under these conditions. Hence he constantly observes them, and this not of necessity, as if he could not have acted otherwise or could not be otherwise, but because, having prescribed them by the freedom of his own choice, he is pleased to observe them constantly. Yet, so that he may show that he is not thereby bound to them, and that he depends on nothing, he sometimes effects something otherwise, and then he is said to work miracles, of which more presently. But, what is chief in this matter, creatures do not posit the existence and circumstances of such conditions; rather God himself posits them all, as has been proved. Therefore when it is said, if such a thing had not been, neither would that which followed have been done, this should be resolved thus: if this had not been, that is, if God had not willed and not posited this, it would have been a sign that he had not willed nor would have posited what followed. The antecedent is the principle: he posits the antecedent; the consequent is the consummation: he posits the consequent; and when he does not posit the antecedent, by that very fact he signifies that he will not posit the consequent. For the ordinary manner in which he acts convinces us of the connection of his operations, and since he observes it, we too ought to observe it carefully. Nor can it be said that the more means God uses in working, the more he seems to be in need and less powerful; on the contrary, the more elaborate the apparatus of means with which he produces a thing, the clearer the proofs he gives of his liberality and power, since he produces the means just as much as the other things. But he convinces man of tangible poverty in this way, and represses his pride, when he subjects him to certain laws, both of matter, of motion, and of the recognition of wretchedness and defect, and of the seeking of another's help, so that by this a transition must be made to his goal.

units.la: XIX. Hisce facile discutiuntur plurimæ cogitationes quæ importune multis hæc ut decet non meditantibus occurrunt, atque eos eo deducunt, ut concludant à positione voluntatis Dei de effectu ad negationem mediorum, quasi quando vult Deus aliquid ex placito ponere, nulla sint media adhibenda. Quam sæpe apud plebejos audiveris, Si Deus eos in vita per certum tempus velit esse, se igitur nolle pericula (quæ sunt conditiones destructionis corporis) evitare, qualia sunt v. g. loca contagio infecta, & quæ periculis sunt obnoxia, & multa ejusmodi. Hæc rebellio est in leges Dei, earumque abdicatio ex barbaro ignaroque fastu procedens: quasi talis homo tantus esset, ut ob illius vitam Deus leges suas debeat deserere, eumque extraordinario modo sustentare: quæ cogitatio insolens tacite subest. At dices de moralibus mediis non posse ita esse, Si enim voluit Deus in me efficere bonum & beatitudinem, ut quid precibus & hortationibus indigeo? Respondeo, has ipsas sic volente Deo esse media essentialia rei seu scopo à Deo intento: Nam cum vera felicitas in hoc consistat ut summe optatis & desideratis fruar, (quod supra ostendimus) ergo cum Deus vult me felicem reddere, eo ipso vult me summe optantem, me desiderantem, sive precantem, efficere, atque boni veri ardorem in me ponere, ut deinceps fruitione optati beatus reddar: Si vero vult me alacriter & summe optantem reddere modo intelligenti, ut rem cogitantem cum intelligentia decet, hoc ipso vult ut alacres & animosæ cogitationes, sive monita & hortationes, Mentem meam subeant. Et sic de cæteris judicare licet.
units.tr: XIX. By these things many thoughts are easily dispelled, which occur unseasonably to many who do not meditate on these matters as they should, and lead them to conclude from the positing of God's will concerning an effect to the denial of means, as if whenever God wills to set something in place by his pleasure, no means are to be employed. How often you will hear among the common people: If God wills that they should be in life for a certain time, then they are unwilling to avoid dangers (which are conditions of the destruction of the body), such as, for example, places infected by contagion, and those exposed to dangers, and many things of that sort. This is a rebellion against the laws of God, and a renunciation of them proceeding from a barbarous and ignorant arrogance: as if such a man were so great that God must abandon his laws on account of his life, and sustain him in an extraordinary way; a strange thought which lies hidden beneath. But you will say that it cannot be so in moral means: For if God has willed to bring about in me goodness and blessedness, why do I need prayers and exhortations? I answer that these very things, when God so wills, are the essential means of the thing and of the end intended by God. For since true happiness consists in this, that I enjoy most highly what is desired and longed for (as we have shown above), therefore when God wills to make me happy, by that very fact he wills to make me desire most highly, to long, or to pray, and to set in me the ardour of a true good, so that afterwards I may be made blessed by the enjoyment of what is desired. But if he wills to make me desire eagerly and most highly in an intelligent manner, as befits a thinking being with understanding, then by that very fact he wills that lively and spirited thoughts, or admonitions and exhortations, should come into my mind. And so it is permitted to judge the rest.

units.la: XX. Dixi modo, Deum aliquando nonnihil efficere aliter quam sub conditionibus ordinariis, eosque effectus miracula vocari. De his jam aliquid dicam, eoque libentius & forte fusius, quod mihi hactenus non licuerit in ullum incidere, ex quo menti cuivis aliquantum perspicaci hac in materia difficili satisfieri possit. Nonnulli ea prorsus negant à Deo vel facta esse, vel fieri debere: Alii disputant an quæ mediantibus Angelis malis, pravisque hominibus fieri vel facta esse dicuntur, sint vera miracula, an vero mirabilia ? Jam, si ea considerentur in ordine ad doctrinas in Religionibus stabiliendas, vel contra, quantæ turbæ! Hic, ut me omnibus istis extricem, considerabo primo miracula in ordine ad statum rerum naturalem: secundo, eorum usum in iis quæ ad cultum Dei spectant. De facto autem, an hæc vel illa quæ hic aut iste narrat, ita facta sint ut dicit, non est hujus loci inquirere; ut neque agetur de illis quæ operatur in mentibus Deus dum eas ad se convertit, sed tantum de illis quæ in rebus corporeis fiunt. Distinctio miraculorum & mirabilium ut hac in re nonnunquam usurpatur, ex earum genere est quibus nonnulli uti possunt ut ea quæ ignorant verbis nil clari significantibus coram imperitis se nosse simulent.
units.tr: XX. I have just said that God sometimes brings about something in a way other than under the ordinary conditions, and that such effects are called miracles. I will now say something about these, and I will do so more willingly and perhaps at greater length, because until now I have not had the chance to come upon any account that could satisfy any reasonably perceptive mind on this difficult subject. Some deny altogether that such things have been done by God or ought to be done. Others dispute whether those things which are said to be done through evil angels and wicked men are true miracles or only wonders. And if these are considered in relation to establishing or overturning doctrines in the religions, what great disturbances arise! To free myself from all these difficulties, I will consider first miracles in relation to the natural state of things, and second their use in matters that pertain to the worship of God. As for whether these or those things which this or that person relates were done in the way he says, it is not the place here to inquire; nor shall I treat of those things which God works in minds when he turns them to himself, but only of those which happen in bodily things. The distinction between miracles and wonders, as it is sometimes used in this matter, belongs to those things by which some people can pretend, before the ignorant, to know what they do not know, using words that signify nothing clear.

units.la: XXI. Ut de miraculis bene judicetur, supponendum est res manere quantum quidem affirmari potest in suo statu: adeoque, posito miraculo, via ejus explicandi quæ minus à statu rerum recedit, & phænomeno clare satisfacit, præferenda est ei, quæ rerum statum magis turbat; eaque plane rejicienda est quæ ipsam naturam rerum omnino subvertit. Hoc ita clarum est, ut ab eo probando, maxime post ea quæ jam de Dei Dominio & Potentia notata sunt, abstineam. Hinc autem sequuntur duæ Regulæ maximi usus. Prima hæc est: Miracula non sunt contra naturam rerum extensarum, sive, non destruunt ideas materiæ, seu extensionis vel spatii, nec ideas motus, aut quietis, aut divisionis materiæ, &c. Non faciunt ut hæc cessent esse id quod sunt in essentia, multo minus ut in existentia maneant, & tamen simul non maneant, sed mutentur, v.g. ut extensio parva sit materia sive extensio magna & non parva; ut eadem extensio ejusque modi maneant, nec tamen res eadem existat, sed alia, cujus natura est extensio major aliter modificata. Examinentur omnia miracula de quibus est consensus, nullum ab hac regula aberrabit. Secunda talis est: Miracula non sunt contra Regulas primariorum modorum rerum extensarum. Primarios modos voco quietem & motum; Secundarios (qui horum primorum quasi modi sunt) quietis situationem & motus determinationem: ex quorum mixturis omnium rerum materialium diversitas, natura particularis, omnisque variatio exurgit, ut ex omnibus Cartesii operibus Physicis evidentissime velut ad oculum patet. Modorum horumce primariorum hæc est lex, ut motus & quies uti jam exstant non pereant, sed in eadem quantitate atque proportione permaneant, adeo ut si aliquid motus incipiat postmodum esse in parte materiæ universi ubi prius nullus erat, tantumdem reciproce quietis in alia materia prius mota inci-piat existere, ut exacte proportio servetur eadem. Nil unquam in natu-ra observatum est quin possit salva hac lege, imo per illam, explicari, ut sciunt, quotquot Dei opera ordinaria cum attentione nonnulla extra Philosophastrorum tenebras inspexerunt. Sed etiam dico, nullum pos-se designari miraculum quod contra hanc legem factum esse dici possit. Nam etsi motus inceperit subito esse in corpore prius quiescente, & tamen nullum aliud ad servandam proportionem videatur quiescere, vel contra; non sequitur tamen motum aliquem de novo fieri contra legem di-ctam, cum (quod in omnibus corporum crassorum motibus fit) materia quædam subtilis, sensibusque subducta, omnia penetrans & cingens, hunc motum ex se, recipiendo in se tantum quietis, in corpus illud potuerit transferre. Hactenus ergo dici non potest, miracula esse contra conditiones sive leges naturæ. Eorum igitur diversitas à cæteris Dei operationibus, quærenda est in rerum modis secundariis, eorumve le-gibus.
units.tr: XXI. To judge rightly about miracles, it must be supposed that things remain, as far as it can be affirmed, in their state; and therefore, when a miracle is posited, the explanation which departs less from the state of things and satisfies the phenomenon clearly is to be preferred to that which disturbs the state of things more; and that explanation is plainly to be rejected which utterly subverts the very nature of things. This is so clear that I will refrain from proving it, especially after what has already been noted about the Dominion and Power of God. From this, however, two rules of very great use follow. The first is this: Miracles are not contrary to the nature of extended things; that is, they do not destroy the ideas of matter, or of extension or space, nor the ideas of motion, or rest, or division of matter, etc. They do not cause these to cease to be what they are in essence, much less to remain in existence and yet at the same time not remain, but be changed; for example, so that a small extension is matter, or a large extension and not a small one; or so that the same extension and its mode remain, and yet the same thing does not exist, but another, whose nature is a larger extension variously modified. Let all the miracles on which there is agreement be examined; none will deviate from this rule. The second is this: Miracles are not contrary to the rules of the primary modes of extended things. I call the primary modes rest and motion; the secondary modes (which are, as it were, modes of these primary ones) are the situation of rest and the determination of motion. From mixtures of these the diversity of all material things, their particular nature, and every variation arises, as is most evidently plain, as if before the eyes, from all the physical works of Descartes. The law of these primary modes is this: that motion and rest, as they now exist, do not perish, but remain in the same quantity and proportion, so that if some motion begins afterwards to be in a part of matter of the universe where previously there was none, just as much rest, reciprocally, begins to exist in other matter that was previously in motion, so that the same exact proportion is kept. Nothing has ever been observed in nature that cannot be explained while this law is preserved, indeed through it, as all know who have looked attentively at God's ordinary works outside the darkness of the pseudo-philosophers. But I also say that no miracle can be designated which can be said to have been done contrary to this law. For although motion may suddenly have begun to be in a body previously at rest, and yet no other body seems to be at rest in order to preserve the proportion, or the reverse, it does not follow that some motion is newly made contrary to the said law, since (as happens in all motions of gross bodies) some subtle matter, withdrawn from the senses, penetrating and surrounding all things, could have transferred this motion from itself into that body, receiving into itself only rest. Thus far, therefore, it cannot be said that miracles are contrary to the conditions or laws of nature. Their difference from the other operations of God is therefore to be sought in the secondary modes of things, or in the laws of these.

units.la: XXII. Secundariorum modorum duplices sunt leges, unæ quæ spectant corpora sola modificata, aliæ quæ respiciunt ea quatenus mentibus nonnullis uniri possunt. Primas vocabimus Leges brutas, alteras vero, rationales. Brutæ leges de motus determinatione sunt 1. Directio in lineam rectam. 2. Reflexio. 3. Refractio (quæ penitus inspicientibus est revera reflexionis species.) 4. Communicatio sui corporibus nonnullis secundum rectam lineam, sed recipiendo, ob jam dictum, tantum quietis. Hæ in operibus in quibus nulla cogitatio creata intervenit, exactissime observantur, sed non in illis, quibus Cogitationem creatam jungere voluit Deus: certum enim est motus corporis illius, cui juncta Mens est, vel ejus partium nonnullarum, quales sunt spiritus animales, non determinari Bruto hoc modo, sed ex ratione & arbitrio cogitationis creatæ ei junctæ, quæ motus ibi existentes determinat, si non omnes, saltem plurimos, quo vult, at, quamdiu sunt in sphæra ejus actioni assignata: nam alioqui cum corpora mota, spiritus videlicet animales, ex eo loco cerebri devenerunt alio, & musculos implent qui pel-lunt corpora externa. Ista, ut jam extra sphæram mentis, Legibus brutis iterum subjiciuntur. Atque in his omnibus quæcunque fiunt, etiamsi miranda sæpe dicantur, pro naturalibus tamen agnoscuntur. Sed notandum est, de nonnullis mentibus quæ Angelicæ vocantur sic disposuisse Deum, ut, etsi forte non omnes, nec semper, nonnullæ at-tamen, sive bonæ sive malæ sint, aliquando cum materiæ quæ est in motu nonnulla portione nexæ sint: unde sequetur, motum hujus ma-teriæ (quam primum & secundum elementum nonnulli appellant, & forte partes tertii subtiliores) non quidem produci, sed determinari alio modo quam si solus regulis brutis esset permissus, nempe pro cogitatione Mentis unitæ, quemadmodum motus spirituum animalium ex arbitrio animæ humanæ determinatur. Hinc materiæ illius agitatissimæ, sensi-busque (ut spiritus animales, qui tamen multo crassiores) subductæ, directiones, reflexiones, refractiones, in corpora crassa & sensibilia oc-cursus, adeoque horum mutationes subitæ & multifariæ oriuntur, quæ cum ultra ordinarium brutumque corporum quæ circa nos sunt regi-men fiant, admirationem in nobis excitant, & miracula nominantur, qualia sunt in tenebris Ægypti, aut Palæstinæ tempore mortis Christi, impeditio motus directi solarium radiorum, eorumque à sola Ægypto & Palæstina reflexio, reflexio item miraculosa in mari rubro, in Jorda-ne, in igne Babylonio, &c. refractio miraculosa in horologio Achazi, quo forte referri posset statio illa Solis Lunæque tempore Josuæ, plane-tis quidem ut antea procedentibus, luminariorum vero radiis miraculose per nubes plurimas ratione extraordinaria dispositas per longum spa-tium tempusque ad terram Canaam ita refractis & reflexis, ut dies inde prolongatus fuerit. Sic dictæ istius materiæ determinatio versus alia cor-pora horum particulas potest ita radere, ita immutare, figurare, & com-pingere, atque ita diversimode disponere, vel in corpore nostro, ejusque ejus organis quibus objecta percipimus, vel in mediis, vel in ipsis objectis perceptis, (nam perinde jam est ubi hæc fiant) ut magnæ fiant muta-tiones, v. g. in objectis externis, ut aëris particulæ coacervatæ ex aëreis fiant aquæ, vel ex aqueis vinosæ, & similia, adeoque naturam particu-larem mutent; atque aliter quam prius in sensus incurrant, aut, si quæ primo mutata sunt immediate non incurrant, ea agant in alia, & hæc forte in alia, quæ tandem quædam extraordinarie in sensus faciant in-currere. Nec ullum est miraculum quod sic volente Deo fieri, adeoque exponi non possit. Quid enim opus est statuere, Deum omnes universi Leges, sapientissime ab ipso statutas & conditas evertere, cum res iis salvis via Deum decenti concipi possit, neque etiam constet miracula in re ipsa sensus feriente fieri immediate, sive sine interventu tum materiæ, quæ correspondeat illi qua corpora nostra, & per hæc alia, moventur; tum etiam mentis cujusdam, illius materiæ motum determinantis? Quid quod in miraculis quæ Scriptura S. recenset, semper fere Angelus unus pluresve intervenisse narrentur, aut saltem Mentes humanæ, quæ ob officium Angelicum, quia nempe ad aliquid speciale à Deo missæ erant, Angelicæ dici possint, atque eadem facultate qua Angeli pollere, aut saltem ea, ut si quid velint id Angeli debeant exequi, prout inter humanas mentes unæ secundum quarumdam jussum, declarationemve, ad extra operari tenentur?
units.tr: XXII. There are two kinds of laws of the secondary modes: one kind concerns bodies considered only as modified, the other concerns them insofar as they can be united to some minds. We shall call the first brute laws, and the second rational. The brute laws concerning the determination of motion are: 1. direction in a straight line; 2. reflection; 3. refraction (which to those who look closely is really a species of reflection); 4. communication of motion to some bodies along a straight line, but receiving, for the reason already given, only rest. These are observed most exactly in works in which no created thought intervenes, but not in those to which God chose to join a created thought.
