For it is certain that the motion of that body to which a mind is joined, or of some of its parts, such as the animal spirits, is not determined in this brute way, but by the reason and will of the created thought joined to it, which determines the motions existing there, if not all, at least most of them, as it wills, provided they are within the sphere assigned to its action. For otherwise, when the moved bodies, namely the animal spirits, have passed from that place of the brain to another and fill the muscles which push external bodies, these, since they are now outside the sphere of the mind, are again subject to the brute laws. And in all these things, whatever happens, even if often called wonderful, is nevertheless recognized as natural. But it must be noted that God has so arranged things concerning certain minds called angelic that, although perhaps not all, nor always, yet some of them, whether good or evil, are sometimes joined to a certain portion of matter that is in motion. Hence it follows that the motion of this matter (which some call the first and second element, and perhaps the more subtle parts of the third) is not indeed produced, but is determined in another way than if it were left to the brute rules alone, namely according to the thought of the united mind, just as the motion of the animal spirits is determined by the will of the human soul. Hence there arise, from that most agitated matter, withdrawn from the senses (as are the animal spirits, though these are far grosser), directions, reflections, refractions, encounters with gross and sensible bodies, and so sudden and manifold changes of these, which, since they happen beyond the ordinary and brute governance of the bodies around us, excite admiration in us and are called miracles. Such are the darkness in Egypt, or in Palestine at the time of Christ's death, the hindrance of the direct motion of the solar rays and their reflection from Egypt and Palestine alone; likewise the miraculous reflection in the Red Sea, in the Jordan, in the Babylonian fire, etc.; the miraculous refraction in the dial of Ahaz, to which perhaps that standing still of the Sun and Moon in the time of Joshua could be referred, the planets indeed proceeding as before, but the rays of the luminaries being miraculously refracted and reflected through very many clouds, arranged in an extraordinary way, over a long space and time, toward the land of Canaan, so that the day was thereby prolonged. Thus the determination of this said matter toward other bodies can so gnaw at, alter, shape and compact their particles, and so dispose them in diverse ways, either in our body and its organs by which we perceive objects, or in the media, or in the perceived objects themselves (for it is all the same where these things happen), that great changes arise; for example in external objects, so that particles of air gathered together become water from air, or wine from water, and similar things, and thus change their particular nature; and so that they strike the senses otherwise than before, or, if those first changed do not directly strike, they act upon others, and these perhaps upon others, which at last by some extraordinary means make certain things strike the senses. And there is no miracle which can be done by God's will in this way and yet cannot be explained. For what need is there to hold that God overturns all the laws of the universe, which he himself most wisely established and ordained, when the matter can be conceived in a way worthy of God while those laws remain intact, and when it is not certain that miracles are made in the thing itself striking the senses immediately, that is, without the intervention either of matter corresponding to that by which our bodies, and through these others, are moved, or of some mind determining the motion of that matter? What of the fact that in the miracles which Holy Scripture recounts, one angel or several are almost always said to have intervened, or at least human minds which, because of an angelic office, since they were sent by God for something special, may be called angelic, and which possess the same faculty as angels, or at least are such that, if they will anything, the angels must carry it out, just as among human minds some are bound to act outwardly at the command or declaration of certain others?

units.la: XXIII. Non jam immorabor in iis refellendis qui causarentur Deo sic fere nihil tribui, sed Angelis: cum supra demonstraverim omnia positiva quæ in mediis & effectis sive mentium sive corporum sunt, à Deo solo effici. Non deprecabor consequentiam quæ ex dictis objici posset, nempe ex his sequi, ea quæ intercedentibus Mentibus pravis, diabolicis & impiis ita accidunt, inter miracula fore numeranda. Omnino miracula sunt dicenda ejusmodi operationes, qualiscunque Mentis, etiamsi Diaboli, etiam Impostoris & Magi interventu existant. Sed causantibus, ea non fore miracula, quæ ita regulatim & per media fierent, respondeo, miracula ideo non dici, quod Deus confuse & turbatim ea operetur quæ naturam ejusque leges destruant ut stulti stupere solum possint; Sed quod sint ejus operationes bene ordinatæ quæ per principium intelligens determinantur circa nos in rebus quæ per brutas Physicasque regulas, aut per Mentis humanæ ordinariam dispositionem, aliter factæ essent, quasque[?], siquidem illæ apud nos eo quo accidunt modo sint insolitæ & extraordinariæ, idcirco non sine gravi & extraordinaria causa à Deo fieri judicandum est. Hæc nos ducunt ad finem sive usum miraculorum, quem ex his verbis patet esse, attentionem ad Deum operantem, deinde etiam ad personas, earumque actiones, aut voces, per quarum interventum operatur, attamen eatenus quatenus ex his regressus ad Deum fieri debet: nam in ipsis mediis, vel quod pejus, in operationibus hærere, nefarium est, & promotio mysterii iniquitatis.
units.tr: XXIII. I will not linger any longer refuting those who object that God is thus attributed almost nothing, but rather the Angels: since I have shown above that all positive things which are in the means and effects, whether of minds or of bodies, are brought about by God alone. I will not shrink from the consequence which might be objected from what has been said, namely that it follows from these things that events which happen through the intervention of wicked, diabolical and impious minds must be counted among miracles. Certainly such operations, of whatever mind, even if they come about through the intervention of the Devil, or of an impostor and magician, are to be called miracles. But to those who argue that those things are not miracles which happen regularly and through means, I reply: they are not called miracles because God works confusedly and in disorder those things which destroy nature and its laws, so that fools can only be astonished; but because they are his well-ordered operations, determined by an intelligent principle, concerning us, in things which would otherwise have come about through the rules of bodies and physics, or through the ordinary disposition of the human mind; and since these, in the manner in which they happen among us, are unusual and extraordinary, it must therefore be judged that they are done by God for no slight and extraordinary cause. These things lead us to the end or use of miracles, which is plainly, from these words, to direct attention to God who works, and then also to the persons and their actions or words through whose intervention he works; yet only so far as a return to God must be made from them: for to rest in the means themselves, or, what is worse, in the operations, is wicked, and a promotion of the mystery of iniquity.

units.la: XXIV. Hinc miraculorum in rebus Religiosis, seu quæ nostram ad Deum relationem concernunt, magnus usus & abusus. Satius fuisset Authori Artis cogitandi hunc lapidem tractatu sat difficilem adversariis suis non movisse, quam multa in operis sui integro capite {a}coacervafse sine ordine, lumine, principiisque sufficientibus, & tamen ita, ut omnes cum adversariis lites ex hoc uno praetendat decidere, & de iis tanquam uno ictu prostratis, secure triumphare; quod amicis commiserationem, inimicis vero risum & confidentiam movet, utpote qui inde praesumptionem capiant arbitrandi omnia per quae impugnantur ejusdem esse commatis. Ut in materia tot dubiis & illusionibus obnoxia certius & clarius eatur per propositiones nonnullas procedemus ex quibus tanquam principiis Mens quaevis integri liberique judicii ea deducet quae sibi hac in re satisfacere apta sint. Sed velim ut prius in animum revocentur ea quae in fine Libri secundi, & passim in hoc Tertio dicta sunt de nihilo, ut sic dicam, omnium quae non sunt Deus, quod nil plane sint a se, quod iis non sit adhaerendum, quod Mens se contemnens, omniaque praetermittens, ad Deum tendere debeat: & quae huc faciunt: quae quidem multi ex ignorantia, multi etiam etsi moniti, ignorare affectantes, non observant. Hisce positis, quaecunque de miraculis circa sacra ad usum qui jam nos concernit dici possunt, quatuor sequentibus propositionibus includimus, quarum prima est.
units.tr: XXIV. Hence there is great use and abuse of miracles in religious matters, that is, those which concern our relation to God. It would have been better for the author of the Art of Thinking not to have stirred up this stone, which is rather difficult to handle, against his adversaries, than to have heaped together so many things without order, light, or sufficient principles in the whole chapter of his work, and yet to claim that he can settle all disputes with his opponents by this one point alone, and to triumph confidently over them as if struck down by one blow; which moves friends to pity, and enemies indeed to laughter and self-assurance, since they thereby take up the presumption of judging that everything which is attacked belongs to the same kind. That in a matter so beset with doubts and illusions we may proceed more surely and clearly, we shall set out some propositions from which, as from principles, any mind of sound and free judgement will deduce what is apt to satisfy itself in this matter. But I would first wish that those things be recalled to mind which were said at the end of the second book and throughout this third about nothing, so to speak, of all things that are not God: that they are of themselves utterly nothing, that one must not cling to them, and that the mind, despising itself and letting all things go, must strive toward God; and the things which bear on this. Many, through ignorance, and many also, though warned, through wishing to remain ignorant, do not observe these. With these matters laid down, whatever can be said about miracles concerning sacred things, for the use which now concerns us, we include in four following propositions, of which the first is this.

units.la: 1. Ut Mentes infirmae creaturis adhaerentes, ab illis ad Deum intellectu & amore, sanctitate doctrinae & vitae, convertantur, vult Deus interdum miracula fieri interveniente voluntate personae quae recte doceat sanctequae vivat, ut ostendat Deus se eam viam ad se redeundi probare quam persona illa verbis atque exemplis proponit. Haec Propositio cum sit perspicua, nec controvertatur, non eget probatione ulteriori.
units.tr: 1. That weak minds clinging to creatures should be converted from them to God, in understanding and love, by the holiness of doctrine and life, God sometimes wills miracles to occur through the will of a person who teaches rightly and lives holily, so that God may show that he approves of that way of returning to himself which that person sets forth by words and examples. Since this proposition is plain and is not disputed, it does not need further proof.

units.la: 2. Secunda Propositio. Ad examinandum sive tentandum, utrum illi qui non amplius infirmi, sed ob veritatem in qua saepe instructi fuere, fortes esse debent, adhaereant Deo ita solide, ut ab illo ob nullam creaturam, dictum factumve, quicquid accidat, avellantur, unde constet eos vero amore soli adhaerere Deo super omnibus; Vult Deus ut fiant miracula per Impostores, falsum cultum inculcantes ut hominem a Deo ad creaturas convertere tentent. Haec propositio est ipsius Dei, & exstat in Deuteronomio Cap. xiii. v. 1. 2. 3, &c. Et notabile est primum miraculum quod post primorum Parentum creationem factum est, tale fuisse, cum per serpentem interventu Diaboli loquentem, homo non in ignorantia constitutus, sed sufficienter intelligens, probatus fuit, utrum Deo, an vero creaturis, adhaerere mallet.
units.tr: 2. The second proposition. To examine or test whether those who are no longer weak, but who, because of the truth in which they have often been instructed, ought to be strong, cling to God so firmly that for no creature, saying or deed, whatever happens, are they torn away from him, whereby it may be clear that they adhere to God alone above all things with true love: God wills that miracles be done through impostors who inculcate a false worship, so that they may try to turn man from God to creatures. This proposition is God's own, and it stands in Deuteronomy chapter 13, verses 1, 2, 3, etc. And it is notable that the first miracle which happened after the creation of our first parents was of this kind: when man, not in ignorance but sufficiently understanding, was tested, through the Devil's intervention speaking by the serpent, to see whether he would prefer to cling to God or to creatures.

units.la: 3. Tertia Propositio. Ut puniantur ii, qui pertinaciter veritati resistunt, adeoque ea sunt indigni, quique mendacium quaerunt & vanitatem, sive cultum & adhæsionem creaturæ, (cum omnis à se sit prorsus nihil,) adeoque qui merentur mendacio mancipari; Vult Deus ut fiant miracula quibus hi pertinaces de mendacio & vanitate persuadeantur, ideoque sub servitute peccati fortiter detenti, severe justo Dei judicio de veritate neglecta puniantur. Hæc propositio etiam Dei ipsius est, & exstat in Epist. 2. ad Thessalon. cap. II. v.9[?] 10. 11. & 12. & sæpe in Apocalypsi occurrit. Nil Deo indignum est, si dicatur, impios operari per Potentiam Dei, cum per illam habeant suum esse, vitam, & motum: Et justum est, Deum de effectibus Potentiæ suæ per illos sic disponere, ut Veritas & Sanctitas contemptæ, vindicentur, luatque contemptor.
units.tr: 3. Third proposition. That those who obstinately resist the truth, and who are therefore unworthy of it, and who seek falsehood and vanity, that is, the worship and adherence of a creature (since every creature is of itself utterly nothing), and who therefore deserve to be given over to falsehood, may be punished: God wills that miracles be done by which these obstinate people are persuaded of falsehood and vanity, and so, held fast under the bondage of sin, they may be justly punished by God's severe judgement for having neglected the truth. This proposition too is God's own, and it stands in 2 Thessalonians chapter 2, verses 9, 10, 11 and 12, and it often occurs in the Apocalypse. Nothing is unworthy of God if it is said that the impious act through the power of God, since by it they have their being, life and motion; and it is just that God should so order the effects of his power through them that truth and holiness, when despised, may be vindicated, and the despiser may pay the price.

units.la: 4. Ultima Propositio sic se habet. In judiciis quæ miracula in particulari concernunt eorumque sequelas, facile homines falli possunt, etiam solertiores, cum nempe simpliciorum & nonnunquam stupidorum, qui apud plerosque pro piis reputantur, & de quibus interdum piaculum esset dubitare, relationibus, patulas aures præbent; vel dum ejusmodi narrationibus in scriptis authorum vita functorum intrusis, locum cedunt; vel, (quæ fraus omnium maxima introduci potest,) dum unusquisque pro mente, vel lubitu, vel præjudicio suo, scopum miraculo assignat. Hæc Propositio per experientiam multorum seculorum probata est. unus ait miraculum factum esse hac de causa, alius aliam assignabit, & sic in infinitum. Augustinus in Confessionibus {a} miraculum factum esse ait ut Arrianismi violentia, & Persecutio Imperatricis Arrianæ in Ambrosium, inhiberentur, adeoque ut ea doctrina cum discipulis suis confirmaretur quæ docet objectum Religiosi cultus, sive Religionis, Deum Creatorem esse, qui Jesus Christus est, ut docebant Orthodoxi; atque reprimerentur ii (Arriani nempe) qui Filium Dei colentes, eundemque pro mera creatura habentes, eam tuebantur doctrinam quæ Creaturam pro objecto Religiosi cultus statuit: At si Author Artis cogitandi hoc aliaque velit referre ad confirmandum omnes abusus qui circa creaturas, materialia, corporea, externa, quibus sæpe multi vel plus quam Deo ipsi religiose, idque aperte, adhærent, à scopo in contrarium recedit: Sique velit inde concludere, eos omnes qui ab ipso in hoc dissentiunt, eapropter convinci se in omnibus à veritate & ab ipso cœlo aberrare, nil ex toto capite concludendum quibusvis relinquit, quam se à sana ratione declinare. Tu vero, Lector, si ad tres propositiones præcedentes redeas, iis, quamvis in facto errares, seu miracula ficta ut facta crederes, tamen à vero scopo, à veritate una & summa, aberrare prohibeberis, neque te ullæ difficultates objectæ re-moramorabuntur. Hæc non latius deducam. De miraculis hactenus satis esto.
units.tr: 4. The last proposition stands thus. In judgements which concern miracles in particular and their consequences, men can easily be mistaken, even the most skilful; namely when they lend open ears to the accounts of simple and sometimes foolish people, who are regarded by most as pious, and about whom it would sometimes be sacrilege to doubt; or when such stories are inserted into the writings of authors who have departed this life, and they yield their place to them; or (which is the greatest deceit of all that can be introduced) when each person assigns an aim to the miracle according to his own mind, or whim, or prejudice. This proposition has been proved by the experience of many centuries. One says that a miracle was done for this reason, another will assign another, and so on to infinity. Augustine in his Confessions says that a miracle was done so that the violence of Arianism and the persecution by the Arian empress against Ambrose might be restrained, and so that that doctrine might be confirmed among his disciples which teaches that the object of religious worship, or of religion, is God the Creator, who is Jesus Christ, as the Orthodox taught; and that those (namely the Arians) who worshipped the Son of God, yet held him to be a mere creature, and defended the doctrine which sets a creature up as the object of religious worship, should be restrained. But if the author of the Art of Thinking wishes to refer this and other things to confirm all the abuses which attach to creatures, material, corporeal and external things, to which many often cling religiously, and even more than to God himself, and openly so, he departs from the aim in the opposite direction. And if he wishes to conclude from this that all who dissent from him in this are thereby convinced that they err in everything from the truth and from heaven itself, he leaves nothing whatever to be concluded by anyone from the whole chapter except that he himself turns aside from sound reason. But you, reader, if you return to the three preceding propositions, you will be prevented, even though you were mistaken in fact, and believed miracles to be feigned as if they were real, from straying from the true aim, from the one and highest truth; and no difficulties that are raised will hold you back. I will not develop these matters further. Let enough be said about miracles so far.

units.la: XXV. Accedo ad tertiam quæstionem de Contingentia & necessitate rerum quæ existere dicuntur, de quibus dico posse asseri, Omnes, nulla excepta, existere contingenter, quatenus confidero[?] eas in se nullam habere necessitatem existendi, imo etiam quatenus Deus eas non ex necessitate statuit ponere atque posuit. Sed cum animadverto, omnem, quæ est eritque, realitatem, non posse nisi à Deo poni, necesse esse determinatam Dei voluntatem non frustrari, Deumque, cum sit Cogitatio perfectissima, infallibiliter omnia quæ determinavit cogitare & nosse; non possum non adduci eo ut concludam omnia quæ existunt, necessario, hoc sensu, existere, cum nulla in rebus major necessitas excogitari possit ea, quæ est ex causa efficienti efficaci & determinata effectus positio & sequela. Quodsi ex rebus ipsis nonnullæ contingenter, aliæ vero necessario existere & fieri dicantur, ea quarundam rerum contingentia aliarum necessitati oppositia nil aliud denotat quam ignorantiam nostram. Nempe cum sciamus experientia Deum per quædam uno modo operari, v. g. per ignem calefacere, possumus id certo prædicere futurum posito igne, nec fallimur, quapropter dicimus id fieri necessario: Sed cum quædam sint per quæ Deus diversa operatur, videlicet per cogitationem hominis, nec ille nobis revelaverit quænam ex pluribus sit operaturus, adeoque id ignoremus, nec possimus certo prædicere certum effectum, dicimus hic contingenter fieri quæ eveniunt.
units.tr: XXV. I come to the third question, concerning the contingency and necessity of things said to exist. Of these I say that it can be asserted that all things, without exception, exist contingently, insofar as I consider them in themselves to have no necessity of existing, and even insofar as God did not decree from necessity to bring them into being, and did not bring them into being. But since I observe that all reality which is and will be cannot be posited except by God, and that the determined will of God cannot be frustrated, and that God, since he is the most perfect Thought, infallibly thinks and knows all the things he has determined, I cannot help being led to conclude that all things which exist exist necessarily, in this sense: no greater necessity can be conceived in things than that which belongs to the positing and consequence of an effect from an efficient, effective and determined cause. If, however, some things are said to exist and come about contingently from the things themselves, and others necessarily, this contingency of some things, as opposed to the necessity of others, signifies nothing other than our ignorance. Indeed, since we know by experience that God works in a certain way in some things, for example that he heats by means of fire, we can predict with certainty that this will happen when fire is present, and we are not mistaken; for this reason we say that it happens necessarily. But since there are some things through which God works in different ways, namely through the thought of a human being, and he has not revealed to us which of several he is going to work, and so we do not know this and cannot predict a certain effect with certainty, we say here that the things which come about happen contingently.

units.la: Etiam ubi omnes rei alicujus causas, quia forte sub sensus cadunt, adesse videmus, rem dicimus necessario fieri, ut, moveri necessario corpus violenter à majore pulsum: at dicimus rem fieri contingenter, cum an causæ, saltem quædam, sub sensum non cadentes, adsint necne, ignoratur; unde nil necessario, sed omne à nobis contingenter sequi dicitur, quia quid secuturum sit ignoratur. Sunt qui & omne quod spontaneè à Mente procedit, contingenter fieri dicant; quibus omnibus sua verba concedamus, modo agnoscant, realitatis cujuscunque, ipsius etiam spontaneitatis, positionem infallibiter poni ex Dei voluntate liberrima, potentissima, nullisque defectibus obnoxia.
units.tr: Even where we see all the causes of some thing present, perhaps because they fall under the senses, we say the thing happens necessarily, as a body struck violently by a larger one is necessarily moved. But we say a thing happens contingently when it is unknown whether the causes, at least some of them which do not fall under the senses, are present or not; hence nothing is said to follow necessarily but everything follows contingently for us, because what is going to follow is unknown. There are some who also say that everything which proceeds spontaneously from the Mind happens contingently. To all of these we may concede their words, provided they acknowledge that the positing of any reality whatever, and of spontaneity itself, is infallibly brought about by the most free and most powerful will of God, which is subject to no defects.

units.la: XXVI. Restat ut quod quarto supra recensui non præteream. Sed cum res jam sint expositæ, quod dicendum est nomina potius spectat. Nempe, prima alicujus substantiæ & modi primarii à Dei voluntate positio, sive existentia, Creatio nominatur, quocunque fiat tempore. Modorum etiam in aliqua substantia extensa vel Cogitante mutatio per vias extraorextraordinarias & miraculosas, sine quibus modi illi non tam cito, vel non omnino secuti fuissent, Creatio dicitur, ut formatio Solis, corporis humani ex luto, mutatio Mentis ignorantis nec Deum amantis in nescentem & amantem Deum, aliaque. Horum autem omnium durans existentia Conservatio dicitur, quæ realiter à Creatione non differt, neque ex parte rei positæ, cum sit ejus existentiæ (ultra primum momentum) positio, neque ex parte Dei, cum sit ejus voluntas una ut res sit prout ei placet. Itaque, cum dicitur, existentiæ rerum momenta esse à se invicem independentia, tantam vim requiri ad positionem secundi vel tertii quam primi momenti creationis, non putandum est, reiterari pro rerum momentis reduplicatis actum illum imperatum, sive conatum à Deo supra repulsum, aut voluntatem divinam: quasi vellet Deus rem esse uno momento, quo posito, & re in nihilum ad momentum sequens tendente, iterum ad sequens momentum efficaciam voluntatis suæ explicaret Deus, atque ita continuo, quemadmodum vox concursus (concursus prævius, concursus simultaneus) inculcare videtur, quæ etsi satis apte rebus applicetur, cum dicat eas currere, fluere, & quasi evanescere, nil constanter possidere, tamen ineptissime tribuitur Deo: etenim non concipiendus est Deus quasi singulis momentis ageret, quasi actus ab eo successive & continua duratione fluerent & terminarentur ad singula creaturæ existentis momenta. proprie Deus non concurrit, hoc est, in ipso & ex ipso nihil est quod durans cum creatura eam faciat existere & agere; sive, ex ipso nihil est quod coexistat & cooperetur cum creaturarum duratione: absurda hæc sunt, & contraria æternitati Dei, ut suo loco videbitur. Una Potens & simplex Dei Voluntas ut talia per tantum temporis existant, ita sufficit ad omnem durationem, ut nulla alia re sit opus: hoc, & illud, & istud, & omne momentum existit & tale est ob Voluntatem illam unam Potentem & Immutabilem, quæ semel omnia momenta decrevit. Ejus unius sufficientiæ sive efficaciæ signa, existentiæ nempe rerum se extendunt ad omne tempus: quo sensu semper operari dicitur. Hæ nihilominus voces, de concursu prævio & simultaneo, quia in usu sunt, sic bene possunt explicari. Nulla creatura à se est vel currit nisi antequam sit vel currat concipiamus ejus causam, nempe voluntatem Dei, positam & determinatam ad hoc ut creatura currat vel sit, adeoque nisi concipiatur Dei voluntas, ut quæ præsit vel præcurrat. (hoc vocarunt concursum prævium.) Deinde cum hoc momento creatura est, concipimus Dei voluntatem esse ut hoc tempore sit & currat, potius quam alio: & sic consideratur Dei voluntas ut determinata ad hoc tempus in quo est creatura, hocque concursus simultaneus dicitur, (qui & ad conservationem extendi-tur,) quia cum res durat, sive fluit, sive durationis stadium decurrit, concipimus voluntatem in Deo de ejus existentia stare, sive non esse mutatam. Nil hic addam specialius de Creaturis, de Decretis Dei, de Providentia, de Regimine universi, de Misericordia, aliisque, quae speciale creaturarum regimen praesupponunt, cum haec sint extra limites ab initio propositos. Sed non possum quin duas difficultates, quae ex occasione huius doctrinae in genere oriundae, nonnullis molestae esse possent, coner removere. quarum Prima est de Cogitationum creatarum Libertate; Altera de earumdem compensatione cuique sua pro suis operibus.
units.tr: XXVI. It remains that I do not pass over what I listed fourth above. But since the things have now been set out, what must be said concerns the names rather. Namely, the first positing or existence of any substance and primary mode by the will of God is called Creation, whatever time it takes place. Also, the change of modes in some extended or thinking substance through extraordinary and miraculous ways, without which those modes would not have followed so quickly or not at all, is called Creation, such as the forming of the Sun, the forming of the human body from clay, the change of a mind that was ignorant and did not love God into one that knows and loves God, and others. But the continuing existence of all these things is called Conservation, which does not really differ from Creation, neither on the part of the thing posited, since it is the positing of its existence (beyond the first moment), nor on the part of God, since it is his one will that a thing be as it pleases him. Therefore, when it is said that the moments of the existence of things are independent of one another, and that no greater power is required for the positing of the second or third moment than for the first moment of creation, it should not be thought that that commanded act, or the effort put forth by God, or the divine will, is repeated for the successive moments of things, as if God wished a thing to be at one moment, and when that was posited, and the thing was tending toward nothingness at the following moment, God again exerted the efficacy of his will for the following moment, and so continually. This is what the word concurrence (prior concurrence, simultaneous concurrence) seems to suggest. Although this word is applied quite fitly to things, since it says that they run, flow and as it were vanish, possessing nothing constantly, it is nonetheless most inappropriately ascribed to God. For God is not to be conceived as if he acted at each moment, as if acts flowed from him successively and in continuous duration and were terminated at each moment of the existence of the creature. Properly speaking, God does not concur; that is, in him and from him there is nothing which, enduring together with the creature, makes it exist and act; or, from him there is nothing which coexists and cooperates with the duration of creatures. These notions are absurd and contrary to the eternity of God, as will be seen in its proper place. The one powerful and simple Will of God is such that things exist for as long as they do, and so it suffices for every duration, so that no other thing is needed: this thing, and that, and this other, and every moment exists and is such because of that one powerful and unchangeable Will, which once decreed all moments. The signs of this one sufficiency or efficacy, namely that the existence of things extends to all time, are the sense in which he is said always to work. Nevertheless, these expressions about prior and simultaneous concurrence, since they are in use, may be well explained thus. No creature is or runs from itself, unless we first conceive its cause, namely the will of God, posited and determined so that the creature may run or be, and thus the will of God is conceived as going before, or preceding. (This they called prior concurrence.) Then, when the creature is at this moment, we conceive the will of God to be that it be and run at this time rather than at another; and so the will of God is considered as determined to this time in which the creature is, and this is called simultaneous concurrence (which extends also to conservation), because when a thing endures, or flows, or runs through a stage of its duration, we conceive that the will in God rests on its existence, or that it has not been changed. I will add nothing more specific here about creatures, the decrees of God, providence, the government of the universe, mercy, and others which presuppose a particular government of creatures, since these lie outside the limits proposed at the beginning. But I cannot refrain from trying to remove two difficulties which, arising from this doctrine in general, might be troublesome to some. The first is concerning the Liberty of created Thoughts; the second concerns the compensation of each for his own works.

units.la: XXVII. Si realitas quaevis, ejusque duratio & conservatio, à sola Dei vi ponantur, in quovis statu, nec minus in mentibus quam in corporibus, tunc omnis libertas creata, non modo ea quae est indifferentiae, sed & illa quam spontaneitatis appellant, videtur tolli. De Libertate indifferentiae in respectu ad malum considerata, sine qua non videtur aliquid malum posse dici, alibi agetur. Quodsi illa ad realitatis sive boni alicujus physici vel ordinis alterius positionem referatur, cum omnem realitatem à Sola Dei Vi poni sit demonstratum, non video qui dici possit, hominem ad ea ponenda esse indifferentem quae ipse non ponit. Si quis vero videatur sibi indifferens ad duo realia, ad hoc vel ad illud, modo ad demonstrata attendat, agnoscet id non inde esse, quod ipse operetur à se independenter, & Deus non efficiat omnia in universum pro voluntate sua; sed tum ex eo quod nesciat quaenam ex duobus sit in ipso tempus sequens operaturus Deus, tum quod non agat Deus in illo & per illum violentomodo[?], sed eo qui consensum quendam secum infert: adeoque Libertas spontanea sic non destruitur, sed potius stabilitur necessario, cum non possit non esse effectus spontaneus ubi Deus eum esse vult potenter. De indifferentia omni, adhuc alibi.
units.tr: XXVII. If any reality whatever, and its duration and conservation, is posited by the power of God alone, in any state, and no less in minds than in bodies, then all created liberty seems to be abolished, not only that which is called liberty of indifference but also that which they call spontaneity. Concerning the liberty of indifference considered with respect to evil, without which it does not seem that anything can be called evil, this will be treated elsewhere. But if that liberty is referred to the positing of reality, or of some physical good or good of another order, since it has been demonstrated that all reality is posited by the power of God alone, I do not see how it can be said that a human being is indifferent to positing those things which he himself does not posit. If anyone seems to himself indifferent to two real things, to this or to that, let him attend only to what has been demonstrated, and he will acknowledge that this is not because he himself acts independently of God, and God does not effect all things in the universe according to his will; but rather because he does not know which of the two God will work in him at the following time, and because God does not act in him and through him in a violent manner, but in one which brings with it a certain consent. Thus spontaneous liberty is not destroyed in this way, but is rather established necessarily, since it cannot fail to be a spontaneous effect when God powerfully wills it to be. Of all indifference, more elsewhere.

units.la: XXVIII. De mali compensatione, sive vituperio & poena, non propositum est quicquam hic dicere: Sed in illis quae de peccato alibi sunt dicenda, ea proponentur, ex quibus sequetur, recte Deum non probare malum & desinere in eo operari, sive, recte malum puniri & vituperari. De iisque positiva & realia sunt, non vero privativa, cum hic solummodo loquamur, difficultas non est extendenda ulterius quam exprimitur verbis hisce, nimirum, sequeretur ex dictis (quod dissicile & durum videtur,) Nullam compensationem, laudes nullas, nullas gratias, ullis mentibus creatis deberi, non tantum à Deo, sed ne quidem à se invicem, dum unarum bonum per aliarum interventum promovetur: Siquidem ipsas ne minimam realitatis umbram ex se contribuere dictum sit; Sed Deum unum omnia. Respondeo, id quod tanquam durum & difficile objicitur, esse omnium veritatum sanctissimam & valde multum memorabilem, qua nihil splendidius, nil evidentius, ab attenta Mente conspiciendum datur. Ecqui concipi posset, Eum à quo sunt omnia, ab illis quaedam accepisse à quibus nihil est, ut illis idcirco aliquid reddere teneretur? Fictio quaevis meritorum sive ex natura dicantur sive ex pacto, qua mens creata aliquid reale ponere posse supponatur, contradictoria est, cum statuat Deum dependentem & independentem, itemque Creaturam dependentem & independentem. Compensationes omnes quae à Deo esse dicuntur & in homines conferri vel immediate vel aliorum interventu, nova dona Dei sunt ex mera ejus placiti liberalitate, quibus priora dona voluit cumulare. Compensatio creaturae à creatura, nulla est, impossibilis est: nam omnia quae dari possunt Dei sunt, nec ab eo alienari possunt, nec ulli alii sunt debita. Ergo omnia sunt Compensatio sive donatio Dei, eaque indebita, quibuscunque mediis ad me perveniant. Nec sequitur, Deum, si is bonum aliquod in me, & per me alicubi, operatus est, teneri ut bonum aliud per alios in me consequenter operetur, multo minus ut ego mihi illas operationes attribuam, vel ut illae ab aliis jure mihi imputentur. Quantum igitur à veritate defecerunt universi ferme homines, dum nemo laborem suum pro alio patitur intervenire, nisi per motivum compensationum, lucri, laudumve exstimuletur, & ne vix ullus libere, ut Dei Bona Potentia per ipsum in aliis manifesta fiat! Fuere tamen vel inter ipsos Ethnicos qui hanc Apostasiam atque defectionem cujusque à Deo ad se,(ut Imperator Antoninus Philosophus in libris de se ipso ad se ipsum,) reprehenderunt, dum per hominem operationes fieri voluerunt haud secus ac fructus per arbores, aut aquae per canalem proveniunt; sine respectu ad compensationem laudemque mutuam. Jam vero omne eorum qui stipites haberi nolunt studium in eo versatur, ut se ipsos mutuo in idola convertant, sibique thura offerant vicissim, dum meritorum, ut vocant, suorum quisque laudes (sacrificium soli Deo ex veritate debitum) alii in alios debacchare, conferre, atque à se invicem accipere summa industria contendunt. Quin à pueritia solent ita à suis ductoribus inescari, & provocari laudibus, ut postmodum per totam vitam non animadvertant (nisi singularis Dei gratia accedat, quoddam ad se unum convertens) se ad exitium ruere, dum continuo furto ea ad se rapiunt quæ ad unam Liberrimam Dei Potentiam unice sunt referenda. Hinc non mirum si Sophistæ, si homines mundo dediti, si ii qui pura ratione ad Principia usque rerum prima non deveniunt, ad hæcce non adeo attendant, vel etiam ea irrideant, causantes, neminem laudi renuntiare nisi prius laudanda facere desierit; (debuissent dicere, nisi prius didicerit omnia laudanda à solo Deo fieri, ubicunque illa fiant.) Sed miror virum recta ratione utentem Cartesium, in hunc scopulum impegisse, dum in Passionum parte Tertia de Generositate & Satisfactione sui verba faciens, asserit hominem se existimare posse, & acquiescere in se ipso ob proprium quoddam meritum, & causam aliunde non pendentem, & similia. nam quamvis de statu naturali loquatur, dicique possit de independentia à creatura, non autem à Creatore sermonem esse, non inde tamen sequitur hominem se existimare, sibique acquiescere debere. Quæcunque ad Deum unum unde omnia, etiam in statu naturali, manarunt, non remeant, ea deficiunt, nec ulla rationis species illam defectionem coram lumine Potentiæ Dei omnia ponentis colorare valet. Hæc veritas cuivis Deum recte agnoscere incipienti ita chara est, ut eam commendare sit superfluum.
units.tr: XXVIII. On the compensation of evil, that is, blame and punishment, I do not intend to say anything here. But in the places where I shall discuss sin, things will be set out from which it will follow that God rightly does not approve of evil and ceases to work in it; or, that evil is rightly punished and blamed. And these are positive and real, not privative, since here we are speaking only of them. The difficulty need not be pressed further than it is expressed in these words, namely: it would follow from what has been said (which seems hard and harsh) that no compensation, no praise, no thanks is owed to any created minds, not only by God but not even by one another, while the good of some is promoted through the intervention of others. For it must be said that they contribute not even the least shadow of reality from themselves, but God alone is all things. I answer: what is objected as harsh and difficult is the most holy of all truths and very worthy of being remembered, and nothing more splendid or more evident is offered for the attentive mind to behold. Could anyone conceive that He from whom all things come has received something from those from whom nothing comes, so that He should be bound to repay them something for this? Any fiction of merits, whether they are said to arise from nature or from a pact, by which a created mind is supposed to be able to posit something real, is self-contradictory, since it makes God both dependent and independent, and likewise the creature both dependent and independent. All the compensations which are said to come from God and to be conferred upon men, either immediately or through the intervention of others, are new gifts of God from the mere liberality of his pleasure, by which he willed to heap up further gifts upon earlier ones. Compensation of a creature by a creature is nothing; it is impossible. For all things that can be given are God's, and cannot be alienated from him, nor are they owed to any other. Therefore all things are compensation or gift of God, and these undeserved, by whatever means they come to me. Nor does it follow that, if God has worked some good in me, and through me somewhere, he is bound to work another good in me consequently through others, much less that I should attribute those operations to myself, or that they should be rightly imputed to me by others. How far, then, have almost all men fallen from the truth, while no one suffers his labour to be put to another's use unless he is stirred up by the motive of compensation, gain or praise; and scarcely anyone acts freely, so that the good power of God may be made manifest through him in others! Yet there have been among the very heathen some who reproached this apostasy and defection of each from God to himself (as the emperor and philosopher Antoninus did in his books addressed to himself), while they wished that operations be done through a man just as fruit comes from trees or water from a channel, without regard to compensation or mutual praise. Now indeed the whole endeavour of those who do not wish to be considered mere stumps is directed to this, that they turn one another into idols and offer incense to one another in turn, while each one of them, with the greatest diligence, strives to vaunt the praises of his so-called merits (a sacrifice owed in truth to God alone), to rail at others, to confer them on others and to receive them from one another. Indeed, from boyhood they are usually enticed and provoked by their teachers with praises in such a way that afterwards, throughout the whole of life, they do not notice (unless a singular grace of God intervenes, turning them back to himself) that they are rushing to their ruin, while they continually steal to themselves those things which must be referred solely to the one most free power of God. Hence it is no wonder if sophists, if men devoted to the world, if those who do not reach the first principles of things by pure reason, pay little attention to these matters, or even ridicule them, arguing that no one renounces praise unless he has first ceased to do praiseworthy things (they should have said: unless he has first learned that all praiseworthy things are done by God alone, wherever they are done). But I am surprised that Descartes, a man who uses right reason, has stumbled upon this rock, when in the third part of the Passions, treating of generosity and self-satisfaction, he asserts that a man can think well of himself and rest in himself on account of some merit of his own, and a cause not depending on anything else, and similar things. For although he speaks of the natural state, and it may be said that this concerns independence from the creature, but not from the Creator, it does not follow from this that a man ought to think well of himself and rest in himself. Whatever has flowed from the one God, from whom all things come, even in the natural state, does not return to him; it fails, and no kind of reasoning can colour that defection before the light of the power of God who posits all things. This truth is so dear to anyone who begins to know God rightly that it is superfluous to commend it.

units.la: XXIX. Non licet igitur, inquies, aliquem aliquid socium suum rogare, ab illo petere, illum deprecari, eum orare, ei gratias agere, & quæ ejusmodi, siquidem hoc agatur agnoscendo quod sit vel fuerit in alterius potestate rem agere, vel secus. Respondeo, petere ab aliquo, &c. non est agnoscere & indicare illi quod ex propria potentia aliquid efficere possit, quod de se acsi solidi aliquid esset, debeat bene opinari: hoc idololatricum esset. Sed cum Deus res ita disposuerit ut per instrumenta intelligentia & spontanea voluerit mihi opitulari, ut ego isti Dei ordinationi morem geram, & instrumentum ex ratione & sponte regatur, ei notifico adesse occasionem quæ ejus interventum secundum Dei ordinationem requirat, idque hortor, ut tanquam Dei instrumentum se ab illo regi hac in re sinat. Sic recte ab hominibus petitur. Eodemque modo cum creaturæ non-nulli gratiæ aguntur, si recte aguntur, his non declaratur, creaturam aliquid ex sese effecisse, nec illi occasio suggeri prætenditur, unde ea sibi hærens seque spectans, de se ipsa sibi congratuletur: Sed tum ei indicatur, Deum, qui solus laudandus est, per illam aliquid boni operatum esse, ut utrinque laudetur Deus, & illa se magis magisque ejus regimini subjiciat; tum ei is cui subventum est testatur optare se esse instrumentum & canalem, quo Deus illi vicissim ossi-cia bona communicet, ad agnitionem & celebrationem Potentiæ & li-beralitatis Dei. Quæ huc non referuntur Cogitationes, tenebræ sunt, quibus accensendi vanissimi discursus qui complementa communiter di-cuntur, subtilia certe & efficacia Satanæ instrumenta, quibus vani ho-mines certo & longe à Deo abducuntur, sub specie rei innoxiæ. Ad-vertat cui volupe est.
units.tr: XXIX. It is therefore not lawful, you will say, to ask someone for something, to beg of him, to entreat him, to pray to him, to give thanks to him, and such things, since this would be done by acknowledging that it is in another's power to do the thing, or the contrary. I answer: to ask of someone, etc., is not to acknowledge and to signify to him that he can effect something by his own power, so that one ought to think well of him as though he were something solid in himself; this would be idolatrous. But since God has so arranged matters that he wishes to help me through intelligent and spontaneous instruments, so that I may obey this ordinance of God, and the instrument is governed by reason and will, I make known to him that there is an occasion present which requires his intervention according to God's ordinance, and I urge him to allow himself to be governed by God in this matter as God's instrument. Thus it is rightly asked of men. And in the same way, when thanks are rightly given to a creature, it is not declared to it that the creature has effected something of itself, nor is an occasion suggested to it, from which, clinging to itself and regarding itself, it might congratulate itself; but rather it is pointed out to it that God, who alone is to be praised, has done some good through it, so that God may be praised on both sides, and it may subject itself more and more to his rule; and then he to whom help has been given testifies that he desires to be an instrument and a channel through which God may in turn communicate good offices to him, for the acknowledgement and celebration of the power and liberality of God. Those thoughts which are not referred to this are darkness, and to them belong the most vain discourses which are commonly called complements: subtle indeed and effective instruments of Satan, by which vain men are drawn surely and far away from God under the appearance of a harmless thing. Let him who is inclined take note.

units.la: XXX. Ergo omnia de Potentia Creaturarum ex se Phantasmata evanescunt, ut Solus maneat Potentissimus Optimusque Omnium Dominator & Author Deus, in quo solo tranquillissime acquiescendum nobis, voluntatis ejus effectis & instrumentis. A cæteris autem ex se quicquam ponere impotentibus, nequicquam etiam vel sperandum vel metuendum. De Dominio, & Potentia, attributisque Dei quæ in relatione ad creata spectantur, si plura quam de aliis dicuntur, meminerimus ænigmatis sacri, Deum à posteriori conspiciendum se præbere.
units.tr: XXX. Therefore all the phantasms about the power of creatures in themselves vanish away, so that God alone remains as the most powerful and best Lord and Author of all things, in whom alone we are to rest most tranquilly, in the effects and instruments of his will. But of the others, who cannot posit anything of themselves, nothing is to be hoped for or feared in vain. Concerning Lordship and Power, and the attributes of God which are regarded in relation to created things, if more is said of them than of others, let us remember the sacred enigma, that God presents himself to be seen from behind.

units.la: CAPUT XIV. (13) COGNITIO sive SCIENTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. (13) COGNITION or KNOWLEDGE.

units.la: 1.2.3. De cognitione Mentis creatæ. Cur non ad omnes res extenditur. 4. Cognitionis inadæquatio & angustia. 5. Ignorantia. Obscuritas. Error. Ratiocinatio. Incertitudo. Opinio. Evidentia. Certitudo. Scientia. 6. Nil de eo quod hac in vita cognitioni nostræ accidet, determinandum.
units.tr: 1.2.3. On the cognition of the created mind. Why it does not extend to all things. 4. The inadequacy and narrowness of cognition. 5. Ignorance. Obscurity. Error. Reasoning. Uncertainty. Opinion. Evidence. Certainty. Knowledge. 6. Nothing is to be determined concerning what befalls our cognition in this life.

units.la: I. QUodcunque illud est quod de Cognitione quam habet Mens utraque, Divina atque creata, dicendum habui, hunc in locum, etsi ante præcedentia proponi potuit, rejeci, non alia de causa, quam quod ejus evidentia & certitudo ex jam dictis accedat. Nam, ut à mea Cognitione incipiam, postquam ex animadversione decima tertia in meis cogitationibus, vidi paucis cognitionis meæ limites & imperfectiones, hoc ipsum ex præcedenti & ante-penultimo capite luculentius per-spiciam.
units.tr: I. Whatever it is that I have to say about the cognition which both minds, the divine and the created, possess, I have put off to this place, although it could have been set out earlier. I did so for no other reason than that its evidence and certainty follow from what has already been said. For, to begin with my own cognition: after I observed in the thirteenth remark in my thoughts the few limits and imperfections of my knowledge, I shall see this more clearly from the preceding chapter and the one before the penultimate.

units.la: II. Rerum naturas, statum, numerum, operationes, regiminis in duratione sua diversitatem cum contemplor quasi exstarent, tales de hisce rebus cogitationes deprehendo, ut non tam earum defectus, quam defectuum inæqualitatem, mirer. Cogito innumerabilia esse, è quibus parparticulam ita parvam novi, ut si-cum cæteris comparetur non sit instar punctuli respectu immensi cœlorum quod imaginamur spatii, & nescio cur hanc particulam novi potius quam aliam. An mea de illa cognitio sit ei adæquata, an etiam esse possit vel non possit, non est quod primo aspectu determinem. Quam etiam de his quæ in ista particula sunt, vel esse possunt, notitiam me habere interdum putare vellem, ita incerta & dubia est, ut nonnunquam male rebus respondeat, adeoque fallar. Denique etsi sciam meam scientiam in posterum augendam, non tamen determinare possum, quousque sit processura. Sed postquam præcedentia percepi, de his omnibus sive de cognitionis meæ perfectione & imperfectione nonnihil certi determinare queo. Et primo quidem, cum omnis omnium rerum perfectio & realitas, adeoque & meæ Cognitionis, sit à placito Dei liberrimo, patet, mensuram meæ Cognitionis de rebus quæ præter Deum & me sunt, non desumendam esse ex respectu ad res ipsas, sed ex placito Dei; (Cognitionem quam de Deo & de Mente mea habeo non quidem hinc excipio, sed nec includo, nec eam hic specto cum alibi de illa sit actum) Atqui natura ipsa Cognitionis meæ non potuit eo determinare Deum ut ipsi placeret me omnia nosse, nam ipse natura & idea Cognitionis creatæ pendet à Dei placito; potuit igitur Deo placere ut Cognitio creata non nosset omnes res, sed quasdam tantum. Non autem constat de placito Dei nisi ex effectis ejus, inter quæ cum cognitionem meam numerem; cumque eam ad paucas rerum particulas, ad paucas mentes, ad pauca corpora, videam extendi; de cæteris autem nihil sciat, nisi ex eo quod Potentiam Dei noscens judicet effecta ejus innumera similitudinem non-nullam habere cum ideis quas ipsa de non-nullis in se experitur; concludo, mihi ratione à priori constare, cur cognitio mea de rebus non sit universalis, sed particularis, & ad quasdam res restricta, inter quas iis mihi vacandum est, quæ mihi magis intimæ & implicatæ sunt. sed de hoc delectu alibi.
units.tr: II. When I contemplate the natures, condition, number, operations and the diversity of governance of things in their duration, as though they were actually present, I find such thoughts about these things that I wonder not so much at their defects as at the unevenness of the defects. I think that there are innumerable things, of which I know only a very small part, so small that, compared with the rest, it is not like a little dot beside the immense space that we imagine the heavens to be; and I do not know why I know this part rather than another. Whether my knowledge of it is adequate to it, or whether it could or could not be adequate, is not something I need to settle at first glance. Sometimes I would like to think that I have some knowledge of what is in this part, or what could be in it, but it is so uncertain and doubtful that now and then it fails to match the things, and so I am mistaken. Finally, although I know that my science will grow in the future, I cannot determine how far it will go. But after I have grasped what came before, I can determine something certain about all these things, that is, about the perfection and imperfection of my cognition. And first, since every perfection and reality of all things, and so also of my cognition, depends on the most free pleasure of God, it is clear that the measure of my cognition of things which exist apart from God and me is not to be derived from their relation to the things themselves, but from the pleasure of God. (I do not exclude from this the cognition which I have of God and of my own mind, nor do I include it, nor do I consider it here, since I have treated of it elsewhere.) But the very nature of my cognition could not have determined God, so that it would please him for me to know all things; for the very nature and idea of created cognition depends on the pleasure of God. It could therefore have pleased God that created cognition should not know all things, but only some. Now, the pleasure of God is known only from his effects, among which I count my cognition; and since I see that it extends to a few particles of things, to a few minds, to a few bodies, but knows nothing of the rest, except insofar as it judges, knowing the power of God, that his countless effects bear some likeness to the ideas which it itself experiences in itself about some things, I conclude that I can know by reasoning a priori why my cognition of things is not universal but particular, and restricted to certain things, among which I must give myself to those which are more intimate and involved to me. But of this choice, elsewhere.

units.la: III. Equidem prima fronte non videtur fuisse opus eo usque ascendere, cum sola Cognitionis creatæ inspectio sufficere vulgo putetur ad reddendam rationem, cur se ad res omnes non extendat: nam multitudine rerum dissiparetur, adeoque in oblivionem atque ignorantiam, sive in non-cognitionem rediret: præterea, inquiunt, si res omnes complecteretur Cognitio creata, esset omniscia, quod Solius Dei est: & hocce ultimum incommodum ratione allegata non evitari dicent, ex qua quippe concludi possit, creatam cognitionem ad omnes res ex indifferenti placito Dei potuisse extendi, adeoque omniscìam, Divinam Deum ipsum fieri. At hæc omnia inepta sunt, & ex falsa Scientiæ Dei idea , atque ex consuetudine male de Divinis cogitandi oriunda. Omniscientia quæ de Dei natura est, & ipse Deus est, sola Dei Intelligentia est, de qua supra capite integro actum, præterquam nil nosse potuisset Deus si placuisset ei nil statuere à se diversum , ut sæpe demonstratum. Scientia quam habet Deus de rebus à se diversis eatenus illi propria est, quatenus à solo ejus placito est , nec ab ulla alia re est dependens : hæc autem non fieret communis creaturæ , etiamsi diceretur, Deum creaturæ dedisse cognitionem rerum omnium quas ipse statuit, & sepositurum voluit : nam hæc cognitio mere ab alia dependens statueretur, nec igitur eadem esset cum Divina cognitione. Non equidem dico cognitionem omnium rerum quas Deus efficere potest , esse in mente creata possibilem, nam sic ad quæstionem de Potentia Dei tandem deveniretur, eaque à Mente finita posse comprehendi esset dicenda : Sed ubi agitur de rebus non quas statuere potest, verum quas jam statuit, quis dicat, eum non posse Mentem efficere, cui, si placeat, omnes res quas statuit notificet ? Certe Potentiam Dei temere circumscriberet, aut hoc de ea negative determinaret. Quod dicatur Mens multitudine dissipari, id in hoc rerum statu quem sic Deo ponere placuit, verum est: at, quidni aliter potuisset ille, eam nempe efficere, in qua omnes rerum ideæ sine dissipatione colligerentur ? Manet igitur Cognitionis meæ ad res quasdam restrictæ ratio firma, non rei naturæ, quæ nil ex se est, sed , quæ est omnium ratio mentem tranquillans, placitum Dei : quod cum de Mentibus quæ sunt in statu à meo differenti alia ac de me velle possit, nec sciam atque experiar quænam ea sint, non permittit, ut de earum cognitione quicquam determinem. De iis mentibus quarum status meo est similis, idem quod de me concludi potest.
units.tr: III. Indeed, at first glance it does not seem necessary to ascend so far, since the mere inspection of created cognition is commonly thought sufficient to give the reason why it does not extend to all things. For (they say) it would be dissipated by the multitude of things, and so would fall back into forgetfulness and ignorance, or non-cognition. Moreover, they say, if created cognition embraced all things, it would be omniscient, which belongs to God alone; and they will say that this last inconvenience is not avoided by the reason alleged, from which it could be concluded that created cognition could have been extended to all things by an indifferent pleasure of God, and so would make it omniscient, that is, would make it God himself. But all this is absurd, and arises from a false idea of the knowledge of God and from the habit of thinking badly about divine things. Omniscience, which belongs to the nature of God and is God himself, is the sole intelligence of God, of which we treated above in a whole chapter; except that God could have known nothing if it had pleased him to posit nothing different from himself, as has often been demonstrated. The knowledge which God has of things different from himself is proper to him only insofar as it depends solely on his pleasure, and depends on no other thing; but this would not become common to a creature, even if it were said that God had given to a creature the knowledge of all things which he himself has decided and wished to set aside. For this knowledge, dependent purely on something else, would be posited, and so it would not be the same as divine knowledge. I do not indeed say that knowledge of all the things which God can bring about is possible in a created mind; for in that case we would come at last to the question of the power of God, and it would have to be said that these things could be grasped by a finite mind. But when we are dealing not with the things which he can decide upon, but with those which he has already decided upon, who would say that he cannot make a mind to which, if he so pleased, he would make known all the things he has decided upon? Certainly, that would rashly limit the power of God, or define it negatively. That the mind is dissipated by the multitude of things is true in the present state of things, which God has thus pleased to establish; but why could he not have made it otherwise, namely, made it such that all the ideas of things would be gathered together without dissipation? Therefore the reason for the restriction of my cognition to certain things remains firm; it is not in the nature of things, which is nothing of itself, but in the pleasure of God, which is the reason of all things and calms the mind. Since he can will for minds which are in a state different from mine something other than what he wills for me, and since I do not know, nor shall I experience, what those minds are, this does not allow me to determine anything about their cognition. Concerning those minds whose condition is like mine, the same conclusion may be drawn as for me.

units.la: IV. Secundo , ex eodem principio deducere possum cætera quæ circa adæquationem cognitionis quarumdam rerum quas præ aliis voluit Deus me nosse, observo. Nempe , si rem aliquam , quam me nosse puto, considerem tanquam in omni statu & tempore in quibus diversimode eam ponere Deus potest, cum Dei Potentiam circa hanc diversitatem comprehendere nequeam , cumque omnis rei status possibilis in ipsa re aliquatenus, vel potentia , ut ajunt , includatur ; concludo evidenter , me, hoc sensu, nullam istarum rerum quas novi, cognitionem adæquatam habere posse: quo sensu etiam me à me ipso non comprehendi supra jam notavi. At si rem aliquam in uno saltem aut altero statu, præsenti, præteritoue, intueor, agnosco facile fieri posse, ut Deo placeat notitiam in me ponere istis rebus adæquatam, meque adeo posse quasdam res adæquate agnoscere, si Deus id velit quod velle posse concipio. Verum cum ex viribus meis mihi non constet, an placitum Dei fuerit, ut quot in re essent perfectiones, earumque gradus, tot etiam in mea cogitatione essent formæ illas repræsentantes, (non enim consilium Divinum perfectione adæquo), cumque mihi à Deo non sit revelatum an ei placuerit plus in re aliqua quam omnium optime me nosse puto, esse positum quam in mea de illa apprehensione; agnosco rationem, cur non possim esse certus meam de ulla re cognitionem esse adæquatam, ut bene Philosophus in responsionibus quartis observavit: Tametsi ex effectu judicem placitum Dei esse, ut nulla ex iis rebus quæ ex portiuncula universitatis cognitioni meæ obječtæ sunt, à me adæquate cognoscatur, siquidem experior in nulla cogitationem meam non deficere. Mentium quas novi nonnullarum Cogitationes præteritas, cum præsentibus, futurisque, earum habitus, &c. ignoro, imo meas ipsius cogitationes quas habui, aut quas mox habiturus sum, nescio. De rebus autem extensis multa miranda desino mirari, cum sit æque ex placito Dei quod quædam me lateant quam quod mihi quædam pateant, adeoque non minus sit mirandum me quasdam res nosse, quam me quasdam ignorare. Desudant Physici in determinanda universi extensione, quam positive infinitam non audent asserere, ne sequatur inde Deum nil illi addere posse; nec finitam, cum si aliquis in extremitate esse supponeretur, spatium, id est extensio ulterior conciperetur. Ita de quavis materiæ particula dicere non sustinent quod sit in partes infinitas positive divisibilis, ne tot habeat partes quot totus mundus; nec quod quædam detur quæ plures alias non contineat, cum figura sub qua esse concipitur habeat partes superiores & inferiores, & laterales, secundum quas in diversis locis à diversis tangitur. hic igitur sunt inter duo opposita eadem de re, finitum & non-finitum, è quibus unum verum esse videri debet, alterum falsum, nec tamen in his sine absurditate aliquid amplecti queunt. nam quod non-nulli de indefinitis partibus, earumve numero indefinito adferunt, est ipsissima suæ ignorantiæ confessio, idem enim est ac si dicant, se hæc nescire definire, quod agnoscit ipse Cartefius. Similes recurrunt diffi-cultates, ubi quæritur de tempore, an in infinitum vel in momenta sit divisibile? item ubi de motu, ejusque celeritatis gradu extremo, an detur, nec-ne? quod iterum sine absurditate, uti nec de ejus tarditatis ultimo gradu, definiri potest. nec scopus est ea hic longius recensere. Mathematici à seculis quærunt lineam rectam circulari geometrice æ-qualem, & adhuc disputant an dari possit ? quæ ex recta peripheriam tangente, ex figuræ rectilineæ comparatione cum circulari, ex quadrati lateris proportione cum ejus diagonali, aliisque plurimis, oriuntur difficultates, eæ sunt,ut ipsos,& quosvis attentos,stupefaciant,suæque ignorantiæ invincibilis in rebus tam tenuibus & simplicioribus admiratores reddant. Ego autem postquam observavi me ex me ipso ad nullam rerum cognitionem ejusque mensuram prætendere debere, in donum reputo quotquot rerum notitiæ mihi ex placito Dei occurrunt : at cum alicubi vere & evidenter Cognitionis meæ terminum expertus sum, colligo me ulterius tendere non debere, & ab eo tanquam à vetito abstinere. Hæc partem istius ignorantiæ constituunt quæ est sine dedecore, & docta dicitur, quia imperiti scioli qui universalem & adæquatam omnium scientiam præ se volunt ferre, cum nihil vere sciant, adeoque non sint experti quousque cognitio in rebus se extendat, quidve eam limitet, nullam, adeoque nec istam ignorantiam, profitentur, sed nil ignorare se simulant, vel temere ad omnia adspirant. Certe ex inspectione rerum quas ex portiuncula universitatis quantulacunque cognitioni meæ objicere Deus voluit, videtur mihi concludi posse, Rerum, utcunque notarum, substantiarum, modorum, istorumque omnium durationis principia, extrema & augmenta summa, sive minima & maxima, mihi meique similibus plane esse occultata, ut nihil pro objecto scientiæ nostræ remaneat, nisi portiuncula status medii paucularum rerum, sive stadium aliquod parvum ingentis decursus quem à carceribus ignotis ad metam ignotam decurrunt : quod etiam in perceptione sensuali, quam effugiunt minima, maxima vero destruunt, media autem fovent, experiri licet.
units.tr: IV. Secondly, from the same principle I can deduce the other things I observe about the adequacy of knowledge of certain things which God willed me to know before others. Namely, if I consider some thing which I think I know as it might be in every state and time in which God can place it in different ways, since I cannot grasp God's power with respect to this diversity, and since every possible state of a thing is included in the thing itself to some extent, or in its power, as they say, I conclude clearly that, in this sense, I can have no adequate knowledge of any of those things which I know; in this sense too I have already noted above that I am not comprehended by myself. But if I look at a thing in at least one state, present, past, or future, I acknowledge that it can easily happen that it pleases God to put in me knowledge of those things adequate to them, and so that I can know certain things adequately, if God wills what I conceive he can will. However, since it is not clear to me from my own powers whether it was God's pleasure that as many forms representing those perfections and their degrees should exist in my thought as there are perfections and degrees in the thing (for I do not equate the divine counsel with perfection), and since it has not been revealed to me by God whether he pleased that more be placed in a thing than I think I know in the best possible way, than in my apprehension of it, I recognise the reason why I cannot be certain that my knowledge of any thing is adequate, as the Philosopher rightly observed in his fourth replies: although from the effect I judge it to be God's pleasure that none of those things which have been presented to my knowledge from the small portion of the universe is known adequately by me, since I find that my thought fails in none. I am ignorant of the past thoughts of certain minds which I know, together with their present and future ones, their habits, and so on; indeed I do not know my own thoughts which I have had, or which I am about to have. As for extended things, I have ceased to wonder at many matters, since it is equally by God's pleasure that some things are hidden from me as that some are open to me, and so it is no less a matter for wonder that I know certain things than that I am ignorant of certain others. Physicists labour over determining the extent of the universe, which they do not dare to assert as positively infinite, lest it follow that God can add nothing to it; nor as finite, since if someone were supposed to be at its extremity, a space, that is a further extension, would be conceived. So too they do not venture to say of any particle of matter that it is positively divisible into infinite parts, lest it have as many parts as the whole world; nor that there is some part that does not contain several others, since the figure under which it is conceived has upper and lower parts and lateral parts, by which it is touched in different places by different things. Here, then, there are two opposites concerning the same thing, finite and non-finite, of which one ought to seem true and the other false, and yet in these matters they cannot embrace either without absurdity. For what some bring forward about indefinite parts and their indefinite number is the very confession of their ignorance, for it is the same as if they said that they cannot define these things, which Descartes himself acknowledges. Similar difficulties recur when it is asked whether time is divisible to infinity or into moments? Likewise when it is asked about motion, and whether an ultimate degree of its speed exists or not? This too can be defined only without absurdity, as can its ultimate degree of slowness. Nor is it my aim to review these things at greater length here. For centuries mathematicians have sought a straight line geometrically equal to a circle, and they still dispute whether it can be found; the difficulties that arise from the straight line touching the circumference, from the comparison of rectilinear and circular figures, from the proportion of a square's side to its diagonal, and from very many other things, are such as to astonish them and any attentive person, and to make them admirers of their invincible ignorance in matters so subtle and simple. Myself, however, having observed that I ought not to claim from myself any knowledge of things nor its measure, I count as a gift whatever knowledge of things comes to me by God's pleasure; but when somewhere I have truly and evidently experienced the limit of my knowledge, I conclude that I ought not to go further, and I abstain from it as from a forbidden thing. These constitute a part of that ignorance which is without shame and is called learned, because unskilled half-learned men, who wish to display a universal and adequate knowledge of all things, when they truly know nothing, and so have not experienced how far knowledge extends or what limits it, profess no knowledge and hence no such ignorance either, but pretend not to be ignorant of anything, or rashly aspire to everything. Certainly from a view of the things which God has willed to present to my knowledge from however small a portion of the universe, it seems to me that it can be concluded that the principles of the durations of things, however known, of substances, of modes, and of all these, together with their extremes and greatest increments, or their least and greatest, are wholly hidden from me and from those like me, so that nothing remains as the object of our knowledge except a small portion of the middle state of a few things, or some small stadium of the vast course which they run from unknown starting-gates to an unknown goal; which can also be experienced in sensory perception, in which the minimal things escape, the maximal things destroy, but the middle ones foster.

units.la: Est igitur Mens humana tanquam tabula, quæ uti non omne, nec ex omni parte, corpus solidum refert, sic nec Mens omnia originalia (Divinas de rebus ideas) nec ulla prima eorum apographa, (res ipsas nempe quæ exactissime originalia referunt) ex omni parte repræsentat, quamvis rebus brutis in eo præcellant, quod repræsentationes quas habet divinarum de rebus illis idearum, vividæ sint, & sui conscientiam inferant.
units.tr: The human mind is therefore like a tablet which does not represent a solid body entirely and from every side, just as a mind represents neither all the original things (the divine ideas of things) nor any first copies of them (namely the things themselves, which represent the originals most exactly) from every side, although it excels brute beasts in this, that the representations it has of those divine ideas of things are vivid and bring with them consciousness of themselves.

units.la: V. Tertio, ex dictis deduco, quid sit ignorantia, obscuritas, error, incertitudo, certitudo, item evidentia sive perspicuitas, & similia quibus cognitio mea afficitur. Ignorantia proprie & specialiter sic à me dicta, in mente esse dicitur, cum res quæ est intra Sphæram ejus cognitionis ab illa non noscitur, ut cum nescitur modus, saltem generalior, for-mationis plantæ, aut animalis. Obscuritatem in mente voco, dum vult ad ea quæ statuit Deus extra capacitatem suæ cognitionis, ut ad difficul-tates jam notatas, attingere: tunc enim eorum ideis, quæ lumen cognitionis sunt, destituta, in tenebris esse dici potest. Hoc autem retuli ad ea quæ non sunt objecta nostræ cognitionis: nam etsi quis dicatur obscurius quædam capere quæ alter evidentius cognoscit, adeoque quod est intra limites cognitionis humanæ, mallem tamen ego id eatenus ignorantiam reputare quatenus ad omnes gradus evidentiæ non pertin-geret: forte etiam error esse possit. Error autem (non loquor hic de peccato) in eo omnis est, quod cogitem, sive judicem, Deo placuisse quædam statuere sive operari, quæ tamen non posuit; aut contra, eum ea non statuisse & operatum esse, quæ statuit & operatus est: adeoque omnis error de rebus creatis circa factum versatur, siquidem omnes res veritatesque creatæ, respectu Dei non sint res juris, sed facti, quas Deus prius indifferens liberrime operatus est, ut sæpe dictum. Exempli gratia, si puto mentem esse corpoream, vel corpus cogitare, est suppositio unius facti pro alio, acsi Deus operans cogitationem esset hoc ipso operans extensionem, vel vice versa. pari modo, si crederem Deum conservantem substantiæ alicujus, puta panis, extensionem & modos, esse tamen rem eam non conservantem, sed aliam, errarem supponendo operi Dei aliud quid: quod cæteris omnibus applicari potest. Inde autem venit error, quod cum placuerit Deo in mea Cogitatione quasdam rerum ideas imprimere, quas etsi statuit veras, non tamen posuit omnes extra me existentes, cumque eæ infinitis inter se modis varientur, & res quæ secundum illas existunt, etiam inter se sint diversissimæ, ego ad unam ex rebus attendens judicem realitatem aliquam idea alia mihi repræsentatam in illa re involvi, sive à Deo positam esse, quæ tamen illic non est, sed vel alibi, vel nullibi, nisi quod sit forte possibilis: adeoque erro ex eo, quod putem Deum voluisse alicubi ea statuere vel operari, quæ vel alibi, vel nullibi ponere voluit. Ergo errorem evitabo si vel ideas rerum in cogitationem ita contempler ut non judicem simile quid illis extra me existere aut non existere, aut hoc illudve quod existere novi, habere has aut illas realitates, eisve carere, quæ ideis meis utcunque repræsentantur. verum hicce erroris evitandi modus cognitionem non promovet, estque ab ignorantia inseparabilis: vel evitavero errorem, si, quod bene præcipuum est, quæsivero & invenero certa indicia, unde constet placitum Dei fuisse ut existerent, idque hic vel ibi, realitates, huic aut illi aut isti ex ideis meis correspondentes, (quod est ratiocinari.) Et in hisce indiciis inquirendis & agnoscendis omnis veritatis detectio versatur. Quodsi vel nulla, vel æquivoca indicia deprehendo, hoc est talia ex quibus fieri possint judi-cia inter se aut ab iis quæ præcise intendo diversa, vel his similia sed de aliis rebus, tunc incertitudo oritur, ex qua procedunt opiniones, nec-dum ad ipsam rei animam, ut sic dicam, deventum est. Si vero talia indicia invenero quæ similitudinem aliquam habeant cum his è quibus veritates de Deo & de Mente creata demonstrantur, ut sunt cum ex in-diciis cogitationis meæ existentis, concludo existere aliquid placitum efficacissimum, seu aliquem efficaciter volentem ut existam, sive ens potentissimum, &c. aut vero quæ cum his nexum aliquem habeant, tunc adest evidentia, & consequenter judicii de cognitione rei certitudo, unde est scientia. Quæ omnia specialius deducere ingentis esset operis. Sufficiat si generalius patescat ratio, cur & quomodo paucæ particula-resque de paucis rerum portiunculis cognitiones hisce omnibus varie possint affici.
units.tr: V. Thirdly, from what has been said I deduce what ignorance, obscurity, error, uncertainty, certainty, likewise evidence or perspicuity, and similar things by which my knowledge is affected, are. Ignorance, properly and specifically so called by me, is said to be in the mind when a thing which lies within the sphere of its knowledge is not known to it, as when the mode, at least the more general mode, of the formation of a plant or an animal is not known. I call obscurity in the mind when it tries to reach those things which God has determined to lie outside the capacity of its knowledge, such as the difficulties already noted: for then, deprived of the ideas which are the light of knowledge, it can be said to be in darkness. I have, however, referred this to those things which are not objects of our knowledge; for although someone may be said to grasp certain things more obscurely which another knows more clearly, and so what lies within the limits of human knowledge, I would nevertheless prefer to count that as ignorance only so far as it does not extend to all degrees of evidence; perhaps it may also be error. Error (I am not speaking here of sin), however, consists wholly in this: that I think or judge that God has pleased to determine or to do certain things which he has not determined; or, on the contrary, that he has not determined and done those things which he has determined and done. Hence every error about created things concerns fact, since all created things and truths, with respect to God, are not matters of right but of fact, which God, being prior and wholly free, has done, as has often been said. For example, if I think the mind is corporeal, or that a body thinks, this is the supposition of one fact in place of another, as if God, by operating a thought, were thereby operating extension, or vice versa.
