In the same way, if I believed that God preserves the extension and modes of some substance, say bread, yet that the thing is not what he preserves but something else, I would err by supposing something other than God's work; which can be applied to all the rest. Error arises, moreover, from this: since it has pleased God to impress in my thought certain ideas of things, which, although he has determined them to be true, he has not placed all of them outside me as existing; and since these vary in infinitely many ways among themselves, and the things which exist according to them are also most diverse among themselves, I, attending to one of the things, judge that some reality represented to me by another idea is involved in that thing, or has been placed there by God, which is nevertheless not there, but either elsewhere or nowhere, unless perhaps it is possible; and so I err in thinking that God has willed to set down or do somewhere those things which he has willed to set down either elsewhere or nowhere. Therefore I shall avoid error if I contemplate the ideas of things in my thought in such a way that I do not judge that something similar to them exists or does not exist outside me, or that this or that which I know to exist has these or those realities, or lacks them, which are represented to my ideas in some way. Yet this mode of avoiding error does not advance knowledge, and it is inseparable from ignorance. Or I shall avoid error if, which is chiefly excellent, I seek and find certain indications from which it is clear that it was God's pleasure that realities corresponding to my ideas should exist, and that they should exist here or there, for this or that or those things (which is to reason). And in seeking and recognising these indications the whole discovery of truth is engaged. But if I find either no indications or equivocal ones, that is, such as from which judgments might be made either between themselves or from those things which I am intending precisely, or which are diverse from them, or similar but about other things, then uncertainty arises, from which opinions proceed, and one has not yet come to the very soul of the thing, so to speak. If, on the other hand, I find indications which have some likeness to those from which the truths about God and the created mind are demonstrated, as when from the indications of my existing thought I conclude that there exists something most efficacious in pleasure, or someone efficaciously willing that I should exist, or a most powerful being, and so on; or indeed which have some connection with these, then evidence is present, and consequently certainty of the judgment about the knowledge of the thing, whence comes science. To deduce all these things more particularly would be a work of great size. It is enough if the reason why and how few particulars and particular things, about small portions of things, can be variously affected by all these kinds of knowledge becomes clear in a more general way.

units.la: VI. Denique, quod quarto notavi, me scilicet nil posse determina-re de cognitionis meæ augmento, vel etiam de ejus diminutione, aut alia quavis mutatione, ex iisdem fontibus manat, ex quibus superiora. Quæ mox dixi, in tempore præsenti ut plurimum ita se habent: sed posterum quod concernit, cum de placito Dei erga id (quod ejus effectus est) non constet, hinc efficitur me scire non posse, quando & quousque augenda sit cognitio, vel an ad res easdem particulares se extensura sit, an ad alias? an sit futura adæquata, an vero contra, minuenda, turbanda, (ut interdum accidit cerebro commoto omnem vel maximi alicujus Doctoris scientiam doctrinamque in Socordiam & fatuitatem evanescere.) Quæ omnia tranquille placito Dei occulto sunt committenda: quod si cuiquam reveletur, is in lucrum id reputet.
units.tr: VI. Finally, what I noted fourthly, namely that I cannot determine anything about the growth of my knowledge, or even its diminution or any other change, comes from the same sources as those I have just mentioned. As for the present time, things are mostly as I have just said. But as for the future, since the pleasure of God toward that which is his effect is not established, it follows that I cannot know when and how far my knowledge is to be increased, or whether it will extend to the same particular things or to others; whether it will be complete, or whether, on the contrary, it will be diminished or disturbed (as sometimes happens when the brain is disordered, and all the knowledge and learning of even the greatest teacher vanishes into dullness and foolishness). All these things must be calmly committed to the hidden pleasure of God; and if it is revealed to anyone, let him count it as gain.

units.la: 7.8.9. Cognitio Dei libera, independens, universalis, particularis, adæqua-ta, certa, infallibilis, immutabilis. 10. Quibus rebus cognitio nostra potissi-mum sit applicanda.
units.tr: 7.8.9. The knowledge of God is free, independent, universal, particular, adequate, certain, infallible, immutable. 10. To what things our knowledge should chiefly be applied.

units.la: VII. Venio ad considerationem Cognitionis sive scientiæ quam Deus de rebus à se diversis habet, nam eam quam de se ipso possidet, malui superius ad intelligentiam referre. Divinam autem Cognitionem cum ex occasione meæ Cognitionis intucor, agnosco esse Liberam & independentem, universalem, adæquatam, certam denique & immutabilem.
units.tr: VII. I come to the consideration of the knowledge or science which God has of things distinct from himself; for I preferred to refer the knowledge he has of himself to the understanding, discussed above. When I look upon the divine knowledge on the occasion of my own knowledge, I recognise that it is free and independent, universal, adequate, certain, and finally immutable.

units.la: VIII. Nam primo, cum Deus omnem quæ ipse non est veritatem, ideam, essentiam atque etiam existentiam ita statuerit & posuerit, ut indifferens fuerit ad ea non ponenda (quod extra dubium supra positum est) sequitur, Cognitionem quam de illis habet Liberam esse dicendam, non vero naturalem, cum Deus hæc non noscat quia noscit suam Naturam, sed quia noscit suum de illis liberum placitum. Quoniam autem res in universum omnes extra Dei voluntatem sunt purum Nihil, nec inferunt quicquam quod sit reale, consequitur, Cognitionem Dei à rebus quibuscunque, à placito alieno, ab eventibus, ab indiciis quibusvis, esse independentem, nec per ratiocinationem fieri; nec Deum ideo res nosse quia illæ sunt, sed contra, illas esse (loquor de realibus) quia placuit Deo ut illas sciret. Non recte itaque Boëthius ut explicaret Libertatis hominis (an indifferentiæ, an vero ejus quæ spontanea dicitur, ipse non dixit) cum divina scientia convenientiam, usus est exemplo visionis, quæ dum res percipit, non tamen, ut apud quemvis experiri datur, infert rerum visarum necessariam positionem. Absurda comparatio. Qui homo videt res præsentes, eas non ponit, sed recipit & ab alieno sentit, ejus de eis visio ab illis pendet: an igitur Deus ab alieno sentit, recipit, cognoscit? Nequaquam. Quod ad mali cognitionem attinet, cum malum non sit aliquid positivi, concipio Deum illud nosse quatenus novit suam operationem in aliquo non ulterius ituram, sive se in aliquo nolle ea operari, quæ etsi absolute posset, non tamen ibi vult ex sapientissima & ut plurimum occultissima ratione operari. Quodsi neque hoc sufficit, id quoque nostrum non est inquirere: in his quippe incomprehensibilis & maxime tremenda Numinis Summi Majestas est adoranda.
units.tr: VIII. For first, since God has so established and posited every truth, idea, essence, and even existence, other than himself, that he was indifferent as to not positing them (which has been placed beyond doubt above), it follows that the knowledge he has of them must be called free, not natural; for God knows these things not because he knows his own nature, but because he knows his own free pleasure concerning them. Since, however, all things in general outside the will of God are pure nothing and contribute nothing that is real, it follows that God's knowledge is independent of things whatever, of any outside pleasure, of events, of any indications whatever, and is not arrived at by reasoning; nor does God know things because they are, but rather they are (I speak of real things) because it pleased God that he should know them. Boethius, therefore, did not rightly use the example of sight to explain how human freedom (whether of indifference, or of what is called spontaneity, he did not say) agrees with divine knowledge; for sight perceives things, yet, as anyone can experience, does not bring about the necessary existence of the things seen. It is an absurd comparison. A man who sees present things does not posit them, but receives them and perceives them from outside; his vision of them depends on them. Does God then perceive, receive, and know from outside? By no means. As for the knowledge of evil, since evil is not something positive, I conceive that God knows it insofar as he knows his own operation going no further in something, or that he is unwilling to work in something those things which, although he could do so absolutely, he does not there wish to work, for the most wise and for the most part most hidden reason. But if even this does not suffice, it is not for us to inquire into this either: in these matters the incomprehensible and most dreadful majesty of the Supreme Deity is to be adored.

units.la: IX. Præterea, cum nihil sit possibile, verum vel existens, nisi quod Deo placet concipere, statuere & ponere tale, recte infertur cognitionem Dei esse absolute universalem, & simul singularem sive ad res singulas se extendentem, etiamque adæquatam, hoc est, Deum omnia & singula perfectissime in omni statu & circumstantia nosse, seu ea jam cum tempore evanuerint, seu jam extent, aut vero à tempore nondum sint exclusa. Omnium natura, principia, media, extrema, maxima & minima, limites & mensuræ, regimen, numerus, omne possibile, omnis variationis casus, motus, vel in quolibet pulvisculo, omnis cogitatio quæ præteriit, aut est, aut fiet, breviter, omnis & quælibet substantia cum omnibus & singulis ejus modis, in fieri, esse, operari, durare, mutari, & si quæ alia, ipsi absolutissime & plene perspecta sunt. Et quia ejus cognitionis objectum est effectus sui lubitus, sive placiti & voluntatis efficacis, nemoque datur qui ejus placitum & potentiam evacuare sive efficacia privare possit, patet inde ejus Cognitionem esse certissimam, atque infallibilem, &, quod plus dicit, immutabilem, non tantum quia creaturæ eam mutare non possunt, sed etiam quod ipsi Deo nil aliud constanter placeat quam quod placet. Hæc evidentiora sunt quam ut pluribus deducantur.
units.tr: IX. Moreover, since nothing is possible, true, or existent except what it pleases God to conceive, establish, and posit as such, it is rightly inferred that the knowledge of God is absolutely universal and at the same time singular, that is, extending to individual things, and also adequate: that is, God knows all things and each thing most perfectly in every state and circumstance, whether they have already vanished with time, or now exist, or are not yet excluded from time. The nature, principles, means, extremes, greatest and least things, limits and measures, government, number of all things; everything possible; every case of variation, motion, even in any little dust particle; every thought that has passed, or is, or will be; in short, every and any substance with all and each of its modes, in becoming, being, acting, enduring, changing, and whatever else there may be, are known to him most absolutely and fully. And since the object of this knowledge is the effect of his own pleasure, or of his purpose and efficacious will, and since no one can be found who could nullify his purpose and power or deprive it of efficacy, it is plain that his knowledge is most certain and infallible and, what says more, immutable, not only because creatures cannot change it, but also because nothing else constantly pleases God himself than what does please him. These things are too evident to need many proofs.

units.la: X. Quæri potest, An Cogitatio nostra ut Dei Cognitionem imitetur, sit applicanda, saltem quantum potest fieri, omnibus objectis quæ Deus novit cognoscendis, præsertim cum illa sint circa nos, nec frustra videantur offerri media ad eorum cognitionem? Cui facile responderi poterit ex comparatione objectorum, & consideratione status in quo versatur Mens nostra. Nempe cum objecta quæ nobis obversantur sint vel necessaria, eaque maxima ut Cogitatio Perfectissima, sive Deus, vel accidentaria, eaque minuta; cum ea sit Mentis nostræ conditio ut unis, utut minima sint, applicata, à cæteris desistat, quod tandem in consuetudinem abit; cum denique is sit ejus status ut tantisper inter corporea degat, mox iisdem valedictura; non dubium est quin applicatio ejus ad cognoscenda temporalia comparata cum occupatione in qua eam esse decet circa objectum æternum, eam servare debeat proportionem, quæ est inter periturum atque momentaneum & inter perpetuum atque æternum; inter creaturam & Deum; vel potius, inter usum tantillorum, necessitate vitæ mortalis & ad aliud tendentis, brevique limite terminatum, & acquiescentiam immutabilem in Deum maximum à cujus placito omnia sunt. Hoc oculo hominum studia si inspicias, possis cum nonnemine dicere omnia vana esse, maxime de illis qui affectum tempusque præcipuum in speculationibus & scientiis materialium, in minutiis, motibus, numeris, figuris disponendis, aut etiam vanius, in verbis fucandis, collocant, uno necessario postposito; quique colligendo pulveri illud paululum incertæ moræ impendunt, quod ipsis ad pretiosum unionem sibi comparandum gratuito concessum erat. Sed, dicet forte nonnullus, cum illa ipsa minuta sint objecta Divinæ Mentis, cur mea Mens illa tanquam sua Cognitione indigna reputabit? An intellectus humanus Divino erit dignior, ut quasi se indigna contemnat ea, quæ Divinus intelintellectus contemplatur, fovet, regit, numerat, disponit, &c. At dixerim ego, quare igitur in capillis tuis enumerandis, aut in conscribenda hystoria passerum quotquot cadunt, quove mortis genere, operam non versas, siquidem hæc etiam Divinæ scientiæ sint objecta? Cogni-tio quam de universis habet Mens Summa, eam à sui notitia & amore non avocat, actusque quo se contemplatur & amat hac non interrumpi-tur nec interpellatur. Sed non ita est de Cogitatione nostra in hoc re-rum statu.
units.tr: X. It may be asked whether our thought, in order to imitate the knowledge of God, ought to be applied, at least as far as can be done, to all the objects which God knows to be known, especially since those objects are around us, and the means for knowing them do not seem to be offered in vain? To this it can easily be answered by comparing the objects and considering the state in which our mind is placed. Indeed, since the objects which present themselves to us are either necessary, and of these the greatest is the most perfect thought, that is God, or accidental, and these are minute; since it is the condition of our mind that, applied to one thing, however small it may be, it turns away from the others, which at length becomes a habit; since finally its state is such that it lives for a little while among bodily things, soon to bid them farewell; there is no doubt that its application to knowing temporal things, when compared with the occupation in which it ought to be engaged concerning the eternal object, ought to keep that proportion which exists between the perishable and the momentary, and between the perpetual and the eternal; between the creature and God; or rather, between the use of very small things, which are necessary for mortal life and tend to something else, and are bounded by a short limit, and the unchanging acquiescence in the greatest God, from whose pleasure all things are. If you look at the pursuits of men with this eye, you may say with some others that all things are vain, especially of those who spend their chief effort and time on speculations and sciences of material things, in arranging minutiae, motions, numbers, and figures, or even, more vainly, in embellishing words, with the one necessary thing set aside; and who devote to gathering dust that little uncertain delay which had been freely granted to them for acquiring for themselves the precious pearl. But, perhaps someone will say, since those very minutiae are objects of the Divine Mind, why should my mind regard them as unworthy of its knowledge? Is the human intellect too worthy for the Divine, that it should scorn, as if unworthy, those things which the Divine intellect contemplates, cherishes, governs, numbers, arranges, and so on? But I would reply: why then do you not take pains in numbering the hairs of your head, or in writing the history of every sparrow that falls, and by what kind of death, since these also are objects of divine knowledge? The knowledge which the Supreme Mind has of all things does not call it away from the knowledge and love of itself, and the act by which it contemplates and loves itself is not interrupted or hindered by this. But it is not so with our thought in this state of things.

units.la: CAPUT XV. (14) SAPIENTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV. (14) WISDOM.

units.la: 1. Animæ Sapientia, unde, ejus imperfectio. 2. Dignior, firmior, certior Sapientia.
units.tr: 1. The origin of the soul's wisdom, and its imperfection. 2. A more worthy, firmer and more certain wisdom.

units.la: I. ANimadversis illis paucis quæ Cognitionem meam subeunt, conscius sum ea in mente mea ex arbitrio varie disponi posse: at ut ea recte disponantur, non ita facile datur assequi. Non dubium est quin res sint concatenatæ certo inter se nexu atque ordine, quem ut cogitatione imiter rerum notiones ordine sic mente constituens, ut rerum ipsarum inter se nexui concordent, arduum est. Datur etiam, sed non sine summa animi contentione, ut quemadmodum rerum unæ sunt media ad alias ponendas, sic cogitatione & in idea quædam tanquam effectus, quædam autem tanquam media ad effectuum consecutionem proponam, & quidem ita, ut si re ipsa media ponantur, sequatur revera effectus intentus. Hic de rebus Cogitandi modus Sapientia dicitur, (scholarum definitiones nil moror) cujus certitudo omnis inde est, quod Deus in cogitatione nostra quasdam rerum earumque modorum, adeoque & ordinis ideas depinxerit, & quod ex observatione circa rerum eventum, quibus mediis, circumstantiis, regulisve hæc aut illa posue-rit Deus, quænam inde sint secuta, &c. possit colligi in futurum, tale quid eventurum si talia ponantur media. quod ultimo in constantiam, qua Deus eodem modo operatur, debet resolvi. At quoniam rerum, mediorum, effectorum, multoque magis placiti divini circa futura co-gnitio quæ in nobis est, non est adæquata, sed incompleta, errori ob-noxia atque incerta, maxime circa res contingentes; cum etiam efficacia cogitationis creatæ res non ponantur, non adeo mirum est in hac Sapientia tantum imperfectionis esse, ut, multos post labores, quæ optime videbantur consulta atque designata mediis certis, non sortiantur eventum, sive per inexpectata, sive quod aliis vi cogitandi nos æquantibus vel superantibus, consulta nostra occulta & abstrusa reddere nequive-rimus.
units.tr: I. Having noticed those few things that come under my cognition, I am aware that I can arrange them in my mind at will in various ways; but it is not so easy to arrange them rightly. There is no doubt that things are linked together by a certain bond and order, and it is hard for me, in thought, to imitate that order by setting up the notions of things in my mind so that they agree with the bond of the things themselves. It is also possible, though not without great exertion of the mind, for me to propose in thought and in idea some things as effects and others as means to the bringing about of effects, and to do so in such a way that, if the means are actually put in place, the intended effect truly follows. This manner of thinking about things is called wisdom (I care nothing for the definitions of the schools); all its certainty comes from this: that God has impressed on our thought certain ideas of things, their modes, and therefore of their order, and that from observing, in the outcome of things, by what means, circumstances or rules God has set this or that in place, and what has followed from them, etc., one may infer for the future that such and such will come about if such means are put in place. This must finally be traced back to the constancy by which God works in the same way. But since our knowledge of things, of means, of effects, and much more of the divine purpose regarding the future, is not adequate but incomplete, prone to error and uncertain, especially concerning contingent things; and since the efficacy of created thought does not establish things, it is not very surprising that there is so much imperfection in this wisdom that, after many labours, things that seemed best planned and designed with sure means do not obtain their outcome, either through unexpected events, or because we have been unable to render our plans hidden and obscure to others whose powers of thought equal or surpass ours.

units.la: II. Non nescio in Mente Creata aliam, quam quæ res creatas concer-nit, posse dari Sapientiam eamque digniorem: cum nempe illa Intelle-ctum suum circa ordinatissimum & Perfectissimum objectum disponit, idque sibi proponit acquirendum quod firmissimum est, nec mutatur, ad quod assequendum media sunt præsentissima, maxime interna, quæ-que idcirco externis rerum cæterarum eventibus non removentur: Hoc est, verbo, cum illa circa Deum intelligendum & amandum versatur. Ultima hac sapientiæ designatione, quamvis in omnibus sit præcipua, nolim tamen hic uti, sed priori, ut ex ea tanquam ex occasione, Dei Sapientiam contempler.
units.tr: II. I am not unaware that in a created mind there can be another wisdom, one that concerns not created things but something else, and that this is more worthy: namely, when the mind orders its understanding toward the most orderly and most perfect object, and proposes to itself to acquire that which is most firm and does not change, for attaining which the means are most present and chiefly internal, and which are therefore not removed by the external events of other things. In a word, this is when the mind is occupied with understanding and loving God. Although this last description of wisdom is in every way the chief one, I would not wish to use it here, but rather the former, so that from it, as from an occasion, I may contemplate the wisdom of God.

units.la: 3. Sapientia Dei. 4. Ejus perfectiones. 5. Quædam meliora, sed non sa-pientius fieri potuissent. 6. Duo extrema vitanda. 7. Prius. 8. Po-sterius. Consilia & fines Dei non scrutanda. 9. Nulli Dei in quibus-cunque fines inquirendi, præter placitum ejus.
units.tr: 3. The wisdom of God. 4. Its perfections. 5. Some things might have been better, but could not have been made wiser. 6. Two extremes to be avoided. 7. The first. 8. The second. The counsels and ends of God are not to be searched out. 9. No one is to inquire into God's ends in whatever matters, except his good pleasure.

units.la: III. Nam quamvis respiciens ad Significationem ultimo notatam, possim in Deo Sapientiam observare quæ creatas res non spectet, sed ipsum Deum, quatenus se ipsum ut objectum possessionis suæ ad quod semper per amorem tendat, proponit, quæque ideo sit ipsa Cogitatio Perfectissima, sive, ipse Deus, ut in Dei definitione, & à creaturis distinctione, & in loco de Dei Intelligentia, quæ hæc ipsa Sapientia est, observatum: attamen siquidem alibi ejus non sim oblitus, hic de ea agam quæ res à Deo diversas, atque ab eo statutas, positas, vel ponendas concernit; quæque per illam quam notavi primo in creata Mente, utcunque adumbratur.
units.tr: III. For although, looking to the meaning noted last, I can observe in God a wisdom which does not regard created things but God himself, insofar as he proposes himself as the object of his possession, towards which he always tends through love, and which is therefore the most perfect Thought itself, that is, God himself, as was observed in the definition of God, in his distinction from creatures, and in the place on the divine understanding, which is this very wisdom: nevertheless, since I have not forgotten that elsewhere, I shall here treat of that wisdom which concerns things diverse from God and established, placed, or to be placed by him; and which is somewhat foreshadowed by that wisdom I noted first in the created mind.

units.la: IV. Utcunque inquam, nam Divina circa res à se diversas Sapientia, nullam involvit cogitationum diversitatem, qualis est in consultando, ratiocinando, concludendo: Sed unum Dei placitum & res diversissimæ, positæ, agnitæ, permissæ, ordineque decenti directæ, cum simul à nobis ob cogitationis nostræ angustiam concipi non possint, nobis licet, dum ad res applicamur multitudinem, variationem, nexumque objectorum comtemplandi gratia, concipere quasi tot essent actus in Divino placito, ex quorum constitutione res ipsæ coordinarentur, sed qui, dum ad Deum reditur, ad actum unum sunt reducendi, quo omnes rerum veritates, naturæ, ideæ, existentiæ, modi, regimen, ita bene disponuntur, nectuntur, concatenantur, & ut verbo dicam constituuntur, ut nil melius, nil convenientius ab ulla creata Mente cogitari possit: adeoque nil inordinati, nil incongrui ibi reperire sit. Ratio evidens est, quia idea bonitatis, decentiæ, convenientiæ, ordinis, &c. non sunt aliquid absolutum ex parte rei atque independens, sed sunt ipsum placitum Divinum determinatum eo modo quo circa ea quæ sunt determinatum est, adeoque eo ipso quo id datur, eo ipso datur bonum, pulchrum, conveniens. Non etiam ab ullo evanida reddi queunt aut pati remoram proposita quæ intendit Deus, cum Omnipotentia omnes obices removeat, & Omniscientiæ nihil inexpectati queat accidere. Quin etiam mala quæ à creaturis fieri finit non modo non impediunt Sapientiæ hujus opera, verum etiam explicatiorem & magis illustrem eam suo tempore proponunt, cum inde patescat ejus Potentia, quæ ultra ens & non-ens, sive ultra id quod simpliciter est negativum extensa conspicitur, atque ultra omnes hominum cogitationes, quibus admirabiles ejus operandi vias ita occultat, ut à prudentioribus ignorentur: inde quoque patescit ejus Felicitas, patescit Bonitas, cum ideo malum sit malum atque idem infelix, quia remotio est à Deo, & sic ita de cæteris Dei attributis, quæ ex occasione mali magis illustrari attendenti cuivis facile est animadvertere, ita ut tenebræ sint ipsi Lux.
units.tr: IV. Somewhat, I say, for the divine wisdom concerning things distinct from itself involves no diversity of thoughts, such as there is in deliberating, reasoning and concluding. Rather, one divine purpose and very diverse things, placed, recognised, permitted, and directed in a fitting order, cannot be conceived by us at once, because of the narrowness of our thought; so we may, while we apply ourselves to things, for the sake of contemplating the multitude, variety and connection of objects, conceive as if there were so many acts in the divine purpose, by whose composition the things themselves would be ordered; but when we return to God, these must be reduced to one act, by which all the truths, natures, ideas, existences, modes and governance of things are so well arranged, bound together, and linked, and, to say it in a word, constituted, that nothing better and more fitting can be thought by any created mind; and so nothing disordered or incongruous can be found in them. The reason is evident: the idea of goodness, fitness, convenience, order, etc., is not something absolute on the side of the thing and independent, but is the divine good pleasure itself, determined in that manner in which it has been determined concerning those things that are; and therefore by the very fact that it is given, the good, the beautiful and the fitting are given. Nor can the things which God intends be made vain by anyone or suffer any hindrance, since Omnipotence removes all obstacles, and nothing unexpected can happen to Omniscience. Indeed, even the evils which God permits to be done by creatures not only do not hinder the works of this wisdom, but in due time even set it forth more clearly and illustriously; for thereby his Power is made manifest, which is seen to extend beyond being and non-being, that is, beyond what is simply negative, and beyond all human thoughts, by which his wondrous ways of working are so hidden that they are unknown to the more prudent. Thereby also his Happiness is made manifest, and his Goodness is made manifest, since evil is evil and likewise unhappy precisely because it is a removal from God; and so it is with the other attributes of God, which it is easy for anyone attending to them to notice are made more clearly visible on the occasion of evil; so that darkness is light to him.

units.la: V. Quæri potest, An ex Dei sapientia omnia ita bene constituta sint, ut nil melius à Deo fieri potuerit? Respondeo, de Potentia Dei & de Universitate rerum, quas non capio, tacendo. At de rebus quibusdam quas novi, concipio eas facile meliores seorsim, sive perfectiores, hoc est, plures realitatis gradus in se possidentes, à Deo fieri potuisse, quamvis concipiam Deum omnia & singula quam sapientissime egisse, ita ut cogitare non detur eum sapientius agere potuisse. Etenim Sapientia Dei in agendo non pendet à gradibus perfectionum quæ in unaquaque re exstant, quasque plus vel minus creaturis impertiri potest; Sed est in occultissima ratione placiti sui, cur ita agat & velit. Deus itaque semper facit optimum, id est, tale bonum, cui plura quidem realia tribuere potuisset, non autem ex consilio meliori & sapientiori & cum scopo convenientiori. Ex quo est, cur non velit omnia bona possibilia existere? cur tali creaturæ tales tantosque perfectionum gradus largiri, tali vero non? cur in illa se magis repræsentare, in ista minus; in hoc magis operari, in illa minus, voluerit? cur mala hæc, hic, hoc tempore, eousque sinat? aliaque infinita, quæ omnia sapientissime constituta & consulta sunt. Nec specialius quid de hisce ulli judicare datur nisi illi cui finis creationis omnium, rerumque Universitas perfecte patefiunt: nam nobis, utrumque ignorantibus, accidere potest ut judicemus aliquid à scopo, quem scilicet imaginati sumus, deviare, quod tamen cum vero scopo, nobis occulto, optime conveniat: atque ut illi cui domus commoditates omnes perspectæ sunt, locum, qui solus spectatus inhonestissimus censetur, habita tamen ratione totius ædificii majorem inferre commoditatem, atque necessariorem & requisitiorem esse quam splendidius forte aliquod ambulacrum, notum est; sic à nobis, qui totius structuræ universi ignari sumus, solumque alicujus portiunculæ utcunque conscii, aliquid ut valde imperfectum, inutile, & rejectaneum reputari potest, quod tamen habita totius, nobis ignoti, ratione, convenientius atque requisitius erit quam quæ perfectiora arbitramur. Quare de hisce non est leviter judicandum.
units.tr: V. It may be asked: Are all things so well constituted by the wisdom of God that God could not have made anything better? I answer that concerning God's power and the totality of things, which I do not grasp, I keep silent. But concerning certain things which I know, I judge that God could have made them easily better taken singly, or more perfect, that is, possessing more degrees of reality in themselves, although I hold that God has acted as wisely as possible in all and each, so that it cannot be thought that he could have acted more wisely. For the wisdom of God in acting does not depend on the degrees of perfection which exist in each thing, and which he can impart to creatures more or less; but it lies in the most hidden reason of his good pleasure, why he acts and wills thus. God therefore always does what is best, that is, such a good that he could indeed have bestowed more real things upon it, but not from a better and wiser counsel and with a more fitting aim. Hence it is that he has not willed all possible goods to exist: why he has granted such and such great degrees of perfection to this creature and not to that one; why he willed to represent himself more in one and less in another, to work more in this and less in that; why he permits these evils, here, at this time, to such an extent; and countless other things, all of which are most wisely constituted and decided. Nor is it given to anyone to judge anything about these matters in particular except to him for whom the purpose of the creation of all things and the totality of the universe are perfectly open; for we, ignorant of both, may happen to judge that something deviates from the aim which we have imagined, though it agrees very well with the true aim, which is hidden from us. And as it is known that to one who has perfectly surveyed all the conveniences of a house, a place which, if viewed alone, is judged most unseemly, yet, taking account of the whole building, brings greater convenience and is more necessary and more required than some more splendid walkway; so by us, who are ignorant of the whole structure of the universe and conscious of only some small portion of it, something may be reckoned as very imperfect, useless and to be cast aside, which nevertheless, taking account of the whole, unknown to us, will be more fitting and more required than what we think more perfect. Therefore one must not judge lightly about these matters.

units.la: VI. Ne autem, cum Dei Sapientia sit abyssus impervia, in temeritatis crimen is qui eam contemplaturus est, incidat, duo extrema evidenter cavenda sunt, alterum, ne de illa secundum apparentiam nonnullarum rerum externam judicetur; alterum, ne nimis exploretur, neve ejus judicia sive agendi rationes impervię, disquirantur: Cum id cuivis sufficere debeat, Perfectissimam Cogitationem nil facere, nil sinere, quod non optime atque perfectissime sit actum & permissum.
units.tr: VI. Lest, since the Wisdom of God is an unfathomable abyss, the one who is about to contemplate it fall into the crime of rashness, two extremes must plainly be avoided: the first, that it not be judged by the outward appearance of some things; the second, that it not be explored too much, nor its judgments or manner of acting be inquired into as if they were beyond our reach. This ought to be enough for anyone: that the most perfect Thought permits and does nothing that has not been done and permitted in the best and most perfect way.

units.la: VII. Horum extremorum prius vitio non caret: etenim cum unaquæque res totius universitatis sit particula, habeatque relationem ad totum suum, quod etiam de tempore asseri potest, quippe cujus momenta singula cum præcedentibus sequentibusque omnibus sint connexa, quis non videt illum qui ex inspectione quorumdam quæ uni aut alteri accidunt personæ, familiæ, regioni, hoc aut illo tempore (quæ omnia particula universitatis rerum & temporis sunt tantummodo) de Sapientia Dei judicium ferret, paria cum illo facturum qui de peritissimi Architecti Solertia ex uno ædificii lapide vellet pronunciare, non attenta constructionis totius structuræ compage, nec expectata ejus absolutione, quæ tamen vel absolutissima solertiam ejus non exhauriret? vel etiam cum eo, qui ex pulcerrima statua aut tabula particulam decerperet ut exinde non modo de tota mole, sed & de peritia fictoris ferret ret sententiam ? Nonne ii qui de Sapientia Divina ex rerum apparente & mutabili facie dijudicant, idem faciunt, acsi quis de ædificii ex-terna inspectione, de interna ejus dispositione optime judicare præ-tenderet?
units.tr: VII. The first of these extremes is not free from fault. For since each thing is a part of the whole universe and has its relation to its whole, which can also be said of time, since each of its moments is linked with all those before and after, who does not see that the one who, from observing certain things that happen to one person, family, region, or at this or that time (all of which are only parts of the universe of things and of time), would pass judgment on the Wisdom of God, would do the same as one who wished to pronounce on the skill of the most expert Architect from a single stone of a building, without attending to the structure of the whole edifice or waiting for its completion, which, even when most complete, would not exhaust his skill? Or the same as one who would pluck a small piece from a most beautiful statue or painting and from it pass judgment not only on the whole mass but also on the skill of the maker? Do not those who judge the Divine Wisdom from the apparent and changing face of things do the same, as if someone claimed to judge very well of a building's inner arrangement from an outside view?

units.la: VIII. Sed nec minori cum temeritate nonnulli conari possent Sapientiam Divinam ita explorare, ut quasi ejus fundum, ut sic dicam, detegerent. In qua occupatione desudare videntur illi qui in fines & rationes, cur Deus res has vel illas condiderit, inquirunt, ut ex hujus imaginaria notitia, demonstrationes suas de rerum natura & modis fulciant. Non facile credi posset quot & quam absurdæ periculosæque sequelæ ex ea temeritate oriantur. Unde, nisi hinc, tot in providentiam Divinam murmurationes scaturiunt? Unde eorum opera infelix, qui notas vitæ regendæ leges postponentes, occulta Dei decreta, maxime de futuris, rimantur? nam ex libidine occultos Divinæ voluntatis fines cognoscendi, facile est transitus ad cupiditatem ipsa Dei consilia quæ per effectus nondum reserata sunt, nec per oracula Divina revelata, intelligendi: & siquidem prioris fruitio possibilis acquisitu habeatur, imo ut principium demonstrationis teneatur, de posteriori idem nullo negotio persuasum esse potest, adeoque in prætensam illam decretorum notitiam demonstrationes practicas, sive vitæ agendæ rationes resolvere multis promptum erit. Nec fluxit aliunde plurimorum phrenetica ratiocinatio quam sceleratæ vitæ sæpe prætexunt, nempe, si Deus hoc de mentis vel corporis statu voluit atque statuit (quanquam malum non est ex statuto Dei, ut suo loco dicendum) quicquid, inquiunt, in posterum fecero, nil mutabit, imo ex statuto Divino erit. Cum tamen voluerit Deus occulta consilia esse extra Cogitationis nostræ limites, nullamque adeo Mentem debere præsupponere in se eorum cognitionem, multoque minus ex illis quasi cognitis & comprehensis se regere. Certe si Deus voluisset ut vita nostra secundum cognitionem decretorum ejus de rebus nobis eventuris dirigeretur, ea utique nobis manifes-tassset: quod cum ei non placuerit, rebellio est velle ea specialiter intueri tanquam principia cognitionis secundum quæ vita regenda sit. Idem dici potest de demonstrationibus circa rerum theoriam, quas ex fine quem Deus sibi in rebus proposuerit, accersere volunt, quasi Sapientiam Dei, in qua absconduntur, penitus exploratam haberent.
units.tr: VIII. But some could try to explore the Divine Wisdom in the same rash way, so as to uncover, as it were, its bottom. In this work those seem to labour who inquire into the ends and reasons why God made these or those things, so that, from this imaginary knowledge, they may support their demonstrations about the nature of things and their modes. It could hardly be believed how many and how absurd and dangerous consequences arise from this rashness. Whence, if not from here, spring so many murmurings against the Divine providence? Whence the unhappy labour of those who, setting aside the known laws for ordering life, pry into the hidden decrees of God, especially concerning the future? For from a desire to know the hidden ends of the Divine will, it is an easy step to the craving to understand the very counsels of God, which have not yet been unlocked through effects nor revealed through Divine oracles. And if the enjoyment of the former is thought to be attainable by acquisition, indeed is held as a principle of demonstration, the same can be persuaded of the latter with no trouble at all; and so it will be easy for many to base practical demonstrations, that is, rules for how to live, on that supposed knowledge of the decrees. Nor does the frenzied reasoning of many arise from any other source, which they often put forward as a pretext for wicked living, namely: if God has willed and decreed this concerning a state of mind or body (though evil is not from God's decree, as will be said in its place), then whatever I do in the future will change nothing, indeed it will be by the Divine decree. Yet God has willed that his hidden counsels lie beyond the limits of our thought, and so no mind ought to presuppose in itself the knowledge of them, much less to govern itself by them as if they were known and grasped. Certainly, if God had willed that our life be directed according to knowledge of his decrees concerning the things that will befall us, he would surely have made them plain to us. Since he has not been pleased to do so, it is rebellion to wish to gaze upon them specially, as principles of knowledge by which life is to be governed. The same can be said of the demonstrations concerning the theory of things, which they wish to derive from the end God proposed to himself in things, as if they had thoroughly explored the Wisdom of God, in which those ends are hidden.

units.la: IX. Non nescio à contentiosis idcirco maxime fuisse conclamitatum, quod Philosophus Cartesius totum causarum genus quod à fine peti solet in rebus Physicis, tanquam inutile ad aliquid demonstrandum rejecerit, existimans se sine temeritate non posse investigare fines Dei qui in thesauro incomprehensibilis ejus Sapientiae absconduntur. Nihi-lominus tamen dicere non verebor, non modo id de rebus Physicis, sed etiam universarum rerum respectu verissimum esse. Absurditatis & arrogantiae est, quaerere quem Deus finem sibi in rerum natura, statu, regimine, proposuerit; quo scopo, quibus rationibus, quo motivo, res ita disposuerit? Et ne quis fervidior hic subito tumultuetur gratis, observandum est, rerum usum cum scopo sive motivo, cur Deus Sapiens res produxerit, non debere confundi, quod facile fieri posset si haec duo diversissima una voce designarentur, ut accidit cum per vocem finis interdum rei usum, interdum productionis ejus motivum, significatur. Itaque, ut distincte procedatur, si in quaestione, cur, aut quo fine tale quid factum est? respiciatur ad rei usum, quasi quaereretur; quisnam hujus rei verus usus est quem ei Deus assignavit, quemque adeo etiam decrevit assignare cum rem produxit? Non modo haec quaestio justa est & aequa, verum etiam [?] maxime necessariis est, cum nil utilius sit notitia legitimae creaturarum occupationis & usurpationis. Hoc sensu affirmari potest finem creationis hominum, id est, usum, occupationemque corporum, Mentium, omniumque facultatum quibus a Deo sunt donati, esse, Deum amare, eique hanc dare gloriam quod sit Solus in quo, praeteritis omnibus, sit acquiescendum. Etiam de rebus materialibus recte quaeruntur in specie usus omnium & singulorum, quae nobis occurrunt, corporum, at quatenus ad necessitatem mortalis vitae uni divino Amori dicandae conferunt; aut caeteroqui vana haec sunt. Si vero in eadem quaestione, Cur vel quo fine aliquid Deus fecerit? respiciatur ad scopum quem sibi proposuit Deus, vel potius, ad motiva, ad rationes, quibus inductus hoc vel illud egerit, ut si quaeratur, quibus de causis permiserit Deus lapsum Angelorum, vel hominum? quid intenderit? quo motivo homines plurimos perire sinat? vel creaverit cunctos? cur tot, & non plures? quibus rationibus rerum naturas & statum sic disposuerit? Hoc quaestionis genus sine temeritate & impietate non fit, cum ea consilia & judicia Dei rimari audeat, quae optime res nobis incomprehensibiles conciliant, simulque adoranda obscuritate teguntur. Non est igitur unde excruciemur in rationibus disquirendis quibus hisce quaesitis respondeatur. Ecquae etiam dari possent? Examinemus, exempli causa, id quod interdum simili quaestioni, responderi solet, Gloriam nempe Dei esse finem creationis rerum quae exstant. Usum & occupationem illarum hic agnosco; at num is est scopus, ratio, motivum, quo Deus res quæ & quales sunt creavit? Quasi vero non potuisset Deus gloriam reportare res naturæ ab his diversæ condendo! unde sequitur rationem positionis earum naturæ non esse à motivo illo desumendam. Præterea, qui posset asseri, gloriam, quæ Deo non est essentialis, quæque extra illum est, esse finem vel motivum quo Deus fuerit inductus ad Creationem rerum? Deus revera in agendo non determinatur à re aliqua quæ extra ipsum sit. quicquid ab eo differt nec motivum, nec finis ejus est. Absurde rationes externæ postulantur, & quæritur, per quam regulam aliquid sit factum ab illo ante cujus placitum nullæ leges, nullæ de rebus ideæ concipiuntur. Suffecerit igitur in hisce unum Dei placitum allegare, quippe quod Sapientia ipsa est, & fundamentum omnium, ultra quod aliquam rerum rationem quærere, enorme est.
units.tr: IX. I am not unaware that the contentious have cried out especially because the philosopher Descartes rejected the whole kind of cause, which is usually sought from the end, in physical matters, as useless for demonstrating anything, judging that he could not investigate the ends of God, which are hidden in the treasury of his incomprehensible Wisdom, without rashness. Nevertheless I will not hesitate to say that this is most true not only of physical matters but also with respect to all things. It is absurd and arrogant to ask what end God proposed to himself in the nature, condition, and governance of things; with what aim, by what reasons, from what motive, he so arranged things? And lest any overheated person be needlessly stirred up at once, it must be noted that the use of a thing and the aim or motive for which God, being wise, produced things, ought not to be confused. This could easily happen if these two very different things were designated by one word, as occurs when the word finis (end) sometimes signifies the use of a thing and sometimes the motive for its production. Therefore, to proceed distinctly: if, in the question why or for what end such a thing was made, one looks to the use of the thing, as if one were asking: what is the true use of this thing which God assigned to it, and which he therefore also decreed to assign when he produced the thing? This question is not only just and fair, but also most necessary, since nothing is more useful than knowledge of the lawful occupation and use of creatures. In this sense it can be affirmed that the end of the creation of men, that is, the use and occupation of bodies, minds, and all the faculties with which they have been endowed by God, is to love God and to give him this glory, that he alone is the one in whom, all others set aside, one may rest. Likewise, concerning material things, it is rightly asked, in regard to the specific use of all and each of the bodies that come before us, insofar as they serve the needs of mortal life, which is to be devoted to the one Divine Love; otherwise these questions are vain. But if in the same question, Why or for what end did God do something? one looks to the aim God proposed to himself, or rather to the motives and reasons by which he was moved to do this or that, as if one asked: for what causes did God permit the fall of the angels or of men? what did he intend? for what motive does he allow so many men to perish? or did he create them all? why so many and not more? by what reasons did he so arrange the natures and condition of things? This kind of question is not made without rashness and impiety, since it dares to search out those counsels and judgments of God which best make these things incomprehensible to us and are at the same time covered by an obscurity to be adored. There is therefore no reason for us to torment ourselves in seeking reasons by which these questions might be answered. Could any even be given? Let us examine, for example, what is sometimes answered to a question like this, namely that the glory of God is the end of the creation of the things that exist. I recognise here the use and occupation of those things; but is this the aim, reason, or motive by which God created things which are and are such as they are? As if God could not have won glory by creating natures different from these! Hence it follows that the reason for the positing of their nature is not to be derived from that motive. Moreover, how could it be asserted that glory, which is not essential to God and which lies outside him, is the end or motive by which God was induced to create things? God, in acting, is not determined by any thing that is outside himself; whatever differs from him is neither his motive nor his end. It is absurd to demand external reasons and to ask by what rule something was made by him, before whose pleasure no laws and no ideas of things are conceived. It will therefore suffice in these matters to allege the one good pleasure of God, which is Wisdom itself and the foundation of all things, beyond which to seek any reason for things is monstrous.

units.la: CAPUT XVI. (15) ÆTERNITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. (15) ETERNITY.

units.la: 1. Ex variabilitate Mentis occasiones ad sequentia. 2. Temporis natura. mensura. successio. prolongatio. effluxus. 3. Mens subtrahenda tempori ad æternitatis adumbrationem.
units.tr: 1. From the variability of the Mind, occasions for what follows. 2. The nature, measure, succession, prolongation and passing away of time. 3. The Mind is to be withdrawn from time, to adumbrate eternity.

units.la: I. Quæ hactenus de mente mea observata mihi materiam de Deo cogitandi suppeditarunt, maximam partem desumpta sunt ex objectis ipsis, (sive ideis rerum) in quorum æqualitate vel inæqualitate, numero, partibus, positione, regimine & similibus, percipiendis, cogitatio occupatur. Sed sequentium pleraque desumentur ex consideratione diversorum modorum quo mens circa objecta versatur. Illa referri possunt ad eam definitionis illius partem qua Mens creata supra dicta est Cogitatio finita; hæc vero sequentia sub illis definitionis verbis includuntur quibus asserta est variabilis. Itaque, primo observo, tanquam generalissimum & primum occurrens, modum quo Cogitatio mea applicatur illis objectis quæ in ejus Sphæra includuntur, non esse simultaneum & uniformem, sed partialem, ut ita dicam, adeoque debere Cogitationem successione produci, & variari, ut ad singula extendatur, & dimissis unis applicetur alteris, & sic deinceps. Hoc tria includit, vel potius, hoc unum trino aspectu intueri potest, unde occasionem desu-mam tria Dei attributa, Æternitatem, Constantiam, & Simplicitatem contemplandi, sed unumquodque seorsim, pro diverso hujus in mente mea observationis respectu. Ab illo incipiam qui ad æternitatis considerationem ducit, qui tamen ideo ab alteris non est separandus, nam si-bi invicem implicantur.
units.tr: I. The things so far observed about my mind, which have supplied me with material for thinking about God, are for the most part taken from the objects themselves (or the ideas of things), in perceiving whose equality or inequality, number, parts, position, government and the like, my thought is occupied. But most of what follows will be drawn from consideration of the different modes in which the mind is engaged with objects. The former can be referred to that part of the definition by which the created mind was said to be a finite thought; the latter, however, are included under those words of the definition by which it was declared to be variable. So, first, I observe, as the most general and first thing that occurs, that the manner in which my thought is applied to those objects which are contained within its sphere is not simultaneous and uniform, but, so to speak, partial; and therefore thought must be produced in succession and varied, so that it extends to each single object, and, having let go of one, is applied to another, and so on. This involves three things, or rather, this one thing can be viewed from a threefold aspect, whence I shall draw occasion for contemplating the three attributes of God, Eternity, Constancy and Simplicity, each separately, according to the different respect in which this observation arises in my mind. I shall begin with that which leads to the consideration of eternity; yet it is not therefore to be separated from the others, for they are mutually entangled.

units.la: II. Quia cogitationis meæ omnia objecta non sunt æque necessaria, (ut dictum cap. 14.) nec omnia simul capit illa, ut per se patet, Cogitatio igitur in plures cogitationes particulares secanda est, quarum quælibet ad unumquodque objectum, sive ad unamquamque objecti differentiam, vel etiam, prout objectum est magis minusve necessarium; ad modum quo ad ea, amore nempe, gaudio, aversatione, aliave passione, ferimur, pertineat. In hac pluralitate occurrit Successio, qua primam cogitationem altera sequitur, & hanc tertia, & sic deinceps; occurrit Mentis continuatio vel prolongatio, sine qua cogitationum ejus successio abrumperetur; occurrit denique effluxus quidam, sive evanescentia, dum priores cogitationes non manent sed evanescunt, sæpe aliquatenus, interdum omnino, posterioribus succedentibus. Et hoc ipsum est quod aliis verbis tempus meum appello, & quo eadem opera ejus successionem, prolongationem, & effluxum percipio, ut non sit nunc opus ad naturam aut mensuram temporis agnoscendam ut recurram ad speculationes rerum materialium, quatenus studii certi, quod motu absolvunt, unæ partes post alias cum præsentia corporis moti succedunt, aut quatenus certæ materiæ fluidæ, puta aquæ vel arenæ, motus ab angusto spatio, ut in clepsydra, remoram patitur, aut quatenus status quorumdam corporum per corruptionem, productionem, aliasve alterationes, evanescunt aut apparent: in quibus plurimi male naturam, nec exacte solam mensuram omnis temporis collocant. Natura temporis quod in hoc statuMenti creatæ proprium est, hoc ipsum est quod dixi, omnisque temporis mensura immediate agnoscitur & ultimo resolvitur in sensu sive in perceptione quam habeo de mutatione & successione objectorum cogitationis meæ, atque modorum cogitandi quibus ad illa feror. Hoc Augustinum integro fere libro, qui est Confessionum suarum undecimum, fatigavit, ut ipse fatetur.
units.tr: II. Since not all the objects of my thought are equally necessary (as was said in chapter 14), nor does it grasp all of them at once, as is plain in itself, thought must therefore be divided into several particular thoughts, each of which pertains to each object, or to each difference of the object, or also to the way in which we are drawn to them by love, joy, aversion or another passion, according as the object is more or less necessary. In this plurality succession occurs, by which one thought is followed by another, and this by a third, and so on; there occurs the continuation or prolongation of the mind, without which the succession of its thoughts would be broken off; and there occurs finally a certain passing away, or evanescence, while the earlier thoughts do not remain but vanish, often in some measure, sometimes entirely, as later ones succeed. And this very thing is what I call my time in other words, and by the same act I perceive its succession, prolongation and passing away. So there is no need now, in order to recognise the nature or measure of time, to have recourse to speculations about material things, insofar as parts of a certain body, moving in a fixed course which they complete by motion, succeed one after another with the presence of the moving body; or insofar as the motion of a certain fluid matter, such as water or sand, suffers a delay from a narrow space, as in a clepsydra; or insofar as the states of certain bodies pass away or appear through corruption, generation or other alterations: in which many men wrongly place the nature of time, and not exactly the measure of all time alone. The nature of time, which is proper to the created mind in this state, is just what I have said: and the measure of all time is immediately recognised and ultimately resolved into the sense, or the perception that I have, of the change and succession of the objects of my thought, and of the modes of thinking by which I am carried towards them. Augustine wearied himself with this through almost an entire book, the eleventh of his Confessions, as he himself confesses.

units.la: III. Dixi hæc de præsenti Mentis statu: de illo vitæ futuræ ob pla-citum Dei occultum non constat sine revelatione: attamen satis intelli-go, tempus, quale hoc est, sive talem modum existentiæ Cogitationis meæ, debere evanescere si Optimæ Menti quæ me sustinet placeat se ipsam mihi secundum meæ Cogitationis plenitudinem jungere. Nem-pe sipe si objectum omne Unum sit & maxime uniforme, sique omni facultatum mearum diversitate cessante omnis mea Cogitatio esset una Intelligentia ardens in objectum vere unum uniformiter defixa, tunc certe omnis successionis causa tolleretur, nec durationem, nec effluxum sentirem, sed omnia unum momentum, ut sic dicam, sive unum præsens mihi essent, & unum momentum esset omnia, quatenus excluderet omnis pluralitatis & diversitatis sive variationis causam. Et unde quæso variationis animadversio esset inde desumenda ubi omnia sunt unum uno modo cogitare? Hæc vita, ubi dabitur non temporaria, sed æterna (quanquam non æternitate Deo propria) erit dicenda, cujus intuitu subsilit Mens Dei cupida, anhelans donec aspiraverit ille dies, & fugerint umbræ, fugerit tempus, pereat successio, pereat effluxus, desinat durationis sensus, & ipsa, qualis jam est, duratio, ut nil in Mente temporariorum remaneat, nil quo à vera Dei æternitate, de qua mox, differat præter hæc duo, dependentiam nempe unam & eandem, totalemque, à Deo, & uniformitatem cogitationis quæ non sit à naturæ suæ perfectione, nec ad illam relata, sed ex Dei placito & ad Deum secundum ejus placitum, omni pluralitate profligata. Plura vetat dicere rei sublimitas & status præsentis incapacitas. Et revera hæc sunt ardua, nec oscitantibus conspicua, nec attendentibus bene perspicua, siquidem cum eousque assurrexerit cogitatio ut ea quasi gustet, continuo ad conceptus temporarios & evanidos quibus hic subjicitur, recidat. Ne tamen hæc ob consequentias stupendas quas quivis attentus elicere inde potest rejiciantur, velim notari similia olim occurrisse Augustino, ut videre est in plurimis capitibus libri Confessionum, ubi Angelos tempori subduxit. omnia lectu digna sunt, sed ob eos quibus ad manus codex non est hæc notabo : Dixisti mihi, (Domine) voce forti in aurem interiorem, quod nec illa creatura tibi coæterna est, cujus voluntas tu solus est, teque perseverantissima castitate hauriens, mutabilitatem suam nusquam & nunquam exerit, & te sibi semper præsentes ad quem toto affectu se tenet, non habens futurum quod expectet, nec in præteritum trajiciens quod meminerit; nulla vice variatur, nec in tempora ulla distenditur. O beata si qua ista est, &c. Quorum ultimorum vim non videtur assecutus eloquens interpres An-dillius dum lingua nobis vernacula sic vertit, sans avoir de passé dont il ne luy reste plus que le souvenir, &c. cum dicendum fuisset, sans avoir de passé dont elle se souvienne, ou dont elle puisse se souvenir. Nempe hic conceptus non caret difficultate, nec ulli hic datur eo frui, sed cum utcunque quasi extra se ipsum intento conamine saliendo attingere. Neque, ut hoc addam, Mentis in illo statu constitutæ existentia cessatura statui putanda est, quod inde sequi nonnullis videri posset, quamvis nec in præteri-tum prolongata, nec in futurum distendenda dici queat: non cessat illa Mens, sed nihil in ea est quod evanescat sive fiat præteritum, nihil etiam ei deest quod de novo ei accidere possit & debeat, adeoque quod sit futurum: omne est præsens, at tale præsens quod se ipso non est, adeoque absolute non est, sed à Deo est, qui solus simpliciter est, atque illud ab ejus placito plenitudinis suæ, alterius (nempe Dei) repræsentativæ, perfectionem haurit. Quamvis autem corpori cuidam, cujus motus & regimen temporum differentiis carere non possunt, Mens talis jungeretur, hoc nihil perfecto isti ejus statui officeret: quemad-modum res temporariæ Deo subjiciuntur, earumque conceptus in Deo sunt, qui tamen non subjicitur ipse tempori, ut mox ex professo dicen-dum, quia per illas ab uniformi sui ipsius intelligentia in qua tota simul præsenti perfecte acquiescit, non revocatur nec impeditur.
units.tr: III. I have said these things about the present state of the mind; about its future life, by the hidden purpose of God, nothing is certain without revelation; nevertheless I understand well enough that time, such as it is here, or such a mode of existence of my thought, must vanish if it pleases the Best Mind which sustains me to join itself to me according to the fullness of my thought. Indeed, if every object were one and most uniform, and if, with all the diversity of my faculties ceasing, all my thought were one burning understanding fixed uniformly upon an object truly one, then certainly the cause of all succession would be removed, and I would perceive neither duration nor passing away, but all things would be one moment, as it were, or one present to me, and one moment would be all things, inasmuch as it would exclude every cause of plurality, diversity or variation. And where, I ask, would the observation of variation be drawn from, where all things are to think one thing in one way? This life, where there will be given a life not temporary but eternal (though not the eternity proper to God), is to be called so; in view of it the mind eager for God leaps up, longing until that day shall dawn and the shadows flee, time flee, succession perish, passing away perish, the sense of duration cease, and duration itself, such as it now is, so that nothing remains in the mind of things temporary, nothing by which it differs from the true eternity of God, of which presently, except these two: one and the same total dependence upon God, and a uniformity of thought which is not from the perfection of its own nature nor referred to it, but from the good pleasure of God and directed to God according to his good pleasure, with all plurality put to flight. The sublimity of the matter and the incapacity of the present state forbid me to say more. And indeed these things are arduous, not evident to the careless, nor very clear to those who attend, since when thought has risen so far that it tastes them as it were, it immediately falls back to the temporary and fleeting concepts to which it is here subjected. Lest, however, these things be rejected on account of the stupendous consequences which any attentive person can draw from them, I would like it to be noted that similar things once occurred to Augustine, as can be seen in many chapters of the book of his Confessions, where he withdrew the Angels from time. All of them are worth reading, but for those who do not have the book at hand I will note these: You said to me, O Lord, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that not even that creature is coeternal with you, whose will is you alone, and which, drinking you in with most persevering chastity, never and nowhere exerts its mutability, and, always present to you, to whom it holds itself with its whole affection, has no future to expect, nor passes into the past to remember; it is never varied by any change, nor is it stretched out into any times. O blessed, if there is any such, etc. The force of these last words does not seem to have been grasped by the eloquent translator Andilly, when in our vernacular he renders them thus: sans avoir de passé dont il ne luy reste plus que le souvenir, etc., whereas it should have been rendered: sans avoir de passé dont elle se souvienne, ou dont elle puisse se souvenir. Indeed this concept is not free of difficulty, nor is it given to anyone here to enjoy it, but only to reach it, as it were, by some effort of attention that leaps somehow outside itself. Nor, to add this, should the existence of a mind established in that state be thought to cease in a state, which some might think follows from it, although it cannot be said either to be prolonged into the past or extended into the future: that mind does not cease, but nothing in it vanishes or becomes past, nothing is also lacking to it that could and ought to happen to it anew, and so nothing is future: all is present, but such a present as is not of itself, and so is not absolutely, but is from God, who alone simply is, and draws its perfection from his good pleasure of fullness, which is the representative perfection of another (namely God). Although indeed such a mind were joined to some body whose motion and government of times cannot be free of differences of time, this would be no hindrance to that perfect state of its: just as temporary things are subject to God, and their concepts are in God, who is not however himself subject to time, as will be said presently and expressly, because by those concepts he is not called back from, nor hindered in, his uniform intelligence, in which he rests perfectly as a whole, all at once present.

units.la: 4. Dei Æternitas demonstratur. 5. Ejus idea. Definitio Boëthii non exacta. 6. Æternitas non coëxistit tempori, nec hoc illi. 7. Essentia rerum non sunt proprie æterna. 5.[?] Res in æternitate facta non sunt. 9. Si mundus non haberet initium existentiæ, non tamen esset æternus. Demonstratur habere initium. 10. Figmentorum circa Æternitatem & præsentiam Dei origines, & destructio.
units.tr: 4. The eternity of God is demonstrated. 5. Its idea. Boethius's definition is not exact. 6. Eternity does not coexist with time, nor time with it. 7. The essences of things are not properly eternal. 8.[?] Things made in eternity are not made. 9. If the world had no beginning of existence, it would still not be eternal. It is demonstrated that it has a beginning. 10. The origins and destruction of fictions concerning the eternity and presence of God.

units.la: IV. Hæc quantum hic datur percipienti non potest non occurrere is de Deo conceptus qui ejus Æternitatem verius & distinctius quam vulgo fit, repræsentet, nosque reddat certos Dei æterni existentiam cum tempore nil habere commune. Omnis quippe, ut visum est, temporis successio, distensio, & effluxus à præterito per præsens in futurum, rei convenit ob ejus dependentiam, & quidem talem, ut ejus realitates repræsentativæ non ponantur omnes, nec simul, sed unæ post alias, prout Summo Domino placuit. Quomodo igitur successionem, continuationem & effluxum in illo conciperemus cujus omnia sunt una perfectissima & Independens Cogitatio? Aut quam absurde ejus Æternitas statueretur esse series infinitorum momentorum quæ initio carentia ita decurrerent ut finem fluendi non essent habitura? Nonne sic Deo tribuerentur imperfectiones, eæque tales, quas à nonnullis creaturis removeri posse vidimus? In cujus Cogitatione est successio, in illo omnia simul[?] non sunt, adeoque is est Naturae limitatae. Cujus Cogitatio pro-longatur, ejus existentia semel, adeoque simpliciter & in se spectata, non est necessaria, sive non est absolute, sed cum conditione ut reproducetur, ut reponatur, sine quo esset ut in nihil evaderet. In fluxu tem-porario a praeterito per praesens in futurum, infinite plus datur imper-sectionis sive non esse, quam perfectionis atque esse: infinitum praeteritum amplius non est, infinitum futurum adhuc non est, super est volucre momentum quo res istis subjecta actu fruitur. Qua fronte similia illi tribuere qui in veritate absolute dicit Ego sum, quasi dicat, In me nil praeteritum est, nil futurum: nil est ante me & nil post me: Sum semel & totus. Existentiae illius nil potest devenire in praeteritum, quae perfectissima est; neque status ejus praesens is est qui sibi non sufficiens egeat re aliqua eum jam deficiente, nempe futura existentia sibi postmodum acquirenda.
units.tr: IV. As far as it can be given to the one perceiving here, this concept of God must come to mind, one which represents his eternity more truly and distinctly than is commonly done, and makes us certain that the existence of the eternal God has nothing in common with time. For all succession, distension and flow from past through present into future, as has been seen, belongs to a thing because of its dependence, and indeed to such a degree that its representative realities are not all posited, nor all at once, but one after another, as the Supreme Lord has pleased. How then could we conceive succession, continuation and flow in him, whose all things are one most perfect and independent thought? Or how absurd would it be to hold that his eternity is a series of infinite moments, which, lacking a beginning, would so run on that they would never have an end to their flowing? Would not imperfections thus be attributed to God, of the sort which we have seen can be removed from some creatures? In whose thought there is succession, in him all things are not together, and so he belongs to limited nature. Whose thought is prolonged, his existence, once taken simply and considered in itself, is not necessary, that is, it is not absolute, but on the condition that it be reproduced and renewed, without which it would pass into nothing. In the temporal flow from past through present into future, infinitely more imperfection or non-being is given than perfection and being: the infinite past no longer is, the infinite future is not yet, there remains only the fleeting moment in which the thing subject to these actually enjoys existence. With what effrontery should we ascribe similar things to him who in truth says absolutely, I am, as if he were saying, In me there is nothing past, nothing future: nothing is before me and nothing after me: I am once and wholly. Nothing of his existence, which is most perfect, can pass into the past; nor is his present state one that, not sufficient for itself, lacks something that is already failing, namely a future existence to be acquired for himself afterwards.

units.la: V. Cum igitur haec omnia a Natura Dei longe abesse ex ante de-monstratis liqueat, consequitur aeternae existentiae rationem esse Meram illam Cogitationem quatenus se ipsam sive suam essentiam totam inde-pendenter & perfectissime semel possidet. Quo pacto Aeternitas Dei exacte designatur, & ab illa repraesentante & dependenti aeternitate, quam supra in Mente possibilem esse animadverti, perfecte distinguitur. Boëthii decantatissimam definitionem {a} qua Aeternitatem dicit esse interminabilis vitae totam simul & perfectam possessionem, omittimus tanquam minus aptam: obscuram, & ambiguam vita vocem non dilucidavit: vox interminabilis quam mundi perpetuae existentiae dicit secundum Platonem tribui posse, quamque Deo, sed ut simul eam possidenti tribuit, videtur dare occasionem cogitandi in aeternitate Dei quasi contractionem mo-mentorum infinitorum, sive spatii infiniti, ac si filum in longissimum extensum, conglobaretur ut simul capi posset: cum tamen nulla res quae creaturis vere inest aut inesse concipi potest, Deo vel ex parte vel ex toto, divisim vel conjunctim, eodem sensu sit tribuenda proprie, ut in definitionibus fieri debet: sed & rationem formalem, ut sic dicam, & conceptum fundamentalem aeternitatis, ipsam nempe Dei independentiam, sive sufficientiam, praetermisit, neque aeternitatem exacte distinxit ab aeterna vita Mentium, quibus etiam quae subjungit de vita temporaria (quam solam ab aeternitate distinctam proponit) non competunt. Possent forte nonnullae harum difficultatum voce perfecta quam interponit, utcunque resolvi, verum id non nisi intercedentibus multis mediis at-que ratiociniis quae exacta definitio non requirit. Sed nec hocce proposi-tum sustinet ut aliorum cogitata discutiantur.
units.tr: V. Since, therefore, it is clear from what has been demonstrated before that all these things are far from the nature of God, it follows that the reason of eternal existence is that pure thought itself, insofar as it wholly and most perfectly possesses itself, that is, its essence, independently and once for all. In this way the eternity of God is precisely designated, and is perfectly distinguished from that representative and dependent eternity which I noted above to be possible in the mind. We omit Boethius's much-celebrated definition, the whole and perfect possession of interminable life all at once, {a} in which he says eternity consists, as less apt: the word life, obscure and ambiguous, is not clarified; the word interminable, which he says according to Plato can be attributed to the perpetual existence of the world, and to God, but as possessing it all at once, seems to give occasion for thinking of the eternity of God as a contraction of infinite moments, or of infinite space, as if a thread extended to the greatest length were rolled into a ball so that it could be grasped all at once: whereas no thing which truly inheres in creatures, or can be conceived to inhere, can properly be ascribed to God, either in part or in whole, separately or jointly, in the same sense, as ought to be done in definitions. But he has also passed over the formal reason, so to speak, and the fundamental concept of eternity, namely the very independence, or self-sufficiency, of God; nor has he exactly distinguished eternity from the eternal life of minds, to which also the things he adds about temporal life (which alone he sets forth as distinct from eternity) do not apply. Some of these difficulties might perhaps be resolved, in whatever way, by the word perfect which he inserts, but this could not be done without many intervening means and reasonings, which an exact definition does not require. But neither does this purpose allow us to examine the thoughts of others.

units.la: VI. Observabimus tamen ob male intellectam Æternitatem Dei, quasdam vulgo proponi quæstiones, propositiones & locutiones absurdas, quas si veram Æternitatis ideam concepissent, nunquam in medium attulissent. Exempli causa, quæritur quomodo Æternitas coëxi-stat tempori, ejusque differentiis, futuro nempe, præsenti & præteri-to? Item, quomodo res temporariæ coëxistant Æternitati? Desuda-tur ut huic quæstioni satisfiat, utque ea explicentur tanquam conve-nientia quæ nullo modo conveniunt, nec à suis explicatoribus conci-piuntur. Dicunt Æternitatem coëxistere omnibus temporum differen-tiis, quatenus simul cum iis est, licet omnes hæ non sint simul: dicit alius, non coëxistit tempori futuro, sed coëxistet: alius, quod coëxi-stat, sed prout columna in foro defixa coëxistit tota omnibus signis Zodiaci, in quantum ista sibi mutuo succedunt in Horizonte, &c. Nu-gæ. verba hæc sunt sine sensu & evidentia. Atqui facile fuissetis cogi-tare Æternitatis existentiam esse ejusdem essentiam: adeoque, petere quomodo Æternitas sit coëxistens tempori, idem esse acsi quæreretur, quomodo illa sit coëssentialis tempori, vel contemporaria, tempusque coæternum? sive quomodo natura Æternitatis & temporis sint ut unum quid & in essentia conveniant? Quomodo unius natura sit sub notione naturæ alterius concipienda? Quæ absurditates revocassent à quærenda illarum rerum convenientia quæ plusquam toto genere differunt ratione ipsius quæsiti. Nos vero, cum supra perceperi-mus Æternitatem Dei esse ipsam Dei essentiam quatenus à se sufficien-tissime est; tempus autem esse res ipsas creatas quatenus suas perfectiones limitatas accipiunt unas post alias; quærentibus, quomodo Æternitas coëxistat tempori, vel, Deus æternus rebus temporariis? non aliter responderi debere putamus quam suam quæstionem cum paraphrasi addita & socia sic remittendo: Quomodo perfectissimum quid, qua-tenus id à se est semel & sufficientissime, conveniat cum alio imper-secto, quatenus hoc est non à se, non plene, sed limitate & vicibus variis? Quomodo perfectissimum est imperfectissimum? Quomodo Deus est non-Deus, sed res temporaria, & vicißim? Minus enor-miter quæreretur, quomodo Mens sit corpus, aut Amor sit qua-dratura circuli? Impertinens est postulare disparatum de disparato. Igitur hæc de Æternitate & tempore cum nullatenus conveniant, nec possint concipi ut convenientia in existentia, sive ut coëxisten-tia quin statuantur coëssentialia, sive ejusdem essentiæ, quæri cum ra-tione non debent.
units.tr: VI. We shall observe, however, that because of a misunderstood eternity of God, certain questions, propositions and expressions are commonly put forward which are absurd, and which, had they conceived the true idea of eternity, they would never have brought forward. For example, it is asked how eternity coexists with time and its differences, namely future, present and past? Likewise, how temporal things coexist with eternity? People sweat to satisfy this question, and to explain these things as agreeing, though they in no way agree, nor are they conceived by those who explain them. Some say that eternity coexists with all the differences of time, insofar as it is together with them, although all these are not together: another says it does not coexist with future time, but will coexist: another, that it coexists, but just as a column fixed in the forum coexists wholly with all the signs of the zodiac, insofar as these succeed one another on the horizon, etc. Trifles. These words are without sense and clarity. Yet you could easily have thought that the existence of eternity is its essence: and so, to ask how eternity is coexistent with time is the same as to ask how it is co-essential with time, or contemporary, and time co-eternal; or how the nature of eternity and of time are such that they agree as one thing and in essence? How is the nature of one to be conceived under the notion of the nature of the other? These absurdities would have deterred them from seeking the agreement of those things which differ by an entire genus, given the nature of what is asked. But we, since we have perceived above that the eternity of God is the very essence of God insofar as he is wholly self-sufficient; and that time is the created things themselves insofar as they receive their limited perfections one after another; when people ask how eternity coexists with time, or, God eternal with temporal things? we think that no other answer should be given than to return their question with an added paraphrase and companion, thus: How can something most perfect, insofar as it is from itself once and most sufficiently, agree with another imperfect thing, insofar as this is not from itself, not fully, but in a limited way and by turns? How is the most perfect the most imperfect? How is God not-God, but a temporal thing, and conversely? It would be less outrageous to ask how mind is body, or love is the squaring of the circle? It is irrelevant to demand the disparate of the disparate. Therefore, since these things of eternity and time in no way agree, nor can they be conceived as agreeing in existence, that is, as coexisting, without being posited as co-essential, that is, of the same essence, they ought not to be asked about with reason.

units.la: VII. At, quod de rerum existentia dubitanter est quaesitum, de ea-rum essentia secure affirmatum est: Rerum inquiunt essentiae sunt Æ-ternae. Hoc falsum est. Attende, an idea rei alicujus creatae involvat ideam verae Æternitatis? Nequaquam. Ergo falso illi attribuitur Æ-ternitas. At dices, est æterna in conceptu Dei, loquor de essentiis rerum, quatenus à Deo concipiuntur. Quid vero hoc est, Essentia rei est æterna in conceptu Dei? An hoc, Deus concipit essentiam rei istius quae est ab ipso diversa æternam esse? Hoc abominandum est.
