Istud inquies non velim, sed hoc, Deus essentias illas concepit ab æterno, vel, ut dictum est, constituit, voluit, ex placito determinavit: quare merito æternae dicuntur, ut etiam passim decreta Dei æterna vocantur. Obscurae & incommodae locutiones, esse æternum ob conceptum ab æterno! an quia res est ab æterno concepta ejus essentia æternitatem involvit? sed etiam, quid illud est, Deus ab æterno hæc concepit, voluit? An, Deus hæc voluit qui æternus est? bene quidem, sed sic mundi existentia esset æterna dicenda, cum ille sit æternus qui eam fecit: An vero, Deus hæc concepit conceptu æterno? sunt in conceptu Dei æterno? Nulla commodior significatio videtur dari posse: examinemus eam aliquantum, visuri, utrum inde sequatur Æternitatem essentiis rerum convenire. Conceptus Dei tria dicit, primo Deum ipsum, secundo objectum aliud à Dei natura, tertio actus Dei. Jam cum conceptus Divinus dicitur æternus, cui ex his tribus Æternitas, & quo sensu, est tribuenda? Si Deo ipsi, hoc nil facit ad rerum essentias? Si ipsis objectis, sive ideis, hæ non involvunt ideam æternitatis, nec cum illa necessario nexæ sunt, absolute non sunt, ex se nihil sunt. vid. Cap.x. Superest actus, quem proculdubio æternum dicentes allegabunt in causam locutionis suæ. Possem respondere infirmando istud quo uti debent ratiocinium, Actus quo rerum essentiae concipiuntur est æternus, igitur & ipsæ essentiae æternae sunt; instando, actus quo idea trianguli à Deo concipitur est omnipotens & omniscius, &c. ergo idea trianguli est omnipotens. sed quia istæ ad absurdum ducentes instantiae etsi convincant, lucem tamen non inferunt, dicam aliud; nempe, Cum actus quo res conceptae, statutae, decretae sunt, æternus dicitur, num significari putandum est eum in Dei Æternitate involvi, ex ea fluere, cum ea ita necti, ut si is actus negaretur, etiam ipsa negaretur Æternitas; nec Dei essentia esset æterna nisi Deus ita egisset, concepisset, voluisset, quae à se diversa sunt? Hæc ita non esse, demonstrant ea quae de Dominio Dei absoluto dicta sunt. Non habet actus Dei liberrimus, indifferentissi-mus, mus, à quo potuit Deus abstinere, nexum necessarium cum essentia Æternitatis Divinæ Naturæ; nec, nisi alio sensu, æternus dici potest, nempe, quatenus res nondum erant, & tamen actu concipiebantur à Deo, vel quatenus conceptus non est in Deo per modum successionis & effluxus temporis correspondentis, sed per alium quem solus novit Deus, quique Naturæ ejus Æternitas certe non est, etsi Eum deceat cujus Natura est æterna. Omnia huc redeunt. Sola Dei Essentia æterna est. Actus seu placitum Dei, sive ejus determinatio, aut conceptus de rebus (&, si vis, rerum essentiæ) sunt libere, non necessario, in illo, ante omne tempus, nec cum successione, quasi alia in Deo præcessissent, alia vero secuta essent. Opera denique Dei sunt in tempore, etsi, ut monitum est, quædam ex his ei subducta esse possint. Hæc sufficiat concipere. Contendat de verbis qui volet, quantum libuerit. Si quis hæc capere nolit, nil mea refert.
units.tr: VII. But what was doubtfully asked about the existence of things, has been confidently affirmed about their essence: they say, the essences of things are eternal. This is false. Consider whether the idea of any created thing involves the idea of true eternity? By no means. Therefore eternity is falsely attributed to it. But you will say, it is eternal in the concept of God; I speak of the essences of things, insofar as they are conceived by God. But what is this, The essence of a thing is eternal in the concept of God? Does it mean, God conceives the essence of that thing, which is diverse from himself, to be eternal? This is abominable. You will say, I would not wish that, but this: God conceived those essences from eternity, or, as has been said, he constituted, willed, determined them by his pleasure: therefore they are rightly called eternal, just as God's decrees are everywhere called eternal. Obscure and inconvenient expressions: to be eternal because of a concept from eternity! Or because a thing has been conceived from eternity, does its essence involve eternity? But also, what is that, God conceived or willed these things from eternity? Does it mean, God, who is eternal, willed these things? Well indeed, but then the existence of the world would have to be called eternal, since he who made it is eternal. Or does it mean, God conceived these things with an eternal concept? Are they in the eternal concept of God? No more convenient meaning seems to be available: let us examine it a little, to see whether eternity thence follows as belonging to the essences of things. The concept of God signifies three things: first, God himself; second, an object other than the nature of God; third, an act of God. Now when the divine concept is called eternal, to which of these three must eternity be attributed, and in what sense? If to God himself, this has nothing to do with the essences of things? If to the objects themselves, or ideas, these do not involve the idea of eternity, nor are they necessarily connected with it; absolutely they are not, of themselves they are nothing. See chap. x. There remains the act, which undoubtedly those who call it eternal will adduce as the cause of their expression. I could answer by refuting the reasoning they must use: The act by which the essences of things are conceived is eternal, therefore the essences themselves are eternal; by urging, the act by which the idea of a triangle is conceived by God is omnipotent and omniscient, etc., therefore the idea of a triangle is omnipotent. But since such instances, which lead to absurdity, though they convince, nonetheless bring no light, I shall say something else; namely, when the act by which things have been conceived, established, decreed, is called eternal, is it to be thought that it is signified as involved in the eternity of God, flowing from it, so connected with it that, if that act were denied, eternity itself would also be denied; and the essence of God would not be eternal unless God had so acted, conceived, willed things which are diverse from himself? That these things are not so, the things said about the absolute dominion of God demonstrate. The most free and most indifferent act of God, from which God could have abstained, does not have a necessary connection with the essence of the eternity of the divine nature; nor can it be called eternal except in another sense, namely, insofar as the things were not yet existing and yet were actually conceived by God; or insofar as the concept is not in God by way of succession and flow of time, corresponding, but by another mode which God alone knows, and which certainly is not the eternity of his nature, though it befits him whose nature is eternal. All things come back to this. The essence of God alone is eternal. The act or pleasure of God, or his determination, or his concept of things (and, if you like, the essences of things) are in him freely, not necessarily, before all time, and not with succession, as if some things had preceded in God and others followed. Finally, the works of God are in time, although, as has been warned, certain of them may be withdrawn from him. Let this suffice to conceive. Let whoever wishes contend about words as much as he pleases. If anyone is unwilling to grasp these things, it matters nothing to me.

units.la: VIII. Ex male intellecta Æternitate est, quod nonnulli sic ratiocinentur: Si cum res non essent nullum tempus erat, ergo Æternitas erat, in qua mundus factus est: quod si in illa non sit successio, igitur omnia simul facta sunt. Hi imaginantur sibi Æternitatem, etiamque tempus, tanquam essent aliquid à Deo æterno, & à rebus temporariis diversum atque indifferens ad Deum & ad res recipiendum, prout spatia imaginaria ficta sunt. Sic dicimus ut difficultati prætensæ non sit locus. Res quæ non sunt perfectissimæ non erant, sed res Perfectissima sufficientissime plenissimeque à se existens (hæc est Æternitas) erat, qua exstante, placuit eidem ex arbitrio quod ex se indifferens erat, res poni quæ limitatas suas perfectiones unas post alias (hoc utique non est in æternitate fieri, vel omnia simul creata dicere) reciperent. In quibus nil video difficultatis, utut ea verbis obscuris, vel insignificantibus, turbari possint.
units.tr: VIII. Some people reason from a misunderstood eternity as follows: If there was no time when things did not exist, then there was eternity, in which the world was made; but if there is no succession in that eternity, then all things were made at once. These people imagine eternity, and time too, as if they were something distinct from the eternal God and from temporal things, and indifferent to receiving God and things, just as imaginary spaces are fabricated. We answer thus, so that the alleged difficulty has no place. Things that are not most perfect did not exist; but the most perfect being, existing of itself with complete sufficiency and fullness (this is eternity), did exist. While it existed, it pleased that being, from its own free choice, since it was indifferent in itself, to posit things which would receive their limited perfections one after another (this, of course, does not happen in eternity, nor do we say that all things were created at once). I see no difficulty in this, however much it may be confused by obscure or meaningless words.

units.la: IX. Asserentibus (Platoni ut ajunt & Aristoteli) mundum existentiæ initio carere, fuit objectum, si id ita se haberet, mundum igitur æternum fore. Ecce, homines isti sibi imaginantur Æternitatem, quasi esset infinitorum momentorum ordo principio atque fine carens. quæ vera æternitatis ignorantia est. Falsum est, mundum statui æternum si dicatur vel semper exstitisse, vel non posse affirmari in eo esse aliquod momentum quod ab alio non fuerit præcessum: quamvis enim hoc esset, nihilominus mundus temporarius esset & dependens, neque hoc quicquam Dei Æternitati aut Potentiæ detraheret. Equidem dogma illud non propugno, sed objectionem qua oppugnatur ineptam esse ostenostendo, & ex falso Æternitatis conceptu oriundam. Fortassis vero ex incidenti postulari posset ut ex veris principiis refelleretur illud dogma, & demonstraretur, mundum non semper fuisse. cui petito ut quantum in me est satisfiat,non pigebit discursus filum digressione parva interrum-pere. Id diu attendentibus non ita facile est ut prima fronte videri pos-set, adeo ut sententiæ contrariæ fautores, siquidem revelatione destitue-bantur, aliquatenus excusari possint. Certe adhuc dum hæc scriberem, postquam videram rerum extrema conceptui nostro esse occulta, non posse cogitari uti spatium vacuum sic nec tempus vacuum, sive in quo nulla res fuerit; postquam aliorum quæ occurrerunt rationes infirmas deprehenderam, alias diu in mente mea quæsieram, putavi seposita revelatione non posse ex lumine naturæ demonstrari Mundum sic esse, ut prius non fuerit. Nam si ab hoc momento, ad quod ejus duratio descendit, retrogrediaris ascendendo quasi ad primum momentum per-venturus, non poteris unquam ullum designare momentum quod non potuerit ab alio præcedi, & hoc ab alio, & sic in infinitum: quod au-tem concipis sic poni potuisse, unde scis, revelatione seposita, non esse positum? Sed postea occurrit, momenta, quæ infinita dicuntur, sive particulas temporis cujus initium non concipitur, non esse tantum sepa-ratim una post alia consideranda, sed, siquidem in unum collecta infini-ta dicuntur, uno etiam intuitu spectanda esse, ut omnibus conjunctim animadvertatur inesse quod est de essentia singulorum separatim. Ani-madverto itaque, Momentum præsens antequam esset præsens fuisse su-turum, quod autem futurum fuit, id non fuit, sive prius non fuit: Er-go, colligendo quotquot momenta per quæ duravit mundus, quæque infinita effluxa esse dicis, omnis & tota mundi existentia præterita, cum omnibus partibus, prius futura fuit quam præsens fuit, hoc est prius nihil fuit, deinde fuit: quod, ni fallor, demonstrat mundum habere existentiæ suæ initium. De mentibus quas suo sensu diximus tempori subduci posse, (nam ex illarum consideratione aliqua instantia fieri pos-set) sciatur eas plus realitatis ex se non possidere quam res temporariæ, & forte omnes prius tempori fuisse subjectas. Sed hæc sufficiant. Redea-mus ad ea quæ Æternitatem concernunt.
units.tr: IX. Those who assert (as Plato and Aristotle are said to have done) that the world lacks a beginning of existence, have raised the objection that, if this were so, the world would therefore be eternal. Look, these men imagine eternity as if it were an ordering of infinite moments having no beginning or end, which is a true ignorance of eternity. It is false that the world is held to be eternal if it is said either that it has always existed, or that one cannot affirm that there is in it any moment which was not preceded by another. For even if this were so, the world would nevertheless be temporary and dependent, and this would take nothing away from God's eternity or power. I, for my part, do not defend that doctrine, but I show that the objection by which it is attacked is inept, and arises from a false concept of eternity. Perhaps, however, it could incidentally be demanded that this doctrine be refuted from true principles, and it be demonstrated that the world has not always existed. To this request, so that it may be satisfied as far as lies in me, I will not hesitate to interrupt the thread of my discourse for a short digression. This is not so easy for those who attend to it for a long time as it may seem at first sight, so much so that the supporters of the contrary opinion, if they were destitute of revelation, could in some measure be excused. Certainly, while I was writing these things, after I had seen that the extremes of things are hidden from our understanding, that an empty space cannot be conceived, nor an empty time (that is, one in which there is no thing), and after I had detected the weak reasons of others that occurred to me, I had long sought other reasons in my own mind, and I thought that, setting aside revelation, it could not be demonstrated from the light of nature that the world is such that it previously did not exist. For if you go back from this moment, to which its duration descends, ascending as if you were going to reach a first moment, you will never be able to designate any moment which could not have been preceded by another, and this by another, and so on to infinity. But what you conceive could have been posited thus, how do you know, with revelation set aside, that it was not posited? But afterwards it occurred to me that moments, which are said to be infinite, or particles of time whose beginning is not conceived, must not only be considered separately, one after another, but, since they are said to be infinite when gathered into one, must also be viewed in a single glance, so that it is observed in all of them together what belongs to the essence of each separately. I observe, therefore, that the present moment, before it was present, was going to be future, and what was future was not, that is, it did not previously exist. Therefore, by gathering together however many moments through which the world has endured, and which you say have flowed by to infinity, the whole existence of the world, past and with all its parts, was future before it was present; that is, it previously was nothing, and then it was. This, unless I am mistaken, demonstrates that the world has a beginning of its existence. Concerning minds, which we said can be withdrawn from time by their own sense (for some instant could be made from the consideration of them), let it be known that they do not possess of themselves more reality than temporal things, and perhaps all of them were previously subject to time. But let these things suffice. Let us return to what concerns eternity.

units.la: X. Plures aliæ locutiones vel propositiones circa Æternitatem obscu-ræ vel falsæ dantur, quam ut hic poni possint omnes, sed facile est eas ad exemplum præcedentium resolvere, si modo clara Æternitatis idea aliquatenus habeatur: alioqui, vel commentariorum plaustra non suf-ficerent. Addam tamen & genefin errorum fere omnium qui in hac materia pullulant, ut ea detecta, isti nullo negotio evitentur. Primo, ho-mines cum essent stulti, &, ut Augustiniano verbo utar, incrassati cor-de, pro rebus omnibus nil aliud supposuerunt & cogitaverunt quam extensionem divisibilem, & quidem spatii pro rerum natura, durationis vero pro actuali existentia. Secundo, cum postea alicunde nonnihil de mente vel de Deo audivissent aut percepissent, etiam eis tale Ubi & Quando extra suam essentiam, extra Cogitationem, in extensione quaesi-verunt & assignarunt. Tertio, ne omnia miscerent, sed ex phantasia sua aliquatenus distinguerent, & primo quidem corpora; quemadmo-dum, postquam figura certa, mensuraque, extensionem spatii determi-navere, eam praesentiae sive τῷ Ubi corporum assignaverunt & locum ap-pellarunt; ita etiam extensionem durationis momentorum certis limiti-bus ex parte anteriori & posteriori limitantes, dixerunt hanc existentiae rerum corruptibilium mensuram sive tempus esse, quod specialiter dixe-runt Quando. Quarto, extensionis spatium fecerunt porro non infinitum quidem, sed nec determinarunt, uti pro corporibus factum est, verum in statu medio indeterminatum reliquerunt, idque creatarum mentium tribuebant praesentiae sub voce Ubi: quo pacto etiam cum extensioni temporariae limites, non omnes, sed quosdam saltem, nempe posterio-res, sustulissent, eam adaptarunt Mentium creatarum existentiae, nec eam tempus appellare placuit, sed aeternitatem a posteriori sive aevum, de digniori Mentium aeternitate nil quicquam solliciti. Et quemadmo-dum, quinto, postquam extensionis spatiosae limites laxassent, eamque infinitam concepissent, Dei praesentiae illam attribuerunt, & Ubique, atque spatia imaginaria nuncupaverunt; ita quoque limitibus extensio-nis durabilis omnibus rejectis, tam prioribus quam posterioribus, illam ad Dei existentiam retulerunt, & quae ante erat aeternitas a posteriori, jam & a priori aeternitas illis est, sive simpliciter Aeternitas, quam ut Deo propriam asseruerunt. Verum uti nescio qua stupenda contradi-ctione omnia iterum miscuerunt, includentes totam Dei essentiam in omnium minimo spatio, causantes Deum ibi praesentem esse quoad essentiam immensam; ita etiam eo devenerunt ut suam Aeternitatem in minima extensione durationis constituerent, docentes eam coexiste-re totam cuivis temporis particulae, &c. Ridicula figmenta haec sunt, & pari modo difflanda: ut enim in primo libro vidimus Dei essentiam, quae ejus omnes perfectiones complectitur, fore limitatam si in creatu-ra esset, imo ipsam creaturam sic fore Deum, quippe in qua esset essen-tia Dei; sic, si existentia Divina sive Aeternitas coexistat tempori ejuf-que que differentiis, & tempus ei, sequeretur istam Æternitatem instar momenti & cum eo limitatam fore, siquidem tota, quæ una est, illi coëxisteret. neque refert, si concipias eam ante & post illud existere, nam hoc proprie est concipere reproductionem rei quæ in se est ejusdem cum tempore naturæ, sive semel, sive pluribus vicibus esse concipiatur. Mensuratur ita Dei existentia, quamvis mensurando limites nec ante nec post deprehendas, omnino prout de spatio imaginario dictum est. Fiunt hoc modo è tempore & rebus temporariis tot Dii, asserendo ista æternitati vel per momentum coëxistere: nam quodcunque semel cum Deo coëxistit, qua Æternus est, id Deus est. Sed quis est ille Deus cujus essentia & existentia in extensum resolvuntur? Miserum cerebri humani, quod vere hoc respectu atheum dici potest, idolum! Sed tandem ut ejus dissolutio non minus pateat quam generatio, quemadmodum præsentiæ Divinæ in spatiis fictio, ex permistione disparatorum orta, evanescit cum unumquodque in sua natura seorsim consideratur; ita hæ de Æternitate fictiones dissipantur, ubi vera Æternitas in sola essentia atque Natura Dei, in pura Cogitatione absolute uniformi inspicitur. quod hic utcunque præstare animus fuit. De his magis magisque meditanti, occurret Æternitatis Entis summi pulchritudo ineffabilis, cujus natura nulli alii communis esse potest, etsi ejus repræsentatio optime inveniatur in illis mentibus, quæ unum illud Æternum objectum cogitantes, tempori vidimus subductas, ut æternæ vitæ addicerentur. Utinam hæc cogitarentur profundius, donec studium temporariorum quæ per momentum præsentia turbant, eo autem elapso incapacia evadunt nos afficiendi, ex animo præ ferventi æternorum cura penitus evaporaret!
units.tr: X. Many other expressions or propositions about eternity are given which are obscure or false, too many to set all of them down here; but it is easy to resolve them after the example of the preceding ones, provided that a clear idea of eternity is had to some extent. Otherwise, not even wagonloads of commentaries would suffice. Yet I will add also the origin of nearly all the errors that sprout up in this matter, so that, once these are exposed, they may be avoided without any trouble. First, men, being foolish and, to use Augustine's phrase, thick-hearted, supposed and thought of nothing else for all things than divisible extension, and indeed of space for the nature of things, and of duration for actual existence. Second, when afterwards they had heard or perceived something from somewhere about mind or about God, they sought and assigned to these also such a "Where" and "When" outside their essence, outside thought, in extension. Third, so as not to mix everything together, but to distinguish them somewhat by their fancy, and first of all bodies: just as, after a certain figure and measure had determined the extension of space, they assigned it to the presence or "where" [τῷ Ubi] of bodies and called it place; so also, limiting the extension of the duration of moments by certain bounds on the anterior and posterior side, they said that this measure of the existence of corruptible things is time, which they specifically called "When." Fourth, they further made the extension of space not indeed infinite, but neither did they determine it, as was done for bodies; rather they left it in an intermediate state, indeterminate, and they assigned this to the presence of created minds under the word "Where." In this way, when they had removed from temporal extension its limits, not all, but at least some, namely the later ones, they adapted it to the existence of created minds, and it did not please them to call it time, but "eternity from a posteriori," or aeon, being in no way concerned about the more worthy eternity of minds. And just as, fifth, after they had loosened the limits of spacious extension and conceived it as infinite, they attributed it to the presence of God, and called it "Everywhere," and named it imaginary space; so also, with all the limits of durable extension rejected, both earlier and later, they referred it to the existence of God, and what before was eternity from a posteriori is now for them eternity from a priori also, or simply Eternity, which they have asserted to be proper to God. But just as they have mixed everything up again by some strange contradiction, enclosing the whole essence of God in the smallest space, claiming that God is present there as to essence, though immense; so too they have come to this, that they establish their eternity in the smallest extension of duration, teaching that it coexists whole with every particle of time, and so on. These are ridiculous fictions, and must be dispelled in the same way. For, as we saw in the first book, the essence of God, which embraces all his perfections, would be limited if it were in a creature; indeed the creature itself would thus be God, since the essence of God would be in it. So, if the divine existence or eternity coexisted with time and its differences, and time with it, it would follow that this eternity would be limited like a moment, and would be limited along with it, since the whole of it, which is one, would coexist with it. Nor does it matter if you conceive it to exist before and after that, for this is properly to conceive a reproduction of a thing which is of the same nature as time, whether it is conceived to exist once or several times. In this way God's existence is measured, although in measuring you find no limits before or after, just as has been said of imaginary space. In this manner, from time and temporal things, so many gods are made, by asserting that these coexist with eternity, even for a moment; for whatever once coexists with God, insofar as he is eternal, that is God. But what is that God whose essence and existence are resolved into extension? Wretched product of the human brain, which in this respect can truly be called an atheist's idol! But finally, so that its dissolution may be as evident as its generation: just as the fiction of divine presence in spaces, arising from the mixing of unlike things, vanishes when each thing is considered separately in its own nature, so these fictions about eternity are dissipated when true eternity is viewed in the essence and nature of God alone, in pure thought absolutely uniform. This is what my purpose has been to set forth here, however I may. As I meditate more and more on these things, there will occur to me the ineffable beauty of the eternity of the supreme Being, whose nature can be common to no other; although its representation is best found in those minds which, thinking of that one eternal object, we have seen withdrawn from time, so that they may be devoted to eternal life. Would that these things were pondered more deeply, until the zeal for temporal things, which disturb us by being present for a moment, and which, once that moment has passed, become incapable of affecting us, were wholly evaporated from the mind through the fervent care for eternal things!

units.la: CAPUT XVII. (16) CONSTANTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. (16) CONSTANCY.

units.la: 1. 2. Unde Mentis inconstantia, ejusque remedium.
units.tr: 1. 2. Whence comes the inconstancy of the mind, and its remedy.

units.la: I. VEnio ad secundam quam principio Capitis præcedentis dixi observationem, quæque inter illas quas in Libri initio de cogitatione mea notavi sexta est post decimam. Infert illa istius modo dictæ prolongationis, quam in Cogitatione mea experior, usum nonnullum, sed eum defectui multo obnoxium. Nempe ejus ope, quod in una dura-tionis parte non possum de objecto aliquo Mente percipere, id partibus sequentibus eo impensis rectius concipio, imo ad alia etiam, ut plurima sunt, objecta, mentis aciem dirigo. At quia Cognitio mea partiaria est, inadæquata, obscuritati, errori, incertitudini aliisque obnoxia, ut superius vidi, hinc in modo quo me non solum objectis pluribus, sed & sæpe uni eidemque applico, & de illo cogito, varietas & inconstantia. Sæpe accidit ut de re una cogitem, postmodum vero de aliis plurimis, & deinde, quasi per circulum ad priorem revertar, quæ quamvis sit eadem, statumque suum nullo modo mutaverit, à me tamen modo qui priori interdum oppositus, interdum ab illo diversus, cogitatione tra-ctatur, ita ut quod mox tale vel tale, verum, bonum, conveniens, gratum, tali modo acquirendum, tractandum, &c. cogitabatur, haud multo post, etsi idem in se manserit, at ob istos, ut dixi cogitationis meæ defectus, aliter reputetur. Et quamvis à voluntate alia causa acce-dere possit, (de qua jam non agimus) atque omnis inconstantia asse-ctibus soleat tribui, attamen experientia cuivis attendenti constare potest, partes potiores tribuendas esse huic cogitationis imperfecta cogni-tione præditæ recursui.
units.tr: I. I come now to the second observation which I mentioned at the beginning of the preceding chapter, and which is the sixth among those I noted at the start of the book concerning my own thinking, after the tenth. It shows that this so-called prolongation, which I experience in my thinking, has some use, but one very liable to defect. Namely, by its means, when I cannot perceive an object with the mind in one part of duration, I conceive it more correctly by devoting my attention to the following parts; indeed, I also direct the edge of my mind to other objects, which are very many. But since my knowledge is partial, inadequate, and liable to obscurity, error, uncertainty and other things, as I saw above, hence there arises, in the manner in which I apply myself not only to many objects but often to one and the same object, and think about it, variety and inconstancy. It often happens that I think about one thing, and afterwards about very many others, and then, as if going round in a circle, I return to the former, which, although it is the same and has in no way changed its state, is nevertheless treated by me now in a way that is sometimes opposed to the earlier thought, sometimes different from it; so that what I had just thought to be such or such, true, good, fitting, pleasing, to be acquired, handled in such a way, and so on, is not much later judged differently, although it has remained the same in itself, but because of those defects of my thinking, as I have said. And although another cause may arise from the will (which we are not now discussing), and although all inconstancy is usually attributed to the affections, yet experience can make it clear to anyone who pays attention that the greater share must be given to this recourse of thought endowed with imperfect knowledge.

units.la: II. Scio equidem hunc inconstantiæ defectum ex me depelli posse, si is qui me tenet, Cogitationi meæ veras necessariasque perfectionum, imperfectionum, veritatis, rerum, ideas evidentes affigat, regatque occulte intima mea, ut in omni actuum cogitationis meæ recursu ad il-las redeam. At vero, si illa mihi indebita deneget, status mei inconstan-tia est deploranda.
units.tr: II. I indeed know that this defect of inconstancy can be driven out of me, if He who holds me fixes in my thinking the true and necessary ideas of perfections, imperfections, truth and things, which are evident, and secretly rules my inmost parts, so that in every turn of my thinking I return to those ideas. But if He denies me those things, which I do not deserve, the inconstancy of my state is to be lamented.

units.la: 3. Deus est constantissimus in Natura sua & placito. 4. Non obstante rerum inconstantia. 5. De promissis, votis, aliisque mediis quibus homines prætendunt se constantes reddere.
units.tr: 3. God is most constant in his nature and his will. 4. Notwithstanding the inconstancy of things. 5. Concerning promises, vows, and other means by which men pretend to make themselves constant.

units.la: III. Ille autem, ad quem reflecto, Deus, non ita se habet, sed mihi ab omni variatione & inconstantia liber conspicitur, sive eum spectem quatenus is se ipso gaudet, sive quatenus alia intuetur; sive ejus naturam, seu ejus de rebus placitum intuear: adeoque ipsum Constantiam habere est agnoscendum, eamque in sensu perfecto, nec talem quam mox in me possibilem esse vidi, quæ in me ex lubitu alieno poni potest. Naturæ suæ statum ipsa natura sua esse Constantem patet ex ejus Intelli[?]gentia & Æternitate simul consideratis, vel nullo negotio, ex eo quod sit Cogitatio Perfectissima. qui enim mutatur fit eatenus alius ab eo quod prius erat, alius autem à perfectissimo non est perfectissimus, sed perfectissimus non fit non-perfectissimus, nec potest, nam hoc sibi contradicit, Ergo non fit alius, nec potest, sive non est inconstans, sed constans, ex naturæ suæ essentia. Id etiam facile de ejus placito sive vo-luntate, quatenus res ab eo statutas & creatas spectat, concludere est: nam in illo non est successio & recursus, ut posterior applicatio à priori diversa sit dicenda, adeoque inconstantiæ subjecta. Neque etiam cogi-tari potest, Deum propositum aliquod deserere & aliud amplecti, quin supponatur, Deum prius propositum quod ipse postea omnimodo defe-rens nullo modo probat, hoc est, (cum in Dei placito non detur prius & posterius) quin supponatur, Deum aliquid simul probare & improba-re: quod absurda contradictione cadit.
units.tr: III. But God, to whom I turn back, is not so disposed; rather he appears to me free from all variation and inconstancy, whether I consider him as he rejoices in himself, or as he regards other things; whether I look at his nature or at his will concerning things. And so it must be acknowledged that he possesses Constancy, and that in the perfect sense, not the kind I have just seen to be possible in me, which can be placed in me at another's pleasure. That his state of being is constant by his own nature is clear from considering together his Intelligence and his Eternity, or with no trouble at all, from the fact that he is Most Perfect Thought. For whatever changes becomes, to that extent, other than what it was before; but what is other than the most perfect is not most perfect; but what is most perfect does not become not-most-perfect, nor can it, for this contradicts itself. Therefore it does not become other, nor can it; that is, it is not inconstant but constant, from the essence of its nature. It is also easy to conclude the same about his will or purpose, insofar as it regards the things decreed and created by him: for in him there is no succession and no recurrence, such that a later application should be said to differ from an earlier one, and so be subject to inconstancy. Nor can it be thought that God abandons some purpose and embraces another, without it being supposed that God first approved the purpose which he afterwards utterly abandons and in no way approves; that is, (since in the divine will there is no before and after) without supposing that God at the same time approves and disapproves of something; which falls into absurd contradiction.

units.la: IV. Atque hisce non officit indifferentia illa quam in Divino placito esse sæpe diximus, siquidem tunc ut indeterminatum, nunc vero ut de-terminatum consideratum est Divinum placitum. Nec ea quæ est in rebus inconstantia evincit illud esse minus constans: nam constanter pla-cet Deo res esse & fore eousque inconstantes, quousque ex effectu patet eas mutari; & ideo mutantur quia voluntas Dei ut mutentur mutari ipsa non potest. Sed & in illa rerum inconstantia egregii constantiæ Di-vinæ characteres conspiciuntur, primo, dum ipsæ rerum substantiæ eorumque modi primarii, sive immediati, cum semel exstiterunt, con-servantur, unde & Mentium, etiam pessimarum, substantia, cogitatio nempe, ejusque facultates, constanter manent: deinde vero, quate-nus rerum statui qui inconstantiæ subjicitur, non accedit mutatio nisi secundum regulas constantissimas, quæ in Mentibus & corporibus con-stanter observantur, ut sciunt illi qui specialius de hisce philosophan-tur. Et quamvis respectu mentium creatarum, quas magis minusve approbare, amare, &c. dicitur Deus, prout illæ bono vel malo dele-ctantur, inconstantia Divinæ voluntati prima fronte quasi videatur in-esse; si tamen quod jam dictum est, nempe uno actu Deum rerum omnium statum & durationem complecti, mente firmiter teneatur, dif-ficultas ita evanescet, ut etiamsi omnia mutarentur, imo in nihilum abi-rent, non pateretur rationis evidentia aliud concludi, quam Divinum placitum, cui visum esset omnia eo modo, & eousque, nec ultra, existere, esse omnino immutabile & constans.
units.tr: IV. And this is not hindered by that indifference which we have often said is in the divine will, since the divine will has been considered sometimes as undetermined, sometimes as determined. Nor does the inconstancy that exists in things prove that the divine will is less constant: for it pleases God constantly that things be and remain inconstant until it is clear from the effect that they change; and they change because the will of God that they change cannot itself be changed. But in this inconstancy of things, too, the distinguished marks of divine constancy are seen: first, while the substances of things themselves and their primary or immediate modes, once they have existed, are preserved; whence also the substance of minds, even the worst, namely thought and its faculties, remain constant; then, moreover, insofar as no change is made to the state of things that is subject to inconstancy except according to the most constant rules, which are constantly observed in minds and bodies, as those know who philosophize more particularly about these matters. And although with respect to created minds, which God is said to approve or love more or less, according as they delight in good or evil, inconstancy seems at first glance to be present in the divine will; yet if one firmly holds in mind what has already been said, namely that God embraces the state and duration of all things in one act, the difficulty will so vanish that, even if all things were changed, or rather went to nothing, the evidence of reason would not allow any other conclusion than that the divine will, to which it seemed good that all things should exist in that way, and so far, and no further, is entirely immutable and constant.

units.la: V. Ex hisce patere potest, quid de illis mediis sit judicandum, quibus homines sese constantes reddere prætendunt in alicujus rei positione vel conservatione, quæque vota, proposita, promissa, juramenta, &c. nuncupant, inconstantiæ suæ scilicet remedia. Nempe cum divinum placitum omnia ponat & conservet, Illudque, etsi sit constantissimum, non inferat rerum quas vult homo, aut quas ipse posuit Deus, forte ad tempus, constantiam; absurdum est ut quis voveat sive sibi spondeat Deum quædam (quæcunque illa sint indiscriminatim) positurum, nisi Dei ipsius de futuro eventu declaratio habeatur, aut jam possideantur primitiæ omnium placiti divini effectorum, quæ cum complemento nexum à Deo statutum dicunt. Stultius vero est te vovere eo sensu affectum, quasi à te penderet alicujus realitatis positio, ejusque prolongatio. Bene de præsenti mentis meæ statu asseverare queo, talem vel talem revera jam in me esse cogitationem, id desiderium, ut hoc jam vel illud velim, imo cupiam, ut Deus conservet hanc voluntatem in me: at quid facturus sit in inconstantia mea, vel de ea permissurus, decet me inter spem & tremorem expectare. Ubi vero certo testimonio constat Deum bona in me positurum, tunc cum voveo me bona præstiturum, vota mea non sunt aliter ab ullo spectanda quam ut confidentiæ meæ signa de Divina veracitate, non vero ut mei Sponsio de mei ipsius propria Constantia.
units.tr: V. From these things it can be seen what is to be judged of those means by which men pretend to make themselves constant in the position or preservation of some thing, and which they call vows, purposes, promises, oaths, and so on, that is, remedies for their own inconstancy. For since the divine will posits and preserves all things, and since it, although it is most constant, does not bring about constancy, perhaps for a time, in the things which man wills or which God himself has posited, it is absurd for anyone to vow or pledge to himself that God will posit certain things (whatever they may be, indiscriminately), unless there is a declaration of God himself concerning the future event, or unless the firstfruits of all the divine decree's effects are already possessed, which they call the connection decreed by God with its completion. But it is more foolish for you to vow with the feeling as if the positing of some reality, and its prolongation, depended on you. I can indeed affirm with confidence concerning the present state of my mind that such or such a thought, such or such a desire, is really now in me, that I now wish or even desire this or that, and that God preserves this will in me; but what he will do with my inconstancy, or what he will permit concerning it, it becomes me to await between hope and trembling. But where it is certain by sure testimony that God will work good things in me, then when I vow that I will perform good things, my vows are not to be regarded by anyone otherwise than as signs of my confidence in the divine truthfulness, and not as my pledge concerning my own constancy.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: (17) SIMPLICITAS.
units.tr: (17) SIMPLICITY.

units.la: 1. Mentis divisio & compositio. 2. Quo simplicior certo sensu, eo confusior. 3. Nunquam absolute simplex futura.
units.tr: 1. Division and composition of the mind. 2. The simpler a thing is in a given sense, the more confused it is. 3. It will never be absolutely simple.

units.la: I. TAles & tantæ variationes jam jam in Mente mea observatæ, non modo excludunt à me vel omnium, vel unius absolutæ perfectionis possessionem aut omnium eorum quæ meæ naturæ alioqui non repugnant, ad quæ tamen ex placito Dei non datur attingere; aut facultatum omnium quæ in me sunt exercitium & actus, ita ut omnibus scientiis, professionibus, objectis, applicer, ad quorum singula seorsim ferri potest mea cogitatio; sed etiam sentio me ita variabilem non simul possidere ea ad quæ pro mei status conditione præsenti applicari possum, aut etiam actu jam memet applicui, ita ut non sim tam comparandus mediocri vasi oris angustioris, quod liquorem paulatim quidem admittit, sed tamen admissum variis vicibus actu omnem simul retinet, siquidem quod variis vicibus cogitatione admisi non omne actu remanet praesens; quam angusto canali, quem aquae, aliorumve liquorum non potest successive subire copia, nisi liquorum portiones in illum fluentes sese mutuo expellant, & evacuatione continua ejiciant: nam experior cogitationes meas sese mutuo ita excludere ut si una adsit, caeteris non det locum; si caeterarum quaedam revocandae sint prior dimittenda est, & sic continuo, non tantum ubi de rebus quae inter se diversae sunt cogito, sed etiam ubi ad objectum quod maxime Unum est, nempe Deum, convertor, cujus perfectionem nonnisi pluribus cogitandi actibus repraesentare mihi hoc in statu possum: huic enim imperfectioni subsunt & istae cogitationes, ut una mihi praesente, caeterae non appareant nec cogitentur.
units.tr: I. Such great and manifold changes, already observed in my mind, not only exclude me from possessing either all absolute perfection or the perfection of any one thing, or the exercise and act of all the faculties that are in me, so that I could apply them to all sciences, professions and objects, to each of which my thought can be directed separately. They also show that I, being so changeable, do not possess at the same time those things to which, given the condition of my present state, I can apply myself, or even those to which I have in fact already applied myself. So I am not to be compared to a vessel with a narrow mouth, which admits liquid little by little but then holds all that it has admitted at once, since what I have admitted in thought at various times does not all remain present at once. I am rather like a narrow channel, which a quantity of water or other liquid cannot pass through successively unless the portions of liquid flowing into it push one another out and are continually expelled by emptying. For I find that my thoughts exclude one another in such a way that when one is present it gives no room to the others, and if some of the others are to be recalled, the first must be dismissed; and so on continually. This happens not only when I think of things that differ from one another, but also when I turn to the object that is most one, namely God, whose perfection I can in my present state represent to myself only through several acts of thinking. For these thoughts too are subject to this imperfection: while one is present to me, the others do not appear or come to mind.

units.la: II. Et quamvis interdum multa cogitando complectar una vice, non tamen ea simul ita complete & clare concipio, quam si singula seorsim sumerem: sed aliquatenus tantum, & confusius, haud aliter acsi liquorum plurium massas in parvo canali simul caperem, nempe portiuncula ex quolibet liquore admissa, unde confusio & dilutio eorum fieret eo major, quo plures essent liquores.
units.tr: II. And although at times I grasp many things together in one act of thinking, I do not conceive them all together so completely and clearly as I would if I took each one separately. I grasp them only to some extent and more confusedly, just as if I took in masses of several liquids together in a small channel, namely a little portion of each liquid being admitted, whence their confusion and dilution becomes greater the more liquids there are.

units.la: III. Interim non sine aliqua admiratione intueor formae cogitationis meae diversitatem. Illic est limitatio, non est unitas, est multiplicitas, sed nec haec simul adest, verum per partes sese mutuo expellentes, quibus adde sis, ex supradictis, quamlibet partem non adaequata cognitione capi. An autem ex hac multiplicitate ad majorem simplicitatem sit olim reducenda Cogitatio mea, id pendet ex placito Dei: quid hac de re velit ex revelatione determinandum relinquitur: quid possit, non determinatur, cum quaestio in Potentiam Dei à nullo capiendam resolvatur. Attamen, quicquid evenire queat, cum Mens creata nunquam unicam Dei perfectionem sit habitura, nedum omnes simul & indivisim possessura, inter simplicitatem ad quam possit pervenire maximam, atque inter illam quae vere Deo propria est, infinita distantia est agnoscenda.
units.tr: III. Meanwhile I look upon the diversity in the form of my thinking with no little wonder. There is limitation there, there is no unity; there is multiplicity, but this too is not present all at once, but through parts that push one another out. To this you may add, from what was said above, that each part is grasped by an inadequate knowledge. Whether my thought will someday be reduced from this multiplicity to a greater simplicity depends on the will of God. What he wishes in this matter is left to be determined from revelation; what he can do is not determined, since the question is resolved into the power of God, which no one can grasp. Yet, whatever may come about, since a created mind will never possess a single perfection of God, much less all of them at once and undivided, we must acknowledge an infinite distance between the greatest simplicity to which it could attain and that which truly belongs to God alone.

units.la: 4. Simplicitas Divina, quæ? Demonstratur. 5. Difficultates tres. 6. Cur nullum aliud simplicitatis exemplum sit? 7. Quæ distinctio inter attributa Dei sit. Ea simplicitati non obstat. 8. Neque diversitas decretorum. 9. Ut adumbretur in materialibus & in mentibus.
units.tr: 4. What is the divine simplicity? It is demonstrated. 5. Three difficulties. 6. Why is there no other example of simplicity? 7. What is the distinction among the attributes of God? It does not stand in the way of simplicity. 8. Nor does the diversity of decrees. 9. How it is shadowed forth in material things and in minds.

units.la: IV. Divina quippe Simplicitas à Summa Perfectione est indissolubilis, eamque optime concipiemus, si missis quisquiliis quibus vulgo eam negative designant, ut quod neget compositionem ex materia & forma, ex genere & differentia, &c. quæ etiam de ipso nihilo dicere queas; de Deo cogitemus secundum viam mox in cogitando de me adhibitam. Sic enim observabimus, omnes quas Deus habet, quasque de illo cogitare utcunque possum perfectiones, non modo simul esse in illius Natura actu præsentes & indivisim unitas, ut nulla deesse possit; sed & illas ita unitas esse, ut una sit altera, & reciproce, imo, una sit omnes, & omnes sint una propriissime & quoad essentiam: nempe v. g. Vita est Spiritualitas, Æternitas, aliæque, & vicissim: vita est omnia attributa, & omnia sunt vita, & sic de cæteris quæ omnia simpliciter unum & idem sunt, sive Unica mera Cogitatio sunt. Id ita in Natura perfectissima esse facile demonstrari potest, & sufficienter in fine libri secundi, quo remittimus, est demonstratum. Id quoque ex cæteris attributis nullo negotio evincitur, exempli causa, ex Sufficientia: Si enim dicas unum attributum non possidere cæterorum perfectiones (hoc est, non esse illa ipsa) peto, an Deus sit sufficiens ad illas ei dandum? Ut neges non permittit Sufficientia Divina: Si affirmes, sequitur eas ab illo attributo actu haberi, cum nil passivi in Deo sit. Ex activitate, quæ negaretur, si unum attributum ab alio separari posse, aut uni perfectiones alterius vel omnium deesse statueretur: sic enim in Dei natura aliquid conciperetur ut capax recipiendi, sive, ut non mere activum. Ex Unitate: Nam quod non exhaurit omnia, id multiplicari potest, si autem multæ possent dari Sufficientiæ, Æternitates, &c. multa darentur Entia sufficientia, multa æterna, adeoque, quia hæc in solo Deo esse agnoscuntur, multi Dii, quod falsi convictum est. Sed, ut plura prætermittam, id & ex attributo immediate præcedenti liquet, quo omnis diversitas & diversitatis capacitas à Divina natura remota est.
units.tr: IV. The divine simplicity is indeed inseparable from supreme perfection, and we shall best conceive it if we set aside the trifles by which it is commonly described negatively, such as that it denies composition of matter and form, of genus and difference, and so on, which you could say even of nothing itself. Let us think of God by the path we just now followed in thinking about myself. For we shall observe that all the perfections God has, and all those which I can in any way think of in him, are not only present together in his nature in act and united without division, so that none can be lacking; but they are also so united that one is the other and reciprocally, indeed one is all of them and all are one most properly and as to essence. For example, life is spirituality, eternity and the others, and conversely; life is all the attributes, and all are life; and so with the rest, which are all simply one and the same, that is, are one pure thought. That this is so in the most perfect nature can easily be demonstrated, and it has been sufficiently demonstrated at the end of the second book, to which we refer. This is also proved without any trouble from the other attributes, for example from sufficiency. For if you say that one attribute does not possess the perfections of the others (that is, is not those very things), I ask whether God is sufficient to give them to it. If you deny it, the divine sufficiency does not allow this. If you affirm it, it follows that they are had by that attribute in act, since there is nothing passive in God. It also follows from activity, which would be denied if one attribute could be separated from another, or if it were held that one lacked the perfections of another or of all the others. For then something would be conceived in the nature of God that is capable of receiving, that is, not purely active. It follows from unity: for what does not exhaust all things can be multiplied; and if there could be many sufficiencies, eternities, and so on, there would be many sufficient beings, many eternal beings, and so, since these are acknowledged to exist in God alone, many gods, which has been shown to be false. But, to pass over many other points, this is also clear from the attribute immediately preceding, by which all diversity and the capacity for diversity is removed from the divine nature.

units.la: V. Fatendum est, nonnullas in hoc concipiendo occurrere posse difficuldifficultates : Primo, ex eo quod in nullis rebus talis Simplicitatis exemplum ullum occurrat : Secundo ex eo quod soleamus plura in Deo attributa tanquam inter se distincta numerare : Denique ex eo quod dicantur esse in Deo plures de rebus conceptus, multa statuta, decretaque, quæ ab illo abesse potuissent, vel aliter esse. Sed hæc omnia Simplicitati Divinæ non obsunt.
units.tr: V. It must be admitted that some difficulties may arise in conceiving this: First, because no example of such simplicity occurs in any things. Second, because we are accustomed to count the several attributes in God as distinct from one another. Finally, because there are said to be in God several concepts of things, many decisions and decrees, which could have been absent from him or could have been otherwise. But all these do not stand in the way of the divine simplicity.

units.la: VI. Nam quod omnia, sive extensa, sive cogitantia non sint ad hunc modum Simplicia, hoc inde est, quod à se non sint, sed à placito alterius qui eis prout placuit dedit esse per particulas. Quod in homine scientia, justitia, gaudium, & quæ ejusmodi, non sint unum, inde est, quod non solum objecta diversa sint, sed & Mens ipsa fit variabi-lis modis multis quorum unus absque altero esse potest, imo uno mentem disponente, alia dispositio mentis quæ per alium modum fieret, impeditur. Sed cum horum causæ in Deo non sint, quippe qui à se sit, unoque invariabili objecto uniformiter gaudeat, nulla difficultate judi-cari potest tales effectus ab eo esse remotos; ut neque ejus Simplicitatem in dubium iis revocari.
units.tr: VI. For the fact that all things, whether extended or thinking, are not simple in this way is because they are not from themselves, but from the will of another, who gave them being in parts as he pleased. That in a human being knowledge, justice, joy and things of this kind are not one is because not only are the objects different, but the mind itself is changed in many ways, one of which can exist without another; indeed, when the mind is disposed in one way, another disposition of the mind that would come about in another way is hindered. But since the causes of these things are not in God, who is from himself and rejoices uniformly in one unchanging object, it can be judged without any difficulty that such effects are far from him, and so his simplicity is not to be called into doubt on account of them.

units.la: VII. De attributorum Divinorum diversitate sive differentia, prout à me concipiuntur & numerantur, sic res se habet. Deus est una mera Cogitatio: At cogitandi in me actus, sive meæ cogitationes de illo, plures sunt, & ex pluribus occasionibus, quæ sæpe rerum objecta diversa involvunt, enatæ: nam, modo ex occasione quod non sim à me, modo quod non omnia possim, modo quod non omnia noscam, & sic deinceps, reflecto ad Divinam Cogitationem. Hæ reflexiones, quæ in respectu ad Deum consideratæ ejus Attributa vocantur, cum contineant relationem non modo ad Deum, sed etiam ad diversitatem actuum, occasionum, objectorum cogitationis meæ, adeoque cum plurium re-rum conceptus complectantur, non possunt non habere aliquam inter se differentiam. At distinctio est in pluralitate actuum mei cogitantis, in occasionibus ex quibus de Deo cogito, & in objectis ad quæ meas de Deo cogitationes aliquatenus relatas esse concipio, non autem in Deo. Una mea cogitatio de Deo non est numero eadem cum altera mea cogitatione de eodem: Una occasio meæ cujusdam de illo Cogitationis est alia ab occasione alterius cogitationis, unum objectum quod ad Deum refero non est idem cum altero quodam quod etiam ad Deum referre possum: Sed quicquid de Deo involvitur in unaquaque & in omnibus istis numero diversis cogitationibus ex diversis occasionibus ortis, & cum diversis objectis implicatis, id unum & idem est indissolubilier uniformiterque in natura Divina spectatum. Cujus veritatis aliud praeter dicta argumentum est, quod nullius attributi vera & clara idea haberi possit si vel unum ex illis negetur, exempli causa, si aeternitatem negas, vitam negas, nam non-cogitatio est non-vita; ubi autem est successio, neque omnes sunt simul perfectiones, ibi est non-cogitatio, non-con-scientia de illis. Et sic de caeteris attendenti videre est.
units.tr: VII. The matter stands thus with regard to the diversity or difference of the divine attributes, as I conceive and count them. God is one pure thought. But the acts of thinking in me, or my thoughts about him, are many, and they arise from many occasions, which often involve diverse objects of thought. For, sometimes from the occasion that I am not from myself, sometimes that I cannot do all things, sometimes that I do not know all things, and so on, I turn back to the divine thought. These reflections, which when considered with respect to God are called his attributes, since they contain a relation not only to God but also to the diversity of the acts, occasions and objects of my thinking, and so embrace the concepts of several things, cannot but have some difference among themselves. But the distinction lies in the plurality of the acts of my thinking, in the occasions from which I think of God, and in the objects to which I conceive my thoughts of God as somehow related, not in God himself. One of my thoughts of God is not numerically the same as another of my thoughts of the same God. One occasion of one of my thoughts about him is other than the occasion of another thought; one object that I refer to God is not the same as another that I can also refer to God. But whatever is involved concerning God in each and all of these numerically diverse thoughts, arising from diverse occasions and bound up with diverse objects, is one and the same, viewed indissolubly and uniformly in the divine nature. Another proof of this truth, besides what has been said, is that no true and clear idea of any attribute can be had if even one of them is denied. For example, if you deny eternity, you deny life; for non-thinking is non-life; and where there is succession, and not all perfections are together, there is non-thinking, non-awareness of them. And so, as anyone who attends to it can see, with the others.

units.la: VIII. Quod attinet ad conceptus, statuta, decreta Dei circa diversissimas res, ea non spectant ad Dei essentiam, siquidem potuissent non esse, vel aliter esse: adeoque nec debet in illis quaeri Simplicitas Essentiae Divinae, nec, si ea ibi non inveniatur, obstat quominus omnes quae in Essentia Divina cogitari possunt perfectiones, una sint eadem-que realitas. Habent tamen & illa suam inter se Simplicitatem, eamque quae placiti Entis perfectissimi & ad haec indifferentissimi determinationem deceat, quippe quae sint omnia actus unus, omnia objecta a Deo diversa complectens, simul & constanter praesens. Sed Simplicitas quae de re summe necessaria & perfectissima est, alia est, nec hujus alterius praesentiam aut absentiam necessario postulat. Difficultatis hujus lucu-lentius solvendae fundamentum in Cap. x. evidentissime detectum est, quo sine, certus sum non posse capi, quomodo statutorum & decretorum, quae aliter esse possent, consideratio, Divinae Simplicitatis conceptui non repugnet.
units.tr: VIII. As for the concepts, the decrees and determinations of God concerning very diverse things: these do not pertain to the essence of God, since they could have not been, or could have been otherwise. Therefore the simplicity of the Divine Essence should not be sought in them, and if it is not found there, this does not prevent all the perfections that can be thought in the Divine Essence from being one and the same reality. Yet those decrees also have their own simplicity among themselves, one fitting the determination of the most perfect Being, which is indifferent to these things. For they are all one act, embracing all objects distinct from God, and at the same time constantly present. But the simplicity that belongs to the most necessary and most perfect thing is another kind, and it does not necessarily require the presence or absence of this other kind. The foundation for solving this difficulty more clearly was most evidently laid out in chapter x., without which, I am certain, it cannot be grasped how the consideration of statutes and decrees, which could have been otherwise, is not inconsistent with the concept of Divine Simplicity.

units.la: IX. Dictum est, nullum in omnibus rebus, praeter Deum, Simplicitatis Divinae exemplum reperiri, quod absolute loquendo verum est, nam nil est absolute simplex, sed si quod est, id aliquo respectu tale est, adeoque non simpliciter simplex est. Attamen ex rebus secundum quid simplicibus, nonnullae satis egregia Divinae Simplicitatis, pro suo modo, suaque natura, signa atque ectypa esse possunt, uti materiae natura, ubi longitudo, latitudo & profunditas ita inseparabiles sunt, ut omnes & singulae in omnibus & singulis materiae partibus sint; nec possit materia in alia quaedam dividi, quorum unumquodque minus habeat quam haec tria simul. Ita motus directio secundum lineam rectam Simplicis Opificis nota est insignis, siquidem nil Simplicius rectitudine quae in toto & in partibus uniformis est, cujus tota totius natura sub qualibet parte est. Unde bene ex Simplicitate operationis Ens Simplicissimum decentis desumitur Lex de motus secundum rectam li-neam directione, quemadmodum ad Constantiam haec altera Lex, quod unumquodque in statu suo conservetur, relata fuit; ad utramque vero Leges de motuum communicationibus & reflexionibus. In Mente autem creata ut Divina Simplicitas quantum fieri potest adumbretur, siquidem ad Simplicitatem Divinæ naturæ non pertineant conceptus de rebus à Deo diversis, ita etiam ad ejus adumbrationem necesse est men-tem creatam iis non hærere, nam attentio ad creata, quæ multiplicia sunt, cogitationes dissipat in multiplicitates infinitas, & inter se diver-sas. Istius supra notatæ æternitatis primitiæ, sola in Deum Simplicem Cogitationis directio recta, genuina, nuda, aperta, sine ambagibus, sine cura varietatis, sine artificiali apparatu, sine dispositione affectata, sine studio ornatuum & phalerarum accidentalium, pompis & fere pupis, in verbis, in gestibus, in subtilitatibus; is in omnibus agendi modus qui nec varietatis nec simplicitatis apparentiam captans, nec animum affigens externis & peregrinis quæ foris pro rerum statu necessario sunt formalitatibus, sit liber ab omni eo quo res grata Deo carere potest; ista inquam Mentem cum Divina Simplicitate conformant, contraria vero à Simplice Deo removere consueverunt. Quo enim plura aliquis possidet quæ à perfectione sive à cogitatione maxime uniformi & constanti, ea videlicet quæ pure Deum amplectitur, distincta sunt, atque idcirco separari & dispergi possunt, is eo magis compositus, multiplex & divisus est, minusque Simplex & similis illi, qui ma-xime repræsentandus est per illud à quo nihil queat amplius sepa-ri, in quo omnia sint unum necessarium, & unum sit omnia. Quemadmodum autem Divinam Simplicitatem inter illa quæ in Deo cognoscendo primum occurrunt jam ante recensuimus; Ita etiam in Mente Deo approximanda vel proxima, primum & præcipuum requisitum est Simplicitas hæc omnia condiens. Hinc etiam Sim-plicitas vere admiranda Divinarum Scripturarum quasi forma & Anima est.
units.tr: IX. It has been said that there is no example of Divine Simplicity to be found in all things except God, which is true speaking absolutely, for nothing is absolutely simple; but if anything is simple, it is so in some respect, and therefore is not simply simple. Nevertheless, from things that are simple in a certain respect, some can be quite fine signs and copies of Divine Simplicity, in their own way and according to their own nature, such as the nature of matter, where length, breadth and depth are so inseparable that all and each are in all and each part of matter, nor can matter be divided into certain parts, each of which has less than these three together. Thus the direction of motion along a straight line is a notable mark of the Simple Maker, since nothing is simpler than rectitude, which is uniform in the whole and in the parts, whose whole nature is under any part. Hence the Law of motion in a straight-line direction is rightly drawn from the simplicity of the operation of the most simple Being, just as this other Law, that each thing be conserved in its state, was related to Constancy; and to both are related the Laws concerning the communication and reflection of motions. In the created mind, however, that Divine Simplicity may be shadowed forth as far as possible, since concepts of things distinct from God do not pertain to the simplicity of the Divine nature, so too for its shadowing it is necessary that the created mind not cling to them, for attention to created things, which are manifold, scatters thoughts into infinite multiplicities, diverse among themselves. Of that eternal primacy noted above, the only right, genuine, bare, open direction of thought toward the Simple God is without circumlocutions, without concern for variety, without artificial display, without affected arrangement, without the pursuit of ornaments and accidental trappings, pomp and almost dolls, in words, in gestures, in subtleties; that is the mode of acting in all things which, seeking the appearance neither of variety nor of simplicity, and not fixing the mind on external and foreign formalities which are necessary outside according to the state of things, is free from everything that a thing pleasing to God can lack. These, I say, conform the Mind to Divine Simplicity, while contrary things tend to remove it from the Simple God. For the more a person possesses things that are distinct from perfection, or from thought that is most uniform and constant, namely those that embrace God purely, and therefore can be separated and scattered, the more composite, manifold and divided he is, and the less simple and similar to him who is best represented by that from which nothing can be further separated, in whom all things are one necessary thing, and one thing is all things. Just as we have already listed Divine Simplicity among the things that occur first in knowing God, so too in the Mind that is to approach or be near to God, this Simplicity, which seasons all things, is the first and chief requisite. Hence also the truly admirable simplicity of the Divine Scriptures is as it were their form and soul.

units.la: CAPUT XIX. (18) LIBERTAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. (18) LIBERTY.

units.la: 1. Mentis libertas in quibus? 2.3. Spontaneitatis. Impetuum gradus, unde? Cautela. Motus Deo addictus. Ea à Deo ponitur, nec ejus ob Potentiam minuitur, &c. 4. Datur Indifferentia. 5. Nec obstant difficultates. 6. An Libertatis creatæ Idea æqualis Divinæ, vel ea minor sit dicenda?
units.tr: 1. In what does the liberty of the mind consist? 2.3. Of spontaneity. Whence the degrees of impulse? Caution. The motion devoted to God. That it is posited by God, and is not diminished by his power, etc. 4. Indifference is given. 5. Nor do difficulties stand in the way. 6. Is the idea of created liberty to be called equal to the divine, or lesser?

units.la: I. Observatis hisce variationum vicibus, occurrunt modi generaliores quibus in me ponuntur, quos partim voluntarios, partim coactos sive peregrinos, partim mixtos animadverto, prout ad diversas objectorum classes, diversamque Mentis cum objectis communicationem referuntur. Et primo quidem, quæ decimæ octavæ observationis materia fuit, adverto eas ex cogitationibus meis quæ circa cognitionem veri & possessionem boni per judicia affirmantia aut negantia, per amorem, cupiditatem, similesque propensiones versantur, non poni in me per externam vim, ita ut sentiam me ad illas recipiendas, seu velim, seu nolim, esse coactum: Sed potius eas ita libere in me venire quasi a me procederent. Hic cogitandi modus vocatur Libertas apud Philosophos, quem melius Spontaneitatem dixeris: neque illa est confundenda cum alia apud Diviniores Scriptores libertate qua Mens peccato soluta, Soli Divinæ voluntati liberrime adhæret.
units.tr: I. Having observed these alternations of changes, there present themselves the more general modes by which they are posited in me. I notice that some of them are voluntary, some compelled or foreign, and some mixed, according as they relate to different classes of objects and to the mind's different communication with objects. And first, the subject of my eighteenth observation: I notice that the thoughts which concern my knowledge of truth and my possession of good, through judgments of affirmation or denial, through love, desire, and similar inclinations, are not posited in me by any external force, so that I feel I am compelled to receive them, whether I wish it or not. Rather, they come into me so freely, as if they proceeded from me. This manner of thinking is called liberty by the philosophers, though you would do better to call it spontaneity. Nor is it to be confused with that other liberty, spoken of by the more divine writers, by which the mind, freed from sin, adheres most freely to the divine will alone.

units.la: II. Prout autem veri & boni cognitio clara est aut obscura, vel ignorantia obnubilata, sic etiam cogitationes quibus de illis judico & in illa feror, sunt aut sponte determinatæ & alacres, aut indifferentes, sive, sponte indeterminatæ & in neutram partem propendentes, unde Libertas modo spontanea modo indifferens ab aliis dicitur, qui forte rectius dicerent Spontaneitatem esse vel indeterminatam vel determinatam, quo loquendi modo malumus uti. De motu illo spontaneo quo in objecta feror, observo, quo major vel minor cognitionis claritas & extensio, verique & boni perfectio est, & quo magis vel minus me concernunt sive mihi necessaria sunt verum & bonum, eo etiam majori aut minori alacritate atque impetu me illuc sponte & libenter ruere, atque adeo Libertatis Spontaneæ determinatæ plurimos esse gradus. Ad hanc veritatem, trianguli duo quæcunque latera simul sumpta sunt majora tertio, sponte quidem feror, cum sit evidentissima, sed cum non sit è præci-puis, remissa valde est mentis meæ circa illam propensio: at in illis quæ majora, nempe Deum & Divina, pro objectis habent, alius sentitur Mentis vigor, percipiturque inclinationis celer, hilaris & vividus tractus sive impetus, omnium maxime spontaneus, quem sive ad passiones animæ spirituales, sive ad sensus internos, quos nonnullus adducit tanquam firmissima post notitias innatas veritatis argumenta, referam, parum interest, modo sedulam adhibeam operam ut cum clara & evidenti veritatis cognitione jungatur, alioqui summa fraus subesse potest, Mensque ignara in chymeras proprias tanquam in Deum vel placita Divina cæco deferri impetu, reputans ex interno sensu fervoris & decursus, totam cogitationem eo temporis penetrante, occupante, & rapiente, se in Divina ruere felicissime, dedocenda tamen per eventum ubi fervor cum phantasmatibus evanuerit. Interim quemadmodum inter idcas quas intellectus percipit, certa quædam est, eaque omnium intima, quæ ad solum Deum est referenda, sic non dubium est quin sit inter hos vo-luntatis motus aliquis qui radices, ut sic dicam, & fundum Mentis se-cretiorem commovens, à solo Deo excitetur nullo intercedente me-dio, quippe qui totus solum Deum immediate spectet, quemque Deus sibi proprium tanquam suum secretiorem operationis locum suumque vectorem elegerit omnis à quibuscunque creaturis commotionis recipiendæ incapacem. Sine quo esset ut Divinæ operationes, inspiratio-nes, verus Dei tactus, veraque mentis conversio, ab imaginariis, quibus tot decipiuntur, nunquam possent ab ullo discerni, nec veræ beati-tudinis, aut etiam miseriæ, ullus certus daretur sensus. Sed hæc pluribus deducere non est hujus loci. Suffecerit notare ea hoc principio niti; Mens apta est à Solo omnipotente Deo intime affici eo modo qui sit di-versissimus ab illis in quibus media creata intercedunt, adeoque ad quem non possint media creata attingere. quo sensu ipsis occultus dicitur & se-cretus, Mensque in fundo reconditissimo (quia cætera eo attingere non possunt) tangi. Et hic vere fiunt mirabilia atque ineffabilia Dei.
units.tr: II. But just as the knowledge of truth and good is clear or obscure, or clouded by ignorance, so too the thoughts by which I judge of these things and am carried toward them are either spontaneously determined and eager, or indifferent, that is, spontaneously undetermined and inclining to neither side. Hence liberty is called by others sometimes spontaneous and sometimes indifferent; those who perhaps would speak more correctly would say that spontaneity is either undetermined or determined, and this is the manner of speaking I prefer. Concerning that spontaneous motion by which I am carried toward objects, I observe that the greater or lesser clarity and extent of knowledge, and the perfection of truth and good, and the more or less they concern me or are necessary to me, the more eagerly and with greater or lesser alacrity and impulse I rush there spontaneously and willingly. Thus there are very many degrees of determined spontaneous liberty. As to this truth, that any two sides of a triangle taken together are greater than the third, I am indeed carried to it spontaneously, since it is most evident; but since it is not among the principal things, my mind's inclination toward it is quite slight. But in those things which have as their objects what is greater, namely God and divine things, another vigor of the mind is felt, and a swift, cheerful, and lively pull or impulse of inclination is perceived, most spontaneous of all. Whether I refer this to the spiritual passions of the soul or to the inner senses, which some adduce as the firmest arguments of truth after innate notions, matters little, provided I take care to join it with a clear and evident knowledge of the truth. Otherwise the greatest deceit may lie hidden, and an ignorant mind, carried on by a blind impulse into its own chimeras as if into God or the divine decrees, may, judging from the inner sense of fervor and flow, which at that time penetrates, occupies and seizes the whole thought, suppose that it is most happily rushing into the divine; yet it must be unlearned through the outcome, when the fervor vanishes along with the phantasms. Meanwhile, just as among the ideas which the intellect perceives there is a certain one, and that the innermost of all, which must be referred to God alone, so there is no doubt that among these motions of the will there is some which, stirring the roots, so to speak, and the more secret ground of the mind, is excited by God alone with no intervening means, since it looks wholly and immediately to God alone, and which God has chosen for himself as his more secret place of operation and his vehicle, incapable of receiving any commotion from any creature. Without this it would come about that divine operations, inspirations, the true touch of God, and the true conversion of the mind could never be distinguished from the imaginary ones by which so many are deceived, and no certain sense of true blessedness, or even of misery, would be given. But to deduce these things at length is not the place for this. It will suffice to note that they rest on this principle: the mind is apt to be inwardly affected by the omnipotent God alone, in a manner most different from those in which created means intervene, and so which created means cannot reach. In this sense he is said to be hidden and secret to them, and the mind is touched in its most hidden ground, since other things cannot reach it there. And here truly the wonders and ineffable things of God are wrought.

units.la: III. Horum omnium, ut ad hactenus dicta redeam, aliam non possum proferre rationem quam naturæ meæ Constitutionem, sive, Dei placitum me ita constituisse; etenim hæc sola essentiæ rerum modorumque primariorum ratio & causa est. Potentia igitur Divina, efficacia & vis sui placiti, Omniscientiaque Libertati Spontaneæ, sive Spontaneitati determinatæ, non obstant, sed contra, eam juvant: nam cum sint ejus causæ quo major earum operatio vel effectus in me ponitur, eo major in me est Spontaneitas; & quo plura placet Deo de voluntate mea praecognoscere, eo magis vere liber sum. Etenim hanc Libertatem esse aliquid positivi per se patet, & supra demonstratum est omnia à Deo poni, ipsamque idcirco libertatem, cum eam vult, ad eum modum mensuramque ab illo conceptam, existere.
units.tr: III. Of all these things, to return to what has been said so far, I can offer no other reason than the constitution of my nature, or that God's decree has so constituted me; for this alone is the reason and cause of the essence of things and of their primary modes. Therefore the divine power, the efficacy and force of his decree, and his omniscience do not stand in the way of spontaneous liberty, or determined spontaneity; on the contrary, they help it. For since they are its causes, the greater their operation or effect is posited in me, the greater my spontaneity is; and the more things God is pleased to foreknow about my will, the more truly free I am. Indeed, that this liberty is something positive in itself is clear, and it has been shown above that all things are posited by God; therefore liberty itself, when he wills it, exists in that manner and measure conceived by him.

units.la: IV. De Spontaneitate indeterminata, quæ in me est cum quid verum & bonum sit non evidenter cognosco, adeoque sponte indeterminatus hæreo, adverto eam esse istius quam modo dixi Spontaneæ determinationis absentiam, unde Mens in objectum affirmatione vel negatione, amore vel odio non fertur. Sed præterea obversatur mihi quædam indeterminationis activæ indifferentis imago, qua Mens habere videtur Potentiam sese à se ipsa determinandi ad quodcunque objectum ex pluribus oppositis, seu diversis, magis minusve bonis, prout ei placuerit. Fatendum est hanc arduam esse difficultatem. Malum non daretur, nisi indifferentia esset vel fuisset. qui culpanda fecit debuit aliter se gerere quam se gessit, ergo, saltem aliquando, aliquo respectu, in aliquo statu, indifferens fuit: nam si alium scopum, alia media, aliam occasionem, aliud principium, non habuit ante determinationem quam post illam, non aberravit igitur à scopo, à regulis nec à principio, unde evidentissime sequitur eum nequaquam peccasse: nisi forte dixeris in hoc esse peccatum, quod is qui agit putans se male agere, agat contra conscientiam, nec attendens an sit ad hoc determinatus: quasi vero, si quis sibi persuaderet omnia promiscue bona esse, & fata suum quemque vocare, minus peccaret; peccatumque consisteret in opinione quod detur peccatum! (quæ Libertinismi ipsa principia sunt). Sed & quomodo illa opinio, quod detur peccatum, esset peccatum ipsum, adeoque in illis culpanda qui illam haberent, nisi prius in illis fuisset indifferentia ad illam amplectendam aut rejiciendam? Necessario igitur Indifferentia est statuenda in Spontaneitate indeterminata.
units.tr: IV. Concerning undetermined spontaneity, which is in me when I do not clearly know what is true and good, and so I remain spontaneously undetermined, I notice that it is the absence of that determined spontaneity which I have just described, whereby the mind is not carried toward an object by affirmation or denial, by love or hatred. But besides this there presents itself to me a certain image of active indifferent indetermination, by which the mind seems to have the power of determining itself from itself to any object out of several opposed, or different, more or less good, as it pleases. It must be confessed that this is a difficult problem. There would be no evil, unless indifference was or had been. The one who is to be blamed ought to have acted otherwise than he did; therefore, at least sometimes, in some respect, in some state, he was indifferent. For if he did not have another aim, other means, another occasion, another principle before the determination than after it, then he did not stray from the aim, from the rules, or from the principle; from which it most evidently follows that he by no means sinned. Unless perhaps you say that the sin lies in this: that the one who acts, thinking he acts badly, acts against his conscience, and does not attend to whether he is determined to this. As if indeed someone who persuaded himself that all things are indiscriminately good, and that fate calls each one to his lot, would sin less, and sin would consist in the opinion that there is sin!
