(These are the very principles of Libertinism.) But also, how would that opinion, that there is sin, be sin itself, and so be blamable in those who held it, unless previously there had been in them an indifference toward embracing or rejecting it? Therefore indifference must necessarily be posited in undetermined spontaneity.

units.la: V. Attamen omnia à Deo non modo sunt determinata, sed &, quod difficultatem auget, determinate posita, ita ut nulla, quanquam minimula, à nullo alio quam ab ipso solo qui omnia determinate statuit se positurum, possint quocunque modo poni. Quomodo hæc cum indifferentia Spontaneitatis indeterminatæ concilianda? At non memini hic sufficere ut obiter tangam ea ex quibus occasionem loquendi de Deo sum desumpturus, nec opus esse ut scrupulos singulos discutiam, hos præsertim qui ex occasione alienæ materiæ, nempe mali, occurrant. Quapropter tractationem difficultatum harum, aliarumque, intermitto, donec de malo sit cogitandum. Tametsi hic brevibus principia ponam unde omnia deducenda. Si certissimum est, (uti est,) omnia positiva à Deo determinate poni, & tamen indifferentem indeterminationem dari, Ergo Indifferens illa indeterminatio non est creaturæ potentia sive capacitas aliqua ponendi vel non ponendi nonnulla positiva & realia; sive, illa non est de perfectione aliqua ponenda, nec ne; adeoque etsi Deus omnia positiva quæ in Mente determinate ponat, hoc non impedit quominus in illa aliquid relinquatur quod concernat imperfectionem sive negationem: & aliud insuper habeo hujus rei, nempe quod indifferentia sit defectus, argumentum, dum mihi perfectionem optanti conscius sum me peroptare illa plane destitui, quemadmodum & Mentes beatas illa spoliatas esse apprime concipio.
units.tr: V. Yet all things are not only determined by God, but also, what increases the difficulty, posited determinately, so that none, however small, can be posited in any way except by him alone, who determinately decided that he himself would posit all things. How is this to be reconciled with the indifference of undetermined spontaneity? But I do not remember that it is enough here to touch on in passing those points from which I shall take occasion to speak of God, nor that there is need to discuss each single scruple, especially those which arise on occasion of a foreign matter, namely evil. Therefore I set aside the treatment of these difficulties, and of others, until evil is to be considered. Yet here I will briefly lay down the principles from which everything is to be deduced. If it is most certain (as it is) that all positive things are posited determinately by God, and yet an indifferent indetermination is given, then that indifferent indetermination is not a power or capacity of the creature to posit or not to posit some positive and real things; or, it is not a matter of whether some perfection is to be posited or not; and so, although God determinately posits in the mind all the positive things, this does not prevent something being left in it that concerns imperfection or negation: and I have, moreover, another argument on this matter, namely that indifference is a defect, since, while I am conscious of desiring perfection, I am conscious that I am wholly destitute of those things, just as I most clearly conceive that the blessed minds too are stripped of them.

units.la: VI. Quæstionem, an tantam Libertatis meæ Ideam me concipere dicendus sim, ut nullius majoris, ne quidem Divinæ (de qua mox) ideam apprehendam, ut minus utilem, utque incommodam atque obscuram confidero. Non est libertas in omnibus meis cogitationibus. Quæ per indifferentiam liberæ dicuntur eo minus perfectæ sunt (non loquor de imperfectione peccaminosa) quo magis liberæ sunt sive indifferentes: itaque hæc libertatis magnitudo cum Divina non est comparanda. Ex meis cogitandi spontaneis actibus inter se comparatis, alios aliis minus alacres & vividos vidi, quid ergo si ad Deum comparandi sint? Quæ omnium maxima in quibusdam est lubentia quomodo cum Divina libertate comparabitur, ut hæc non dicatur illa major? esse majus vel minus proprie dicitur de æqualitate aut inæqualitate graduum realitatis in rebus earumve modis, quæ quæstio inter Creatorem & creaturam locum habere nequit. Dices, coactionem vel potius sensum coactionis non magis abesse à Libertate Dei quam à Libertate Mentis creatæ, adeoque recte hoc sensu cum Cartesio Medit. IV. dici posse, utramque Libertatem sic præcise consideratam æqualem esse nec alteram altera majorem. Respondeo, me hæcce quidem ut vera admittere, nempe, Omnis coactionis sensus abest à Deo, abest etiam ab iis ex cogitationibus meis quæ liberæ dicuntur: Sed quia id utrobique non est eadem de causa, eodemque modo, cumque id quod tanquam positivum hac voce non-coactio significatur, nempe vel indifferentia, vel lubitus, se non habeat ut in Deo sic in Creatura, nolim idcirco vocibus comparativis uti: nam nullo respectu aliquid in Deo est positivi & in creatura, quod præcise æquale, nec majus, nec minus dici proprie possit, uti nec quid in illis magis vel minus æternum, omnipotens, magis vel minus Deus, &c. dicitur apte. Hæc diversissimi generis nullum vere parallelismum patiuntur. Addo, non fuisse opus Philosopho ad erroris causam investigandam (quod ibi faciebat) ista realitatis cujusdam inter Deum & creaturam comparatione uti: nec etiam ibi clare processisse videtur. attendat quivis: nam revera ibi inque illa materia quam ibidem tractat, superest obscuritas. Dicit ex evidentia sequi Spontaneam allubescentiam (quam diximus Cogitationis spontaneam determinationem;) indifferentiam (spontaneam indeterminationem) esse ex ignorantia vel obscuritate; esse minimum gradum libertatis; adeoque nullam perfectionem sed potius imperfectionem sive defectum, inferre, etiamsi ad ea extendatur quæ intellectus vel non cognoscit, vel non perspicue cognoscit, adeoque latius pateat quam intellectus: Subjungit eo majores esse agendas Deo gratias, quo illa amplior est, sive quo se magis ultra intellectum extendit. Quod cum præcedentibus non congruit, nam hîc supponit illam magnitudinem esse perfectionem quod supra negaverat, quodque etiam falsum est: alioqui actus ei magnitudini conveniens, hoc est, judicium se extendens ultra perceptionem intellectus, esset perfectio, (quod aliquo modo præsensisse videtur) neque culpandus esset, neque error esset. quod absurdum est. Sufficiisset dixisse, Deum, qui Menti creatæ nil debet, ei dedisse quasdam perfectiones, sed non omnes quas potuit; reliquisse adeo in illa imperfectiones, inter quas & illa est, ut dum in illa non datur determinatio spontanea ex evidenti perceptione oriunda, Mens maneat sponte cogitans vel in statu negativo, hoc est, cogitet se hoc vel illud vel istud non nosse; vel in statu privativo, hoc est feratur ad non-Ens quasi esset ens, unde error. Hæc ex alibi dicendis magis illustrabuntur.
units.tr: VI. The question whether I should be said to conceive so great an idea of my liberty that I grasp no greater idea of it, not even the divine idea (of which presently), I consider to be a matter of less use, and of an inconvenient and obscure kind. Liberty is not present in all my thoughts. Those things which are called free through indifference are less perfect (I am not speaking of sinful imperfection) the more free, or indifferent, they are; therefore this magnitude of liberty is not to be compared with the divine. Comparing my spontaneous acts of thinking with one another, I have seen some less eager and lively than others. What then if they are to be compared with God? In some cases the greatest of all is the delight; how will it be compared with divine liberty, so that it is not said to be the greater? To be greater or less is properly said of equality or inequality of degrees of reality in things or in their modes, a question which cannot hold between the Creator and the creature. You will say that coercion, or rather the sense of coercion, is no more absent from the liberty of God than from the liberty of a created mind, and so, in this sense, it can rightly be said with Descartes (Med. IV) that both liberties, considered precisely in this way, are equal and neither is greater than the other. I reply that I admit this as true: the sense of all coercion is absent from God, and it is also absent from those of my thoughts which are called free. But because this is not for the same reason and in the same way on each side, and because that which is signified as positive by this word non-coaction, namely either indifference or delight, does not stand in God as it does in the creature, I would not for that reason wish to use comparative words; for in no respect is there something positive in God and in the creature which can properly be said to be precisely equal, or greater, or less, just as it is not aptly said that one thing is more or less eternal, omnipotent, or more or less God, and so on. Things of such utterly different kinds admit no true parallel. I add that the philosopher had no need, in investigating the cause of error (which was his task there), to use this comparison of a certain reality between God and the creature; nor does he seem to have proceeded clearly there. Let anyone attend to it: for indeed there remains obscurity there, and in the matter which he treats in that place. He says that from evidence there follows spontaneous delight (which we called the spontaneous determination of thought), and that indifference (spontaneous indetermination) arises from ignorance or obscurity, is the least degree of liberty, and therefore implies no perfection but rather imperfection or defect, even if it is extended to those things which the intellect either does not know or does not know clearly, and so reaches more widely than the intellect. He adds that thanks are to be given to God the more, the greater that freedom is, or the more it extends itself beyond the intellect. This does not agree with what came before, for here he supposes that magnitude to be a perfection, which he had denied above, and which is also false; otherwise an act corresponding to that magnitude, that is, a judgment extending itself beyond the perception of the intellect, would be a perfection (which he seems in some way to have foreseen), and it would neither be blameworthy nor be error; which is absurd. It would have sufficed to say that God, who owes nothing to the created mind, has given it certain perfections, but not all that he could; he has thus left in it imperfections, among which is this: that while there is in it no spontaneous determination arising from clear perception, the mind remains spontaneously thinking either in a negative state, that is, it thinks that it does not know this or that or the other; or in a privative state, that is, it is carried toward non-being as though it were being, whence error. These matters will be made clearer from what is to be said elsewhere.

units.la: 7. In Deo esse Libertatem non Indifferentem. 8. Esse & Indifferentem, quæ positiva, & solius Dei prærogativa.
units.tr: 7. That in God there is a liberty which is not indifferent. 8. That indifference, which is positive, is also present, and is a prerogative of God alone.

units.la: VII. Quamvis in Divina Cogitatione nulla sit imperfectio, adverto nihilominus in illa Libertatem quæ cum mea nonnullam habet similitudinem, eamque tum mere Spontaneam sive determinatissimam, tum etiam Indifferentem ad determinationem, pro diversitate objectorum, veritatis, bonitatis rerum de quibus cogitat Deus. Libertatem in illo agnosco, non quæ sit mera coactionis absentia, aut quæ solum dicat principium Cogitandi esse in ipso, sed quæ dicat esse id à se ipso & ad se ipsum. Spontaneam Libertatem sive allubescentiam determinatam in Deo esse adverto, quæque nequaquam est indifferens, cum illius Cogitatio in objectum absolutæ Veritatis & Bonitatis, hoc est, in se ipsum, fertur: nam proculdubio Deus non est indifferens ad se ipsum, ad se noscendum, approbandum, sibi acquiescendum, quamvis maxime Spontaneè atque lubenter in his versetur. Æque est de Essentia Dei ut non sit ad hæc indifferens, ac de ejus natura est ut non sit sibi ipsi contrarius, ut necessarius sit. Nec est quod quis offendatur, quod hunc quem in Deo concipimus, actum, quo in sui notitiam & approbationem fertur, ad Libertatem revocaverim, si quidem hac voce tantum notare volui actus principium esse in ipsa re, & ab ipsamet. Nec etiam obstat quod ante dixerim Scientiam sive Notitiam Dei de se, non esse Liberam, sed Naturalem, illam vero solam quam de rebus cæteris habet liberam esse dicendam: nam illic Libertatis vox, quam hic latius diduco, ad indifferentiam restringebatur. adeoque de solo nomine esset quæstio.
units.tr: VII. Although there is no imperfection in the divine thought, I nevertheless observe in it a liberty which has some likeness to mine, and this both purely spontaneous or most determinate, and also indifferent as to determination, according to the diversity of the objects of God's thought: the truth and goodness of things. I acknowledge in him a liberty which is not merely the absence of coaction, nor one which only says that the principle of thinking is in him, but one which says that it is from himself and toward himself. I observe that in God there is a spontaneous liberty, or a determinate delight, which is by no means indifferent, since his thought is carried toward the object of absolute truth and goodness, that is, toward himself; for undoubtedly God is not indifferent toward himself, toward knowing, approving, and resting in himself, although he moves most spontaneously and gladly in these things. It is the same with the essence of God as with his nature: that he is not indifferent to these things is as necessary as that he is not contrary to himself. Nor need anyone take offence that I have referred to liberty this act which we conceive in God, by which he is carried toward the knowledge and approval of himself, if indeed I wished only by this word to note that the principle of the act is in the thing itself and from itself. Nor does it stand in the way that I said before that God's knowledge or understanding of himself is not free but natural, while that alone which he has of other things is to be called free; for there the word liberty, which I here extend more widely, was restricted to indifference, and so the question would be about the name alone.

units.la: VIII. Cum vero considero Cogitationem Divinam ut relatam ad naturas, essentias, veritates, bonitatem, cæteraque, quæ ipse Deus non sunt, quia ea nec absoluta nec independentia sunt, judico Divinam voluntatem nullum cum illis habere nexum necessarium, sed erga illa fuisse indifferentem, hoc est, potuisse statuere, ponere, conservare ea, aut plane non, aut hoc aut alio modo, & , quæ determinarit, ex indifferentia mera placiti determinasse. Atque hoc tam fuse supra Cap. x. est expositum, & tam sæpe inculcatum, ut malim ea suis in locis inspicere quam eadem hic reponere. Sed notari velim hanc indifferentiam positivam solius Dei Privilegium esse, omni creaturæ incommunicabile, cum involvat independentiam & Potentiam, sive, Vim res statuendi atque ponendi.
units.tr: VIII. But when I consider the divine thought as related to natures, essences, truths, goodness, and other things which are not God himself (because these are neither absolute nor independent), I judge that the divine will has no necessary connection with them, but was indifferent toward them; that is, it was able to establish, place, or preserve them, either not at all or in this or that way, and whatever it has determined, it determined from mere indifference of pleasure. This has been set out at length above in Chapter X, and so often impressed that I prefer to look at those things in their places than to set them down again here. But I would wish it to be noted that this positive indifference is the privilege of God alone, incommunicable to any creature, since it involves independence and power, that is, the force of establishing and positing things.

units.la: CAPUT XX. (19) IMPASSIBILITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. (19) IMPASSIBILITY.

units.la: I. Passiones Animæ in genere, multæ. 2. Mirabilis Dei de hisce dispensatio. 3. 4. Sensationes non tendunt in falsum. 4. Ex solis sensationibus regere corpus, brutum est.
units.tr: I. The passions of the soul in general are many. 2. God's wonderful arrangement concerning these. 3. 4. Sensations do not tend toward falsehood. 4. To govern the body by sensations alone is brutish.

units.la: I. Dixi hanc Libertatem, quam in me modo animadverti, ad omnes cogitationes meas non extendi, utpote qui multas sen-tiam pro voluntatis meæ arbitrio in me non excitari. Quædam sunt quæ etsi interdum ex occasione Cogitationum quarumdam liberarum in me ponantur, tamen præter voluntatem eis annexæ sunt, adeo ut nexus hic non sit liber: tales sunt nonnullæ animi passiones & commotiones turbidæ, quæ quasdam liberas cogitationes nonnunquam ita se-quuntur, ut his positis vix non possint illæ non sequi: nec aliud in his pro libertate fieri potest, nisi quod antecedentibus sponte remotis vel po-sitis, sequentes removeantur vel ponantur: quod tamen in omnibus passionibus locum non habet, nam cum eæ oriuntur ex humorum dis-positione constanti, jam utique plus adest extranei violentique impetus, quamvis partim tanquam in mente mea sentiantur. Aliæ sunt in me Cogitationes quas tanquam ex corpore certo, quod meum appello, imo quasi in illo, percipio, quales illæ sunt doloris, appetitus, famis, sitis, & ejus fortis similes. Aliæ denique quas tanquam ex corporibus extra meum sitis[?], & quasi in illis percipio, ut sunt lucis, colorum, sonorum, & ejusmodi aliæ, quas patet, ubi motus adsunt vel absunt requisiti, quorum perpauci sponte mea disponuntur, me invito adesse vel abesse, nec per voluntatem sisti aut amoveri. Unde consequitur, me multa pati ex occasione rerum mente mea ignobiliorum.
units.tr: I. I have said that this freedom, which I have just now observed in myself, does not extend to all my thoughts, since I feel that many are stirred up in me without the choice of my will. Some are such that, although at times they arise in me on the occasion of certain free thoughts, they are nonetheless attached to them apart from my will, so that the connection is not free. Such are certain passions and turbulent emotions of the mind, which sometimes follow certain free thoughts in such a way that, once these are posited, they can scarcely fail to follow. Nor in these can anything be done in the name of freedom, except that, when the antecedents are voluntarily removed or posited, the consequents are removed or posited as well. This, however, does not hold for all passions, for when they arise from a settled disposition of the humours, there is then much more of an external and violent impulse, although they are partly felt as in my mind. Other thoughts arise in me which I perceive as coming from a certain body that I call my own, or rather as being in it, such as the thoughts of pain, appetite, hunger, thirst, and others of that kind. Still others I perceive as coming from bodies outside my own, and as being in them, such as those of light, colours, sounds, and other such things; it is clear that these occur when the requisite motions are present or absent, and that very few of them are arranged by my own will, nor can they be brought to a halt or removed by my will, whether I wish them present or absent. Hence it follows that I suffer many things on the occasion of things less noble than my mind.

units.la: II. Libet autem in transitu intueri mirabilem circa hæcce Dei dis-pensationem, qui cum Mentem meam cum corporibus, & specialius cum uno ex illis, vel cum una ejus parte nexum habere vellet, non ef-fecit ut turbatim & confuse quævis perceptio cuivis corpori aut motui responderet, sed convenientissime omnia fecit, & prout corpora eorumque motus meam cum illis unitatem magis vel minus spectant, etiam impetus per ideas in mentem meam vividiores, urgentiores, aut vero dilutiores & remissiores fieri statuit. Hinc ubi id quod nexui mentis cum corpore nocet vel prodest, in ipsis (ut vocantur) spiritibus animalibus (nobilissima & immediata Mentis instrumenta) invenitur, eosque fortiter afficit, impetus in Mentem omnium urgentissimi, puta per dolores, vel etiam deliria, aut per raptus inter se contrarios, fiunt; ubi id extra ipsum corpus est, remissiores; ubi partim extus, partim intus, medii, mixtæque sensationes, quæ partim in corpore, partim extra illud, terminantur, quales sunt calor, fames, sitis; ubi quod extra corpus est, ipsum remotius est, vel non vehementer afficit, neque potest; indifferentes quoque, hoc est indifferenter spectatæ perceptiones, excitantur, quales ex visu & auditu ordinarie habentur; at ubi illud tanquam in corpus facile & subito offensurum, idque vel destructurum, vel perfecturum exhibetur, tunc commotiones adduntur vehementiores, quibus corpus disponitur ad occursum vel fugam externorum. Hæc generaliora si specialius deducantur, pulcritudinem mirabilem Divinæ ordinationis contemplantibus sistent. Est etiam in his unde Deus laudetur, quod per coactiones, turbationes, anxietates, fastidia, terminationes ad externa, & similes imperfectiones quæ in istis occurrunt, & mentem quasi à seipsa & à Deo revocant, me monuerit ea non esse solida bona, ne illis sponte mea, præter necessitatem nexus mei cum corpore adhærere quæram.
units.tr: II. It is worth pausing here to consider God's wonderful arrangement in these matters. Since He wished my mind to be joined with bodies, and more particularly with one of them, or with one part of it, He did not ordain that every perception should respond to every body or motion in a disordered and confused way; rather He arranged all things most suitably, and decreed that, according as bodies and their motions bear more or less on the union of my mind with them, the impulses conveyed to my mind through ideas should be made more vivid and urgent, or else fainter and more remiss. Hence, where what harms or benefits the bond of the mind with the body is found in the animal spirits themselves (as they are called, the noblest and most immediate instruments of the mind), and strongly affects them, the most urgent impulses upon the mind arise, as in pains, or even in delirium, or in mutually contrary raptures. Where it is outside the body itself, the impulses are more remiss. Where it is partly outside and partly inside, there arise intermediate and mixed sensations, which terminate partly in the body and partly outside it, such as heat, hunger and thirst. Where what is outside the body is more remote, or does not strongly affect it, or cannot, indifferent perceptions are also excited, that is, perceptions regarded with indifference, such as we ordinarily have from sight and hearing. But where something is presented as likely to strike the body easily and suddenly, and either to destroy it or to bring it to completion, then stronger emotions are added, by which the body is disposed to meet or to flee external things. If these more general matters are deduced more particularly, they will present to those who contemplate them a wonderful beauty of divine ordering. There is also in these matters something for which God is to be praised: by the constraints, disturbances, anxieties, disgusts, the determinations towards external things, and similar imperfections that occur in these, which call the mind back, as it were, from itself and from God, He has warned me that these are not solid goods, so that I should not seek to cling to them of my own accord, beyond what the necessity of my bond with the body requires.

units.la: III. Perfectiones igitur quæ in hisce, utut limitatæ atque imperfectionibus mixtæ, tamen culpandæ non sunt.
units.tr: III. Perfections, therefore, which are found in these things, however limited and mixed with imperfections, are nonetheless not to be blamed.

units.la: Sed non videtur posse ita extra culpam poni, quod hæc interdum positive & ex naturæ suæ conditione fallere videantur, nempe cum vel passiones, vel sensus, Mentem ad ea revocant quæ vel non ita se habent uti repræsentantur, vel nexui ejus cum corpore sunt obfutura, ut cum dolor sentitur in illis partibus quæ tamen absunt, aut cum sitis hydropicum ad potum ei nociturum disponit. Quæritur, quomodo hæc, & quæ his similia, quæ Dei sunt operationes, conciliari possint cum eis quæ demonstrata sunt, quod Deus non tendat in non-ens, quod ejus Sapientiæ sit media ad scopum ducentia, nec, quatenus abillo reguntur, deviantia, adhibere? Cartesius circa finem Sextæ Meditationis nodum hunc dissolvere tentat, sed, ut quod mihi videtur efferam, non dissolvit: concludit enim naturam hominis ut ex mente & corpore compositi non posse non aliquando esse fallacem. Manet tota difficultas, An operatio Dei possit interdum positive in falsum tendere? Certe rationes quibus evincitur non esse de Deo reputandum quod interdum in quocumque actu tendat in non-ens, ens, sive, operationes edat fallaces, omni exceptione majores sunt; nec causæ quas enarrat Philosophus, quod Mens indivisa quæ juncta corpo-ri divisibili, ejusque parti speciali, affectæ à partibus contiguis, à ner-vorum funiculis eodem modo cum funiculis in principio, aut medio, aut extremo moventur, debeat potius ad extremitates nervorum per sensum reduci quam ad eorum principia aut media, quia illuc utplurimum commodum vel incommodum quo afficimur est referendum; & ex unoquoque motu unum eum sensum percipere qui quam frequentissi-me ad conservationem sani hominis conducit; Hæ, inquam, causæ, ut-ut materialiter sive in re ipsa ita se habeant, non tamen tantum realitatis habent, ut ideo hæc realissima veritas, Deus agens nunquam fallit positive, sive, Nulla ejus actio est positive fallax, sit infringenda. Quin potius minus incommodum esset statuere, perceptiones de corpore in Mente excitari debuisse, non pro identitate vel diversitate motuum, sed quæ statui cor-poris bene aut male dispositi, immediate, quocunque modo se habeant motus, constanter sint correspondentes; quam si dicatur fallax positive nonnulla Dei operatio. Prius tamen non fit: sed quæ de sensibus à Cartesio observata sunt, & de occasione qua excitantur, ita se habent in re ipsa. Quid igitur ad difficultatem propositam facies? Dico omnia quæ de sensationibus istis recensita sunt, experientia suffragante, non esse rejicienda; sed non debere inde concludi subesse in illis fallaciam, sive positive fallere atque per se erronea esse interdum quædam Dei opera.
units.tr: But it does not seem possible to exempt these entirely from blame, in that they sometimes seem positively to deceive, and by their very nature: namely, when either the passions or the senses recall the mind to things that either are not as they are represented, or will prove harmful to its bond with the body, as when pain is felt in those parts which are in fact absent, or when thirst disposes the dropsical man to a drink that will harm him. The question is how these things, and others like them, which are operations of God, can be reconciled with what has been demonstrated: that God does not tend toward non-being, that His wisdom employs means that lead to the end, and that it does not, in so far as it is governed by them, employ deviating means. Descartes, near the end of the Sixth Meditation, tries to untie this knot, but, to state what seems to me, he does not untie it. For he concludes that the nature of man, being composed of mind and body, cannot but at times be fallacious. The whole difficulty remains: can the operation of God sometimes tend positively toward falsehood? Certainly the reasons by which it is proved that one should not think that God, in any action whatever, tends toward non-being, or produces deceptive operations, are greater than any exception. Nor are the causes which the Philosopher sets out convincing: that the undivided mind, joined to a divisible body and to a particular part of it, when affected by the contiguous parts, is moved along the cords of the nerves in the same way as those cords are moved at their beginning, middle or end; that it ought to be referred through sense rather to the extremities of the nerves than to their origins or middles, because it is there that the advantage or disadvantage by which we are affected is mostly to be located; and that from each motion it perceives that one sensation which most frequently conduces to the preservation of a healthy man. These causes, I say, although they may be so in material fact, or in the thing itself, do not have so much reality that the most real truth, God acting never deceives positively, or, No action of His is positively deceptive, ought therefore to be overturned. Rather, it would be less of an inconvenience to hold that perceptions of the body ought to be excited in the mind not according to the identity or diversity of motions, but so that they should constantly correspond, immediately, to the state of the body as well or ill disposed, whatever the condition of the motions may be; than to say that some operation of God is positively deceptive. The former, however, does not happen; but what Descartes has observed concerning the senses, and concerning the occasion on which they are excited, is so in the thing itself. What, then, will you do with the difficulty proposed? I say that everything that has been recounted about these sensations, with experience lending its support, is not to be rejected; but it must not be concluded from this that there is falsehood in them, or that some works of God positively deceive and are in themselves erroneous at times.

units.la: IV. Quod ut clarius perspiciam, inquiram quid in hisce error dici possit? Nempe nihil aliud quam deviatio sensationum à scopo atque usu quem Deus ipsis voluit assignare. Observo hunc scopum, sive usum, mentis cum corpore connexionem spectare. Observo præterea Deo non placuisse ut hæc connexio, saltem in hoc statu, inter corpus & Mentem esset indissolubilis. Observo denique connexionem mentis cum corpore non esse mere coactam, &, ut sic dicam, brutam sive ἄλογον, sed ex parte rationalem esse, sive in qua ratio suas habeat partes, ut inde patet, quod ex arbitrio & ratione corpus regi possit. Ex his concludo, Eas sensationes non esse dicendas fallaces quæ ob incertitu-dinem sive obscuritatem, non impediunt interdum quominus Mens à corpore dissolvatur; quomodo errarent, sive deviarent à scopo, siquidem is, qui est Mentis nexus & corporis, ab authore suo non sit indis-folubilis decretus? Secundo, infero easdem non esse fallaces reputandas, si cum solæ consuluntur, mentis cum corpore conjunctionem de-strustructum eunt, ut in hydropico sitiente: nam cum illæ non sint regulæ adæquatæ secundum quas corpori consulatur, sed adhibenda sit quæ & in his partem habet ratio, si hac neglecta, nocitura amplectaris illas sequendo, id negligenti tuo judicio voluntatique adscribe, non autem ipsis sensationibus, quæ ad hoc non datæ sunt ut ex iis solis cæce corpus regeremus. Brutalitatis principium est, secundum sensus appetitusque solos regere corpus, cibum, potum, cætera usurpare, prout appetitus adsunt, durant, evanescunt vel absunt omnino. Ut quid rationi jus & partem in illis concessit Deus? De illis quidem in quibus nullus adhuc rationis usus esse potest, nempe infantulis, videmus ita esse dispositum, ut viribus destituti, & se regere impotentes, alienæ rationis regimini subjiciantur: At, qui ratione uti debent, humanitate sunt indigni cum cæce suos sequuntur impetus, quales delicatuli, voluptuantes, & quot-quot sensibus addicti sunt in corporis sive sani sive ægroti regimine, & quasi bestiæ merito reputantur. Consule intelligentiam, illa te docebit quædam assumenda, quædam item à corpore esse relegánda, interdum cum sensationibus appetituque, interdum sine illis, interdum con-tra, interdum cis vel præter illos, atque etiam judicia similiter de corporis statu efformare. Quodsi sine ratione spirituales impetus, qui spi-rituale bonum nobis proponunt, sequi non debeamus, ut in capite præ-cedenti est observatum, multo minus brutos, qui corporea nobis osse-runt. Quare sensus interni sive sint Spirituales, sive corporei (facultates tantopere à Herberto decantatæ) non tuto soli ad aliquid probandum adducuntur. Et specialius de corporeis, non putandum has perceptio-nes non-spontaneas ad hoc esse datas ut ex iis immediate impellamur ad agendum id ad quod obscure revocare videntur, aut judicandum secun-dum eas: Sed datæ sunt tanquam monita & signa, ex quorum appulsu ratio nostra, imo & aliena cum imbecilles sumus, in consilium vocatur, & admonetur statui corporis attendendum esse, eique debite prospi-ciendum. Hic ergo usus est: Mentem de corpore sollicitam reddere; & hunc assequuntur. An autem ei sit consulendum eo modo & in eo membro, quæ subobscure indicantur, & quo revocant illæ sensationes, suus rationi non frustra in corpus jus habenti, locus relinquatur, quæ etsi quam frequentissime cum illis concordet, interdum tamen alio revocat quam illuc quo sine illa ruissemus: eodem prorsus modo, quo perceptionibus caloris, colorum, &c. etsi ad externa per has sensatio-nes videamur revocari, ratio tamen intus non revocat, docetque simi-lia in rebus externis non esse, sed intus, in Mente: unde nemo recte
units.tr: IV. That I may see this more clearly, I shall inquire what can be called error in these matters. Surely nothing other than the deviation of sensations from the aim and use which God wished to assign to them. I observe that this aim, or use, concerns the connection of the mind with the body. I observe further that it did not please God that this connection, at least in this state, between body and mind should be indissoluble. I observe finally that the connection of the mind with the body is not merely forced and, so to speak, brute or ἄλογον, but is in part rational, that is, one in which reason has its own parts, as is clear from the fact that the body can be governed by choice and reason. From these things I conclude: those sensations are not to be called fallacious which, on account of their uncertainty or obscurity, do not at times prevent the mind from being dissolved from the body; how would they err, or deviate from the aim, since that which is the bond of the mind and the body has not been decreed indissoluble by its author? Second, I infer that the same sensations are not to be reckoned fallacious if, when they alone are consulted, they lead to the destruction of the union of mind and body, as in the thirsty dropsical man. For since they are not adequate rules by which the body is to be cared for, but reason, which also has a part in these matters, must be applied, if you neglect this and embrace those things which will harm you by following them, ascribe that to your negligent judgement and will, and not to the sensations themselves, which were not given for this purpose, that we should blindly govern the body by them alone. The principle of brutishness is to govern the body by the senses and appetites alone, to take food, drink and other things as the appetites are present, last, fade or are altogether absent. Why, then, has God granted reason a right and a part in these matters? For those in whom no use of reason can yet exist, namely little infants, we see it so arranged that, being destitute of strength and unable to govern themselves, they are subjected to the government of another's reason. But those who ought to use reason are unworthy of humanity when they blindly follow their impulses, as do the delicate, the pleasure-seekers, and all who are given over to the senses in the governance of the body, whether sound or sick, and are rightly reckoned as beasts. Consult understanding: it will teach you that some things are to be assumed, and some likewise to be banished from the body, sometimes together with sensations and appetite, sometimes without them, sometimes against them, sometimes either apart from them or beyond them; and likewise it will teach you to form judgements about the state of the body. But if we ought not to follow spiritual impulses, which set a spiritual good before us, without reason, as has been observed in the preceding chapter, much less should we follow brute impulses, which present corporeal things to us. Therefore the internal senses, whether they are spiritual or corporeal (faculties so much praised by Herbert), are not safely brought forward alone to prove anything. And more particularly concerning the corporeal senses, it should not be thought that these non-spontaneous perceptions are given for this purpose: that we should be driven immediately by them to act in the very thing to which they seem obscurely to call us, or to judge according to them. But they are given as warnings and signs, by whose impact our reason, and even that of others when we are weak, is called into counsel, and it is admonished that attention must be paid to the state of the body and that due provision must be made for it. This, then, is their use: to make the mind solicitous about the body; and this they achieve. Whether, however, it is to be attended to in that manner and in that member which these sensations somewhat obscurely indicate, and to which they call us, is left to reason, which has a right over the body not in vain; and although reason agrees with them as often as possible, yet at times it calls us elsewhere than where we would have rushed without it. In exactly the same way, with perceptions of heat, colours, etc., although through these sensations we seem to be called towards external things, reason nonetheless does not call us there, and teaches that things of this kind are not in external objects but within, in the mind; whence no one rightly

units.la: Ceremonies of underlined words: "ratio", and the lines "Brutalitatis principium est ... Ut quid rationi jus &" are underlined in the print. ratiocinans concludet sic sensus statui proprie & ex natura sua fallaces atque erroneos. Similiter de aliis perceptionibus est judicandum. Si quid datum ut pars socia, & adhibitum ut totum, nil efficit recti, non illud fallaciae, sed qui sic illo utitur ipse erroris & inconsiderantiae insimulari debet.
units.tr: Underlined in the print: "ratio", and the lines "Brutalitatis principium est ... Ut quid rationi jus &". Reasoning will conclude in this way: the senses, taken by themselves and by their own nature, are deceptive and erroneous. Similarly, the other perceptions must be judged. If something given as a partner part is used as the whole, it produces nothing right; the fault lies not in that thing as a source of deception, but the person who uses it in this way must be charged with error and thoughtlessness.

units.la: 5. Deus nil in se patitur. Ejus sensus perfectissimus.
units.tr: 5. God suffers nothing in himself. His sense is most perfect.

units.la: V. Ab operationibus illis Dei in me non spontaneis sed nec fallacibus, transeo ad ipsius Dei contemplationem. Sed quae in illo ex hac occasione observo, difficultate carent: nam quocunque modo eum intuear, facile concipio eum esse absolute Impassibilem, & ab alio nil actu recipientem. Talis est primo in Notitia atque voluntate sua quatenus ad se ipsum terminantur. Secundo in Cogitatione sua de rebus, suaeque de illis voluntatis determinatione, quippe quae a rebus ipsis ad Deum non veniunt, ut saepius probatum. Tertio, in sensibus: nullos enim habet nostris similes qui aliunde procedant, cum imperfectio sit aliunde recipere. Quomodo autem conscius sit nostrarum sensationum, temerarium est inquirere. Sed sensus Divinus, sensus sui ipsius cum gaudio perfectissimo, de ipso negandus non est, etsi non sit dicendus passio, quippe qui aliunde non manat, qui spontaneus est, nullam involvit imperfectionem, & ab Entis perfectissimi Natura est indissolubilis. Nam, qui perfectissimus diceretur ille qui omnes perfectiones possidere asseveraretur, nec tamen in illis haberet complacentiam, delectationem, gaudium summum, quod a conscientia omnium perfectionum suaeque Felicitatis non differt? Interim quisquis sensus impressionem ab alieno, aut inconstantiam, aut aliam quamcunque imperfectionem infert, illi proprie non convenit, neque irascitur aut odit, aut poenitentia erga quenquam ducitur serenissima Mens, sed Scriptores Sacri illis verbis utentes, ejus operationum vices, praesentiam aut absentiam erga peccatores, designant. Hoc attributum Impassibilitas, etsi verbo negativum, est tamen sensu positivum: ejusque ab Activitate differentia alibi exposita est.
units.tr: V. Having set aside those operations of God in me, which are not spontaneous yet are not deceptive either, I pass on to the contemplation of God himself. The things I observe in him on this occasion, however, present no difficulty: for in whatever way I look at him, I easily conceive that he is absolutely Impassible, and receives nothing actually from another. Such he is, first, in his knowledge and will, insofar as these terminate in himself. Second, in his thought about things, and his determination of will concerning them, since these do not come to God from the things themselves, as has been proved often. Third, in his senses: for he has no senses like ours that proceed from elsewhere, since imperfection consists in receiving from elsewhere. How he is conscious of our sensations it is rash to inquire. But the divine sense, his sense of himself with most perfect joy, is not to be denied to him, although it is not to be called a passion, since it does not flow from elsewhere, is spontaneous, involves no imperfection, and is inseparable from the nature of the most perfect Being. For who would be called most perfect, if he were said to possess all perfections, yet had no complacency, delight, or supreme joy in them, which does not differ from the consciousness of all perfections and of his own blessedness? Meanwhile, whatever sense brings an impression from another, or inconstancy, or any other imperfection, does not properly belong to him; the most serene Mind neither grows angry, hates, nor is moved to repentance toward anyone. Rather, the Sacred Writers, using those words, designate the vicissitudes of his operations, his presence or absence toward sinners. This attribute, Impassibility, though negative in word, is positive in sense; and its difference from Activity has been set out elsewhere.

units.la: CAPUT XXI. (20) JUSTITIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI. (20) JUSTICE.

units.la: 1. Imperfectiones voluntariæ, injustæ. 2. Justitia in homine. 3. Injustitia, adductis aliquot exemplis. 4. Ea hominem, non vero Deum attingunt.
units.tr: 1. Voluntary imperfections are unjust. 2. Justice in man. 3. Injustice, with several examples adduced. 4. These touch man, not God.

units.la: I. Non modo animadverto in Libertate mea limites atque imperfectiones, quatenus omnes Cogitationes secundum illam in me non excitantur: (quæ impressio est involuntaria:) Sed & alias imperfectiones in illa deprehendo, quæque sunt voluntariæ, quatenus fieri potest, atque etiam nimis sæpe fit, ut sponte libertate mea abutar, atque eam ipsam improbem, negando, exempli causa, me ea sponte commisisse in cogitationibus, in judiciis, in corporis regimine, aliisque, quæ tamen me commisisse vere percepero; vel etiam eam regere aliter volendo ac fieri deberet. Sic enim ejus tum verus usus, tum regimen, abnegatur: quæ quidem imperfectio magna est, & jure injustitia appellatur. Antequam autem ex hujus occasione id quod per Justitiam Dei intelligi debet, considerem, nonnihil de illa mei injustitia, deque justitia quæ illi in me opposita deberet inesse, specialius inquiram, ut conceptus & verba distinctiora reddantur.
units.tr: I. I notice not only the limits and imperfections in my liberty, insofar as not all thoughts are stirred up in me according to it (which impression is involuntary). I also detect in it other imperfections, which are voluntary, insofar as it can happen, and indeed happens all too often, that I of my own accord abuse my liberty and misuse it, by denying, for example, that I have committed of my own accord things in my thoughts, in my judgments, in the governing of my body, and in other matters, which nevertheless I have truly perceived that I committed; or by willing to govern it otherwise than it ought to be governed. For thus both its true use and its government are denied. This imperfection is great, and rightly called injustice. Before, however, I consider on the occasion of this what ought to be understood by the Justice of God, I shall inquire somewhat more specifically into this injustice of mine, and into the justice which ought to be opposed to it in me, so that the concepts and words may be rendered more distinct.

units.la: II. Id justum est, quod rei alicujus naturæ & regimini est congruens, conveniens, decens, atque iis dignum: etenim voces istæ, justum, decens, conveniens, tanquam synonymæ recte usurpari possunt. Adeoque, quoniam quicquid est realitatis in mea natura, in meæ Mentis corporisque mei regimine, in regiminis regulis, & verbo, in omnibus quæcunque in me sunt, aut esse possunt, quoniam inquam illud omne operatio Dei est, sequitur justum esse, ut sinam me, (effectum quippe Dei) à Deo regi, de me secundum ejus placitum & regulas disponi, in me quicquid vult fieri, me per illum (omnia operantem) ad illum (omnium scopum) duci, nec impediam quominus illa omnia quæ mihi annexuit, corpus, externa, proximi, ad illum mediante nexu quem mecum habent, rapiantur. Hæc justitia mea in statu naturæ, eaque jure est indispensabilis. sic decet verum Dei opus disponi.
units.tr: II. That is just which agrees with, suits, and becomes the nature and governance of some thing, and is worthy of it. For these words, just, becoming, and suitable, may rightly be used as synonyms. Accordingly, since whatever reality there is in my nature, in the governance of my mind and of my body, in the rules of governance and in the word, in all things whatever that are or can be in me, since, I say, all that is the work of God, it follows that it is just that I allow myself (being an effect of God) to be ruled by God, to be disposed of by him according to his pleasure and rules, that whatever he wills to be done in me, that I be led through him (who works all things) to him (the goal of all things), and that I not hinder those things which he has joined to me, my body, external things, and my neighbour, from being carried off to him through the connection they have with me. This is my justice in the state of nature, and it is by right indispensable. Thus it becomes God's work to be arranged.

units.la: III. At si huic resisto, tunc operationi Divinæ resistens patro[?] injustitiam, cujus natura, vel potius absurditas, in eo non est quod aliquid ex inde incongrui in Natura Dei sequatur, aut in ejus placito, aut in ejus opere quatenus ab ipso est, sed quatenus in me debet admitti. Si ego debeo esse merum opus Dei, & tamen resisto operi Dei, tunc mihi ipsi, quatenus illud deberem esse, noceo & resisto: & hoc est absurdum, incongruum, male conveniens naturæ illi meæ quæ opus Dei est & esse debet. Hæc est injustitia. Si ex me vane operari tentem, injustitia est, nam sic volo esse non-opus Dei, sed opus mei, hoc est, nihil: atqui incongruum est alicui, ut positive tendat in nihil. Si in me optem operationes Dei fieri ad lubitum sive placitum meum, injustitia: nam natura operis Dei est effectus placiti solius Dei, volo autem ut sit effectus placiti non-Dei, hoc est, ut non sit, quod incongruum. Si in me optem operationes Dei fieri, at non ita in aliis, in proximis, quos non curem in conspectu Dei, injustitia: nam verum opus Dei repræsentat Deum secundum ejus placitum, estque canalis per quem operationes Dei ad alios fluunt; Sed hoc modo non repræsento Deum omnes curantem, & nolo me esse eum qui gerat ea quæ sunt operis Dei: opus vult esse non-opus. absurdum. Si lubens ita corpus rego ut proximus non approximetur Deo, sed alienetur potius ab illo, injustitia: Deo subtrahere tento opera sua in me & in aliis, ut fiant non-opera sua, adeoque nihil. hoc non decet Dei opus. Si postquam injustitiam commisero eam negem me commisisse; aut postquam justum quid in me factum fuerit, illud inficias eam, utrumque nova injustitia: posterius, quia sic operatio Dei directe, prius autem quia indirecte negatur, & pro ea obtruditur quod non est Dei operatio. Etenim negando me injuste egisse, eopse affirmo Deum semper in me operatum esse, adeoque injustitiam quæ vere in me est, tanquam esset opus Dei in me, jacto, sive eam pro me ipso quatenus opus Dei sum, sumo. Atqui indecens & incongruum est mihi, quatenus sum Dei opus, asseverare me talem ab illo esse factum. Econtra, justum & conveniens est illi qui est opus Dei, ut se ipsum manifestet quatenus & quousque tale est vel non est: id est, non debet negare sua Dei bona, & sua ipsius mala.
units.tr: III. But if I resist this, then, resisting the divine operation, I commit injustice. Its nature, or rather its absurdity, lies not in this, that something incongruous would follow from it in the nature of God, or in his pleasure, or in his work insofar as it is from him, but insofar as it ought to be admitted in me. If I ought to be purely the work of God, and yet I resist the work of God, then I harm and resist myself, insofar as I ought to be that work; and this is absurd, incongruous, and ill-suited to that nature of mine which is and ought to be the work of God. This is injustice. If I try to work of my own vain accord, it is injustice, for thus I will to be not the work of God but my own work, that is, nothing; but it is incongruous for anything to tend positively toward nothing. If I wish in myself that the operations of God be carried out according to my own pleasure or whim, it is injustice; for the nature of God's work is to be the effect of God's pleasure alone, while I want it to be the effect of a pleasure that is not God's, that is, that it should not be, which is incongruous. If I wish that God's operations be carried out in me, but not so in others, in my neighbours, whom I do not care for in the sight of God, it is injustice; for the true work of God represents God according to his pleasure, and is the channel through which God's operations flow to others. But in this way I do not represent God caring for all, and I am unwilling to be the one who bears what belongs to God's work: I wish the work to be a non-work. Absurd. If I willingly govern my body so that my neighbour is not brought near to God, but is rather estranged from him, it is injustice: I try to withdraw from God his works in me and in others, so that they become non-works, and so nothing. This does not become the work of God. If, after I have committed an injustice, I deny that I committed it, or, after something just has been done in me, I deny it, both are a new injustice: the latter because God's operation is thus denied directly, the former because it is denied indirectly, and what is not God's operation is foisted in its place. For by denying that I have acted unjustly, I thereby affirm that God has always worked in me, and so I assume the injustice that is truly in me as if it were a work of God in me, as if I took it on behalf of myself insofar as I am the work of God. But it is unbecoming and incongruous for me, insofar as I am the work of God, to assert that I have been made such by him. On the contrary, it is just and fitting for him who is the work of God to manifest himself as he is, and as far as he is or is not such: that is, he must not deny God's good things and his own evils.

units.la: IV. Hæc omnia justitiæ Dei agnoscendæ, & ab ea quæ in hominibus esse debet distinguendæ, inserviunt, modo ne hæc ex principio corrupto ullus intueatur, reputans ex amore corruptionis suæ, in hoc esse justitiam, ut quæ sibi ex depravatione convenire judicat, assequatur. Nil aliud in dictis videre volui, nisi justitiam naturæ Dei, ut & justitiam placiti Dei, etsi hæc sit regula justitiæ hominis, non esse tamen ipsam justitiam hominis, sive ipsam rem, sive ipsum opus justum in homine: sed hoc hominem ipsum esse quatenus in illo nihil est quod non sit Dei opus, sive quod non deceat hominem quatenus is est Dei opus. Sic percipio, quam vere sacra clamet pagina, hominem peccantem non tam in Deum quam in se ipsum inque suam animam peccare (siquidem sic minus operationum Dei sint in illo;) justitias, aut injustitias nostras ad Deum non attingere, quanquam indirecte sint conamen inutile ut Deus non sit Deus, nempe quatenus placito & dependentiae ab illo volunt subduci, adeoque, Deum non habere jus, potentiamque in omnia, neque sic Deum esse: Ex quo est quod motivum poenitentiae sive doloris ob injustitiam, non sit desumendum a consideratione nostri, sed Dei: imo, si vis, a consideratione nostri, quatenus nos omnino nostri non sumus, sed ejus, & tamen in multis, in regimine, in omnibus voluimus esse non-ejus. Nam alioqui absurdum esset dolere, perinde quasi Naturae Dei aut ejus placito nocuissemus, cum hoc, quod indirecte tentavimus, sit impossibile.
units.tr: IV. All these things serve to recognise the justice of God and to distinguish it from that which ought to be in men, provided that no one looks at these things from a corrupt principle, reckoning, out of love for his own corruption, that justice consists in attaining whatever he judges to suit him by reason of his depravity. I have wished to see nothing else in what has been said than that the justice of God's nature, as also the justice of God's pleasure, although this is the rule of human justice, is not itself the justice of man, whether the thing itself or the just work itself in man; but that this is man himself, insofar as in him there is nothing which is not the work of God, or which does not become man insofar as he is the work of God. Thus I perceive how truly the sacred page cries out that man, sinning, sins not so much against God as against himself and his own soul (since to that extent there are fewer of God's operations in him); and that our justices or injustices do not reach God directly, although indirectly they are a useless attempt to make God not God, namely insofar as they want to withdraw themselves from his pleasure and dependence upon him, and thus to hold that God has no right or power over all things, and that God is not thus God. Hence it follows that the motive of repentance or grief for injustice is not to be drawn from consideration of ourselves, but of God; indeed, if you will, from consideration of ourselves insofar as we are not ours at all but his, and yet in many things, in governance, in all things, we have wished to be not-his. For otherwise it would be absurd to grieve, as though we had harmed the nature of God or his pleasure, since what we have attempted indirectly is impossible.

units.la: 5. In Dei natura, placito, opere, justitia est. 6. Ea ultra vindictam mali extendenda. 7. Justitia vindicativa ut Deo essentialis. ut postulat satisfactionem. 8. Nempe ut peccator sit æternum miser, 9. vel ex amore Dei summe doleat. 10. Quod interventum subjecti præstantissimi & innocentissimi requisivit. 11. Conscientia hisce suffragatur quoad jus. Veritas facti ex revelatione & experientia depromenda.
units.tr: 5. Justice is in the nature, pleasure, and work of God. 6. It must be extended beyond the punishment of evil. 7. Vindictive justice as essential to God, since it demands satisfaction. 8. Namely that the sinner be eternally wretched, 9. or grieve most deeply out of love for God. 10. Which required the intervention of a most excellent and most innocent subject. 11. Conscience supports this as to right. The truth of the fact is to be drawn from revelation and experience.

units.la: V. In Cogitatione summa non eæ sunt imperfectiones quas jamjam in Cogitatione mea animadverti. Nam seu illa se ipsam contempletur ac velit, seu alia velit vel operetur, equidem nil incongrui ullibi adverti potest. Naturam mere unam perfectissimam, simplicem, esse sibi maxime congruam, decentem, atque adeo in se justam, ita evidenter percipio, ut operosiorem probationis deductionem non requiram. Non etiam concipere possum Deum aliquid statuere aut operari quod eo sit indignum, sive quo testetur aut se plane non esse, hoc est, aliquid quod non habeat notam Dei existentis; aut se non esse id quod est; aut se nolle id quod vult, aut velle id quod non vult. Adeoque non potest ab illo aliqua operatio proficisci quae ostendat eum esse non independentem, non sapientem, non potentem, non omnis boni Authorem, non alienum a nihilo vel ab odio sui, sive a malo, non approbantem opus suum: Sive, Cogitari nequit in Deo ejusque actionibus ullum indecens, ulla justitia.
units.tr: V. In the supreme Thought there are not those imperfections which I have just now noticed in my thought. For whether it contemplates and wills itself, or wills or works other things, indeed nothing incongruous can be noticed anywhere. I perceive so evidently that the nature which is purely one, most perfect, and simple is most congruous with itself, becoming, and therefore just in itself, that I do not require a more laborious deduction of proof. Nor can I conceive that God decides or works anything which would be unworthy of him, that is, anything by which he would show himself not to be at all, that is, anything that does not bear the mark of the existing God; or that he is not what he is; or that he does not will what he wills, or wills what he does not will. Accordingly, no operation can proceed from him which would show him to be not independent, not wise, not powerful, not the author of every good, not remote from nothingness or from hatred of himself, or from evil, not approving his own work. In short, nothing unbecoming, no injustice, can be thought in God or in his actions.

units.la: VI. Econtra, Cum Deum deceat se, qualis est, operationibus suis, si quas producere vult, adumbrare, justum est igitur (hæc enim Ju-stitia ultra vindictam mali est extendenda) ut iis testetur se summum, se Potentem, se Sapientem esse, se bonum & boni fontem, se operis approbantem. (hinc omnia conservat, ipsæque substantiæ quæ malo implicatæ sunt, quia substantiæ sunt, hoc est, quia opus ejus sunt, ab eo sustentantur, & ab annihilatione præservantur.) Ita quoque Deum sui amantem & approbantem, decet esse improbantem ejus quod ipsum non amat, in quo si aliquid realitatis & bonitatis ponit, decet etiam ut ostendat indubitatis notis, & valde seriis, se non ideo malum, sui neglectum, probare, sed potius improbare. Hoc ultimum Justitia Vindi-catrix dicitur, & Simpliciter Justitia; At improprie ad solam vindictam mali restringitur Justitia, quæ vere latius quid est quam vulgo putatur, cum ad Dei Naturam, ad omne ejus placitum, & ad omne ejus opus viderimus eam ita esse referendam, ut nihil in illis ab ea deflectat, quamvis ejus viæ in occulto Sapientiæ Divinæ interdum ad tempus lateant.
units.tr: VI. On the other hand, since it becomes God to reflect in his operations, if he wishes to produce any, what he is in himself, it is therefore just (for this Justice must be extended beyond the punishment of evil) that by them he should bear witness that he is supreme, that he is powerful, that he is wise, that he is good and the fountain of goodness, and that he approves his own work. (Hence he preserves all things, and the substances themselves which are entangled with evil, because they are substances, that is, because they are his work, are sustained by him and preserved from annihilation.) Likewise, since God loves and approves himself, it becomes him to disapprove of what he does not love, and if he posits in it any reality and goodness, it becomes him also to show, by indubitable and very serious signs, that he does not approve evil, the neglect of himself, but rather disapproves of it. This latter is called Avenging Justice, and simply Justice; but Justice is improperly restricted to the mere punishment of evil, whereas it is truly something broader than is commonly thought, since we see that when it is referred to the Nature of God, to all his good pleasure, and to all his work, it is so related that nothing in them turns aside from it, although its ways sometimes lie hidden for a time in the secret of Divine Wisdom.

units.la: VII. De Justitia Dei vindicativa pauca ex hisce specialius & evidentius deducere conabor, siquidem horum fructus præcipuus sit ut iis sacra illustrentur. Cum Justitia Vindicativa, quæ Creaturas malas pro objecto habet, dicitur Deo essentialis, non cogitandum est, aliquid per creaturas Deo sive Divinæ Naturæ subtrahi posse aut subtractum esse, quod ei reddere oporteat ut Divina natura sibi constet: nam sic aliquid Naturæ sive Essentiæ Dei deesset. Sed Deo volente se operibus suis ad placitum pingere qualis est, decens est ut in illis operibus sint testimonia, notæ, signa seria, grandia, indubitata, quod Deus se ipsum & sui amorem probet, non probet autem sui contrarium, sui neglectum. Hæc igitur decentia, sive Justitia, proprie dicenda est essentia-lis placito Dei de se, qualis est, per creaturas quales jam voluit libere statuere, repræsentando, non vero directe ipsi Essentiæ Dei. Quod si talia adsint testimonia, nil est quod placitum sive voluntas Dei ad sui decentiam, justitiamve, ad hoc ut tanquam Deo digna concipiatur, ulterius requirat: hisce testimoniis ei satisfit, nam sic illa vindicatur à contumelia & blasphemia qua impeti posset, quasi probaret id quod Deo contrarium est, quod revera esset injustissimum, sive non decens voluntatem Dei, ipsumque Deum.
units.tr: VII. I shall try to deduce a few things more specifically and evidently from these concerning the vindictive Justice of God, since the principal fruit of these things is that the sacred matters be illuminated by them. When Vindictive Justice, which has evil creatures for its object, is said to be essential to God, we must not think that anything can be taken away from God or from the Divine Nature through creatures, or that something has been taken away which he must restore so that the Divine nature may remain consistent with itself; for thus something would be lacking to the Nature or Essence of God. But since God, willing to depict himself in his works as he is according to his good pleasure, it is becoming that in those works there should be testimonies, marks, and serious, great, and indubitable signs that God proves himself and his love, and does not prove the opposite of himself, his neglect. This propriety, or Justice, is therefore properly to be called the essential good pleasure of God concerning himself, as he is, by representing him through creatures as he has freely willed to establish them, and not directly to the Essence of God itself. And if such testimonies are present, there is nothing further which the good pleasure or will of God requires for his propriety or justice, so that he may be conceived as worthy of God: he is satisfied by these testimonies, for thus they are vindicated from the insult and blasphemy by which they might be assailed, as if they proved what is contrary to God, which would truly be most unjust, or unbecoming to the will of God and to God himself.

units.la: VIII. Jam vero, si Ego, qui sum opus Dei, su[?]issem me Deo subjici, tunc certe nil in me esset quod Decentiam placiti Dei de se in me repræsentando in dubium revocaret. At postquam volui esse mei juris, sive Deum nolui esse omnia in me, sed eum abnegavi, & peccavi, tunc quamvis essentia & existentia mea, sive τῷ[?] conscium esse, declarent Dei potentiam sustentantem, (adeoque non sint eatenus à Deo improbandæ sive annihilandæ :) attamen illa abnegatio Dei non potest concipi esse Divinæ voluntati grata,congrua,decens. decet itaque Deum testari negationem sui in me sibi non placere. Qui id testabitur? Quale illud testimonium? An si Deus illa bona in me operetur in posterum quæ operatus fuisset si non peccassem, sique me rebellem ita sustentet, ut in meo statu delicier, mihi placeam, & acquiescam? Stulta cogitatio hæc est. Quin potius si omittat in me operari bona quæ ni peccassem fuisset operatus, gaudiaque iniqua inquietudine percellat: quomodo omnibus bonis privatus summe miser equidem in posterum redderer, imo & in Dei negatione pergens, Dei operationibus optimis privari æternum pergerem; sed tamen hoc modo miseria mea vindicaret Decentiam sive Justitiam Divinam, alte clamans, Deum sui negationem summe improbare, & ab ea esse summe alienum & abstinentem. Sic igitur postulat voluntas quæ Ens se ipsum non improbans decet, ut peccator sit æternum miser.
units.tr: VIII. Now, if I, who am the work of God, had submitted myself to God, then certainly there would be nothing in me which would call into doubt the propriety of God's good pleasure concerning himself, represented in me. But after I willed to be my own master, that is, did not want God to be all things in me, but denied him and sinned, then, although my essence and existence, or my being conscious, declare the sustaining power of God (and so, to that extent, they are not to be disapproved or annihilated by God), nevertheless that denial of God cannot be conceived to be pleasing, agreeable, or becoming to the Divine will. It is therefore fitting that God should testify that my denial of him does not please him. Who will testify this? What kind of testimony? Would it be if God, in future, were to work in me the good things which he would have worked had I not sinned, and sustained me in my rebellion in such a way that I should delight in my state, take pleasure in myself, and acquiesce? This thought is foolish. Rather, if he were to omit working in me the good things which he would have worked had I not sinned, and were to strike my joys with unjust disquiet, then I would indeed, deprived of all good things, become supremely miserable in future, and moreover, persisting in the denial of God, I would persist to be eternally deprived of God's most excellent operations; yet in this way my misery would vindicate the Propriety or Justice of God, crying aloud that God supremely disapproves of the denial of himself, and is wholly alien to it and abstains from it. Thus, then, the will which becomes a Being that does not disapprove of itself requires that the sinner be eternally miserable.

units.la: IX. Attamen concipio, quodsi in Dei negatione & mei ipsius præ Deo amplexu non pergerem, & præterea si maxime & amarissime ex displicentia peccatorum commissorum & amore Dei, ex eo quod voluerim Dei juri subtrahi & mei juris esse, dolerem, totusque inquietus essem respectu mentis & corporis, tunc me fore in eo statu restitutum in quo bona Dei voluntas decentissime in me operaretur denuo quæ intermissa erant, atque consummaret ea quæ absente peccato fuisset factu-ra, aut forte eadem mensura majori. Sine hoc impossibile est ut cogitem Deum sese mecum feliciter communicaturum. Nam quocunque medio Deum uti posse putem, Si tamen in me non cessaret Dei negatio, non desinere voluptas in non-Deo, non reponeretur Divinus amor; tunc res eo rediret, ut Deus probaret & amplecteretur sui neglectum; mediumque, qualecunque id cogitari posset, dicendum esset intervenire ut maneret constans Dei negatio, non-amor Dei, & delectatio in non-Deo. Quod absit ut cogitemus.
units.tr: IX. Yet I conceive that if I did not persist in the denial of God and in embracing myself before God, and moreover if I grieved most bitterly from displeasure at the sins committed and from love of God, because I had willed to withdraw from the right of God and to be under my own right, and if I were wholly restless in mind and body, then I would be restored to that state in which the good will of God would most becomingly work in me again those good things which had been interrupted, and would complete those things which, had sin been absent, I would have done, or perhaps in an even greater measure. Without this it is impossible for me to think that God would communicate himself happily with me. For by whatever means I might suppose God could be used, if, however, the denial of God did not cease in me, if delight in the non-God did not cease, and the Divine love were not restored, then the matter would come to this: that God would approve and embrace the neglect of himself; and whatever means could be conceived, it would have to be said that it intervened so that the denial of God, the non-love of God, and delight in the non-God, would remain constant. Far be it from us to think this.

units.la: X. At quomodo cessatio negationi Dei, hujus amor, destructio delectationis extra Deum, quomodo dolor sanctus ex amore Dei & negatione mei oriundus (res bona, perfecta, realissima, quæ in se mala & execranda non est, sed talis si dicitur, ideo dicitur, quia rei execrandæ, nempe peccati, nota est.) quomodo, inquam, talia bona in me ponerentur, nisi is qui operatur omnia, ea quoque operetur? quomodo vero tanta bona in me rejectaneo peccatore decenti modo operari Deum concipiam nisi concipiam antecedenter quod Deus testatus sit solide malum meum sibi non placere? Prior difficultas primumque obstaculum redit. Haec maxima bona ipsumque adeo sanctum dolorem, non concipio a voluntate Deum neglectum sui improbantem decente, poni posse in subjecto improbo, nisi Deus in antecessum testatus sit sui de illo improbationem summam, quod obstaculum ut per circulum redit continuo, donec detur tale subjectum, quod nil habeat in se praecedente Dei improbatione & displicentia dignum, sed quod sit praestantissimum & pretiosissimum, in quo non fuerit prava voluntas, negatio Dei, quodque Deus sui amore, &, in testimonium odii erga peccatum, doloribus summis ex Summo Dei amore & displicentia peccati oriundis repleat. Dico autem & sanctos dolores illos summos, & subjectum illud pretiosissimum atque praestantissimum esse debere. Nam cum Deus ultra quam cogitari potest a peccato distet, sic quod in hujus testimonium debet adduci, ultra quam dici vel cogitari potest decet esse memorabile & notabile: quod in me hoc quoque respectu plene fieri non poterat. Atqui cum tale subjectum in naturali hominum statu non detur, alibi quaerere sapientiae Dei, exhibere liberae gratiae est. Sed ubi tale subjectum innocens, taleque in eo Dei opus fuerit, quid postea impediet quominus Dei Bonitatem deceat mihi ita bene velle ut ad sui mecum communionem divinos in me atque etiam in aliis, ut ipsi placebit, dolores efficiat, cessationem negationi Dei injiciat, adque easdem quae prius ante peccatum operationes fuissent, ponat, etsi gradatim & alio modo? An jam dicetur quod locus huic contumeliae superfit, nempe, Divinam voluntatem haec bona in peccatore operantem sic agere, acsi ab eo quod Deum negat, sive a peccato, non esset aliena? Siquidem se ab hac contumelia sufficientissime purgaverit & vindicaverit, efficiendo dilectum in quo antecedenter nil erat reprobandum, ex amore Divino summe ob peccata dolere? Non impediet igitur Justitia Dei, sive decentia ejus voluntatis, quin consequenter in me bona ista ponat, videlicet primo, ut amare atque ex amore doleam quod noluerim Deum mihi esse omnia, fuerimque causa dolorum innocentis; deinde finem imponat abnegationi suae quae in me fuit; & tandem priores suas operationes in me restituat, quae aliis verbis ex eventu possis sic efferre: Chri-stus morte sua Dei Justitiam vindicavit, mihique acquisivit poenitentiam, resipiscentiam, & sanctitatem; sive, ut feram ejus crucem, abnegem me, & ipsum sequar; (quæ trina eodem recidunt) ut ne Deus mecum communionem habens putetur cum eo quod adhuc in impuritate maneret & sui negatione, commisceri. Et huc respexit Deus cum voluit justitiam suam non priori altero modo, quo semper miser fuissem, sed hoc posteriori, mihique salutari, vindicari.
units.tr: X. But how could the cessation of the denial of God, the love of him, the destruction of delight outside God, and holy sorrow arising from love of God and denial of myself (a good, perfect, most real thing, which is not in itself evil and to be execrated, but if it is called so, it is called so because it bears the mark of a thing to be execrated, namely sin), how, I say, could such goods be placed in me, unless he who works all things also worked these? And how could I conceive that God, in a becoming manner, would work such great goods in a rejected sinner, unless I conceived beforehand that God had solidly borne witness that my evil does not please him? The first difficulty and the first obstacle return. These greatest goods, and that very holy sorrow, I do not conceive can be placed by the will of God, disapproving of the neglect of himself in a becoming way, in an unworthy subject, unless God has beforehand borne witness to his supreme disapproval of it; and this obstacle returns continually in a circle, until there is given such a subject as has nothing in itself worthy of God's prior disapproval and displeasure, but which is most excellent and most precious, in which there was no perverse will, no denial of God, and in which God, by his love for himself, and, as a testimony of hatred toward sin, may fill it with the greatest sorrows arising from the Supreme love of God and displeasure at sin. I say, moreover, that those greatest sorrows and that subject, most precious and most excellent, must be given. For since God is distant from sin beyond what can be conceived, the thing which must be brought forward as a testimony of this ought to be memorable and remarkable beyond what can be said or conceived; and this, in my case, could not be fully done in this respect either. But since such a subject does not exist in the natural state of men, to seek the wisdom of God elsewhere is to exhibit free grace. But where there has been such an innocent subject, and such a work of God in him, what then will prevent it from becoming the goodness of God to will me well in such a way that he may bring about, both in me and in others, divine sorrows for communion with himself, as it pleases him, may cast a cessation of the denial of God upon me, and may restore the same operations which would have been before sin, though gradually and in another manner? Will it now be said that there is room for this insult, namely, that the Divine will, working these goods in a sinner, would act as if it were not alien to him who denies God, that is, to sin? Provided that he has most sufficiently cleansed and vindicated himself from this insult, by bringing about a beloved one in whom beforehand there was nothing to be reproved, grieving most greatly from Divine love on account of sins? Therefore the Justice of God, or the propriety of that will, will not prevent him from consequently placing these goods in me, namely, first, that I should love and, from love, grieve, that I had been unwilling for God to be all things to me, and had been the cause of sorrows to the innocent; then, that he should put an end to my denial of him which was in me; and finally that he should restore in me his former operations, which in other words could be expressed from the outcome thus: Christ by his death vindicated the Justice of God, and acquired for me repentance, resipiscence, and holiness; or, that I may bear his cross, deny myself, and follow him (which three things come to the same thing); so that God, having communion with me, might not be thought to mix with what still remained in impurity and in the denial of himself. And to this God looked when he willed that his justice be vindicated, not in the first way, by which I would always have been miserable, but in the latter way, salutary to me.

units.la: XI. Hisce ex naturalis conscientiæ discussione sua constat veritas juris: sunt enim meræ notitiæ communes, evidentissimæ, cuilibet ad Deum agnitum attendenti: adeoque Herberti, Deistarum, aliorumque dogma, de Justitia Dei per solam peccatoris pœnitentiam vindi-canda est plane absurdum, & ad vindicandum Deum à contumelia ine-ptum. Quod attinet ad veritatem facti, cum illa potuerit non esse (potuit enim Deus post malum admissum nolle amplius bona in peccatore operari, & suam Justitiam per peccatoris miseriam perpetuam declarare) ejus certitudo & modus executionis ex revelatione & experientia, bina eventus rerum possibilium argumenta, unice est depromenda, totaque res ex duobus hisce principiis penitius & specialius est proponenda.
units.tr: XI. From the examination of his own natural conscience the truth of the law follows: these are plain, common notions, most evident to anyone who attends to the known God. Therefore the doctrine of Herbert, of the Deists and of others, that the justice of God is to be vindicated solely by the repentance of the sinner, is plainly absurd and an inept way of vindicating God from reproach. As for the truth of the fact: since it could have been otherwise (for after the evil had been committed God could have been unwilling any longer to work good in the sinner, and could have declared his justice by the sinner's perpetual misery), its certainty and the mode of its execution must be drawn solely from revelation and experience, the two proofs of the outcome of possible things; and the whole matter must be set forth more thoroughly and more particularly from these two principles.

units.la: CAPUT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: (21) VERACITAS.
units.tr: (21) VERACITY.

units.la: §. A. I. Mendacii, fraudis, perfidiæ, &c. injustitiæ.
units.tr: §. A. I. Of lying, fraud, faithlessness, etc., of injustice.

units.la: I. INter præcedentes Spontanearum Cogitationum imperfectiones hæc etiam numeranda est, quod contingere possit, me ea de me-negaturum, quæ vera esse non modo scivero, sed & ipse voluero, pro-bavero, & promisero. Hæc injustitiæ species est, & speciali nomine Mendacium dicitur, vel potius perfidia. Si aliquid promisero, nec tamen præstitero, non potest non illic injustitia latere, vel in promisso ipso, vel in ejus denegatione. Nam si testatus fuero me optare & velle ut Deus certis circumstantiis aliquid in me operetur quod ad alios tendat (etenim id promittere est sano sensu) atque illud non placeat Deo quod per me fieri volui, equidem recte tunc violatur promissio, at id in illa injustum erat, quod non-placitum Dei sumebatur pro opere à Deo per me faciendo. Quodsi promissum fuerit de bono, atque de re Deo grata, nec tamen præstetur, injustitia est: nam quod eam rem ab ipso & à me approbatam ille per me non præstet, id inde est, quod ejus operationi restiterim: ego, inquam, qui ejus opus sum, restiti ejus operi mihi convenienti: quod satis patet ad Injustitiam esse accensendum.
units.tr: I. Among the preceding imperfections of spontaneous thoughts, this too must be counted: that it may happen that I deny things about myself which I not only know to be true but have myself willed, approved and promised. This is a species of injustice, and is called by the special name lying, or rather faithlessness. If I have promised something and yet not performed it, injustice must lie hidden there, either in the promise itself or in its denial. For if I have declared that I desire and wish that God would work in me, under certain circumstances, something that tends toward others (for to promise this is in a sound sense), and that what I wished to be done through me does not please God, then indeed the promise is rightly broken; but the injustice lay in this, that what did not please God was taken to be the work to be done by God through me. But if something good and pleasing to God was promised, and yet is not performed, there is injustice: for the fact that he does not carry out through me that thing which he and I both approve is due to this, that I have resisted his working. I, I say, who am his work, have resisted his work fitting for me; which is plain enough to be counted as injustice.

units.la: 2. Veracitas Dei in promissis. 3. Promissa verbalia & naturalia.
