units.tr: 2. The veracity of God in promises. 3. Verbal and natural promises.

units.la: II. Satis etiam patet ex dictis de Justitia Dei, hancce Injustitiam esse ab illo removendam: Cum nequeat cogitari decere Ens summum ut improbet quæ probat; aut vero mutetur. Econtra, decet constantem Deum, atque à placito suo non alienum, se promissi sui ostendere approbatorem per ejus eventum. Justitia sive decentia hæc Veracitas nuncupatur. Quare, si promiserit se, quamvis olim ab illo regi noluerim, recturum attamen singulari modo omnes cogitationes meas, sive, si gratiam mihi suam non obstante meo peccato promiserit, eam ab illo postulare queo per Justitiam suam, hoc est, veracitatem, quia nempe decet & justum est, eum non negare, sed ponere suum promissum.
units.tr: II. It is also sufficiently clear from what has been said about the justice of God that this injustice must be removed from him, since it cannot be thought fitting for the supreme Being to disapprove what he approves, or to change. On the contrary, it befits a constant God, not alien to his own purpose, to show himself the approver of his promise through its outcome. This propriety or fitness of justice is called veracity. Therefore, if he has promised that, although I once refused to be ruled by him, he will nevertheless govern all my thoughts in a singular manner; or, if he has promised me his grace notwithstanding my sin, I can ask him for it by his justice, that is, his veracity, because it is fitting and just that he should not deny but fulfil his promise.

units.la: III. Notandum inter promissa Dei, objecta hujus veracitatis, non solum debere ea reponi quæ Deus vocibus vel literis quibusdam se factu-rum significavit, sed etiam quicquid quibuscunque signis, ideis, testi-moniis ut certa objecit menti, vel per corpora, vel immediate per suas ipsius cogitationes: imo quicquid de statu rerum non modo futuro, sed & præsenti ostendit Deus menti per ideas, se habere instar promissorum. Nam omnia efficit ille, & extus ea efficit impletque quæ clare constat eum intus signare, & quasi promittere vel præmittere. Notitia hæc, Recte utenti intellectu veritas occurrit, quam Deus eo modo in Mentibus operatus est, ut de illa non possit dubitari, est quasi primum promissum. Cæteræ, quas Deus etiam Menti impressit, & ex quibus recte animadversis, infertur aliquarum rerum aut modorum existentia, ex hoc priori roborantur, nec in suspicionem falsi debent induci, quia Deus Verax est. Quod invicte & insuperabiliter voluit à Mente tanquam præsens, vel etiam futurum cognosci; id ipsum, eam sui voluntatem, non putandus est per eventum improbare & rejicere. Hæc de illo Cogitatio contumeliosa esset.
units.tr: III. It must be noted that the objects of this veracity among God's promises are not only those things which God has signified by certain words or letters that he will do, but also whatever he has presented to the mind as certain by any signs, ideas or testimonies, whether through bodies or immediately through his own thoughts. Indeed, whatever God shows to the mind through ideas concerning the state of things, not only future but also present, has the force of promises. For he produces all things, and he produces outwardly and fulfils those things which it is clear he signifies inwardly, and as it were promises or foreshadows. This notion, truth presents itself to the intellect using it rightly, which God has so wrought in minds that no doubt can be cast on it, is as it were the first promise. The others, which God has also impressed on the Mind, and from which, when rightly considered, the existence of certain things or modes is inferred, are strengthened by this first one, and ought not to be brought under suspicion of falsehood, because God is true. What he has willed to be known by the Mind, invincibly and irresistibly, as present or even future, that very will of his is not to be thought to be disapproved and rejected by the outcome. To think this of him would be a blasphemous thought.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII. (22) SANCTITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. (22) HOLINESS.

units.la: I.[?] Animæ Impuritas & Sanctitas.
units.tr: 1. Impurity and Holiness of the Soul.

units.la: I. HÆc quoque una est ex numero imperfectionum mox notata-rum, quæque ex abusu libertatis meæ oriuntur, nempe quod cogitationes meas, affectusque spontaneos totos, lubens ita deprimere possim, ut adhæream atque affigar rebus vilioribus quam ego sim; sive quam sint operationes Dei in me statui meo decentissimæ & convenientissimæ: nimirum si ad ea quæ inferioris sunt naturæ me dejiciam, aut ea ad me usque devehere coner, aut vero eorum gratia operationibus Dei in mente divinioribus injiciam moram, aut his renuntiem ut infe-rioribus, quasi ea præstarent, locum concedam: ut si, exempli causa, dedo animum & affectus divitiis metallisque, si curæ sensualis massæ mox perituræ, si vanis rumoribus cogitationibusve de me cassis & inef-ficacibus, si denique Mens quæ inter lutosa ad momentum est constitu-ta, ut probetur an Deo præ his adhærere malit, atque adeo ab his sepa-rari, nisi quatenus necessario quibusdam utendum, eaque ad Deum re-ferri possunt & debent; si, inquam, illa nihilominus istis sese immisceat divino in mente opere postposito. In istis quanta imperfectio & quan-tum culpanda! cum pessime sic confundantur quæ Deus optime separa-vit atque etiam natura distinxit. Ordinatius cælum terræ, aqua igni, pretiosa sordibus, omniaque à suis vinculis dissoluta omnibus misce-rentur, quam Mentis cogitationes luto subjiciantur, eoque occupari, penetrari & repleri velint. Quare non immerito eæ ubi hoc fit, ab impuritate, dissolutione, sordibusque, sordidæ, impuræ & dissolutæ denominantur. Uti è contra, actus quibus quæque res seponitur cum iis ejusdem status, in suo gradu & usu recte disponi & sanciri censentur, & à puritate atque sanctitate recte nomina sortiuntur: siquidem voces Sanc-titatis, sancti, & similes, designent statum sive commercium rei cum iis rebus quæ non sunt ea indignæ.
units.tr: I. This too is one of the imperfections noted above, and it arises from the abuse of my freedom: namely, that I can willingly press down all my thoughts and my spontaneous affections, so that I cling to and fasten myself upon things viler than I am, or than the operations of God in me are fittingly and suitably for my state. That is, if I cast myself down to those things which belong to a lower nature, or try to drag them up to myself, or if for their sake I place a hindrance in the way of God's operations in the divine mind, or give them room by renouncing these as lower, as if those lower things were of greater worth. For example: if I give my mind and affections to riches and metals; to the care of a sensual mass that will soon perish; to vain rumours and to thoughts about myself that are empty and ineffective; or finally, if the mind, which has been placed among muddy things for a moment, so that it may be tested whether it prefers to cling to God rather than to these, and so be separated from them (except insofar as some of these must be used, and can and ought to be referred to God), nevertheless mingles itself with these, setting aside the divine work in the mind. In these things, how great is the imperfection, and how much to be blamed! For things which God has most excellently separated, and nature has distinguished, are so terribly confused. Heaven would sooner be mixed with earth, water with fire, precious things with filth, and all things loosed from their bonds would be mingled together, than the thoughts of the mind be subjected to mud and wish to be occupied, penetrated and filled with it. Therefore, not without reason, those thoughts where this happens are called foul, impure and dissolute, from impurity, dissolution and filth. On the contrary, acts by which each thing is set apart from those of a different state, and are rightly ordered and sanctioned in their own degree and use, are judged to be pure, and rightly receive their names from purity and holiness; for the words holiness, holy, and similar terms signify the state or relation of a thing with those things which are not unworthy of it.

units.la: 2. 3. 4. Dei Sanctitas, quæ? Demonstratur. Declaratur in Creaturis viis oppositis. Ad justitiam referenda.
units.tr: 2. 3. 4. What God's Holiness is; it is shown. It is declared in creatures by opposite ways. It is to be referred to justice.

units.la: II. Hæcce me juvant ut concipiam quid per Attributum Sanctitatis Deo relatum significari intelligendum sit. Nempe facile adverto nil aliud eo significari posse, nisi quod Deus sit ab omni eo separatus quod vile est, vel indignum ipsius Natura, aut ejus placito, aut ejus opere: imo ab omni eo quod plane non resolvitur in ipsum. Nam omne quod est non-Deus est Deo indignum. Et quamvis opus Dei non sit ipse Deus, Deus tamen in illo ad se recurrit, estque illic omnia: ideo est opus Dei, quia Deus illic videt se ipsum volentem, operantem, omnia. Deus à se abest nunquam, in re, in placito, in opere ullo; omnia ab illo, per illum, ad illum; à quovis alio principio, motivo, scopo, actione, re, alienus est; nulla re indiget; omne quod plane ab eo est alienum, & cujus omnia non resolvuntur in Deum unum, excludit. Ergo si vult aliquid, vult se ipsum, vult suum placitum, sui repræsentationem in illa re: vult ipse sibi occurrere. Is ipse in se per adorandam generationem & sui secum communionem se ipsum quærit: Is idem extra se in rerum umbratilem productionem, & sui cum illis communionem, se ipsum quoque quærit, sive id quærit, quod ipsum in principio, medio, fine, omnibus, referens, tandem in se solum, quem unice intendit, omne & totum resolvatur. Alioqui nil Deo dignum quocum communicet invenire est.
units.tr: II. These things help me to conceive what must be understood to be signified by the attribute of holiness, as ascribed to God. Namely, I readily perceive that nothing else can be signified by it than that God is separated from everything that is vile, or unworthy of his nature, or of his pleasure, or of his work; indeed, from everything that is not wholly resolved into himself. For everything that is not God is unworthy of God. And although the work of God is not God himself, yet God returns to himself in it, and is there all things: it is therefore a work of God, because God there sees himself willing, working, and all things. God is never absent from himself, in essence, in purpose, or in any work; all things are from him, through him, and to him; he is alien to every other principle, motive, aim, action or thing; he needs nothing; he excludes everything which is wholly alien to him, and into which not all things are resolved into the one God. Therefore, if he wills anything, he wills himself, wills his own pleasure, his own representation in that thing: he wills to meet himself. He seeks himself within himself, through his adorable generation and communion of himself with himself; he seeks himself also outside himself, in the shadowy production of things, and in his communion with them; or he seeks that which, referring all things in beginning, middle and end, is at last resolved entirely into himself alone, whom he alone intends. Otherwise, it is impossible to find anything worthy of God with which he might communicate.

units.la: III. Atque hæc est Dei Sanctitas Deo essentialis & in eo concipienda, facillime quidem si nullas creaturas existere supponamus; evidenter quoque positis creaturis. Nam quicquid fit, Conceptus Entis perfectissimi, sufficientissimi, quod sibi est omnia, est conceptus entis nil præter se vel quærere, vel invenire potentis quod non sit ipse vel ipsius. Ergo existente, ut sic dicam, malo, quod à Deo non est, nec Deum refert, sed potius eum, quantum in se est, negat, ostendet Deus se ab eo, omnique impuritate, esse quammaxime alienum, tum quos amat, sive in quibus sui ipsius amorem & repræsentationem, vel se ipsum, amat, à malo præservando; tum deferendo & puniendo eos qui id voluerint & habuerint. Sicque in utrisque Sanctus declarabitur viis oppositis.
units.tr: III. And this is God's holiness, essential to God and to be conceived in him: most easily indeed if we suppose that no creatures exist; and evidently also, creatures being posited. For whatever is done, the concept of a most perfect and self-sufficient Being, who is all things to himself, is the concept of a Being able to seek or find nothing beyond himself that is not himself or of himself. Therefore, if evil exists, so to speak, which is not from God and does not refer to God, but rather, as far as it is in itself, denies him, God will show himself to be as far as possible removed from it and from all impurity: both by preserving from evil those whom he loves, that is, in whom he loves his own love and representation, or himself; and by forsaking and punishing those who have willed and held it. And thus he will be declared holy, in both respects, by opposite ways.

units.la: IV. Ex his patescit, Sanctitatem Dei ad ejus Justitiam esse referendam: nec conceptum quem de Sanctitate habemus à conceptu de Justitia differre, nisi quod conceptus Sanctitatis habeatur cum oppositione specialiori ad specialiorem peccati notionem, Justitiae vero juxta cum oppositione generaliori ad quodcunque indecens quod fingi possit. Sed de hisce disceptare haud justum esset.
units.tr: IV. From these things it is plain that God's holiness is to be referred to his justice: nor does the concept we have of holiness differ from the concept of justice, except that the concept of holiness is held in a more specific opposition to the more specific notion of sin, whereas justice is in a more general opposition to whatever unbecoming thing can be imagined. But it would not be right to dispute about these matters here.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV. (23) INFINITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. (23) INFINITY.

units.la: 1. Mens augmenti capax est limitata, non habito respectu ad spatia.
units.tr: 1. The mind is capable of limited increase, without regard to spaces.

units.la: I. QUas hactenus de Cogitatione mea observationes habui, utcunque particulariores, recolens, redeo ad generaliores, quibus hasce concludam animadversiones, quarum prima numero vicesimo secundo recensita est, nullas in me perfectiones esse quae novos augmenti gradus, eosque indefinitos, recipere non possint, hoc est, quae magis magisque perfectae non possint fieri. Non equidem concipio eas magis prope essentiam Dei quam sint, vel, absolute loquendo, quam ipsum etiam nihil sit, posse accedere, nam infinite ab hac distant omnia: Sed tamen eam magis minusve adumbrare vel repraesentare pro placito Dei possunt. Quare inde concludo Cogitationis meae perfectiones limitibus quibusdam circumscribi, siquidem augmentum nil aliud sit quam rei limitatae, sive ejus limitum, ulterior extensio. Nec tamen hic loquor de extensione spatiosa, spatiorumque limitibus: stultum esset ea menti, ejusque cognitioni, judiciis, amori, &c. tribuere; Sed, ut dictum, de limitibus perfectionum sive realitatum naturae cogitationis meae convenientium. Nil hic observo quod non antea passim cum evidentia viderim.
units.tr: I. Recalling the observations I have so far made concerning my thought, however particular they are, I return to the more general ones, by which I shall conclude these remarks. The first of them was listed as number twenty-two: that there are in me no perfections which cannot receive new degrees of increase, and those indefinite, that is, which cannot be made more and more perfect. I do not indeed conceive that they can come nearer to the essence of God than they are, or (speaking absolutely) that they can approach it at all, since all things are infinitely distant from it. Yet they can, by the pleasure of God, shadow it forth or represent it more or less. Hence I conclude that the perfections of my thought are circumscribed by certain limits, since increase is nothing other than the further extension of a limited thing, or of its limits. Nor do I here speak of spatial extension and the limits of spaces: it would be foolish to attribute these to the mind and its knowledge, judgments, love, etc. But, as I said, I speak of the limits of the perfections or realities which belong to the nature of my thought. I observe nothing here that I have not often seen before with evidence.

units.la: 2. Deus positive Infinitus.
units.tr: 2. God is positively Infinite.

units.la: 3. Non spatii extensione, sed Cogitationis perfectione.
units.tr: 3. Not by extension of space, but by perfection of thought.

units.la: 4. Infinitum sufficienter concipitur.
units.tr: 4. The infinite is sufficiently conceived.

units.la: 5. De repraesentatione infiniti.
units.tr: 5. On the representation of the infinite.

units.la: 6. Quae requirit Deum existentem.
units.tr: 6. What requires God to exist.

units.la: II. De Deo non possum similes habere conceptus, in cujus quippe idea nullae sunt perfectiones quae prorsus completae non sint, atque infinitae habendae positivo modo, hoc est, non tantum quoniam nulli de eis limites sunt noti, sed etiam quod eas nullos habere, nec quidem pos-se habere, verum plenissimam possidere abundantiam quæ ab homini-bus & à Deo concipi possit, queque nulli additamento intelligibili locum relinquat, positivis rationibus convincamur. Et hoc ipsum sine ratiocinatione in conceptu Entis summi, perfectissimi, Meræ Cogitatio-nis, immediate habetur.
units.tr: II. Concerning God I cannot have similar concepts, since in his idea there are no perfections which are not wholly complete, and which must be held infinite in a positive way: that is, not only because no limits of them are known to us, but because we are convinced by positive reasons that they have no limits, nor indeed can have any, but possess a most full abundance which can be conceived by men and by God, and which leaves no room for any intelligible addition. This very thing is had immediately, without reasoning, in the concept of the supreme and most perfect Being, of pure Thought.

units.la: III. Atque hoc est quod per Divinam Infinitatem intelligendum venit, non vero crassum aliquod phantasma quale in scholis sæpius imaginati sunt, Infinitatem videlicet spatiosæ extensionis, quam, ad modum Divinæ præsentiæ explicandum, absurde protruserunt, necnon tanquam rem veritatis inconcussæ in medium attulerunt ut aliquid repelle-rent quod suæ fictioni videbatur obstare. Nempe cum à nonnullis dictum fuisset mundi extensionem ita esse concipiendam ut nulli limites ei præscribantur, objecerunt illi, sic mundo tribui Infinitatem, quæ tamen soli Deo competat, poni absurde mundum esse infinitum, cum solus Deus sit talis, quem negare est si alius infinitus dicatur. En cogitationes Infinitatem Dei valde decentes! Quid enim? An Immensitas Divina eadem est quæ Infinitas spatiosæ extensionis, qualem isti mundo tribui (etsi, non infinitus, sed indefinitus ab aliis dicatur,) conque-runtur? Id certe cogitant, siquidem conquerantur mundo tribui quod soli Deo proprium est, dum putant mundum statui infinite extensum. Absurda hæc de Deo figmenta alibi profligata sunt. Falsum est, mundo, quamvis extensione infinitus diceretur (qui non dicitur, ut neque hac de re determinate judicari potest) tribui Infinitatem Dei. Mundi Infinitas, si qua esset, esset natura ab Infinitate Divina diversissimæ, multas quippe imperfectiones involvens, quales in extensione omni reperiri non ignorat ullus, adeoque esset infinitas non absoluta, sed aliquo respectu, eoque finitæ perfectionis, extensionis nempe. Cum econtra, Divina Infinitas absoluta sit, omnes Imperfectiones excludat, quippe quæ sit Infinitas Cogitationis, Infinitas Intelligentiæ, Infinitas Dominii, Bonitatis, Potentiæ, Sapientiæ, Constantiæ, & uno verbo, Omnium & Singulorum Attributorum, quorum quodlibet infinitum dicitur, quia nulla realitas & perfectio ab illo abest, sed unumquodque & omnia sunt una & eadem maxima & perfectissima realitas. Quomo-do ad Simplicitatem reducimur. Hæc igitur est vera, solique Deo pro-pria Infinitas: de qua memorabilia Augustini in Confessionibus {a} ver-ba exstant inter alia, quæ non possum non huc referre. Anima mea fe-cerat sibi Deum per infinita spatia locorum omnium, & cum putaverat esse Te, & eum collocaverat in corde suo, & facta erat rursus templum idoli sui abominandum tibi. Sed postea quam fovisti caput nescientis, & clausisti oculos meos ne viderent vanitatem, cessavi de me paululum, & consopita est insania mea. Et evigilavi in Te, & vidi Te infinitum aliter, & visus iste non à carne trahebatur.
units.tr: III. And this is what is to be understood by the divine Infinity, not some crude phantom such as the schools have often imagined: namely, the infinity of spatial extension, which they absurdly thrust forward to explain the divine presence, and also brought forward as a matter of unshakable truth, in order to repel something which seemed to stand in the way of their fiction. For when some had said that the extension of the world must be conceived so that no limits are prescribed to it, they objected that in this way infinity is attributed to the world, which nevertheless belongs to God alone; it is absurd to posit the world as infinite, since God alone is such, and to say that another is infinite is to deny him. Behold thoughts very fitting for the infinity of God! For what? Is the divine immensity the same as the infinity of spatial extension, such as they complain is attributed to this world (although it is said by others not to be infinite but indefinite)? Surely they think this, if they complain that what belongs to God alone is attributed to the world, while they suppose the world is set up as infinitely extended. These absurd fictions about God have been refuted elsewhere. It is false that the infinity of God is attributed to the world, even if it were said to be infinite in extension (which it is not said to be, nor can it be determinately judged in this matter). The infinity of the world, if it had any, would be a nature most unlike the divine infinity, since it would involve many imperfections, such as everyone knows are to be found in every extension; and so it would be an infinity not absolute but in some respect, and of a finite perfection, namely that of extension. On the contrary, the divine infinity is absolute and excludes all imperfections, being the infinity of Thought, the infinity of Understanding, the infinity of Dominion, of Goodness, of Power, of Wisdom, of Constancy, and in a word, of all and each of the Attributes, each of which is called infinite because no reality or perfection is absent from it, but each and all are one and the same most great and most perfect reality. Thus we are led back to Simplicity. This, then, is the true infinity, and the one proper to God alone: concerning which there are, among other things, memorable words of Augustine in the Confessions, which I cannot help citing here. My soul had made for itself a God through the infinite spaces of all places, and when it had thought that you were such, and had placed him in its heart, it had again become a temple of its idol, abominable to you. But after you warmed my head, which did not know, and closed my eyes lest they should see vanity, I ceased a little from myself, and my madness was lulled to sleep. And I awoke in you, and I saw you infinite in another way, and that sight was not drawn from the flesh.

units.la: IV. Nonnulli hic difficultates excitare tentarunt, ubi tamen nullae sunt, cum nil conceptu sit facilius quam infinitum, utpote quod nos ponat extra periculum & metum ei tribuendi plus quam habeat, quod nullis limitibus obscuretur perceptuque difficilius reddatur, denique omnes cogitationes simplicius cum acquiescentia quam ullum aliud quid impleat. Nihilominus tamen dicunt de eo absurde loqui, eo quod non capiatur ab intellectu nostro, adeoque esse verba sine mente: aut vero si capi dicatur, id esse contra notionem Infiniti ut capiatur à finito. Respondeo, quamvis non capiatur, non inde sequi nullos plane de eo sermones esse habendos, sed tantum non debere de eo verba fieri veluti de re quae caperetur aut capi posset. Deinde advertendum est, aliud esse cognitione adaequata Infinitum comprehendere, aliud vero concipere Infinitum inadaequate & obscure quidem respectu cognitionis quam id ipsum de se habet, attamen satis clare & sufficienter ad hoc, ut simus certi in illo esse complementum omnium perfectionum. Priori assertio-ne limitibus caperetur Infinitum, nempe, si assereretur, Mentem creatam posse habere ejus conceptum ita exactum & plenum, videlicet concep-tum Potentiae infinitae, Sapientiae infinitae, & sic de caeteris, quem-admodum ipsum de se habet Infinitum. Sed ab hac absurditate declina-tur dum in sensu posteriore affirmatur, humanam Mentem sat noscere Divinam Cogitationem ut judicet eam carere omni imperfectione, sive, omni perfectione esse praeditam, hoc est, infinitam esse; sufficienter concipere ejus Potentiam, ut, etsi de objectis nil determinare possit, agnoscat tamen ei nil resistere posse, & ita de caeteris quae in Deo animadverti possunt, quorum notitiae in nobis satis sunt claerae ut judicemus ea esse in Deo realissima, simplicissima, adeoque Infinita. Quod homines istos decepit duplex phantasma fuit; primo attenderunt ad infinitatem spatii, secundo ne quidem intellectu, sed imaginatione in hoc usi sunt: & cum imaginari non potuerint (ut nec vere potest) infinitum extensione, hoc perperam ad Dei conceptum applicuerunt. Num igitur profitebuntur se non cognoscere Deum sine defectibus esse? sed hoc est concipere Deum Infinitum.
units.tr: IV. Some have here tried to raise difficulties, where there are none, since nothing is easier to conceive than the infinite, inasmuch as it places us beyond danger and fear of attributing to it more than it has, and it is not obscured by any limits, and it is made no more difficult to perceive; finally, it fills all thoughts more simply, with acquiescence, than anything else. Nevertheless they say that to speak of it is absurd, because it is not grasped by our intellect, and so these are words without mind; or, if it is said to be grasped, that this is contrary to the notion of the infinite, that it should be grasped by the finite. I answer: although it is not grasped, it does not follow that there should be no discourse about it at all, but only that words should not be spoken about it as about a thing which is or could be grasped. Next it must be noted that it is one thing to comprehend the infinite by adequate knowledge, and another to conceive the infinite inadequately and obscurely, indeed with respect to the knowledge which it has of itself, yet clearly enough and sufficiently for us to be certain that in it is the completion of all perfections. By the first assertion the infinite would be grasped within limits, namely, if it were asserted that a created mind can have its concept so exact and full, that is, the concept of infinite power, infinite wisdom, and so on for the rest, as the infinite has of itself. But this absurdity is avoided when it is affirmed in the latter sense that the human mind knows the divine thought well enough to judge that it lacks every imperfection, or, in other words, is endowed with every perfection, that is, is infinite; that it conceives his power sufficiently to acknowledge that, although it can determine nothing about objects, nothing can resist him; and so on for the rest of what can be observed in God, of which our knowledge is clear enough for us to judge that they are in God most real, most simple, and therefore infinite. What deceived these men was a twofold phantasm: first, they attended to the infinity of space; second, they used not the intellect but the imagination in this matter; and since they could not imagine the infinite by extension (as indeed it truly cannot be), they wrongly applied this to the concept of God. Will they then profess that they do not know God to be without defects? But this is to conceive God as infinite.

units.la: V. Quaeritur à nonnullis, An partem infiniti concipiam, an vero totum infinitum? Respondeo, τὸ [?] infinitum esse sensu allato, ut & simplicissimum esse, negat partes quascunque: adeoque absurde quaeritur, An partem infiniti concipiam? Concipiam-ne partem ubi est de essentia ejusmodi conceptus nullas concipere partes? An igitur, inquies, totum concipis infinitum? An infinitum, ejus ratio & forma, infinitas, est in tuo intellectu, in conceptu, in cogitatione? Dico, nec infinitum ipsum, neque infinitas, sunt in mea cogitatione & cognitione, ut ne-que etiam ullum aliud Dei attributum, alioqui cogitatio sive cognitio mea esset Deus: Sed in illa sunt talia delineamenta, tales tabulae, umbratilesque designationes, è quibus percipio infinitum existere Deum. neque est necesse ut delineamenta ista in se possideant easdem perfectiones ejus quod repraesentant, alioque non jam tabulae, sed originale ipsum forent; ut neque dedecet infinitatem Divinam eo modo repraesentari qui non sit perfectissimus: Sed contra, eam non deceret perfectissime repraesentari per rem à se ipsa diversam, siquidem praeter Deum sic poneretur aliquid perfectissimi, hoc est, negaretur Deus, cum duo perfectissima se tollant, ut visum est ubi de Unitate. Neque est quod dicas, hic quaeri de infinito repraesentando perfectissime objectivo modo, non autem subjectivo, quae duo non videntur sese tollere in rebus diversis: Nam hoc ultimum falsum est. Etenim quando agitur de rebus Cogitantibus, si dixero, haec Cogitatio repraesentat perfectissime hanc Cogitationem perfectissimam & infinitam, idem est ac si dicerem, Haec Cogitatio habet Cogitationem perfectissimam & infinitam perfectissime, sive illam perfectissime cogitat, aut est perfectissime cogitans, hoc est, ipsamet est cogitatio infinita & perfectissima. Adeoque dari nequit perfecte objectiva repraesentatio sive imago infiniti, nisi in subjecto infinito. hinc est quod Filius Dei, imago sive repraesentatio objectiva Dei, fit agnoscendus Deus subjective, quia perfectissima ejus imago est. Non ita de mente nostra, in qua praeter umbras, mirabiles tamen, nil absolute perfecti exstat.
units.tr: V. Some ask whether I conceive a part of the infinite, or rather the whole infinite? I answer: the infinite, in the sense stated, is also most simple, and denies any parts whatever; therefore it is absurd to ask, "Do I conceive a part of the infinite?" Do I conceive a part where it is of the essence of such a concept to conceive no parts? Will you then say, "Do you conceive the whole infinite?" Is the infinite itself, its reason and form, infinity, in your intellect, in your concept, in your thought? I say that neither the infinite itself nor infinity is in my thought and knowledge, just as no other attribute of God is, otherwise my thought or knowledge would be God. But in it there are such outlines, such tablets and shadowy designs, from which I perceive that the infinite God exists. Nor is it necessary that these outlines possess in themselves the same perfections of that which they represent; otherwise they would no longer be tablets but the original itself. Nor does it unbecome the divine infinity to be represented in a way that is not most perfect. But, on the contrary, it would not befit it to be represented most perfectly by a thing different from itself, since in that case something most perfect would be posited besides God, that is, God would be denied, as two most perfect things cancel each other out, as was seen when we treated of Unity. Nor is there reason for you to say that here we are asking about representing the infinite most perfectly in an objective way, and not in a subjective way, which two do not seem to cancel each other out in different things: for this last is false. For when we are dealing with thinking things, if I say, "This thought represents most perfectly this most perfect and infinite thought," it is the same as if I said, "This thought has most perfectly a most perfect and infinite thought," or that it most perfectly thinks it, or is most perfectly thinking, that is, is itself an infinite and most perfect thought. Hence a perfectly objective representation or image of the infinite cannot exist except in an infinite subject. Hence it is that the Son of God, the image or objective representation of God, is to be acknowledged as God subjectively, because he is his most perfect image. It is not so with our mind, in which, besides shadows, yet wonderful ones, nothing absolutely perfect exists.

units.la: VI. Mirabiles inquam, nam certe fatendum est hic aliquid esse mi-rabile, & omnino, quicquid explicetur, stupendum: nempe a re mi-nimula, & fere nulla, repraesentari infinitum, qualicunque modo id fiat, attamen modo infinitum non dedecenti. Quomodo res ulla (cogitatio mea) possit se ipsam, conditionem naturae suae, excedere? repraesentationes, sive cogitationis variationes & modos habere excellentiores quam sua sit natura? An potest modificatio ulla excedere naturam substantiae suae? An potest ferrum, tale manens, modificationes quæ in corpore humano sunt, admittere, aut aqua modos auri sufci-pere, aut pulvis instar massæ ingentissimæ modificari? Qui igitur Cogitatio finita habebit cogitationem sive modum cogitandi natura sua excellentiorem? Certe mirabilis & incomprehensibilis hujus effectus causa extra meam naturam assignanda est plane mirabilis, stupenda, extra ordinem rerum creatarum, incomprehensibilis, hoc est, existens Deus, qui, ut Sanctus, se ipsum quærens, vult se etiam ut infinitum & incomprehensibilem depictum invenire; quique, ut justus, operari vult modo Ens Infinitum & incomprehensibile decenti, adeoque modo qui non capi possit & sit maxime mirabilis. Si hæc mirabilia & in impiis operetur Deus, (hi enim ideam hancce Dei habent) quæ demum stupenda illa erunt quæ in sanctis ab illo posita, magisque in posterum ponenda, nullam cum illis, quæ in exteris sunt, patientur comparationem?
units.tr: VI. Wonderful, I say; for certainly it must be admitted that there is something marvellous here, and altogether stupendous, however it is explained: that the infinite should be represented by a thing very small, and almost nothing, in whatever manner this happens, provided only that it is a manner not unworthy of the infinite. How can any thing (my thought) exceed itself, exceed the condition of its own nature? How can it have representations, that is, variations and modes of thinking, more excellent than its own nature is? Or can any modification exceed the nature of its own substance? Can iron, remaining iron, admit the modifications that are in the human body, or water take on the properties of gold, or dust be modified like a very great mass? How then will a finite thought have a thought, or mode of thinking, more excellent than its own nature? Surely the cause of this wonderful and incomprehensible effect must be assigned outside my nature: it must be plainly wonderful, stupendous, beyond the order of created things, incomprehensible; that is, God existing, who, as holy, seeking himself, wills also to be found depicted as infinite and incomprehensible; and who, as just, wills to work in a manner fitting an infinite and incomprehensible Being, and so in a manner that cannot be grasped and is most wonderful. If God works these wonders even in the impious (for these have this idea of God), what then will those stupendous works be which he has placed in the saints, and which he will place in them more and more in time to come, which will suffer no comparison with those that are found in outsiders?

units.la: CAPUT XXV. (24) IMMORTALITAS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. (24) IMMORTALITY.

units.la: I. Anima, si Deus vellet, ad nihilum devenire posset. 2. Ex quibus demonstranda sit animæ immortalitas. 3. Mortis significationes generaliores. Anima non moritur ut corpus. 4. Ea quadruplici sensu mortalis, imo, mortua dici potest. 5. De modis Mentis, an cessaturi? De substantia Mentis quæstio præcipua, Num Deo placuerit eam tantum durare donec corpus dissolvatur? 6. Id sine revelatione solvi potest. 7. Corporis menti uniti dissolutio non infert Mentis annihilationem. 8. Nodus præcipuus de Animæ immortalitate. Solvitur eadem de causa qua allegabatur. 9. Animæ immortalitatis demonstrationes primariæ ex Dei attributis. 10. Ex Justitia. 11. Ex Constantia. 12. Ex Sapientia. 13. Ex vindicativa Justitia. 14. Ex Sanctitate. 15. 16. Ex veracitate. 17. 18. 19. 20. De statu Animarum post mortem.
units.tr: I. The soul, if God willed, could come to nothing. 2. From these points the immortality of the soul is to be demonstrated. 3. More general senses of death. The soul does not die as the body does. 4. In four senses it can be called mortal, or even dead. 5. Do the modes of the Mind cease? The chief question concerns the substance of the Mind: did God will that it should endure only until the body is dissolved? 6. This can be resolved without revelation. 7. The dissolution of the body united to the mind does not entail the annihilation of the Mind. 8. The chief knot concerning the immortality of the soul. It is solved by the same cause by which it was alleged. 9. The primary demonstrations of the immortality of the soul from the attributes of God. 10. From justice. 11. From constancy. 12. From wisdom. 13. From vindictive justice. 14. From holiness. 15. 16. From truthfulness. 17. 18. 19. 20. On the state of souls after death.

units.la: Non modo gradus possibiles in mei augmentum percipio, verum etiam in mei decrementum, ita ut realitatis meæ qualiscunque gradus vel quidam, vel omnes, paulatim, vel etiam simul, possint diminuere ad ipsum usque nihil, ut Cogitatio, sive Mens mea, in absolutum nihil, quale olim fuit, evanescat. Nolim equidem asserere Mentem in hoc rerum statu perituram esse, sive mortalem esse: dico tantum me percipere, quod si Deo placuisset eam cum hac conditione creare ut ad certum tempus existeret, postea vero cessaret esse, id fuisset futurum. Etenim, cum ego non sim opus mei, non pendet à me ut plus vel minus in me sit existentiæ quam vellem, sed qualia meo Fictori placuit de hocce statuere sunt mihi expectanda: quæ quidem, si aliter ac nunc voluisset, per breve stetissent tempus; perpetua tamen non possunt non esse, quatenus quod Deo placuit, non potest non ad eum modum eventum sortiri, quem de placito suo circa durationem mentis imperituram evidentissime ipsis Mentibus testatus est.
units.tr: I perceive not only possible degrees of increase in myself, but also of decrease, so that the degrees of whatever reality I have, some or all, could gradually, or even at once, diminish to absolutely nothing, so that my thought, or my Mind, would vanish into absolute nothing, as it once was. I would certainly not wish to assert that the Mind will perish in this state of things, or that it is mortal: I say only that I perceive that if it had pleased God to create it with this condition, that it should exist for a certain time and afterwards cease to be, that would have come to pass. For since I am not my own work, it does not depend on me whether I have more or less existence in me than I would wish; rather, what kind of thing it pleased my Maker to decide concerning this is what I must await. Indeed, had He willed otherwise than He does now, they would have stood only for a brief time; yet they cannot but be perpetual, inasmuch as what has pleased God cannot but obtain an outcome in the manner in which He most evidently attested to the Minds themselves, by His good pleasure, that the Mind is to be imperishable.

units.la: II. Non forte ludetur opera, si coner hic inquirere & brevibus exponere rationes è quibus Mentis humanæ Immortalitas evincatur. Eæ autem ex consideratione naturæ Mentis, quæ ipsa Cogitatio est, & quorumdam Dei attributorum sunt deducendæ. Verum, & ratio habenda est vocis Mors sive mortalis, quæ plures significationes admittit. Et sic perspicue habebitur quicquid hac de re est concludendum.
units.tr: II. It may not be idle labour if I attempt here to inquire into, and briefly set out, the reasons by which the immortality of the human Mind is proved. These are to be deduced from a consideration of the nature of the Mind, which is thought itself, and from certain attributes of God. But the meaning of the word Death, or mortal, which admits of several senses, must also be taken into account. And thus what is to be concluded in this matter will be clearly seen.

units.la: III. Mors in genere, sensu simpliciori, tanquam aliqua cessatio intelligitur, atque diminutio existentiæ; & referri potest vel ad substantiam, vel ad ejus modos; ad eoque, ad extensam substantiam ejusve modos, vel ad cogitantem substantiam, aut modos ejus: quæ quadruplicem mortis significationem pariunt, quarum quælibet forte subdivisionibus plurimis, quas omitto, multiplicari potest. (De composito ex pluribus substantiis, quarum separatio etiam mors dicitur, non opus est ut hic agatur.) Jam, quoniam substantia extensa cum ejus modis, à Mente ejusque modis cogitandi realiter est distincta, quis non videt nullum superesse locum huic dubitationi vel quæstioni, An mens sit mortalis eo sensu quo corpus mortale est? Equidem nullam ullius corpusculi substantiam sive extensionem annihilari constat: Sed quamvis supponeretur, omne corpus esse mortale quoad substantiam suam, hoc est, omne extensum aliquando cessaturum, quid hoc ad mentem? An illa quoque hoc ipso eo sensu moreretur, hoc est, desineret esse extensa? Absurdum. Quomodo illa cessabit id esse quod ab illa alienum semper fuit? Ita etiam de morte quæ modos corporis certos qui ante aderant cessare facit, est judicandum. Cum corpora illa, quæ generari proprie dicuntur, in particulas resolvuntur, quæ alias figuras, alios motus, aliam structuram habent quam antea, cum eorum organa corruunt, partes seu sensibiles, sive insensibiles, separantur, disperguntur in auras tenues, miscentur cum terra, cum aquis, quibuscum alia, vapores, lutum, gramen, infecta, &c. componunt; tunc mori dicuntur, quia modi priores, quibus omnia ista erant coagmentata & sustentata in uno Systemate, cessant. An per hoc ipsum, & hoc sensu Mens erit mortalis, sive an depositura est priores quas habuerit figuras, motus, particularum coagmentationem, situm, & per partes aliis mo-dis figuratas, motas, dispositas, cum aëre vel aqua vel terra miscebi-tur, atque cum illis quædam corpora componet? Quam inepte de hoc quæreretur, num Mens sit depositura modos quos habuit nunquam, nec per naturam suam habere potest! Opusne est ut dicatur expresse, non esse Mentem mortalem eo sensu quo corpus mortale dicitur; & hoc argumentum tanquam egregium aliquod inventum, & valde memorabile, commendare? Equidem id argumenti genus necessarium red-diderunt crassissima eorum præjudicia, qui Mentes instar corporum, aut tenuis portionis aëreæ, aut ignis, sunt imaginati. Sed suffecisset il-lis ostensa mentis à corpore realis differentia, qua posita, non videtur opus monere, unum alterius modos non posse deponere, hoc est, eo sensu mori.
units.tr: III. Death in general, in its simpler sense, is understood as some cessation and diminution of existence; and it can be referred either to a substance or to its modes; and so, either to an extended substance or its modes, or to a thinking substance or its modes: which yields a fourfold meaning of death, each of which can perhaps be multiplied by very many subdivisions, which I omit. (There is no need to treat here of a composite of several substances, whose separation is also called death.) Now, since the extended substance with its modes is really distinct from the Mind and its modes of thinking, who does not see that there is no room left for this doubt or question: whether the mind is mortal in the sense in which the body is mortal? Indeed, it is agreed that the substance or extension of no little corpuscle is annihilated. But even if it were supposed that every body is mortal as to its substance, that is, that every extended thing will at some time cease, what has this to do with the mind? Would it too, in this very same sense, die, that is, cease to be extended? Absurd. How will that cease to be what has always been alien to it? The same judgment must be made of death, which causes certain modes of the body that were previously present to cease. When those bodies which are properly said to be generated are resolved into particles, which have other figures, other motions, another structure than before, when their organs collapse, their parts, whether sensible or insensible, are separated and scattered into thin air, mixed with earth, with waters, with which they compose other things: vapours, mud, grass, infusions, and so on; then they are said to die, because the former modes by which all those things were joined and sustained in one system cease. Will the Mind, by this very fact, and in this sense, be mortal, or will it lay down the former figures, motions, arrangement of particles, situation it had, and, its parts being figured, moved and disposed in other ways, be mixed with air or water or earth and compose certain bodies with them? How foolishly would one ask whether the Mind is going to lay down modes which it never had and cannot by its nature have! Is there any need to say expressly that the Mind is not mortal in the sense in which a body is called mortal, and to commend this argument as some outstanding and very memorable discovery? Indeed, the crassest prejudices of those who have imagined Minds to be like bodies, or like a thin portion of air or of fire, have made this kind of argument necessary. But it would have sufficed for them to be shown the real difference of the mind from the body; once this is granted, there seems no need to warn that the one cannot lay down the modes of the other, that is, cannot die in that sense.

units.la: IV. Sed si ad eam mortis significationem veniamus quæ ad mentem relata, denotet quæri, An ejus cogitandi modi quidam vel omnes, vel ipsa Cogitatio, sive Mentis substantia, existere cessatura sint? jam ad modum difficultatis propius accedetur, etsi non sit par in istis omnibus difficultas. Nam quantum ad modos mentis quosdam, cum non dubium sit quin nonnulli sint in mente cessaturi, & quotidie ad longissi-mam moram, imo nonnunquam ad perpetuum cessent, non dubitan-dum est quin mens mortalis dici queat eatenus, istorum quorumdam respectu. Itaque Mens mortalis, imo mortua dici potest, quatenus v. g. omnes cogitandi modos de rebus terrestribus, vilibus, & sordidis depositit: quæ sanctorum mors est & vere grata Deo. Mors itidem omni menti à corpore separatæ tribui potest, quatenus modis cogitandi qui fiunt per sensus externos, fame, siti, dolore corporeo, voluptate, quæ illa ex occasione corporis percipiebat, spoliatur. Etiam nil prohi-bet cum mens destituta est modis cogitandi nobilissimis & excellentissi-mis, dotibus & perfectionibus suis maximis, contemplatione & amore Dei, eam appellare mortuam, & quidem majori jure quam corpus egre-giis suis modis privatum, inepta & inutilis moles, putidumque cada-ver redditum, dicitur mortuum. Hæc mors spiritualis & moralis dicitur, de qua sæpe sacri agunt Authores. Denique cum mens omnibus jucundis, ex quacunque occasione provenerint, cogitandi modis exuta est omnino, quibus atri, horrendi, durandi, nulla lenitate nec spe inter-mixti, succedunt, etiam mortem subire dicitur. Sed jam de his omnibus quaestio non fit praecipue.
units.tr: IV. But if we come to that meaning of death which, when related to the mind, signifies the question whether some or all of its modes of thinking, or thought itself, that is, the substance of the Mind, are going to cease to exist, then we come closer to the nature of the difficulty, though the difficulty is not equal in all these cases. For as to certain modes of the mind, since there is no doubt that some will cease in the mind, and daily cease for a very long delay, and sometimes cease altogether, there is no doubt that the mind can be called mortal to that extent, with respect to these certain modes. And so the Mind can be called mortal, or even dead, insofar as, for example, it lays aside all modes of thinking about earthly, base and sordid things: which is the death of the saints and truly pleasing to God. Likewise, death can be ascribed to every mind separated from the body, insofar as it is stripped of the modes of thinking which arise through the external senses, of hunger, thirst, bodily pain, and the pleasure which it perceived on the occasion of the body. Nothing prevents us, too, when the mind is deprived of its most noble and most excellent modes of thinking, of its greatest endowments and perfections, the contemplation and love of God, from calling it dead; and indeed with greater right than the body, deprived of its excellent modes, is called dead, becoming a useless and unprofitable mass, a stinking corpse. This is called spiritual and moral death, of which the sacred authors often speak. Finally, when the mind has been wholly stripped of all pleasant modes of thinking, from whatever occasion they arose, and dark, dreadful, lasting modes, mixed with no mildness or hope, succeed them, it is said to undergo death too. But the question is not chiefly about all these things now.

units.la: V. Quaeritur, an omnes modi cogitandi cessaturi sint in mente creata, ita ut nulla ullo modo, quisquis is sit vel esse possit, amplius cogitet & percipiat? quae dormitantium quorumdam opinio est, asserentium Mentem à separatione corporis ita omnibus cogitationibus spoliari, atque sic mortuam esse ad certum usque tempus. Respondeo, quamdiu ipsa Mentis substantia actu remanere supponitur, concludendum est illam tamdiu cogitare actu, sive esse conscium: nam haec est ipsa mentis natura & substantia, ut alibi demonstratum est. Et quemadmodum corpus actu existens non potest omnibus corporeis modis simul spoliari, sed est necesse ut aliquibus sit praeditum; sic non potest Mens sive cogitatio existere quae non se aliquo modo habeat, sive aliquo modo, quisquis is sit, cogitet. At si supponatur, quod Mentis substantia sive Cogitatio radicalis cesset, hoc ipso evidenter infertur, omnes cogitandi modos etiam desinere: adeo ut tum hujus, tum totius rei difficultas in hanc quaestionem resolvatur, An substantia cogitans, sive ipsa Mens, sit existere cessatura? De Potentia Dei absoluta non est quaestio, An Deus id possit absolute loquendo? Sed de eo quod secundum Dei placitum eventurum est: An nempe Deo placuerit, ut Mens quae cum corpore juncta est, eousque duret, donec corpus dissolvatur: quo facto ipsa cesset existere?
units.tr: V. It is asked whether all modes of thinking are going to cease in the created mind, so that it no longer thinks or perceives in any way, whoever it is or could be? This is the opinion of certain sluggish persons, who assert that the Mind, on separation from the body, is so stripped of all thoughts that it is thus dead until a certain time. I answer: as long as the substance of the Mind itself is supposed to remain in act, it must be concluded that it thinks in act, that is, is conscious; for this is the very nature and substance of the mind, as has been demonstrated elsewhere. And just as a body existing in act cannot be stripped of all bodily modes at once, but must necessarily be endowed with some; so a Mind or thought cannot exist which does not somehow be disposed, or somehow, whoever it is, think. But if it is supposed that the substance of the Mind, or radical thought, ceases, it is evidently inferred by this very fact that all modes of thinking also cease: so that the difficulty of both this and the whole matter is resolved into this question: whether the thinking substance, that is, the Mind itself, is going to cease to exist? There is no question here concerning God's absolute power, whether God can do this absolutely speaking. But concerning what will happen according to God's good pleasure: namely, whether it has pleased God that the Mind, which is joined with the body, should endure only until the body is dissolved, after which it ceases to exist?

units.la: VI. Hanc quaestionem multi putant non posse solvi sine revelatione Dei verbali, inter quos sic Cartesius {a}Quod additis ex distinctione animae a corpore non sequi ejus immortalitatem; quia nihilominus dici potest talis naturae illam a Deo factam esse, ut ejus duratio simul cum duratione vitae corporeae finiatur, fateor a me refelli non posse, &c. & postea, Solius est Dei respondere; & protinus ad revelationem recurrit. Ratio ejus est, quia haec pendent a Dei libera voluntate & decreto. Sed ratio ea nil valet ad rem, siquidem etiam rerum essentiae, ideae, veritatesque a Dei libera voluntate pendeant, ut ipse agnoscit, & tamen de illis quamplurima, etiam futura, ut in physicis, sine revelatione determinamus, vel potius ut determinata a Deo agnoscimus, & enunciamus: quidni & idem de Mentis perpetua existentia tentaturi? Profecto credibile non est, Deum, qui plurima, eaque minuta satis, in natura nobis patefecit, nos in natura celasse rem inter omnes maximi momenti, qualis nempe haec est, ut nos nobis, ille nobis, omnia nobis, respective fiant vel nihil, vel omnia. Quin ipsa revelatio, quæ ingratitudinis redarguit eos qui ex operum Dei inspectione ipsi gratias debitas non egerunt, convincit eo ipso dari in natura testimonia de laudibus Deo bene & potenter in natura operanti debitis, adeoque de animæ immortalitate, quippe ob quam maximæ ei laudes debentur, cum sit Divinum ejus Potentiæ opus in natura omnium continuandum, & multarum aliarum ejus operationum basis. Quare ea testimonia quæremus, quibus ostendit Deus Mentium existentiam nequaquam esse defuturam, etsi dissolvatur corpus.
units.tr: VI. Many think this question cannot be resolved without God's verbal revelation. Among them Descartes, who says: "Granting the distinction of soul from body, it does not follow from it that the soul is immortal; for it may still be said that God made it of such a nature that its duration ends together with the duration of bodily life. I admit I cannot refute this," etc. And afterwards: "It belongs to God alone to answer," and at once he has recourse to revelation. His reason is: "because these things depend on God's free will and decree." But this reason is of no weight in the matter. For even the essences, ideas and truths of things depend on God's free will, as he himself acknowledges, and yet about these we determine very many things, including future ones, without revelation, or rather we recognise and state them as determined by God. Why then should we not also attempt the same concerning the perpetual existence of the mind? Surely it is not credible that God, who has disclosed to us in nature very many things, and quite minute ones, has concealed from us in nature a matter of the greatest importance among all, namely whether, for us to ourselves and for him to us, and all things for us, they become either nothing or everything. Indeed revelation itself, which rebukes those who, from looking at the works of God, have not given him the thanks due to him, proves by that very fact that in nature there are witnesses to the praises due to God, who operates in nature well and powerfully, and so also to the immortality of the soul, for which the greatest praises are owed, since it is a divine work of his power to be continued in nature, and the basis of many of his other operations. Therefore we shall seek those witnesses by which God shows that the existence of minds will by no means fail, even if the body is dissolved.

units.la: VII. Testimonia ea vel ex Dei, vel ex ejus operum contemplatione exurgunt. Ad hæcce ultima referimus, quod sic Deus de rebus dispo-suerit, ut quamvis omnes quibus Mens jungi potest, destrui concipe-rentur, non tamen sequatur necessario conceptus destructionis mentis. In creatis palàm est nil dari quod in mentem magis agat, & à quo Mens vicissim plura patiatur, quam corpus Menti cuique proprium: adeo ut si ab alicujus destructione sit metuenda ruina, missis rebus cæteris à nulla magis metuenda sit quam à propria ruina domicilii quod suum quæque inhabitat Mens, cujus forsan casu opprimatur. Sed hoc dubium ratione caret: nam, 1. Corpus, (substantia ignobilis & minus perse-cta,) non annihilatur cum mens ab illo separatur: cur igitur mens, (nobilior res atque perfectior,) putaretur annihilari cum illud ab hac se-paratur? Nulla pro substantiæ corporeæ ab anima solutæ duratione po-test allegari ratio, quæ non majori jure Menti competat. Quod si dixe-ro ex sensibus constare corpus, remanere postquam anima illud reliquit, non autem ita de illa; id nec de omnibus corporis partibus quæ resol-vuntur verum est, nec perceptio sensuum tam firmum medium est pro-bandi corporum existentiam, quam rationes mox allegandæ ad Men-tium immortalitatem ex perceptione attributorum Dei. 2. Corpus moritur, sive mutat modos, Ergo ideo mens annihilanda; absurdum fuerit ratiocinium. Neque enim ab uno subjecto ad aliud, natura di-versum, transit solum; (acsi dicerem, aqua evaporat, ergo & adamas qui in illa est, qui tamen magis cum natura aquæ convenit quam Mens cum natura corporis.) verum etiam prave concludit, cum ad summum concludi potuisset, etiam fieri mutationes modorum cogitandi in men-te, cum in corporis modis simile quid accidat. 3. Cum Mentis cogita-tiones intimæ atque nobilissimæ à corpore non pendeant, neque id concurrat ad intellectionem, ad ratiocinia, ad contemplationem, ad amo-rem rerum spiritualium, aliaque, nisi quemadmodum compedes cum captivo ambulante concurrunt, ut in primo Libro visum est, sequitur remoto corpore eas, adeoque nec mentem ipsam, minime tolli, ut ne-que captivum solutis catenis annihilari aut ambulandi facultate privari; sed potius eas augeri & perfici, tuncque mentem maxime esse activam & vividam. Perierint licet facultatum istarum exercitia quae medium corporeum postulabant, qualia sunt quae sensus externos, quae dolo-rum corporeorum, voluptatumque, crassam seriem concernunt, imo, si Supremo placet, facultates illae ipsae, sive potentia hisce modis, in posterum percipiendi; Ideone Mens crassamentis tortoribusque sic libera-ta, perire dicenda est? Certe majori jure corpus quod invulnerabile, quod inalterabile redderetur, quod ab iis, à quibus ei noceri posset, li-beraretur, ipsum ideo perire & mori esset dicendum. Forte vero Men-tis facultates nobiliores earumque exercitium à corporis debito statu pendere inde suspicaberis, quod in somno Mens videatur cum omni facultatum vigore absorpta: quod tamen fieri non deberet, si à corpore semota vividis polleret facultatibus. nam cum in somno multis objectis corporeis sit liberata, nonne, si independens esset à corpore, deberet tunc, ubi sibi magis restituta, liberior esse? Respondeo, in somno Mentem à corpore non esse liberam, sed ei bene junctam: Corpus autem sive Spiritus animales, eorumque instrumenta, quibus Mens riga-tur, cum non sint tunc in eo statu ut de eorum motibus, utpote extra vigiliam languidis, inconstantibus, interruptis, evanidis, possit sponte Mens disponere; hinc inter dormiendum in mente vi conjunctionis adhuc durantis, excitari cogitationes languidas, interruptas, non spontaneas, evanidas, quae vel fere nullae, vel totae absorptae fuisse videntur. Magis in somno gravatur Mens quam in vigilia. Catenae tunc ita ingra-vescunt ut captivum non sinant libere ambulare, sed eum dejiciant. At si mens vel in somno, vel in quocunque alio statu minus esset alligata corpori quam esse solet, non dubium est quin facultatum intellectua-lium exercitium solito nobilius & magis spontaneum esset habitura. Hinc in morbis qui Mentis cum corpore vinculum relaxant, interdum raptus nobiles, cogitationes sublimes, & quae occulta prius, detegentes. Et de magnae Mentis viro {a} memoriae proditum est, quod cum ejus corporis vires paulatim resolverentur, is per aliquot menses non nisi somniis inter dormiendum mere speculativis & ratiocinationibus sine absur-ditate phantasmatum ordinaria refertis, fruitus sit, quae pro signis dissolutionis Mentis suae à corporis consortio ipse, & vere quidem, eventu testante, habuit. An etiam ii qui Mentem eatenus à corporis consortio subducunt, ut assuescant puro intellectu sine imaginatione uti, non ha-beant beant interdum in somno cogitationes quasdam sublimes, solidas, subtiles, novas notitias vel ratiocinia detegentes, quibus vel ex professo inter vigilandum vix potuissent attingere; id expertis determinandum relinquitur. Huc igitur redeundum est, Mentis facultates excellentiores corporis casu non impediri, nedum plane deleri. 4. Denique suspicari nequeo quod corpus ipsum, vel ulla creatura, proprie possit esse causa mortis sive annihilationis animae: nam cum vita morti isti opposita nil sit nisi sustentatio existentiae mentis, mors vero cessatio ab illa sustentatione; id non potest desinere sustentare Mentem, sive mortem ei inferre, quod eam non sustentat: corpus autem ut olim non creavit, ita nec jam sustentat mentem, neque, eadem de causa, ulla creatura; Ergo non potest esse causa ejus annihilationis, nec etiam ulla creatura, aut ullius creaturae voluntas, potestas, actio. Deus igitur Creator & Conservator sic omnia disposuit ut nulla de mentis immortalitate suspicio justa haberi possit. quod merito in rebus maxime necessariis pro affirmante argumento habendum est.
units.tr: VII. These witnesses arise either from the contemplation of God or from the contemplation of his works. To the latter we refer the fact that God has so arranged things that, although all the things to which the mind can be joined were conceived as destroyed, the concept of the destruction of the mind would not necessarily follow. Among created things it is plain that there is nothing that acts more upon the mind, and from which the mind in turn suffers more, than the body proper to each mind; so that, if the ruin of any being is to be feared, then, with other things set aside, nothing is to be feared more than the ruin of the dwelling which each mind inhabits as its own, by whose collapse it might perhaps be crushed. But this doubt lacks reason. For: (1) the body (a base and less perfect substance) is not annihilated when the mind is separated from it; why then should the mind (a nobler and more perfect thing) be thought to be annihilated when the body is separated from it? No reason can be alleged for the duration of a bodily substance once loosed from the soul which does not belong to the mind with greater right. And if I should say that it is known from the senses that the body remains after the soul has left it, but not so with the soul, this is true neither of all the parts of the body, which are dissolved, nor is the perception of the senses so firm a means of proving the existence of bodies as the reasons about to be alleged for the immortality of minds from the perception of God's attributes. (2) The body dies, or changes its modes; therefore the mind must be annihilated: this would be an absurd inference. For it is not merely passing from one subject to another of a different nature (as if I were to say: water evaporates, therefore the diamond which is in it must also, although the diamond agrees more with the nature of water than the mind agrees with the nature of body). Rather, it is also a false conclusion, when at most it could have been concluded that changes of modes of thinking also happen in the mind, since something similar happens among the modes of body. (3) Since the mind's most inward and noblest thoughts do not depend on the body, and the body does not contribute to understanding, to reasoning, to contemplation, or to the love of spiritual things, and to other such things, except as chains contribute to a captive who walks about, as was shown in the first Book, it follows that when the body is removed those thoughts are not taken away, and therefore not the mind itself either, any more than a captive is annihilated or deprived of the power of walking when his chains are loosed. Rather, those thoughts are increased and perfected, and then the mind is most active and lively. The exercises of those faculties which required a bodily medium may perish, such as those which concern the external senses and the gross series of bodily pains and pleasures; indeed, if it pleases the Most High, those very faculties, or the power of perceiving in these ways in the future, may perish. Is the mind, then, thus freed from gross matter and tormentors, to be said to perish? Certainly with greater right the body, which would be rendered invulnerable and unalterable, freed from those things by which it could be harmed, should on that account be said to perish and die. But perhaps you will suspect that the nobler faculties of the mind and their exercise depend on the proper condition of the body, because in sleep the mind seems to be absorbed with all the vigour of its faculties; yet this ought not to happen if, separated from the body, it possessed lively faculties. For since in sleep it is freed from many bodily objects, should it not, if it were independent of the body, then be freer when it is more restored to itself? I answer: in sleep the mind is not free from the body, but is well joined to it. The body, however, or the animal spirits and their instruments, by which the mind is watered, are not then in such a state that the mind can freely dispose of their motions, being, outside waking, languid, inconstant, interrupted and fading. Hence, while sleeping, in the mind, by the force of the union still lasting, there are excited thoughts which are languid, interrupted, not spontaneous, and fading, which seem either almost none at all or wholly absorbed. The mind is more burdened in sleep than in waking. The chains then grow so heavy that they do not allow the captive to walk freely, but bring him down. But if the mind, either in sleep or in any other state, were less bound to the body than it usually is, there is no doubt that it would have an exercise of its intellectual faculties nobler and more spontaneous than usual. Hence in diseases which loosen the bond of the mind with the body, sometimes there are noble raptures and sublime thoughts, disclosing things previously hidden. And of a man of great mind it is reported that, when the strength of his body was gradually dissolving, for some months he enjoyed nothing but dreams, purely speculative during sleep, and reasonings filled with no absurdity of ordinary images; these he himself, and truly, as the outcome bore witness, took for signs of the dissolution of his mind from its fellowship with the body. Whether also those who withdraw the mind so far from fellowship with the body that they accustom themselves to use pure understanding without imagination do not sometimes have, in sleep, certain sublime, solid, subtle thoughts, disclosing new notions or reasonings, which they could scarcely have reached while awake, even by deliberate effort, is left for those with experience to determine. We must therefore return to this: the more excellent faculties of the mind are not impeded by the fall of the body, much less utterly destroyed. (4) Finally, I cannot suspect that the body itself, or any creature, can properly be the cause of the death or annihilation of the soul. For since life, which is opposed to that death, is nothing but the sustaining of the mind's existence, and death is the cessation of that sustaining, that which does not sustain the mind cannot cease to sustain it or inflict death upon it. But the body, just as it did not create the mind, so now does not sustain it, and for the same reason no creature does. Therefore neither the body nor any creature can be the cause of its annihilation, nor the will, power or action of any creature. God therefore, the Creator and Conserver, has so arranged all things that no just suspicion of the immortality of the mind can be held. This, rightly, among the most necessary matters, is to be regarded as an argument of affirmation.

units.la: VIII. Forte sic possit aliquis reputare: Quamvis corpus non sit causa Mentem producens & sustentans, imo quamvis necessarium nexum non habeat cum mente, nec absolute sit opus concipere mentem corpore concepto, nec mentis destructionem percepta corporis dissolutione, uti nec mentis praesentiam concepta corporis praesentia: attamen quemadmodum nihilominus posita corporis generatione placuit Deo mentem incipere existere; ita quis scit, sepolita revelatione, num posita corporis corruptione, placuerit Deo Mentem non amplius existere, quamvis, ut dictum, conceptus positionis & destructionis Mentis, in conceptu generationis & destructionis corporis praecise non involvatur, ut attendenti patet? Et haec quidem est ultima dubitationis meta, ultra quam ire non datur. Cui sufficeret respondere, allegata instantia & comparatione, utut adversa videatur, vim nostrae assertionis nequaquam infirmari, sed potius corroborari: etenim, quemadmodum posita corporis generatione non eo ipso concipimus Mentem, quae prius non fuit, idcirco existere, neque hoc ideo affirmamus, sed experientia & certissimis indiciis edocti, eam adesse judicamus: Sic posita corporis destructione, quae conceptum annihilationis Mentis antea existentis non involvit, non putandum est Mentem desinere esse, nisi certissimis experimentis & rationibus id constet; quae cum deficiant, continuare priorem Mentis existentiam judicandum est. Nam, qua ratione suppo-ncre[?] non licet existere quicquid nobis placet, nisi illud existere certis convincamur rationibus, sine quibus id in primo suo statu, hoc est in nihilo, manere recte judicamus; eadem etiam adducimus ut non supponamus quicquid nobis lubet desinere esse, nisi de hac ipsa rei annihilatione certa ratio & causa valida habeatur, sine qua res in priori statu, hoc est in existentia qua ante fruebatur, manere judicanda est, nisi velimus sine causa aliqua de re judicare contrarium ejus quod eam mox fuisse constat, hoc est, nisi libeat scientes errare.
units.tr: VIII. Perhaps someone might reason in this way: although the body is not the cause that produces and sustains the mind, and even though it has no necessary connection with the mind, nor is it absolutely necessary to conceive the mind when the body is conceived, nor to perceive the destruction of the mind when the dissolution of the body is perceived, just as the presence of the mind is not conceived from the presence of the body: nevertheless, just as, although the generation of the body being posited, it pleased God that the mind should begin to exist; so who knows, revelation being set aside, whether, the corruption of the body being posited, it has pleased God that the mind should no longer exist, although, as has been said, the concept of the positing and destruction of the mind is not precisely involved in the concept of the generation and destruction of the body, as is plain to one who attends to it? And this, indeed, is the last limit of doubt, beyond which one cannot go. It would be enough to answer to this that, the instance and comparison adduced, however adverse they may seem, by no means weaken the force of our assertion but rather strengthen it. For just as, the generation of the body being posited, we do not on that account conceive the mind, which previously was not, to exist, nor do we affirm this on that account; but, taught by experience and the most certain indications, we judge that it is present: so, the destruction of the body being posited, which does not involve the concept of the annihilation of a mind that previously existed, it is not to be thought that the mind ceases to be, unless this is established by the most certain experiments and reasons; and since these are lacking, the prior existence of the mind must be judged to continue. For by the same reasoning by which it is not permitted to suppose that whatever pleases us exists, unless we are convinced of its existence by certain reasons, without which we rightly judge it to remain in its first state, that is, in nothing; by that same reasoning we also conclude that we should not suppose that whatever we like ceases to be, unless a certain reason and a valid cause for this very annihilation of the thing is held, without which the thing must be judged to remain in its prior state, that is, in the existence which it enjoyed before, unless we wish to judge without any cause the contrary of what is known to have just been the case, that is, unless we choose to err knowingly.

units.la: IX. Sed ut omni disceptationi & conflictui terminus sit, jam dicam quomodo affirmative constet Deum velle, ut mens nulla existere cesset. Hoc, ut dictum est, pendet à placito Dei. Placitum autem Dei praeter revelationem extraordinariam (quae prophetica est) etiam constat praecipue ex iis quae in Mentis notitiis internis descripta sunt, vel in illis fundantur. Ex quibus quia nil clarius, nil evidentius est notitia Divinorum attributorum, ut ex omnibus dictis constat, unde firmissime concludimus Deum sic velle à nobis agnosci; ita quoque si notitiae attributi alicujus divini perspicue jungatur conceptus attributi alicujus Mentem meam concernentis, (v. g. me amore debere ferri in Deum) quod negare non possim nisi obscurando divinum attributum, eique tribuendo quae id non decent, quaeque id contumelia afficiunt; palam est eum de mente mea conceptum, sive id mentis meae attributum, pro verissimo & Deo grato, & ab eo statuto atque decreto esse habendum. Certe firmius probandi medium in tota rerum universitate non novi quam illud quod ita in notitia attributorum Divinorum fundatur, ut nequeat negari quin haec, non dico corruant, sed contumeliose traducantur: non quod sit periculum pro attributis Dei: quicquid statuant homines ea in se tuta sunt: sed si quod periculum est, id in nostra de illis notitia est, quae deturpari posset, iisque falsitatibus obscurari, quibus cognitionis Dei lumen nobis interciperetur. Illud autem certo accidit hoc in casu. Nam asserta Animae mortalitate, Dei Justitia, Constantia, Sapientia, Justitia retributiva sive vindicativa, Sanctitas, Veracitas, Bonitas & Gloria, eo ipso traducuntur, & percipiendae proponuntur cum tali decore, quod sine horrore illis attribui nec cogitari quidem possit. Ubi econtra, cum in suo decore contemplamur eorum ideas quas pro Dei placito habemus, infertur ab illis animae Immortalitas, quae ipsorum vicissim notitiam quammaxime illustrat. Atque haec ita patent.
units.tr: IX. But so that there may be an end to all dispute and conflict, I will now say how it is affirmatively established that God wills that no mind should cease to exist. This, as has been said, depends on the pleasure of God. Now the pleasure of God, apart from extraordinary revelation (which is prophetic), is established chiefly from those things which are described in the inner notions of the mind, or are founded upon them. Of these, since nothing is clearer or more evident than the notion of the divine attributes, as is plain from all that has been said, we conclude most firmly that God wills to be acknowledged by us in this way. So too, if the notion of some divine attribute is clearly joined with the concept of some attribute concerning my mind (for example, that I ought to be carried in love toward God), which I cannot deny except by obscuring the divine attribute and ascribing to it things that do not befit it and that bring it into disgrace; it is plain that the concept of this about my mind, or this attribute of my mind, is to be held as most true and pleasing to God, and as established and decreed by him. Certainly I know of no firmer means of proof in the whole universe of things than that which is so founded upon the notion of the divine attributes that it cannot be denied that these, I do not say collapse, but are shamefully misrepresented. This is not because there is danger to the attributes of God: whatever men may determine, those are safe in themselves; but if there is any danger, it lies in our knowledge of them, which could be defiled and obscured by those falsehoods by which the light of the knowledge of God would be taken from us. Now in this case it certainly comes about that, the mortality of the soul being asserted, the justice, constancy, wisdom, retributive or vindictive justice, holiness, truthfulness, goodness and glory of God are by that very fact misrepresented and are presented to be perceived with such a lack of fitness that they cannot even be conceived to be ascribed to him without horror. Where, on the contrary, when we contemplate their ideas in their proper fitness, which we hold to be God's pleasure, the immortality of the soul is inferred from them, which in turn illuminates most greatly the knowledge of those very attributes. And these things are thus evident.

units.la: X. (1) Ex Justitia Dei. Deus ex placito condidit mentem, quae in ipsa sua substantia Dei perfectiones aliquatenus adumbraret; dignum placiti & Potentiae suae opus; ac proinde, non annihilandum. Nam de[?]eet Deum se statuentem, se operantem approbare, proindeque suum ipsius verum opus non improbare. Gratis autem affirmarem Deum se ipsum ut statuentem, utque operantem non probare, si putarem eum opus suum destruere, & se tanquam non bene acti, non bene consulti, arguere. Nonne sic cogitando decentia sive Justitia Dei, à me impugnaretur? At, in mente invenitur malum, quod est non-opus Dei. Quid inde? Etiam mox videbitur ideo non debere Mentem annihilari. Sed jam suffecerit annotare, ipsam mentis substantiam malam non esse. Ipsa radicalis perceptio, conscientiave, bona est, opus Dei est, & mansit: cur Deum eam improbare statueres? Opus alienum, peccatum, concipe eum improbare, opere suo subsistente.
units.tr: X. (1) From the justice of God. God, by his pleasure, has created a mind which in its very substance shadows forth to some degree the perfections of God; a work worthy of his pleasure and power; and therefore not to be annihilated. For it is fitting that God should approve himself as the one who establishes and who works, and therefore should not disapprove his own true work. But I would be asserting without warrant that God does not approve himself as establishing and as working, if I thought that he destroys his work and accuses himself as one who has not acted well or planned well. Would not the decency or justice of God be impugned by me if I thought in this way? But in the mind there is found evil, which is the non-work of God. What follows from this? It will soon be seen that for this reason the mind ought not to be annihilated either. But it will suffice for now to note that the substance of the mind itself is not evil. The radical perception itself, or consciousness, is good, is the work of God, and has remained so: why would you determine that God disapproves it? Conceive him disapproving the alien work, sin, while his own work continues to subsist.

units.la: XI. (2) Ex constantia cum Justitia. Teneor de Ente Perfectissimo reputare, ipsum decere ut opera sua quam realissimam, quantum experientia non reclamat, nec contrarium ratione evincitur, suæ constantiæ gerant imaginem. Ut concipiam quamdignissime, & modo decentiæ sive Justitiæ Dei conveniente, Constantiam Dei, tenendum est Deum ipsam probare in se ipso, in placito suo, & in suis operibus, sive sui tabulis & adumbrationibus: Ac proinde id quod in ejus operibus bonum est, nec unquam quicquid accidat, malum fieri potest, (Substantia nempe rerum, & specialiter Mentium, præciso earum statu, de quo non loquor, substantia inquam, rerum, semper opus Dei,) constanter remanere judicandum est. Contrarium statui nequit nisi ab illo, qui quæ possent esse Constantiæ Divinæ imagines ipse pro phantasia sua mutans, ac penitus è medio tollens, non vereretur jactare sic suos conceptus Deo constantissime dignos esse.
units.tr: XI. (2) From the constancy together with the justice.
