I am bound to reflect concerning the Most Perfect Being that it befits him that his works should bear, as far as experience does not object and the contrary is not proved by reason, the image of his constancy as fully as possible. In order to conceive, in the most worthy manner and in the way that is suitable to the decency or justice of God, the constancy of God, it must be held that God approves it in himself, in his pleasure, and in his works, that is, in his tablets and shadowings forth. Accordingly, what is good in his works, and whatever may happen, can never become evil (the substance of things, and especially of minds, taken apart from their state, of which I am not speaking, I say the substance of things is always the work of God), must be judged to remain constantly. The contrary cannot be stated except by one who, changing at his own whim the things which could be the images of divine constancy and utterly removing them from the midst, would not hesitate to boast that his concepts are most constantly worthy of God.

units.la: XII. (3) Ex Sapientiæ notitia eadem Immortalitas evincitur. Sapientiam Dei in statuendo & ponendo ea quæ extra se sunt, quis dicat à me recte & decenter concipi, si statuerem Deum substantiæ alicui simpliciori dedisse facultatem simpliciorem, nobilissimam, spectabilem valde, omniumque quasi basin, quæ continuo ferme ad aliquid tendat, nec tamen hoc aliquid sive ejus objectum, dandum esse, adeoque frustraneam & nullius usus facultatem cum ejus inclinatione, à Deo factam esse? Quis Sapientiæ Dei tribuere audeat, eam donasse homines facultatibus videndi, esuriendi, sitiendi, amandi, &c. inclinationes ad objecta in illis posuisse, sed tamen nil visibile, nil manducabile, nil potabile, nil amabile, quo illæ unquam, quicquid agant, fruantur, ponere voluisse? Quis non erubescat Sapientiam Divinam in agendo sic calumniari? Et dederit illa facultatem realissimam & nobilissimam, Desiderium Immortalitatis, ad objectum cum vehementia, fervore & constantia in omnibus inclinatam, (siquidem tam probi quam improbi, quorum hi in modo errantes, voluptuose crasseque perpetuo velint versari, omnes immortalitatem peroptent,) & tamen objecti possessionem, immortalitatem ipsam, nullo modo acquirendam proposuerit, siquidem Mentes in nihilum sit redacturus! Inepta haec est impietas. Ne quis autem locus captioni relinquatur, causando, multos habere facultates regnandi, docendi, & alias, destitui tamen objectis, regno, discipulis, &c. notetur, hic quaestionem esse, de re, de facultate, ejusque inclinatione, quae inter omnia creata sunt simplicissima & communia; de objecto, non quod particulare sit, quale a pluribus possideri non potest, non quod sit naturae ab optante diversae, quod externum, quod fictum, quod impossibile sit dicendum: Sed econtra agi de objecto communi, quod est naturae rei cogitantis, siquidem sit ipsa cogitatio continuata; adeoque de objecto interno, vero, jamjam materialiter exstante (nam est existentia), ad cujus durationem Mens plena anhelat cupiditate.
units.tr: XII. (3) From the notion of the wisdom of God the same immortality is proved. Who would say that I rightly and fittingly conceive the wisdom of God in establishing and positing the things that are outside himself, if I were to hold that God has given to some simpler substance a simpler faculty, most noble and very conspicuous, the basis, as it were, of all things, which tends almost continually toward something, and yet that this something or its object is not to be given, and that therefore a useless faculty and one of no use has been made by God together with its inclination? Who would dare to ascribe to the wisdom of God that he has given men the faculties of seeing, of hungering, of thirsting, of loving, etc., and has placed inclinations in them toward objects, but yet has wished nothing visible, nothing edible, nothing drinkable, nothing lovable to be set there, in which those faculties might ever, whatever they do, take delight? Who would not blush to slander the divine Wisdom so in its working? And would it have given a most real and most noble faculty, the Desire for Immortality, inclined toward its object with vehemence, fervour and constancy in all (since both the upright and the wicked, of whom the latter, erring in their manner, wish to dwell perpetually in pleasure and gross things, all desire immortality), and yet would have proposed the possession of the object, immortality itself, to be acquired in no way, if indeed it were going to reduce minds to nothing! This is a foolish impiety. But lest any opening be left for a captious objection, by alleging that many have faculties of ruling, teaching, and others, yet are deprived of objects, of kingdom, of disciples, etc., let it be noted that here the question concerns a thing, a faculty, and its inclination, which are among all created things the simplest and most common; and concerns an object, not one that is particular, such as cannot be possessed by many, not one that is different in nature from the one who desires it, which is external, feigned, or said to be impossible: but on the contrary, the discussion is about a common object, which is of the nature of a thinking thing, since it is continued thought itself; and so about an internal object, true, already materially existing (for it is existence), to whose duration the mind eagerly longs with full desire.

units.la: (4) Praeterea quis sine horrore Sapientiam eandem secundum quam omnia disposita sunt, velit ita concipi, ut quae disposuerit Mentes probas noxis & crucibus ab impiis ita esse (quod saepe accidit) afficiendas, ut horrendo fine per destructionem corporis in nihilum eae redigantur ab istis, qui postquam tranquille diu vixissent, dulcis vitae terminum absolute ultimum, diu ditatum, tandem simpliciter cum illis subeunt, in eundemque cum illis nihili statum deveniant?
units.tr: (4) Moreover, who could think without horror that the same Wisdom by which all things are ordered should be conceived in such a way that the minds of the good are, as often happens, afflicted by the wicked with harms and torments, and then brought to nothing by destruction of the body, with a dreadful end; that these same wicked, after having lived quietly for a long time, at last reach together with the good the utterly final end of a sweet life, long enjoyed, and arrive in the same state of nothingness as they?

units.la: XIII. (5). Justitia vindex malarum mentium substantiam annihilari non postulat, ut suo loco dictum est: quin & negatur hujus Justitiae conceptus verus, supponendo Deum, commisso peccato, peccatrices mentes in nihilum reducere, sive eas non amplius sustentare. Sic enim statuitur de Deo, eum tacere, se gerere peccato admisso acsi nil plane factum, nil admissum esset; id enim est annihilare, se gerere acsi nil factum esset. Sic Deus non magis a malo censeretur alienus quam a nihilo: mentem peccare, ipsi idem esset ac lapidem visu carere: atque perinde ipsi esset testari se sui odium improbare, & aliquid in nihilo relinquere. Quae omnia in notitias quas habemus de Deo impingunt.
units.tr: XIII. (5) Avenging justice does not demand that the substance of evil minds be annihilated, as has been said in its place. Indeed, the true concept of this justice is denied if one supposes that God, once sin is committed, reduces the sinning minds to nothing, or ceases to sustain them. For in that case God would be held to keep silent and to conduct himself, after the sin has been committed, as if nothing at all had been done or committed; for to annihilate is to behave as if nothing had been done. So God would be no more regarded as opposed to evil than to nothing: for a mind to sin would be to him the same as a stone lacking sight; and it would be just the same to him to bear witness that he disapproves of his own hatred and to leave something in nothingness. All these things clash with the notions we have of God.

units.la: XIV. (6) Sanctitas Divina, nisi Sanctarum probarumque Mentium immortalitatem confitear, non potest recte a me concipi. 'Nam qui Mentes Sanctas Dei amantes amicasque, Deum in omnibus repraesentantes, asseram destruendas a Deo illo qui se ipsum, suum placitum, suam imaginem in omnibus quærit & probat ? Cui, nisi sanctitatis amo-risque Divini osori & inimico, tribuenda est voluntas destruendi simul cum mentibus puris eam quam amplexantur & fovent sanctitatem & di-lectionem Dei ? Hoc atrocius est, quam ut Deo esse applicandum co-gitetur.
units.tr: XIV. (6) The holiness of God cannot rightly be conceived by me unless I confess the immortality of holy and upright minds. For how could I assert that minds which love and are friends of God, which represent God in all things, are to be destroyed by that God who seeks and approves himself, his own good pleasure, and his own image in all things? To whom, unless to one who hates and is the enemy of divine holiness and love, could be attributed the will to destroy, together with pure minds, the holiness and love of God which they embrace and cherish? This is too atrocious to be imputed to God.

units.la: XV. (7) Etiam ex veracitate Dei animæ immortalitatem concludo. Deus impressit in mente mea evidentissimam immortalitatis ideam: proposuit illam tanquam scopum acquisitu possibilem: positive illuc inclinat Mentem: omnia, quam diligentissime fieri potest, cum circum-spiciuntur, nova de immortalitatis certitudine testimonia (quæ præcef-serunt) in operibus Dei deteguntur. Qui optime suis facultatibus utun-tur, omnibus perspectis non possunt non eo sponte & sine indifferentia deduci ut de animorum immortalitate persuadeantur: imo ipsi impii cum crassis objectis quocunque modo valedicentes spiritualia intuentur, omnibus latibulis perreptatis, futuri status conscii ita sunt, ut nullis ar-gutiis & considerationibus eam conscientiam possint deponere. Nisi hæc omnia à Deo sint, nisi sint ejus placiti testimonia, insculptaque de su-turo statu promissa, dic, quæso, quænam apta erunt voluntatem Dei testandi? Ecquis neget iis, quibus positive, potenter & inevitabiliter in-ducimur ad aliquid affirmandum, Dei operationibus in mente nostra clarissime perspectis, quis, inquam, his neget non respondere eventum, nisi improbus veracitatis Divinæ calumniator, ejusque notitiæ in Men-te delector? Ergo, quam verum est homines à contumelia in Deum debere abstinere, tam verum est eos convinci Mentes creatas esse ex pla-cito Divino clare mentibus ipsis insculpto Immortales. Quod nullo pro-babili argumento vel negabatur vel in dubium revocabatur, sed nullis, ineptis, impiis de causis. Si quis vero vult sine multis ratiocinationibus de hac veritate secure persuaderi, is caveat tantum sibi ab ea morte quæ spiritualis initio dicta est. Alioqui non adeo mirum est, si mali ut mortem æternam declinent, in nihilum relabi peroptent, & ex con-suetudine, justo Dei judicio occæcati, id futurum nonnulli sibi per-suadeant.
units.tr: XV. (7) I also conclude the immortality of the soul from the veracity of God. God has impressed on my mind the most evident idea of immortality; he has set it before us as a goal attainable by acquisition; he positively inclines the mind thitherward. When all things are examined as carefully as possible, new testimonies to the certainty of immortality (which surpass all others) are discovered in the works of God. Those who use their faculties well, all things having been surveyed, cannot fail to be led to this of their own accord and without indifference, so as to be persuaded of the immortality of souls: indeed the impious themselves, bidding farewell in whatever way to gross objects, look upon spiritual things; having crept through all hiding places, they are so aware of a future state that by no subtleties and considerations can they lay aside that consciousness. Unless all these things come from God, unless they are the testimonies of his good pleasure and promises of a future state engraved within us, tell me, I pray, what fitting means there would be for God to bear witness to his will? Who would deny that the outcome corresponds to those things to which we are positively, powerfully and inevitably led to affirm something, when the operations of God in our mind are most clearly perceived? Who, I say, would deny this except a wicked calumniator of divine truthfulness who delights in the knowledge of it in his mind? Therefore, just as true as it is that men must abstain from insult against God, so true is it that they are convinced that created minds are, by the divine good pleasure clearly engraved upon the minds themselves, immortal. This was either denied or called into doubt by no probable argument, but only for unfitting, impious and baseless reasons. But if anyone wishes to be securely persuaded of this truth without many lines of reasoning, let him take care only that he avoid that death which was spoken of at the beginning as spiritual. Otherwise it is not very surprising if wicked men, in order to avoid eternal death, wish greatly to slip back into nothingness, and, blinded by habit and by the just judgment of God, some persuade themselves that this will happen.

units.la: XVI. Plures demonstrationes, ut quæ ex Bonitate & Gloria Dei (de qua ultima specialius nil adhuc dictum est) solide possunt deduci, prætermittimus; cum ex dictis sufficienter patescat veritas hujus Propo-sitionis, Mens humana nunquam existere cessabit. Quod assertum non opponitur priori ab initio à me allato, nempe, Si Deus absolute voluif-set res aliter disponere, suaque attributa alio in me modo adumbrare, nil ex parte mei obstitisset quominus in nihilum posset relabi eo me sustentare desinente. Quod autem jam id non futurum sit, id non fit vi naturae meae, quo sensu anima mea non est dicenda immortalis ex natura sua, sed vi voluntatis Dei, qui solus, ut mox dicendum est ex vi naturae suae Immort[?]alis.
units.tr: XVI. We pass over several demonstrations, such as those which can be solidly deduced from the goodness and glory of God (of which last nothing more particular has yet been said), since from what has been said the truth of this proposition is sufficiently clear: the human mind will never cease to exist. This assertion is not opposed to the earlier one I advanced at the beginning, namely, that if God had absolutely willed to arrange things otherwise and to shadow forth his attributes in me in another way, nothing on my part would have hindered me from falling back into nothingness once he ceased to sustain me. But that this will not now happen is not due to the force of my nature; in this sense my soul is not to be called immortal by its own nature, but by the will of God, who alone, as shall soon be said, is immortal by the force of his own nature.

units.la: XVII. De statu Mentis à corpore solutae, (ut hic nonnihil dicatur de eo) nil praecise & specialius determinari potest, quia hoc à placito Dei non omnino manifestato pendet. Interim ejus idea generalior potest haberi, si praeter id quod mutari constat nulla alia subita & violenta mutatio accidere supponatur, hoc est, nulla talis mutatio, quae fiat de statu contrario in contrarium: sed omnia putentur in praecipuo suo statu, quantum fieri posse concipitur, remanere; atque in eo per habitus intellectus & voluntatis magis magisque radicari, & , quae status mentium regula est, robore morum & consuetudinum gradibus indefinite augeri. Non est quod in concipiendo Mentis immortalis à corpore solutae statu, à binis hisce regulis, quas hic veras esse constat, quaeque sine causa, imo falso, alibi assererentur mutari, recedatur. Igitur Primo, putandum est Mentes à corporibus solutas, siquidem solutae sint & cum illis nullum nexum amplius habeant, nullas etiam amplius habere perceptiones ex illis quae immediate sive directe excitantur in nobis per organa corporea sine quibus nunquam perciperentur: adeoque Mentes, quamdiu corpus non resumunt, perceptionibus sensuum externorum visus, auditus, aliorum, eorumque adeo objectorum, item voluptatum aut dolorum corporeorum omnino destitui. Quapropter proprie dici nequit, Animas à corpore separatas igne nescio quo torqueri. Nam quamvis dolor, etiam corporeus, non sit nisi in Mente, ignisque corporeus, sic disponente Deo, doloros perceptionis occasionem dare possit, ut bene observavit Author Artis Cogitandi, hoc tamen fieri in Mentibus corpore solutis nequit supponi, {a}ut fit ab illo, nisi destruatur eo ipso hypothesis, quod Mentes illae sint corpore solutae. Si enim censeantur per mortem à corpore mentem sensibus subjiciente separari, censeri non possunt igne tartareo aliove corporeo torqueri: nam ad hoc supponendum est eas cuidam corpori manere unitas, vel de novo uniri (ipsi saltem igni), quod cum ex natura non pateat, non sine divini placiti patefactione est affirmandum.
units.tr: XVII. Concerning the state of the mind loosed from the body (since something is to be said of it here), nothing can be determined precisely and in more detail, because this depends on the good pleasure of God, which has not been wholly made manifest. Meanwhile a more general idea of it can be had, if, besides what is known to change, no other sudden and violent change is supposed to occur, that is, no such change as would pass from a contrary state into its contrary; rather, all things are to be thought to remain, so far as it can be conceived, in their chief state; and in that state they are to be rooted ever more firmly through the habits of intellect and will, and increased indefinitely by degrees of strength of character and of custom, which is the rule of the states of minds. There is no reason, in conceiving the state of an immortal mind loosed from the body, to depart from these two rules, which are plainly true here and which are asserted elsewhere to change without cause, or rather falsely. Therefore, first, it must be thought that minds loosed from bodies, provided they are loosed and no longer have any bond with them, also no longer have any perceptions from those things which are excited in us immediately or directly through the bodily organs, without which they would never be perceived: and so minds, as long as they do not resume a body, are wholly deprived of perceptions of the external senses, of sight, hearing and the others, and of their objects, and likewise of bodily pleasures or pains. Wherefore it cannot properly be said that souls separated from the body are tormented by some fire or other. For although even bodily pain exists only in the mind, and bodily fire, God so ordaining, can give occasion for painful perception, as the author of the Art of Thinking rightly observed, yet this cannot be supposed to happen in minds loosed from the body, as it happens according to him, unless the very hypothesis that those minds are loosed from the body is destroyed. For if they are held to be separated from the body by death, which subjects the mind to the senses, they cannot be held to be tormented by infernal fire or any other bodily thing: for to suppose this one must suppose that they remain united to some body, or are united anew (to fire itself at least), which, since it does not appear from nature, must be affirmed only by the revelation of the divine good pleasure.

units.la: XVIII. Secundo, est ex iisdem regulis quod cogitemus, eas mentes quae in corporea vita corporeis praeter necessitatem nexus à Deo cum suis corporibus instituti, adhaeserunt; ita ut principium ex quo corporeis applicatæ sunt, fuerit spontanea cogitatio qua se præter necessitatem lubentes excitabant ad terrestria cogitanda, quærenda, amplectenda, cumulanda, ut illic delectarentur; quæque assueverunt ob horum præsentiam aut absentiam amore, spe, odio, ira, angore, percelli & abripi; est, inquam, quod cogitemus mentes eas hosce habitus, non obstante nexus cum corporeis dissolutione, retenturas, siquidem ii non à necessitate ejus nexus, sed à mente ipsa sponte orti sint, ibidemque sponte radicati. Et cum Mentes istæ plerumque soleant esse habitualiter ignorantes, adeoque tales sint etiam remansuræ; cum phantasmatibus illæ suis firmiter infixis, quorum objectis non amplius tunc frui dabitur, indesinenter sint vexandæ; cum suis illæ passionibus, quibus consueverunt ob optatorum defectum sese torquere, sint percellendæ & discerpendæ, quanta hujus immortalis status miseria est reputanda!
units.tr: XVIII. Second, from the same rules we may think that those minds which, in corporeal life, clung to bodily things beyond the necessity of the bond which God established with their bodies, so that the beginning from which they were applied to bodily things was a spontaneous thought by which they, beyond necessity and willingly, roused themselves to think upon, seek, embrace and heap up earthly things, in order to take delight in them; and which were accustomed, through love, hope, hatred, anger and anguish, to be struck and carried away by the presence or absence of these things: we may think, I say, that those minds will retain these habits even after the dissolution of the bond with the body, since these did not arise from the necessity of that bond but spontaneously from the mind itself, and there they took spontaneous root. And since such minds are for the most part wont to be ignorant as a habit, and will remain so; since they, firmly fixed to their phantasms, whose objects will then no longer be enjoyed, will be tormented without end; since they will be struck and torn apart by their passions, with which they were accustomed to torment themselves on account of the lack of what they desired: how great the misery of this immortal state is to be reckoned!

units.la: XIX. Tertio, habemus ex iisdem, Mentes eas quæ in hac Vita intellectum suum cum affectu applicuerunt scientiis & Cognitionibus de corporeis & terrestribus, ut in Physicis, Mathematicis, Historicis plerisque, & ejusmodi aliis; vel de Divinis, ut in Theologicis, in iis quæ circa Religionem, in studio scripturæ litterali, &c. acquirendis, quæque in his cum sui amore, delectatione, satisfactione, superbia & existimatione versantur, quærendo, lætando, deliciando, se tantas, tam doctas, subtiles, & spirituales esse & haberi; aut si non tales ab aliis habeantur, vel etiam à se, non invenientes quod in suæ scientiæ & præstantiæ idea acquiescant ut vellent, dolendo suffocatæ ira, angore, odio: tales intelligimus post separationem sui à corpore evadere in Mentes Diabolicas, seu Diabolicis similes: Nam Mens pura, id est, corpore soluta, intelligens, docta, & superba, de actibus passionibusque suis secundum existimationem sui spiritualem disponens, Diabolica Mens est. Hic est scientiarum, earumque quæ de Divinissimis & Spiritualissimis tractant, ubi sine humilitate & abnegatione sui possidentur à quoquam, certissimus eventus. Noli igitur superbia elevari, sed time. Non aliud ex scientia evidentiori sequetur, nisi importuna Magnitudinis Boni absentis moneta, ac mali lapsusque ingentis clara & non reclamanda convictio, ex habitu amoris proprii (principio pessimo & Deo non grato) perpetuos cogitationum laniatus reverberans.
units.tr: XIX. Thirdly, we may infer from the same things that those minds which in this life have applied their understanding, together with their affection, to the sciences and cognitions of corporeal and earthly things, as in physics, mathematics, most of history and suchlike, or of divine things, as in theology, in what is acquired concerning religion and in the study of the literal Scripture, and which in these pursuits are occupied with self-love, delight, self-satisfaction, pride and esteem, seeking, rejoicing and delighting that they are, and are held to be, so great, so learned, subtle and spiritual; or, if they are not so regarded by others, or even by themselves, and do not find what they wish in the idea of their own knowledge and eminence, are choked with anger, anguish and hatred from grief: such minds, we understand, after separation from the body, pass into diabolical minds, or minds like the devils. For a pure mind, that is, one loosed from the body, understanding, learned and proud, which arranges its acts and passions according to its own spiritual estimation, is a diabolical mind. This is the most certain outcome of those sciences, and of those which treat of the most divine and most spiritual things, where they are possessed by anyone without humility and self-denial. Do not, therefore, be lifted up with pride, but fear. Nothing else will follow from more evident knowledge except the importunate reckoning of the absent Good and a clear and undeniable conviction of the great evil and fall, reverberating from the habit of self-love (a most wicked principle, and not pleasing to God) perpetual lacerations of thoughts.

units.la: XX. Sequitur & inde ultimo, Mentes quarum status & habitus ante suam à corpore dissolutionem is fuerit', ut terrestribus præter necefsitatem non adhæserint, sed iis subductæ fuerint, se ipsas omniaque prætermiserint ut Deum contemplarentur, amarent, in eo acquiescerent, non ob sui utilitatem, sed quia sic Deo placet; quæque doluerint se alio olim inclinatas fuisse, siquidem id Deo displiceat; & eas pravas inclinationes penitus delere omni opere conatæ fuerint; fore post relictum cadaver, à vanis malisque non amplius inquietandas, sed à Dei notitia & amore habitualiter & constanter absorbendas. Nam status fundamentalis ut malus in aliis, ita & bonus in his constans manet perseveratque. Et quamvis dum solutio Mentis à corpore fiebat, labor ille quem desudabat Mens in eliminandis & delendis malarum inclinationum minimis plicis notisque ultimis, atque in acquirenda habituum sanctissimorum Divinæ sui Deo in omnibus traditionis perfectione, non fuerit adhucdum plane ad ultimas metas absolutus; attamen siquidem principium constans atque exercitatum aversationis à vanitate, & applicationis ad Deum unum, manet alta mente repostum, fixum, penetrans fundum animæ, sese semper offerens, semper gratum; solutione facta, remotis tentationum obstaculis quæ imperfectiones involuntarias fovebant, delebuntur brevi facileque si qua manent priscæ vestigia fraudis, & obtinebitur scopus ad quem unice collimatum fuit. De iis quæ ubi corpora resumentur accident, consulenda est Divina revelatio, unum cognoscendi in his principium. At illa sic de præcipuis bonis, Quod erimus nondum patefactum est.
units.tr: XX. Lastly, it follows from this: minds whose state and habit before their dissolution from the body was such that they did not cling to earthly things beyond necessity, but were withdrawn from them, and set aside themselves and everything else in order to contemplate, love and rest in God, not for their own advantage but because it so pleases God; and which grieved that they had formerly been inclined elsewhere, if indeed this displeases God; and which have striven by every effort wholly to destroy those wicked inclinations: after the corpse is left behind, these will no longer be disturbed by vain and evil things, but will be habitually and constantly absorbed by the knowledge and love of God. For as the fundamental state remains constant and persists as evil in others, so in these it remains and persists as good. And although, while the mind was being loosed from the body, the labour which the mind sweated through in eliminating and blotting out the smallest folds and last marks of evil inclinations, and in acquiring the most holy habits of a perfect divine surrender of self to God in all things, had not yet been fully brought to the final goals, nevertheless, provided the constant and practised principle of aversion from vanity and of application to the one God remains laid up in the deep mind, fixed, penetrating the bottom of the soul, always presenting itself and always welcome, then once separation has taken place, with the obstacles of temptations removed which used to nourish involuntary imperfections, whatever traces of the old deceit remain will be quickly and easily blotted out, and the goal at which the mind alone has aimed will be attained. Concerning what will happen when bodies are resumed, the divine revelation must be consulted, the one principle of knowledge in these matters. But it has thus not yet been revealed concerning the chief goods: What we shall be has not yet been made manifest.

units.la: 21. Deus est Immortalis sensu nobiliori quam sit Anima, sibique soli proprio.
units.tr: 21. God is immortal in a nobler sense than the soul is, and in a sense proper to himself alone.

units.la: XXI. Quicquid de Immortalitate Dei post hæc dicendum est; cum per se pateat; verbo annotare sufficiet. Nempe non modo Deum non esse mortalem concipio, sed ne quidem esse immortalem eo sensu quo Mentem immortalem dixi. Non diminuentur ullæ Dei perfectiones ullo modo, multo minus eo qui ad nihilum absolutum redigat. Sed nec si illæ à diminutione manent immunes, tales manent vi & placito alieno, ut de Mentis immortalitate dictum est; verum ex virtute & præstantia propria decrementi sunt incapaces, quippe quæ sint perfectissimæ, sibi sufficientissimæ, & à se ipsis. Posse minui, etsi actus diminutionis sequi numquam deberet, est nota dependentiæ ab alio qui pro placito plus minusve realitatis queat largiri; aut etiam nota est contrarietatis & repugnantiæ internæ inter principia aliquid componentia, quæ sese pau-latim nisi id impediretur, labefactarent, quæ omnia ab Ente simplicissimo quamlongissime sunt removenda. Deus igitur ut cætera, sic Immortalitatem eo habet sensu qui nulli præter ipsum solum est tribuendus. Quomodo inter ejus propria attributa Immortalitas recensenda est.
units.tr: XXI. Whatever must be said after this concerning the immortality of God, since it is evident in itself, it will suffice to note in a word. Indeed I hold not only that God is not mortal, but not even that he is immortal in the sense in which I have called the mind immortal. No perfections of God are diminished in any way, much less by him who would reduce them to absolute nothingness. But even if they remain free from diminution, they do not remain so by force and pleasure of another, as was said of the immortality of the mind; rather, they are incapable of decrease from their own power and excellence, since they are most perfect, wholly sufficient to themselves, and from themselves. To be able to be diminished, even if the act of diminution ought never to follow, is a mark of dependence on another who could bestow more or less reality at will; or it is also a mark of contrariety and internal repugnance among the principles composing something, which would gradually weaken one another unless this were prevented; all of which must be removed as far as possible from the most simple Being. God therefore has immortality, as he has other things, in a sense which must be ascribed to no one but himself alone. Hence immortality is to be counted among his own proper attributes.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: (25) GLORIA.
units.tr: (25) GLORY.

units.la: I. Gloriæ Mentis de se occasio nulla. 2. Probatur id ex vano Mentis de se phantasmate. 3. Ex consideratione operantis Dei. 4. Ex consideratione operis ipsius in genere. 5. Ex consideratione operis quatenus id est cogitans.
units.tr: I. The mind has no occasion for glorying in itself. 2. This is proved from the empty phantasm the mind forms of itself. 3. From consideration of God as the one who works. 4. From consideration of the work itself in general. 5. From consideration of the work insofar as it is thinking.

units.la: I. VEnio ad ultimam qua numerum superiorum de Mente mea observationum clausi, considerationem: videlicet, omnibus hisce visis mentis meæ imperfectionibus quibuscunque, perfectionumque dependentia omnimoda ex alterius placito, nil esse cur adeo de me ipso bene opiner, mihique memet conspiciendum & spectandum sistam.
units.tr: I. I come now to the last consideration with which I close the list of observations on my Mind: namely, that, having seen all these imperfections of my mind, and that all its perfections depend entirely on another's pleasure, there is nothing that would warrant my thinking well of myself, and I should set myself before my own eyes to be looked at and contemplated.

units.la: II. Nolim dicere silentio vel cogitatione esse prætereunda, aut etiam contemnenda Dei in nobis dona atque opera, vel cæterum falsa humilitatis affectatione neganda & dissimulanda esse. Mendacio locus dandus non est, nec operationes & imagines Dei sunt improbandæ ubicunque sint, illi qui justitiam amat. Sed accidit plerumque ut homines sua (quæ à Deo sunt) bona considerantes, (non enim loquor de illis qui ob mala sua efferuntur.) accidit inquam ut reflectentes ad opera Dei in sese, instar ejus quod fit in omni reflexione in qua quis se quasi à se ipso diversum & à se alterum spectat, sic se ipsos tanquam ab operibus Dei in se diversos considerent, adeoque sui ideam phantasticam, ab opere Dei distinctam (quæ revera nihil est, siquidem omne non-opus Dei sit nihil) contemplantes, ad ipsam ea bona referant, acsi hæc illis esset digna præ aliis quas quisque alius sibi de se format phantasticis ejusmodi sui ideis, & acsi magis apta ad illa dona quam alii sint, fuisset. Sic vanum quisque sui spectrum ex Dei donis æstimat, laudat, inflat;gaudet illam sui ideam, quam contradistincte ad Dei dona contemplatur , pluribus ornari dotibus quam aliorum de seipsis phantasma-ta. Et hoc est gloria interna ,ridiculum exosæ Deo superbiæ fundamen-tum atque cor.
units.tr: II. I would not say that the gifts and works of God in us are to be passed over in silence or in thought, or despised, or that they are to be denied and concealed under a false affectation of humility. No room should be given to falsehood, and the operations and images of God, wherever they are, are not to be condemned by one who loves justice. But it commonly happens that men, considering their own goods (which are from God; for I am not speaking of those who are puffed up by their own evils), when they reflect upon the works of God in themselves, as happens in every reflection in which someone regards himself as distinct from himself and as another, so they consider themselves as distinct from the works of God in themselves; and thus, contemplating a phantastic idea of themselves, distinct from the work of God (which in truth is nothing, since every non-work of God is nothing), they refer those goods to it, as if these were owed to it above others, and as if it were better suited to those gifts than others are. Thus each one values, praises and inflates his own empty specter, drawn from the gifts of God; he rejoices that his idea of himself, which he contemplates in contrast to the gifts of God, is adorned with more endowments than the phantasms other men form of themselves. And this is inward glory, the ridiculous foundation and heart of pride, which God abhors.

units.la: III. Certe si in me multa, & ea quidem utcunque egregia Dei dona & opera sint, ad quæ contemplando reflectere velim , eaque ut in me posita considerare; quicquid pro me , pro illo subjecto in quo opera illa essent supponere possem , convincor id nil posse aliud esse quam unum ex illis ipsis operibus Dei quod ipse omnium primum ex mera liberalitate liberrimi sui placiti statuerit, posuerit, sustentaverit; huicque tanquam basi alia itidem ex mera voluntatis libertate quot quantaque placuit, imposuerit: adeo ut si quæratur, quare hoc sit positum , eique illud , & istud , aliudque , superadditum ? nil vere assignari possit quam Dei placitum & operatio: Deo videlicet pro arbitrio placuisse hoc primum operari, statuere nexum hujus primi cum altero, & hoc alterum ex libertate esse operatum, & sic deinceps opus operi ob solum suum placitum addidisse. Ergo si positionis alicujus realitatis causa est alleganda, probanda, de ea gaudendum, gloriandum, præter voluntarium Dei placitum, præter bonam Dei erga me aliosque voluntatem, nil omnino occurrit quod proferam. quare in hoc solo est gloriandum, & gaudendum hoc unicum esse in omnibus omnia, præter quod sit nihil, & sic ad Deum in omnibus reflexionibus est tendendum.
units.tr: III. Certainly, if there are in me many gifts and works of God, and indeed in some way excellent ones, to which I might wish to turn by contemplation, and to consider them as placed in me; whatever I might suppose on my own behalf, for that subject in which those works are, I am convinced that it can be nothing other than one of those very works of God, which he himself, out of pure generosity of his most free pleasure, first established, placed and sustained; and upon this as a base he has likewise placed, from the mere freedom of his will, as many and as great others as he pleased. So that if it is asked why this has been placed, and that to it, and this other, and another, has been added besides, nothing truly can be assigned except the pleasure and operation of God: namely, that it pleased God at his discretion to act first in this way, to establish the bond of this first with another, and that this other was produced from freedom, and so on, one work added to another solely by his own pleasure. Therefore, if the cause of the reality of any position is to be alleged, proved, rejoiced in or gloried in, beyond God's voluntary pleasure, beyond God's good will toward me and others, nothing at all occurs that I could put forward. Therefore it is in this alone that one should glory and rejoice: that this one thing is everything in all things, apart from which there is nothing; and so in all reflections one must turn toward God.

units.la: IV. Opus, umbratile opus, non necessarium opus, non est quid absolutum sed relatum, & relatum ad operantem, ad operantem solidum, ad solidissimi operantis liberum placitum. Quicquid realitatis ego sum, & in me est, continuo tale opus est umbratile & non necessarium. Ergo in illius consideratione non debet vel minima cogitatione ad ipsum, vel ad aliquod phantasma non operans omnia ex placito, non-Deum, fieri terminus, eique, acsi solidum quid esset, adhæreri, ipsum ut ipsummet probare approbatione in illud ipsum terminata, & ab aliis velle id probari: nisi libeat sic Deum omnium originem & exemplar atque finem, tollere, negare, eique absurdum nihilum substituere. Nec etiam decet me de aliis aliter quam de me, modo jam demonstrato, cogitare, nam ipsi, & omnia, præter occasiones laudandi & probandi Deum solum ex bonitate omnia operantem, à se, ad se, & per se sunt, non opus, non umbra, non accidentarium quid; sed absolutum nihil.
units.tr: IV. A work, a shadowy work, an unnecessary work, is not something absolute but relative, and relative to the one who works: to the one who works solidly, to the free pleasure of the most solid worker. Whatever reality I am, and whatever is in me, is at once such a shadowy and unnecessary work. Therefore, in its consideration, not even the least thought should make either myself or some non-God phantasm, which does not work all things by pleasure, the terminus, and cling to it as if it were something solid, wishing to prove it by an approval terminated in itself, and to have it proved by others; unless one is willing thus to remove God, the origin, pattern and end of all things, to deny him, and to substitute an absurd nothing in his place. Nor is it fitting for me to think of others otherwise than of myself, as has just been demonstrated; for they themselves, and all things, apart from the occasions for praising and proving God alone, who works all things from goodness, are from him, to him and through him: they are not a work, not a shadow, not an accidental thing, but an absolute nothing.

units.la: V. Deus operatus est in me, & operatus est me & multa alia; sed &, quod de multis non fecit, cogitantem & conscium me fecit, non ut simpliciter essem cogitans, non ob operationem illam, hoc est, ut illa esset id quod est, nam & de brutissimis simile dici posset, & creatura esset scopus sui: adeoque nec etiam ut essem conscius mei, ut conscientia mea sciret se esse, conscia esset de se terminative, ut sic dicam: nam nec habeo mei solius ideam, neque illi perceptio acquiescentiæ sive termini mei juncta est: Sed cogitans factus sum ut essem conscius operationis Divinæ, ut perciperem operationem quæ in me est esse à Deo, hoc scirem, cogitarem, in hoc acquiescerem, gauderem, gloriarer. Neque cogitationis, idearum nobilissimarum, facultatumque ejus, excellentiorem usum rationemque assignare datur. Et quod præter Dei in me operantis conscientiam, is ipse Deus me utcunque conscium de quibusdam aliis reddidit, cum aliorum ideas mihi dedit, sive notificavit mihi se in aliis operari, & efficere ut glorientur illi in ipso agnito; Id mihi ostendit, non ut ego cæterorum sim solum conscius (quod est scientiæ vanæ) eosve laudem: sed ut ego sim conscius & læter, & glorier quod Deus sit & habeatur ab aliis ut existens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: V. God has worked in me, and has worked me and many other things; but also, what he has not done for many, he has made me thinking and conscious, not merely so that I should be a thinking being, nor for that operation, that is, so that it should be what it is (for something similar could be said of the most brutish creatures, and the creature would be its own goal), and so not even so that I should be conscious of myself, so that my consciousness should know that it is, and be conscious of itself as its terminus, so to speak: for I have no idea of myself alone, nor is any perception of rest or of my own terminus joined to it. Rather, I have been made thinking so that I might be conscious of the divine operation, so that I might perceive that the operation which is in me is from God, know this, think it, rest in this, rejoice, and glory. Nor is it granted to assign a nobler use and purpose of thought, of the most noble ideas and of its faculties. And that, besides the consciousness of God working in me, this same God has in some way made me conscious of certain other things, when he gave me the ideas of others, or made known to me that he works in others and brings it about that they glory in him who is acknowledged: this he has shown me, not so that I should be conscious of others only (which is the knowledge of vanity), or praise them; but so that I should be conscious, and rejoice, and glory, that God is, and is held by others as the one who exists and is all in all.

units.la: 6. Gloria Deo essentialis. 7. Gloria relativa Dei in creaturis. Gloria quomodo datur Deo. Deus cur glorificandus & laudandus.
units.tr: 6. Essential glory of God. 7. Relative glory of God in creatures. How glory is given to God. Why God is to be glorified and praised.

units.la: VI. Sed cum Deus ad se ipsum reflectens & seipsum, quantum concipi potest ut à se ipso differens, contemplatur, sit ille ipse unus sibi uni obvius, sibique omnia, sibi suæ perfectiones omnes indivisim; cumque eorum quæ in se sunt approbans existat, non potest non ad se ipsum approbationem existimationemque perfectissimam proprie referre, & primo atque ultimo terminare. Et hæc vera est Gloria Dei, Deo essentialis, ut à se, ad se, per se perfectiones suas, se ipsum, consideret, approbet, bonum de se ipso sibi testimonium habeat, bonamque sui ipsius de se conscientiam.
units.tr: VI. But when God, reflecting upon himself, contemplates himself as far as he can be conceived as differing from himself, he is that one being, present to himself alone, and to himself all things, and to himself all his perfections together, undivided. And since he exists approving of what is in himself, he cannot but refer his most perfect approval and esteem properly to himself, and terminate it first and last in himself. This is the true glory of God, essential to God: that from himself, to himself, through himself, he considers his perfections and himself, approves them, and has within himself a good testimony concerning himself, and a good consciousness of himself.

units.la: VII. Concipitur gloria in Deo quæ non nisi mediantibus ejus placito atque effectibus eum respicit: nempe percipimus Deum omne suum placitum & opus approbare, æstimare, & ad se ipsum, ut ad exemplar & authorem scopumque referre. Hoc sensu dicitur Deus omnia ad gloriam suam statuisse, nempe ut essent umbræ & imagines quibus repræsentaretur Deus ut se ipsum approbans, ut existens omnia. Quare etiam hæc gloria dicitur esse in creaturis objective, & creaturas, vel brutissimas, gloriam dare Deo. Quod autem specialior quædam gloria à mentibus Sanctis Deo tribui dicatur, codem recidit, nam hæc gloria est opus Dei in mentibus illis, neque putandum est aliquam Dei gloriam à Creatura, ut à se ipsa, posse procedere: Deus ipse efficit illam sui gloriam in illis & per illas, sive se gloriosum reddit in illis, & creat illas (beneficio singulari) ad gloriam suam. Ipse ponit sui in illis delineationes excellentiores, & efficit ut Mentes tum ad Dei naturam gloriosam intelligendam & amandam sponte dirigantur, tum ut Divini placiti opus in seipsis fieri sinant, & illud ut gloriosissimi Dei effectum & tabulam considerent. quomodo sic vere omnia per sanctos fiunt ad gloriam Dei. Sed interim advertatur, ut dictum, Naturæ Dei hanc Gloriam non esse essentialem, quippe quæ, si Deus voluisset nil à se diversum velle, non exstitisset: nil autem concipi potest superaddi posse ab ullo, nequidem à Deo, Divinæ Naturæ ut ei essentiale. Non magnificentior illa & ornatior in se redditur. omne hoc in placitum Dei sic debet resundi, ut si effecerit suæ gloriæ imagines in mentibus, sique illæ Deum laudent, non sit cogitandum hoc ideo esse quod eo opus habeat, idve illi sit necesse: Sed ideo vult in suis gloriosus adumbrari, & illi in hoc summo fervore debent ferri, quia Illi gratiose placuit ut hoc vellet ita esse. Gloria verbalis, loqui, canere, &c. quàm stupide multi pro vera Dei (imo & sui) gloria amplectuntur, hic, ubi de cogitatione sola agitur, locum non habet; atque cum sola est, fumus & mendacium meretur dici.
units.tr: VII. Glory is conceived in God which regards him only through his decree and effects. We perceive, namely, that God approves and values every decree and work of his own, and refers it to himself as to its pattern, author and goal. In this sense God is said to have ordained all things for his own glory, namely, that they should be shadows and images by which God would be represented as approving himself, as existing in all things. Hence this glory is also said to be objectively in creatures, and even the most senseless creatures give glory to God. As for the claim that a certain more special glory is given to God by the holy minds, it comes to the same thing, for this glory is the work of God in those minds, and we must not think that any glory of God can proceed from a creature as from itself: God himself produces his glory in them and through them, or makes himself glorious in them, and creates them (by a singular benefit) for his glory. He himself puts in them more excellent outlines of himself, and brings it about that minds are spontaneously directed both to understand and to love the glorious nature of God, and to allow the work of the divine decree to be done in themselves, and to regard it as an effect and portrait of the most glorious God. In this way, truly, all things are done through the saints for the glory of God. But meanwhile let it be noted, as has been said, that this glory is not essential to the nature of God, since, had God wished to will nothing different from himself, it would not have existed; and nothing can be conceived as being added by anyone, not even by God, to the divine nature as something essential to it. It is not rendered more magnificent or more adorned in itself. All this must be referred to the decree of God in such a way that, if he has produced images of his glory in minds, and these praise God, it should not be thought that he has this need, or that it is necessary for him; rather he wills to be shadowed forth gloriously in his people, and our minds ought to be carried towards this with the highest fervour, because it has pleased him graciously that he should will it to be so. Verbal glory, speaking, singing, and so on, which many foolishly embrace as the true glory of God (indeed even of themselves), has no place here, where only thought is in question; and when it is alone, it deserves to be called smoke and lies.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII. CONCLUSIO hujus PARTIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII. CONCLUSION OF THIS PART.

units.la: §. 1. Reflexio ad præcedentia. 2. Attributorum Divinorum distributio generalior. 3. Specialior. 4. Via facilior ad ea cognoscenda. 5. 6. Hic non hærendum, sed ad notitiam infusam tendendum. 7. Remoto obstaculo, nempe malo, de quo postea tractabitur.
units.tr: §. 1. Reflection on what precedes. 2. A more general distribution of the Divine attributes. 3. A more specific one. 4. An easier way to know them. 5. 6. Here one must not stop, but strive towards infused knowledge. 7. The obstacle removed, namely evil, which will be treated later.

units.la: I. HÆc sunt quæ de Mente creata & de Deo dicenda erant, post quæ operæ erit pretium si ad conceptum Simplicitatis Dei recursus fiat, ne nimia cogitationum multitudine dissipetur Mens. Cæterum suffecerit Attributorum Divinorum generaliorem ideam hic proposuisse, vel saltem id conatum fuisse, quæ sit instar fundamenti vel potius areæ in qua quæ aliunde ex ratione circa hæc occurrent specialiora, vel quæ ex his ipsis deducentur, possint cum majori facilitate disponi: nam forte vix aliquid de hisce rebus ostendi poterit, quod non possit per hæc satis commode illustrari. Quare etiam omnes quæ de hisce ab aliis habentur opiniones, difficultates, controversiæ, non recensitæ sunt, siquidem una veritatis præsentia se ipsa sufficiat dispellendis qui-busvis nebulis, absque ulteriori apparatu.
units.tr: I. These are the things that had to be said concerning the created mind and concerning God. After them it will be worth the effort to return to the concept of the simplicity of God, lest the mind be scattered by too great a multitude of thoughts. Moreover, it will suffice to have proposed here a more general idea of the divine attributes, or at least to have attempted it, which serves as a foundation, or rather as a level area, on which the more specific considerations that arise from reason elsewhere, or that will be deduced from these very things, can be arranged with greater ease. For perhaps scarcely anything can be shown about these matters that cannot be sufficiently clearly illustrated through these. For this reason I have also not listed all the opinions, difficulties and controversies that others hold about these matters, since the mere presence of truth is enough in itself to disperse any mists whatsoever, without further apparatus.

units.la: II. Jam si consuetudinis ergo postuletur attributorum Divinorum distributio, & dictis sat patet eam esse omnium primam & utilissimam, quæ est attributorum ratione Naturæ sive Essentiæ, ut Intelligentia, Altitudo, Infinitas, &c. & attributorum ratione Placiti, ut cognitio, Indifferentia, &c. Imo sub quolibet ferme attributo, vel potius attri-buti nomine, latet ista distributio, ut sæpissime suis in locis fuit nota-tum: sed quod vulgo neglectum, confusum, permissum, non parum obfuit claritati facilitatique conceptuum de hisce.
units.tr: II. Now, if for the sake of custom a distribution of the divine attributes is demanded, it is quite clear from what has been said that the first and most useful one is that which divides the attributes by reason of nature or essence, such as Intelligence, Loftiness, Infinity, etc., and the attributes by reason of pleasure or will, such as knowledge, indifference, etc. Indeed, this distribution lies hidden under almost every attribute, or rather under the name of the attribute, as has been noted very often in its proper places. But because it is commonly neglected, confused and overlooked, it has not little hindered the clarity and ease of the concepts concerning these things.

units.la: III. Quodsi memoriæ causa, ut facilius attributa Divina certo or-dine enarrentur, specialiores eorum petantur distributiones, vix aliæ dari poterunt, quàm quæ ex occasione rerum à Deo diversarum desu-mentur. Inter quas præter illam quam quisque ex occasione suæ cogi-tationis, ut observatum est, desumere valet, sequentem adhibere licet. Attributa Divina concipi possunt, vel ex occasione universitatis rerum in genere, quæ universitas cum sit una, variata, cujus membra sibi invi-cem communicent, magna, cui tamen addi potest, nec tota comprehen-datur: hic de Deo cogitari datur, Unitas, Simplicitas, Bonitas, Altitudo, Infinitas, Incomprehensibilitas; vel ex specialiori consideratione rerum, quarum si spectes existentiam quoad ejus principium, inde Sufficientia, Potentia; quoad ejus durationem, Æternitas, Constantia; quoad finem, Immortalitas, tanquam ex occasionibus concipiuntur: Si rerum essen-tiam intuearis, & quidem in genere, seu res sint cogitantes aut secus, futuræ nec ne, Dominium; si in specie Essentiam rerum cogitantium naturamque earum ob oculos ponas, occurrent tibi de Deo, Vita, Spiritualitas, Activitas, Intelligentia, Libertas; Si earum naturæ statum aut perfectionum gradus, Cognitio, Impassibilitas, Felicitas; si regimen, Sapientia, Justitia, Veracitas, Sanctitas & Gloria. quæ quidem omnia sunt quæ in præcedentibus capitibus hactenus sunt proposita, etsi alio ordine. Modus quo attributa hæc occurrunt ex istis considerationibus, in sex prioribus notatus est, in cæteris vero quia est facillimus, est prætermissus. Ut autem neminem moveat quod Intelligentia quam ut hypo-stasin multi concipiunt, hic attributum appelletur, sciatur animum non esse hic de rebus istiusmodi disputare, adeoque per attributum nil aliud hic significari quam quicquid de Deo cogitari potest. Quod prius mo-nendum erat.
units.tr: III. But if, for the sake of memory, so that the divine attributes may be set out more easily in a certain order, more specific distributions are sought, scarcely any others can be given than those drawn from the occasion of things different from God. Among these, besides the one that each person can draw from the occasion of his own thinking, as has been observed, the following may be used. The divine attributes can be conceived either from the occasion of the universe of things in general, which universe, since it is one, varied, and its members communicate with one another, is great, yet it can be added to and is not wholly comprehended. Here we may think of God as Unity, Simplicity, Goodness, Loftiness, Infinity, Incomprehensibility. Or they are conceived, as from occasions, from a more specific consideration of things: if you look at their existence with respect to its principle, thence Sufficiency, Power; with respect to its duration, Eternity, Constancy; with respect to its end, Immortality. If you contemplate the essence of things, and indeed in general, whether they are thinking things or not, future or not, Dominion; if you set before your eyes the essence of thinking things in particular and their nature, there will present themselves to you concerning God Life, Spirituality, Activity, Intelligence, Freedom; if their state of nature or degrees of perfection, Knowledge, Impassibility, Happiness; if their government, Wisdom, Justice, Truthfulness, Holiness and Glory. All of these are the things that have so far been set forth in the preceding chapters, though in another order. The manner in which these attributes arise from these considerations has been noted in the first six, but in the rest, because it is very easy, it has been passed over. Yet so that no one may be troubled that many call Intelligence a hypostasis, and it is here called an attribute, let it be known that it is not our intention here to dispute about such things; accordingly, by attribute nothing else is meant here than whatever can be thought about God. This had to be noted first.

units.la: IV. Ultimam hanc viam attributa Divina enarrandi & cognoscen-di postposuerim illi, quæ ab initio ex inspectione solius Cogitationis est proposita & postmodum adhibita. Nam ultima hæc ex rebus extraneis & ignotis & partim ex terminis scholasticis, non cuivis per-spectis, non parum obscuritatis contrahit: Prior vero, quam sum se-cutus, ita naturalis, ita facilis est, ut nil evidentius faciliusque in statu naturali & discursivo inveniri potuerit. Naturalis est, cum sponte sua sine artis operosæ adminiculo sese cuilibet cogitationes, ordine fere eo-dem qui supra, sistere possint, quales mihi de me occurrerunt ex qui-bus ad Deum recurri: est quoque maxime facilis, cum fundetur tum in quibusdam perfectionibus quæ sunt in nobis, vel quæ potius à nobis ipsis non differunt; cum, & quidem utplurimum, in detectione im-perfectionum multarum nobis ita cognitarum, ut fieri nequeat, quin eas quisque in se sentiat, convincaturque eas esse revera imperfectiones, adeoque habeat statim actualem ideam absolutarum perfectionum eis oppositarum, hoc est, Dei ipsius. Non enim videtur posse aliquid tan-quam imperfectum agnosci, quin comparetur cum notitia perfectionis oppositæ, eo ipso cognitæ, ut ante demonstratum. Ergo cum & ipsæ Cogitationis imperfectiones adhibeantur ut inserviant ad eum cognitio-nis de Deo gradum qui in præcedentibus expositus est, non videtur esse ulla Mens, utut imperfecta sit, quæ ratione utens eousque attingere non possit, quo acquisito, ad ulteriora adspiret: hic enim ultimus gra-dus non est, imo ne vix quidem initium.
units.tr: IV. I would have placed this last way of setting out and knowing the divine attributes after that which was proposed at the beginning from the inspection of thought alone and afterwards employed. For this last way draws obscurity from things foreign and unknown, and partly from scholastic terms, which are not familiar to everyone, and so it contracts no small obscurity. But the former, which I have followed, is so natural and so easy that nothing more evident and easier could have been found in the natural and discursive state. It is natural, since the thoughts can present themselves spontaneously to anyone, without the aid of laborious art, in almost the same order as above, such as occurred to me about myself, from which I recurred to God. It is also most easy, since it is founded both on certain perfections that are in us, or which do not really differ from ourselves, and, and indeed for the most part, on the detection of many imperfections known to us in such a way that it cannot happen that each person does not feel them in himself, and is convinced that they are truly imperfections; and so he at once has an actual idea of the absolute perfections opposed to them, that is, of God himself. For it does not seem possible for anything to be recognised as imperfect without being compared with the knowledge of the opposite perfection, known by that very fact, as was demonstrated before. Therefore, since the imperfections of thought themselves are used to serve for that degree of knowledge of God which has been set out in the preceding chapters, there does not seem to be any mind, however imperfect, which, using reason, cannot attain so far that, having attained it, it aspires to higher things. For this is not the final degree, indeed not even scarcely the beginning.

units.la: V. Quapropter ne perniciola hic fiat confusio, etiam atque etiam monitum velim, Dei cognitionem, cum ejus acquirendæ ratione, prout hucusque tractata est, non proponi nisi ut naturalem, ut quæ ex prin-cipiis innatis, per rectam rationem, secundum veriores ratiocinandi le-ges, cuivis occurrere potest; ut ea maneat intemerata & intacta Dei no-titia ineffabilis & longe perfectior, quam in statu abnegationis & rege-nerationis infundit Spiritus Dei, ejus solus Doctor & distributor, quæ demum vere Theologica & Christiana Dei cognitio appellari meretur; & priori non quidem contrariatur, sed eam implet, vel potius absor-bet. Sed hodie non raro pro Cognitione Dei Theologica ea venditatur, quæ artibus obliquis acquisita & obscurata, & Scripturæ (si ea interdum adhibeatur) verbis sine Spiritu & ratione perceptis incrustata, sit vel ipsa naturali, imo Ethnica, in multis deterior.
units.tr: V. Therefore, lest a harmful confusion arise here, I would wish to be warned again and again that the knowledge of God, together with the way of acquiring it as it has been treated up to now, is proposed only as natural, as that which can occur to anyone from innate principles, through right reason, according to the truest laws of reasoning; so that the knowledge of God remains inviolate and untouched, that knowledge which is ineffable and far more perfect, which the Spirit of God pours in during the state of self-denial and regeneration, He being its sole teacher and dispenser, and which at last deserves to be called truly theological and Christian knowledge of God. It does not indeed contradict the former, but fulfils it, or rather absorbs it. Yet today there is often hawked as theological knowledge of God that which, acquired and darkened by crooked arts, and encrusted with the words of Scripture (if these are sometimes used) perceived without the Spirit and without reason, is in many respects worse than the natural, indeed the heathen, knowledge.

units.la: VI. Ne igitur hic hæreas & pauses. Ut quid tibi subsistendum in ea Dei cognitione quam Mentes perpetuo impuræ, infelices, Deoque exosæ, acquirere, & etiamnum atque in posterum possidere possint? Parum est quod ex Cogitationis tuæ & facultatum tuarum generaliorum qualicunque consideratione superficiarias de Deo cogitationes atque ratiocinia acquiras, ad quæ etiam ex imperfectionibus, imo ex illis quæ culpandæ sunt, introduci possis, ut hactenus plerumque factum est, ex consideratione Mentis, secundum primam suam definitionem, qua variabilis & limitata asserta est (lib. II. cap. VI.) consideratæ. Dignius Deum cognosces per tui in omnibus abnegationem: quam & nobilior sequetur Notitia à Deo speciali modo producta, cum nempe Deo in nobis miras suas operationes efficiente, istis perfectionibus tanquam Dei imaginibus & tabulis, licebit intueri, quæ quantaque sit Archetypi & Authoris pulchritudo. Quo pervenies, si secundum alteram Mentis definitionem, quod hæc tendat amore intelligendi ad Deum, cum sui ipsius despectu, progrediaris. Et hæc sunt praxeos, non ratiocinationis. Sed (quæ tertia Dei cognoscendi via est, juxta tertiam Mentis descriptionem) ubi abnegatio, &, ut sic dicam, oblivio nostri, atque Dei operatio, perfectæ sunt futuræ, tunc perfecta erit Dei cognitio, multiplicitasque conceptuum volatilium in unum solidum nescio quid absorbebitur, & velut perdetur, instar guttulæ cui torrens, cui fluvius, cui mare, superadderentur, à quibus esset absorpta. Et hoc tertium est ex genere eorum, in quibus homo, ut nihil activi sese habens, facultatem de illis loquendi & ratiocinandi non habet: quæ proprie ineffabilia sunt, & dici queant manna absconditum, quod soli Sancti interdum hic gustant; nomenque nulli nisi possessori notum; Ab inexpertis hæc non exspectanda: cæci sunt, etsi sibi videre videantur. Si de his aliquid fando audire lubet, consule Divinum & horum expertum Taulerum in omnibus ejus operibus.
units.tr: VI. Do not, then, stop and linger here. Why should you stay content with that knowledge of God which minds, perpetually impure, unhappy, and hateful to God, can acquire, and still possess now and in the future? It is too little that by some consideration of your thought and of your more general faculties you acquire superficial thoughts and reasonings about God, to which one could also be led from imperfections, indeed from those things which deserve blame, as has mostly been done hitherto, by considering the mind according to its first definition, by which it has been declared variable and limited (book II, chapter VI). You will know God more worthily through the denial of yourself in all things; and a nobler knowledge will follow, produced by God in a special manner, since, when God works in us His wonderful operations, it will be permitted to behold, in these perfections as in images and pictures of God, how great and what kind of beauty there is in the Archetype and Author. You will arrive there if, according to the second definition of the mind, you advance, in that it tends by the love of understanding towards God, with contempt for yourself. And these belong to practice, not to reasoning. But (which is the third way of knowing God, according to the third description of the mind) when denial, and, as I may call it, the forgetting of ourselves, and the operation of God shall be perfected, then the knowledge of God will be perfect, and the multiplicity of fleeting concepts will be absorbed into a certain solid something I know not what, and as it were lost, like a little drop to which a torrent, a river, or the sea were added, by which it would be swallowed up. And this third is of the kind of things in which man, having nothing active in himself, has no power of speaking and reasoning about them: they are properly ineffable, and may be called the hidden manna, which only the saints sometimes taste here; and its name is known to none except the possessor. These things are not to be expected from the inexperienced: they are blind, though they seem to themselves to see. If it pleases you to hear anything about these matters by report, consult the divine Tauler, who has experience of them, in all his works.

units.la: VII. Quoniam autem in nobis universis existat obstaculum quod Divinissimæ huic Dei Notitiæ ita opponitur, ut nisi illud removeatur, hanc non sit nobis largiturus Deus, danda est opera ut hoc agatur, atque adeo ut quamprimum recte & evidenter agnoscatur id obstaculi (quod malum & peccatum appellatur) quo deinceps nullus ei aditus in Mente patefiat. Et hoc est quod in sequenti Libro tractabitur. Hoc agnito, si Mens eo purgari peroptet constanter & sincere, non dubium est quin Deus opitulatum veniat atque operatum, nec quin det ipse quæcunque ad Divinissimam sui Notitiam & fruitionem pertinent, etiam nullo intercedente humano externoque discursu : Etenim si creaturæ rebus externis undique circumstrepentibus circumcinctæ, eisque applicatæ, nimisque occupatæ, malo peccatoque penetratæ, hoc nihilominus gratiæ præstat Creator, ut in illo statu copiam atque ideam sui, quam deduximus, mirandam sane, excitet, & magis magisque promoveat, utendo vel ipsis rebus externis & imperfectis, literis, characteribus, sonis, quæ nexum necessarium cum illo non habent, imo ipsismet imperfectionibus à quibus abhorret; multo magis cum illa istis erit libera & vacua solique Creatori dedita, Hic Illi Ideam sui & Copiam per se, istis velis remotis, immediate impressurus & aucturus[?] censendus est.
units.tr: VII. Since there exists in all of us an obstacle that opposes this most holy knowledge of God in such a way that, unless it is removed, God will not bestow it upon us, care must be taken to deal with it, and so, as soon as possible, that obstacle (which is called evil and sin) must be recognised correctly and clearly, so that no entrance for it opens in the mind thereafter. This is what will be treated in the following Book. Once this is recognised, if the mind desires constantly and sincerely to be purged of it, there is no doubt that God will come to help and to work, and that he will himself give whatever pertains to his most holy knowledge and enjoyment, even without any intervening human or external discourse. For if the Creator, while the creature is surrounded on every side by external things clamouring about it, and is applied to them, too much occupied, and penetrated by evil and sin, nevertheless grants this grace: that in that state he stirs up and more and more advances the abundance and idea of himself, which we have set out, truly wonderful, making use even of external and imperfect things, letters, characters, sounds, which have no necessary connection with him, indeed even of the very imperfections from which he shrinks; how much more, when the mind is free and empty of these and given wholly to the Creator alone, is he to be thought to impress and increase his own idea and abundance immediately in it, by himself, with these veils removed.

units.la: O Deus, quis Similis Tibi? Psal. 71: 19.
units.tr: O God, who is like unto thee? Ps. 71:19.

units.la: Nullus plane est sicut Tu, Domine. Jerem. x. 6.
units.tr: There is plainly none like thee, O Lord. Jer. 10:6.

units.la: LIBER QUARTUS IN QUO DE MALO sive PECCATO AGITUR. CAPUT I.
units.tr: BOOK FOUR, IN WHICH EVIL, OR SIN, IS TREATED. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De iis quæ ad sequentia sunt prænotanda.
units.tr: Concerning what must be noted in advance of what follows.

units.la: I. DE Realitate Summa, & de intermediis, præ-sertim vero cogitantibus, sive de Deo & de creaturis, maxime de spiritualibus, hactenus dictum est. Sed cum hæ posterioris generis malo sint obnoxiæ, eoque nonnullæ, specia-liter vero omnes Mentes humanæ, interdum contaminentur, necesse est, ut rerum omnium in genere fundamentales notitiæ habeantur, de malo quædam meditari. Quare de eo in posterum agetur, Deo juvante; Sed prius monita hæc animadvertantur.
units.tr: I. Up to now we have spoken of the Supreme Reality and of intermediaries, especially thinking beings, that is, of God and of creatures, and most of all of spiritual creatures. But since creatures of the latter kind are subject to evil, and since some of them, and especially all human minds, are at times contaminated by it, it is necessary, if we are to have fundamental notions of all things in general, to meditate on evil to some extent. Therefore it will be treated hereafter, God helping; but first let the following remarks be noted.

units.la: II. Primo, ne malum culpæ, cujus natura, non vero sequelæ, hic est proponenda, cum malo poenæ confundatur, sæpissime hic nomine peccati designabitur.
units.tr: II. First, since the evil of guilt, whose nature and not its consequence is to be set out here, is confused with the evil of punishment, it will very often be designated here by the name of sin.

units.la: III. Secundo, scopus hic non est, ut cujusvis cupiditati curiosi-que quæstionibus satisfiat, quod ipsum à peccato non esset alienum: sed tantum ut quilibet de peccatis propriis inquirere serio volens eo ducatur, ut Deo soli det gloriam agnoscendo omnia realia esse ab ipso; se ipsum vero, à quo nil reale est, deprimat usque ad nihil; atque etiam se non modo ad nihil usque deprimat, verum quoque ob malum admissum infra nihil sese dejectum videat, sentiat, odiosum & juxta inexcusabilem habeat. Quæ tria certe apta sunt satisfacere quantum hac in re potest requiri, cujusvis conscientiæ. Si quis autem de peccatis aliorum, velut infantum, specialius inquirat, quia hoc non tam ad bonum eorum de quibus sic quæritur, utpote qui disciplinæ sunt incapaces, quam ad curiositatem quærentium postulatur, responsa aliunde exspectet. De adultis non quidem quoad species, gradus, durationem peccati, sed quoad ejus radicem, fundum, rationem, vel potius absurditatem, quilibet hæc capiens, ex se ipso, sive ex sui ipsius experientia, facile judica-bit. bit. Nam uno nequam agnito, cæteros omnes ejusdem farinæ nullo labore noscere licet.
units.tr: III. Second, the aim here is not to satisfy the desire or the curious questions of anyone at all, which would not be foreign to sin itself; rather, the aim is only that whoever seriously wishes to inquire into his own sins may be led to give glory to God alone, by acknowledging that all things real are from Him; and that he himself, from whom nothing real comes, may be brought down to nothing, and may see, feel and hold himself not only brought down to nothing, but also, on account of the evil he has committed, cast down below nothing, and hateful and inexcusable. These three things are certainly suited to satisfy, as far as in this matter can be required, the conscience of anyone. If, however, someone wishes to inquire more particularly into the sins of others, such as infants, since this is demanded less for the good of those about whom such questions are asked (as they are incapable of discipline) than for the curiosity of those who ask, let him look for answers elsewhere. As for adults, anyone who grasps these matters will easily judge, from himself, or from his own experience, not indeed the kinds, degrees or duration of sin, but its root, foundation and reason, or rather its absurdity. For once one villain is recognised, all the others of the same stamp can be known without any labour.

units.la: IV. Tertio, Cum hic scholastico modo locum communem de peccato proponere non sit animus, sed tantum ea ostendere quæ ex principiis Menti innatis, ut hactenus factum est, secundum recte rationis normam circa peccata quæ actuali modo admittuntur, possunt demonstrari; non est quod ullus commoveatur si principia, si methodus, si nomina quæ eorum scriptis vulgantur, non sint adhibita; si peccatorum definitiones communes, sive veras, sive falsas, si partitiones in peccata originis, imputationis, propagationis, habitus, & similes, silentio prætereamus. Quæ de his similibusve ab aliis scripta sunt, suis in locis relinquuntur, neque de illis quicquam hic vel negatur, vel quidem judicatur. Quodsi quis sua in sequentibus dogmata desideret, nolim idcirco eum magis indignari, quam cum in scriptis Philosophicis non invenit sermones de mysterio Incarnationis aut Resurrectionis. Nam Philosophi ista omittentes, eo quod ex principiis quibus utuntur non vident illa manare, non ideo negant eadem ex aliis principiis posse & inveniri & demonstrari. Hic autem non utimur nisi principiis naturalibus; quanquam tamen ex illis ea possint deduci quibus cæteræ peccati species magis quam à multis credi possit, illustrentur. Sed hæc prætermittimus.
units.tr: IV. Third, since it is not my intention to set out here, in the scholastic manner, a common topic on sin, but only to show what can be demonstrated, according to the rule of right reason, concerning actual sins, from the principles innate to the mind, as has been done up to now, there is no reason for anyone to be disturbed if the principles, the method and the terms that are circulated in their writings are not employed; if we pass over in silence the common definitions of sin, whether true or false, and the divisions into sin of origin, of imputation, of propagation, of habit, and the like. What has been written about these or similar matters by others is left in its own place, and nothing is either denied or indeed judged here about them. But if anyone desires in what follows his own doctrines, I would not wish him to be the more indignant on that account than when he does not find in philosophical writings discourses on the mystery of the Incarnation or the Resurrection. For philosophers, omitting those things because they do not see them flowing from the principles they use, do not therefore deny that the same things can both be found and be demonstrated from other principles. Here, however, we use only natural principles; although from them those things can be deduced by which the other species of sin may be illustrated more than many believe possible. But we set these aside.

units.la: V. Ut autem, quod quartum est, in antecessum de istorum, quibus hic utimur, principiorum valore certior detur persuasio, velim adverti ea esse quæ non modo ad syntheresin possint referri, suamque adeo secum certitudinem attendenti inculcent, verum etiam quæ à scriptis sacris commendentur, dum his asseritur, legem in mentibus dari inscriptam, principium discretionis boni & mali, hominesque secundum ejus tenorem esse judicandos.
units.tr: V. Now, as to the fourth point, so that a more certain persuasion may be given in advance of the value of the principles we use here, I would have it noticed that these are principles which can not only be referred to synteresis, and which impress their own certainty on anyone who attends to it, but also which are commended by the sacred writings, while it is asserted in these that a law is given written in minds, a principle of discernment of good and evil, and that men are to be judged according to its tenor.

units.la: VI. Denique velim ut ea mente teneantur quæ in Libro secundo, capitibus sexto & octavo, item quæ in Tertio de Dei Dominio, de Bonitate, de Potentia, de Libertate, maxime Indifferentiæ, de Justitia, de Sanctitate, & de Gloria dicta sunt: etenim in his sequentium principia omnia continentur & probantur; & quidem ita, ut reliquus labor omnis in eorum dispositione, conclusionum ex iis deductione, eorumque ad hoc negotium applicatione consistat.
units.tr: VI. Finally, I would wish these things to be held in mind which were said in the second book, in chapters six and eight, likewise what was said in the third concerning the Dominion of God, concerning His Goodness, Power, Liberty (especially Indifference), Justice, Holiness and Glory: for in these all the principles of what follows are contained and proved; and indeed in such a way that all the remaining labour consists in their arrangement, in the deduction of conclusions from them, and in their application to this business.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: I. Generalissima notio peccati. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. A peccato generalius subducuntur quae ad illud non spectant, Deus, Dei placitum, Dei opus ut a Deo est, Absolutum nihil, nihil existentia, & nihil admixtum realitati, quatenus id a Deo est. 7. Non autem quatenus est ab homine.
units.tr: I. The most general notion of sin. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Those things that do not pertain to sin are set aside from the more general account: God, God's pleasure, God's work as it is from God, the Absolute Nothing, nothing of existence, and nothing mixed with reality, insofar as it is from God. 7. But not insofar as it is from man.

units.la: I. SEd ad majorem evidentiam, res ab ovo, ut ajunt, est exponenda. Principio itaque peccati generalior notio habenda est, etsi confusior, ut saltem non nesciamus quid quaeratur: neque absurde petitur in antecessum generalior illius notitia, cujus speciialius natura inquirenda est. Eam autem recte desumemus ex notione Justitiae, oppositum ejus Mente percipientes, indecentiam videlicet, incongruitatem, repugnantiam in re secum, vel cum suo statu. Quae sit illa res, quae repugnantia in ea, singularius est detegendum.
units.tr: I. But for greater clarity, the matter must be set out from the egg, as they say. First, then, we must have a more general notion of sin, though a more confused one, so that at least we do not fail to know what is being sought. Nor is it absurd to seek beforehand a more general knowledge of that thing whose nature is to be investigated more specifically. We shall rightly derive it from the notion of justice, conceiving in the mind its opposite, namely indecency, incongruity, and inconsistency in a thing with itself, or with its own state. What that thing is, and what the inconsistency in it is, must be disclosed more particularly.

units.la: II. Ut autem hic nihil alieni assumatur, nullum phantasma quo er-rori locus dari possit, removeo quantum possum omnia, & quam minimum potero resumam.
units.tr: II. But so that nothing foreign is assumed here, and no phantasm is left by which error could find a place, I remove as far as I can all things, and I will take up as little as I possibly can.

units.la: III. Primo igitur, omnia quae possent non esse, suppono non esse, sic apud me cogitans: Si Deus ita solus esset, ut praeter illum, praeter ejus Essentiam, ejus Naturae veritates, nihil plane esset, non modo nulla res existens, sed & nulla essentia, nulla idea, nulla veritas statuta, verum absolutum omnium rerum, essentiarum, veritatum, idearum Nihil, (quod se ita habere potuisse ex dictis de Dominio Dei demonstratum est) tunc non posset esse peccatum.
