Et hoc satis per se manifestum est, siquidem Natura Dei perfectissima est, sibi convenientissima, concordantissima, unitissima ut sic dicam; Neque esset ei incongruum & male conveniens eive contraveniret ut Una & Sola omnibus quibuscunque absolute exclusis, esset. (ex Dominio.) Quare concludo Divinam Essentiam sive Naturam incapacem esse peccati; & praeterea, absolutum omnium rerum nihil non esse peccatum.
units.tr: III. First, then, I suppose that all things which could not be are not, thinking thus within myself: If God were so alone that, apart from him, apart from his Essence and the truths of his Nature, there were absolutely nothing, not only no existing thing, but no essence, no idea, no established truth, but the absolute nothing of all things, essences, truths and ideas (which, as has been shown from what was said about the Dominion of God, could have been so), then there could be no sin. And this is clear enough in itself, since the Nature of God is most perfect, most fitting to itself, most harmonious, and most one, so to speak. Nor would it be incongruous or ill-fitting for it, or contrary to it, to be One and Alone, with all other things absolutely excluded (from the Dominion). Therefore I conclude that the Divine Essence or Nature is incapable of sin; and moreover, that the absolute nothing of all things is not sin.

units.la: IV. Secundo, si Deus (quem cum placito suo jam confidero) ita solus esset, ut praeter ejus placitum de rebus statuendis, ponendis, gubernandis, nil esset, sive, si res illae nondum existerent, sed, ut ante creationem, essent adhuc existendae; tunc nondum peccatum fore facile percipio. Peccatum ergo in placito inque conceptu Dei quaeri non debet: nam qualecunque effet vel esse posset id Dei placitum, id tamen effet Deo dignum, (ex Justitia) & bonum, (ex Bonitate) Deusque se in illo quæreret, (ex Sanctitate) adeoque effet illud Dei repræsentatio & imago, haberetque Deum pro principio, medio & scopo, quæ omnia optima, & secum in Deo convenientissima sunt, adeoque peccatum non inferunt. Imo ne possibilitati quidem peccati dat ex se locum Dei placitum, sic absque opere externo consideratum, quod quamdiu ita est, peccatum ne potest quidem existere vel existendum concipi. Dices, inde tamen haberi sive concipi, peccatum possibile esse, adeoque conceptum sive notionem ideamve peccati, à placito Dei esse desumendam, absque quo peccatum plane non esset, ne quidem potentia nec in conceptu. Respondeo primo, neque possibilitatem peccati, neque conceptum sive notionem ejus peccatum esse. Præterea, peccati notionem atque possibilitatem esse quidem eatenus à placito Dei quatenus si Deo non placuisset ullam rem statuere faciendam, etiam peccatum esse & nosci non posset, velut si me non statuisset esse, non à me peccatum committi & nosci potuisset: Sed hoc nihil aliud est quam dicere, possibilitatem subjecti in quo esse & nosci potest peccatum, à Dei placito esse desumendam. At vero ipsa notio, idea, natura possibilitatis peccati non est à placito Dei, nec ideo quod res statutæ sint; sed ab eo est, quod res, si quæ statuantur, ex se & sine interventu placiti Dei, sint nihil solidum, nil subsistens, nil se conservans, sint non-Deus. quare ut deficiendi sint capaces, non opus est placitum Dei positive intervenire. Hac ergo de causa & hoc sensu sine placito Dei peccatum est possibile, sive datur ejus possibilitatis conceptus, cujus ratio & causa non est placitum Dei.
units.tr: IV. Second, if God (whom I now consider together with his pleasure) were so alone that, apart from his pleasure concerning things to be decreed, established and governed, there were nothing; or if those things did not yet exist, but, as before creation, were still to be brought into existence, then I readily perceive that there would not yet be sin. Sin, therefore, must not be sought in the pleasure or in the conception of God. For whatever that pleasure of God was, or could be, it would still be worthy of God (from justice), and good (from goodness), and God would seek himself in it (from holiness), and it would be a representation and image of God, and would have God as its principle, means and end; all of which are most excellent and most fitting together in God, and so do not imply sin. Indeed, God's pleasure, considered thus without external work, does not in itself even give a place to the possibility of sin; and as long as it is so, sin cannot even be conceived as existing or to be existing. You will say that from this it is nonetheless had, or conceived, that sin is possible, and so the conception, notion or idea of sin must be derived from God's pleasure, without which sin would not be at all, not even in power nor in conception. I answer, first, that neither the possibility of sin nor the conception or notion of it is sin. Moreover, the notion and the possibility of sin are indeed derived from God's pleasure only in this respect: that if it had not pleased God to establish anything to be made, sin could neither be nor be known, just as, if he had not willed that I should be, I could not have committed or known sin. But this is nothing other than to say that the possibility of the subject in which sin can be and be known is to be derived from God's pleasure. But the very notion, idea and nature of the possibility of sin is not from God's pleasure, nor because things have been established; it is from the fact that things, if any are established, are of themselves, and without the intervention of God's pleasure, nothing solid, nothing subsisting, nothing preserving itself, are non-God. Therefore, in order that they be capable of failing, it is not necessary for God's pleasure to intervene positively. For this reason, and in this sense, sin is possible without God's pleasure, or there is a conception of this possibility whose reason and cause is not God's pleasure.

units.la: Ex quibus evidenter elucescit, Deum ut Essentiarum, naturarum, formarum, veritatumque causa statuens dicitur, (ex Dominio) non ita dici posse peccati formam essentiamque, (quæcunque sit) statuisse, nedum ejus existentis causam efficientem esse: Nam cum efficere sit vim & simulacrum placiti externo opere testari, qui id operabitur quod ne quidem statuit? non autem statuit quod se non decet suumque opus. Objectum placiti est realitas & decentia. Quod placitum est, eo ipso decens & bonum est. Quod nil perfectionis habet causam statuentem non requirit, nec statuitur, sed linquitur, ut sic dicam, intactum. Improprie itaque dicitur, Deum decernere ut fiant peccata, ut & improprie quoque, peccata esse contra placitum Dei: Nam quemadmodum Deus cum ejus placito, quanquam omnis realitas quæ in subjecto peccati ab ipso pendeat, non tamen tangit ulla quæ in peccato sunt, sic neque ab illis tangitur, nec ejus placitum per contrarium positive premitur, à quo evacuetur. Magis proprie dici posse putaverim, peccatum esse sine placito Dei, sinentis id fieri in subjectis iis quæ bene voluit statuere, efficere, regere. Hoc de Deo cogitare indignum non est. Si quis culpæ conceptus in hoc involvatur, ejus rationem esse à subjecto peccati desumendam, eique jure tribuendam, postea videbimus.
units.tr: From these things it clearly appears that, although God is said (from Dominion) to be the cause of the establishing of essences, natures, forms and truths, it cannot in the same way be said that he established the form or essence of sin (whatever it may be), much less that he is the efficient cause of its existence. For since to effect is to show forth power and the image of a pleasure by external work, who would effect what he does not even establish? But he does not establish what is not fitting for him and for his work. The object of pleasure is reality and fittingness. What is pleasing is by that very fact fitting and good. What has no perfection does not require an establishing cause, and is not established, but is left, so to speak, untouched. It is therefore improperly said that God decrees that sins should come about, and likewise improperly that sins are against the pleasure of God. For just as God with his pleasure, although every reality that is in the subject of sin depends on him, does not touch any of the things that are in sin, so neither is he touched by them, nor is his pleasure positively pressed by the contrary, by which it would be emptied. I would think it more proper to say that sin is without the pleasure of God, in that he permits it to happen in those subjects which he willed well to establish, effect and govern. To think this of God is not unworthy. If the conception of guilt is involved in this, we shall see later that its reason is to be derived from the subject of sin, and rightly attributed to it.

units.la: Ex his quoque evincitur, quod si quid sit decretum nec tamen adhuc existat, id peccatum non esse, sive nihil existentiæ non esse peccatum.
units.tr: From these things also it is proven that, if something is decreed and yet does not yet exist, that is not sin; or that nothing of existence is not sin.

units.la: V. Hisce tum de Deo solo, tum de Deo cum ejus placito considerationibus, tertiam adjungo quæ rerum decretarum existentiam involvit. Nempe, si quæ Deo placuit statuere, ita essent producta atque existerent, ut in illis nihil præterquam quod sint placiti Divini opus, considerandum occurreret, ne tunc quidem ullum peccatum eatenus deprehendo. Non enim est incongruum, sed è contra valde decens est ut placitum Dei Deumque decens, à Deo complementum sortiatur. (ex Potentia.) Et res effecta non potest non eatenus esse perfecta, cum sit effectus repræsentans Sapientissimam causam. Quare nullum Dei opus, nullas res existentes & durantes peccatum esse concludo; seu omnes res sint æque perfectæ, seu non sint æque perfectæ; seu simul ponantur, sive unæ post alias; imo etiamsi suas quæque perfectiones non adipiscantur simul, sed gradatim, v. g. si gradatim dentur & augeantur in corporibus quidem organa, moles, vires, in mentibus vero cognitio, scientia, prudentia, sive etiam secus omnia simul darentur. Non est incongruum, nec ulli decentiæ contravenit ut ea sive semel sive per vices accipiant realitates, quæ à mera Creatoris nil cuiquam debentis liberalitate proficiscuntur. Quare realitas admixta nihilo, hoc est, nondum adhuc eas adepta perfectiones quas in posterum adeptura sit, non infert ex sese peccatum.
units.tr: V. From these considerations, first of God alone, and then of God together with his pleasure, I add a third, which involves the existence of decreed things. Namely, if the things which it pleased God to establish were so produced and existed that in them nothing were to be considered except that they are the work of the divine pleasure, then I do not detect any sin even so far. For it is not incongruous, but on the contrary very fitting, that the pleasure of God, and God who is fitting, should receive completion from God (from power). And an effected thing cannot but be perfect to that extent, since it is an effect representing the most wise cause. Therefore I conclude that no work of God, no existing and enduring things, is sin; whether all things are equally perfect or not equally perfect; whether they are posited together or one after another; indeed even if they do not obtain all their perfections at once but gradually, for example if in bodies organs, bulk and powers are given and increased gradually, and in minds knowledge, science and prudence; or even if all things were given at once otherwise. It is not incongruous, nor does it contravene any fittingness, that they should receive realities, whether once or by turns, which proceed from the mere liberality of the Creator, who owes nothing to anyone. Therefore reality mixed with nothing, that is, not yet having obtained those perfections which it is to obtain in future, does not of itself imply sin.

units.la: VI. Animadverto itaque Dei τὸ εἶναι[?], placere, statuere, velle, decernere, efficere, plane non tangere peccata: Deum non habere in se, in statuto, in opere, aliquid positivi quod peccatum ullo modo attingat sive illuc tendat. Blasphemè contrarium assereretur. Peccatum est quid plane derelictum à Deo, qui non habet commercium in esse, in statuendo, in agendo, nisi cum realitate & perfectione. Sive ergo Dei naturam solam spectem, sive eam cum placito, sive eam cum operibus, nullum peccatum eatenus, nullam peccati causam deprehendo: & tamen datur peccatum, & in me datur, & non est merum nihil, sed aliquid habet, quodcunque sit, quod instar formæ & essentiæ sit. Non est quid existens, & tamen non est mere non-existens. Non est placitum & opus Dei, ego sum opus placiti Dei, & nihilominus habeo peccatum. Quo-modo hæc incomposita in congruum ordinem redigemus? At qui con-gruere possent, siquidem est de natura peccati ut fit absurdum & inordi-natum? Interim tamen cum conceptus peccati non fit peccatum, cum-que absurdi recta possit haberi cognitio, etsi forte non undique clariffi-ma, siquidem omnis absurditas aliquid obscuri involvat, tentabo eam qualitercunque adipisci. Quapropter circumspiciam me diligentius. Nam utut ex jam dictis collegero peccatum esse aliquod nihil, quod pra-ve, indebite, indecenter, imitatur formam realitatis; esse non placi-tum, non opus Dei; esse placiti operationisque Dei absentiam in eo sub-jecto cujus omnis realitas est effectus placiti Dei; his tamen similibusve definitionibus non sufficienter effecero, ut, (caeteris quaestionibus præ-termissis) ubi, unde, quid, quove modo existat peccatum, quam cla-riffime fieri possit percipiatur.
units.tr: VI. I observe, therefore, that God's τὸ εἶναι [being?] — his willing, purposing, decreeing, effecting — does not touch sins at all: God has in himself, in his decree, in his work, nothing positive that reaches sin in any way or tends towards it. To assert the contrary would be blasphemy. Sin is something utterly abandoned by God, who has no dealings in being, in decreeing, or in acting except with reality and perfection. Whether, then, I consider God's nature alone, or that nature together with his decree, or together with his works, I find no sin and no cause of sin in any of these respects. And yet sin exists, and it exists in me, and it is not sheer nothing, but has something, whatever it is, which serves as its form and essence. It is not something existing, and yet it is not purely non-existent. It is not the decree and work of God; I am the work of God's decree, and nevertheless I have sin. How shall we bring these incongruous things into a fitting order? Could they agree at all, since it is of the nature of sin to be absurd and disordered? Meanwhile, however, since the concept of sin is not sin itself, and since a correct knowledge of the absurd can be had, even if perhaps not altogether clear (for every absurdity involves something obscure), I shall try to attain it in whatever way I can. Therefore I shall look around myself more diligently. For although from what has been said I have gathered that sin is a certain nothing which wrongly, improperly and indecently imitates the form of reality; that it is not a decree or work of God, but the absence of God's decree and working in that subject whose whole reality is the effect of God's decree; yet by these and similar definitions I have not sufficiently managed to make it clearly perceived (setting other questions aside) where, whence, what, and in what manner sin exists.

units.la: VII. Forsan vero id clarius confecero, si animadvertens peccatum non esse Ens seorsim consideratum, neque esse nihil seorsim spectatum, suspicatus fuero id in mixtione utriusque esse deprehendendum. Nam quid, & ubi, & unde præterea esset? Atqui mox vidi realitatem admix-tam nihilo peccatum non involvere. Sed esto. Mixtio ista quatenus à Deo est facta, vere recteque facta sit, cum potentissimum Ens possit revera in nihilo realitatem ponere, si velit: Attamen si mixtio ista fiat indebite, nempe ab Ente impotente, à me qui nihil ex me sum, si vide-licet tentem nihilo interponere realitatem, sive Entitatem quandam, nonne hoc pro absurdo & malo habendum erit? Certe hic aliquid subest ejus quod quaerimus. At quia ista hoc modo valde abstracta sunt, ter-minique non usitati, satius est ea ut sunt in subjecto quod corpore & Mente constat, considerare, & verbis quantum fieri potest vulgaribus exprimere; quam persequi modo nec satis intelligibili, nec ob abstra-ctionem, fixo satis. Entis igitur & nihili generaliores considerationes præ-termitto, ut assumam quid determinatius.
units.tr: VII. Perhaps I would have confirmed this more clearly if, noticing that sin is neither being considered in isolation nor nothing considered in isolation, I had suspected that it is to be found in the mixture of both. For what, and where, and whence would it otherwise be? Yet I soon saw that reality mixed with nothing does not involve sin. But granted. This mixture, insofar as it is made by God, is truly and rightly made, since the most powerful Being can indeed place reality in nothing, if he wills. Yet if this mixture is made improperly, namely by a being that is powerless, by me who am nothing of myself, if I should try to interpose some reality or certain entity into nothing, must not this be regarded as absurd and evil? Certainly something underlies what we are seeking here. But since these matters are very abstract in this way, and their terms unusual, it is better to consider them as they are in the subject which consists of body and mind, and to express them in ordinary words as far as possible, rather than to pursue them in an abstract manner that is neither sufficiently intelligible nor, on account of the abstraction, sufficiently fixed. I therefore set aside the more general considerations of being and nothing, so that I may take up something more determinate.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: I. 2. 3. 4. Quid specialius à peccato sit subducendum (1) in Corpore. 5. (2) In sensibus & passionibus. 6. 7. 8. (3) in Mente. Mentis materiale & formale, error, facultates, habitus, actus, ignorantia, notitia, spontaneitas, ut ad illud se habeant? Non est explicita Dei rejectio. 9. Peccati specialior designatio. 10. ad illud reflexio non requiritur.
units.tr: I, 2, 3, 4. What more specifically must be removed from sin: (1) in the body; 5. (2) in the senses and passions; 6, 7, 8. (3) in the mind. The material and formal of the mind: error, faculties, habits, acts, ignorance, knowledge, spontaneity, and how these stand in relation to it. There is no explicit rejection of God. 9. A more specific designation of sin. 10. Reflection upon it is not required.

units.la: I. Concipio Deum & nihil, me vero quasi inter utrumque, quatenus à me ipso plane nihil, quatenus autem à Dei placito, aliquid, quod nec sit, nec habeat omnia. Intuebor itaque tum realitates quasdam quas possideo, tum quarumdam quæ mihi desunt absentiam, ut sciam quid sit in his non modo subjectum proprium sed & formale peccati. Et posset id quidem solam Mentem, ut hactenus factum est, contemplando, breviori via absolvi, quæ veritatis præsentia errorem depelleret: at quoniam multi plurimis, iisque solitis impediuntur ambagibus, in quas ex consuetudine recidunt, non advertentes eas veris principiis repugnare nisi de hoc expresse moneantur; cum etiam nihil communius sit illo superstitionis principio, quo justitia vel peccatum in rebus extensis corporeisque, in mole, in motibus quæratur, & præcipue collocetur; corpus juxta cum mente inspiciendum resumam, siquidem constem ex utroque.
units.tr: I. I conceive of God and of nothing; I myself stand as it were between the two: from myself I am plainly nothing, but from God's pleasure I am something, which neither is nor has all things. I shall therefore consider both certain realities which I possess and the absence of certain realities which are lacking to me, so that I may know what in these is not only the proper subject but also the formal element of sin. And indeed this could be settled by contemplating the mind alone, as has been done so far, by a shorter way, which the presence of truth would drive out error; but since many people are hindered by many and familiar entanglements, into which they fall out of habit, not noticing that these are opposed to true principles unless they are expressly warned of this; and since nothing is more common than that superstitious principle by which righteousness or sin is sought in extended and bodily things, in mass, in motions, and is chiefly placed there, I shall take up the body as well, to be examined alongside the mind, since I consist of both.

units.la: II. Corporis mei naturam quod concernit, non possum eam in suspicionem peccati adducere si eam in genere, quatenus cum aliis communis est, extensa est, divisibilis, mobilis, mota, quiescens, &c. considepo: nam eatenus merum opus Dei est, & brutum opus, quale ne subjectum quidem esse peccati, indubium est. In peccatum quoque non imputari debet absentia quarumdam realitatum, ut quod non habeat omnes partes, omnem molem, omnes motus, &c. possibiles, quorum absentia est merum nihil. Hæc ad omnia corpora debent extendi: nam ex uno potest hic tuto inductio fieri.
units.tr: II. As far as the nature of my body is concerned, I cannot bring it under suspicion of sin if I consider it in general, insofar as it is extended, divisible, mobile, moved, at rest, etc., and in common with other things. For so far it is purely the work of God and a brute work, and it is beyond doubt that it is not even the subject of sin. Nor should the absence of certain realities be imputed to it as sin, such as that it does not have all parts, all mass, all possible motions, etc., whose absence is pure nothing. This must be extended to all bodies, for from one case a safe induction can be made here.

units.la: III. Corpus quoque qua humanum est, certa mole donatum, alia carens, certis figuris, motibus, humoribus, temperamentis præditum, certisque destitutum, peccati culpam non infert. Si quæ de ejus motibus vel humoribus est difficultas, facile elevabitur. Omnis quippe corporis motus, ejusque gradus, varietas, determinatio, sunt opus Solius Potentiæ Divinæ; eorumque positio nec ab hominis, nec ab Angeli, nec ab ullius creaturæ vi accedit; quod ex Dei Potentia demonstratur. Atque hîc expresse ad motus determinationem omnem pronunciatum extendo, omnis quippe non à me, sed à Deo est: & quamvis mihi videantur quamplurimæ motuum corporis mei determinationes à me esse, quoniam fiunt cum interventu meæ voluntatis, attamen rem penitius inspiciendo nulla apparet necessaria connexio inter mentis voluntatem de movendo membro, quod fit per effluxum Spirituum animalium (quos illa ignorare potest) in tubulos & canales incognitos, ad certa receptacula, (quæ etiam non novit,) & de quibus nil cogitat :) & inter effectuum horumce executionem. Quomodo unum vi existentiæ suæ alterius existentiam inferret, cum utrumque se ipsum ne ponat quidem, neque cum altero conveniat essentia, cum unum sit cogitationis, alterum extensionis modus? Sed & experientia constat non pendere à nobis, ut spiritus animales, principium motuum, in quam vellemus corporis partem determinemus, alioqui morbos, vitam, mortem, suo quisque sibi arbitrio dispensaret. Pleniorem hujus deductionem demonstratic-nemque fere palpandam alicubi {a}exhibuit Lud. Forgeus. Hic hæc est Veritas: Omnia ista esse à Deo agente, movente, determinante motum, etsi ex occasione & interventu cogitationis Spontaneæ, ut dictum est, ubi de Potentia. Quare nullum in his præcise est peccatum, cum sint operationes Dei. Præterea iidem motus communes sunt probis cum improbis, quare si in illis esset peccatum, in utrisque esset, cum nulla in motu esset diversitas: interimens bestiam & interimens hominem, assumens sua & apprehendens aliena, & sic de cæteris, quo ad corpus similiter moti, similiter peccarent. Denique quotquot rationis usu non pollent, vel ob somnum, vel ob morbum, aliamve causam naturalem, ob irregulares motus non solent culpari. Quicquid de corpore vel motibus ejus in relatione ad peccatum dici potest, illud est, nempe, ista peccati vel occasiones, vel instrumenta, vel notas & signa esse posse, ipsa scriptura teste: adeoque corpus & omnia quæ circa illud sunt, quæque in ejus sensuum organa incurrunt, vanitati & peccato subjici, non culpa sua, sed culpa subjicientis: quare in subjiciente, qui sane corpus non est, quærenda est culpa, sive malum ipsum. Absurde in objecto quod est occasio mali constituitur malum, nam & lex bona nonnunquam est mali occasio: absurde in instrumentis, absurde in signis. Ridicule intemperantiæ v.g. turpitudinem vino, aut pateris, aut doliis, aut suspensæ adscribes hederæ: homicidii, gladio: falsitatis, verbis: superbiæ, vestibus aut gestibus, &c. Ultra cortices hosce penetrandum est, neque in apparentibus hærendum. Vide in quibus scriptura homicidia, calumnias, furta, aliaque consistere dicat. Oppones forte fructus cujusdam vetiti esum à parentibus primis commissum pro peccato habe-ri. Atqui non motus, non manducatio ipsum peccatum erat, sed si-gnum peccati prius in mente admissi, quod etiam sine comestione æque peccatum, etsi latens, fuisset.
units.tr: III. The body also, insofar as it is human, endowed with a certain mass, lacking others, furnished with certain figures, motions, humours and temperaments, and deprived of certain things, does not incur the guilt of sin. If there is some difficulty concerning its motions or humours, it will easily be removed. For every motion of the body, and its degree, variety and determination, is the work of the Divine Power alone, and its positing comes neither from the power of man, nor of an angel, nor of any creature; this is demonstrated from the Power of God. And here I expressly extend this pronouncement to every determination of motion: for every such determination is from God, not from me. And although it may seem to me that very many determinations of my bodily motions are from me, since they occur with the intervention of my will, yet, looking more deeply into the matter, no necessary connection appears between the will of the mind to move a limb, which happens through the outflow of animal spirits (which the mind may not know) into tubes and channels unknown to it, toward certain receptacles (which it also does not know, and of which it thinks nothing), and the execution of these effects. How could one thing by the force of its existence imply the existence of another, when neither posits itself, nor do their essences agree, since the one is a mode of thought and the other a mode of extension? But experience also shows that it does not depend on us to direct the animal spirits, the principle of motions, into whatever part of the body we wish; otherwise each person would dispense diseases, life and death at his own discretion. A fuller deduction of this, and an almost tangible demonstration, Lud. Forgeus has set forth somewhere. Here this is the truth: all these things are from God, acting, moving, determining the motion, although on the occasion and with the intervention of spontaneous thought, as has been said, where we spoke of Power. Therefore there is strictly no sin in these, since they are operations of God. Moreover, the same motions are common to the good and the wicked; therefore if there were sin in them, it would be in both, since there is no difference in the motion: killing a beast and killing a man, taking one's own and seizing what belongs to another, and so on for the rest, would, as regards the body, be similarly moved and similarly sin. Lastly, all who do not possess the use of reason, whether because of sleep, or disease, or some other natural cause, are not usually blamed for irregular motions. Whatever can be said of the body or its motions in relation to sin is this: that they can be occasions, instruments, marks and signs of sin, as Scripture itself bears witness; and so the body and all that is about it, and whatever runs into the organs of its senses, is subjected to vanity and sin, not through its own fault but through the fault of the one who subjects it; therefore the fault, or evil itself, is to be sought in the subjecter, who is certainly not the body. It is absurd to constitute evil in the object which is the occasion of evil, for even a good law is sometimes an occasion of evil; it is absurd to do so in instruments, absurd in signs. You would ridiculously ascribe the shamefulness of intemperance to wine, or to goblets, or to casks, or to the ivy hung up; of murder to the sword; of falsehood to words; of pride to clothes or gestures, and so on. One must penetrate beyond these husks and not cling to appearances. See in what Scripture says murders, slanders, thefts and other things consist. You might perhaps object that the eating of a certain forbidden fruit committed by our first parents is held to be sin. But the motion and the eating were not sin itself; rather they were a sign of sin previously admitted in the mind, which, even without the eating, would equally have been sin, though hidden.

units.la: IV. De humoribus quoque & temperamento corporis idem agno-scere licet: nam si hæc à cogitatione semota consideres, nihil aliud sunt quam materiæ sive sanguinis modificationes & motiones. Quamvis autem disponant Mentem ad tristitiam, vel iram, vel ad affectus alios, attamen nec passiones istæ in sua natura vitiosæ sunt ut dicetur mox, nec, si vitiosæ essent, malum idcirco esset in humoribus: quemadmodum libellus nonnulus potest mentem ejus characteres perlustrantem ad malum disponere, neque tamen charta ejus vel atramentum ipsum peccatum fuerint. Ergo recte concludam, peccati naturam non esse in materia, nec in ullis quæ materiam concernunt, semota cogitatione creata. Quodsi illis juncta sit cogitatio, tunc illa, remissis materialibus, sola adeunda est.
units.tr: IV. One may recognise the same about the humours and the temperament of the body: for if you consider these apart from thought, they are nothing other than modifications and motions of matter or blood. Although they dispose the mind to sadness, or anger, or other affections, nevertheless these passions are not in their own nature vicious, as will be said presently, nor, even if they were vicious, would evil on that account lie in the humours: just as a certain little book which leads the mind of one who reads its letters to evil does not thereby make its paper or ink itself the sin. Therefore I shall rightly conclude that the nature of sin is not in matter, nor in anything which concerns matter and is created apart from thought. But if thought is joined to these, then that thought, with the material things set aside, alone must be approached.

units.la: V. Et quanquam non negaverim esse quasdam in mente perceptiones quarum consideratio à materiæ motibus non videtur dissolvenda, quales sunt perceptiones sensuum & affectuum ex dispositione sanguinis oriundæ, quidam item corporis motus qui à cogitatione spontanea non separandi sunt, (quibus de causis corpus aliquod meum appello): Attamen omnia illa non esse mala assero, quatenus vi conjunctionis mentis cum corpore oriuntur. Quibus in motibus intercedit Cogitatio spontanea, illis omissis, hæc, ut dictum est, consideretur. Perceptiones quæ tanquam à corpore ad mentem promanantes, bonæ sunt omnes, Deumque authorem habent. Non potest malum in corpore esse qua meum est, sive, quia certe perceptiones in mente ex ejus motibus, & certi motus in eo ex mentis cogitatione pro Dei placito & ordinatione potenti præ aliis perceptionibus vel motibus oriuntur. De sensibus res evidentior fiet si hæc tria in illis occurrentia distincte seorsimque perpendero, primo motum, sive occursum tum objectorum in corporis organa, vel corporis in objecta, de quo jam actum; secundo principium, motivum, scopum, intentionem, consensum cogitationis creatæ in appropinquatione objectorum ad corpus, vel hujus ad illa, ut in se agant: & hoc proprie non ad sensum, sed ad cogitationem spontaneam, de qua postea, est referendum; tertium est, ipse qui ex actione objectorum in corpus resultat sensus, cujus extrema, titillatio & dolor, perperam à vulgo pro bono & malo habentur: cum tamen utrumque, & ipsa adeo dolorum tormenta extrema à Deo efficiantur sapien-tissime & decentissime. Tot in passionibus considerari possunt, quo-rum ultimum, ipsam sensionem sive perceptionem commotionis, quae proprie passio est, non esse natura sua malam, ex dictis se-quitur. Caeterum quod dixi mox de corpore & motibus, posse ea esse vel occasiones, vel instrumenta vel signa peccati, id de hisce, & de aliis in quibus adhuc dicam non consistere peccatum, asseveratum esse reputandum est repu-tandum est.
units.tr: V. And although I would not deny that there are certain perceptions in the mind whose consideration does not seem to be separable from the motions of matter, such as the perceptions of the senses and affections arising from the disposition of the blood, and likewise certain motions of the body which are not to be separated from spontaneous thought (for which reasons I call it some body of mine), nevertheless I affirm that all those are not evil, insofar as they arise by virtue of the union of the mind with the body. In those motions in which spontaneous thought intervenes, these being set aside, that thought is to be considered, as has been said. Perceptions which proceed from the body to the mind, as it were, are all good and have God as their author. Evil cannot be in the body insofar as it is mine; that is, certain perceptions in the mind arise from its motions, and certain motions in it arise from the thought of the mind, according to God's pleasure and powerful ordering, rather than other perceptions or motions. The matter will become clearer regarding the senses if I weigh separately and distinctly the three things occurring in them: first, the motion, or the encounter of objects with the organs of the body, or of the body with objects, which has already been treated; second, the principle, motive, aim, intention, and consent of created thought in the approach of objects to the body, or of the body to them, so that they act upon it: and this is properly to be referred not to sense but to spontaneous thought, which will be discussed later; third, the sense itself which results from the action of objects on the body, whose extremes, titillation and pain, are wrongly held by the common people to be good and evil; yet both, and indeed the very torments of pains, are brought about by God most wisely and most fittingly. Many things can be considered in the passions, of which the last, the sensation or perception of the commotion itself, which is properly the passion, does not, from what has been said, follow to be evil in its own nature. Moreover, what I said just now about the body and its motions, that they may be occasions, instruments or signs of sin, is to be taken as affirmed of these things too, and of others in which I shall say that sin does not consist.

units.la: VI. Restat igitur ut Mentem meam sine respectu ad corpus, in se ipsa, sive quatenus sum Cogitatio Spontanea, considerem. Certe ad id attendens quod alicubi materiale Cogitationis appellavi, nempe, Conscium esse, vel percipere actu quae in me sunt, non possum eousque quicquam mali reperire: hoc enim opus Dei est, nec ipsi improbi peccare ideo dicuntur, quod eorum quae in se sunt sint conscii, quae ratio cum optimis quoque mentibus esset communis. Inter formas autem Cogitationis sive Mentis quas supra {a} intuitus sum, e quibus quasdam magis, alias vero minus praecipuas animadverti; si in harum quibus carere possem, quales sunt cogitare de rebus mere terrestribus, speculari naturas rerum materialium, scientias humanas, &c. si inquam in harum speculatione ex ignorantia vel etiam errore deficerem, & si defectus vel privatio realitatis cujusdam in mente mea hoc ipso daretur, non tamen idcirco peccatum, sed errorem commisisse dicendus essem. Peccatum igitur jam specialius quam supra factum sit, designare licet, non quamvis indebitam realitatis cujuscunque repraesentationem, non merum non-placitum & non-opus Dei, siquidem haec ipsa sint in error quovis: sed ad praecipuas & maxime proprias mentis formas redeundum est, quarum vel indebita imitatio, vel inordinatio, vel alius quis circa illas defectus, peccatum sit. Eae autem mentis formae supra relatae sunt ad limitationem cum variatione; at tendentiam ad Ens aliud à Mente ipsa, nempe ad Ens Summum, sive, quod idem est, ad repraesentationem alterius; & ad dependentiam ab illo: quae omnia à Spontaneitate permeantur.
units.tr: VI. It remains, then, that I consider my mind without reference to the body, in itself, or insofar as I am a spontaneous thought. Certainly, attending to that which I have elsewhere called the material of thought, namely, being conscious of or actually perceiving what is in me, I cannot find anything evil up to this point. For this is the work of God, and wicked men are not said to sin because they are conscious of what is in them; this condition would be common even to the best minds. But among the forms of thought or mind that I looked at above, of which I noticed some more and others less important: if I were to fall short, through ignorance or even error, in the contemplation of those forms I could do without, such as thinking about purely earthly things, speculating about the natures of material things, human sciences, and so on, and if, I say, in the contemplation of these I were deficient, and if a defect or privation of some reality were thereby given in my mind, I should still not be said to have committed a sin, but an error. Let us therefore now designate sin more specifically than above: it is not any improper representation of any reality whatever, nor mere displeasure and not-work of God (since these very things are in every error), but we must return to the principal and most proper forms of the mind, of which the improper imitation, or disorder, or some other defect concerning them, is sin. Now these forms of the mind were referred above to limitation with variation, but to a tendency toward an Being other than the mind itself, namely the Supreme Being, or, which is the same, to the representation of another; and to dependence upon that Being. All of these are pervaded by Spontaneity.

units.la: VII. Sed ut in his cum minori confusione agatur, singula seorsim resumam. Ex eo quod cogitatio limitata sit & variabilis, animadvertuntur in ea facultates, habitus, actus. Facultates percipiendi in posterum ea quæ nondum percipio. At illæ tametsi actus absentiam involvant, non tamen ideo malum complectuntur, cum nec debuerint omnia menti simul inesse, nec vel ipsa quidem peccandi capacitas, (nolim dicere facultatem) quæ positiva non est, sit peccaminosa, ut mox notatum fuit. Ignorantia igitur ex hoc fundamento recte dicitur non esse peccatum, neque etiam parvulis in quibus viget illa in peccatum reputatur, uti neque ejus oppositum, videlicet notitia, constituit justitiam. Quod ignorantiam juris hinc excipiant cum id ea fiat de causa, quod ex principio libero sponte occasio discendi sit prætermissa, nil aliud infert, quam Spontaneitati potius quam ignorantiæ, quæ peccati sequela est, ejusdemque in futurum occasio, peccatum attribuendum esse. Ad habitus quod attinet, nil mali est si ex iteratione actuum præterita mens ad eosdem in posterum iterandos disponatur: hoc in se spectatum bonum est, atque effectus Divini placiti. Quod habitum specificat ut sic dicam, sive reddit atque denominat bonum vel malum, actio est: quare hæc, non ille, venit huc consideranda. Quod si per actiones, quæ præteritæ sint, peccaminosas, ubi proprie malum invenire est, malos habitus sum adeptus, quibus tamen in præsenti atque in futuro tempore sponte totus restitero, non puto me pro eo reputatum iri qui adhucdum & ideo actu peccatum faciam; sin vero iis actu consensero & dedar[?], hoc ipso actiones criminari oportet. Ergo superest ut in actibus cogitationis limitatæ quæram peccatum, quod si non consistat in ignorantia atque in limitibus ipsis cogitationis, multo minus in Cognitione, sive realitate quæ est inter ipsos limites, non modo in cognitione veri aut boni, in Dei ejusque placiti ad certam mensuram notitia, sed nec in ea quæ est de falso & malo: etenim quamvis cognovero errores, vitia, enormitates, blasphemias, & monstra ejusmodi, quamvis Menti sisterentur cogitationes Diabolicæ & horrendæ, modo illis sponte non consentiam, sed resistam, non pecco. Quin potius hoc sæpe utile est, & ad mali confutationem & virtutis confirmationem: acciditque interdum ut malum esset quorumdam horum non habere experientiam, sive cognitionem. Hæc propositio, Satanas est adorandus, est abominanda, nihilominus tamen cognitionem Christi, suggerente ipso Satana, subiit, cum horrore quidem & repulsione, at subiit tamen. Hinc tentationes Diabolicæ intellectuales ubi sponte displicent non nocent, sive malum non inferunt menti tentatæ.
units.tr: VII. But so that these may be handled with less confusion, I will take up each one separately. From the fact that thought is limited and variable, faculties, habits, and acts are observed in it. The faculties are of perceiving in future those things which I do not yet perceive. But although these involve the absence of an act, they do not on that account embrace evil, since neither ought all things to be present to the mind at once, nor is even the capacity to sin itself (I would prefer not to call it a faculty), which is not positive, sinful, as was noted shortly before. Ignorance, therefore, on this ground is rightly said not to be sin, nor is it imputed as sin to little children in whom it flourishes; nor does its opposite, namely knowledge, constitute righteousness. That they exclude ignorance of law from this, since it comes about for this reason, that the occasion of learning has been freely neglected by a spontaneous principle, implies nothing else than that sin is to be ascribed to Spontaneity rather than to ignorance, which is a consequence of sin, and an occasion of it for the future. As for habits, there is no evil if, through the repetition of acts, the mind is disposed to repeat the same in the future: viewed in itself this is good, and an effect of the divine good pleasure. What specifies a habit, so to speak, or renders and names it good or evil, is the action; wherefore it is this, not that, which must be considered here. But if, through past acts that were sinful, where evil is properly to be found, I have acquired evil habits, to which nevertheless in the present and in future time I wholly resist of my own accord, I do not think I shall be reckoned as one who still sins and therefore sins actually; but if indeed I should consent to them in act and yield, by that very fact I must be charged with the actions. Therefore it remains that I seek sin in the acts of limited thought; and if it does not consist in ignorance and in the very limits of thought, much less does it consist in knowledge, or in the reality which lies between those limits, not only in the knowledge of the true or good, of God and of his good pleasure to a certain measure, but not even in that which concerns the false and evil. For although I may have known errors, vices, enormities, blasphemies, and monstrosities of this kind, and although diabolical and horrible thoughts were presented to my mind, provided I do not consent to them of my own accord but resist them, I do not sin. Indeed this is often useful, both for the refutation of evil and the confirmation of virtue; and it sometimes happens that it would be evil not to have experience or knowledge of certain of these things. This proposition, Satan is to be worshipped, is abominable, yet nevertheless Christ's knowledge, Satan himself suggesting it, came under it, indeed with horror and repulsion, yet it came. Hence intellectual diabolical temptations, when they are displeasing of one's own accord, do not harm; that is, they do not inflict evil upon the mind that is tempted.

units.la: VIII. Præterea in forma mentis consideravi tum quod Cogitatio non sisteretur in se ipsa, seque adeo ipsam non repræsentaret, sed utut imperfecta & limitata, ad Deum tenderet, inque eo repræsentato sisteretur: Tum hoc denique, quod ab illo esset omnimode atque absolutissime in fieri, esse, operari, regi, & verbo, in omni realitate dependens. Quæ omnia optima sunt & nobilissima. Spontaneitas quoque hæc permeans, quippe opus Dei actu præsens, in se bona est, & maxime bona cum determinata est ut hisce applicetur. Ecce igitur cum coram Deo omnia quæ in me sunt intueor, Cogitationis materiam, formas, facultates, habitus, actus, determinationem spontaneam, nulla mala sunt: & quod istis multæ, ut vidi, desint realitates, adeoque de nihilo eatenus participent, non est malum. Ista omnia bene se habent, & tamen abundo peccatis. Unde vero hoc? An quod determinate negem rejiciamque formam Mentis quatenus directe Deum respicit, quasi explicite dicam, Nolo à Deo esse limitatus, nolo ad illum tendere, illum repræsentare, ab illo esse & regi? Hoc quidem peccatum esset, nec forte multum alienum ab illo quod irremissibile dicitur. Sed id jam nec examinabo, nec in clariores ideas resolvere tentabo, siquidem in communibus peccatis non inveniatur. Verum velim tantum hinc caveri ne multi sibi adulentur, quasi non peccarent ubi Deum non expresse reiciunt. Nam peccatum, non dico aliquod in specie aut in gradibus, sed in communi genere, non est explicita Dei in cogitatione repræsentati, rejectio.
units.tr: VIII. Besides, I considered in the form of the mind both that thought does not rest in itself, nor therefore represent itself, but, however imperfect and limited it may be, tends toward God, and rests in that represented object; and finally that it depends from him in every way and most absolutely, in being, in becoming, in acting, in being governed, and in a word in all reality. All of these are most excellent and most noble. This Spontaneity also, which pervades all things, being in act the work of God present, is good in itself, and most good when it is determined to be applied to these things. Behold, therefore, when I look before God at all that is in me, the material of thought, its forms, faculties, habits, acts, and spontaneous determination: none of these is evil; and that many realities, as I have seen, are lacking in them, and so partake of nothing to that extent, is not an evil. All these things are well, and yet I abound in sins. Whence then is this? Is it because I determinately deny and reject the form of the mind insofar as it directly regards God, as if I were to say explicitly: I do not want to be limited by God, I do not want to tend toward him, to represent him, to be from him and governed by him? This indeed would be a sin, and perhaps not very remote from that which is called unforgivable. But I shall neither examine this now nor try to resolve it into clearer ideas, since it is not found among common sins. Yet I would only wish this caution to be given, that many may not flatter themselves, as if they did not sin when they do not expressly reject God. For sin, I do not say some particular sin or in its degrees, but sin in the common genus, is not an explicit rejection of God represented in thought.

units.la: IX. Illa Mentis meæ forma quæ mihi Deum undique sistit limitantem, repræsentatum, operantem, mihi etiam ideam sistit mei, prout ego solus sine Deo sum, videlicet ut qui nihil sim, ne vel minimum quidem realitatis gradum, in me habens, nihil quod ab aliquo debeat repræsentari, vel scopus aut originale alterius esse, nihil denique quod à se quicquam operetur. Et quemadmodum hoc non habeo à Deo, nempe ut sim nihil, quippe quod non habet opus causa, sed à me ipso quatenus à me sum, seu quatenus nihil sum; sic non opus est à Deo poni determinationem in me spontaneam quæ sit à me, ad me, & per me: hoc esset contradictorium & absurdum; sicque ego memet amplecterer ut Ens à me, ut aliquid per me, mei scopum, &c. quod est imperfectio, tenditque in non-ens. Deus hoc neque statuit neque efficit, nec occasionem positivam, ut talis in me esset determinatio, obtulit, siquidem omnia in me & extra me contrarium mihi sistant, clamentque, Deum omnia esse, me nihil. Quare hic à Deo relictus sum ad hoc non-determinatus. Et quia sum variabilis à me ipso quatenus natura mea non sum Ens Summum & constantissimum, fieri potest ut deficiam ab hoc statu non-determinationis in quo sum non-determinatus à me, ad me, per me, ad inane aliquod spectrum pejus quam nihil, cui, quanquam ei subsit cogitatio realis & spontanea, absurda inest forma, quasi nimirum à me essem, possem, facerem aliquid reale. Et hoc est quod, ubi accidit, peccatum est, imo hoc ipsa radix est & fundum peccati intimum unde manant reliqua. Quia vero ad hoc eram indifferens, hinc culpa à peccato est indissolubilis. Sed ut haec clarius percipiantur, de libertate ex professo, maxime de indifferentia, nonnulla sunt explicanda, & quantum ad peccatum conferat, ostendendum. Post quae aliquot difficultates, quaestiones, conclusiones, ex hisce oriundae subjicientur.
units.tr: IX. That form of my mind which presents God to me on every side as limiting, represented, and working, presents to me also an idea of myself, as I am alone without God, namely as one who is nothing, having not even the least degree of reality in me, having nothing that ought to be represented by anyone, or to be the end or origin of another, nothing finally that works anything of itself. And just as I do not have this from God, namely that I should be nothing, for what has no work has no cause, but from myself insofar as I am from myself, or insofar as I am nothing; so it is not necessary that a spontaneous determination in me, which is from me, to me, and through me, should be posited by God: this would be contradictory and absurd; and thus I would embrace myself as a being from myself, as something through myself, my own end, and so on, which is imperfection and tends toward non-being. God neither establishes this nor effects it, nor did he offer a positive occasion for such a determination to be in me, since all things in me and outside me present to me the contrary, and cry out that God is all things and I am nothing. Wherefore I am left by God here undetermined for this. And because I am variable, insofar as by my own nature I am not the Supreme and most constant Being, it can come about that I fall away from this state of non-determination in which I am undetermined by myself, toward me, through me, toward some empty phantom worse than nothing, in which, although a real and spontaneous thought underlies it, there is an absurd form, as if forsooth I were from myself, could do, or made something real. And this is what, wherever it happens, is sin; indeed this itself is the root and innermost foundation of sin, from which the rest flow. But since I was indifferent to this, hence guilt is inseparable from sin. But that these things may be perceived more clearly, some things must be explained concerning liberty, especially concerning indifference, and it must be shown how much it contributes to sin. After these, some difficulties, questions, and conclusions arising from these will be subjoined.

units.la: X. Sed hoc adhuc notandum est, naturam commissionemque peccati actualem non requirere ut Mens reflexivo modo ad illud se gerat, quasi apud se esset dicendum, volo à me ipsa determinari, à me, ad me, per me, pro me regi, considerari, nonnihil haberi, me ipsam repraesentare, volo hoc vel illo modo non limitari, & si quae ejusmodi: quae quidem si adsint peccatum reddunt gravius, elatum nempe & contra conscientiam; Sed sufficit ad peccatum ut sine reflexione cogitatio sic se habeat quasi talis quae jam dicta est, esset illa: Sic enim Ego, quatenus à me nihil sum; Ego, quatenus per Deum aliquid sum; Deus ipse, quatenus me statuit & fecit; Ipse etiam, quatenus se repraesentavit; ipseque adeo, quatenus ille ipsemet est, consequenter negantur.
units.tr: X. But this must further be noted: the nature and commission of an actual sin do not require that the mind should relate itself to it in a reflexive way, as if it were said within itself: "I want to be determined by myself, from myself, to myself, through myself, for myself to be ruled, considered, to be held in some esteem, to represent myself, I want not to be limited in this or that way," and so on. Such things, if present, make the sin graver, namely when they are proud and against conscience. But it is enough for sin that a thought, without reflection, is so disposed as if it were of the kind just described: thus, "I, insofar as I am nothing from myself"; "I, insofar as I am something through God"; "God himself, insofar as he has established and made me"; "He himself also, insofar as he has presented himself"; and "he himself, insofar as he is that very self," are consequently denied.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 1. De libertate notiones clariores. 2. 3. 4. De Indifferentia, eam dari. 5. Ea multiplex. 6.--12. In creatura non est positiva, sed negativa. Demonstratur, repulsis contrariis probationibus. 13. Ejus termini Duo. 14. Peccati specialissima designatio.
units.tr: 1. Clearer notions of liberty. 2., 3., 4. That indifference is given, concerning Indifference. 5. It is manifold. 6.–12. In a creature it is not positive but negative. This is demonstrated by rejecting the contrary proofs. 13. Its two terms. 14. The most special designation of sin.

units.la: I. DE intellectu voluntate, libertate tum spontaneitatis tum Indifferentiae, tam saepe apud scholasticos, & ut fieri solet, iis cum tenebris disputatum est, ut ex illa consuetudine vix ulla ex istis vocibus adhiberi possit quin aliquod praeteritarum obscuritatum, vel etiam chymerarum statim recurrat. Quare hic voces aliae, eaque evidentiores, quantum fieri poterit, nullisque nugis adhuc contaminatae adhibebuntur cum principio perspicuo unde deducentur. si tamen aliqua ex illis retineatur, expositione clara non carebit. Sit haec propositio Concipio sponte Deum meum, principium, sive occasio, unde hæc deducentur. Concipio : hoc referunt ad Intellectum ut ejus actum , nos id simpliciter cogitationis sive Mentis perceptionem dicimus. Sponte concipio : hoc, quod voluntati tanquam ejus actum adscribunt, qua de causa etiam Libertatem ei attribuunt, dicimus allubescentiam , sive lubitum, vel potius Spontaneitatem. Deum meum sponte concipio: Id jam ad Libertatem Spontaneitatis quam vocant , referunt: Sed evitandæ, ut dixi, obscuritatis causa, malo dicere, illum actum quo mens percipit sponte objectum sibi conveniens, esse spontaneitatis determinatæ, sive esse spontaneam determinationem. Nulla est obscuritas in resolutione hujus propositionis quoad formam , & patet hinc quid per Intellectum , Voluntatem , Libertatem, Libertatem spontaneitatis, intelligendum veniat. quæ clarius sic comprehendes & efferes, Mens percipit Sponte determinata; quam si cum scholis dixeris, Anima habet Intellectum & Voluntatem quæ est libera libertate Spontaneitatis.
units.tr: I. CONCERNING the intellect, the will, and liberty, both of spontaneity and of indifference, much has been disputed by the schoolmen, so often and, as usually happens, in such darkness, that from that habit hardly any of these words can be used without some obscurity of the past, or even some chimera, at once coming back. Therefore other words, and more evident ones, not yet contaminated by any trifles, will be used as far as possible, together with a clear principle from which they will be derived. If, however, some of those words are retained, they will not lack a clear explanation. Let this proposition be the principle, or occasion, from which these things will be derived: I conceive God of my own accord. I conceive: this they refer to the intellect as its act; we call it simply a thought, or the perception of the mind. Of my own accord I conceive: this, which they ascribe to the will as its act, for which reason they also attribute liberty to it, we call an inclination to delight, or rather spontaneity. I conceive my God of my own accord: this they now refer to the liberty they call the liberty of spontaneity. But, as I said, for the sake of avoiding obscurity, I prefer to say that the act by which the mind perceives of its own accord an object suited to itself is of determined spontaneity, or is a determined spontaneous determination. There is no obscurity in the resolution of this proposition as to its form, and from this it is plain what is to be understood by intellect, will, liberty, and liberty of spontaneity. These you will comprehend and express more clearly thus: the mind perceives, being determined spontaneously; whereas if you speak with the schools, you would say: the soul has an intellect and a will, which is free with the liberty of spontaneity.

units.la: II. Hæc omnia , & nominatim Spontaneitatem determinatam interventu perceptionis, esse à Deo, demonstratum est expresse ubi de Divina Potentia & Libertate actum est. Quare omnis quæ restat difficultas est de Indifferentia, quam quasi in ortu & radice ex hac consideratione videre licet. Nempe, si quod mea Mens sponte percipit, non videt seu quia realitati in perceptione aliquid deficit, seu in objecto ipso, convenire cum eo quod Deus in forma Mentis manifestavit de seipso, de placito , de opere suo , tunc indeterminatus maneo, sive hæreo, an id meum mente faciam, hoc est, an in illud spontanea cogitatione ferar, inque eo maneam tanquam id esset quod Dei ideæ , aut placito, aut operi conveniat ? Hoc malim spontaneitatem indeterminatam , vel non-determinationem spontaneitatis dicere, quam libertatem indifferentiæ : nam de hac demum spontaneitate indeterminata quæritur, an sit indifferens, nec-ne ?
units.tr: II. All these things, and especially that determined spontaneity through the intervention of perception, are from God; this has been expressly demonstrated where we treated of the divine power and liberty. Therefore the only remaining difficulty concerns indifference, which can be seen in its origin and root from this consideration. Namely, if what my mind perceives of its own accord does not appear to it, either because something is lacking in the reality of the perception or in the object itself, to agree with what God has manifested of himself in the form of the mind, of his good pleasure, of his work, then I remain undetermined, or I hesitate whether I shall make that my own by thought, that is, whether I shall be carried by spontaneous thought into it and remain in it as though it were what agrees with the ideas, the good pleasure, or the work of God? I would rather call this indeterminate spontaneity, or the non-determination of spontaneity, than the liberty of indifference: for it is of this indeterminate spontaneity that the question is asked at last, whether it is indifferent or not?

units.la: III. Inde notare est, indifferentiæ in Mente creata suspicionem, ejusque , si qua ibi detur, fundamentum , esse negationem , sive, non-positionem determinationis ex eo quod Mens non inveniat vel detegat objectum perceptioni & allubescentiæ conveniens. Ex quo quid de indifferentia illic fundata sit judicandum, sitne perfectio aut secus , decidere facile est. Sed id ex sequentibus sat patebit. Videndum prius, quid sit indifferentia.
units.tr: III. From this it is to be noted that the suspicion of indifference in the created mind, and its foundation, if any such is there, is a negation, or non-positing of determination, from the fact that the mind does not find or detect an object suited to perception and inclination. From this it is easy to decide what must be judged of the indifference grounded there, whether it is a perfection or not. But this will be sufficiently plain from what follows. First it must be considered what indifference is.

units.la: IV. Si scholastice loquendum esset, dicerem , hic non quæri de indifferentia in sensu morali, vel Physico, sed in sensu Metaphysico ; at dicere malim, hic non agi de ratione qua res nonnullæ nec bonæ nec malæ, sed adiaphoræ nominantur; neque de ea quæ est aptitudo passiva alicujus subjecti ad recipiendum has illasve ab operante formas, prout operanti placebit: quo sensu homo indifferens est ad hoc ut Deus hoc aut illud realitatis, aut plane nihil, in illo operetur. Indifferentia de qua hic agitur, est concipienda instar principii in quo ratio & causa naturæ atque existentiæ rerum ad quas indifferentia dari dicitur, quæratur, atque plene inveniatur sine ulteriori provocatione. Talem indifferentiam in Deo dari respectu omnium rerum quæ ipsius natura non sunt, sæpe dictum est: unde is potuit hoc aliove modo statuere & efficere earum naturas, existentias, veritates, & quarum omnium, quocunque modo se habuissent, ratio, principiumque præter ejus placitum nullum datur. Ex simili, hoc est, indifferenti principio debere provenire peccatum, demonstratum est expresse in libro tertio, ubi de libertate. Et certe, aut à nullo plane principio, sive, quod sit instar principii, est peccatum, atque sic non daretur peccatum; aut à necessario, quale vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi, præter Deum, ejus placitum, & ejus opus, quæ in se extra culpam omnino sunt, nullum habetur; aut ab indifferenti. Dubitari-ne etiam potest rationem peccati vel admissi, vel negative non admissi (non loquor de positione boni) in mente creata certo respectu considerata sine ulteriori provocatione dari? quæ est ipsa indifferentiæ ratio.
units.tr: IV. If we were to speak scholastically, I would say that here we are not inquiring about indifference in the moral or physical sense, but in the metaphysical sense; but I would rather say that here we are not dealing with the manner in which certain things are named neither good nor evil, but adiaphora; nor with that passive aptitude of some subject to receive these or those forms from the agent, as the agent shall please; in which sense man is indifferent to this, that God should work in him this or that reality, or plainly nothing. The indifference with which we are here concerned is to be conceived as a principle in which the reason and cause of the nature and existence of things, to which indifference is said to be given, is sought, and is fully found without any further appeal. That God possesses such indifference with respect to all things which are not his own nature has often been said: whence he could decide and bring about, in this or that way, their natures, existences, truths, and of all of these the reason and principle, however they might have been, lies in nothing but his good pleasure. It has been expressly demonstrated in the third book, where we treated of liberty, that sin must arise from a like principle, that is, from an indifferent principle. And certainly, either sin is from no principle at all, or from something that is in place of a principle, and thus sin would not exist; or it is from something necessary, of which there is, either absolutely or by hypothesis, nothing besides God, his good pleasure, and his work, which are in themselves wholly outside of fault; or it is from the indifferent. Can it also be doubted whether the reason of sin, either committed or negatively not committed (I am not speaking of the positing of good), is given in the created mind, considered in a certain respect, without any further appeal? This is the very reason of indifference.

units.la: V. Occurrit ex allatis exemplis indifferentiam prout est in Cogitatione firma vel infirma, aut etiam prout ejus termini sunt positivi vel negativi, ipsam positivam vel negativam esse agnoscendam: Cum enim res aliqua potens est ponere hoc vel illud vel istud bonum, ejus indifferentia pure positiva est; at si ponere bonum, aut id intermittere, positiva est ex una parte; si vero indifferens sit ad hoc, ut vel plane nihil à se ipsa faciat, vel malum patret[?], tunc negativa est ejus indifferentia. Duas priores Soli Deo competere exclusive ad omnem creaturam, ex Potentia Divina demonstratur: quare si quæ est creaturæ tribuenda, ut tribuendam ostendi, restat sola ultima, quæ negativa est.
units.tr: V. From the examples brought forward it appears that indifference, as it is in a firm or weak thought, or also as its terms are positive or negative, is to be acknowledged as itself positive or negative. For when a thing is able to posit this or that or that good, its indifference is purely positive; but if it is able to posit good, or to omit it, it is positive on one side; and if it is indifferent to this, so that it either does nothing at all of itself or commits evil, then its indifference is negative. The first two, it is demonstrated from the divine power, belong exclusively to God, and not to any creature. Therefore if anything is to be attributed to the creature, as I have shown it should be, only the last remains, which is negative.

units.la: VI. Sed hoc non omnibus placet, qui à se aliquid esse sibi videri volunt. hinc positive se esse indifferentes asserunt, vel in alterutrius ex duobus boni positione, vel saltem inter boni positionem aut omissionem. Quare plurimi mali originem rationemque hinc deducunt, quod cum indifferentes sint, vel saltem ante admissum malum fuerint, si ex duobus bonis minus eligant, majori postpositio, minus quidem; si vero bonum omne plane facere desistant, tunc gravius peccent. Quibus-cum videntur Scriptura sacra atque hominis debitum consentire.
units.tr: VI. But this does not please everyone, who wish that something should seem to be of themselves. Hence they assert that they are positively indifferent, either to the positing of one of two goods, or at least between the positing or the omission of a good. Therefore most derive the origin and reason of evil from this: that, since they are indifferent, or at least were indifferent before the evil was committed, if out of two goods they choose the lesser, they postpone the greater, a lesser fault; but if they stop doing every good altogether, then they sin more gravely. To these, it seems, holy Scripture and the debt of man agree.

units.la: VII. Quantum ad hasce duas, quae adferuntur, instantias, rem non ita esse ut prima fronte videtur, posthac manifestum fiet. De In-differentia vel ex parte, vel ex toto positiva, manet invicta ex Potentia Dei deducta demonstratio, eam nulli Creaturae in quocunque statu convenire, ne Angelis, ne homini quidem in statu innocentiae. Nil ille unquam, nil alius praeter Deum, vi sua aliquid reale ponere valuit vel valet, qui igitur fuisset indifferens ad ponendum vel secus? Quam verum est Dei Potentiae nil ab alio addi posse, nullam rem esse ejus terminum qui eam excludat, Solum Deum esse independentem, nil esse sine vi voluntatis suae, nil esse a seipso, denique Deum esse Deum; tam verum est neminem praeter illum esse aliquid reale ponen-tem, vel ad id positive indifferentem. Aut Deus & omnium evidentissi-mae & Sanctissimae veritates hic negandae sunt, aut blasphemum istud positivae indifferentiae idolum, quod, utpote notitiis de Dei potentia, de Creaturae dependentia, communibus adversum, imo noxium, in-utile, fundamento destitutum, exterminare praestat. Nam quod non-nulli id amplectantur ne sibi ipsis nimis vilescant, neve, quod allegat quidam, sequatur inde aliquid Deo, nil vero creaturis tribuendum esse, id abominandum est; nec aliunde venit quam ex eo quod Mens Diabo-licis insistens vestigiis, in se gloriari quaerat.
units.tr: VII. As to these two instances which are brought forward, it will afterwards become clear that the matter is not as it seems at first sight. Concerning indifference, positive either in part or in whole, the demonstration deduced from the power of God remains unshaken: that it belongs to no creature in any state, not even to the angels, nor even to man in the state of innocence. He never, and no other except God, by his own power, was or is able to posit anything real; who then would have been indifferent to positing or not? As true as it is that nothing can be added to the power of God by another, that there is no thing which is its limit to exclude it, that God alone is independent, that nothing is without the power of his will, that nothing is from itself, and finally that God is God; so true is it that no one except him positively posits anything real, or is positively indifferent to it. Either God and the most evident and most holy truths must be denied here, or that blasphemous idol of positive indifference must be cast out, which, being contrary to the common notions of the power of God and the dependence of the creature, nay harmful, useless, and lacking foundation, it is better to exterminate. For that some embrace it lest they become too cheap in their own eyes, or lest, as a certain man alleges, something should follow from it for God and nothing should be attributed to creatures, is to be abhorred; nor does it come from anywhere else than from this: that the mind, treading in the footsteps of the Devil, seeks to glory in itself.

units.la: VIII. Sed forte etiam nonnulli ex iis qui indifferentiam istam propugnarunt, ex alio motivo, non ita malo, egerunt. forte consequentias omnes quae ex ejus cum Divina Potentia comparatione oriuntur, non animadverterunt; verum aliis de causis ad indifferentiam positivam recurrerunt; alii ut ostenderent peccatum esse inexcusabile & culpabile; alii quia ipso sensu conscientiaque propria de se ipsis convinci videntur, se indifferentes esse. Non video quid aliud possit praetexi.
units.tr: VIII. But perhaps some of those who defended this indifference acted from another motive, not so bad. Perhaps they did not notice all the consequences that arise from comparing it with the Divine Power; but for other reasons they had recourse to positive indifference. Some did so in order to show that sin is inexcusable and culpable; others because their own sense and conscience seem to convince them that they are indifferent. I do not see what else could be put forward as a pretext.

units.la: IX. Sed haec nihil habent roboris ad probandum quod assumitur. Nam, ut a primo initium fiat, sufficit ad culpam peccati agnoscendam consideratio indifferentiae negativae in mente, quae poterat vel in statu nihilum suum decens manere, nil a se gerere; vel ab illo ad statum privativum sive indecentem peccaminosumque descisere. Ergo praeter necessitatem allegatur ejusmodi positiva Indifferentia. Sed & inutilis quoque & noxia est. Quod ut perspiciatur, sciendum est, ut quid sit culpabile & inexcusabile, oportere ejus oppositum, quod fieri debebat, tale esse, ut ex eo nulla necessario sequatur culpa. Jam vero, quamvis ille maxime culpandus videatur qui bonum quod ipse ponere potuisse dicitur, omisit, cum supponis tamen eum fuisse bonum illud operatum, tunc quoniam ei præbes occasionem de se ipso gloriandi, patet (ex Dei Justitia & gloria) eum in majus inconveniens inde lapsum fore. Quod si dixeris eum teneri omnem Deo gloriam reddere, tunc, siquidem ve-rum fuisset (ut velles) eum positive indifferentem se habuisse, is referen-do suum opus alteri, non autem sibi ipsi, qui tamen id potuisset, men-tiretur, gloriamque mendacem tribueret Deo: sed hic non postulat per mendacium commendari, neque falsa ratione ejus gloria est illustran-da. Itaque supposita Indifferentia positiva, quicquid facias in culpam cadis, eamque minorem ex parte boni omissi quam boni commissi. Proinde suppositio absurda est.
units.tr: IX. But these arguments have no force for proving what is assumed. For, to begin with the first point, it is enough for recognising the guilt of sin to consider a negative indifference in the mind, which could either remain in its state, fitting its nothingness and doing nothing of itself, or fall away from that state into a privative state, unbecoming and sinful. So a positive indifference of this kind is alleged to no purpose. But it is also useless and harmful. To see this, it must be understood that, for something to be culpable and inexcusable, the opposite of what ought to have been done must be such that no fault necessarily follows from it. Now, although he who is said to have omitted a good that he could have put in place seems most deserving of blame, yet, since you suppose that he did perform that good, then, because you give him an occasion of glorying in himself, it is plain (from God's justice and glory) that he would fall thereby into a greater evil. And if you say that he is bound to give all glory to God, then, supposing it were true (as you wish) that he was positively indifferent, he would be lying if, in ascribing his work to another and not to himself, though he could have done it, he attributed a false glory to God. But God does not require to be commended by a lie, nor is his glory to be illustrated by a false reasoning. Therefore, on the supposition of a positive indifference, whatever you do you fall into fault, and a fault less in respect of the good omitted than of the good committed. Hence the supposition is absurd.

units.la: X. Quod secundo prætendebatur etiam cassum est. Multi nempe ad sensum provocant. En, inquiunt, experimur nos indifferentes esse ad rerum positionem, id percipimus, id sentimus. Quod constat sensu intimo non debet negari quia forte cum re incomprehensibili, Potentia nempe & concursu Dei, conciliari a nobis non potest. Quod clare per-cipitur non est negandum ob id quod natura sua incomprehensibile est. Hæc sic inverto: Res clara hæc est, & evidens, Deum esse Authorem & Effectorem omnium realium; nullam rem a se, præter illum, quic-quam esse vel operari; Indifferentiam in Creatura positivam non modo non posse conciliari cum Divina Potentia, sed ei è diametro repugnare, eam negare & tollere. Quod autem est, vel saltem quod primo intuitu videtur esse incomprehensibile, id hocce est, In nobis aliquid ab alio esse vel poni (nempe quodcunque reale in nobis sponte est) quod ta-men non sentiamus tanquam ab alio pendere, verum quod quasi a no-bis ipsis venire percipiamus. Quapropter, si quod evidens est non debet ob incomprehensibile quoddam negari, concludendum est, illud pri-mum, utpote evidentissimum, Deum videlicet omnia solum facere, Creaturam ad nil quicquam indifferentem esse positivo sensu, non de-bere ideo negari, quia non statim comprehendimus, quomodo id quod quasi a nobis ipsis sponte vel ex indifferentia videmur sentire, non tamen a nobis ponatur. Quid mirum aut incongruum si modus quo Deus in Mentibus agit non omnino comprehendatur? Sed id demum incon-gruum esset, si Divinæ Potentiæ, Impotentiæ autem creaturæ princi-pia patefacta non essent, aut ut depravata sisterentur. Nam Deus de-center agnoscitur, &, ut sic dicam, tractatur, his patefactis, illo, modo nempe agendi, occulto: non vero contra, cum hicce evidenter percipi dicitur, illa autem vel dissimulantur vel ignorantur, stat Deo in Mente suus honos.
units.tr: X. What was put forward in the second place is also empty. Many, to be sure, appeal to sense. Behold, they say, we experience that we are indifferent to the placing of things; we perceive it, we feel it. What is established by inner sense must not be denied merely because perhaps we cannot reconcile it with an incomprehensible thing, namely the power and concurrence of God. What is clearly perceived is not to be denied on account of the fact that it is incomprehensible in its nature. I turn the matter around thus: this thing is clear and evident, that God is the author and effector of all real things; that no thing is or acts of itself, apart from him; and that a positive indifference in a creature not only cannot be reconciled with the Divine Power, but is diametrically opposed to it, denying and removing it. But what is, or at least what seems at first sight to be incomprehensible, is this: that something in us is caused or placed by another (namely, whatever is real in us arises spontaneously), which yet we do not feel as depending on another, but which we perceive as coming, as it were, from ourselves. Therefore, if what is evident must not be denied on account of some incomprehensible thing, it must be concluded that the first point, as the most evident, namely that God alone does all things and that the creature is in no positive sense indifferent to anything, must not be denied for the reason that we do not at once comprehend how that which we seem to feel as if from ourselves, spontaneously or from indifference, is nevertheless not placed by us. What wonder or incongruity is there if the manner in which God acts in minds is not wholly comprehended? But that would indeed be incongruous, if the principles of the Divine Power and of the creature's impotence were not laid open, or were presented as corrupted. For God is rightly acknowledged, and, so to speak, handled, when these things have been laid open, while that manner of acting remains hidden; but not the reverse, when the latter is said to be clearly perceived while the former are either dissembled or unknown. In that case God's honour in the Mind stands.

units.la: XI. Sed insuper falsum esse dico, ullos sese positive indifferentes sentire. Etenim omne quod se sentire dicunt, referri potest vel ad indifferentiam subjecti, cum ex pluribus operationibus quæ à Deo in illo poni possunt, ignorat hasce an illas sit experturus; vel ad indifferentiam negativam; vel ad spontaneitatem positive determinatam, quam, cum ea non sentiatur ut ab alieno, putat ideo esse à se. Sic vero omnis spontanea Cogitatio esset ex natura sua à Dei Potentia subtracta atque independens, & ne quidem posset Deus in illa operari. quod undique profligatum est. Verum aliæ sunt rationes, cur ab alieno & externo non sentiatur, ut non sit opus ad nodum hunc dissolvendum Creaturam in Creatorem transmutare, aut vice versa. Ipsa conservatio nostri continua spontanea est, nec sensu percipitur ut ab alio procedens, eam tamen à nobis non esse evincitur intellectu. Quod autem ipsa, cum aliis ejusmodi operationibus, non percipiatur ut ab alieno, ratio est quod nobis sit intima, nec sit in nobis magis intimum cum quo comparata, aliena sentiri possit. Omnis directe percipiens aliquid ut à se diversum & ab alieno, eatenus est diversus à re ita percepta: quare etiam ex sensu crasso & corporeo concluditur dari aliquid à nobis diversum. Sed opus Dei, cogitationem spontaneam in nobis efficientis, est nobis intimum, vel potius, est nostrum intimum. Nos ipsi in fundo id opus sumus. Quid in nobis, præter id, restat, quod ejus operis tanquam rei à nobis differentis possit directum recipere sensum, & cujus comparatione id possit sentiri ut extraneum? tametsi per reflexionem intellectus percipiamus, omne reale, utut nobis sit intimum, sitque vel tota ipsa spontaneitas nostra, à Deo positum esse. Herbertus ipse, {a} qui tantopere sensum urget internum, si nomine Libertatis non confudisset in unum quæ distincta esse vidimus, sique ad id quod tanquam notitiam communem proponit, attendisset, Deum omnium finem, principium & medium esse, hæc neque negaret, neque, ut facit, diceret, hoc pacto Libertatem non nisi ex inepto vexari & limitari discursu.
units.tr: XI. But I say further that it is false that any persons feel themselves to be positively indifferent. For everything they say they feel can be referred either to the indifference of the subject, since, out of several operations which God can produce in it, it does not know which of these it is going to experience; or to negative indifference; or to a positively determined spontaneity, which, since it is not felt as coming from another, they think is therefore from themselves. Yet in that way every spontaneous thought would by its nature be withdrawn from the Divine Power and independent of it, and God could not even act in it; which has been refuted on all sides.
