But there are other reasons why it is not felt as coming from something alien and external, so that there is no need, to loosen this knot, to transform the creature into the Creator, or the reverse. The continual spontaneous preservation of ourselves is not perceived by sense as proceeding from another, yet by the intellect it is proved that it is not from ourselves. And the reason why this preservation, together with other such operations, is not perceived as coming from another is that it is intimate to us, and nothing in us is more intimate with which it could be compared so that it might be felt as alien. Whoever directly perceives something as different from himself and as coming from another is, to that extent, different from the thing so perceived; hence it is also concluded from crude and bodily sense that something different from us exists. But the work of God, which produces spontaneous thought in us, is intimate to us, or rather is our very innermost. We ourselves are that work at bottom. What remains in us, apart from that, which could receive a direct sense of that work as a thing different from us, and by comparison with which it could be felt as foreign? Although by reflection of the intellect we perceive that everything real, however intimate to us, and indeed our whole spontaneity itself, has been placed by God. Herbert himself, {a} who so strongly insists on inner sense, if he had not confused under the name of Liberty things that we have seen to be distinct, and if he had attended to that common notion which he puts forward, that God is the end, the beginning and the means of all things, would neither deny these things, nor, as he does, say that in this way Liberty is harassed and limited only by an unskilled reasoning.

units.la: XII. Cartesius, qui omnia multis in locis à Deo dependere, bene demonstrat, quæque indifferentiam creaturæ alicubi{b} inter defectus enumerat, non videtur hisce veritatibus consentaneum quid proferre in suis Epistolis, ubi{c} de indifferentia loquitur ut de facultate positiva, de potentia positiva sequendi deteriora præ melioribus agnitis, dicitque, nos ab-
units.tr: XII. Descartes, who rightly demonstrates in many places that all things depend on God, and who in one place counts the creature's indifference among its defects, does not seem to put forward anything consistent with these truths in his Letters, where he speaks of indifference as a positive faculty, as a positive power of following the worse in preference to the better known, and says that we are absolutely always able to do so, and that a greater use is made of this positive power in that than otherwise.

units.la: {b} Cartes. Medit. IV.
units.tr: {b} Descartes, Meditation IV.

units.la: {c} Cartes. Tom. I. Epist. CXII. solute id semper posse, atque in eo majorem hujus potentia positiva usum fieri, quam si secus. Hæc vel falsa vel male expressa sunt. Ipse in Medit. iv. dicit non esse opus facultate positiva ad errandum: an igitur ea opus ad peccandum? Non loquendum est de potentia positiva sequendi pejus, sed de imperfectione, sive impotentia negativa ex qua in privationem cadere datur: neque tam dicendum est, nos id absolute posse, quam nos semper satis à nobis esse imperfectos qui huic defectui obnoxii simus.
units.tr: {c} Descartes, Tome I, Letter CXII. These statements are either false or badly expressed. In the Fourth Meditation he himself says that no positive faculty is needed for erring: is one needed, then, for sinning? We ought not to speak of a positive power of following the worse, but of imperfection, or negative impotence, by which one is given to fall into privation; nor ought we to say so much that we are absolutely able to do this, as that we are always sufficiently imperfect in ourselves to be subject to this defect.

units.la: XIII. Sola itaque negationis indifferentia restat, quæ creaturæ tributatur. Nec novum est in subjecto positivo, ut neque etiam in actu, vel objecto, aliquid negativum considerandum dari. At quomodo respectu nihili potest dari indifferentia, siquidem ad indifferentiam duo ad minimum requirantur termini? Verum, nota est differentia quæ est inter nihil mere negativum, & inter nihil quod privativum dicitur: vel, ut dicam clarius (quia id forte in recto atque convenienti sensu à nonnullis ignoratur aut obscuratur), aliquando τὸ nihil adest, ut sic loquar, ubi adesse debet: debet autem in eo quod ex sese plane nihil est, respectu essentiæ, existentiæ, conservationis, omnium, adesse nihil determinationis propriæ, nihil scopi ad se, nihil principii à se, nihil repræsentationis sui quasi aliquid esset: & hoc sensu, nihil mere negativum dicitur; Aliquando vero τὸ nihil, ubi adesse deberet, deest, & in ejus loco inane realitatis phantasma, cassaque imitatio, adest, quod nihil, privativum dicitur. Atque horum duorum respectu datur in Mente indifferentia, vel saltem antequam peccaretur, & habitu prave deficiendi corrupta fuisset Mens, exstabat illa. Negari enim nequit, Deum liquisse mentem non determinatam à se ipsa & ad se ipsam: qui unus est ex Indifferentiæ terminis; & constat ex eventu, alterum terminum (nihil privativum) isti oppositum jam actu dari, & olim fuisse in potentia. In quocunque autem ex his Mens mansisset, ejus, sic præcise sine realitate consideratî, ratio, &, si ita vocanda sit, causa, in Mente fuisset quærenda. (quæ ratio est indifferentiæ.) Nam cum utriusque status ita spectati forma sit nihil, imo alterius sit pejor nihilo, non requiritur causa positiva, idque quantum ad hoc posterius extra dubium esse debet: Sed nec in priori ulla est ratio difficultatis: etenim quanquam Deus operando res in mente maxime positivas, Mentem ex indifferentia sic eripuisset, ut illa in nihilo respectu sui ipsius constanter mansisset, (quod in Angelis sanctis factum est) attamen dici nequit, statum mentis, quæ à se ipsa nihil est, fuisse ante peccatum insufficientem ad hoc ut mens maneret à se ipsa talis, quale decet ut quod nihil est à se ipso, maneat, nempe non se spectans, nec de se ipse acsi id à se aliquid esset, disponere tentans.
units.tr: XIII. Only the indifference of negation therefore remains, which is attributed to the creature. Nor is it new that something negative should be considered in a positive subject, just as also in an act or object. But how can indifference exist with respect to nothing, since indifference requires at least two terms? Indeed, there is a difference between nothing that is purely negative and nothing that is called privative. Or, to say it more clearly (since this is perhaps ignored or obscured by some in its correct and proper sense): sometimes τὸ nothing is present, so to speak, where it ought to be present. It ought to be present in that which of itself is plainly nothing, with respect to essence, existence, preservation, and all things: nothing of its own proper determination, nothing of purpose toward itself, nothing of principle from itself, nothing of representation of itself, as if it were something. In this sense it is called purely negative nothing. But sometimes τὸ nothing, where it ought to be, is absent, and in its place there is present an empty phantom of reality and a hollow imitation, which is called privative nothing. With respect to these two, indifference exists in the Mind, or at least it existed before sin, and before the Mind was corrupted by a habit of perverse falling away. For it cannot be denied that God left the mind undetermined by itself and toward itself, which is one of the terms of indifference; and it is clear from the outcome that the other term, the privative nothing opposed to this, is now actually given and was formerly in potency. But whichever of these the Mind had remained in, the reason, and if it must be so called, the cause, would have had to be sought in the Mind itself (this is the reason of indifference). For since the form of each state, so considered, is nothing, or rather one of them is worse than nothing, no positive cause is required; and this must be beyond doubt as regards the latter. But in the former there is also no ground for difficulty: for although God, by operating on the mind's most positive things, would have snatched the Mind out of indifference in such a way that it would have remained constantly in nothing with respect to itself (which happened in the holy Angels), yet it cannot be said that the state of the mind, which is of itself nothing, was insufficient before sin for the mind to remain of itself such as it becomes, which is nothing of itself, namely not regarding itself, nor trying to dispose of itself as if it were something from itself.

units.la: XIV. Si itaque Ego qui per Deum Cogitatio sum Spontanea, maneam in nihilo quod est non-determinatio à me, ad me, per me, pro me, simque mihi ut qui ex me, ad me & per me nihil sum, volo, opto, eligo, operor, &c. tunc non pecco. Sed si illud nihil absit, id est si Ego, res sponte cogitans, deficiam à nihilo, à non-determinatione à me, ad me, per me, &c. adsitque aliqua realitatis larva inanis, qua Ego, qui nihil sum, mihi is videar qui à me aliquid sim, sciam, bene optem, velim, operer, tunc eo ipso pecco. Unde patet peccatum, non Cogitationem spontaneam, ejusve positionem actualem esse, sed esse absentiam nihili in mente debiti, sive nihili privationem, ipso nihilo longe imperfectiorem & deteriorem, etiamsi id vel Dei proxima imitatio interdum esse videatur.
units.tr: XIV. If therefore I, who am a spontaneous thought through God, remain in the nothing which is non-determination by me, toward me, through me, for me, and I am to myself as one who is nothing from myself, toward myself and through myself; if I will, desire, choose, act, etc., then I do not sin. But if that nothing is absent, that is, if I, a thinking thing acting spontaneously, fall away from nothing, from non-determination by me, toward me, through me, etc., and some empty larva of reality is present, so that I, who am nothing, seem to myself to be something from myself, to know, to wish well, to desire, to act, then by that very fact I sin. Whence it is plain that sin is not the spontaneous thought, nor its actual positing, but the absence of the nothing due in the mind, or the privation of nothing, far more imperfect and worse than nothing itself, even if sometimes it may seem to be the nearest imitation of God.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. Difficultates notabiles ex præcedentibus septem. 2. 3. An homo debeat ex se aliquid positivi agere? 4. Num status negativus faveat negligentiæ. 5. 6. 7. An Mens possit in illo manere? quantæ perfectiones eum sequantur. 8. Num Menti inde occasio gloriandi. 8. 9. 10. Admisso peccato an maneat indifferentia? Quæ causa ad sublationem peccati. Primariæ species peccati, tres. 11. 12. De præscientia & Regimine Dei circa peccata. 13. An Deus indifferentiam tollere potuerit, & cur non sustulerit?
units.tr: 1. Notable difficulties arising from the preceding seven. 2. 3. Whether a man ought to produce anything positive from himself? 4. Whether the negative state favours negligence. 5. 6. 7. Whether the Mind can remain in that state; what perfections follow it. 8. Whether the Mind thereby has an occasion for boasting. 8. 9. 10. Once sin is admitted, does indifference remain? What is the cause of the removal of sin? The primary kinds of sin, three. 11. 12. Concerning the foreknowledge and government of God with respect to sins. 13. Could God have removed indifference, and why did He not remove it?

units.la: I. HOc, inquam, modo omnia positiva soli Deo omnium Authori asseruntur, Menti vero nil eorum tribuitur quod ad Deum efficientem sit referendum. Nam si mens quæ à se nihil est, ad se non est, neque ex sese regenda est, sit, maneatque, non à se, non ad se, non per se, tunc nihil ponit, se gerit ut nihil, & eatenus nihili, sive sui ipsius, quatenus à se nihil prorsus est, gerit imaginem. Hoc decet nihil. Eatenus nulla adest ipsi perfectio: Si vero illa peccat hæc non admittendo, vel potius non permittendo, tunc aliquid adhuc minus reale, ob quod etiam culpanda venit, perpetrat. Sed hic occurrunt nonnullæ difficultates, quas per modum quæstionum proponemus, & resolvere tentabimus.
units.tr: I. In this way, I say, all positive things are asserted to belong to God alone, the author of all things, while nothing of those things that must be referred to God as efficient cause is attributed to the Mind. For if the mind, which is nothing of itself, is not from itself, is not toward itself, is not governed by itself, and yet is and remains, then it is not from itself, not toward itself, not through itself; then it posits nothing, it conducts itself as nothing, and to that extent it bears the image of nothing, or of itself insofar as it is nothing at all of itself. This is fitting for nothing. To that extent no perfection is present in it. But if it sins by not admitting this, or rather by not permitting it, then it commits something still less real, for which it also comes to be blamed. But here several difficulties arise, which we shall propose by way of questions and try to resolve.

units.la: II. (1) De prima mentio jam supra facta est ubi indifferentia positiva repulsa fuit, & assertum creaturam nil ex se ponere, adeoque peccatum non esse proprie cessationem creaturae à bene operando. Quæri potest, an non homo debeat operari? nonne opera, & quidem bona, tenetur edere? Quam Deus hoc sæpe ab homine postulat? Cur ergo id supra negatum est, etiam de homine Sancto & innocenti, imo de omnibus creaturis? Respondeo, rationes asserti tales fuisse suo loco allegatas, ut, si confidenter interdum loqui liceat, non putem eas ab ullo unquam infirmari posse. De Scriptura dico, eam, quamvis verbis utatur quæ proprie rerum positionem significant, dicatque homines operari bona, imo à quibusdam proximos suos salvari; non tamen se ipsam evertere, quæ ubique clamat omnia à Deo esse facta, sine illo nihil; omnia ab eo, per eum & ad eum esse, & ejusmodi quamplurima. Quare phrases illas improprias esse dicimus, & intelligendas secundum eum loquendi modum, quo instrumento verbis tribuitur effectus qui ad causam efficientem est referendus. Deus ideas rerum ut voluit concepit, statuit, illas extra se expressit per earum existentiam, productionem, regimen: homini, qui ex illis est, dedit Deus ut quasdam ex his imperfecte conciperet, vultque illo uti tanquam instrumento, quod placet ei ad quarumdam positionem intervenire: ita ut homo sit respectu Dei quasi infans aliquis spectans characteres à se non inventos, nec pictos, cujus manus à præceptore tanquam instrumentum, à se quidem ad hoc immotum & ineptum, assumeretur & dirigeretur ad rectam similium scriptionem, verum ad quam nihil ex se contribueret, nisi forte quod quantum in se esset, injiceret remoram, dum ex semetipso ductus phantasticos vellet exarare. (quod nihili privativi instar se habet). Jam vero prout cum assereretur verbo scriptio illa infanti, ut solet, stultum esset tamen inde concludere infantis esse hoc opus; ita etiam male ex verbis Scripturæ concluditur, hominem positive, ut causa propriæ efficiens, operari. Similes itaque locutiones in Deum sunt refundendæ, quatenus is per hominem, qui ipse ejus opus est, operatur.
units.tr: II. (1) The first point was already mentioned above, where positive indifference was rejected, and it was asserted that a creature posits nothing from itself, and so that sin is properly not a cessation of the creature from doing good. It may be asked: ought not a man to act? Is he not bound to produce works, and indeed good works? Does God not often demand this from man? Why then was it denied above, even of a holy and innocent man, indeed of all creatures? I answer that the grounds of this assertion were set forth in their proper place, so that, if it is permissible to speak with some confidence, I do not think they can ever be weakened by anyone. I say of Scripture that, although it uses words that properly signify the positing of things, and says that men do good works, and even that some are saved by their neighbours, yet it does not overturn itself, since it everywhere cries out that all things were made by God, that nothing was made without him, that all things are from him, through him and to him, and very many things of this kind. Hence we say those phrases are improper, and are to be understood according to that manner of speaking by which an effect that belongs to the efficient cause is attributed to the instrument. God conceived the ideas of things as he willed, established them, and expressed them outside himself through their existence, production and government. God gave to man, who is one of those things, that he should conceive some of these imperfectly, and he wills to use him as an instrument, which pleases him to intervene in the positing of certain things. So man is, with respect to God, like a child looking at characters which he has neither invented nor painted, whose hand is taken up and guided by the teacher as an instrument, which of itself is indeed unmoved and unfit for this, toward the correct writing of similar characters, yet to which it contributes nothing of its own, except perhaps that, as far as it lies within it, it would throw in a hindrance, while, led by itself, it wished to scrawl fanciful lines. (This stands in the manner of a privative nothing.) Now, just as when that writing is attributed to the child by word, as is customary, it would nonetheless be foolish to conclude from this that the work is the child's; so likewise it is wrongly concluded from the words of Scripture that man acts positively, as the proper efficient cause. Such expressions must therefore be referred back to God, insofar as he acts through man, who is himself his work.

units.la: III. Quod autem hæ loquendi formulæ hic à me adhibitæ non sint, inde est, quod simpliciores & propriæ magis cum philosophico discursu convenire videantur, utpote à quo omnis ambiguitas, vel occasio extraneos conceptus per tropicas formulas introducendi, exulare debet. Itaque hac de causa de solo Deo dictum est, eum operari & ponere aliquid reale; De homine vero, eum nihil à se esse in fieri, esse, operari, regi, in principio, medio, fine; vel, si sit peccator, eum minus adadhuc esse. Positivum Deo, negativum homini, privativum peccatori tribuitur. Germanæ & propriæ locutiones: nam res ita genuine & simpliciter se habent. Quicquid reale est, fuit, eritque unquam in homine, aut est opus Dei, aut nihil. Quicquid de homine quæri & postulari potest in respectu ad causam efficientem, ad principium, ad scopum, quatenus id non est operatio Dei, sed ut opus hominis considerari potest, est nihil. Et ut illud nihil sit mere negativum, officium hominis est. Non potest quicquam nobilius à creatura posci vel exspectari quam nihil, quam negatio propriæ operationis, proprii scopi, proprii principii, & si quæ ejusmodi. Quapropter (quod seorsim forsan videretur mire falsum) verissimum est, hominem à Deo non obligari ad positivum opus efficiendum, sive, ad operandum positive: neque mandata Dei sunt ejusmodi obligationes ad hoc ut aliquid reale à creaturis ponatur. Cum enim concipi nequeat, hominem aliquid positivum à se, distincte à Deo, operari, quin ei hoc modo tribuatur quod Soli Deo, cujus Potentia, & consequenter Natura, sic negatur, proprium est; multo minus concipere datur, hominem à Deo ad hoc absurdum, quod Divinæ Naturæ repugnat, obligari. Hinc omnia Dei mandata ad homines debent ultimo in negativa resolvi, ut revera qualia sunt percipiantur. Teneant se homines ut merum nihil, cætera operari Dei est. Sed & ex Decalogi inspectione omnia fere negativa esse apparet, & id quod affirmativum videtur, quietem, cessationem, negationem operationis propriæ injungere. Quod Theologi de fœdere operum,cum homo nondum peccasset, loquantur, in quo fuerit possibile meritum, & quod gloriationem non excludat; ea patet non posse nisi negativo Sensu intelligi: nempe ut τὸ operari relatum ad hominem, sit se ex se gerere ut nihil: quod à creatura ut opus suum requiritur. mereri, sit, esse ex se per certum studium in tali statu negativo, quem sequuntur remunerationes, sive certa quædam dona, secundum Dei promissum. gloriari vero, sit cogitare vere, se non deflexisse ab isto statu nihili cui merces est annexa, sed in illo mansisse, nec se per peccatum reddidisse indignum effectu promisso. Alioqui in sensu positivo homo neque obligari potest ad operandum ex se, ut mox dictum; neque positive potest mereri, ut probatum est ubi de potentia Dei; nec denique habere potuit unde de positione ullius realitatis à se, posset gloriari: quod animadversum est in cap. de Gloria Dei; & mox ad Quæst. 4. ostendetur, Impropriam in statu nihili futuram fuisse gloriationem. Interim tamen homo fastuoso propriæ Potentiæ phantasmate insolescens, eò verbis provocari potest, test, ut, siquidem prætendat se ipsum regere, & multum posse, det hujus imaginariæ potentiæ specimen faciendo bonum, vel etiam creando sibi cor novum, unde appareat quantum revera possit præstare.
units.tr: III. That these forms of speech have not been used by me here is because simpler and proper expressions seem better to accord with philosophical reasoning, since all ambiguity, or occasion of introducing foreign concepts through figurative formulas, ought to be banished from it. Accordingly, for this reason it has been said of God alone that he acts and posits something real; but of man, that he is nothing of himself in becoming, being, acting, being governed, at the beginning, middle and end; or, if he is a sinner, that he is still less. The positive is attributed to God, the negative to man, the privative to the sinner. These are genuine and proper expressions, for things genuinely and simply stand thus. Whatever is real, was, or will ever be in man, is either the work of God or nothing. Whatever can be asked or demanded of man with respect to the efficient cause, the principle, the end, insofar as it is not the operation of God but can be considered as the work of man, is nothing. And so that this nothing may be purely negative, it is man's duty. Nothing more noble can be required or expected of a creature than nothing, that is, the negation of its own operation, its own end, its own principle, and things of that sort. Therefore (what perhaps might seem wonderfully false when taken alone) it is most true that man is not bound by God to produce a positive work, or to act positively; nor are God's commandments obligations of this kind, that something real should be posited by creatures. For since it cannot be conceived that man should act something positive from himself, distinct from God, without this being attributed to him in a manner that belongs to God alone, whose power, and consequently whose nature, is thus denied, it is far less possible to conceive that man is bound by God to this absurdity, which is repugnant to the divine nature. Hence all God's commandments to men must in the end be resolved into negative ones, so that they may be perceived as they truly are. Let men hold themselves as mere nothing; it is God's to do everything else. But also from an inspection of the Decalogue it appears that nearly all are negative, and that what seems affirmative enjoins rest, cessation, the negation of one's own operation. As for the theologians who speak of a covenant of works, when man had not yet sinned, in which merit was possible, and which does not exclude boasting: it is plain that this can only be understood in a negative sense; namely, that to work, as referred to man, is to conduct oneself from oneself as nothing, which is required of the creature as its work. To merit is to be, from oneself, through a certain zeal, in such a negative state, which is followed by rewards, or certain gifts, according to God's promise. To glory, however, is to think truly that one has not turned aside from that state of nothing to which the reward is attached, but has remained in it, and has not by sin rendered oneself unworthy of the promised effect. Otherwise, in a positive sense, man could neither be bound to act from himself, as has just been said, nor positively merit, as has been proved where we spoke of the power of God; nor finally could he have had anything from which he might glory in the positing of any reality from himself: which was noted in the chapter on the Glory of God; and it will be shown shortly, at Question 4, that boasting would have been improper in a state of nothing. Meanwhile, however, man, puffed up with the proud phantom of his own power, may be provoked by words to this extent: that, if he claims to govern himself and to be very powerful, he should give a specimen of this imaginary power by doing good, or even by creating for himself a new heart, whereby it may appear how much he can really accomplish.

units.la: IV. (2) Secundo quæri potest, An hoc non faveat hominum desidiæ & negligentiæ? siquidem videatur inde posse desumi occasio nil curandi, nil amandi, nil agendi, sese ad nihil applicandi, nullum conatum exprimendi, sed omnia ita Deo permittendi ut otiosi spectent res vadere prout vadunt, manibus suis in sinum reconditis. Respondeo, status hujusce otiosi, qui objicitur, formam non esse nihil mere negativum, sed esse potius nihili absentiam, sive præsentiam phantastici spectri sui ipsius, proprii placiti, propriæ delectationis, esse reditum inanem ad se ipsum, acsi cujusque blandum otium sui ipsius scopus esset. Hoc vero non esse se gerere coram Deo ut merum nihil. Præterea inter operationes quibus Deus statum privativum ex hominibus pellit, quasque in illis post hunc expulsum, sed modo pleniori & diviniori quam ante, efficit, sunt curæ ipsæ, diligentia, conatus, amor, actiones, labores, iiqueefficacissimi. quæ omnia tantum abest ut à nihilo quod est in homine negativo tollantur, quin potius eo locus illis conceditur amplissimus & aptissimus, ut jam amplius dicetur.
units.tr: IV. (2) Secondly, it may be asked whether this does not favour human idleness and negligence. For it might seem that an occasion is thereby taken for caring about nothing, loving nothing, doing nothing, applying oneself to nothing, making no effort, but leaving everything to God in such a way that one looks on idly while things go as they go, with one's hands hidden in one's bosom. I answer: the state of this idleness that is objected is not a form of pure nothingness; it is rather the absence of nothing, or the presence of the phantom of oneself, of one's own pleasure and one's own delight, an empty return into oneself, as if one's agreeable leisure were its own goal. But this is not to conduct oneself before God as sheer nothing. Moreover, among the operations by which God drives the privative state out of people, and which He brings about in them after this expulsion, but in a fuller and more divine manner than before, are the cares themselves, diligence, effort, love, actions, labours, and the most effective of them all. Far from these being removed from the negative nothing that is in a person, the nothing is instead given the widest and most suitable place for them, as will be said further on.

units.la: V. (3) Quæritur tertio, Num Mens possit esse vel manere in isto nihilo, in ista non-determinatione? Ratio dubitandi est, quod cum illa sit Cogitatio spontanea actu continuo posita, non videatur esse posse sine objecto ad quod feratur & determinetur quocunque modo, quemadmodum materia non potest esse sine aliqua figura modoque positivo. Non potest forma Cogitationis actualis esse & manere nihil, præsertim ejus Cogitationis quæ sit ad Dei imaginem, ejusve repræsentativa. Quomodo igitur id à Mente constanter exigitur? Respondetur, non posse quidem Mentem absolute & simpliciter in illo statu esse, ut sit & maneat sine determinatione ad aliquod objectum cui applicetur, ut velit nihil, ut tendat in nihil, neque etiam id assertum est: Sed posse eam respectu sui ipsius, quatenus illa à se nihil est, se præter-mittere, non determinare, non spectare, non gerere se ut principium à quo, & secundum quod, & ob quod regi debeat. Quæ negationes sui si adsint, in hoc ipso momento Deus in illa operabitur Divinam determinationem, Divinum scopum, Divina motiva, Divina principia, (quæ omnium operationum Dei dignissimæ sunt, siquidem aliis tanquam media non subjiciantur, sed dominentur in corde:) denique media, modi, omnia Deo placita, non deerunt. Negationem sive præter-mifmissionem sui ipsius sequitur immediate positio Dei, atque certius, quam in natura spatium ab aliquo corpore desertum ab alio statim occupatur: neque enim & hic vacuum absolutum dari potest. Mens se ipsa debite vacua simulque Divinis vacua operationibus nequit esse.
units.tr: V. (3) Thirdly, it is asked whether the mind can be, or remain, in this nothing, in this non-determination. The reason for doubting is this: since that is a spontaneous thought, actually posited in continuous act, it does not seem able to exist without an object towards which it is directed and by which it is determined in some way, just as matter cannot exist without some shape and positive mode. The form of an actual thought cannot be and remain nothing, especially of a thought that is directed to the image of God or that represents Him. How, then, is this constantly required of the mind? The answer is that the mind cannot indeed be in that state absolutely and simply, so as to exist and remain without determination towards some object to which it might apply itself, so as to will nothing or tend towards nothing; nor is this asserted. But it can, with respect to itself, insofar as it is nothing of itself, pass itself over, not determine itself, not look to itself, not conduct itself as the principle from which, according to which, and for the sake of which it ought to be ruled. If these negations of itself are present, at that very moment God will work in it the divine determination, the divine aim, the divine motives, the divine principles (which are most worthy of all God's operations, provided they are not subordinated to other things as means, but rule in the heart); finally, the means, the modes, and everything pleasing to God will not be lacking. The negation, or passing over, of oneself is immediately followed by the positing of God, and more surely than a space in nature deserted by one body is at once occupied by another; for here too no absolute void can exist. A mind that is rightly emptied of itself cannot at the same time be empty of divine operations.

units.la: VI. Hæc ita esse experti testantur. Sed & in non expertis Deus sat luminis sive operationum suarum, quas universas nunquam retrahit, vel in pessimis, reliquit, ex quibus de hacce veritate possint convinci. Interroget se ipsum quisque, Quid, si nihil, sive in se, ut notitias, voluntatem, affectus, & similia, sive in universitate rerum, objectum nullum, à se ipso & ob se ipsum vellet, eligeret, optaret, aversaretur? Quid inquam fieret si ego huncce ad me respectum omitterem? Procul dubio siquidem à Deo sponte cogitans conservaret, nec, ut dictum, cogitatio mea omni objecto atque determinatione posset carere, neque etiam à me ad ullum quid determinarer, restaret ut Deus hoc in me operaretur. Quid vero, quove modo? Non certe quicquam contra se ipsum suumve placitum, sed profecto secundum se. Itaque cum is à se non alienus ad se ipsum determinetur, se amet, seque, suumque placitum atque opus propter se ipsum approbet, in me etiam mei ad se determinationem, & sui omniumque suorum propter se amorem atque approbationem operaretur: cumque unus ille sit omnium principium, finis scopusque, omnia quoque quæ in me ad se referret, & à sui motivo inciperet. Hoc modo non relinqueret in me imaginem mei nihili solitariam, sed ea tanquam loco uteretur quem suis operationibus, ipsum illum optime repræsentantibus, repleret; atque, ut graphice dicam, is esset in me se ipsum, suum placitum, suum opus contemplans, amans, volens, se ipsum orans, esset in me eligens, rejiciens, disponens, agens, denique omnia esset. quod tamen respectu essentiæ suæ nolim ita intelligi quasi ejus Natura esset in me subjectum quod hosce modos in se admitteret: Sed is hæc esset operatione, effector esset; vel si cum scholis loquendum, hæc ille esset causaliter & efficienter, non vero subjective & essentialiter.
units.tr: VI. Those who have experienced it testify that this is so. But even in those who have not experienced it, God has left enough light, or enough of His operations, which He never wholly withdraws, even from the worst people, from which they can be convinced of this truth. Let each person ask himself: what, if he were to choose, desire, long for, or shrink from nothing, either in himself, as in knowledge, will, affections, and the like, or in the universe of things, no object, from himself and for his own sake? What, I say, would happen if I were to omit this regard to myself? Without doubt, since I think spontaneously and am preserved by God, and as has been said, my thought could not lack every object and determination, nor would I be determined by myself to anything; it would remain that God should work this in me. But what, and in what way? Certainly not anything against Himself or His own pleasure, but surely in accordance with Himself. Therefore, since He is not alien to Himself, and is determined to Himself, He loves Himself and approves Himself and His own pleasure and work for His own sake; He would also work in me a determination towards Himself, and a love and approval of Himself and of all that is His, for His own sake. And since that one is the principle, end and goal of all things, He would also refer everything in me to Himself and begin from His own motive. In this way He would not leave in me a solitary image of my nothing, but would occupy the place which He would fill with His operations, which best represent Himself; and, to speak graphically, He would be in me contemplating Himself, His own pleasure, His own work, loving, willing, praying to Himself; He would be in me choosing, rejecting, disposing, acting; in short, He would be all things. Yet I would not wish this to be understood, with respect to His essence, as if His nature were in me as a subject admitting these modes in itself; rather He would be the one who works these things, the effector; or, if we are to speak in the manner of the schools, He would be these things causally and efficiently, not subjectively and essentially.

units.la: VII. Et tunc revera tantum abesset ut ob statum mei nihili Divina imagine destituerer, quin hoc modo, cui divinæ junctæ sunt operationes, illa in me esset maxime conspicua. Etenim nonne si operetur ille in me diligentiam, curas, laboresque sanctiores, hoc ipso suæ ipsius Activitatis adumbrationem sistet? Nonne si patientiam, ex. gr. si in rebus adversis tolerantiam atque hilarem acquiescentiam efficiat, sese quasi imagine ostendet felicem sufficientemque, quippe qui sic videatur menti, quamquam externis undique conquassatæ & omnibus destitutæ, & sufficere & gaudium esse? Sapientem, cum sine murmure mihi ac-quiescentiam in se dabit? Viventem atque Spiritualem, cum in eo statu præ cogitationibus, quas potenter sustinebit, cætera materialia non vi-debitur adeo curare? Annon operando in me absolutam omnium quæ in me esse possent sibi ipsi ob se ipsum submissionem, optime ejus abso-lutum Dominium, ejus Bonitatem, Potentiam & Altitudinem sic il-lustrat? Sed innumera sunt, & ineffabilia quæ huc pertinent, quæque nec vidit oculus, nec audivit auris, nec mundanus animus est assecu-tus. Ea vero detexit Deus & operatus est in illis qui à se ipsis quicquam agere aut velle non prætenderunt, ut patuit in humanitate Filii Dei, & in ejus genuinis sectatoribus. Hic status nihili præbet materiam cui for-ma veri Christiani (rarae avis in terris) superinducatur; mensque eo dispositæ instar materiæ est, obscurae quidem & indigestæ eatenus, sed in qua tamen futurum est ut dicatur potenter, fiat lux: vel potius illa spatium hoc inane & informe est, in quod novi mundi forma intro-ducenda; & dum omnia reliquit, invenit illa clavem qua ad thesau-ros penetret cæteris occultatos. Hoc est Nihil illud, quod à Viris Sanctis in mysticis & Divinis suis contemplationibus est tantopere commen-datum.
units.tr: VII. And then indeed I should be so far from being deprived of the divine image on account of the state of my nothing, that in this way, to which the divine operations are joined, that image would be most conspicuous in me. For if He worked in me greater diligence, cares and holier labours, would this not itself present a shadow of His own activity? If He produced patience, for example, endurance and cheerful acquiescence in adverse circumstances, would He not show Himself, as it were, in an image of happiness and sufficiency, since He appears to the mind as both sufficient and joy, although the mind is shaken on every side by external things and deprived of everything? Would He not give me acquiescence in Himself without murmuring, as a wise person does? Would He, when in that state, not seem so much to care for material things, because of the thoughts which He powerfully sustains, as one living and spiritual? Does He not, by working in me an absolute submission of everything that could be in me to Himself for His own sake, illustrate in the best way His absolute dominion, His goodness, power and loftiness? But the things that pertain to this are countless and ineffable, which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has the worldly mind attained. God, however, has revealed them and has worked in those who did not claim to do or will anything of themselves, as was manifest in the humanity of the Son of God and in His genuine followers. This state of nothing provides the material upon which the form of the true Christian (a rare bird on earth) is superimposed; and the mind thus disposed is like matter, obscure and undigested to that extent, but in which it will nevertheless be powerfully said, Let there be light. Or rather, it is that empty and formless space into which the form of a new world is to be introduced; and while it has left everything, it finds the key by which it penetrates to treasures hidden from others. This is that Nothing which has been so highly commended by holy men in their mystical and divine contemplations.

units.la: VIII. (4) At, (quæ quarta sive quæstio, sive difficultas est) cum illud Nihil tantum habeat bonum secum annexum, cumque assertum sit nihil illud à mente esse; nonne possit inde mens gloriari si illa à se in statu nihili maneat, eumque quem tanta bona sequuntur, præstatu nihili privativi teneat? nonne dicere posset, se, si non peccet, esse causam cur non peccet? Respondeo primo, illa bona quæ statum nihili negativi sequuntur, non sequi ex vi nihili, non esse vel ab ipso nihilo, vel etiam à mente, ne quidem Angelica, posita; sed à Sola Dei liberalitate & placito ejus liberrimo, ut ex Dominio Dei videre licet, pendere, qui illa gratis à nullo externo motivo impulsus, distribuit quæ & quanta placet; ita ut quamvis omnes mentes instar SS. Angelorum mansissent respectu sui in ejusmodi statu, non habuissent unquam unde de ullius vel minimæ realitatis positione potuissent gloriari. hoc æternum ab omni creatura abest. Secundo, velim notari, quod de indifferentia inter statum nihili & statum peccati dictum est, illud non fuisse assertum exstare in Mente postquam se statui peccaminoso mancipavit, quasi illa postquam pravitati se subjecit, posset ex se ab ea se liberare, & ad statum negativum regredi, hoc est, ex statu magis imperfecto minus imperfe-ctum [?]ctum sistere, atque gloriari de diminutione mali ante positi. De hoc non adhuc dictum est. forsan quid sit de eo sentiendum aperietur in posterum. Mens hactenus spectata est ut nondum pravo privativum eli-gendi actu corrupta. Tertio, non peccare, in Mente ita considerata, quod etiam in nihilo vel in materia videre licet, non est in se aliquid positivi. Mentem per se non peccare, nil aliud est quam dicere, Mentem quatenus est Dei opus, non esse peccati insimulandam, ut etiam principio monitum est; eandemque quatenus à se nihil est, non esse quoque ream peccati: hoc est, opus Dei, & merum nihil, non esse peccatum, nec peccatum in se præcise involvere. Quod incongruum non est. De-nique absurdum, contradictorium & impossibile est, Mentem in statu nihili posse in se gloriari, proprie & in sensu positivo, nam non-gloriari in se est ipse status nihili, & qui in se gloriari quærit eo ipso ex illo statu decidit, & se ad se ipsum determinat; qui vero in eo statu manet, eo ipso se non spectat, se prætermittit atque linquit. Sed quæso, quæ glo-riandi ansa, glorior in me quia sum vel quia fui hactenus in statu ni-hili! hoc est, quia nihil respectu mei, non modo substantiæ sed & regiminis sum, & hactenus fui ut decet τὸ nihil respectu sui esse, ideo geram me ut dedecet τὸ nihil se gerere: quod idem est ac, gloriabor in me. Hæc certe ex permanentia in statu negativo nequaquam pul-lulant.
units.tr: VIII. (4) But (which is the fourth question or difficulty), since that Nothing has so great a good annexed to it, and since it has been asserted that this nothing is from the mind, could not the mind boast, if it remains of itself in the state of nothing, and holds to the state of privative nothingness, which is followed by such great goods? Could it not say that, if it does not sin, it is itself the cause of its not sinning? I answer, first, that the goods which follow the state of negative nothingness do not follow from the force of nothing, nor do they depend on nothing itself, nor on the mind, not even an angelic mind; they depend solely on God's liberality and His most free pleasure, as can be seen from God's dominion. He, moved by no external motive, freely distributes these goods, both in what kind and in what amount He pleases; so that even if all minds had remained, like the holy angels, in such a state with respect to themselves, they would never have had any ground for boasting of the positing of any, even the smallest, reality. This is eternally far from every creature. Second, I would have it noted that what was said about the indifference between the state of nothing and the state of sin was not asserted to exist in the mind after it has given itself over to a sinful condition, as if, after it has submitted to wickedness, it could free itself from it of its own accord and return to the negative state, that is, from a more imperfect state set a less imperfect one, and boast of the diminution of the evil posited before. This has not yet been discussed. Perhaps what is to be thought about it will become clear hereafter. Thus far the mind has been considered as not yet corrupted by the act of privatively choosing evil. Third, not to sin, in the mind so considered (as can also be seen in nothing or in matter), is not in itself anything positive. For the mind not to sin in itself is nothing other than to say that the mind, insofar as it is God's work, is not to be accused of sin, as was also warned at the beginning; and likewise insofar as it is nothing of itself, it is not guilty of sin either; that is, God's work, and sheer nothing, is not sin, nor does it in itself precisely involve sin. This is not incongruous. Finally, it is absurd, contradictory and impossible for the mind in the state of nothing to be able to boast in itself properly and in a positive sense; for not to boast in itself is itself the state of nothing, and whoever seeks to boast in himself by that very fact falls from that state and determines himself to himself; but whoever remains in that state, by that very fact does not look to himself, but passes himself over and leaves himself behind. But I ask, what ground for boasting is there? Do I boast in myself because I am, or because I have hitherto been, in the state of nothing? That is, because with respect to myself I am nothing, not only in substance but also in governance, and have hitherto been as it befits nothing to be with respect to itself, therefore I conduct myself as it is unbecoming for nothing to conduct itself; which is the same as saying, I shall boast in myself. Certainly these things do not spring up at all from remaining in the negative state.

units.la: IX. (5) Quinto, ex occasione membri secundi responsionis proximæ quærere licet, non quæ de indifferentia mentis inter nihil negationis & privationis dicta sunt, ita se habeant, ut Mens æque sit indif-ferens post peccatum admissum quam ante? Cui responderi potest ex notitia illa communi, omne manere in statu suo nisi à Pontentiori alio deturbetur, quam in omnibus advertere licet, imo & in ipsa commis-sione peccati. Nam quod hominem à statu negativo dejecit in privati-vum, phantasma aliquod fuit, spectrum sui ipsius, proprii regiminis, quod potentius quid apparet quam merum nihil; non quod sit, sed quod appareat, nam in peccato omnia, quatenus id concernunt, sunt apparentiæ absurdæ, nil reale: si enim id revera potens fuisset, pecca-tum tunc, utpote positivæ causæ realis effectus, peccatum non esset. Sed cum status nihili negativi non sit inane aliquod phantasma, non spectrum falsum, aliter se habens aliter vero apparens, ejus reductionis in subjectum unde ille per peccatum abfuit, causa & ratio non debet esse phantastica, nec tantum potentior malo per apparentiam. Quodsi causa non detur, neque status negativus redire potest, neque adeo potest illic indifferentia concipi. Quænam autem esset illa hujus redu-ctionis causa? Indifferentia prior? Sublata est. Indifferentia determina-tione, cum hæc fit, tollitur; post illam, ut post actum, habitus se-quitur indifferentiam infirmans. Mens privativo modo determinans se, tollit ex se indifferentiam, adest determinatio peccaminosa, hæc manet igitur id quod est, continuat, durat, roboratur in suo statu & sublatione indifferentiæ, nisi detur causa mutationis: cur enim sine causa mutari supponeretur?
units.tr: IX. (5) Fifthly, following on from the second member of the previous reply, one may ask whether what has been said about the mind's indifference between the nothing of negation and of privation is such that the mind is equally indifferent after sin has been committed as before. To this it can be answered from that common notion: everything remains in its own state unless it is thrown down by something more powerful, which can be observed in all things, and even in the very commission of sin. For that which cast the human being from the negative state into the privative one was some phantasm, a spectre of itself and of its own rule, which appears to be something more powerful than mere nothing; not because it is, but because it appears so. For in sin all things, insofar as they concern it, are absurd appearances, nothing real. If, indeed, that thing had truly been powerful, sin would then not be sin, since it would be the effect of a positive and real cause. But since the state of negative nothing is not some empty phantasm, not a false spectre that is otherwise than it appears, the cause and reason of its return into the subject from which it was removed by sin must not be phantastic, nor merely more powerful than evil through appearance. Now if no cause is given, the negative state cannot return, and indeed no indifference can be conceived there. But what would be the cause of this return? Prior indifference? It has been removed. Indifference is removed by the determination, when that takes place; after it, as after an act, a habit follows which weakens indifference. The mind, determining itself in a privative manner, removes indifference from itself; the sinful determination is present; this therefore remains what it is, continues, endures, is strengthened in its state, and indifference is abolished, unless a cause of change is given. For why would it be supposed to change without a cause?

units.la: X. Sed jam quæret forte aliquis, quænam causa requiratur? Negativa, dicet forsan alius, adeoque quæ à creatura fit. Quæ ergo illa? An status meri nihili? Is vero per peccatum à creatura peccante expulsus est. An Indifferentia? ea etiam expulsa, daturque à nihilo defectio ad privationem ejus, datur deflexio ab uno extremo & propensio ad alte-rum: quod negotium non conficit, sed contra. Quid igitur causæ as-signandum, siquidem præter recensita nil sit in creatura quod possit suspicari ab ipsa esse? Certe patet hinc ad sublationem privationis in subjecto quod permanet requiri realissimam causam operantem. Quid vero operantem? An ut nihil redeat operandum est positive? Imo, ut phantasmata vana omnia ejiciantur, multis opus est intus & extus acti-bus particularibus, exercitiis, modis & formis diversis incompletisque: his enim & privatio, modusque quo in mente viguit, evacuantur: & mens vacua sic reducitur ad nihili statum, quem, ut ad quæstionem ter-tiam dictum est, sequuntur operationes novæ, simpliciores, puriores, magis immediatæ, directæ, completæ, solidæ & uniformes. Possit igitur privationis sublatio cum sublatione nihili, quæ per positionem fit, comparari, similemque postulare causam. Sumamus rem à principio. Ad status nihili meri sublationem datur causa: ergo & ad status privativi sublationem. Status nihili tollitur duobus modis, uno bono, altero malo, hinc duo causarum genera: forte & idem de statu privativo videbimus. Status nihili tollitur, sed male, ab homine, sua ipsius prava positione, quæ causa, nisi ex falsa apparentia, non est τῷ[?] nihilo potentior, quin revera imperfectior est, & recte ad privationem nihili, sive ad minus quàm nihil reducitur. Tollitur & status nihili, & quidem recte, à Deo, per positionem operationum suarum, dum non sinit vel omnia manere nihil; vel in homine, (ut ad tertiam quæstionem dictum est,) cum meri nihili solitariam gerere imaginem, sed suam ei superin-ducit, quæ Causa realissima est, maxime positiva, omnemque nihili extensionem potentiæ immensitate superans. (ut de Potentia Dei suo loco vidimus.) Ita quoque de privativo statu dicere licet. Prave tollitur, hoc est, non tollitur, sed potius roboratur & reduplicatur, si creatura illum à se ipsa & per se ipsam tollere praetendat: sic absurde iterat phantasma sui ipsius, à se ipsa quae jam semel suae impotentiae, & mali quod in sui amplexu, convicta est, ad se ipsam se convertit, sibique potentiae idolum immensum, ultra limites nihili efficax, in se effingit: qui status priore pejor, fere est insanabilis & desperatus, ad quem crediderim dari in peccatore indifferentiam novam, ita ut, quia hic status non est idem cum illo qui simpliciter privativus est, sed omnino est alius naturae deterioris, etiam sit indifferens peccator ad hoc ut ei satis sit status suus priori peccaminosus, vel ad hunc deteriorem amplectendum. Quemadmodum, ut hoc ex occasione addam, postquam in hunc deteriorem lapsus est, iterum indifferens videtur esse concipiendus vel ad subsistendum in hoc ipso in quo se gerere praetendit acsi esset plusquam Creator, nempe & Ereptor à malo; vel ad deficiendum ad statum peccati alterius naturae, in quo convictus, illuminatus, doctusque eatenus à Deo, ut sciat se jam duplici crimine teneri, neque se ipsum, sed Deum esse Creatorem, & Liberatorem à malo, nihilominus Deum sciens sponteque praetermittat & sinat; sui ipsius vero idolum, quod conscit à se nihil, & nihilo deterius, nil facere vel servare potens, amplectatur. quod genus peccati & ultimum & immedicabile habetur: neque enim concipere datur Deum unquam, ulloque modo, magis à Mente abesse posse, quam isto. Quod autem ut ante primum peccatum, quod rejicit Deum ut Creatorem, sic & ante secundae peccati speciei statum, qui est in Deum Liberatorem, atque tertiae, in Deum Illuminatorem, indifferentia suo cuique statui conveniens posita fit; ejus rationes ad similitudinem earum quae in prima specie peccati recensitae sunt, deducendas, & à difficultatibus, quae prioribus fere correspondent, vindicandas, relinquimus. Id enim haec percipientibus operosum non est. Sed nec erat hujus instituti de hisce agere, tametsi quoniam hic in mentem inciderunt, ea non recusaverim tanquam incidentia illico reponere, addito, negata indifferentia inter peccati naturam statumque ex his tribus primum & secundum, vel inter secundum & tertium, inde sequi radices peccati ultimae naturae esse in peccatoribus omnibus, sive eos potentia commisisse peccatum ultimum, hoc est, pro iis esse habendos qui in illud incidissent, nisi Deus quod futurum erat, & cujus jam exstabat principium, impediisset, remediumque admovisset: quomodo id peccatum naturae principiique sui respectu non esset, quale tamen esse agnoscitur, immedicabile. Quam profunde igi-tur, & horrende, ut eo unde digressi sumus, redeamus, ex regressu sui ad se ipsum gradatim evenit cadere! Quare, omisso cujusque ad se re-cursu, ut recte è medio statu privativus sive peccaminosus tollatur, si-stenda causa, quæ, siquidem malum sit pejus quam nihil, sit, si sic loqui liceat, plusquam realissima, ultra vagos vastosque nihili limites transcendens, vincens & implens plusquam π[?] minus nihilo; placitum extraordinarium, ut sic dicam, & novi generis; operatio plusquam or-dinarie efficax, plusquam potens expellere simplex nihilum, plusquam Creatrix, bona, liberalis; in qua non jam ut ante potentia, sed virtus potentiæ roboris; non liberalitas, sed thesaurus immensus divitiarum; non bonitas, sed ingens misericordia deprædicentur. Hæc illa est effi-cax & victrix Gratia, Creatio nova & secunda priori magis stupenda, quæ à statu nihilo minori reducit ad statum, qualem diximus, nihili meri sive negativi, nam hac (quæ depositio veteris hominis) transeun-dum est; & ab illo ad omnis realitatis excellentiam (indutionem homi-nis Novi) quam Deus pro placito suo operatur. Nonne hisce ex Dei gratia suum intus in mente invenire est testimonium? An autem cæteri in quibus ista omnia non sic operatur Deus, reducantur tamen omnes per Deum ad eum indifferentiæ statum, ut ipsis de novo per aliquam temporis periodum integrum relinquatur se ipsos amplecti vel non am-plecti? non est hujus loci inquirere. Sed & id asserere non infert ullam absurditatem, nihil enim sic tribuitur homini, nil detrahitur Deo, cui omnis mali diminutio & repressio adscribitur: quin potius, id aptum est Dei misericordiam commendare. Hinc non est quod quis offenda-tur quibusdam loquendi formulis, quibus nonnulli vere probi, gloriæ-que Dei (cui omnia referunt) studiosi, nonnunquam utuntur; v. g. homines habere adhucdum liberum arbitrium, libertatem eligendi vi-tam aut mortem, Deum aut Diabolum, salutem aut damnationem, imo, faciendi bonum vel malum: quibus (quanquam iis superbi abuti possint) recte intelligere est, hominem non tantum esse semper non-coa-ctum in istis, sed & Deum homini servare eum statum in quo ei liceat se gerere aut modo privativo (quod est amplecti mortem, &c.) aut ne-gativo modo, quem sequitur operatio vitalis & salutaris Dei. Et hoc respectu putandus est homo indifferens seu liber dici ad operandum bo-num, nempe non immediate, quasi bonum ab homine poni posset; at bene indifferens ad id (statum negativum) cujus præsentiam sequitur operatio boni quæ à Deo est & fit. Quo sensu etiam bene capi possunt quæ supra vidimus à Scriptura hominibus tribui, quasi ipsi bona operarentur.
units.tr: X. But perhaps someone will now ask: what cause is required? A negative one, another might say, and therefore one that comes from the creature. What, then, is it? Is it the state of mere nothing? But that has been driven out of the creature by sin, the creature having sinned. Is it indifference? That too has been driven out, and there is a falling away from nothing into its privation, a deflection from one extreme and an inclination toward the other; this business does not come to completion, but the reverse. What cause, then, is to be assigned, since, apart from what has been listed, there is nothing in the creature which could be suspected to come from itself? Clearly, from this, it is evident that for the removal of a privation in a subject which remains, a most real operating cause is required. But what operating cause? Must something be operated positively, so that nothing may return? Indeed, so that all empty phantasms may be cast out, there is need of many particular acts, both inward and outward, of exercises, of various and incomplete modes and forms; for by these both the privation and the manner in which it flourished in the mind are emptied out. And the mind thus emptied is brought back to the state of nothing, which, as was said in the third question, is followed by new operations, simpler, purer, more immediate, direct, complete, solid and uniform. The removal of privation can therefore be compared with the removal of nothing, which is effected by a positing, and it demands a similar cause. Let us take the matter from the beginning. For the removal of the state of mere nothing a cause is given; therefore also for the removal of the privative state. The state of nothing is removed in two ways, one good and the other bad; hence two kinds of causes. Perhaps we shall see the same concerning the privative state. The state of nothing is removed, but badly, by the human being, through his own perverse positing, which cause, unless from a false appearance, is not more powerful than nothing; indeed it is actually more imperfect, and is rightly reduced to privation of nothing, or at least to less than nothing. The state of nothing is also removed, and indeed rightly, by God, through the positing of his operations, since he does not allow everything to remain nothing; and he superinduces in the human being (as was said in the third question) not the solitary image of mere nothing, but his own, which is the most real cause, most positive, and surpassing every extension of nothing in the immensity of power (as we saw in its place concerning the power of God). It is likewise permissible to say the same of the privative state. It is removed badly, that is, it is not removed but rather strengthened and redoubled, if the creature claims to remove it from itself and through itself. Thus absurdly the phantasm of itself is repeated: the creature, already once convicted of its own impotence and of the evil it embraces, turns itself back to itself, and fashions in itself an immense idol of power, effective beyond the limits of nothing. This state, worse than the former, is almost incurable and hopeless. I would believe that in the sinner there is a new indifference with respect to it, so that, since this state is not the same as that which is simply privative, but is wholly of another and worse nature, the sinner may be indifferent to this, so that his own sinful state is enough for him, or so that he embraces this worse one. Just as, to add this by way of occasion, after he has fallen into this worse state, he must again be conceived as indifferent, either to remaining in this very thing in which he pretends to behave as though he were more than Creator, namely also Deliverer from evil; or to falling away into the state of sin of another nature, in which, convicted, enlightened and taught by God so far that he knows he is now held by a double crime, and that not himself but God is Creator and Liberator from evil, he nevertheless, knowing God and willingly, lets this pass and allows it; but he embraces the idol of himself, which he knows to be nothing of himself, and worse than nothing, able to do or preserve nothing. This kind of sin is held to be both the last and incurable. For it cannot be conceived that God could ever, in any way, be further removed from the mind than by this. But as for the indifference suited to each state being posited before the first sin, which rejects God as Creator, and likewise before the state of the second species of sin, which is against God as Liberator, and of the third, against God as Illuminator, we leave it to be deduced from the reasons which were listed for the first species of sin, by analogy with them, and to be vindicated against the difficulties which almost correspond to the earlier ones. For this is not laborious to those who perceive these things. But it was not the purpose of this undertaking to treat of these matters, although, since they have come to mind here, I would not refuse to set them down at once as incidental, adding that, indifference being denied between the nature of sin and the state of the three, the first and second, or between the second and third, it follows from this that the roots of the last nature of sin are in all sinners, whether they have been able to commit the ultimate sin, that is, whether they are to be held as those who would have fallen into it, had God not impeded what was to come, and of which the beginning already existed, and applied a remedy; how this sin, with respect to its nature and principle, would not be such, though it is acknowledged to be such, and incurable. How deeply and horribly, then, to return to where we digressed, does it come about, from a return of self to self, that one falls step by step! Wherefore, leaving aside the recourse of each to himself, in order that the privative or sinful state may rightly be removed from the middle, a cause must be posited which, since evil is worse than nothing, must be, if one may so speak, more than most real, transcending the vague and vast limits of nothing, conquering and filling more than π[?] minus nothing; an extraordinary and, so to speak, new kind of decree; an operation more than ordinarily effective, more than able to expel simple nothingness, more than creative, good, liberal; in which not power as before, but the virtue of strength of power, is proclaimed; not liberality, but an immense treasure of riches; not goodness, but great mercy. This is that effective and victorious Grace, a new creation and a second, more stupendous than the first, which leads from the state less than nothing back to the state, such as we have said, of mere or negative nothing; for through this (which is the putting off of the old man) one must pass, and from that to the excellence of all reality (the putting on of the new man), which God works by his own good pleasure. Is it not possible to find within the mind, from the grace of God, testimony of these things? But whether the others, in whom God does not work all these things in this way, are nevertheless all led back by God to that state of indifference, such that for them there is left, anew, for some whole period of time, the power to embrace themselves or not to embrace themselves, is not a matter for inquiry in this place. But to assert this too does not entail any absurdity, for nothing is thereby attributed to man, nothing is taken from God, to whom all diminution and restraining of evil is ascribed; rather, this is suited to commend the mercy of God. Hence there is no reason for anyone to take offence at certain forms of speech which some truly upright men, zealous for the glory of God (to whom they refer all things), sometimes use: for example, that human beings still have free choice, the liberty to choose life or death, God or the Devil, salvation or damnation, indeed to do good or evil. By these (although the proud can abuse them) it is rightly understood that the human being is not only always unconstrained in these matters, but also that God preserves for him that state in which it is permitted for him to behave either in a privative manner (which is to embrace death, etc.) or in a negative manner, which is followed by the vital and saving operation of God. And in this respect the human being is to be thought of as called indifferent or free to work good, namely not immediately, as if good could be posited by the human being; but rightly indifferent to that (the negative state) whose presence is followed by the operation of good which is from God and is done by God. In this sense also those things which we saw above are attributed by Scripture to men, as if they themselves worked good, can well be understood.

units.la: XI. (6) Sed & adhuc difficultas, quam sexto ponimus loco, resolvenda proponi potest. Si ante peccatum, imo ante quemlibet ex tribus speciebus peccati statum, creatura sit indifferens eo modo qui dictus est, ita ut in quocunque ex istis illa postmodum sit, ejus ratio & causa in illa sit, non in Deo; quomodo Deus certo prænoscet peccatum? Aut ejus notitia non dependebit ab indifferentiæ mentis incerto habitu? aut vero, Nonne operationes quas si peccatum non fuisset, operatus esset, eatenus dependebunt à creatura, ut possint per illam impediri? Quomodo denique circa hæc competet certum Deo regimen? Respondeo, Caveat Cogitatio creata ne in his ultra Sphæram suam se tentet efferre, atque sic peccet. Hæreamus hactenus demonstratis. Si quædam accedant quæ non capiamus, memores simus sortis Cognitionis nostræ. Difficultas ex eo maxime accedit, quod peccati notitiam instar notitiæ realium entium considerare velint. Cæterum hæc conclusa teneantur. Cum omnia essent absolutissimum nihil, respectu & essentiæ & substantiæ, & existentiæ; dependet à solo Dei placito indifferenti, ut essent & efficerentur quæ & quot vellet & voluit. Cum omnia vel aliqua sunt in nihilo determinationis, dependet à solo Dei placito, ut in illis operetur quæ & quanta, & quo modo vult. Cum omnia sunt in statu nihili privativi, sive peccati, dependet à Solo Dei placito, ut in quibus vult quæ & quanta & quomodo vult, operetur. Itaque notitia quam habet Deus de harum realitatum essentia, existentia, & modis, est ab illo solo, idque independenter ab omni creatura. Ulterius: Operatio Divina peccato opposita, generalius spectata sine determinatione graduum, &c. eatenus à me pendet, ut si illa in me non sit, ego sim causa ejus absentiæ. Hæc non est proprie dependentia operationis, quemadmodum non dependet à me lux Solis, quamvis claudens oculos ea me destitui causser. Pergamus. Quod detur peccati idea, notio, atque existentia, causa omnino Deus non est. Deus quocunque modo noscat peccatum, in minima suæ cognitionis realitate à nullo, neque etiam à tempore, dependet. Privationes sive peccata ita Deo prævidentur (quocunque illud fiat modo) ut prævisio hæc non sit causa cur peccata existant vel sint, sive, non efficiat illa, utpote quæ positivam causam non requirunt. Hæc omnia suis in locis demonstrata sunt, & sufficiunt. Sed inquies, quomodo illa simul cum notitia Dei de peccato conciliabis? aut vero, quomodo putas Deum nosse peccatum & prænosse? Difficultas est de primo quoque ex tribus speciebus recensitis peccato, non de illis quæ prima admissa sequuntur, quæque primis præsuppositis prænosci, facile concipiuntur. At de primis quid? Dico, postquam diu cogitavi, huc & illuc oculos conjeci, redeundum esse ad hanc ingenuam confessionem, nescio, nec possum scire, nec debeo scire, neque adeo amplius opto scire. {a}Admirabilis scientia tua superat me, & ita excelsa est, ut ad eam attingere non possim, ait divinus Vir. Et exclamat alius, {b}Divinam cognitionem ita esse profundam, ut ejus viæ inveniri nequeant. Nonne hactenus evidenter conclusa atque perspecta conscientiam sufficienter hac in re tranquillare valent? Num opus est ad quietem animi mei ut sciam quomodo se habeat cognitio in Deo? Hæc igitur temeraria relinquimus, contenti clare agnitis.
units.tr: XI. (6) But a further difficulty, which we place sixth, can also be raised for resolution. If, before sin, or indeed before any of the three kinds of sinful state, the creature is indifferent in the way just described, so that whichever of these states it later falls into, the reason and cause of that lie in the creature and not in God, how does God foreknow sin with certainty? Either his knowledge will not depend on the uncertain disposition of an indifferent mind; or else, will not the operations which, had there been no sin, he would have performed, depend on the creature to that extent, so that they could be hindered by it? Finally, how can a certain government of God be exercised over these things? I answer: the created thought should take care not to try to raise itself beyond its own sphere in these matters, and so sin. Let us hold to what has been demonstrated so far. If some things arise which we cannot grasp, let us remember the lot of our knowledge. The difficulty arises chiefly from the fact that they wish to consider the knowledge of sin as like the knowledge of real beings. Otherwise, let these conclusions be held fast. Since all things were absolutely nothing, with respect to their essence, their substance and their existence, it depends on God's sole indifferent pleasure that they should be, and be made, which and how many he wished and willed. Since all things, or some of them, are in the nothing of determination, it depends on God's sole pleasure that he works in them what and how great and in what manner he wills. Since all things are in the state of privative nothingness, or sin, it depends on God's sole pleasure that he works in those in whom he wills, what and how great and in what manner he wills. Therefore the knowledge which God has of the essence, existence and modes of these realities is from him alone, and independent of every creature. Further: the divine operation opposed to sin, viewed more generally without the determination of degrees, etc., depends on me to this extent, that if it is not in me, I am the cause of its absence. This is not properly a dependence of the operation, just as the light of the sun does not depend on me, although I am the cause of its being withdrawn from me when I close my eyes. Let us go on. That there is an idea, notion and existence of sin, God is by no means the cause. Whatever way God knows sin, he depends in the smallest reality of his knowledge on no one, not even on time. Privations or sins are foreseen by God (in whatever way that takes place) in such a manner that this foreknowledge is not the cause why sins exist or are, that is, it does not produce them, since they do not require a positive cause. All these things have been demonstrated in their places and are sufficient. But you will say: how will you reconcile these things with the knowledge of God concerning sin? Or rather, how do you think God knows and foreknows sin? The difficulty concerns the first of the three recounted kinds of sin, not those which follow once the first is admitted, and which, given the first, are easily conceived as foreknown. But what of the first? I say, after I have thought about it for a long time and cast my eyes here and there, we must return to this ingenuous confession: I do not know, nor can I know, nor ought I to know, nor indeed do I any longer wish to know. "Your knowledge is wonderful; it surpasses me, and it is so lofty that I cannot attain to it," says the divine man. And another exclaims that the divine knowledge is so deep that its ways cannot be found. Do not these conclusions, clearly reached and examined so far, suffice to quiet the conscience in this matter? Is it necessary for the peace of my mind that I know how knowledge stands in God? Therefore we leave these rash questions aside, content with what is clearly recognised.

units.la: XII. De Divino regimine & providentia circa ea quæ uno ex præcipuis admisso specialiora sequuntur peccata, vel potius circa peccati diversas apparentias & facies, res facile concipitur. Peccati apparentias aut facies, aut vestes, aut signa appello, modos particulares, & plerumque extus se prodentes, quibus manifestatur quod Mens à statu nihili sui ad inane idolum deflexit. quod una ostendit absurde versando circa metalla vel opes, altera circa carnalia, aliave, quæ interdum maxima, imo maxime spiritualia putantur, quæque unius peccati intus præsentis & durantis, unius status privativi qui in Mente est, malim diversas appellare vestes & apparentias, quam species aut naturas. Jam ad peccatum ipsum quod attinet, Deus, si proprie loquendum, illud non regit, etenim nihil positivi in Deo est quod ad peccatum, ad non-ens, proprie terminetur; sed subjectum peccati, Cogitationem Spontaneam, item corpus, ejus modos, motus, corpora quæ circum illud hoc vel modo, tempore, & cætera, quæ ex se peccata non sunt, atque realitates sunt, à Deo ex liberrimo placito, ut de omni realitate demonstratum est, ponuntur & reguntur. & hinc Mens peccatrix illis juncta & implicata suum peccatum, in se intus conceptum & jam factum, diverse, pro diversitate innumera rerum circumstantium apparere facit, unde etiam diversa id nomina nanciscitur, v. g. homicidium, furtum, avaritia, luxuries, &c. prout per diversa media apparet mentem à nihilo suo debito deflexisse, seque ut sui Dominam, principium, scopum, absurde spectare, & regere velle. Ista vero particularia mittimus. Sufficiat hic advertisse, quam certo Deus, qui suum placitum certissime novit, hanc etiam secundum illius reales operationes diversitatem accidentem prævideat; & quam sancte præsideat ille tanquam Rector isti diversitati secundum abscondita Sapientiæ & Justitiæ suæ judicia variandæ : siquidem prout plus vel minus realitatis hoc vel illo modo, tempore, circumstantia operari vult, appareat peccatum per hanc aut per illam viam, ejusve apparentia per aliam reprimatur, vel, prout placet illi, plane tollatur. Sic via hominis, etiam peccantis, (media per quæ peccatum suum vadat, prodeat, appareat, unde diversæ vitiorum denominationes) non est ejus; nec passus sui (actus apparentiæ, quoties hoc vel illo modo appareat,) etiam sui non sunt, ut divinum ait oraculum. Quod si quis peccando putet se Dei regimini posse subduci, quia (ut de indifferentia positiva dicebatur) id sibi sentire videtur, fallitur omnino; eique præter opinionem nihilominus subjicietur, imo Deum, ejusque attributa, (quod nolebat peccans) repræsentabit nolens, etsi alio modo, ad eundem tamen finem summum & bonum. Nam nihil potest à Deo evadere & elabi: Impossibile est creaturam sese à Dei Potentia subducere, & independentem facere: manet igitur, quicquid ei videatur, totaliter sub ejus regimine. Quia vero quicquid à Deo regitur, id bene eatenus regitur & fit; hinc Deus ex istis bonum elicit, omniaque in finem bonum, sibique gloriosum & convenientem, non obstante peccato illis permixto convertit. Tenebræ sunt ipsi Lux, vel Lucis ejus pulchritudinem commendant. Et facile est attendenti divina attributa omnia ex inspectione peccati suo modo, eoque vere admirabili, illustrare.
units.tr: XII. Concerning the divine government and providence with regard to those more specific sins that follow upon one of the principal admitted sins, or rather concerning the various appearances and faces of sin, the matter is easily grasped. I call the appearances, faces, garments or signs of sin the particular modes, for the most part outwardly revealed, by which it is made plain that the mind has turned aside from the state of its nothingness toward an empty idol. One such mode shows itself in absurd dealings with metals or wealth, another with fleshly things, and others again which are sometimes thought to be very great, even most spiritual things; I would rather call these diverse garments and appearances, rather than species or natures, of one sin present and abiding within, of one privative state which is in the mind. As for sin itself, God, properly speaking, does not govern it, for there is nothing positive in God which terminates properly on sin, which is a non-being. But the subject of sin, the spontaneous thought, likewise the body, its modes and motions, bodies which are around it in this or that way, at this time, and other things which are not sins in themselves but are realities, are posited and governed by God from his most free pleasure, as has been demonstrated of every reality. And hence the sinful mind, joined and entangled with these things, causes its sin, conceived and already made within itself, to appear in various ways, according to the countless diversity of the surrounding things; whence it also acquires various names, for example homicide, theft, avarice, luxury, etc., according as through diverse means it appears to have turned the mind aside from its proper nothingness, and to look upon itself absurdly, as its own mistress, principle and goal, and to wish to rule. But we pass over these particulars. It is enough here to have noted how certainly God, who knows his own pleasure most certainly, foresees this diversity which accompanies his real operations; and how holily he presides over it as Ruler, to be varied according to the hidden judgments of his Wisdom and Justice; for according as he wills to work more or less of reality in this or that mode, time or circumstance, sin appears by this or that way, or its appearance is repressed by another, or, as it pleases him, it is wholly removed. Thus the way of man, even of the sinner (the means by which his sin goes forward, comes forth and appears, whence the diverse names of vices), is not his own; nor are his steps (the acts of appearance, however often it appears in this or that way) his own either, as the divine oracle says. But if anyone, sinning, thinks he can withdraw himself from the government of God, because (as was said of positive indifference) he seems to himself to feel this, he is wholly mistaken; and he will nevertheless be subjected to God against his expectation; indeed he will represent God and his attributes, which the sinner did not wish, though unwillingly, and in another way, yet to the same supreme and good end. For nothing can escape or slip away from God: it is impossible for a creature to withdraw itself from the power of God and make itself independent; it remains, whatever it may seem to itself, wholly under his government. And since whatever is governed by God is well governed and done to that extent, therefore God draws good out of these things, and turns all things to a good end, glorious and fitting to himself, notwithstanding the sin mixed with them. Darkness is light to him, or it commends the beauty of his light. And it is easy for one who considers to illustrate all the divine attributes from the contemplation of sin, in its own way and truly admirable manner.

units.la: XIII. Quod si quis ultimo quærat, Annon Deus potuisset indifferentiam illam negativam ex Mente tollere, ita ut hæc semper se respectu sui ut nihil habuisset? & cur eam non sustulerit? Responsum habeat, potuisse quidem, sed non decere ꝝ[?] nihil, vel ens stultum, obmurmurare Enti sapientissimo; non fuisse Deum obligatum ut eam tolleret; ut neque etiam illa mala est, sed ejus non-rectus usus, ad quem Deus nullam dedit occasionem: quin contra, monuit Mentem ex creatione, ex conservatione, ex Idea Dei, ex sui ipsius forma limitata, ad alium tendente, ab alio existente, quod ea ex se ipsa respectuque sui fit nihil omni modo & tempore. Imo, qui scit se posse deficere, is minus occasionis habet sese habendi ut non-nihil, magisque impellitur ad nihili sui agnitionem: ut dicendum sit, peccare fuisse difficilius quam non peccare: hoc quippe leve, facile, ad quod non-agere, non-operari à se, quod nihilo naturale est, sufficiebat; illud durum, ad id vana conatuum spectra, violenta, & tamen cassa naturæ nihili, ut sic dicam, transgressio, quæ omnia neque bene possunt comprehendi neque exprimi, & hinc peccato absurditas ingens & inexcusabilitas accedit. Hinc etiam peccatum per dolorem, laborem, pondus grave, parturire & parere inania, & similes loquendi formulas, saepe notatur; ubi status ei oppositus per somnum, quietem, jugum leve, onus facile, designatur. Sunt & plura alia, quae de peccato dicta, ex ejus idea hactenus exposita possunt satis apte illustrari; nec alienum erit si eorum nonnulla sequenti capite proponantur.
units.tr: XIII. But if anyone finally asks: could God not have removed that negative indifference from the mind, so that it would never have been related to itself as nothing? And why did he not remove it?
