Let him have this answer: God could indeed have done so, but it was not fitting for nothing, or for a foolish being, to mutter against the most wise Being; God was not obliged to remove it; nor is it in itself evil, but its wrong use, for which God gave no occasion. Rather, on the contrary, he warned the mind, from its creation, from its preservation, from the Idea of God, from its own limited form, which tends toward another and exists by another, that it is in itself and in relation to itself nothing in every way and at every time. Indeed, he who knows that he can fail has less occasion to regard himself as something, and is more driven to the acknowledgment of his own nothingness: so that it must be said that sinning was more difficult than not sinning. For the latter was light and easy, a matter for which not-acting and not-operating of itself, which is natural to nothing, sufficed; the former was hard, requiring for it empty phantoms of efforts, violent and yet vain transgression, as it were, of the nature of nothing; all of which can be neither well comprehended nor expressed, and hence great absurdity and inexcusability attach to sin. Hence too sin is often described by such forms of speech as bringing forth and bearing empty things through pain, labour and a heavy burden; whereas the opposite state is designated by sleep, rest, a light yoke and an easy burden. There are also many other things said of sin which, from its idea set out so far, can be quite aptly illustrated; nor will it be out of place if some of them are set forth in the following chapter.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Peccati proprietates sive denominationes nonnullae exponuntur.
units.tr: Some properties or names of sin are set out.

units.la: 1. Quod sit injustum. 2. Negatio Dei. 3. Privatio. 4. Adhaerentia sibi ipsi, appropriatio, propria voluntas, &c. 5. Superbia. 6. Peccator ut reputandus.
units.tr: 1. That it is unjust. 2. The denial of God. 3. Privation. 4. Adherence to self, appropriation, self-will, etc. 5. Pride. 6. The sinner as to be reckoned.

units.la: I. Patet ex dictis, Primo, Cur peccatum dicatur injustum & indecens. Nam sive ego me spectem ut sum opus Dei, absurdum est ut me habeam pro non-opere Dei, vel pro opere mei, quod tamen fit, dum a me non-nihil esse volo, & a me ipso regi; Sive ego me spectem quatenus opus mei ipsius sum, hoc est, quatenus nihil omnino sum, itidem injustum est ut non geram me erga me tanquam nihil.
units.tr: I. It is clear from what has been said, first, why sin is called unjust and unbecoming. For whether I consider myself as the work of God, it is absurd that I should regard myself as not the work of God, or as the work of myself, which nevertheless happens when I wish to be something of my own and to be governed by myself. Or whether I consider myself as I am the work of myself, that is, insofar as I am absolutely nothing, it is equally unjust that I should not behave toward myself as toward nothing.

units.la: I I. Secundo, patet quomodo peccatum sit negatio Dei. Deus omnium Rector, scopus, principium, solus aliquid à se, unus & idem est: & sic repraesentatur per formam Mentis meae, quatenus haec per illum est limitata, ad illum tendit, ab illo est posita. At dum non maneo in nihilo decenti, sed me tento limitare vel non limitare per me, ut mihi, qui nihil sum, videtur; tunc Deum Rectorem tollo; & cum me, qui nihil, pro scopo habeo, tollo Deum Scopum; denique cum tanquam à me agere praetendo, nego in me Deum Principium: hoc est, improbe nego Deum. Hinc licet advertere quanta sint in nobis peccato infecta. Omnis actus corporis vel mentis hanc vel futuram vitam spectans, unde abest Deus Rector, Finis, Principium, peccato commaculatus est. Facultas sive corporis, sive Mentis, bona est, objectum bonum, actus bonus, sed negatio Dei, non-relatio ad illum per positionem absurdam mei qui nihil sum, mala est. Exempli gratia: facultas & actio gaudendi, bonae sunt, scientia vel divitiae materiales, etiam bonae; sed si de illis gaudeo sine Deo, id est, ob me ipsum, quoniam hoc mihi gratum videtur, idque forte me ipsum mihi aliisve commendando inservire puto, non autem quoniam hoc per Deum ita accidit & dispensatum est, & Deum repræsentat, ei inservire impendique debet; peccatum in ista absentia Dei, cujus vices inane phantasiæ propriæ idolum sustinere sibi videtur, includitur. Hæc est negatio Dei quam omnibus peccatoribus inesse ait Divinus Psaltes: Stultus dicit in corde suo, non est Deus: item, in omnibus ejus cogitationibus non Deus est. Quod de explicita & reflexa Dei existentiæ negatione interpretari strictum nimis esset. Adverte ex hac occasione quid vero sensu sit Deum, Dei nomen, (Christum quoque) affirmare, confiteri, profiteri: nempe, eum Solum Principium, Finem, Rectorem omnium vere, intus & extus, habere.
units.tr: II. Second, it is clear how sin is a denial of God. God, the Ruler, goal, and principle of all things, the only one who is something of himself, is one and the same. And so my mind is represented through the form that it has, insofar as this is limited by him, tends toward him, and is placed by him. But when I do not remain in the fitting nothingness, and instead try to limit or not limit myself by myself, as it seems to me, who am nothing, then I remove God as Ruler; and when I take myself, who am nothing, as my goal, I remove God as Goal; finally, when I pretend to act as if from myself, I deny God as Principle in me: that is, I wickedly deny God. From this one may notice how many things in us are infected with sin. Every act of body or mind, looking to this life or the future life, from which God the Ruler, End, and Principle is absent, is stained with sin. A faculty, whether of body or mind, is good; its object is good; its act is good; but the denial of God, the non-relation to him through the absurd positing of myself, who am nothing, is evil. For example: the faculty and act of rejoicing are good; knowledge or material riches are also good; but if I rejoice in them without God, that is, on account of myself, because this seems pleasing to me, and perhaps I think I serve myself or commend myself to others, and not because this has happened and been dispensed so by God, and represents God, and ought to be served and devoted to him; then sin is included in this absence of God, whose place a vain idol of one's own fancy seems to take. This is the denial of God which the divine Psalmist says is in all sinners: "The fool has said in his heart, there is no God"; likewise, "God is not in all his thoughts." It would be too narrow to interpret this as the explicit and reflexive denial of God's existence. Notice on this occasion what it truly means to affirm, confess, and profess God, and the name of God (and Christ too): namely, to hold him alone as the Principle, End, and Ruler of all things truly, within and without.

units.la: III. Videre est tertio, quomodo Peccatum sit privatio. Est privatio sive absentia indebita istius status nihili in quo debebam permanere. Est & privatio seu absentia indebita operationis Dei in me. Non quod Deus in me operari debuerit vel ad id obligatus fuerit: Sed cum ejus ex liberalitate operatio absit mea culpa, absentia hoc respectu indebita dicitur, & recte indebita, quia ea absentia pugnat cum forma mentis meæ, eamque quantum in se est tollit & negat. Forma quam Mens a Deo recepit, est, ut vidi, (1) Limitari aut etiam augeri, & variari secundum Dei placitum, sive poni & exerceri ab illo in statibus diversis, modo plus, modo minus realitatis habentibus. (2) Ad illum tendere, (3) ab illo plane pendere: Ego vero peccans ei repugno, cum me habeam ut non per Deum, non ad illum, non ab illo: adeoque in me peccante est mei ipsius, quatenus opus Dei sum, meæ formæ, vel saltem ejus complementi dignioris, privatio. Hinc Mens peccatrix est revera monstrum informe sive absque forma.
units.tr: III. Third, it can be seen how sin is privation. It is the undue privation or absence of that state of nothingness in which I ought to remain. It is also the undue privation or absence of God's operation in me. Not that God ought to operate in me or was obliged to do so; but since his operation is absent from me through my own fault, the absence is called undue in this respect, and rightly undue, because that absence conflicts with the form of my mind and, as far as it is in itself, removes and denies it. The form which the mind receives from God is, as I have seen: (1) to be limited, or even increased and varied according to God's pleasure, or to be placed and exercised by him in different states, having now more and now less reality; (2) to tend toward him; (3) to depend wholly on him. But I, in sinning, resist him, since I hold myself as not through God, not toward him, not from him: and so in the sinning self there is a privation of my own form, insofar as I am the work of God, or at least of its more worthy completion. Hence the sinful mind is truly a monster, shapeless or without form.

units.la: IV. Quarto, elucescit inde quam energetice peccatum dicatur ad-hærentia sibi ipsi, sibi placere, propria voluntas, appropriatio, furtum, &c. quorum nil verbo adhærere sibi significantius est. Nam his formulis notatur spectrum illud inane quod negati Dei & expulsæ nihili debitæ præsentiæ vices gerit. Nempe cum Mens peccat, se non prætermittit, se ipsam non habet & tenet ut decet id quod a se ipso nihil est; sed se ponit actu aliquid a se, ad se & per se esset, continuanque hoc tenore, quicquid habet facultatum & actuum ista sui larva inficit. quod proprie est actu & habitu adhærere sibi. Imo vero, cum se considerat ut opus Dei, & conservandum opus, si se sui conservandi causa spectet, adhibeatque omnia, & sæpe quidem ex placito, tanquam media conservationis suæ, ut si ego ad me venio, sisto me meæ durationis Judicem & directorem, peto à me (ut à principio) quæ optima & mihi placita vivendi ratio? eligo eam quæ mentem & corpus honore, copia, gratoque sensu demulcent, quæque à probris, inopia, doloribus, removeantur; statuo scientiæ seu cognitionis, amoris, odii, tristitiæ, gaudii, aliarumque facultatum & passionum qualia mihi,non autem qualia Deo,ejus placito, dispensatricique providentiæ, videntur objecta; tunc mea Mens adhæ-ret sibi ipsi, seque sibi ipsi vendicat, & quasi suum ipsius opus esset à se & ob se curandum atque regendum per media quæ tanquam sua usurpat, se propriam, se sui juris, sibique habet, furtumque adeo committit. Atque hoc à peccato ut explicitum est, venit: nempe se absurde ponit Mens pro directrice fine & principio, cum sit nihil horum respectu. Sed & interdum accidit ut nobis videamur adhærere Deo, cum miserrime sumus nostri mancipia. Nam si spiritualibus bonis, notitiis, meditatio-nibus, precibus, ipsique Dei amori atque placito ita dedar, ut sic commodum mei in hac futuraque vita intendam allectus sensu istorum grato, vel timore incommodorum oppositorum perculsus; tunc non tam Deo quam mihi adhæreo: illi ut medio quidem, mihi vero ut fini cujus gratia medium curatur & expetitur affigor: hoc est, Deo adhærere volo quia mihi prius adhæresco magisque adhærescere cupio; me talem habeo cujus gratia Deus & omnia cætera existant. Sic adhibetur Deus tanquam scala & gradus qui subjiciuntur ut ad fastigium commodi proprii fiat ascensus. Sic is peccator qui respectu rerum omnium non est tantus quantus est capillus ad humanum corpus, absurdius agit quam si omnia corporis ex unius capilli commodo mensurarentur, perinde quasi corpus factum fuisset ut capillus unus nutriretur; mensque corpori illi esset juncta ut pilus is bene & curaretur & gubernaretur. Cavendum est autem ne quis sibi adhæreat mox ut principio, mox ut medio, mox ut fini, aut tribus istis modis, aut solum uni, altero ex his ad Deum relato. Si velim quædam bona ob Deum & ad illum solum, & tamen spectem me, meas resolutiones, promissiones, industriam, habitus, ut principium agens; tunc amplectens Deum finem mihi adhæreo ut principio. Si adhærens Deo ut principio, ut ille ex vi sua faciat ea quæ me delectent, tunc Deum pro principio habens adhæreo mihi ut scopo. Denique si Deum finem & principium intuens velim ea quæ is in me ob se facturus est, fieri secundum meam ratiocinationem, phantasiam, vias; tunc mihi ut medio adhæreo, tolloque, ut mox dixi, Deum jam finem, jam principium, jam medium, per adhærentiam amplexumque vanistivanissimi idoli mei ipsius. Quamvis autem & in adhærentia rebus aliis peccatum consistere videatur, ut cum homo sibi non fidens bona vel apparentia vel vera non putat se posse consequi sine aliorum studio, in-dustria, opere, favore, perinde quasi sine illis impotens esset Deus; attamen quia hæc ex propria cujusque phantasia vim illam suam mutuan-tur, refunduntur in adhærentiam cujusque suam sibi ipsi. Omne quod est in Creaturæ statu, conservatione, actione, regimine, cujus ratio à creatura reddenda allegatur Ego, ego volo, mihi placet, & ejusmodi, non vero, nec vere Dei placitum, peccaminosum est. Istud Ego, cui adhæretur, pessima positio est Idoli Zelotypiæ.
units.tr: IV. Fourth, it becomes clear from this how forcefully sin is called adherence to oneself, pleasing oneself, self-will, appropriation, theft, etc., of which nothing is more expressive than the word "to adhere to oneself." For by these expressions is marked that empty specter which takes the place of the denied God and of the absent presence that ought to be there. Indeed, when the mind sins, it does not set itself aside; it does not have and hold itself as is fitting for what is nothing of itself; but it sets itself up in act as something of itself, from itself and through itself, and, continuing in this manner, it stains with this mask of itself whatever faculties and acts it has. This is properly to adhere to oneself in act and habit. Indeed, when it considers itself as the work of God, and a work to be preserved, if it regards itself for the sake of preserving itself, and employs all things, and often indeed by its own choice, as means of its own preservation, as when I come to myself, set myself up as judge and director of my own duration, and ask of myself (as of a first principle) what is the best and most agreeable way of living for me? I choose that which delights mind and body with honor, plenty, and pleasant sensation, and which removes disgrace, want, and pains; I establish the objects of knowledge or cognition, of love, hatred, sadness, joy, and of the other faculties and passions, as they seem desirable to me, not as they seem to God, his pleasure, and his dispensing providence; then my mind adheres to itself, claims itself for itself, and, as if it were its own work to be cared for and governed from itself and for itself, through the means which it usurps as its own, it holds itself as its own, under its own authority and as its own, and so commits theft. And this arises from sin as it has been explained: namely, the mind absurdly sets itself up as the directing end and principle, when with respect to these it is nothing. But it also sometimes happens that we seem to adhere to God, while we are most miserably the slaves of ourselves. For if I give myself to spiritual goods, to knowledge, meditations, prayers, and to the very love and pleasure of God, in such a way that I aim at my own advantage in this life and the future, enticed by the pleasant feeling of these things or struck by fear of opposing disadvantages; then I adhere not so much to God as to myself: I am attached to him as to a means indeed, but to myself as to the end for whose sake the means is cared for and sought. That is, I want to adhere to God because I first adhere to myself and desire to adhere more; I hold myself as one for whose sake God and all other things exist. Thus God is employed as a ladder and steps which are put beneath so that the ascent may be made to the summit of one's own advantage. So that sinner who, in comparison with all things, is not so great as a hair is to the human body, acts more absurdly than if all the body's parts were measured by the advantage of a single hair, as though the body had been made so that one hair might be nourished, and the mind were joined to that body so that this hair might be well cared for and governed. But one must beware lest anyone adhere to himself, now as to the beginning, now as to the means, now as to the end, or in these three ways, or in only one, with the other two referred to God. If I wish to do certain good things for God and to him alone, and yet regard myself, my own resolutions, promises, industry, and habits, as the acting principle; then, by embracing God as the end, I adhere to myself as the principle. If, adhering to God as principle, I want him by his power to bring about what pleases me, then, holding God as principle, I adhere to myself as the goal. Finally, if, looking to God as end and principle, I want the things which he is to do in me for his own sake to be done according to my own reasoning, fancy, and ways; then I adhere to myself as means, and I remove God, now as end, now as principle, now as means, through the adherence and embrace of my own most vain idol. Although sin also seems to consist in adherence to other things, as when a man, distrusting himself, does not think he can obtain good things, whether apparent or true, without the zeal, industry, work, or favor of others, as though God were powerless without them; nevertheless, since these borrow that power of theirs from each person's own fancy, they are referred back to each one's adherence to himself. Everything that is in the state, preservation, action, or governing of the creature, for which the reason to be given by the creature is alleged as "I, I want, it pleases me," and the like, and not the pleasure of God, truly or in fact, is sinful. This "I," to which one adheres, is the most wicked position of the idol of jealousy.

units.la: V. Quinto, clarum est & ex his recte peccatum Superbia nomine de-signari, siquidem hæc nihil aliud sit quam plus de se sentire atque æquum est, veritatem excedere in opinione sui ipsius de se aut regimine sui: quod à peccante fit dum nihilum suum deserens, sibi non-nihil à se esse videtur, aut sui ipsius inspectione, aut cum aliis comparatione, atque dum se gerit tanquam esset aliquid magni. Quomodo etiam, ut visum est, negatur & pellitur Deus ut ejus locum peccans quasi dignior esset, occupet. Re-cursus Mentis ad Deum ut ad medium quoad scopum, quem Mens pec-cans sui ipsius commodum statuit, perveniatur, cum ponat Deum Mente inferiorem, jure ut detestanda superbia habendus est. Reputa hinc quid sit vera humilitas, quanta ejus sit necessitas, & quam vere omnem illa virtutem includere dicatur.
units.tr: V. Fifth, it is clear, and from these points it follows rightly, that sin is designated by the name Pride. For pride is nothing other than to think more of oneself than is fitting, so that one exceeds the truth in one's opinion of oneself or of one's own governance. This is what the sinner does, when, forsaking his own nothingness, he seems to himself to be something from himself, either by looking at himself or by comparing himself with others, and when he behaves as if he were something great. In this way, as has been seen, God is also denied and thrust out, so that the sinner may occupy His place as though he were more worthy. When the mind returns to God only as a means toward the end which the sinning mind has set for its own advantage, and when it places God below itself, such pride is rightly to be regarded as detestable. Consider from this what true humility is, how great its necessity is, and how truly it is said to include every virtue.

units.la: VI. Denique hinc scitur quod peccator se non modo ut nihil debeat reputare, se omittere, prætermittere, abnegare: sed etiam se odio habere, sibi indignari, se detestari, à se horrere, sibi contrariari & inimicus esse cum luctu & dolore. Nam si in statu inculpato mansisset, tunc quidem se ut nihil spectare simpliciter debuisset, nec dubium est quin priori hoc modo puræ Angelorum Mentes se gerant, seque ipsas, utpote quæ per se merum nihil sunt, nilque ex se omnino habent, etiam ut nihil spe-ctantes, nil quoque de se prorsus prætendant. At vero id quod à se pejus nihilo est, nempe peccatorem, à quo non modo nil boni, nil quo se Deo gratum exhibeat proficisci potest; sed etiam à quo quicquid est, magis nihilo rejectaneum est, qui ut talis nil à se proprii habet nisi quod nihilo est deterius & Deo injuriosius magisque inimicum; talem, inquam, decet ut minus nihilo tractari, hoc est, summa aversatione, summisque, qua talis est, querelis, prosequi, & tam abominandum censeri, quam ejus oppositum, quod eo tollebatur, Deus videlicet cum ejus placito, amari atque optari debet.
units.tr: VI. Finally, from this it is known that the sinner must regard himself not merely as nothing, and must put himself aside, pass himself over, and deny himself, but also must hate himself, be indignant with himself, detest himself, shudder at himself, stand against himself, and be his own enemy with grief and sorrow. For if he had remained in the uncorrupted state, he would indeed simply have had to regard himself as nothing in that former manner; and there is no doubt that the pure minds of the angels conduct themselves in this way, and that, since they are in themselves mere nothing and have absolutely nothing from themselves, they, regarding themselves as nothing, also claim nothing at all for themselves. But the sinner, who is in himself worse than nothing, from whom not only nothing good can proceed, nothing by which he might show himself pleasing to God, but from whom whatever he is, is more than nothing to be cast away, and who as such has from himself nothing of his own except what is worse than nothing, more injurious to God and more hostile to Him; such a person, I say, ought to be treated as less than nothing, that is, to be pursued with the utmost aversion and the greatest lamentations, befitting what he is, and to be judged as abominable as the opposite of what was removed by his sin, namely God, who with His good pleasure ought to be loved and desired.

units.tr: 1.2.3.4. A few words on the extension or restraint of sin in actions and in the root. 5.6. On the difference between the sins of the upright and of the wicked. 7. On the certainty of one's own state. 8. Conclusion of all.

units.la: I. Videre est, tum ex hactenus deductis, cum ex aliis quae possent quidem, at quae non necesse est allegari, peccati ideam, prout exposita est, maxime inservire ut de eo recte judicetur & noscat quisque quousque vel ab illo liber est, vel illi mancipatus. Fallitur vulgus de illo secundum externum, apparentias, imo actiones splendidiores, quae quosvis, etiam maxime stupidos, feriunt atque commovent, judicia sua componens, quasi peccati natura in corticibus hisce consisteret. Ea vita ut proba decantatur quae in oculis hominum nil probitatem ( hoc est, mores eorum, judicia quae de bono, quaeque saepe pessima ) offendens ostentat: At prout magis minusve ea extus producit quae ab illis desciscunt, ea quoque magis minusve mala censetur. Neque modo alius de alio ita censet, sed &, quod pejus est, quisque de se ipso. Quod quid aliud est quam turpiter se ipsum decipere? Ad radices usque cogitationum intimas principiaque Entis & nihili descendendum est in conspectu Entis summi, & tunc demum quid inter probum & improbum, peccatum majus minusve interfit discriminis, clarum fiet. Tunc forte nonnulli, aliorum suaque opinione justissimi probissimique, sese continuo peccantes esse eo modo agnoscere possent: Sed quotusquisque est qui studeat ut sua sibi turpitudo nota sit & perspecta?
units.tr: I. From what has been deduced so far, and from other things that could be cited but need not be, it can be seen that the idea of sin, as it has been set out, serves above all to enable each person to judge rightly about it and to know how far he is either free from it or enslaved to it. The crowd is mistaken about it when it judges by the external, by appearances, and indeed by the more splendid actions, which strike and move everyone, even the most stupid, as if the nature of sin consisted in these outward shells. A life is proclaimed upright when it displays, in the eyes of men, nothing that offends propriety (that is, their customs and their judgments about good, which are often very bad). But the more or less it produces outwardly the things that depart from those standards, the more or less bad it is judged to be. And people judge in this way not only about one another but, what is worse, each about himself. What else is this than to deceive oneself shamefully? One must descend to the innermost roots of thoughts and the principles of Being and nothing, in the sight of the supreme Being; only then will it become clear what difference there is between the upright and the wicked, and between a greater and a lesser sin. Then perhaps some, who by their own opinion and that of others are most just and most upright, could recognise in this way that they are sinning continually. But how few there are who take pains that their own baseness should be known and thoroughly seen!

units.la: II. Sunt quorum peccatum est quid interrupte durans & permanens, a quibus continuo abest debitum suum nihil, abest omissio sui cujusque ut existentis, non-scopi, non-principii, non-Domini; abest consequenter Deus omnia, Deus Scopus, Deus Principium atque Dominus; adest sui ipsius cujusque acsi aliquid esset, cassa umbra, eaque in omnibus actionibus, propositis, votis, amore, electione, caeterisque ejusmodi: qui si suum nihil interdum patiantur intervenire, admittendo se nihil esse vel posse a se, vel mereri, similiaque, sic intendunt ut idolo suo aliquid acquirant a Deo vel ab hominibus, atque ut illud hacce veluti humilitatis umbra, conspicatius reddant: Deum quoque, undique circumstantem & ingredi paratum, interesse forte permittant, at cum ut medium, ut servum, ut executorem suae libidinis, non autem, (qualem praerogativam suo phantasmati servant) ut omnium Principium, Directorem, finemque unum. Talium peccata non ita sunt enumeranda quasi essent actus interrupti, huc illucve sparsim & ex in-terrupto per eorum vitam disseminati, quemadmodum externa quaedam irregularia interdum perpetrant: Sed tota eorum vita unum, idque con-tinuum peccatum est, idve involvit, siquidem una debiti absentia, indebiti praesentia, continuo durent. Ergo quicquid ejusmodi Mentes agant vel omittant, apparenter probe vel apparenter improbe, (perinde enim est in hac disquisitione) peccant. Earum ignorantia, notitia, amor, sensus, passiones, proposita, non quidem materialiter mala sunt, sed malo sunt contaminata, quippe quae extra respectum ad Deum sint, & ex rationibus atque motivis alienis, iisque diversis, prout ea sibi quisque diversimode finxit ex variis occasionibus: quae tamen omnia in unam peccati ideam facile est resolvere. Itaque, sive Deum tales ignorent, peccant, ex adhaerentia negligentiae suae; seu eum etiam noscant, peccant, notitiam ejus injuste acquirendo & detinendo, vel quia curiosi, vel quia docti, aut Sancti, aut Deo familiares, eique quasi a secretis haberi a se vel ab aliis volunt. Peccant non precantes, nam deseritur Deus; peccant precantes, hoc est, concupiscentias suas coram Deo effundentes, ut is cum illis consentiat, easque impleat. Peccant temperantia atque sobrietate utendo, quo nempe sui idolum, ad quod omnia referunt, diutius duret, vel ut sobrium celebretur; Sed & intemperantia peccant, voluptatem pro vitae agendae Consultatrice & Rectrice eligentes. Peccant eleemosynas erogando, nam se ipsos spectantes, Deum ad sua commoda sic flectere arbitrantur, ejusve judicia in eos debita donariis corrumpere praetentant; etiam avaritia & cordis duritie eos peccare non est dubium, & obscurum. Seu operentur, seu otientur, peccant; ab illo nihilum sui, totumque Dei, absunt; adest huic suae mollitiei positio. Sontes puniunt, fures, homicidas, Atheos, blasphemos ? nil minus peccant. Sui ipsius, suarum commoditatum proprius amor, ne illis etiam noceatur; item cupiditas ut sibi aliisque tanquam Zelo Divino ferventes videantur, eos regit: Sin impunitos dimittunt, sceleri consentientes ejus rei quoque evadunt. Quid ultra dicam, nisi cum Sacris, nil boni illis inesse, malam arborem fructus bonos ferre non posse, eos ad omne bonum opus ineptos, nihilque puri in impuris esse? Quocunque se vertant, quacunque veste, apparentia, etiam sanctissima & Angelica, tegantur, peccati fontem ferunt quaquaversum rivulos derivantem, quibus omnia, omnia prorsus quæ in ipsis, non ex interrupto, sed uno tractu continuo infi-ciuntur. Totus ejusmodi vitæ decursus, quæ ad Deum ut decet non re-fertur, Deum quantum in se est, tollit; nihilque debite Deum fatetur nisi vel indirecte, ut status nihili debitus, vel directe, ut omne reale quod in creatura est, confiteatur in re ipsa Deum esse solum omnia à se, ad se, & per se operantem. Adhibere continuo bonum opusque alienum sine Authore & possessore suo, inconsulto illo, atque ad illum quantum fieri potest tollendum, continuus hostilitatis actus est: quod facit pecca-tor, mente, corpore, tempore, creaturisque plurimis utens, etiamsi eo modo qui homines extrinsecus non offendat: nec datur ab illo liberari, & in amicitiam cum Ente Summo redire nisi per sui ipsius cujusque pecca-toris odium, conditamque dolore displicentiam, atque etiam duraturi æternum nihili, in quo coram Deo nos esse decet, restitutionem: siqui-dem horum indebita absentia, peccati principia, fomenta, & incrementa sint; præsentia vero, area operationum Dei.
units.tr: II. There are those whose sin is something continuous and lasting, from whom their due never ceases to be absent: the absence of acknowledging each one's own existence, the absence of the goal, the principle and the Lord; and consequently God, who is all things, God the goal, God the principle and Lord, is absent. Present in its place is the self of each person, as if it were something, an empty shadow, and this in all actions, purposes, vows, love, choice and other things of this kind. Even if such people sometimes allow their own nothingness to intervene, by admitting that they are nothing, or can do nothing of themselves, or deserve nothing, and similar things, they nevertheless strive in such a way as to gain something for their idol from God or from men, and to make it more conspicuous under this shadow of humility. They may also perhaps permit God, who surrounds them on every side and is ready to enter, to be present; but they regard Him as a means, a servant, an executor of their lust, and not (which is the privilege they reserve for their phantasm) as the Principle, Director and sole End of all things. The sins of such people are not to be counted as if they were interrupted acts, scattered here and there and spread out in their life from time to time, as some outward irregular deeds they sometimes commit. Rather, their whole life is one sin, and a continuous one, or includes one, since the absence of what is due and the presence of what is not due last without interruption. Therefore whatever such minds do or omit, whether apparently well or apparently badly (for it makes no difference in this inquiry), they sin. Their ignorance, knowledge, love, feelings, passions and purposes are not evil in their material nature, but they are contaminated with evil, since they lie outside any reference to God and proceed from reasons and motives that are alien and diverse, which each has shaped for himself in different ways from various occasions. Yet all of these can easily be resolved into the one idea of sin. Thus, whether such people are ignorant of God, they sin, by reason of their adherence to their own negligence; or whether they also know Him, they sin by acquiring and retaining the knowledge of Him unjustly, either because they are curious, or because they are learned, or holy, or familiar with God, and wish to be regarded by themselves or by others as, so to speak, in God's confidence. They sin by not praying, for God is then forsaken; they sin by praying, that is, by pouring out their desires before God so that He may agree with them and fulfil them. They sin by using temperance and sobriety, namely so that their idol, to which they refer everything, may last longer, or so that they may be celebrated as sober; but they also sin by intemperance, choosing pleasure as the counsellor and guide of the life they lead. They sin by giving alms, for looking to themselves they think that they can thus bend God to their own advantage, and they try to corrupt His judgments concerning them by gifts; it is also beyond doubt, and clear, that they sin by avarice and hardness of heart. Whether they act or whether they are idle, they sin; they are absent from the nothingness of themselves and from the whole of God; and in their place stands the positing of their own softness. They punish the guilty, thieves, murderers, atheists, blasphemers: they sin no less. The proper love of self and of their own conveniences governs them, so that they themselves may not even be harmed; likewise a desire to appear to themselves and to others as burning with divine zeal. But if they let the guilty go unpunished, they also escape, as consenting to the crime. What more shall I say, except with the Sacred Writings, that there is no good in them, that an evil tree cannot bear good fruit, that they are unfit for every good work, and that there is nothing pure in the impure? Wherever they turn, whatever garment, whatever appearance, even the most holy and angelic, they may be clothed in, they carry the fountain of sin, sending its streams out in every direction, by which all things, all things entirely, which are in them, are tainted, not by interruptions but in one continuous stroke. The whole course of such a life, which is not referred to God as it ought to be, takes God away as far as it lies in itself; and it acknowledges God in no due way, except either indirectly, as the due state of nothingness, or directly, by confessing in fact that God alone is all things, working everything from Himself, towards Himself and through Himself, of every real thing that is in a creature. To use continuously a good work that belongs to another, without its author and owner, without consulting Him and, as far as possible, removing Him from it, is a continuous act of hostility; and this is what the sinner does, using his mind, his body, his time and very many creatures, even when he does so in a manner that does not offend men outwardly. Nor can he be freed from this and return into friendship with the supreme Being, except through the hatred of each sinner for himself, and a displeasure seasoned with sorrow, and also the restoration of that nothingness which is to last for ever, and in which it is fitting for us to be before God. For the absence of what is due in these things is the principle, the fuel and the growth of sin; their presence, on the other hand, is the field of God's operations.

units.la: III. Nolim tamen concludi, omnes qui pro vere dolentibus, seque abnegantibus habendi sint, eos demum esse qui prorsus non amplius peccant, adeoque neminem aliquatenus peccato obnoxium extra statum peccati esse. Sed, inquies, cur hoc non esset? Cur ex uno Mentis actu quo illa primo ad peccatum se contulit, secuta sunt talis continuatio ha-bitusque peccati, ut mens inepta inde fit facta ad oppositum, atque pure peccatrix, sine ulla justitiæ mixtura sit constituta; neque eodem mo-do ex uno odii sui, suæ abnegationis, divinæque operationis actu (si ve-re is adest) reddatur ita inepta ad peccandum, ut peccatum plane non amplius intermisceatur, sed mera justitia? Nonne videtur, nisi hoc ita sit, bonum esse impotentius & imperfectius malo? Atqui si in statu ab-negationis rediret peccatum, nonne eo ipso, ut post primum peccatum factum est, rediret status habitualis iniquitatis meræ? Rediret certe, ut hoc hic antecedenter respondeam, nisi Deus potenti sua gratia illud im-pediret. Sed de hisce omnibus dico, non ita de malo ac de mali eradica-tione & de boni positione, esse judicandum: Nam malum non debet sustentari positive ut duret, sed semel admissum, perpetuo, per se, sine ulla causa positiva, sine Deo, durat mere & constanter, modo plane sibi sinatur, (quod non est in ipso perfectio ulla,sed imperfectio ingens.) Sed non ita est de eradicatione mali & de positione boni, quæ causam quam-maxime positivam requirunt; nam inceptæ à potentissima causa, si per eam non continuentur, cessant; & semel positæ, non sese sustentant, sed continuo ab alio reproduci debent, à Deo nempe, qui ex placito agens, regulas, modum, mensuram suis operationibus in initio & continuatione statuit, ita ut nil impediat, quominus velit aliquid incipere & augere interruptim & gradatim, & nihilominus id vere constanterque agere, & ad consummationem tandem perducere: privationem non statim primo momento ejicere, sublimiaque operari; Sed prius, & nonnunquam diu, per infirmia crassaque incipere, quae crassiora quibus inerat peccatum aggrediantur, impugnent, & paulatim vincant; tum sensim sublimiora fortioraque ponere, quae in robustiora mali praelien-tur, donec tandem victoria obtenta, id pace Divina fruatur quod in Mente à parte Divina stat. Hinc in primis, imo & in mediis mentium restituendarum reparationis periodis pausae, hiatus olim implendi, infirmitates postmodum sanandae, à Deo, & quidem sapientissimis de causis, ad nostri agnitionem, ad hoc ut magis nobis diffidamus, nos ut nihil, ut minus nihilo abnegemus, ad cautelam, stimulum ad preces, ad humilitatem, aliorum compassionem, &c. denique ad ejus gloriam, re-linquuntur. Quare non est quod ea Mens quae mali odio Deique amore tangitur, cum non videt in se tantam operationum Dei abundantiam, sed infirmitates animadvertit, animum plane despondeat, multoque minus in Deum murmuret, aut cum eo expostulet: quin decet nos, dolere quidem quod nostra culpa adsint mala, desintque bona, quae, nisi peccassemus, nobis fuissent data: at si respiciamus ad Deum juste sic de gratia sua peccatori non debita disponentem, judicia ejus de nobis cum silentio, acquiescentia & adoratione revereri. Et certe in hoc ipso latet maxima sui abnegatio, atque Dei operatio.
units.tr: III. I would not, however, have it concluded that all who are to be regarded as truly sorrowing and denying themselves are only those who no longer sin at all, and that therefore no one who is in any way subject to sin is outside the state of sin. But you will say: why should this not be so? Why, from the one act of the mind by which it first turned itself to sin, has there followed such a continuation and habit of sin, that the mind thereby became unfit for the opposite and was constituted purely sinful, with no admixture of righteousness; and why, in the same way, from the one act of self-hatred, self-denial and divine operation (if it is truly present), is it not made so unfit for sinning that sin is no longer mixed in at all, but there is mere righteousness? Does it not seem that, unless this is so, good would be weaker and more imperfect than evil? And yet, if sin returned in the state of self-denial, would not the habitual state of pure iniquity, just as it was after the first sin, return by that very fact? It would certainly return, to answer this beforehand here, unless God, by His powerful grace, prevented it. But concerning all these things I say that it is not to be judged in the same way about evil and about the eradication of evil and the positing of good. For evil need not be sustained positively in order to last; once admitted, it lasts of itself, purely and constantly, without any positive cause, without God, provided it is simply left to itself (and there is in it no perfection at all, but a huge imperfection). But it is not so with the eradication of evil and the positing of good, which require a most powerful positive cause; for once begun by the most powerful cause, if they are not continued through it, they cease; and once posited, they do not sustain themselves, but must be continually reproduced by another, namely by God, who, acting by His good pleasure, establishes at the beginning and in the continuation the rules, manner and measure of His operations, so that nothing hinders Him from willing to begin something and to increase it by interruptions and by degrees, and nevertheless to work at it truly and constantly, and at length bring it to completion: not to cast out the privation at once in the first moment and to work on high things, but first, and sometimes for a long time, to begin with weak and coarse things, which attack and overcome the grosser things in which sin was present, and gradually conquer them; then little by little to set up higher and stronger things, which are put in front of the more robust parts of evil, until at last, when victory is obtained, the mind enjoys by the divine peace that which stands in the mind on the divine side. Hence, in the first place, and even in the middle periods of the restoration of minds, there are pauses, gaps to be filled in time, weaknesses to be healed afterwards, which God leaves in place, and indeed for the most wise reasons: for our recognition of ourselves, so that we may distrust ourselves the more, may deny ourselves as nothing, or less than nothing, for caution, as a spur to prayer, to humility, to compassion for others, and so on, and finally for His glory. Therefore the mind that is touched by hatred of evil and love of God has no reason to lose heart altogether when it does not see in itself such an abundance of God's operations, but notices its weaknesses; still less should it murmur against God or complain to Him. Indeed, we ought to grieve, it is true, that through our fault evils are present and goods are absent, which would have been given to us had we not sinned; but if we look to God, who thus justly disposes His grace, which is not owed to the sinner, we should revere His judgments concerning us with silence, acquiescence and adoration. And certainly in this very thing lies the greatest self-denial and the operation of God.

units.la: IV. Omnino, quicquid sit de reliquiis peccati in illis quos Deus assumit reparandos, non permittit ille fundum Mentis intimum & ultimum, ut sic dicam, à malo tangi; nec conscientiam cum intelligen-tia, nisi maxime extraordinarie, idque nec directe, commaculari; neque majorem vitae partem, habitusque, eo ligari & teneri. Praesidet in mentis intimis sui ipsius (peccatoris assumpti) odium, utut debili, tamen sincero modo, adest nihilum sui, reflexio ad haec frequenter iterata, unde habitus gignantur; adsunt & quamplurimae aliae Dei operationes, notitiae, amor, quibus Deus Principium, medium, scopus omnium, in mente fit. At cum Mentis natura, qualem hic statuit Deus, non patiatur ut semper directe ad unum objectum, puta Deum, fiat actualis & expressa reflexio, (quis enim vel in rebus unde abest peccatum requirat hanc continuo adesse, siquidem intentio vel habitus referendi ea ad Deum, in quibus ob cogitationis limites de Deo actu non cogitatur, sufficiat?) Cum etiam Mentis cogitationes interdum corpus necessa-rio detineat, cum denique noluerit Deus simul & semel omnem ignorantiam, omnem mali habitus plicam, ex mente profligare, omne-que bonum statim operari, hinc illi in mente interdum languores atque defectus, quibus tamen ita admirabiliter utitur optimus Deus, ut inser-viant tanquam murus, ut ne peccatum ad fundum Mentis insanabiliter penetret. Cogita quaeso, Mentis amplissimam celerrimamque cogitan-di facultatem, qua illa vel semper, vel saepe, ad Deum reflectere possit; libertatem, qua à corpore nullo invita detineatur; scientiam, qua igno-rantia non obnubiletur; plenam spontaneitatem, quae praecedentibus pravorum habituum plicis, variisque & quasi invitis impulsionibus, non alliciatur; quod haec, ubi peccatum superaccidit, illis profuerint qui ea habuerunt, nisi quod omnia totaliter & profunde devastata insa-nabile subjectum reddiderint: ut patet in Mentibus Angelicis; quae cum hisce praerogativis essent praeditae, peccatum, sed non desendum, admi-serunt? At si peccatum accidat ubi limites cogitandi stricti sunt, ubi corpus cogitationem necessario detinet, ita ut eo tempore de Deo ne-queat cogitare, tunc hisce impeditum est ne ex intima Mentis petulan-tia oblivioni destinatus sit Deus, neve ex liberrima electione & libidine terrena prae illo admissa sint: Si, ubi ignorantia superest, cavetur hoc mo-do ne intelligentia & conscientia funditus malo penetrentur, quod fie-ret, si clara semper adesset notitia; denique si peccetur ubi malorum praeteritorum horumque habituum plicae, impetum in mentem praeter voluntatem & saepe cum gemitu haec patientem faciunt, praepeditur ne voluntatis purus intimusque consensus violetur ex mere spontaneo lubi-tu malum amplexandi. Atque sic Intelligentiae, Voluntatis, Mentisque adeo intima ita servantur, ut peccatum accedens, in ea quae magis exter-na sunt impingat, vimque suam, ut Serpens in calcem, exerat, imo ex-spiret, interioribus secretius reconditis. Sic admirandus Deus tenebras circa tabernaculum suum, Mentem in qua maneat, disponit, iisque ad ejus custodiam utitur. Ita sunt ejus viae admirabiliter benignae, ut ubi saepe putamus debitum fere esse querelae locum, gratiae ei agendae sint tantae ut captum nostrum excedant. Interim hoc nollem accipi quasi ad peccatum palliandum, eive patrocinandum essent dicta. Nemo non tenet Diabolica peccata mere humanis esse atrociora; & inter humana, ea quae scienter, mere, sponte, & nullo impulsu violento, praepondera-re illis quae secus fiunt; perfectiorumque lapsus graviores & fere im-medicabiles esse. Quod hic obiter illustrare, intentum.
units.tr: IV. Whatever the remnants of sin may be in those whom God takes up to be restored, he does not permit the innermost and utmost ground of the mind, so to speak, to be touched by evil; nor does he allow conscience along with understanding to be defiled, except most extraordinarily, and then not directly; nor does he allow the greater part of life and its habits to be bound and held fast by it. In the innermost mind there presides the hatred of oneself (of the sinner who has been taken up), feeble though it is, yet genuine in its way; there is the sense of one's own nothingness, and a reflection upon these things often repeated, from which habits are born; and there are also very many other operations of God, knowledges and love, by which God becomes the beginning, the means and the goal of all things in the mind. But since the nature of the mind, as God has established it here, does not allow an actual and explicit reflection to be made continually and directly upon one object, namely God (for who would require this to be always present even in things where there is no sin, since an intention or habit of referring them to God is enough, and in these things God is not actually thought of because of the limits of thought?), and since also the body sometimes necessarily holds the thoughts of the mind, and since, finally, God has not willed to drive out from the mind all ignorance and every fold of bad habit at once and in a single moment, and to perform every good immediately, therefore in the mind there are at times languors and defects of this kind; yet the most good God uses them so admirably that they serve as a wall, so that sin may not penetrate incurably to the bottom of the mind. Consider, I beg you, the very ample and very swift faculty of thinking of the mind, by which it can always, or often, turn back to God; its freedom, by which it is not held by the body against its will at all; its knowledge, by which it is not clouded over by ignorance; its full spontaneity, which is not enticed by the preceding folds of depraved habits and by various impulses that are, as it were, against its will; that these gifts, when sin has supervened, would have benefited those who possessed them, except that they, by wholly and deeply laying waste everything, made the subject incurable: as is evident in the angelic minds; which, though they were endowed with these prerogatives, admitted sin, but not defence? But if sin happens where the limits of thinking are narrow, where the body necessarily holds the thought, so that at that time one cannot think of God, then it is prevented, by these means, that God should be consigned to oblivion through the inward wantonness of the mind, or that anything should be admitted in preference to him from the freest choice and earthly lust. If, where ignorance remains, care is taken in this way that understanding and conscience are not penetrated to the root by evil, which would happen if clear knowledge were always present; finally, if sin is committed where the folds of past evils and of these habits, which make an assault upon the mind against the will and often with groaning endure these things, are a hindrance, it is prevented that the pure and inmost consent of the will be violated by the mere spontaneous desire to embrace evil. And thus the innermost parts of the understanding, the will and the mind are so preserved that sin, when it comes, strikes the things that are more external, and puts forth its power, like the serpent into the heel, indeed breathes out its last, while the interior things lie hidden more secretly. Thus God, who is admirable, arranges the darkness around his tabernacle, the mind in which he dwells, and uses it for its guarding. So admirably kind are his ways that where we often think there is almost cause for complaint, the thanks owed to him are so great that they exceed our comprehension. Yet I would not wish this to be taken as if these words were meant to excuse sin or to plead for it. Everyone holds that diabolical sins are far more atrocious than merely human ones; and among human sins, those that are committed knowingly, purely, willingly and with no violent impulse outweigh those that happen otherwise; and the lapses of the more perfect are graver and almost incurable. This I have intended to illustrate here in passing.

units.la: V. Neque est quod improbi sese cum probis jungi putent, eo quod utrique in nonnullis convenire dicantur. Doctus & indoctus saepe eousque conveniunt, ut uterque defcientiis[?] interdum non cogitet, uterque circa aliquid simile occupetur, aliquid simile agat, imo uterque eodem errore inficiatur, ut cum uterque intuens Solem, extemplo eam de illo admittit cogitationem quae illum sistit acsi non esset majorquam apparet. At si ad intimam usque mentis, habituum, actuumque ordinariorum & praecipuorum dispositionem veniatur, quanta inter utrumque differentia! Ita etiam, imo & magis, differunt probi, qui interdum in actu, & impro-bi qui semper in statu peccaminoso sunt, eorum quoque inter se peccata. Est lapsus justi in subjecto, in Mente, cujus intimum, principium, habitus, proposita, & maximus vitae agendae modus, bona atque Divi-na sunt. Deinde in eo non perseverat, sed mens ab eo statim deflectit ad Deum, haud secus ac acus magnete tacta, quae violento impedimento à directione sua detorta & humi detenta, retento nihilominus in se viae suae principio, statim atque sibi in libero aere redditur & erigitur, polum suum continuo respicit. Denique indies diminuitur, donec ad perfectio-nis eam mensuram, qua hic frui per divinam gratiam licet, attingat. Est peccator resipiscens quasi infans qui inobedientiam suam, desertionem-que paternae voluntatis serio abominatus, affectus proprios non amplius sequi paratus, ex amore Patris tenerrimo domum redit, laboremque à Pa-tre assignatum desudat; at quia ex praeterita desidia membra habet minus agilia & assueta labori quam si nunquam exiisset, fuisset-que passus se à Patre exercitari, hinc in labore resumendo lente initio procedit, pausatur, multa errata admittit, sunt tamen ea non in destruendo sed in construen-do opere Paterno; non studio, sed invite aut incogitanter; non semper, sed ex intervallo, sed quam minime potest, sed indies corrigitur, donec tandem ad perfectionem evadat operationis Paternae. Caeteri per plateas civitatis discurrunt, voluntarie ignorantes & otiosi, aut etiam iis dediti quae sunt Domino odiosa.
units.tr: V. Nor is there reason for the wicked to think that they are joined with the good because both are said to agree in some respects. The learned and the unlearned often agree so far that each at times does not think, each is occupied with something similar, each does something similar, indeed each is infected with the same error, so that when each looks at the sun, each straightway admits that thought which holds it fixed as if it were not greater than it appears. But if we come to the innermost disposition of the mind, of its habits, and of its ordinary and principal acts, how great is the difference between the two! So too, and even more so, the good, who at times sin in act, and the wicked, who are always in a sinful state, differ also in their sins. There is the lapse of a righteous man in the subject, in the mind, whose innermost ground, principle, habits, purposes and greatest manner of living are good and divine. Then he does not persist in it, but the mind turns away from it at once and back to God, just as a needle touched by a magnet, which, having been turned from its direction by a violent hindrance and held down to the ground, yet retaining within itself the principle of its course, as soon as it is set free and raised up into the open air, continually looks back to its pole. Finally, it is diminished day by day until it reaches that measure of perfection which, by divine grace, it is allowed to enjoy here. The penitent sinner is like a child who, having seriously abhorred his disobedience and desertion of the father's will, no longer ready to follow his own desires, returns home from the most tender love of his Father and toils at the labour assigned by his Father; but because from past idleness his limbs are less nimble and less accustomed to labour than if he had never gone out, and had suffered himself to be exercised by his Father, therefore in resuming the work he proceeds slowly at first, pauses, makes many mistakes; yet these are not in destroying but in building up the Fatherly work; not from zeal, but unwillingly or thoughtlessly; not always, but at intervals, and as little as possible; yet he is corrected day by day, until at last he attains to the perfection of the Fatherly operation. The others run about the streets of the city, wilfully ignorant and idle, or even given over to those things that are hateful to the Lord.

units.la: VI. Ex his patet quid de justorum peccatis eorumque apparentiis sit cogitandum; quibus si sibi adulando abutantur improbi Dei neglectores, sui vero curatores, quid demum est quo abuti non possint? Quod attinet ad operationes Divinas in quibus sui magis magisque exercentur donec perficiantur, eas docebit ipse Deus, operabiturque in illis. Atque ut de eorum corporum regimine verbum fiat, extra dubium est Deum sic corpus per Mentem recturum, ut haec per illud à Deo non alienetur; cumque proximi (ut de modo erga illos agendi non taceatur), non possint cogitationes operationesque Divinas in sancta tali mente inspicere, ut eis ducantur ad Deum, efficiet Deus ut Sancta Mens has illis faciat certis signis in corpore apparere, ita disponendo de lingua, deque membris omnibus, de externis bonis, de vita externa, ut illi nil ibi conspicati quod non tendat ad Deum solum per praetermissionem omnium quae ipse non sunt, excitentur ad similis vitae studium, cujus modus & forma Deo placens praestat in illa humanitate quam Deus ipse sibi conjunctissime univit, in Θεάνθρωπω Jesu Christo, qui vitam vixit simplicem, humilem, patientem, vim nescientem, non mollem, non splendidam, quae adhaesionem creaturis, rebus terrestribus, sensibus, voluptatibus, passionibus, honori gloriaeque mundi, prudentiae seculi, artificiis & subtilitatibus discursuum & scientiarum mundanarum; omnes formas viles & terrestres cogitationum, & similia quaecunque in quibus solent se quaerere homines, quaeque statum abnegationis necessarium removent, conculcavit; ut disceret homo se in omnibus deserere, nullis haerere, sui scopus & motivum non esse, ut Divina forma pro Dei placito in illo, quamvis eo modo qui saepe informis, vilis, amarus, ingratus, apparet, restituatur. Qua vivendi ratione, aut si mavis, Religione, nulla magis vere evidenterque rationalis est.
units.tr: VI. From these things it is clear what is to be thought about the sins of the righteous and their appearances; if the wicked, who neglect God and care only for themselves, abuse these things by flattering themselves, what then is there at last that they cannot abuse? As for the divine operations in which the godly are exercised more and more about themselves until they are perfected, God himself will teach them, and will work in them. And that a word may be said about the governing of their bodies: it is beyond doubt that God will so rule the body through the mind that the mind is not alienated from God through the body; and since neighbours (that nothing be left unsaid about how we ought to act toward them) cannot look into the divine thoughts and operations in such a holy mind, so that they might be led by them to God, God will bring it about that the holy mind makes these appear to them by certain signs in the body, disposing thus of the tongue, of all the members, of external goods, of outward life, so that they, seeing nothing there that does not tend to God alone, through the leaving aside of everything that is not God himself, are stirred to the zeal of a similar life, whose manner and form pleasing to God is shown in that humanity which God himself has most intimately united to himself, in the God-man Jesus Christ, who lived a life simple, humble, patient, not knowing violence, not soft, not splendid, which trampled underfoot adhesion to creatures, earthly things, the senses, pleasures, passions, the honour and glory of the world, the prudence of the age, the arts and subtleties of reasonings and of worldly sciences, all base and earthly forms of thought, and all similar things in which men are wont to seek themselves, and which remove the state of self-denial that is necessary; so that man might learn to forsake himself in all things, to cling to nothing, not to be his own goal and motive, so that the divine form might be restored in him according to God's pleasure, although in a manner that often appears unformed, base, bitter and ungrateful. By no way of living, or, if you prefer, by no religion, is anything more truly and evidently rational.

units.la: VII. Interim, quae nostra est caecitas, fatendum difficile esse non falli, non dicam in judicando in genere & abstracte, ut hic, de statu peccati, nihili, operationumque Dei; sed in sui cujusque & aliorum subjectiva agnitione. Nonnulli interdum de se putant sibi male esse, cum bene est; interdum bene, cum pessime se habent. De aliis invidia, aut complacentia, vel morum conformitas, judicia pervertit. Quomodo igitur an peccatum, an vero operatio Dei in me, an in aliis, sit, recte certoque cognovero? Multi putant se peccato mortuos, se sui abnegatores, se regenitos, se divinarum operationum plenos esse, & tamen falluntur. Praeter ipsius Divinae veritatis experientiam particularem, nil certi est. Etiam in naturalibus quamplurimi se doctissimos esse reputant, qui praeter nugas nil possident. Quemadmodum nemo scit intime quid sit veritas naturalis, quid sit clara & distincta perceptio, nisi is qui revera illam possidet, etenim is demum certissimus est illam esse quam possidet, seque illam possidere, alios non ita dispositos illa privari, (quanquam & errantes persuasissimi sint suos errores esse veritatem, suos conceptus esse claros & distinctos) veritas enim modo aliquo qui errori inimitabilis est, mentem afficit, & radices cogitationis tangit, quo error non potest attingere, etsi non experti id non notent, vel etiam id se experiri putent; Sic solus ille qui veritatem supernaturalium Dei operationum expertus est & recepit, scit vere quid illa sit,& testari potest cum certitudine se non falli,& scit suum testimonium esse verum,Deumque esse in se singulari modo operantem: alteri vero id non experto, qui tamen putat eadem de se, error suus per perceptionem veritatis oppositae non potest ab homine ostendi; nam ne-mo sic alterius intima commovere & afficere potest uti quidem ipse a Deo afficitur. Et praeterea, genus operationis Dei certissimum tale est ut Deus sine ullo medio mentem afficiat eo modo qui sibi propriissimus est & diversissimus ab illis omnibus in quibus media intercedunt, quare hoc non potest ab ullo alteri ostendi, demonstrari, neque nominari, hoc est, verbis idea ejus excitari, siquidem omne medium respuat, aut non esset operatio Dei immediata cujus praesentiam sistere Solius Dei meri, ut sic dicam, & per se, sine aliis, esset. Interim quemadmodum sciens aliquando a scientia non afficitur actu; sic saepe latent operationes Divinae sine directo sensu, & putantur abesse, unde Sanctissimorum querelae lamentabiles, & tamen adsunt proxime verissimeque. Sed in hoc ultimo casu, optimum est, non adhaerere sensui operationum, nec ipsis quidem operationibus Dei quatenus eae ad nos spectant, verum nil eligere,nil optare, velle, non dulcia, amara, magna, parva, spectabilia, despecta, scientiam, ignorantiam, latere, patere, mirabilia facere, vel non facere, ea videre aut secus; sed absolute, sine conditione aut respectu ad nos, indeterminate,se-se Divino placito offerre, & peroptare ut illud, qualecunque Deo visum sit, fiat in nobis, de nobis, & a nobis sive nobis consentientibus. nam postea Deus suas divinissimas operationes simul cum illo manifestabit, tutif-simeque eae admittentur & cognoscentur: at sine hoc periculum est ne optimi quique suos pro illis amplectantur sequanturque affectus. Si au-tem quaestio sit judicandi de aliorum statu, id ab illis recte fieri non po-test qui in malo sunt. Multitudo quamdiu carnalis manet ea judicat quo-rum oppositum tenendum est: nam & ipsi Sophistae, ubi quaestio est de rebus facilioribus, nec concupiscentiis hominum adversantibus,dum ine-ptas nugas per tot secula hucusque proponunt, coram turba, caeteris ex-pulsis, triumphant. Quid igitur ubi de rebus altioris indaginis agetur?
units.tr: VII. Meanwhile, it must be admitted that, by our blindness, it is hard not to be deceived, not to say in judging in general and in the abstract, as here, about the state of sin, of nothing, and of the operations of God; but in the subjective recognition of each person's own state and of others'. Some sometimes think they are unwell when they are well, and sometimes that they are well when they are in the worst condition. Envy, complacency, or conformity of morals perverts judgments about others. How, then, shall I rightly and certainly know whether it is sin or the operation of God in me, or in others? Many think they are dead to sin, self-denying, regenerate, and full of divine operations, and yet they are deceived. Apart from the particular experience of divine truth itself, nothing is certain. Even in natural things very many think themselves most learned who possess nothing beyond trifles. Just as no one knows inwardly what natural truth is, what a clear and distinct perception is, except one who truly possesses it (for he alone is most certain that it is the thing he possesses, and that he possesses it, and that others not so disposed are deprived of it, although even those who err are most firmly persuaded that their errors are truth and their concepts clear and distinct), for truth affects the mind in a way that is inimitable by error and touches the roots of thought, which error cannot reach, even though those who have not experienced it do not notice this, or even think they experience it; so only he who has experienced and received the truth of God's supernatural operations knows truly what it is, and can testify with certainty that he is not deceived, and knows that his testimony is true, and that God is operating in him in a singular manner. But to another who has not experienced it, yet thinks the same things of himself, his error cannot be shown to him by the perception of the opposite truth; for no one can so move and affect another's inmost being as he himself is affected by God. Moreover, the kind of operation of God that is most certain is such that God affects the mind without any intermediary, in a way that is most his own and most unlike all those in which means intervene. Hence this cannot be shown, demonstrated, or named to anyone else, that is, its idea cannot be excited in him by words, since it rejects every means; otherwise it would not be an immediate operation of God, whose presence belongs, so to speak, to God alone, and is by itself, without others. Yet just as one who knows does not always actually feel the effect of his knowledge, so the operations of God often lie hidden without direct sense, and are thought to be absent; hence the most holy people's lamentable complaints, and yet they are most truly and closely present. But in this last case, it is best not to cling to the sense of the operations, nor even to the operations of God insofar as they concern us, but to choose nothing, desire nothing, will nothing: not sweet or bitter, great or small, conspicuous or despised, knowledge or ignorance, hidden or open, to work wonders or not to work them, to see these things or otherwise; but absolutely, without condition or regard to ourselves, indeterminately, to offer ourselves to the divine pleasure, and to desire above all that whatever seems good to God be done in us, concerning us, and by us, or with us consenting. For afterwards God will reveal his most divine operations together with that, and they will be most safely admitted and known; but without this there is danger that the best people embrace and follow their own affections in place of them. If, however, the question is of judging the state of others, this cannot rightly be done by those who are in evil. As long as the multitude remains carnal, it judges things whose opposite must be held; for even the Sophists themselves, when the question concerns easier matters that do not oppose human desires, while they have so far put forward silly trifles through so many ages, triumph before the crowd, with the others driven out. What then, when the matter concerns things of a higher inquiry?

units.la: VIII. Quanquam ut de hoc rerum statu aliquid dicatur, operam de-dit mundus, ne si lucem divinam per suos agnoscere non licet, suae tamen tenebrae, quas vel omnium manibus palpandas praebet, ignorentur, ut jam sine difficultate animadverti possit mundum, opus haereditatemque Dei, alienatum esse a Deo suo, & in rebellione obfirmatum maxime Atheum devenisse, in malo demer-sum jacere, vanitati, quae jam in regu-las transiit, & pro morum probitate, honestate,& gloriandi materia habe-tur, tur, totum subjici. Non attenderunt ad notitias communes in mentibus suis descriptas, & monita perChristumDominum susq; deque habuerunt, & pejus quam ante fecerunt: Eum tanquam Patronum & Protectorem majoris nequitiæ, tanquam venerit ut qui daret materiam loquendi, concionandi, opinandi, adhibuerunt: ejus verba & tesseras ita assumpserunt, ut sub illis ei rebellantes, sibi ipsis vero servientes, se à judicio Dei esse tutos persuadere sibi possint. Sui Ductores atque Doctores præter opiniones, sectas, divisiones, disputationes, scientias de theoria, ceremonias, externa, politico fastu & affectu exposita, nil aliud remedii plerumque obtruserunt: passionem passione ejecerunt. Eos qui tanquam divino affinitatis nexu juncti, se fratres Christianos appellavere, quique à Christo se redemptos professi, ad ejus nutum & mandatum, quodcunque esset, ut-ut eis durissimum & absurdissimum appareret, corpus, Mentem, vitam, bona, quæ non suæ, sed Domini dispositionis erant, profundere debuissent, eos, inquam, ne cæteras iniquitates commemorem, præ aliis, non-obstantibus Domini sui in hocce patientiæ suæ regno prohibitionibus, mandatis, dogmatibus, parabolis, sacramentis, vexillo amoris, precum formula, dispositione testamenti ultima, suo denique exemplo, videre licuit ob terrenas quisquilias in se sævire, & quem Patrem communem vocabant, reclamare, quo ipsis de animo, de gladiis, de furore prospiceret, ut animose omnia cæde sociorum suorum implerent, & Patri eo ampliores canerent gratias, quo plures jugulassent, & quo perfectius & profundius divina Charitas in eorum cordibus esset exstincta: Et hæc hactenus, & etiamnum se ita habent, probanturque ab omnibus, ab illis etiam qui sunt, si credere fas est, luminaria mundi. O tempora! quo genuinus evanuit Christianismus, ut ne quidem Ethnicismo moderatiori superfit locus? Sed quid exspectandum, quamdiu, (quod fons mali est) quisque putat se habere jus de se deque rebus aliis, vel omnibus, vel quibusdam, disponendi ad placitum suum, & ita quidem ut multi sibi imaginentur se id juris habere à Deo vel à natura? Quid autem estDeum in Authorem peccati efficere, nisi hoc sit? Scilicet Deus proprium hominis Idolum ejusque cultum & regulas, ut id agat, & de se aliisque disponat ex principio sui placiti, & ad se, & ob se, quia ei placet, statuerit, & effecerit! Et hæc diversimode mixta & translata, legitima fuerint Societatis humanæ, (si cæcum aliquem sequi licet) fundamenta! Imo certe Babylonicæ Civitatis, quæ una jam fere ita ubique obtinet, ut in illa à bonis serviatur, & quibuscunque impiis, parvis & magnis, idola sua laudantibus; administrentur in vasis Domini, (quorum usus discriminis signa inter pios impiosque esse deberet,) ea, qui inebriandis ipsis magis magisque inserviunt: tanta est servitutis calamitas: ut nisi cito veneris, ô Reparator omnium Deus, in quem unum oculi tuorum sunt defixi, opera tua extremam ruinam videantur passura. Atque utinam, uti equidem promisisti, ô Deus verax, mox operaturus adsis, ut deletis nostris sceleribus, reductis nobis per odium nostri ad nihili statum debitum in nobis efficias, caeteris omnibus tanquam quisquiliis dimissis, unum Tui, ut in Sancta humanitate spectandum Te praebuisti, studium; nosque tanquam infantulos qui omnia deinceps ignorare velimus ut tibi uni committamur, assumas in discipulos tui Spi-ritus ab illo docendos quae reservasti amantibus Te; quo sic expulso vano nostri phantasmate tu solus in omnia regnes, omnia possideas, impleas, operum tuorum perfectione sis omnia in omnibus. Domine, velis quo-que pro beneplacito tuo quicquid hic boni est (nam si quid est, a te to-tum est) benigne acceptare; & quicquid mali in his est commissum, etsi quid te non decens sit dictum, non imputare; & omnia ad laudem & glo-riam Nominis tui promovendam adhibere: non quod putem quod tu verbis ejusmodi arte, pro hodierna consuetudine, nec sine taedio ita com-positis, egeas, & scis me non intendere ut homines inde affectent artificia-lem de te scientiam atque notitiam. Sed si quid boni venire possit ex Phi-losophandi, ut inter homines vocatur, studio, veriore & sinceriore, id in-tendebam tibi, Deus, offerre in Sacrificium, ut si qui ex iis qui sapere in studiis praetendentes saepe stultescunt, inspiciant cogitationes ad te ascen-dere, ii relictis verborum, apparentiarum & imperfectionum quae hic sunt cineribus, pelle, imo & excrementis & fumo; sequendo vero, si quis est sensus versus superiora, vigorem, oculos & cor sic convertant ad te unum, Domine, qui per media, utut imperfecta sint, nos ad te, sic volui-sti, deducis; quisque neque metalla, quanquam ex origine impuritatibus permixta, neque ea spolia quae in Ægypto vanitati subjecta erant, ad tabernaculi Tui constructionem recusasti.
units.tr: VIII. Yet, that something may be said of this state of things, the world has taken care, lest, if it is not permitted to recognise the divine light through its own people, its darkness, which it offers to be felt even by everyone's hands, should go unnoticed; so that it can now be observed without difficulty that the world, the work and inheritance of God, has been alienated from its God, has hardened itself in rebellion, has become most atheistic, lies sunk in evil, and has submitted everything to vanity, which has now passed into rules and is held as the material of moral uprightness, honesty and boasting. They have not attended to the common notions described in their minds, and have treated the admonitions given through Christ the Lord with contempt, and have done worse than before: they have used him as the patron and protector of greater wickedness, as if he had come to give matter for talking, preaching and opining; they have taken up his words and tokens in such a way that, while rebelling against him under them and serving themselves, they can persuade themselves that they are safe from the judgment of God. Their own leaders and teachers, beyond opinions, sects, divisions, disputations, sciences of theory, ceremonies, externals, exposed to political pride and passion, have for the most part pressed upon them no other remedy: they have driven out passion by passion. Those whom they called brothers in Christ, joined as if by the bond of divine kinship, and who professed to be redeemed by Christ, ought to have poured out body, mind, life and goods, which were not their own but at the disposal of the Lord, at his nod and command, whatever it was, however very hard and absurd it might seem to them: these, I say, not to mention other iniquities, were seen, in spite of the prohibitions, commands, doctrines, parables, sacraments, banner of love, form of prayer, final disposition of the testament, and lastly the example of their Lord in this kingdom of his patience, to rage against one another for earthly trifles, and to cry out against him whom they called the common Father, that he might provide for them concerning their minds, their swords, their fury, so that they might fill everything with the slaughter of their companions, and sing the more thanks to the Father the more they had slain, and the more perfectly and deeply divine charity had been extinguished in their hearts. And these things so far, and even now, stand so, and are approved by all, even by those who are, if it is right to believe it, the lights of the world. O times! When genuine Christianity has vanished, so that not even a place is left for a more moderate heathenism? But what is to be expected, as long as (which is the source of evil) each person thinks he has the right to dispose of himself and of other things, or of all or some, at his own pleasure, and indeed so that many imagine they have this right from God or from nature? What else is it to make God the author of sin? Surely God is made the proprietor of man's own idol, its worship and rules, that man may act and dispose of himself and others from the principle of his own pleasure, and may establish and effect it toward himself and for himself, because it pleases him! And these things, variously mixed and transferred, would be the lawful foundations of human society (if it is permitted to follow a blind man)! Indeed, surely of the Babylonian city, which now almost everywhere prevails so that in it the good serve, and whatever impious people, small and great, praising their idols, are administered in the vessels of the Lord (whose use should be a sign of distinction between the pious and the impious), those who serve more and more to make them drunk: such is the calamity of servitude that, unless you come soon, O God, Restorer of all, on whom alone the eyes of your people are fixed, your works seem destined to suffer extreme ruin. And would that, as indeed you have promised, O true God, you would be present to work soon, so that, our crimes being destroyed and we being brought back through hatred of ourselves to the state of nothing that is due, you may effect in us, all else being dismissed like trifles, the one zeal for you, which you have shown yourself to be looked upon as in holy humanity; and take us, like little children who would thereafter wish to be ignorant of everything, so that we may be committed to you alone, as disciples of your Spirit to be taught by him those things you have reserved for those who love you; so that, our vain phantom being cast out, you alone may reign over all, possess all, fill all, and be all in all by the perfection of your works. Lord, may you also, according to your good pleasure, graciously accept whatever good is here (for if anything is good, it is wholly from you); and not impute whatever evil has been committed in these things, even if anything has been said that is unbecoming to you; and bring everything to advance the praise and glory of your Name: not that I think you need words of this kind, composed by art after the present custom and not without weariness, and you know that I did not intend to bring men to affect an artificial knowledge and acquaintance of you from them. But if any good can come from the study of philosophising, as men call it, of a truer and more sincere kind, I intended to offer it to you, God, as a sacrifice, so that if any of those who, claiming to be wise in their studies, often become foolish, should look at the thoughts that ascend to you, they might leave aside the words, appearances and imperfections that are here: ashes, skin, indeed dung and smoke; and, pursuing instead, if there is any sense toward higher things, let them turn their vigour, eyes and heart to you alone, Lord, who through the middle things, however imperfect, lead us to yourself, as you have willed; you who have not refused, for the building of your tabernacle, either the metals, though by origin mixed with impurities, or those spoils which in Egypt were subject to vanity.
